projects.name: Reaction-time game (Sandy's first build)
projects.power_supply: USB cable from your laptop to the Uno (5V via the Uno's USB-B port). No batteries, no wall plug.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little red light blinks on after a surprise pause. You slap the button as fast as you can, and your reaction time pops up on the laptop screen in milliseconds. **Why it's fun**: Race your dad, your brother, anyone who walks past, and see who has the fastest thumb in the house. Most grown-ups land around 250 ms, so if you beat that you get to brag about it forever. **Goal:** Arduino lights an LED after a random 2-5 second pause. Player slaps the button as fast as possible after the LED comes on. Reaction time prints to the Serial Monitor in milliseconds. Aiming for sub-250 ms on a good day. **First electronics project, age 10, no soldering needed.** ## Parts list (allocated below) - Arduino Uno R3 (CH340 clone) - Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm - 1x red 5mm LED - 1x 220R resistor (colour bands: red-red-brown-gold) - 1x tactile push-button, 4-pin (3x6x3.1mm) - 4x M-M jumper wires - USB cable for the Uno - check the clone (USB-B "square printer", mini-USB, or USB-C; grab one in advance) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **D0 to D13** - the digital pins along the top edge. When the code says `pin 9`, find the one marked **D9**. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. There are a few pins marked GND. Any of them work. - **5V** - the power input pin. It hands out 5 volts from the USB cable. You will not use it in this build, but it is good to know. - **USB-B** - the big square USB socket on the end of the Uno. The cable from your laptop plugs in here. - **RESET** - a tiny black button on the board. Press it to restart the program from the beginning.
**Step 1 - Get to know the breadboard.** Before you plug anything in, look at the white board with all the little holes. - The two long red and blue strips on the sides are called **rails** - they are the long red/blue strips running down the side of the breadboard. The red one is for power, the blue one is for ground (0V). - In the middle, the holes are grouped into short rows of 5. Every hole in the same numbered row (like row 5) is secretly connected under the plastic. So if you push two legs into the same row, they are touching each other. - The big gap down the middle splits the left side from the right side. A leg in row E5 is NOT connected to a leg in row F5 unless you add a wire. We will use the **blue rail on the right** as our GND rail (the 0V side). Nothing else plugs into the rails in this build except for the GND wire later.
**Step 2 - Plant the LED and its little brother, the resistor.** The red LED is the light that will flash when the game says GO. The resistor is the tiny tan part with colored stripes. - The LED has two legs. The **long leg** is the plus side. The **short leg** is the minus side. There is also a flat spot on the rim of the LED on the short-leg side - that is a backup clue if the legs got trimmed. - Push the **long leg** into hole **F5**. - Push the **short leg** into hole **F6**. - Take the 220 ohm resistor. It does not care which way around it goes. Push one leg into hole **J6** (same row as the LED's short leg) and the other leg into any hole on the **blue GND rail** on the right side. **Why this matters:** The resistor is there to slow down the electricity going through the LED. If you skipped it, the LED would gulp too much current and pop in a puff of magic smoke. 220 ohm is the perfect size for a 5V build like this one - bright light, no smoke.
**Step 3 - Plant the GO button.** The push-button is the little square black part with 4 metal legs sticking out. - Push the button across the gap in the middle of the breadboard so that it straddles row **15**. Its 4 legs should land in **E15, F15** on one side and **E14, F16** on the other side (the exact rows depend on which way you turn it, that is fine). - The important thing is that the **E15** hole has one of the legs in it. That is the leg we will wire to the Uno. - This is a tricky one: the button has 4 legs but only 2 of them are actually "the switch". The other 2 are just held together inside the button. If pressing the button later does not register, gently lift it out, turn it 90 degrees, and push it back in.
**Step 4 - Run the wires.** Grab 4 jumper wires from the rainbow bag. They have a stiff metal pin on each end (M-M means male-to-male). The color does not matter electrically, but using red for power and black for ground makes life easier later. - **Wire 1 (signal to the LED):** from the pin marked **D9** on the Uno, into hole **F5** on the breadboard. That is the same row as the LED's long leg, so this wire will switch the LED on and off. - **Wire 2 (signal to the button):** from the pin marked **D2** on the Uno, into hole **E15** on the breadboard. That goes to one leg of the GO button. - **Wire 3 (other side of the button to GND):** from hole **F17** on the breadboard (on the far side of the button) into any hole on the **blue GND rail** on the right side. - **Wire 4 (ground the rail):** from one of the **GND** pins on the Uno, into any hole on the **blue GND rail**. This connects the whole blue rail to 0V. **Why this matters:** The Uno uses a quiet trick called an internal pull-up inside D2. That means when nothing is touching D2, the pin floats up to 5V on its own. When you press the GO button, you tie D2 down to the GND rail through wires 3 and 4, and the Uno notices the drop. That is how the code can tell "button pressed" vs "button not pressed" without a second resistor.
**Step 5 - Power it up.** Plug the USB cable from your laptop into the square **USB-B** socket on the end of the Uno. The other end goes into a USB port on your laptop. You should see one or two tiny green lights come on near the USB socket. That is the Uno saying "I am awake." If anything smells warm, smells weird, or a part gets hot to the touch, unplug right away and check the wiring against the diagram before plugging back in.
## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):** 1. Install the Arduino IDE and open it once so it finishes setting itself up. 2. Plug the Uno in. Windows will go "ding" and install the CH340 USB-to-serial driver. If it doesn't, grab the CH340 driver from [sparks.gogo.co.nz/ch340.html](https://sparks.gogo.co.nz/ch340.html) and run it. 3. **Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno.** 4. No extra libraries needed for this sketch - everything it uses is built in. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into the laptop with its USB cable (the square "printer" USB-B end goes into the Uno). The green `ON` LED on the board should light up straight away. 2. **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that says **COM\*** (some number like COM3 or COM5). If two ports show up, unplug the Uno, see which one disappears, plug back in - that's the Uno. 3. Open the sketch (File -> New, paste the code in, File -> Save As, give it a name like `reaction_game`). 4. Nothing to fill in - no WiFi password, no placeholder. The code is ready to go. 5. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow `->` icon in the top-left, next to the tick). The bottom of the screen will say *Compiling sketch...* then *Uploading...*. The two little `TX`/`RX` lights on the Uno will flicker for a second or two. When it says **Done uploading** you're flashed. 6. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window, set the baud rate to **9600** (that's what `Serial.begin(9600)` in the code is asking for). Anything else and you'll get gibberish like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`. 7. You should see `Get ready ...` appear. Wait 2-5 seconds, the red LED snaps on, slap the button, and the laptop prints something like `Your reaction: 243 ms`. That means it works. Try to beat 250. **Common gotchas:** - **Serial Monitor showing garbled characters** (`⸮⸮⸮`) - the baud rate dropdown in the bottom-right is wrong. Set it to **9600** to match `Serial.begin(9600)` in the code. - **LED never lights up** - it's in backwards. No damage done, just pull it out, flip it 180 degrees, and re-seat. Long leg goes to the Arduino pin 9 side, short leg goes to the resistor / GND side. - **Pressing the button does nothing** - the tactile switch only connects two of its four legs (the other two are the same pair, rotated 90 degrees). Pull the button out, turn it a quarter-turn, push it back in, try again. ## Talking points while he wires it up Drip-feed one at a time, not all at once. - **LEDs have a long leg (+) and a short leg (-).** Backwards = no light, but no damage. - **The resistor stops the LED getting too much current** and burning out. Garden-hose analogy: too much water blows the nozzle. - **A breadboard's short rows are joined under the plastic.** The two long rails on the sides are usually power and ground. - **The code's `loop()` runs forever**, top to bottom, then starts again. That's why the game keeps coming back round. - **Average human reaction time is about 250 ms.** That's the benchmark to beat. ## Things to change once it works Give him the goal, let him hunt for the change in the code. - Make the random pause longer or shorter. - Cheat-detect: if the button is pressed *before* the LED lights, print "Too early!" instead of a time. - Best-of-five mode: track and average over 5 rounds. - Add a second LED that turns on when he beats his previous best time. ## Prep checklist for Andy - [ ] Install the Arduino IDE from [arduino.cc](https://arduino.cc) - free, Windows. - [ ] Plug the Uno in once yourself first. Windows will prompt for a CH340 USB driver - let it install. - [ ] Open the IDE: **Tools -> Port** should show a COM port. Set **Tools -> Board -> Arduino Uno**. - [ ] Confirm the USB cable type the clone uses. - [ ] Pre-count one 220R resistor (red-red-brown-gold) so he isn't squinting at colour bands on the first try. ## Next project once he's hooked **Wave-controlled lamp.** Same Uno, same breadboard, swap the button for the HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor. LED brightens as your hand gets closer, dims as you move it away. Two extra wires and one extra component beyond this build.

projects.name: Bedroom Temperature Dashboard
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from a laptop or USB charger to the XIAO (5 V on the USB rail, regulated to 3.3 V on-board)
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug in a tiny chip the size of your thumbnail. Open a web browser on any phone or laptop in the house, type in its address, and a real web page pops up showing a live temperature number that refreshes itself every 5 seconds. **Why it's fun**: You just built a website. Not on the internet, on YOUR desk - a thing smaller than a stick of gum is hosting a page your dad can open on his phone from the couch, and you made it. ## Parts list - 1x XIAO ESP32-C3 - 1x USB-C cable (data-capable, plugged into a laptop or any 5 V USB charger) - GeeFam WiFi (2.4 GHz) within range of where the XIAO sits That is the entire bill of materials. No breadboard, no jumpers, no sensor module - the chip measures its own internal temperature. **Before flashing:** open the sketch and replace `PASSWORD_HERE` on the `WIFI_PASSWORD` line with the real GeeFam WiFi password. The sketch will compile either way, but it cannot join the network without the real password. ## Wiring notes Good news: this project has zero wires. The XIAO ESP32-C3 board has a temperature sensor built right inside the chip, so all you need is a USB-C cable. That is it. No breadboard, no jumper wires, no resistors. If you have ever wanted a "first build" that just works, this is the one. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the XIAO ESP32-C3 board:** - **USB-C** - the small oval-shaped plug on one end. This is where power and code come in. - **5V** - the power input pin. It carries 5 volts from the USB cable. We are not using it today. - **3V3** - the pin that gives back 3.3 volts after the on-board regulator drops the USB power down. Not used today either. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every project needs it, but this one hides it inside the USB cable. - **D0 through D10** - the labeled pins along the edges of the board (the silkscreen labels). We will not use any of them today, but you will see them on the chip. - **BOOT** - a tiny button next to the USB-C plug. You press it to put the board into "ready-to-flash" mode when uploading code for the first time.
**Step 1 - Plug the USB-C cable into the XIAO.** Find the USB-C end of your cable and push it gently into the small oval plug on the XIAO board. It only goes in one way, but it is reversible (you cannot put it in upside down with this connector, which is nice).
**Step 2 - Plug the other end into a laptop or a USB charger.** Either works. The laptop is best while you are uploading code, because you need the USB connection for both power AND for sending the program. Once the code is loaded, you can move the cable to any USB phone charger and the board will keep running on its own. A tiny green or orange light on the XIAO should turn on. That means the board is alive. **Why a short, good cable matters:** The XIAO is small but the WiFi radio inside it briefly pulls a lot of current when it first connects to your network. A thin, cheap, or super-long cable can sag in voltage during that moment and cause the board to restart. Use a short cable (under 1 meter is great) that you know carries data, and plug it straight into the laptop, not through a USB hub.
**Step 3 - First-time upload trick (BOOT button).** The very first time you send code to a brand-new XIAO, the computer sometimes cannot get its attention. If your upload fails or hangs, do this: - Unplug the USB-C cable. - Hold down the small BOOT button on the board (it is right next to the USB-C plug). - While still holding BOOT, plug the USB-C cable back in. - Let go of BOOT after a second. - Try the upload again. This forces the chip into a special "I am listening for new code" mode. After the first successful upload, you will not have to do this trick again - normal uploads will just work.
**Step 4 - Warmup note.** The temperature sensor lives inside the same chip that runs your code. The chip warms up a little when it is busy, especially when WiFi is sending data. So the reading is usually a degree or two warmer than the actual room. That is normal and expected. If you want a true room reading, this project is a great first step, and later you can add an outside sensor like a DHT11 or DS18B20 on a wire away from the chip. That is the whole wiring section. One cable. You are done. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. **Add the ESP32 board manager.** In Arduino IDE: *File → Preferences → Additional Boards Manager URLs*, paste this URL and click OK: ``` https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json ``` 2. **Install the ESP32 boards.** *Tools → Board → Boards Manager*, search `esp32`, install **esp32 by Espressif Systems** (any 3.x version). It's a ~500 MB download - go grab a snack. 3. **Pick the board.** *Tools → Board → ESP32 Arduino → XIAO_ESP32C3*. **Every time you flash:** 1. **Plug the XIAO into your laptop via USB-C.** Use a short, known-good *data* cable plugged straight into the laptop, not through a hub. Thin charge-only cables cause brownouts when the WiFi radio kicks in. 2. **Pick the port.** *Tools → Port → COM whatever* (Windows) or `/dev/cu.usbmodem*` (Mac) or `/dev/ttyACM0` (Linux). If you don't see a new port appear, hold the BOOT button on the XIAO and re-plug the cable. 3. **Set your WiFi password.** In the sketch, find the line: ```cpp const char* WIFI_PASSWORD = "PASSWORD_HERE"; ``` Replace `PASSWORD_HERE` with your real GeeFam password (keep the quotes). 4. **Click Upload** - the right-arrow icon in the toolbar, or *Sketch → Upload*. First upload after a fresh boardloader install may need you to hold the **BOOT** button on the XIAO until "Connecting..." switches to "Writing". 5. **Open Serial Monitor.** *Tools → Serial Monitor*, set baud rate **115200** in the bottom-right dropdown. Within a few seconds you should see: ``` XIAO Chip Temperature starting... Connecting to GeeFam ..... Connected. Open this address in a browser: http://192.168.88.42 RSSI: -65 Web server listening on port 80. ``` 6. **Visit that IP** (e.g. `http://192.168.88.42`) in Chrome / Safari / Firefox on any phone or laptop on the same WiFi. The big green number is your XIAO talking to you. **Common gotchas:** - *"Failed to connect / Wrong boot mode"*: hold BOOT, click Upload, release BOOT when "Connecting..." starts. - *"No IP printed"*: WiFi password wrong, or the XIAO isn't seeing 2.4 GHz (it can't see 5 GHz). Double-check the `WIFI_PASSWORD` line. - *Page doesn't load*: your phone is on a different WiFi network than the XIAO, or your router has client isolation on. Connect to the same SSID and try again. ## Talking points - This is the first project where the XIAO does two things at once: it joins WiFi AND it answers HTTP requests from a browser. The Arduino core handles the messy networking parts so the sketch stays short. - **Honest framing of the "sensor":** every ESP32 has a small thermal diode used internally for thermal management, and `temperatureRead()` exposes it as a Celsius value. But the chip warms itself by running, so the reading is the *chip* temperature, not the *room* temperature - it will typically sit at 40-55 C even in a cool room. The web page says this in a yellow note so nobody is confused. Honesty about what a sensor is actually measuring is a real engineering skill. - The web page is one self-contained HTML string built in the sketch. It uses `` to tell the browser to reload itself every 5 seconds. No JavaScript, no separate JSON endpoint - the simplest possible "live" web page. - Why no breadboard / resistor / external sensor? Because the goal of this project is to *just* learn how to host a web page on a microcontroller, with nothing else in the way. The next project adds the real sensor. ## Things to change once it works - Add a real external temperature sensor like a DHT22 or BME280 to measure the *room* instead of the chip. Now it is a useful bedroom thermometer (and the page title can honestly say "Bedroom Temperature"). - Once a real sensor is in, keep the last N readings in memory and draw a small graph in the browser. (That is the natural next step up in difficulty - it adds a ring buffer, JSON, and HTML canvas drawing.) - Have the XIAO publish each reading over MQTT to the Orange Pi (once the Pi is booted). That is the bridge from "one device with a webpage" to "a real home-automation network". ## Why this is interesting This is the smallest possible "real" IoT project: a device on the network that you open in a browser like any other website. Once Andy sees a temperature reading updating in Chrome that is being served by a thumbnail-sized chip on his desk, the rest of the kit makes sense - the ESP32s are tiny web servers / data sources, and the Orange Pi will eventually be the always-on hub that collects from all of them. It also reuses the already-working WiFi connect logic from `XIAO_ESP32C3/Wifi/connect-wifi.ino`, so the only new idea is "host a page".

projects.name: Mood Meter (touch the dot, change your face)
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from laptop to the XIAO ESP32-C3 (5V in, regulated to 3.3V on-board; 3.3V powers the OLED and the TTP223B via the breadboard rails)
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little screen shows a face - happy, sad, surprised, sleepy. Touch the metal dot with your finger and the face flips to the next mood. No buttons, no switches, just tap. **Why it's fun**: It feels like magic the first time - you barely brush the pad and the face changes, like it can read your mind. Stick it on your bedroom door and make it match your mood so your brother knows whether to knock or run. ## Parts list - 1x XIAO ESP32-C3 (the brain - runs the sketch, drives the screen) - 1x 0.96" SSD1306 OLED, I2C version (4 pins: VCC, GND, SCL, SDA) - 1x TTP223B capacitive touch module (3 pins: VCC, GND, I/O) - 1x breadboard (shared 3.3V and GND rails) - 8x F-M jumper wires (XIAO header to breadboard rails and modules) ## Wiring notes This whole project runs on 3.3V power. The XIAO ESP32-C3 takes 5V from the USB-C cable and turns it into 3.3V on its own little board. The OLED screen and the touch pad both love 3.3V, so we feed them from the XIAO's 3V3 pin. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the XIAO ESP32-C3 board:** - **3V3** - the pin that gives back 3.3V power for your other parts. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs one wire going here. - **D0 to D10** - the silkscreen labels next to each pin. The chip inside calls them by different numbers (GPIO), but you only ever read the D labels. - **USB-C** - the little oval socket where the laptop cable plugs in. - **SDA / SCL** - the two "talking wires" the OLED screen uses to chat with the XIAO.
**Step 1 - Set up the power strips on the breadboard.** The breadboard has two long strips running down one side - the long red/blue strip running down the side is called a rail. The red one is for power, the blue one is for ground (0V). - Run a jumper wire from the XIAO's **3V3** pin to the **red** rail. - Run a jumper wire from the XIAO's **GND** pin to the **blue** rail. Now any part you push into the breadboard can grab power from the red rail and ground from the blue rail. Easy.
**Step 2 - Wire up the OLED screen.** Push the OLED into the breadboard so each of its 4 pins sits in its own row. The pins are labeled on the little board: **GND**, **VCC**, **SCL**, **SDA**. - OLED **GND** -> blue rail (0V / ground). - OLED **VCC** (power input) -> red rail (3.3V). - OLED **SCL** -> the pin marked **D5** on the XIAO (that's GPIO 7 inside). - OLED **SDA** -> the pin marked **D4** on the XIAO (that's GPIO 6 inside). SDA and SCL are the two "talking wires." SDA carries the actual message ("draw a smiley face here!") and SCL is the clock tick that keeps both ends in sync. The order matters - if you swap them, the screen will stay black. **Why this matters:** The OLED is a tiny computer of its own. It will not light up unless it gets clean power AND both talking wires hooked up correctly. If the screen stays blank after you upload the code, 9 times out of 10 it's SDA and SCL swapped, or the address in the code is wrong (some screens want 0x3C and some clones want 0x3D - try both).
**Step 3 - Wire up the touch pad.** The TTP223B is the little board with a metal square on top. When you touch the metal, the **I/O** pin fires. It has 3 pins: **VCC**, **GND**, **I/O** (sometimes called SIG or OUT). - Touch pad **VCC** (power input) -> red rail (3.3V). - Touch pad **GND** -> blue rail (0V / ground). - Touch pad **I/O** -> the pin marked **D0** on the XIAO (that's GPIO 2 inside). That's it - only 3 wires. The chip on the bottom of the touch pad does all the hard work of noticing your finger. **Why this matters:** You don't need a button or a resistor here. The touch pad watches for tiny electrical changes when your finger gets close to the metal pad. The chip on board already takes care of "is this a real touch or just noise?" - so the XIAO just reads the I/O pin and sees a clear "yes, finger!" or "no finger."
**Step 4 - Plug in the USB-C cable and warm-up.** Plug the USB-C cable into the XIAO's little oval socket, then into your laptop. A small light on the XIAO should glow. When the touch pad first powers on, it spends about half a second figuring out what "no finger" feels like in your room. **Don't rest your finger on the metal pad while you press the reset button** - if you do, it will think your finger is the new "normal" and the screen will never react. Let go, plug in, then touch. If after all that the screen stays blank: unplug, double-check that SDA and SCL aren't swapped, then try changing `0x3C` to `0x3D` in the code (some screens are made by a different factory and use a different address).
## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open File -> Preferences. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Open Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager. Search for "esp32" and install "esp32 by Espressif Systems". It is a big download, give it a minute. 3. Open Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> and pick **"XIAO_ESP32C3"** from the list. 4. Open Tools -> Manage Libraries. You need two libraries for the screen: - Search "Adafruit GFX" and install **Adafruit GFX Library**. - Search "Adafruit SSD1306" and install **Adafruit SSD1306**. If it asks to install dependencies, say yes. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the XIAO into your laptop with a **USB-C** cable. The little orange LED on the board should glow. 2. Open Tools -> Port and pick the new one that appeared when you plugged in (Windows: `COM4` or similar; Mac: `/dev/cu.usbmodem...`; Linux: `/dev/ttyACM0`). 3. There are no passwords or WiFi names to fill in for this sketch - it runs offline. Skip straight to upload. 4. Click the **right-arrow Upload button** at the top left. The IDE will say "Compiling..." then "Writing...". The XIAO ESP32-C3 flashes over USB without needing the BOOT button trick, so you should not have to hold anything down. 5. Open Tools -> Serial Monitor and set the baud rate (bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window) to **115200** - that has to match the `Serial.begin(115200)` line in the code. 6. What you should see: the OLED lights up with a smiley face and the word "happy" along the bottom. The Serial Monitor prints a startup line. Touch the metal pad on the TTP223B with your fingertip - the face flips to sleepy, then grumpy, then surprised, then back to happy. Each tap also prints a line in the Serial Monitor like `mood -> sleepy @ 12s`. **Common gotchas:** - **Blank screen, code uploaded fine?** The OLED address is probably 0x3D instead of 0x3C. Change `#define OLED_ADDR 0x3C` to `0x3D` and re-upload. - **Face changes by itself the moment you reset?** You were touching the pad while the TTP223B was still calibrating (the first half-second after power on). Unplug, let go of the pad, then plug back in. - **Serial Monitor shows alien gibberish?** The baud rate dropdown in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor is not on 115200. Change it. ## Talking points - I2C uses just two wires (SDA = data, SCL = clock) and can talk to up to ~120 devices in theory. The OLED listens on address 0x3C; if we added a second I2C gadget (temperature sensor, real-time clock, another screen) it would share the same two wires with a different address. - "Capacitive touch" means the chip is measuring how much electrical charge the pad can hold. A finger nearby adds a tiny bit of capacitance, the chip notices the change, and flips the output pin. No moving parts, no wear. - The face is drawn from primitives: `drawCircle`, `drawLine`, `fillCircle`, plus a couple of stray pixels for the smile curl. It's the same toolbox an old 8-bit game would have used. ## Things to change once it works - Add more moods. Adding a fifth case is one enum entry, one name string, one extra `case` in `drawFace`, and bumping the modulo from 4 to 5. - Make the eyes blink every few seconds when idle (timer + extra draw call). - Connect to WiFi (SSID `GeeFam`, password `PASSWORD_HERE`) and pull the real time from an NTP server so the log timestamp is a clock time instead of seconds-since-boot. - Hold-to-confirm: instead of cycling on every tap, require a 300ms hold so accidental brushes don't change the face. - Once the Orange Pi is running Mosquitto, publish each mood change as an MQTT message - first cross-device milestone for the kit. ## Why this is interesting Two of the most useful "building block" skills for everything else in the kit live in this project: talking to an I2C peripheral, and reacting to a non-button input. Once OLED graphics feel familiar, every future sensor reading (temperature, distance, humidity) has somewhere nice to show up. And capacitive touch is the gateway to projects that don't look like electronics at all - hidden touch points behind wood, glass, or a 3D-printed shell.

<![CDATA[// Mood Meter - touch the dot, change your face
// Hardware: XIAO ESP32-C3 + SSD1306 0.96" I2C OLED + TTP223B touch module
//
// Libraries to install via Arduino IDE Library Manager:
//   - Adafruit GFX Library
//   - Adafruit SSD1306
//
// Board: "XIAO_ESP32C3" (under ESP32 Arduino)
// Serial baud: 115200

#include <Wire.h>
#include <Adafruit_GFX.h>
#include <Adafruit_SSD1306.h>

// ---- Pin assignments (match the wiring diagram) ----
// XIAO ESP32-C3 default I2C pins:
//   SDA = GPIO 6  (silkscreen "D4")
//   SCL = GPIO 7  (silkscreen "D5")
// TTP223B signal:
//   TOUCH = GPIO 2 (silkscreen "D0")
const int PIN_TOUCH = 2;

// ---- Display setup ----
#define SCREEN_WIDTH 128
#define SCREEN_HEIGHT 64
#define OLED_RESET   -1     // share the XIAO reset
#define OLED_ADDR    0x3C   // most cheap 0.96" SSD1306 boards
Adafruit_SSD1306 display(SCREEN_WIDTH, SCREEN_HEIGHT, &Wire, OLED_RESET);

// ---- Mood state ----
enum Mood { HAPPY = 0, SLEEPY = 1, GRUMPY = 2, SURPRISED = 3 };
const char* MOOD_NAMES[4] = { "happy", "sleepy", "grumpy", "surprised" };
Mood currentMood = HAPPY;

// ---- Touch debounce ----
int lastTouchState = LOW;
unsigned long lastTouchChangeMs = 0;
const unsigned long DEBOUNCE_MS = 50;

// ---- Timestamp (seconds since boot - good enough without WiFi) ----
unsigned long lastChangeSec = 0;

// ---------- Drawing helpers ----------

// Draw the face inside a circle in the upper portion of the screen.
// Center at (64, 24), radius 20. That leaves the bottom for the log line.
void drawFace(Mood m) {
  const int cx = 64;
  const int cy = 24;
  const int r  = 20;

  // outline of the face
  display.drawCircle(cx, cy, r, SSD1306_WHITE);

  // eyes - default position
  int eyeLx = cx - 7;
  int eyeRx = cx + 7;
  int eyeY  = cy - 5;

  switch (m) {
    case HAPPY:
      // round eyes
      display.fillCircle(eyeLx, eyeY, 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.fillCircle(eyeRx, eyeY, 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      // smile - arc-ish: a short horizontal line with curled ends
      display.drawLine(cx - 6, cy + 4, cx + 6, cy + 4, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawPixel(cx - 7, cy + 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawPixel(cx + 7, cy + 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
      break;

    case SLEEPY:
      // closed eyes - horizontal lines
      display.drawLine(eyeLx - 3, eyeY, eyeLx + 3, eyeY, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawLine(eyeRx - 3, eyeY, eyeRx + 3, eyeY, SSD1306_WHITE);
      // tiny "o" mouth
      display.drawCircle(cx, cy + 5, 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      // a little "Z" floating up-right
      display.setTextSize(1);
      display.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.setCursor(cx + r - 4, cy - r);
      display.print("z");
      break;

    case GRUMPY:
      // angled eyebrows over round eyes
      display.drawLine(eyeLx - 4, eyeY - 4, eyeLx + 3, eyeY - 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawLine(eyeRx + 4, eyeY - 4, eyeRx - 3, eyeY - 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.fillCircle(eyeLx, eyeY + 1, 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.fillCircle(eyeRx, eyeY + 1, 2, SSD1306_WHITE);
      // frown - line that curves the other way
      display.drawLine(cx - 6, cy + 7, cx + 6, cy + 7, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawPixel(cx - 7, cy + 8, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawPixel(cx + 7, cy + 8, SSD1306_WHITE);
      break;

    case SURPRISED:
      // wide round eyes
      display.drawCircle(eyeLx, eyeY, 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
      display.drawCircle(eyeRx, eyeY, 3, SSD1306_WHITE);
      // open "O" mouth
      display.drawCircle(cx, cy + 7, 4, SSD1306_WHITE);
      break;
  }
}

// Format seconds-since-boot as M:SS so the log line looks like a timestamp.
void formatTimestamp(unsigned long totalSec, char* out, size_t outLen) {
  unsigned long minutes = totalSec / 60;
  unsigned long seconds = totalSec % 60;
  snprintf(out, outLen, "%lu:%02lu", minutes, seconds);
}

void drawLogLine() {
  char ts[16];
  formatTimestamp(lastChangeSec, ts, sizeof(ts));

  display.setTextSize(1);
  display.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE);

  // bottom log area: line + text
  display.drawLine(0, 50, SCREEN_WIDTH - 1, 50, SSD1306_WHITE);
  display.setCursor(2, 54);
  display.print("[");
  display.print(ts);
  display.print("] ");
  display.print(MOOD_NAMES[currentMood]);
}

void redraw() {
  display.clearDisplay();
  drawFace(currentMood);
  drawLogLine();
  display.display();
}

// ---------- Arduino entry points ----------

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(300);
  Serial.println();
  Serial.println("Mood Meter starting...");

  pinMode(PIN_TOUCH, INPUT);

  // Start I2C on the XIAO's default SDA=6, SCL=7
  Wire.begin();

  if (!display.begin(SSD1306_SWITCHCAPVCC, OLED_ADDR)) {
    Serial.println("SSD1306 not found at 0x3C - check wiring");
    while (true) {
      delay(1000);
    }
  }

  display.clearDisplay();
  display.setTextSize(1);
  display.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE);
  display.setCursor(0, 0);
  display.println("Mood Meter ready.");
  display.println("Touch to cycle...");
  display.display();
  delay(800);

  redraw();
}

void loop() {
  int reading = digitalRead(PIN_TOUCH);

  // Debounced edge detection - act on LOW -> HIGH transition (touch start)
  if (reading != lastTouchState) {
    if (millis() - lastTouchChangeMs >= DEBOUNCE_MS) {
      lastTouchChangeMs = millis();

      if (reading == HIGH) {
        // Cycle to next mood
        currentMood = static_cast<Mood>((static_cast<int>(currentMood) + 1) % 4);
        lastChangeSec = millis() / 1000UL;

        Serial.print("Mood -> ");
        Serial.print(MOOD_NAMES[currentMood]);
        Serial.print(" at ");
        Serial.print(lastChangeSec);
        Serial.println("s");

        redraw();
      }
      lastTouchState = reading;
    }
  }

  delay(5);
}

projects.name: Theremin Lite
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (5V via the micro-USB port, regulated on-board to 3.3V for the chip and broken out as VIN/5V for the ultrasonic sensor)
projects.description:
**What it is**: Wave your hand over the breadboard. The red LED blinks slowly when your hand is far away, then pulses faster and faster as you move it closer, like a heartbeat speeding up. No touching anything - just air. **Why it's fun**: You are literally controlling a light with your hand from across the desk, like a wizard. Challenge your dad to guess the distance just by watching the blink speed - then move your hand and prove him wrong. ## Parts list - ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - reads the sensor, blinks the LED) - HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance sensor (the "eye" that bounces sound off your hand) - 5mm red LED (the visible heartbeat) - 220R resistor (current limiter for the LED - keeps it from burning out) - 1K resistor + 2.2K resistor (voltage divider on the Echo line - see Wiring notes) - Breadboard, 400 tie-points - A handful of male-male jumper wires - A USB cable from your laptop to the ESP32 (power and code-upload in one) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **VIN** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. We use this to power the sensor. - **3V3** - 3.3 volts out. We do not need this one for this project. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs to share a GND. - **D5, D18, D19** - pins marked on the silkscreen. The numbers in the code match what is printed on the board. - **EN** - reset button. Press this if the board gets stuck.
**Step 1 - Place the breadboard and the ESP32.** - The breadboard has a long red strip and a long blue/black strip down each side. Those long strips are called rails. The red one is for power, the blue one is for ground (0V). - For this build the ESP32 sits next to the breadboard (not on it). We will run jumper wires from the ESP32 pins into the breadboard holes. - Plug the USB cable from your laptop into the micro-USB port on the ESP32. That is what powers everything.
**Step 2 - Wire up the distance sensor.** The HC-SR04 is the part with two silver "eyes". Those eyes click out a sound your ears cannot hear and listen for it to bounce back. The closer your hand is, the faster the bounce comes back. The sensor has four pins labeled VCC, TRIG, ECHO, and GND. Push it into the breadboard so each pin sits in its own row. - **VCC (power input, 5V in)** on the sensor goes to the red rail on the top of the breadboard. Then run a red wire from that red rail to the **VIN** pin on the ESP32. VIN gives us back the 5V from the USB cable. - **GND** on the sensor goes to the blue/black rail on the top of the breadboard. Then run a black wire from that rail to a **GND** pin on the ESP32. - **TRIG** on the sensor goes to the pin marked **D5** on the ESP32 with a yellow or orange wire. Trig is how the ESP32 tells the sensor "go ping now!". - Leave **ECHO** for the next step. Echo is special.
**Step 3 - Build the little resistor pair for Echo.**
The sensor sends its Echo signal back at 5V, but the ESP32 only likes 3.3V on its input pins. We need to step the voltage down with two resistors before it hits the ESP32. The 1K resistor has bands brown-black-red, and the 2.2K has bands red-red-red. - Run a blue wire from the sensor's **ECHO** pin to an empty row on the breadboard. - Plug the **1K resistor** with one leg in that same row and the other leg in another empty row a few holes away. This is the "middle" row. - Plug the **2.2K resistor** with one leg in that middle row and the other leg in the GND rail. - Run a yellow wire from the middle row to the pin marked **D18** on the ESP32. **Why this matters:** Two resistors in a line like this share the voltage between them. The 1K is the smaller share and the 2.2K is the bigger share, so the ESP32 only sees about 3.4V instead of the full 5V. Without this little pair, the 5V Echo signal could damage the ESP32 pin over time. If your sensor always reads -1 (no echo) even when your hand is right in front of it, you may have a sensor clone that needs a stronger Trig push. Try a different HC-SR04 before tearing apart the wiring.
**Step 4 - Add the LED with its safety resistor.**
Look closely at the LED. One leg is longer than the other. The long leg is the plus side, and the short leg is the minus side. The 220R resistor has bands red-red-brown. - Push the LED into the breadboard so the **long leg** and **short leg** sit in two different rows. - Plug the **220R resistor** with one leg in the same row as the long leg of the LED, and the other leg a few holes away in a fresh row. - Run a yellow wire from that fresh row (the far side of the 220R resistor) to the pin marked **D19** on the ESP32. - Run a black wire from the row with the **short leg** of the LED to the blue/black GND rail. **Why this matters:** An LED is greedy. If you connect it straight to a pin, it will try to pull as much electricity as it can and burn itself out in a flash. The 220R resistor is a tiny traffic gate that keeps the current safe and slow. The resistor can go on either side of the LED, the LED does not mind which side it is on.
**Step 5 - Double-check before you plug in the USB.** - Long leg of the LED is wired through the 220R resistor to D19. Short leg of the LED goes to GND. - Sensor VCC goes to VIN (5V). Sensor GND goes to GND. - Sensor TRIG goes straight to D5. - Sensor ECHO goes through the 1K resistor to D18, and the 2.2K resistor goes from that middle spot down to GND. - Nothing is touching the wrong row, and no bare resistor legs are crossing each other. Now plug the USB cable in. The board will boot, the code will start, and waving your hand over the sensor should change the pitch of the buzzer (or in the Serial Monitor) and brighten the LED as your hand gets closer. If the LED never lights at all, flip the LED around. You almost certainly have the long leg and short leg swapped, and that is the most common first-try mistake. It cannot hurt the LED to wire it backward, it just will not glow. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open File -> Preferences. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Go to Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager. In the search box type `esp32`, find "esp32 by Espressif Systems", and click Install. It is a big download (a few hundred MB) - go grab a snack. 3. Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> **NodeMCU-32S** (it is in a long list, scroll patiently). 4. No extra libraries needed for this sketch. Everything it uses (`pulseIn`, `digitalWrite`, `Serial`) is built into the Arduino core, so you can skip Tools -> Manage Libraries entirely. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with a micro-USB cable (the cable matters - some cheap micro-USB cables are "charge only" and have no data wires, so the laptop will not see the board at all. If nothing shows up in the next step, try a different cable first). 2. Tools -> Port. Pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged the board in - on Windows it looks like `COM4` or `COM7`, on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`. 3. No passwords or placeholders to edit in this sketch - it does not use WiFi. You can leave the code exactly as it is. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, top-left, next to the checkmark). The IDE will compile for about 20 seconds, then start uploading. You should see a row of orange dots `....__....__....` marching across the bottom black panel. If it stalls on `Connecting........_____........` for more than 10 seconds, **hold down the BOOT button on the ESP32** (the little button labeled BOOT or IO0) until the dots start moving, then let go. Some boards need this every time, some only the first time. 5. When upload finishes you'll see `Hard resetting via RTS pin...`. Now open Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. In the dropdown at the top-right of the Serial Monitor panel, set the baud rate to **115200** (it has to match the `Serial.begin(115200)` line in the code, or you'll just see garbage characters). 6. You should see `Theremin Lite ready. Wave your hand!` print once, then a stream of distance readings like `distance: 24.3 cm` once per loop. Wave your hand over the sensor and watch the number change. The red LED should be blinking - slowly when your hand is far, faster as you bring it closer. If the readings say `(no echo)` non-stop, point the sensor at the ceiling - if the number then drops to something sensible, your hand was just out of range or off-axis. **Common gotchas:** - **Upload stuck on "Connecting..."** - hold the BOOT button on the ESP32 until the orange dots start moving, then release. The chip needs to be nudged into flash mode on some boards. - **Serial Monitor shows garbage like `@#~~?@`** - the baud rate is wrong. Set it to 115200 in the dropdown at the top-right of the Serial Monitor. - **LED never lights up** - the LED is in backwards. The long leg (anode) goes to the 220R resistor side; the short leg (cathode, also the flat side of the plastic dome) goes to GND. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees, and push it back in. You can't damage it by getting it wrong. ## Talking points - **How ultrasonic distance works:** the sensor chirps a 40kHz "click" your ears can't hear, then listens for the echo. The ESP32 times how long the click takes to come back. Sound travels about 343 metres per second in air, so distance in cm = duration in microseconds * 0.0343 / 2 (the "divide by 2" is because the sound made a round trip). - **Why the LED gets faster when your hand gets closer:** the code maps distance to a blink delay. Far away -> long delay -> slow blink. Close -> short delay -> rapid pulse. That mapping is a simple linear interpolation (lerp). - **Why three resistors for one LED:** one limits LED current (220R), the other two protect the ESP32 from 5V on its Echo input. Two different jobs. - **Why GPIO 5/18/19:** these are "safe" output pins on the ESP32. Some pins (like 0, 2, 12, 15) are tied to boot behaviour and pulling them HIGH or LOW at startup can prevent the board from booting. Sticking to 5, 18, 19, 21, 22, 23 avoids that whole class of headache. ## Things to change once it works - Swap the LED for the onboard blue LED on GPIO 2 (one less wire on the breadboard). - Print distance to the Serial Monitor (115200 baud) so you can see numbers next to the blinking. - Add a buzzer in parallel with the LED for an actual Geiger-counter sound effect. - Use `ledcWrite` (PWM) instead of digital ON/OFF to make the LED smoothly fade brighter as your hand approaches, instead of blinking. - Hook three LEDs (green / yellow / red) and light them like a traffic light based on distance bands. ## Why this is interesting This is the smallest possible bridge between the physical world and code. There are no buttons, no switches - you wave your hand in mid-air, sound waves bounce, and a light reacts. That's the same loop every smart device on Earth runs: sense, decide, act. Once this works, every other sensor in the kit (PIR motion, photoresistor, tilt switch, IR obstacle) becomes "the same project with a different sensor block at the top."

projects.name: Don't-Touch-The-Wire steady-hand maze
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S micro-USB port (5V in; ESP32 runs on 3.3V on-board, TM1637 display fed from the 5V VIN pin)
projects.description:
**What it is**: Guide a little metal loop along a bendy wire track without letting them touch. Every time you bump the wire, the red light flashes, a number on the display ticks up, and your strike count climbs. Hold steady and the green light stays on instead. **Why it's fun**: It's the classic carnival "buzz wire" game, but you built it yourself, and the screen keeps score so you can finally settle who in the family has the steadiest hand. Bend the track into a tougher shape every round to mess with whoever goes next. ## Parts list - **ESP32 NodeMCU-32S** - the brain. Watches the wand and updates the score. - **4-digit 7-segment Display Module (TM1637, 4-pin: VCC/GND/CLK/DIO)** - shows the strike count. Powered from 5V (see wiring notes). - **LED 5mm Red + 220R resistor** - lights while the wand is touching the wire. - **LED 5mm Green + 220R resistor** - lights while the wand is in the clear. - **Tactile Push-button Switch (3x6x4.3mm, white pin)** - reset-to-zero button. - **Stiff bare wire (~30 cm)** bent into a wavy track. **Wand loop (~3 cm)** of the same wire on a short insulated handle. (Both physical-craft parts, not on the board.) - **Heat-shrink tubing / electrical tape / pen barrel** - the insulated handle for the wand so the player's hand doesn't complete the circuit. - **Breadboard + jumper wires** to hold everything together. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **GND** = the 0V side, ground. The wire that finishes the circuit. - **VIN** = the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. We use it to feed the display. - **3V3** = the 3.3V pin. We will not use it in this build. - **Dx pins** (like D18, D23) = the pins you can control from code. The number printed on the board matches the number in the code. - **EN** = the reset button on the board itself. Don't worry about it.
**Step 1 - Get the breadboard ready.** The breadboard has two long red/blue strips running down each side. These strips are called rails. The red one is the +5V power rail, and the blue (or black) one is the 0V ground rail. Inside the white middle part, every row of 5 holes is connected from side to side. - We will use the top rails (near the top of the board) for the ESP32's 5V and GND. - We will use the bottom rails (near the bottom) for the display's 5V and GND.
**Step 2 - Power the breadboard from the ESP32.** Plug the ESP32 in next to the breadboard. We need to send its 5V out to the top red rail, and ground out to the top blue rail. - ESP32 pin **VIN** -> top red rail (+5V). - ESP32 pin **GND** -> top blue rail (GND). The USB cable from the laptop is what actually feeds power to the ESP32. The VIN pin just hands that 5V back out so the breadboard can use it too.
**Step 3 - Put in the red "you lose" LED.** The LED has a **long leg** (the + side) and a **short leg** (the - side). Push the long leg into hole **E5** and the short leg into hole **E6**. - One end of a 220 ohm resistor into **A5** (same row as the long leg), other end into **A2**. - Short jumper wire from **A6** (same row as the short leg) over to the top blue rail (GND). - Long jumper wire from the ESP32 pin marked **D18** over to **A2**. When the code makes D18 high, current flows: D18 -> resistor -> long leg -> through the LED -> short leg -> GND. Red LED lights up. **Why this matters:** the 220 ohm resistor is a "current limiter". An LED is greedy and will burn itself out if you let it drink all the power. The resistor sits in the way and only lets a small, safe sip through.
**Step 4 - Put in the green "you won" LED.** Same trick as the red one. Long leg into **E10**, short leg into **E11**. (We don't have a photo of the green one on file, but it looks just like the red one, only green.) - 220 ohm resistor from **A10** to **A8**. - Short jumper from **A11** to the top blue rail (GND). - Long jumper from the ESP32 pin marked **D19** to **A8**.
**Step 5 - Add the reset button.** The little tactile button has 4 legs. The two legs on one side are joined inside, and the two on the other side are joined inside. Pressing the button connects those two pairs together. The easy way to handle this is to push it across the middle gap of the breadboard so two legs land on each side. - Push the button in at **E15** (one corner of the button there, the diagonally opposite corner ends up somewhere around row 17 on the other side). - Short jumper from **A15** down to the top blue rail (GND). - Long jumper from the ESP32 pin marked **D5** over to **C15**. Now when the kid presses the button, D5 gets pulled to GND for a moment, and the code uses that as the "start a new game" signal. **Why this matters:** D5 is a special "strapping pin" - the ESP32 peeks at it the instant it turns on, to decide how to start up. With our wiring, the button is **not** being pressed at power-on, so D5 reads high, which is exactly what the chip wants. This is safe. Just don't add another wire to D5 later that holds it down at start-up, or the board won't boot.
**Step 6 - Plug in the timer display.** The TM1637 is the little board with 4 red number digits. It has 4 pins along one edge labelled **CLK, DIO, VCC, GND**. Push it into the breadboard so the pins land in row 22 (VCC), 23 (GND), 24 (DIO) and 25 (CLK), on the F column. - From **J22** (same row as VCC) -> bottom red rail (+5V). - From **J23** (same row as GND) -> bottom blue rail (GND). - Long jumper from the ESP32 pin marked **D21** to **J24** (DIO). - Long jumper from the ESP32 pin marked **D22** to **J25** (CLK). Now we need to feed that bottom red rail. Use a short jumper to connect the top red rail to the bottom red rail (they need to be joined), and the top blue rail to the bottom blue rail. That way the 5V and GND coming from the ESP32 reach the display too. **Why this matters - why VIN and not 3V3 for the display?** This display is built for 5V. If you only give it 3.3V, the digits look faded or flicker. VIN gives us the full 5V coming straight from the USB cable, which is what the display wants. The ESP32's data pins (D21, D22) are happy talking to a 5V display like this one - it's the normal way to hook up a TM1637.
**Step 7 - The game piece: the maze wire and the wand.** This is the fun bit. Take a longer piece of bare wire and bend it into a wiggly maze shape - that's the **maze wire**. Take another piece of wire, bend a small loop at one end, and tape the other end of the loop's wire to a chopstick or pencil so it has an insulated handle - that's the **wand**. Thread the wand's loop around the maze wire so it can slide along it. Use the long female-to-male jumper wires (the ones with a sleeve on one end) so you can clip onto the bare ends of the maze wire and wand without soldering: - Maze wire -> long jumper -> ESP32 pin marked **D23**. - Wand loop -> long jumper -> bottom blue rail (GND). **Why this matters:** in the code we tell D23 to use an "internal pull-up". That means the ESP32 quietly holds D23 at 3.3V from the inside. The wand's loop is connected to GND (0V). When the loop touches the maze wire, suddenly D23 is yanked all the way down to GND. The code spots that drop and shouts "you touched it!" That whole loop-vs-maze-wire setup is one giant switch.
**Step 8 - Plug in and check.** Plug the USB cable into the ESP32 and into your laptop. The display should light up with four bright red digits. If you touch the wand loop on the maze wire on purpose, the red LED should flash. Tap the reset button and the green LED gives the all-clear so you can start a fresh run. If the display stays dark, the most common fix is that the bottom rails are not joined to the top rails - check those two short jumpers from Step 6. If only the display is dark but the LEDs work, swap the DIO and CLK wires (D21 and D22) - it is easy to put them on the wrong row. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and click **Install** on "esp32 by Espressif Systems". Give it a few minutes - it's a big download. 3. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries**, type `TM1637` in the search box, and click **Install** on **"TM1637" by Avishay Orpaz**. That's the one the sketch uses for the 4-digit display. 4. Now pick the board: **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **micro-USB cable** (make sure it's a real data cable - some "charge only" cables won't show up). The little red power LED on the board should light up. 2. **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that just appeared (looks like `COM5` on Windows, `/dev/cu.usbmodemXXXX` on a Mac, or `/dev/ttyUSB0` on Linux). If you only see one option, that's it. 3. This sketch has no WiFi passwords or other placeholders to fill in - it's ready to go as-is. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling..." then "Connecting..." with dots scrolling across the bottom. **First-upload tip:** if it sits at "Connecting......_____......" for more than 10 seconds, hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 down until the upload actually starts, then let go. After the first successful flash you usually don't need that trick again. 5. When it finishes (you'll see "Hard resetting via RTS pin..." in green), open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the monitor, set the baud rate to **115200** (that matches `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch). 6. You should see `Steady-hand maze: starting up` followed by `Reset - new round`. At the same time the **4-digit display lights up showing `0`**, the **green LED comes on**, and the red LED stays off. Touch the wand to the maze wire - the red LED should snap on, the green should snap off, the display should tick to `1`, and the Serial Monitor will print a strike message. Press the reset button and the count jumps back to `0`. That's the whole game. **Common gotchas:** - **Display is dark or shows weird symbols:** the TM1637 module is wired to **VIN (5 V)**, not 3V3. At 3.3 V many modules are too dim to read or flicker. Double-check the red VCC wire on the display goes to the pin labelled `VIN` on the ESP32. - **"Connecting....." never finishes on upload:** hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 board while the IDE shows the dots, then let go once it starts writing. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need this every single upload, others only the first time. - **Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `??????`:** the baud rate dropdown in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor is wrong. Set it to **115200** to match the sketch. ## Talking points - **Pull-ups in one sentence:** "The pin is held HIGH by a tiny resistor inside the chip until something outside drags it LOW. We use the wand-to-maze contact as the thing that drags it LOW." If you skip the pull-up, the pin is *floating* - touching nothing, but picking up stray noise from the air - and you'll see random ghost strikes with the wand sitting still. The pull-up is what makes "not touching" a definite, repeatable state. - **Why a resistor on every LED:** an LED is basically a short-circuit with a glow, so the resistor sets the current. A red LED drops about 2.0 V, so across a 220R resistor on a 3.3 V GPIO the current is (3.3 - 2.0) / 220 = about **6 mA**. That's gentle - plenty visible as an indicator, well under the ESP32's ~20 mA-per-pin comfort limit. If you ever want it brighter, drop to 150R for about 8.7 mA, or move the LED to the 5 V VIN rail (still through the resistor) for around 13 mA. - **Edge detection:** we only count a strike on the *moment* of contact - the HIGH-to-LOW transition - not every single loop where the pin happens to be LOW. That way, holding the wand against the wire doesn't rack up hundreds of strikes; one touch = one strike, no matter how long you linger. - **Debouncing (the lighter version):** real metal contacts are jittery and can register as a few touches in 1 ms. After the edge fires we wait 20 ms and re-check; if the pin is still LOW it was a real touch, not noise. For the reset button it's even simpler: a 50 ms `delay()` before a second read. We can get away with that because nothing time-critical is happening during a reset press. ## Things to change once it works - Add a buzzer (when one shows up in inventory) on GPIO 4 for the actual "bzzzt" sound. - Use the reset button held for 2 seconds as "hard reset to zero" and a short tap as "new round." - Add a timer: count seconds until the player either finishes (touches a designated "end pad" wire) or hits the max strikes. Display the time on the 7-segment between rounds. - Wire two maze wires in parallel and use both ends as "start pad" and "end pad" so the game knows when the run is complete. - Upgrade to a millis()-based non-blocking loop once the game logic is comfortable - that's a natural next step into intermediate territory. ## Why this is interesting It's the smallest possible useful circuit - "two pieces of metal that complete a circuit when they touch" - dressed up as a game. The maze itself is the sensor. There's no module hiding the physics; the kid can see exactly *why* the score ticks, because they watched you bend the wire that does it. It also turns two software concepts (pull-ups and edge detection) into something tangible: without the pull-up the score creeps up on its own, and without edge detection holding the wand still while touching racks up dozens of strikes. Add them both and the game suddenly feels fair. Great moment.

projects.name: Temperature Mood Dial
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from laptop (or any 5V USB charger) to the XIAO ESP32-C3; the XIAO's 5V pin feeds the SG90 servo, and the XIAO's 3V3 pin feeds the DHT11.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little cardboard dial with a pointer that swings to show how warm or cold the room is. When the air is freezing it points at BRRR, when it's hot it swings all the way to LAVA, and it keeps re-checking every couple of seconds on its own. **Why it's fun**: Breathe on the sensor and watch the needle creep toward TOASTY in real time, or stick it by a window and catch the moment the sun comes out. You built a thing that feels the world and reacts - no buttons, no app, just your dial quietly paying attention. ## Parts list - 1x Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 (the brain - reads the sensor, drives the servo). - 1x DHT11 Temperature & Humidity Sensor module (3-pin breakout: VCC / DATA / GND). - 1x SG90 Servo (the moving needle). - 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (gives the XIAO and DHT11 a home and shared power rails). - 1x 470uF electrolytic capacitor (sits across 5V and GND near the servo to absorb its current spikes). - 1x Jumper Wire F-M, 20pc pack (servo lead and DHT11 module both need female-ended jumpers to reach the breadboard). - 1x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc pack (a few short wires for the 5V, 3V3 and GND rails on the breadboard). - Craft supplies (not in inventory, grab from a drawer): a square of cardboard, a marker, a thin cardboard strip for the needle, sticky tape. ## Wiring notes This is the brain of the project: the **Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3**. It is a tiny computer that we will plug parts into. It runs on power from a USB-C cable. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the XIAO ESP32-C3 board:** - **5V** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. Use this for the servo motor. - **3V3** - a pin that gives 3.3V (a smaller voltage). Use this for the DHT11 sensor. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs a wire going to GND so electricity has a way home. - **D2, D3** - the silkscreen labels for two of the pins where we plug in signal wires. On this board D2 is really GPIO 4 inside the chip, and D3 is really GPIO 5. The code uses the GPIO numbers but you only need to find the labels printed on the board. - **USB-C** - the little oval jack where the cable plugs in.
**About the two power pins:** The servo motor is hungry and wants 5V to be strong. The DHT11 sensor is happy with the smaller 3.3V, and using 3.3V for the sensor makes its talking wire safer for the XIAO. So we will use **5V for the servo** and **3V3 for the sensor**. Don't swap them.
**Step 1 - Plant the XIAO on the breadboard.** - Push the XIAO ESP32-C3 down into the middle of the breadboard so the row of pins on each side lands in its own column of holes. - The USB-C jack should stick out over the edge so you can plug a cable in later. The breadboard has two long red strips and two long blue strips down the sides. We call these the "rails" - long red/blue strips that share electricity all the way down. Red rails will carry power, blue rails will carry ground.
**Step 2 - Build the power rails with M-M jumper wires.** Use the **M-M (male-to-male) jumper wires** for this step. They have stiff metal pins on both ends and push straight into the breadboard. - Red wire from the XIAO pin marked **5V** to the **red (+) rail** at the top. - Black wire from the XIAO pin marked **GND** to the **blue (-) rail** at the top. Now every hole along the red rail has 5V power, and every hole along the blue rail has ground (the 0V side).
**Step 3 - Make a small 3V3 spot for the sensor.** The XIAO pin marked **3V3** gives a smaller 3.3V power. Most breadboards only have two rails, so we don't need a whole rail for this - the sensor is the only thing that uses 3.3V. - Run one M-M jumper from the XIAO pin marked **3V3** straight to an empty row of holes near where the DHT11 will sit. That row is now your "3V3 spot".
**Step 4 - Wire in the DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor.** The **DHT11** is a little blue box that reads how warm and how damp the air is. It has three pins. Different brands label them differently, but it's always power input, data, and ground. - Push the DHT11 into the breadboard so each of its 3 pins lands in its own row. - Pin marked **VCC** or **+** (power input) -> connect to your **3V3 spot** with a M-M jumper. Not the red 5V rail! - Pin marked **DATA** or **OUT** (the talking wire) -> connect to the XIAO pin marked **D2** (GPIO 4) with a M-M jumper. - Pin marked **GND** or **-** (the 0V side, ground) -> connect to the **blue rail** with a M-M jumper. The DATA wire is how the sensor tells the XIAO the temperature. Because the sensor is running on 3.3V, the words it sends down DATA are also 3.3V, which is just right for the XIAO.
**Step 5 - Plug in the SG90 servo motor.**
The **SG90 servo** is the little motor that will swing the arrow. It has 3 colored wires ending in female sockets, so use the **F-M (female-to-male) jumper wires** to extend each one into the breadboard. The female end goes onto the servo's pins, the male end goes into the breadboard. - **Red** servo wire -> **red rail** (5V). The servo wants the bigger 5V to be strong. - **Brown** (or black) servo wire -> **blue rail** (ground). - **Orange** (or yellow) servo wire -> XIAO pin marked **D3** (GPIO 5). This is the wire that tells the servo where to point.
**Step 6 - Add the 470uF capacitor near the servo.** The **470uF capacitor** is the little black cylinder with two legs. This one cares which way around it goes - look at the side and you'll see a white stripe with a "-" mark. The leg next to the white stripe is the **short leg** (negative). The other one is the **long leg** (positive). - **Long leg** -> push into the **red rail** (5V). - **Short leg** (the one by the white stripe) -> push into the **blue rail** (ground). - Put it as close as you can to where the servo's red and brown wires plug in. **Why this matters:** When the servo motor jerks, it gulps a big sip of power all at once. The capacitor is a tiny power tank - it holds a little extra electricity right next to the servo and tops up the rail during that quick gulp, so the XIAO doesn't suddenly lose power and reset. If you skip the capacitor and the XIAO keeps restarting whenever the servo moves, you'll know why.
**Step 7 - Build the mood dial face.** - Tape a thin cardboard arrow onto the white plastic servo horn (the X-shaped piece that came with the servo). Press the horn onto the servo's metal shaft. - Cut a bigger piece of cardboard into a half-circle. Draw five equal zones across the curve and label them: **BRRR / CHILLY / NICE / TOASTY / LAVA**. - Tape the servo behind the half-circle so the arrow pokes through and points at one of the zones.
**Step 8 - Power it up.** Plug the USB-C cable into the XIAO and into your laptop (or any 5V USB phone charger). The XIAO's little LED should glow. If the servo twitches once and the arrow lands somewhere, you're wired up right - the code will take it from here. **If it acts weird:** If the servo keeps twitching and the XIAO's LED blinks oddly, double check that the capacitor's short leg is in the blue (ground) rail and the long leg is in the red (5V) rail. Also try a different USB cable plugged straight into the computer, not through a USB hub. Hubs sometimes don't give enough power for the servo to move smoothly. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open the IDE, then go to **File -> Preferences**. Find the box called "Additional boards manager URLs" and paste in: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click OK. 2. **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. In the search box type `esp32`. Install the one called "esp32 by Espressif Systems" (it's a big download, give it a few minutes). 3. **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> XIAO_ESP32C3**. That tells the IDE which chip it's talking to. 4. Now install the three libraries the sketch needs. Go to **Tools -> Manage Libraries** (or click the books icon on the left side bar). For each one: type the name in the search box, then click Install on the matching result. - Search `DHT sensor library` -> install the one by **Adafruit**. When it asks if you want to install dependencies, click "Install all" - that grabs Adafruit Unified Sensor too. - Search `Adafruit Unified Sensor` -> install it by **Adafruit** (skip this if step above already installed it). - Search `ESP32Servo` -> install the one by **Kevin Harrington, John K. Bennett**. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the XIAO into the laptop with a **USB-C cable**. A tiny light on the XIAO should glow. 2. **Tools -> Port** -> pick the one that just appeared (on Windows it's `COM4`, `COM5`, or similar; on a Mac it's `/dev/cu.usbmodem...`). If you only see one port, that's the one. 3. Open the sketch (paste the code into a new IDE window and save it as `TempMoodDial.ino`). There are no WiFi passwords or placeholders to fill in on this project - you can leave the code exactly as it is. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the round arrow pointing right, top-left of the IDE). It will say "Compiling sketch..." for a while, then "Uploading...", then "Done uploading." If the upload hangs or fails with a "Failed to connect" message, hold down the tiny **BOOT** button on the XIAO, click Upload again, and let go of BOOT once you see "Connecting..." in the bottom panel. 5. **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right corner of the Serial Monitor pane, set the baud rate to **115200** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). 6. Within a couple of seconds the servo should swing to a starting position, and the Serial Monitor should print a line every 2 seconds showing the temperature, the mood word (BRRR / CHILLY / NICE / TOASTY / LAVA), and the angle the needle is pointing at. Cup your hand around the DHT11 and breathe on it - the number should climb and the needle should glide toward TOASTY. That's how you know it worked. **Common gotchas:** - **"Failed to connect" on the first upload.** The XIAO ESP32-C3 sometimes needs the BOOT button trick described in step 4. Hold BOOT, hit Upload, release BOOT once "Connecting..." appears. - **Capacitor in backwards.** The 470uF cap has a stripe with a "-" on one leg - that leg goes in the GND (blue) rail, the other leg in the 5V (red) rail. If you flip it, the cap can puff out smelly smoke when you plug in USB. If anything smells warm, unplug right away and check the stripe. - **Servo jitters or the XIAO keeps resetting.** That's the servo yanking too much current. Make sure the 470uF capacitor is plugged in right next to the servo's red and brown wires, not way over on the other end of the breadboard. Also double-check the servo's red wire is on the **5V** rail, not the 3V3 rail - 3V3 isn't enough juice for the motor. - **`nan` (not-a-number) shows up instead of a temperature.** The DHT11's DATA wire is loose or in the wrong hole. Check it goes to **D2 (GPIO 4)** on the XIAO, and that VCC is on the **3V3** rail (not 5V). ## Talking points - The DHT11 is "one-wire-ish": you ask, and one wiggling pin gives back both temperature and humidity. The Adafruit DHT library does all the timing for us. - A servo isn't told a speed - it's told an angle. We `map()` Celsius into degrees so 15 C -> 0 deg, 30 C -> 180 deg. - The DHT11 is slow. It only updates about once a second and only in whole degrees (no half-steps), so we read it once every two seconds and slowly nudge the servo toward the new angle. That avoids the dial jittering on tiny readings. - Why a capacitor near the servo? When the servo motor starts moving, it grabs a big gulp of current for a split second. A thin USB cable can't deliver that fast enough, so the 5V rail dips, the XIAO sees a brown-out, and the whole board can reset. The cap is a tiny bucket of charge sitting right next to the servo - the servo drinks from the bucket, then the USB cable refills the bucket more slowly. Same idea as a header tank in a plumbing system. - 3.3V vs 5V picking sides: running the DHT11 at 3V3 means its DATA line idles at 3.3V (safe for the XIAO). Running the SG90 at 5V keeps the motor strong. Each part gets the voltage it likes, and the XIAO's 3.3V signal is enough to tell the servo where to go. ## Things to change once it works - Change the temperature range in `MIN_TEMP_C` / `MAX_TEMP_C` to match the room - if it never gets to 30 C indoors, narrow the range so the needle uses the whole gauge. Re-space the mood thresholds in `moodFor()` to match, keeping them equal-width. - Add humidity to the dial too - print it to serial first, then maybe a second servo for "DRY / OK / SWAMP". - Smooth the reading by averaging the last few values before mapping to an angle. - Swap the DHT11 for a DHT22 or BMP280 later for finer-grained readings (the DHT11 only reports whole degrees, which is why the serial line shows no decimal). ## Why this is interesting It turns an invisible thing (room temperature) into a physical, kid-friendly object that moves. The cardboard gauge is the canvas - Andy and his son can re-draw it as a volcano, a dragon's mouth, a thermometer in a desert, anything. The electronics underneath stay the same; the storytelling on top is theirs.
