projects.name: Shake-to-roll electronic D6 dice
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S micro-USB port (5V in, regulated to 3.3V on board for all modules)
projects.description:
**What it is**: Shake the breadboard like a pair of dice in your hand. A little green light flashes, numbers blur across the screen, and then it stops on your roll - 1 through 6, just like a real die. **Why it's fun**: No more lost dice under the couch on board game night. Plus the numbers slow down as they land, so every shake feels like a real tumble - your brain totally falls for it. ## Parts list - ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - reads the shake sensor and drives the display) - SW-420 vibration switch module (digital "did something shake?" sensor) - 4-digit 7-segment display module (TM1637 driver - only needs two data pins) - 1x 5mm green LED + 1x 220 ohm resistor (lights up while the dice is "rolling") - Breadboard + DuPont jumper wires - Micro-USB cable from your laptop to power the ESP32 ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the pin that gives out 3.3 volts of power to small parts. - **GND** - the 0 volt side, also called ground. Every part needs a GND wire. - **D18, D19, D26, D27** - signal pins. The number on the silkscreen matches what we write in the code. - **EN** - the reset button is right next to it. Press it to restart the program. - **USB** - the micro-USB port. This is how the laptop sends power and uploads the code.
**Step 1 - Place the ESP32 across the middle of the breadboard.** The breadboard has a small gap running down the middle. That gap is there on purpose so chips like the ESP32 can straddle it - one row of pins on the left side, one row on the right side. Push it in gently and evenly until the black plastic is flat against the board. The long red and blue strips down each edge are called rails. The red rail is for power, the blue rail is for ground (0 volts). We will feed both rails from the ESP32 in the next step.
**Step 2 - Feed power into the breadboard rails.** We will use the male-to-male jumper wires for everything. Use red for power and black for ground if you can - it makes mistakes much easier to spot. - ESP32 pin marked **3V3** -> red rail (long red strip on the side) - ESP32 pin marked **GND** -> blue rail (long blue strip on the side) Now every part we plug into the rails gets power and ground without any extra wires running back to the ESP32. Neat, right?
**Step 3 - Wire the vibration sensor (the shake detector).** The SW-420 is a tiny module with a little spring inside that wiggles when you shake it. It has 3 pins labeled VCC, GND, and DO. - **VCC** (power input, 3.3V) -> red rail - **GND** (the 0V side - ground) -> blue rail - **DO** (the "shake!" signal) -> ESP32 pin marked **D27** The small blue box on the SW-420 is a tuning screw. If the dice rolls without you shaking it, turn the screw a tiny bit with a small screwdriver to make it less twitchy. If you have to shake really hard to get it to react, turn the other way. *Why this matters:* we picked D27 because it is a normal, safe pin. Some pins on the ESP32 control how the chip starts up - if a sensor is connected to one of those, the chip can get confused when you plug in the USB cable. D27 leaves the boot pins alone.
**Step 4 - Wire the 4-digit number display.** This is the display that will show the dice number. It has 4 pins: CLK, DIO, VCC, and GND. - **VCC** (power input) -> red rail - **GND** (ground) -> blue rail - **CLK** (clock signal) -> ESP32 pin marked **D18** - **DIO** (data signal) -> ESP32 pin marked **D19** Only 2 signal pins for 4 whole digits! The chip on the back of the module does all the clever timing work for us. The ESP32 just needs to send numbers and the module figures out how to light up the right segments.
**Step 5 - Wire the green "rolling" LED with its resistor.**
The LED has two legs of different lengths. Look closely! - The **long leg** is the plus side. - The **short leg** is the minus side (it also has a flat spot on the rim of the plastic). Build this little chain from the ESP32 to ground: - ESP32 pin marked **D26** -> one end of the **220 ohm resistor** - Other end of the resistor -> **long leg** of the green LED - **Short leg** of the LED -> blue rail (ground) *Why this matters:* an LED is greedy. If you plug it straight into a pin, it tries to grab as much electricity as it can and burns itself out in a flash (sometimes with a tiny pop). The 220 ohm resistor is like a narrow doorway - it only lets a safe amount of electricity through, so the LED glows happily forever. You can put the resistor either side of the LED and it works the same, but putting it on the pin side first is a tidy habit.
**Step 6 - Plug in the USB cable and check.** Plug the micro-USB cable from the laptop into the small port on the ESP32. A little red power light on the ESP32 should glow. If the green LED also lights up the moment you tap the breadboard, congratulations - the shake sensor is working before you have even uploaded the code! If nothing lights up, unplug the USB and check: - Long red rail and long blue rail are not mixed up. - The ESP32 is sitting flat across the middle gap. - The LED's long leg is on the resistor side, not on the ground side.
**Tune-up tip.** Once the code is running, give the breadboard a gentle bump. The display should roll digits and then settle on a number from 1 to 6. If a tiny bump always triggers it, turn the blue screw on the SW-420 a quarter turn one way. If you have to whack the table to trigger it, turn the screw the other way. Tiny adjustments only - the screw is sensitive. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open the IDE, go to **File -> Preferences**. Find the box labelled "Additional boards manager URLs" and paste in: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click OK. 2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. In the search box, type `esp32`. Find "esp32 by Espressif Systems" and click Install. It takes a few minutes - good time for a snack. 3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**. That tells the IDE which chip it's talking to. 4. Install the display library: **Tools -> Manage Libraries**. Search for `TM1637`. Install the one called **"TM1637" by Avishay Orpaz**. That's the library the code uses to talk to the 4-digit display. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop using a **micro-USB cable**. Make sure it's a real data cable, not a charge-only one - some cheap cables only have the power wires, and the laptop won't see the board at all. 2. Go to **Tools -> Port**. Pick the new port that just appeared (on Windows it'll be something like `COM4`, on a Mac it's `cu.usbserial-*` or `cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`, on Linux `ttyUSB0`). If nothing new shows up, you might need the **CP210x USB driver** from Silicon Labs - install it, unplug, plug back in. 3. There are no passwords or WiFi names to fill in for this sketch - it runs entirely offline. Just open the `.ino` file. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top left). The IDE will compile for a few seconds, then start flashing. If you see "Connecting......_____" stuck for more than 10 seconds, hold down the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until you see the dots turn into percentages, then let go. NodeMCU-32S boards usually don't need this trick, but it's good to know. 5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of the monitor window) to **115200**. The sketch itself doesn't print anything chatty, but the Serial Monitor is still useful for spotting error messages if the board resets unexpectedly. 6. **How to know it worked:** the 4-digit display lights up but stays blank. Now give the breadboard a gentle shake. The green LED should switch on, a number should flicker through the rightmost digit of the display for about two seconds, slow down, then land on a number between 1 and 6. The LED blinks three times to "announce" the roll and then goes dark. Your result stays on the display until your next shake. **Common gotchas:** - **"Connecting..." never finishes on upload.** Hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 while the IDE shows the connecting dots, then release it once the upload actually starts. This is the classic first-flash problem. - **No new port appears when you plug in the ESP32.** Almost always the USB cable (try another one - lots of cables are charge-only) or a missing **CP210x driver** on Windows. Install the driver from Silicon Labs and unplug/replug. - **It rolls non-stop, or every tiny bump triggers a roll.** The SW-420 has a tiny blue trimpot on the module - turn it gently with a small screwdriver. Clockwise makes it less sensitive, counter-clockwise makes it more sensitive. Aim for "a real shake fires it, but tapping the desk doesn't." ## Talking points - **Why the SW-420 is "noisy":** one shake makes the spring inside rattle on and off many times. The code handles this with a classic two-step debounce: read once, wait 50 ms for the bouncing to settle, read again. If both reads agree, it was a real shake. The exact same trick works for noisy push buttons. - **Why the dice slows down:** the animation array `delays[]` has shorter delays at the start and longer ones at the end. That alone makes it feel like a real tumbling die. No physics needed. - **Where the randomness comes from:** `esp_random()` uses the ESP32's hardware random number generator. On an Arduino Uno you'd have to "seed" the random function with noise from a floating pin - on the ESP32 you get true hardware randomness for free. - **Why 3.3V is fine for all of this:** the TM1637 chip is happy from 3.3V to 5.5V, the SW-420 just needs enough voltage to drive a logic-level signal, and the LED is comfortable too. Worth knowing: at 3.3V drive with a 220 ohm resistor and a typical green LED (forward voltage ~2V), the LED current is about (3.3 - 2) / 220 = 6 mA, which is visible but not super bright. If you want the announce-blink to really pop, swap to a 150 ohm resistor - that pushes the current up to ~9 mA, still well under the LED's limit. ## Things to change once it works - Twist the sensitivity trimpot on the SW-420 so it triggers from a firm shake but ignores you bumping the table. - Show the previous roll in the leftmost digits and the new roll on the right - the display has 4 digits, you're only using 1. - Add a second LED that lights up only when you roll a 6 (a "critical hit" indicator). - Replace the dice with a 2d6 simulator (two dice at once, one per pair of digits) for board games. - Add a piezo buzzer that beeps faster and faster as the roll slows down. ## Why this is interesting You're replacing a physical object (a die) with code, but the *feel* of using it is what makes it work - the spin-down animation tricks your brain into accepting it as a real roll. That's the core lesson of human-computer interaction in one tiny project: the math is trivial (`random() % 6 + 1`), but the perceived experience is everything. It also introduces a sensor that isn't a button or a knob. Once you've used the SW-420, you understand the general pattern for "event-driven" sensors: read, debounce, then act.

projects.name: Motion-Triggered Jump Scare Box
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop into the NodeMCU V3. The NodeMCU plugs into the I/O Expansion Shield - the shield exposes every NodeMCU pin as a 3-wire (signal + 5V + GND) header, so the PIR and servo plug straight in. A 470 uF capacitor across the servo's 5V/GND s
projects.description:
**What it is**: Set the little cardboard box on a shelf and walk away. When someone wanders past, the lid flips open and a paper spider pops out at them. **Why it's fun**: Hide it outside your sister's bedroom door and wait for the scream. The box sits perfectly still until the exact second someone walks by - it feels less like electronics and more like the box is alive. ## Parts list - 1x NodeMCU V3 (ESP8266) on the I/O Expansion Shield - the brain. Reads the PIR, blinks the LED, twitches the servo. - 1x HC-SR501 PIR Motion Sensor - the "eye". Detects warm bodies moving past. - 1x SG90 Servo (9g micro) - the muscle. Tape it under the lid; horn flips the lid open. - 1x 5mm Red LED - "armed" indicator so you know the trap is live. - 1x 220R resistor - current-limiter for the LED so it does not burn out. - 1x 470 uF electrolytic capacitor - soaks up the servo's start-up current spike so the NodeMCU V3 does not brown out and reset when the lid snaps. Long leg (+) to the 5V rail, short leg (-) to GND. Polarity matters - backwards can pop the cap. - 1x Breadboard - holds the LED, resistor, capacitor, and power rails. - Jumper wires (F-M for the PIR/servo headers, M-M for breadboard hops). - USB cable from laptop to power the NodeMCU V3. - (Not in the inventory) a small cardboard box and a paper spider on a spring or rubber band. ## One-time software setup Before this sketch will compile, install the **NodeMCU V3Servo** library: 1. Arduino IDE -> Tools -> Manage Libraries... 2. Search for `NodeMCU V3Servo` (by Kevin Harrington / John K. Bennett). 3. Click Install. Done - this is a one-time step. If you skip this you will get `NodeMCU V3Servo.h: No such file or directory` when you try to upload. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you'll see on the NodeMCU V3 board:** - **VIN** (or **VV**, depending on the variant) = "voltage in". When the USB cable is plugged in, this pin gives you back the **5V from the USB**. We use it to power the PIR sensor and the servo (both want 5V). - **GND** = "ground", the 0V side of the circuit. Every part needs a GND wire so electricity has a path back to the battery / USB. - **D5, D2, D7** = pin labels printed on the board's plastic. The NodeMCU turns these on and off to talk to the LED, the servo, and the PIR. (The board labels are **D**-numbers; the underlying chip numbers are GPIO 14, GPIO 4, and D5 - the IDE handles that translation for you.)
**Step 0 - put the NodeMCU on the I/O Expansion Shield.** The shield is the green board with **three rows of pin headers** on each side. Plug the NodeMCU into the middle of it so each NodeMCU pin sits on top of the shield's matching label. The three rows of holes do this, for every labeled pin: - **Outer row** = the **signal** (the D-label) - **Middle row** = **+5V** (handy for that pin) - **Inner row** = **GND** (handy for that pin) So when a sensor module has a 3-wire cable (signal / 5V / GND), you can plug all three pins straight into one column on the shield - no separate jumper wires to the rails.
**Step 1 - the PIR (motion sensor).** The HC-SR501 has 3 pins on the back labelled **VCC**, **OUT**, **GND**. ("VCC" is just another word for "5V in".) Plug a 3-wire female-to-female cable into the PIR, then plug the other end into the **D5 column** of the I/O shield, matching: - PIR **VCC** -> shield **middle row** of the D5 column (+5V) - PIR **GND** -> shield **inner row** of the D5 column (GND) - PIR **OUT** -> shield **outer row** of the D5 column (signal) When the PIR sees movement, the OUT wire jumps from 0V to 3.3V. The NodeMCU reads that on D5 as "MOTION!".
**Step 2 - the servo (the lid flipper).** The SG90 already has a 3-wire cable on it. The wires are: - **Red wire** -> shield middle row of the **D2 column** (+5V) - **Brown wire** -> shield inner row of the **D2 column** (GND) - **Orange wire** (the signal) -> shield outer row of the **D2 column** (signal) The whole servo cable goes into one column. That's it.
**Step 3 - the 470 uF capacitor. DO NOT SKIP THIS.** The capacitor is a small black cylinder with two legs - one **long leg (+)** and one **short leg (-)**. There's also a white stripe down the side near the short leg. We need it bridging 5V and GND, **right next to where the servo is plugged in**. The neatest place is on the breadboard: 1. Run a jumper from the shield's D2 **middle row** (+5V) to one row on the breadboard. 2. Run another jumper from the shield's D2 **inner row** (GND) to a second row on the breadboard. 3. Plug the **long leg** of the cap into the +5V row, the **short leg** into the GND row. **Why this matters:** when the servo yanks the lid open, it gulps a big slug of power for a split second. Without the capacitor, that gulp drops the voltage just long enough to crash the NodeMCU - the lid snaps once, the NodeMCU reboots, the sketch starts over, and you can't figure out why it broke. The capacitor stores up a little reserve power so the NodeMCU doesn't notice the gulp. Tiny part, huge job.
**Step 4 - the "armed" LED.** The LED has a **long leg (+)** and a **short leg (-)**. We need it on the breadboard. - **Long leg** -> one end of the 220 ohm resistor (gold-brown banded "fence post" of a part) - Other end of the resistor -> a jumper that runs to the shield's **D7 outer row** (signal) - **Short leg** -> a jumper that runs to the shield's **D7 inner row** (GND), or any GND hole on the shield The resistor stops the LED from burning out. If you plug the LED in backwards by mistake, it just won't light - no damage. Pull it out, flip it, plug it back in.
**Step 5 - tune the PIR.** Look at the back of the HC-SR501. There are two small orange screws and a tiny yellow jumper. - **Left orange screw (Sensitivity)**: start with it roughly in the middle. Clockwise = sees farther, counter-clockwise = sees closer. - **Right orange screw (Time delay)**: turn it all the way counter-clockwise. That sets the shortest hold (about 3 seconds). - **Yellow jumper**: there are two pins it could sit on, marked **L** and **H**. Move it onto the **L** pair. - **L** = "fire once, then go quiet for a moment". This is what we want for a jump scare - one motion, one snap. - **H** = "stay on as long as you keep seeing motion". Useful for a porch light, but wrong here - it would keep re-firing while a kid is still in the room. **Warm-up note.** The PIR needs 30 to 60 seconds to settle after power-up. During that time it sometimes thinks it sees motion when nothing's there, so the sketch deliberately ignores motion for the first minute. While it's warming up, the LED blinks fast to tell you "not ready yet". When the LED goes solid, the box is armed. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any NodeMCU V3):** 1. File -> Preferences. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-NodeMCU V3/gh-pages/package_NodeMCU V3_index.json` then click OK. 2. Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager. Search for `NodeMCU V3` and install **"NodeMCU V3 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download - wait for "INSTALLED" to appear next to the version. 3. Tools -> Board -> NodeMCU V3 -> **"NodeMCU V3 Dev Module"** (the NodeMCU-32S uses this board profile). 4. Install the servo library: Tools -> Manage Libraries... Search for `NodeMCU V3Servo` (by Kevin Harrington / John K. Bennett) and click Install. Without this, the sketch will not compile - you will see `NodeMCU V3Servo.h: No such file or directory`. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the NodeMCU V3 into your laptop with a **USB cable that has data lines** (the thin charge-only cables that come with some phone chargers will not work). The little red power LED on the NodeMCU V3 should come on. 2. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that appeared when you plugged in (`COM5` on Windows, `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` on a Mac, `/dev/ttyUSB0` on Linux). Not sure which one? Unplug the board, look at the menu, plug it back in - the new one is yours. 3. This sketch has no WiFi passwords or placeholders to fill in. Pin numbers and timings at the top of the file already match the wiring above - leave them alone for the first run. 4. Click the **Upload** button (right-arrow icon, top-left of the IDE). The bottom of the screen says "Compiling sketch..." for a while, then "Connecting..." with a row of dots. If the dots keep going and it says "Failed to connect", hold down the small **BOOT** button on the NodeMCU V3 while it connects, and let go once you see "Writing..." start. 5. When the IDE says "Hard resetting via RTS pin..." the flash is done. Open Tools -> Serial Monitor. In the dropdown at the top-right of the monitor, set the baud rate to **115200** (matches `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code - anything else gives garbled junk like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`). 6. What you should see: - `Jump Scare Box booting...` - `Warming up PIR (60s)...` and the red LED starts blinking fast. - About a minute later: `PIR ready. ARMED.` and the LED goes solid on. - Wave your hand in front of the white PIR dome. The monitor prints `MOTION! Flipping lid.` and the servo snaps to 120 degrees, holds 2 seconds, then eases back to 0. If all that happens, the trap is live. Tape the servo horn to the inside of the box lid and go scare somebody. **Common gotchas:** - **No COM port shows up.** Almost always a charge-only USB cable. Try a different cable - one you know syncs your phone with a computer. - **"Failed to connect" during upload.** Hold the **BOOT** button on the NodeMCU V3 while the IDE shows the "Connecting......" dots, release once "Writing..." starts. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need this every time, some only on the first flash. - **NodeMCU V3 reboots every time the lid snaps open** (Serial Monitor restarts with `Jump Scare Box booting...` on every motion event). The 470 uF capacitor is missing, in the wrong row, or in **backwards**. Long leg (+) into the 5V rail, short leg (-) into the GND rail, right next to where the servo's red and brown wires plug in. Backwards electrolytics can bulge or pop, so double-check before powering up again. - **LED never lights, even during warm-up.** It is in backwards. No damage - just pull it out, flip it 180 degrees, and put it back. Long leg through the 220R resistor toward D7, short leg to GND. ## A note on USB power The NodeMCU V3's `VIN` pin is *not* a clean 5V. After the USB connector and the board's protection diode, you typically see 4.5-4.7 V under load. That is fine for an LED and a PIR, and the SG90 will move on it, but the servo will be a little weaker than its datasheet rating and the PIR can occasionally false-trigger on the supply dip. If the lid feels gutless or the box keeps firing on its own, the upgrade is a separate 5V phone-charger-style supply feeding the servo (with its GND tied to the NodeMCU V3's GND). For learning on the desk, USB-from-laptop plus the 470 uF cap is fine. ## Talking points - A PIR (Passive InfraRed) sensor does not emit anything. It just watches for *changes* in infrared (heat) hitting its dome. If a warm body crosses one zone but not the next, the chip flags motion. - A hobby servo does not turn freely - it goes to a specific *angle* between 0 and 180 degrees and holds it. So "open the lid" is "go to 120 degrees" and "reset" is "go back to 0 degrees". - Servos draw a big current spike when they first start moving (the SG90 can briefly pull 600-700 mA, several times its idle draw). Without help, that spike pulls the 5V rail down, the NodeMCU V3 sees a brown-out, and resets. The 470 uF capacitor is a tiny local "battery" right next to the servo: it dumps stored charge to cover the spike, then refills from USB. - The NodeMCU V3 has lots of GPIOs but they are not all equivalent. Some are **strapping pins** (0, 2, 4, 5, 12, 15) that the chip reads at boot to decide how to start - and a few of them also pulse PWM-like signals during boot. **GPIO 14** is one of those boot-noisy pins, which is why we put the servo on **D2** instead. D2, 26, 32 and 33 are quiet at boot and a good default choice for actuators. D5 (PIR input) and D7 (LED) are also safely behaved. ## Things to change once it works - Add a small piezo buzzer on another GPIO and play a scream when the lid pops. - Build a paper spider on a thin spring so the lid-flip also launches it upward instead of just opening the lid. - Lengthen the cool-down in code so the box only fires once every 30 seconds (no double-spooking). - Move from USB-from-laptop power to a proper 5V supply (phone charger + USB cable, or a barrel-jack 5V brick into VIN) so the servo gets its full punch. - Once the Orange Pi is up, send an MQTT message every time the box fires so you get a phone notification "the trap got someone". ## Why this is interesting This is the simplest possible "sensor sees something -> something physical happens" loop, which is the core idea of every home-automation project. There is no WiFi yet, no app, no cloud. Just: read a digital pin, decide, move a motor. Once this works, every future project is a variation: swap the PIR for a door sensor, swap the servo for a relay, swap the spider for a light switch.

projects.name: Hidden-Magnet Treasure Hunter
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (5V via the micro-USB port; ESP32 regulates down to 3.3V on board)
projects.description:
**What it is**: Hide a magnet anywhere - under a couch cushion, inside a book, behind a wall. Wave the sensor near it and a red LED lights up while a little screen counts higher and higher the closer you get. **Why it's fun**: It is a real treasure detector that sees through stuff your eyes cannot. Make your dad hide the magnet, time how fast you find it, then swap and try to stump him. ## Parts list From the kit: - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - reads the Hall sensor, blinks the LED, drives the display) - 1x KY-024 Linear Magnetic Hall Sensor (4-pin: A0 analog out, D0 digital out, +, -). This is the *linear* Hall sensor - its analog output voltage swings up or down depending on the magnet's pole and how close it is. We only use the A0 (analog) pin. - 1x 4-digit 7-segment Display Module (TM1637-based, 4 pins: VCC, GND, DIO, CLK) - 1x LED 5mm Red (any colour works, red is most visible against couch cushions) - 1x Resistor 220R 1/8W 1% (the LED's bodyguard - keeps it from burning out) - 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) - 1x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc bundle (for breadboard-to-breadboard hops) - 1x Jumper Wire F-M, 20pc bundle (for ESP32 header pin to breadboard, and to the KY-024 / TM1637 modules) You supply: - 1x small neodymium magnet - the "treasure". A fridge magnet works in a pinch; a small neodymium is much more dramatic. - 1x USB cable (laptop to ESP32 NodeMCU-32S, micro-USB). ## Libraries to install Open Arduino IDE > Tools > Manage Libraries... and install: - **TM1637Display** by Avishay Orpaz - drives the 4-digit display. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the 3.3V power output pin (we use this as our "power" wire). - **GND** - the 0V side, ground. Every part needs a wire back here. - **D2, D21, D22, D34** - the pins we plug into. On this board the "D" number matches the GPIO number in the code. - **D34** - this one is special: it can only listen, not talk. Perfect for reading a sensor. - **EN** - the reset button on the board. Press it to restart the program. - **micro-USB** - the port at the end where the USB cable plugs in to power and program the board.
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard power strips.** The long red and blue strips down the side of the breadboard are where we share power and ground. We will call the red strip "+5V" (even though we are feeding it 3.3V from the ESP32 - the name on the strip is just a label) and the blue strip "GND". - Using a male-to-male jumper wire, connect the ESP32 pin marked **3V3** to the red strip. - Using another male-to-male wire, connect the ESP32 pin marked **GND** to the blue strip. This way any part can grab power and ground from the nearest red or blue hole instead of running long wires back to the ESP32 every time.
**Step 2 - Plug in the KY-024 magnet sensor.** The KY-024 has four little pins underneath: A0, G, +, and D0. Push the little board into the breadboard so the pins sit in row 3, 5, 7, and 9 on side A. Then: - KY-024 **A0** (in hole A3) goes to the ESP32 pin marked **D34**. Use a male-to-male wire from hole B3 over to D34. - KY-024 **G** (in hole A5) goes to the blue strip (GND). Use a wire from hole B5 to the blue strip. - KY-024 **+** (in hole A7) goes to the red strip (our 3.3V power). Use a wire from hole B7 to the red strip. - We do not use the **D0** pin at all - leave it empty. **Why this matters:** A0 is the "analog" pin - it sends out a smoothly changing voltage that gets bigger or smaller as a magnet gets closer. D34 on the ESP32 is built to read those smooth changes (it is an "input-only" pin, meaning it can only listen). The D0 pin only flips on or off like a light switch, which is not what we want for a treasure hunter that gets warmer and warmer as you get closer.
**Step 3 - Wire up the red "getting warmer" LED.** Look at your red LED. One leg is longer than the other - that is the **long leg**. The shorter one is the **short leg**. - Push the 220 ohm resistor across the gap between hole E15 and hole E18. - Push the LED's **long leg** into hole F18 and the **short leg** into hole F19. - Run a male-to-male wire from hole A15 to the ESP32 pin marked **D2**. - Run a male-to-male wire from hole J19 to the blue strip (GND). **Why this matters:** The resistor is the LED's seatbelt. If you wire an LED straight to a pin, too much electricity rushes through it and pop - the LED burns out in a second. The 220 ohm resistor slows the flow down to a safe trickle so the LED can shine for years. Always put a resistor in line with an LED. There is also a fun bonus: pin D2 on the ESP32 is also connected to the little blue LED already on the board. So when your red treasure-hunter LED blinks, the blue one on the board blinks at the same time, for free. **A note about pin D2:** D2 is a "strapping pin" - the ESP32 peeks at it the moment it powers on to decide how to start up. The pin needs to be low (off) at that exact moment. The code is written carefully to set the pin to LOW *before* telling it to be an output. Do not change the order of those two lines in `setup()` or your ESP32 might refuse to boot.
**Step 4 - Plug in the 4-digit number display.** This is the little red 7-segment display that will count up as you get closer to the magnet. It has four pins: CLK, DIO, VCC, GND. Push it into the breadboard so its pins sit in holes A24, A26, A28, and A30. - Display **CLK** (in hole A24) goes to the ESP32 pin marked **D22**. Wire from hole B24 to D22. - Display **DIO** (in hole A26) goes to the ESP32 pin marked **D21**. Wire from hole B26 to D21. - Display **VCC** - which is just the power input pin - (in hole A28) goes to the red strip. Wire from hole B28 to the red strip. - Display **GND** (in hole A30) goes to the blue strip. Wire from hole B30 to the blue strip. **Why this matters:** This kind of display only needs two signal wires (CLK and DIO) instead of one wire per segment. CLK is a tick-tock pin that keeps time, and DIO is the pin that sends the actual numbers. The ESP32 wiggles them really fast to draw whatever number we want.
**Step 5 - Power up and warm up.** Plug the USB cable from your laptop into the micro-USB port on the ESP32. The board should light up. Now do not move anything for about 2 seconds - the program needs to take a "resting" reading of the magnet sensor when no magnets are nearby. This baseline is what it compares against later. After the warmup, slowly bring a magnet close to the flat side of the KY-024. The number on the display should climb higher and higher, and the red LED should blink faster. Pull the magnet away and the number falls back to zero. **A tip on magnets:** The KY-024 reacts to both poles of a magnet, but in opposite directions. The code is clever - it measures how far the reading moves away from the resting value in either direction, so either side of the magnet works. If a magnet seems to do nothing, try flipping it over and trying the other face.
## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open File -> Preferences. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Open Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager. Search for "esp32" and install **esp32 by Espressif Systems** (it is a big download, give it a few minutes). 3. Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> **NodeMCU-32S**. 4. Tools -> Manage Libraries. Search for **TM1637Display** and install the one by **Avishay Orpaz**. This is the library that talks to the 4-digit number screen. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with the **micro-USB** cable. A light on the board should glow. 2. Tools -> Port. Pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged in (on Windows it looks like `COM5`, on a Mac like `/dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX`). If nothing new appeared, try a different USB cable - some cables are "charge only" and have no data wires inside. 3. There are no passwords or placeholders to fill in for this sketch. (If the magnet is super strong or super weak, you can tweak `STRENGTH_AT_MAX` near the top - bigger number = magnet has to be closer to peg the meter.) 4. Click the **Upload** button (the round arrow icon, top-left). It will say "Compiling..." then "Connecting...". If it gets stuck on "Connecting......_____" dots, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. You usually only need that trick once. 5. When it says "Done uploading", open Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor, set the baud rate to **115200** (it must match the number in `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code, or you will get gibberish). 6. You should see `Hidden-Magnet Treasure Hunter starting up.` and then a baseline number being printed. Keep the sensor away from anything magnetic for the first second while it calibrates. Now wave your magnet near the little chip on the KY-024 board - the red LED should start blinking, faster and faster as you get closer, and the 4-digit screen should count up. **It works!** **Common gotchas:** - **"Connecting......_____" upload failure.** Hold the BOOT button on the ESP32 until "Writing..." appears, then release. Some boards need this every upload, most only the first time. - **Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`.** The baud rate dropdown in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor is not set to 115200. Change it and the text will appear properly. - **LED never lights up, even with the magnet touching the sensor.** Either the red LED is in backwards (swap the two legs - the longer leg is the one that goes through the 220R resistor to GPIO 2), or you forgot to install the TM1637Display library and the sketch is still sitting on the "Compiling..." step with red errors at the bottom. ## Talking points - Magnetic fields are invisible but the LED makes them visible - that's the whole magic moment. - The sensor uses the "Hall effect": moving electrons in the sensor get pushed sideways by a magnetic field, which produces a tiny voltage. The ESP32 reads that voltage as a number from 0 to 4095. - One pole of the magnet pushes the voltage up, the other pole pushes it down. Flipping the magnet over flips the direction. That's why we measure distance from baseline rather than just "high" or "low". - The 4-digit display shows the raw "strength" number so you can watch it climb as you get closer. Great for the kid - it's a literal number going up. ## Things to change once it works - Add a buzzer alongside the LED for a metal-detector beep. - The sketch already auto-calibrates the baseline on startup - try holding the magnet *near* the sensor at power-on and see how that messes things up. Good lesson in why calibration matters. - Make it wireless: post each "find" to MQTT once the Orange Pi hub is alive. - Swap the single LED for a strip and light up more LEDs the closer you get (Cylon eyes). ## Why this is interesting It's a sensor that detects something humans literally cannot perceive. Andy's son can hide the magnet under a book, in a cushion, behind a wall, and the ESP32 will still find it. That moment of "wait, it can see through stuff?" is the hook. It also teaches the analog-to-digital pipeline (real world -> voltage -> number -> behaviour) which is the foundation of basically every interesting sensor project that comes later.

projects.name: Plant SOS
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from laptop to the XIAO ESP32-C3 (5V); the XIAO's onboard regulator powers the OLED from its 3.3V rail, and the soil sensor's VCC is gated by a GPIO (D2) so it only sees 3.3V during the ~10 ms read window.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Stick the two metal prongs into your plant's dirt. A tiny screen shows a happy face when the soil is wet, a sleepy face when it's getting dry, and a crying face when the plant is thirsty - and a red LED blinks at you until you water it. **Why it's fun**: Your plant basically gets a face and tells you how it feels. Spit on the prongs, dunk them in a glass of water, hold them in the air - the little face changes right in front of you like the plant is reacting to what you do. ## Parts list - 1x Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 (the brain - reads the sensor, drives the OLED and LED) - 1x Soil Moisture Sensor (the two-prong probe + small comparator board; we only use the analog "AO" pin) - 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) (the little blue/white screen; talks over 2 wires) - 1x LED 5mm Red (the "thirsty" warning blinker) - the legs plug directly into the breadboard, no jumper needed - 1x Resistor 220R (current limit for the red LED - never wire an LED straight to a GPIO) - leads plug directly into the breadboard, no jumper needed - 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (no soldering - everything plugs in) - Jumper wires M-M (for the OLED and sensor connections - not for the LED itself) ## Wiring notes This is the **Plant SOS**. The XIAO ESP32-C3 is the tiny brain that checks how thirsty your plant is, flashes a red LED when it needs water, and shows the moisture level on a little screen. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the XIAO ESP32-C3 board:** - **3V3** - the pin that gives out 3.3V of power input. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs one wire going here. - **D0 to D10** - the pins you can plug things into. The board says "D0", "D1", etc., but inside the chip they have different numbers (GPIO numbers). We will use the "D" labels because that is what is printed on your board. - **USB-C** - the little port where the cable from your laptop plugs in. The cable gives the board power AND lets you upload code.
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard.** A breadboard has two long strips down the side - the red strip is the "+" power line, and the blue strip is the "-" ground line. Think of them like little extension cords. Anything you plug into the red strip gets power; anything in the blue strip is connected to ground. Push the XIAO ESP32-C3 into the breadboard so it straddles the center gap, near the top. Don't plug in the USB cable yet - we want all the wires connected first.
**Step 2 - Wire up the power strips.** Use two short jumper wires to feed power from the XIAO to the strips: - XIAO **3V3** pin -> the red (+) strip on the breadboard - XIAO **GND** pin -> the blue (-) strip on the breadboard Now every part that needs 3.3V power can grab it from the red strip, and every part that needs ground can grab it from the blue strip. Easy.
**Step 3 - Wire up the OLED screen.** This little screen talks to the XIAO using only 2 data wires (plus power and ground). That style of talking is called I2C. Push the screen into the breadboard with its 4 pins in a row, then connect: - OLED **VCC** (power input) -> red (+) strip - OLED **GND** -> blue (-) strip - OLED **SDA** -> the pin marked **D4** on the XIAO (GPIO 6 - this is the default SDA pin) - OLED **SCL** -> the pin marked **D5** on the XIAO (GPIO 7 - this is the default SCL pin) **Why this matters:** Most of these little screens answer to a "name" called **0x3C**, but some answer to **0x3D** instead. The code tries the first name, and if nobody answers, it tries the second name - so you don't have to figure it out by hand.
**Step 4 - Wire up the soil moisture sensor.** This sensor has two metal prongs you poke into the plant's soil. The wetter the dirt, the easier electricity flows between the prongs, and the sensor turns that into a voltage we can read. The sensor has 4 pins. Plug it into the breadboard and connect: - Sensor **VCC** (power input) -> the pin marked **D2** on the XIAO (GPIO 4) - **not** the red strip! - Sensor **GND** -> blue (-) strip - Sensor **AO** (the analog output) -> the pin marked **D0** on the XIAO (GPIO 2) - Sensor **DO** (the digital output) -> leave this one empty, we don't need it **Why this matters:** Did you notice the sensor's power doesn't go to the red strip like everything else? Here is the trick: if you leave the sensor powered ALL the time, the wet soil eats the metal prongs (it's called corrosion) and they go rusty in a few weeks. So we let the XIAO turn the power on for a tiny moment (about 10 milliseconds, which is way faster than you can blink), take the reading, then switch the power off again. That makes the sensor last way longer. One thing to check: most of these sensor boards are happy with 3.3V coming out of D2. If yours has writing on it that says "5V only", let your parent help - it needs a different setup.
**Step 5 - Wire up the warning LED.**
The red LED is the "SOS" light - it flashes when your plant is thirsty. LEDs only work in one direction, so look carefully: the **long leg** is the + side, the **short leg** is the - side. Plug the resistor and LED straight into the breadboard (no jumper wires needed for these little parts): - The pin marked **D1** on the XIAO (GPIO 3) -> one leg of the 220 ohm resistor - Other leg of the 220 ohm resistor -> **long leg** of the red LED - **Short leg** of the red LED -> blue (-) strip **Why this matters:** The little resistor in front of the LED is super important - it's like a speed bump for electricity. Without it, too much current would zoom through the LED and burn it out in a flash (sometimes a literal puff of smoke!). The resistor keeps the LED at a safe brightness so it lights up nicely for years. When the code turns the **D1** pin on, electricity flows through the resistor, through the LED (long leg to short leg), down to ground, and the LED lights up.
**Step 6 - Last check before powering up.** Go down this list before you plug in the USB-C cable: - Red strip has only 3V3 wired to it (not 5V). - Blue strip is wired to GND. - The LED's **short leg** is on the ground side. - There is exactly **one** resistor between the XIAO's D1 pin and the LED. - The soil sensor's power wire goes to **D2**, not to the red strip. - Nothing metal is touching anything else metal (no loose wires bridging the strips). If everything looks good, plug the USB-C cable from your laptop into the XIAO. The board should light up its little power LED. If it doesn't, unplug right away and check the wiring with your parent - a wrong connection can make the board very hot.
## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click **OK**. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type **esp32**, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download - grab a snack. 3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"XIAO_ESP32C3"** from the list. 4. Install the two screen libraries. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and: - Search **Adafruit GFX** and install **"Adafruit GFX Library"** by Adafruit. - Search **Adafruit SSD1306** and install **"Adafruit SSD1306"** by Adafruit. If it asks to install dependencies (like Adafruit BusIO), click **Install All**. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the XIAO into your laptop with a **USB-C cable**. The tiny orange LED on the XIAO should light up. (If nothing lights up, try a different cable - lots of cheap USB-C cables are charge-only with no data wires.) 2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that just appeared. On Windows it is **COM3**/**COM4**/**COM5**; on a Mac it is **/dev/cu.usbmodem...**; on Linux it is **/dev/ttyACM0**. Unplug-and-replug to see which port disappears and comes back - that one is yours. 3. There are no WiFi passwords or secrets to fill in for this sketch - nothing to edit. (You can tune `WET_BELOW` and `DRY_ABOVE` near the top later, but leave them alone for the first run.) 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-pointing arrow). The status bar shows **"Compiling..."** for 30-60 seconds, then **"Uploading..."**. If it hangs at "Connecting..." for more than 10 seconds, **press and hold the small B (BOOT) button on the XIAO, tap the R (RESET) button next to it, then let go of B**. That forces flashing mode. After the first successful upload you almost never need this trick again. 5. When you see **"Done uploading"**, open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. Set the baud rate dropdown on the right to **115200** (must match the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch or you get gibberish). 6. **What should happen:** The OLED lights up with a face within a second or two. The Serial Monitor prints `OLED found at 0x3C` (or `0x3D`) and then a moisture number every second, like `soil raw: 3100`. Now the fun part - pinch the prongs with wet fingers or dunk them in a glass of water: the number changes a lot, and the face changes from crying to sleepy to happy. Hold the prongs in the air and the red LED starts blinking once per second to say "I'm thirsty!" **Common gotchas:** - **Stuck on "Connecting..." during upload.** Do the **BOOT + RESET** dance from step 4: hold **B**, tap **R**, release **B**, then click Upload again. - **Serial Monitor shows gibberish.** Baud rate dropdown is wrong - set it to **115200**. - **OLED stays completely black but Serial Monitor prints sensor numbers.** Either SDA and SCL are swapped (SDA goes to **D4**, SCL goes to **D5**), or the sketch says "OLED not found" - meaning the screen isn't being detected at 0x3C or 0x3D. Re-check the VCC and GND wires to the screen. - **Face never changes - always the same expression.** Your sensor's polarity is reversed. Watch `soil raw:` in Serial: dunk the prongs in water, then hold them in air. If **air gives a smaller number than water**, change `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW = true;` to `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW = false;` near the top and upload again. ## Talking points - Soil sensors work by measuring how easily electricity flows between the two prongs. Wet soil conducts; dry soil resists. The little board on the sensor converts that into a voltage on the AO pin. On the most common (LM393) boards a wet probe gives a **low** number and a dry probe gives a **high** number, but a few clones (and most capacitive replacements) flip that. The code has a `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW` flag at the top - watch the Serial Monitor while you dunk the probe in water vs. hold it in air, and flip the flag if the relationship is reversed. The thresholds below it stay readable either way. - The ESP32-C3 ADC turns that voltage into a number between **0 and 4095** (12 bits). We map "raw number" -> "happiness" with two thresholds. - I2C is wonderful: SDA + SCL + power, and you can chain more sensors on the same two wires later (each with a unique address). Each device has its own address - that's why we needed to find the OLED at 0x3C or 0x3D. - The face is drawn with three primitives: two filled circles for eyes, and either the bottom half of a circle (smile), a straight line (sleepy), or the top half of a circle plus two tear drops (crying). The "half a circle" trick uses `drawCircleHelper`, which is Adafruit_GFX's quadrant-selectable arc - cheaper than drawing a full circle and clipping. - The LED only blinks when truly thirsty. A solid LED would be annoying; blinking screams "do something" without being constant. ## Things to change once it works - **Calibrate the thresholds.** The defaults in the sketch are a starting guess. Hold the probe in air -> note the number printed to Serial; that's your "very dry". Stick it in a glass of water -> note that number; that's "very wet". Pick thresholds about a third and two-thirds of the way between. (And confirm which end is which - that's what `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW` is for.) - Plant the probe to the depth shown on the prongs (about 4 cm). Deeper isn't better - the metal contacts must stay above the water line of the pot's drainage saucer. - Swap to a **capacitive** soil sensor when the resistive prongs corrode (gated power buys you weeks-to-months instead of weeks, but capacitive probes don't corrode at all). Same wiring, just better hardware - and remember to recheck `SENSOR_WET_IS_LOW`, capacitive boards often invert. - Add a buzzer on another GPIO for an audible "feed me" chirp once a day instead of just the LED. - Have the XIAO publish moisture to MQTT once the Orange Pi is online, so the plant's mood appears on a phone dashboard. - Add a small smoothing average (e.g. 10 readings) so a single noisy sample doesn't flip the face. ## Why this is interesting It turns an invisible thing (soil moisture) into something a 10-year-old can read at a glance. There's a real, immediate consequence: water the plant and the face changes. It's also a clean introduction to the two most useful sensor categories - **analog** (a voltage you read with `analogRead`) and **I2C** (a digital bus you talk to with a library) - in the same small project, plus one quietly important trick (gating sensor power from a GPIO) that the same beginner can reuse on every battery-or-corrosion-sensitive sensor they meet next.

projects.name: Earthquake Cam
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 (5V in). The ESP32's VIN pin re-exposes that 5V to power the MAX7219 matrix; the ESP32's onboard 3V3 regulator powers the SW-420 sensor and drives the GPIO logic.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Thump the table next to it. A yellow lamp lights up while it counts your shakes, then a tiny 8x8 grid of red lights draws a bar graph showing how big your "earthquake" was, with a label that scrolls past like "TINY TREMOR" or "GODZILLA". **Why it's fun**: It is basically a Richter scale for whacking the desk. Take turns with your dad or your brother and see who can pound out the biggest quake without knocking the breadboard off the table. ## Parts list - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU (the brain) - 1x SW-420 vibration switch module (the "earthquake" sensor) - 1x 8x8 LED matrix with MAX7219 driver board (the display) - 1x yellow LED (the warning lamp that lights while a quake is being measured) - 1x 220 ohm resistor (current-limit for the yellow LED) - 1x breadboard, ~12 DuPont jumpers - 1x USB cable (laptop to ESP32; this is also where the 5V for the matrix comes from) ## Wiring notes This project is a tiny earthquake detector. When the board gets bumped or shaken, a yellow light blinks and the matrix of red dots draws a little wave. Cool, right? **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the pin that gives out 3.3 volts of power. Used to feed small parts like the shake sensor. - **VIN** - the pin that gives back the 5 volts that comes in from the USB cable. We use this to power the LED matrix. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part has to share a ground or nothing works. - **D5, D18, D23, D26, D27** - signal pins. The number on the silkscreen matches the GPIO number in the code. - **MOSI / SCK** - fancy names for D23 and D18 when they are used to send fast data to the LED matrix.
**This build needs TWO red power strips, not one.** Look at the long red strip running down the side of the breadboard - that is called a rail. We are going to use one red rail for 3.3V (for the shake sensor) and a separate red rail for 5V (for the LED matrix). The blue rail along the side is GND, and both red rails share that same blue GND rail. - ESP32 **3V3** pin to the first red rail. This is the 3.3V rail. - ESP32 **VIN** pin to the second red rail (near column 22 on the breadboard). This is the 5V rail. - ESP32 **GND** pin to the blue rail. **Why this matters:** The LED matrix really wants 5V to light up nicely, but the shake sensor and the ESP32 itself only deal in 3.3V signals. Keeping the two red rails separate makes sure the matrix does not try to suck so much power that it browns out the little 3.3V helper chip on the ESP32.
**Step 1 - Plug in the shake sensor.** The SW-420 is the part with a little spring inside that wiggles when you tap it. - Sensor **VCC** (power input) at hole B3, with a wire from A3 to the 3.3V red rail. - Sensor **GND** at hole B4, with a wire from A4 to the blue GND rail. - Sensor **DO** (the data wire that says "I felt a shake!") at hole B5. Run a jumper wire from the pin marked **D27** on the ESP32 to hole A5. Press the sensor firmly into the breadboard so it does not wiggle on its own jumper wires. If it wobbles, the wires themselves will shake and tell your ESP32 there is an earthquake when there really is not.
**Step 2 - Add the yellow warning light.**
The yellow LED blinks every time a shake is detected. LEDs have a long leg and a short leg, and they only work one way around. - Yellow LED long leg into hole B12. - Yellow LED short leg into hole B13. - 220 ohm resistor across holes E12 and E16. (It does not matter which way around the resistor goes.) - Jumper wire from the pin marked **D26** on the ESP32 to hole A16. - Jumper wire from hole A13 to the blue GND rail. **Why this matters:** The 220 ohm resistor is a current-limit resistor. Without it, the LED would gulp down way too much electricity in one go and burn out in a puff of smoke. The resistor is like a thin straw that slows the drink down so the LED only sips what it can handle.
**Step 3 - Wire up the 8x8 LED matrix.** This is the grid of 64 red dots that draws the wave shape. It has a little chip on the back called a MAX7219 that does all the hard work of lighting up the right dots. It has 5 pins on one edge. - Matrix **VCC** (power input) at hole B22, with a wire from A22 to the **5V** red rail (not the 3.3V one). - Matrix **GND** at hole B23, with a wire from A23 to the blue GND rail. - Matrix **DIN** (data in) at hole B24. Jumper wire from the pin marked **D23** on the ESP32 to hole A24. - Matrix **CS** (chip select) at hole B25. Jumper wire from the pin marked **D5** on the ESP32 to hole A25. - Matrix **CLK** (clock) at hole B26. Jumper wire from the pin marked **D18** on the ESP32 to hole A26. **Why this matters:** The matrix needs 5V to make its 64 dots bright. The three signal wires (DIN, CS, CLK) are how the ESP32 quickly whispers "light up dot 1, dot 2, dot 3..." to the MAX7219 chip. Even though those whispers are only 3.3V, the chip is happy to listen at that level.
**Step 4 - Plug in the USB cable.** Connect the USB cable from your laptop to the ESP32. That powers everything - the laptop pushes 5V into the ESP32 over USB, the VIN pin gives that 5V back out to the matrix, and the onboard 3.3V chip on the ESP32 powers the shake sensor.
**Step 5 - Tune the shake sensor.** Look closely at the SW-420 module. You will see a tiny blue box with a little screw on top - that is called a trim pot, and it sets how easily the sensor triggers. There is also a small red LED on the module that lights up when a shake is detected. - If the trigger LED is on all the time even when nothing is moving, the sensor is too sensitive. Turn the screw clockwise (a quarter turn at a time) until the LED only flashes when you actually tap the breadboard. - If it never seems to notice when you tap, turn the screw counter-clockwise a little to make it more sensitive. This is a tricky one - you might need to play with the screw for a couple of minutes to find the sweet spot. Once it is set, give the breadboard a gentle thump and watch the yellow LED blink and the dot matrix come to life. Earthquake detected! ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a chunky download, give it a couple of minutes. 3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> ESP32 Dev Module**. That is the right pick for the NodeMCU-32S. 4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries**, type `MD_MAX72XX` in the search box, and install **"MD_MAX72XX" by majicDesigns**. This is the library that talks to the 8x8 matrix; without it the sketch will not compile. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a USB cable. The NodeMCU-32S uses a **Micro-USB** cable (the small flat one, same shape as on older phones). Make sure it is a *data* cable, not a charge-only cable - if the laptop does not go "ding" when you plug it in, try a different cable. 2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged the board in (on Windows it looks like `COM5` or `COM7`, on Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*`). If nothing new shows up, unplug and re-plug the cable. 3. There are no WiFi passwords or secrets to fill in for this sketch - it runs fully offline, so you can skip straight to upload. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." for a bit, then "Connecting...". If you see a row of dots and dashes that never finishes (`....____....____`), hold the small **BOOT** button on the ESP32 down until you see "Writing at 0x..." start scrolling, then let go. Most NodeMCU-32S boards auto-reset and do not need this, but if yours is stubborn, the BOOT-button trick fixes it every time. 5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate dropdown in the bottom-right to **115200** (that is what `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch expects - any other number gives you garbled junk). 6. Tap the breadboard with your finger. The yellow LED should snap on, and the 8x8 matrix should start drawing a little bar graph. After 10 seconds the bar freezes for a beat, then a label like `MOUSE FART` or `BUMP` scrolls across the matrix and the yellow LED switches off. You should also see the pulse count print in the Serial Monitor each round. If you see all of that, it worked! **Common gotchas:** - **Display looks scrambled, mirrored, or upside-down.** Cheap 8x8 matrix modules come wired in four different layouts. Find the line `#define HARDWARE_TYPE MD_MAX72XX::FC16_HW` near the top of the sketch and try the other three values in the comment above it (`GENERIC_HW`, `PAROLA_HW`, `ICSTATION_HW`), re-uploading after each change, until the bar graph draws upright. - **Yellow LED never lights.** Long leg (anode) goes through the 220 ohm resistor to GPIO 26, short leg (cathode) goes to GND. If it is in backwards, no damage - just pull it out, flip it around, and push it back in. - **The matrix triggers a quake the instant power touches it, without you tapping anything.** The little blue trim-pot on the SW-420 module is too sensitive. Turn it clockwise a quarter-turn at a time until the on-board trigger LED only blinks when you actually tap the breadboard. - **Upload fails with "Failed to connect to ESP32: Timed out waiting for packet header".** Almost always the BOOT-button trick from step 4 - hold BOOT until "Writing at..." appears, then let go. ## Safety notes Nothing in this build runs above 5 V, so the mains-safety warnings that apply to the 2-channel relay project explicitly do NOT apply here. The only real hazards are: (a) backwards LED polarity will simply not light, no damage; (b) shorting 5V to GND on the breadboard will trip the laptop's USB port protection but not hurt the ESP32. Unplug USB before re-wiring anything. ## Talking points - The SW-420 isn't really a "sensor" in the analog sense - it's a tiny spring around a pin that briefly closes a circuit when shaken. So we don't measure shake *strength*, we count shake *pulses* per unit time. Lots of pulses in 10 seconds = bigger quake. - We use a hardware *interrupt* on the sensor pin. Interrupts let the chip drop whatever it's doing the instant a pulse arrives and bump a counter. That way we never miss a bump even while the matrix is busy drawing. The interrupt is armed only *after* the boot animation, so bumps during startup don't trick the board into thinking a quake started before you arrived. - The bar graph is drawn column by column. Eight columns, eight "Richter" levels. Each level also gets a label that scrolls across afterwards using a small built-in font. - 25 ms debounce: a single physical tap can ring the spring several times within a few milliseconds. We ignore extra pulses inside a 25 ms window so one tap counts as one bump. - We deliberately stick to the low-level `MD_MAX72XX` library and write the scrolling text by hand instead of mixing in the higher-level `MD_Parola`. Mixing the two on the same panel can cause one library's internal buffer to overwrite the other's drawing - confusing to debug as a beginner. ## Things to change once it works - If the matrix shows garbled, scrambled, mirrored or upside-down output, change `HARDWARE_TYPE` in the code. Try `GENERIC_HW`, then `PAROLA_HW`, then `ICSTATION_HW` until it looks right. This is the single biggest gotcha with cheap matrix modules. - Lower the SW-420 sensitivity pot (turn clockwise) to make it harder to trigger - then you have to really thump the table to reach "GODZILLA". - Add a second LED (red) for "BIG ONE" and above, so the warning lamp escalates. - Replace the verdict labels with funny ones aimed at Andy's son. - Once the Orange Pi is online, publish each quake's count + level to MQTT so the Pi can keep a high-score table. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project that *reacts* to the physical world instead of timing or button presses. It teaches three new ideas at once: reading a digital sensor through an interrupt, accumulating events over a time window, and driving a real graphical display (the 8x8 matrix) with a library. And the feedback loop is irresistible: you hit the table, the matrix lights up, you hit it harder, it scrolls "GODZILLA". Hard to put down.

projects.code:
<![CDATA[// Earthquake Cam
// ESP32 NodeMCU + SW-420 vibration switch + MAX7219 8x8 LED matrix + warning LED.
// On any shake, count the bumps over a 10-second window and show a Richter-style
// bar graph + a verdict label ("MOUSE FART" ... "GODZILLA").
//
// Library needed (install once in Arduino IDE Library Manager):
//   "MD_MAX72XX"  by majicDesigns
//
// Arduino IDE board:  ESP32 Arduino > ESP32 Dev Module
//
// POWER NOTE: the matrix VCC goes to the ESP32's 5V / VIN pin (USB-powered),
// NOT to 3V3. The MAX7219 datasheet wants 4.0 to 5.5 V. The ESP32 GPIO logic
// is 3.3 V but the MAX7219 reads anything above ~2 V as HIGH, so direct
// connections from GPIO to DIN/CS/CLK work fine.

#include <SPI.h>
#include <MD_MAX72xx.h>

// ---- Pin map (matches the wiring diagram) ----
const int PIN_SW420    = 27;   // SW-420 digital OUT
const int PIN_LED_WARN = 26;   // Yellow warning LED through 220R
const int PIN_MATRIX_CS = 5;   // MAX7219 CS / LOAD
// MOSI = GPIO 23, SCK = GPIO 18 (hardware SPI defaults on ESP32)

// ---- Matrix config ----
// If the display looks garbled, scrambled, mirrored, or upside-down,
// try the OTHER values below in order. This single line is the #1
// thing that varies between cheap 8x8 modules.
//   FC16_HW       <- most common on "FC-16" red modules (try first)
//   GENERIC_HW    <- many no-name eBay/Aliexpress modules
//   PAROLA_HW     <- original Parola-branded boards
//   ICSTATION_HW  <- IcStation-branded boards
#define HARDWARE_TYPE MD_MAX72XX::FC16_HW
#define MAX_DEVICES   1
MD_MAX72XX matrix = MD_MAX72XX(HARDWARE_TYPE, PIN_MATRIX_CS, MAX_DEVICES);

// ---- Event counting ----
const unsigned long WINDOW_MS   = 10000UL;   // 10 second measuring window
const unsigned long DEBOUNCE_MS = 25UL;      // ignore re-triggers inside this gap

volatile unsigned long lastPulseMs = 0;
volatile unsigned int  pulseCount  = 0;

void IRAM_ATTR onShake() {
  unsigned long now = millis();
  if (now - lastPulseMs >= DEBOUNCE_MS) {
    lastPulseMs = now;
    pulseCount++;
  }
}

// Map a count to a 1..8 "Richter" level for the bar graph.
int countToLevel(unsigned int count) {
  if (count <= 1)   return 1;
  if (count <= 3)   return 2;
  if (count <= 6)   return 3;
  if (count <= 10)  return 4;
  if (count <= 18)  return 5;
  if (count <= 30)  return 6;
  if (count <= 50)  return 7;
  return 8;
}

const char* levelToVerdict(int level) {
  switch (level) {
    case 1: return "MOUSE FART";
    case 2: return "TIPTOE";
    case 3: return "BUMP";
    case 4: return "STOMP";
    case 5: return "TRUCK";
    case 6: return "QUAKE";
    case 7: return "BIG ONE";
    default: return "GODZILLA";
  }
}

// ---- Tiny 5x7 font for the scrolling verdict (uppercase + space only). ----
// Each glyph is 5 columns wide; bit 0 = top row, bit 6 = bottom row.
struct Glyph { char c; uint8_t col[5]; };
const Glyph FONT[] = {
  {' ', {0x00,0x00,0x00,0x00,0x00}},
  {'A', {0x7E,0x11,0x11,0x11,0x7E}},
  {'B', {0x7F,0x49,0x49,0x49,0x36}},
  {'C', {0x3E,0x41,0x41,0x41,0x22}},
  {'D', {0x7F,0x41,0x41,0x22,0x1C}},
  {'E', {0x7F,0x49,0x49,0x49,0x41}},
  {'F', {0x7F,0x09,0x09,0x09,0x01}},
  {'G', {0x3E,0x41,0x49,0x49,0x7A}},
  {'H', {0x7F,0x08,0x08,0x08,0x7F}},
  {'I', {0x00,0x41,0x7F,0x41,0x00}},
  {'K', {0x7F,0x08,0x14,0x22,0x41}},
  {'L', {0x7F,0x40,0x40,0x40,0x40}},
  {'M', {0x7F,0x02,0x0C,0x02,0x7F}},
  {'N', {0x7F,0x04,0x08,0x10,0x7F}},
  {'O', {0x3E,0x41,0x41,0x41,0x3E}},
  {'P', {0x7F,0x09,0x09,0x09,0x06}},
  {'Q', {0x3E,0x41,0x51,0x21,0x5E}},
  {'R', {0x7F,0x09,0x19,0x29,0x46}},
  {'S', {0x46,0x49,0x49,0x49,0x31}},
  {'T', {0x01,0x01,0x7F,0x01,0x01}},
  {'U', {0x3F,0x40,0x40,0x40,0x3F}},
  {'Z', {0x61,0x51,0x49,0x45,0x43}},
};

const uint8_t* glyphFor(char c) {
  for (size_t i = 0; i < sizeof(FONT)/sizeof(FONT[0]); i++) {
    if (FONT[i].c == c) return FONT[i].col;
  }
  return FONT[0].col;  // space if missing
}

// Build a column buffer for a whole message: 5 cols per glyph + 1 blank gap,
// plus 8 blank cols of padding at the start and end so it scrolls cleanly.
size_t buildMessage(const char* msg, uint8_t* out, size_t outCap) {
  size_t n = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < 8 && n < outCap; i++) out[n++] = 0x00;
  for (const char* p = msg; *p && n + 6 < outCap; p++) {
    const uint8_t* g = glyphFor(*p);
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) out[n++] = g[i];
    out[n++] = 0x00;
  }
  for (int i = 0; i < 8 && n < outCap; i++) out[n++] = 0x00;
  return n;
}

// Scroll a 1..N column buffer across the 8-column matrix, ~60 ms per step.
void scrollColumns(const uint8_t* cols, size_t n) {
  for (size_t start = 0; start + 8 <= n; start++) {
    matrix.clear();
    for (int c = 0; c < 8; c++) {
      matrix.setColumn(7 - c, cols[start + c]);
    }
    delay(60);
  }
}

// Draw a vertical bar graph: `level` columns lit from the left, full height.
void drawBar(int level) {
  matrix.clear();
  for (int col = 0; col < level && col < 8; col++) {
    matrix.setColumn(col, 0xFF);   // light all 8 rows in this column
  }
}

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(200);
  Serial.println();
  Serial.println(F("Earthquake Cam booting..."));

  pinMode(PIN_LED_WARN, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(PIN_LED_WARN, LOW);

  // INPUT_PULLUP is defensive: most SW-420 breakouts have an LM393 comparator
  // with its own pull-up, but bare-module variants without the comparator
  // need the MCU to pull the line high. Adding INPUT_PULLUP is harmless on
  // the comparator boards and saves the bare ones.
  pinMode(PIN_SW420, INPUT_PULLUP);

  matrix.begin();
  matrix.control(MD_MAX72XX::INTENSITY, 4);   // 0..15
  matrix.clear();

  // Friendly boot "READY" scroll BEFORE we arm the interrupt, so that bumps
  // landing during setup don't leave a stale pulseCount > 0 when loop() starts.
  uint8_t buf[64];
  size_t n = buildMessage("READY", buf, sizeof(buf));
  scrollColumns(buf, n);
  matrix.clear();

  // Now arm the shake interrupt and zero the counter for a clean start.
  pulseCount  = 0;
  lastPulseMs = 0;
  attachInterrupt(digitalPinToInterrupt(PIN_SW420), onShake, FALLING);

  Serial.println(F("Ready. Bump the sensor to start a measurement."));
}

void loop() {
  // Idle: wait for the very first pulse to open a measurement window.
  if (pulseCount == 0) {
    delay(10);
    return;
  }

  // A shake just happened. Light the warning LED and count for WINDOW_MS.
  digitalWrite(PIN_LED_WARN, HIGH);
  unsigned long windowStart = millis();
  Serial.println(F("Quake window opened."));

  // Show a small "live" tick on the matrix while counting (column 0 blinks).
  bool tick = false;
  unsigned long lastTickMs = 0;
  while (millis() - windowStart < WINDOW_MS) {
    if (millis() - lastTickMs >= 250) {
      lastTickMs = millis();
      tick = !tick;
      matrix.clear();
      matrix.setColumn(0, tick ? 0x18 : 0x00);  // middle two rows blink
    }
    delay(5);
  }

  // Snapshot the count, then reset for the next quake.
  noInterrupts();
  unsigned int finalCount = pulseCount;
  pulseCount = 0;
  interrupts();

  int level = countToLevel(finalCount);
  const char* verdict = levelToVerdict(level);

  Serial.print(F("Pulses in window: "));
  Serial.print(finalCount);
  Serial.print(F("  ->  level "));
  Serial.print(level);
  Serial.print(F("  ("));
  Serial.print(verdict);
  Serial.println(F(")"));

  // Show the bar graph for 2 seconds...
  drawBar(level);
  delay(2000);

  // ...then scroll the verdict label across the matrix once.
  matrix.clear();
  uint8_t buf[96];
  size_t n = buildMessage(verdict, buf, sizeof(buf));
  scrollColumns(buf, n);
  matrix.clear();

  // All done. Turn the warning lamp off and go back to idle.
  // Drain any pulses that arrived during the display so we don't immediately
  // re-trigger from the user celebrating their GODZILLA score.
  noInterrupts();
  pulseCount = 0;
  interrupts();
  digitalWrite(PIN_LED_WARN, LOW);
  Serial.println(F("Quake window closed. Waiting for the next bump."));
}
