projects.name: Simon Says - 4-color memory game
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (5V in via the board's USB port, 3.3V on the GPIO header)
projects.description:
**What it is**: Four colored LEDs flash a pattern at you - red, yellow, green, blue. You press the buttons underneath in the exact same order. Get it right and the pattern grows by one. Get it wrong and the game is over. **Why it's fun**: It is the classic Simon Says toy, but YOU built it. Challenge your dad to see who can remember the longest sequence, and watch the flashes get faster and faster until your brain melts. ## Parts list - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - runs the state machine and the randomizer) - 1x Red, 1x Yellow, 1x Green, 1x Blue 5mm LED (the four "Simon" pads) - 4x 220 ohm resistors (one in series with each LED so the LED does not burn out) - 4x tactile push-buttons (one under each LED) - 1x breadboard, ~18 DuPont jumpers - USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 (also how power gets in) No external pull-up resistors are needed because every button GPIO chosen here (32, 33, 13, 19) supports the ESP32's internal pull-up. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. This is where electricity "comes home". - **3V3** - the pin that gives 3.3V power. We do not use it in this build. - **VIN** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. We do not use it either. - **D25, D26, D27, D14** - pins that will light up the LEDs. - **D32, D33, D13, D19** - pins that will listen for button presses. - **USB port** - where the laptop cable plugs in to give the board power and load the code.
**Step 1 - Get the breadboard ready.** A breadboard lets you plug parts in without any soldering. The two long blue strips running down each side are called the "ground rails" - the long blue strip on the side of the breadboard. We will use both of them as our 0V (ground) lines so every part has a short trip back to the ESP32's GND pin. - Sit the breadboard flat in front of you with the long blue strips on the top and bottom. - The numbered holes in the middle are where the LEDs, resistors, and buttons will plug in. Holes in the same column are joined inside the board.
**Step 2 - Park the ESP32 next to the breadboard and link its GND to both ground strips.** Jumper wires are little wires with stiff metal tips that push right into the holes. - Take a black jumper wire. Push one end into a hole marked **GND** on the ESP32. Push the other end into the top blue ground strip on the breadboard. - Take another black jumper wire. Push one end into a second **GND** hole on the ESP32 (the board has a few). Push the other end into the bottom blue ground strip. - Now every "-" hole on the breadboard, top and bottom, is at 0V. Why this matters: every LED and every button in this game needs a path back to GND. Wiring both ground strips at the start means the rest of the build is just little hops to the nearest "-" hole.
**Step 3 - Wire the RED LED.** LEDs only work one way around. The **long leg** is the plus side, the **short leg** (on the same side as the flat notch in the plastic) is the minus side. - Push the LED's **long leg** into hole **E3**. - Push the LED's **short leg** into hole **E4** (right next to it). - Take a 220 ohm resistor (it has red-red-brown bands). Resistors do not care which way around they go. Push one leg into hole **A3** (same column as the long leg). Push the other leg into the top blue ground strip. - Take a short jumper wire. Push one end into hole **E4** (same column as the short leg). Push the other end into the top blue ground strip. - Take a jumper wire and connect the pin marked **D25** on the ESP32 to hole **A3**. Why the resistor matters: an LED is hungry. If you plug it straight into the ESP32, it will pull too much current, get hot, and burn out in a second. The 220 ohm resistor sits in the path like a little speed bump and limits the current to a safe amount. Every LED in this build gets its own resistor.
**Step 4 - Wire the YELLOW LED.** Same pattern as the red one, just a few holes further down the breadboard. - Yellow LED **long leg** into hole **E9**, **short leg** into hole **E10**. - 220 ohm resistor from hole **A9** to the top blue ground strip. - Short jumper wire from hole **E10** to the top blue ground strip. - Jumper wire from the pin marked **D26** on the ESP32 to hole **A9**.
**Step 5 - Wire the GREEN LED.** Same pattern again. - Green LED **long leg** into hole **E15**, **short leg** into hole **E16**. - 220 ohm resistor from hole **A15** to the top blue ground strip. - Short jumper wire from hole **E16** to the top blue ground strip. - Jumper wire from the pin marked **D27** on the ESP32 to hole **A15**.
**Step 6 - Wire the BLUE LED.** Last one, same pattern. - Blue LED **long leg** into hole **E21**, **short leg** into hole **E22**. - 220 ohm resistor from hole **A21** to the top blue ground strip. - Short jumper wire from hole **E22** to the top blue ground strip. - Jumper wire from the pin marked **D14** on the ESP32 to hole **A21**.
**Step 7 - Plant the four buttons across the middle of the breadboard.** The tactile buttons have four little metal legs that bend slightly outward. They are designed to straddle the gully in the middle of the breadboard. Press each one gently so all four legs click into their holes. - Place the **RED button** so two of its legs sit in row **F2** and the other two in row **E2** (it bridges the middle gap, sitting near the red LED). - Place the **YELLOW button** the same way at row **F8** / **E8** (near the yellow LED). - Place the **GREEN button** at row **F14** / **E14** (near the green LED). - Place the **BLUE button** at row **F20** / **E20** (near the blue LED). If a button will not push in flat, lift it back out and gently bend the legs a tiny bit straighter with your fingernail, then try again. Never force it.
**Step 8 - Connect each button to a pin and to ground.** Each button needs two wires: one to a listening pin on the ESP32, and one to the bottom blue ground strip. - **RED button:** jumper from the pin marked **D32** on the ESP32 to hole **F2**. Short jumper from hole **J2** to the bottom blue ground strip. - **YELLOW button:** jumper from the pin marked **D33** on the ESP32 to hole **F8**. Short jumper from hole **J8** to the bottom blue ground strip. - **GREEN button:** jumper from the pin marked **D13** on the ESP32 to hole **F14**. Short jumper from hole **J14** to the bottom blue ground strip. - **BLUE button:** jumper from the pin marked **D19** on the ESP32 to hole **F20**. Short jumper from hole **J20** to the bottom blue ground strip. Why no extra resistor on the buttons: the ESP32 has a tiny built-in resistor inside each pin that we can switch on with code. When the button is not pressed, that built-in resistor gently holds the pin at 3.3V (the code reads it as a "1"). When you press the button, the pin gets yanked down to 0V through your wire (the code reads it as a "0"). So the code fires when the button is pressed - no extra parts needed.
**Step 9 - Plug in the USB cable.** Take the USB cable from your laptop and plug the small end into the USB port on the end of the ESP32 board. The little red power light on the ESP32 should glow. - The USB cable carries 5V into the board. The board uses that to make its own 3.3V for the LEDs and buttons. You do not need a separate power supply. - If nothing glows: unplug, check that no LED is in backwards (long leg should be the one going to the resistor side), and try again.
**A few pin tips for grown-ups helping out:** - Pins D34 and D35 are listen-only and have no built-in pull-up resistor. They look handy because they are right there on the header, but a button wired between one of those pins and GND will give random readings. If you ever want to use one, add a real 10,000 ohm resistor from the pin to 3V3. - Avoid D0, D12, and D15 for buttons. Those pins help the ESP32 figure out how to start up, and holding them at the wrong voltage at power-on can stop the board from booting. - D2 is the on-board blue LED on this board. Do not double up a button there - the LED and the button would argue. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open File -> Preferences. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager. Search for "esp32" and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"** (it is a big download, takes a minute or two). 3. Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> **"NodeMCU-32S"**. 4. No extra libraries are needed for this sketch - only `Arduino.h`, which is built in. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with a USB cable. Use a **data** USB cable, not a charge-only one (if the board's red power LED comes on but the laptop never makes the "device connected" sound, swap the cable). 2. Tools -> Port. Pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged the board in (on Windows it looks like `COM4` or `COM5`, on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX`, on Linux it is `/dev/ttyUSB0`). 3. Nothing to edit in the sketch this time - there are no WiFi passwords or placeholders to fill in for Simon Says. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, second from the left at the top). The bottom of the IDE will say "Compiling..." for a few seconds, then "Connecting....." while it flashes. If "Connecting....." dots keep scrolling for more than 10 seconds, **hold the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see "Writing at 0x..." appear, then let go. Most NodeMCU-32S boards auto-flash without this, but a few stubborn ones need the trick. 5. When it says **"Hard resetting via RTS pin..."** the upload worked. The game starts immediately - you should see the four LEDs do a short startup blink, then flash the first one-color "sequence". 6. (Optional) Tools -> Serial Monitor, and set the baud rate dropdown (bottom right) to **115200** to match the sketch's `Serial.begin(115200)`. You will see messages like `Round 1` and `Sequence: RED` so you can peek at what Simon is "thinking". Press the button under the LED that just flashed. If the next round adds one more flash, you are playing! If all four LEDs blink three times together, you got it wrong - it will start a fresh game on its own. **Common gotchas:** - **LED in backwards.** No damage, just no light. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees so the long leg (anode) is on the resistor / GPIO side and the short leg (flat side of the plastic) is on the GND rail, push it back in. - **Button feels "stuck on".** Tactile buttons have **four** legs but only two pairs are actually connected - the other pair shorts when you press. If a button reads pressed all the time, rotate it 90 degrees in the breadboard so the correct pair straddles the gap. - **"Connecting....." never finishes on upload.** Hold the BOOT button on the ESP32 until you see writing progress, then let go. If that still fails, try a different USB cable - charge-only cables are the #1 culprit and they look identical to data cables. ## Talking points - The "memory" of the game is just an array of numbers. Each new round appends a fresh random value (0-3) and replays the whole array from the start. - Debouncing: when you press a tactile button the metal contacts bounce for a few milliseconds, so the GPIO sees several rapid LOW/HIGH/LOW transitions. The sketch reads the pin, waits a tiny moment (`DEBOUNCE_MS`), and reads again to confirm. - `INPUT_PULLUP` flips your intuition: pressed = LOW, not pressed = HIGH. That is because the internal resistor pulls the pin to 3.3 V by default, and the button shorts it to GND when you press it. This is why pin choice matters - GPIOs without a built-in pull-up have nothing to flip back to HIGH. - The speed-up: every successful round trims the gap between LED flashes. That is the difficulty curve, baked into one variable. ## Things to change once it works - Add a tiny passive buzzer on another GPIO and play a different tone per colour (real Simon does this). - Save the high score to flash with the `Preferences` library so it survives a reset. - Add a 2-player mode: alternate who has to repeat the sequence. - Replace the four discrete LEDs with a single WS2812 strip and use colour directly. - Make it WiFi-aware and POST the high score to the Orange Pi hub (once the Pi is online). ## Why this is interesting Pure software project - no sensors, no analog, no I2C. Everything interesting happens in the code: the array, the random call, the loop that plays it back, the loop that reads the player. It is the perfect introduction to a finite state machine (SHOW_SEQUENCE -> WAIT_FOR_PLAYER -> CHECK -> WIN/LOSE) without any new electrical concepts. And the game is genuinely fun, which keeps a 10-year-old engaged long enough to ask "but how does it remember?" - which is exactly the question worth answering.

projects.name: Stopwatch + Lap Memory on Serial Monitor
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (5V in via USB, the onboard regulator makes 3.3V for the chip; no external parts so nothing else needs feeding).
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug the ESP32 into your laptop and open the Serial Monitor. Tap the BOOT button to start a stopwatch, tap again to stop, hold it down to save a lap time, and a tiny blue light blinks once a second while the clock is running. **Why it's fun**: Race your dad down the hallway, time how long you can hold your breath, or see who can stack ten cups the fastest, and every lap gets saved so you can compare runs. One little button does three different jobs depending on how you press it, which feels a bit like a secret code your fingers know. ## Parts list - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the entire project - nothing else needed) - 1x USB-C cable from your laptop That is the whole shopping list. This version of the project was deliberately re-scoped so it can be built with **only the hardware already in Andy's kit**. An earlier draft used a TM1637 4-digit display, an SSD1306 OLED, two tactile push-buttons, a breadboard, and jumpers - none of which are in the kit yet. When those parts arrive, see "Things to change once it works" for the upgrade path. ## Wiring notes This is the easiest wiring job in the whole inventory: there is no wiring. Everything we need is already baked into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board. Read the glossary, then follow the three short steps. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **USB jack** - the little metal port at one end of the board where the USB cable plugs in. Power and code both come through here. - **EN button** - the tiny button next to the USB jack labeled "EN". It means "enable" and is really a reset button. Pressing it reboots the chip. Do not touch it while timing. - **BOOT button** - the other tiny button near the USB jack labeled "BOOT". This is the one button we will use to start, stop, and save laps. - **Built-in blue LED** - a small blue light on the board (not the red one, which just means "power is on"). It blinks while the stopwatch is running. - **Pin marked D2** - the pin on the side of the board with the silkscreen label "D2". The blue LED is wired to this pin inside the board, so we do not run any wires for it. - **Pin marked D0** - the pin labeled "D0" on the silkscreen. The BOOT button is wired to this pin inside the board, so again, no wires from us.
**Step 1 - Plug in the USB cable.** Take the USB cable from your laptop and push it into the USB jack on the end of the ESP32 board. The red "power" LED should light up right away. That cable does two jobs at once: it carries 5V power from your laptop into the board (the board's own little chip turns that 5V into the 3.3V the brain needs), and it also carries the code from the Arduino IDE down to the chip. You do not need a wall plug, batteries, or any other parts.
**Step 2 - Find your one button (BOOT) and leave the other one (EN) alone.** Look at the two tiny buttons near the USB jack. One is labeled **BOOT** and the other is labeled **EN**. The BOOT button is our user button - we will press it to start the timer, press again to record a lap, and hold it to stop and clear. The EN button is a hardware reset; if you press it, the chip reboots and you lose the run. Try to remember which is which before you start timing. Why this matters: the BOOT button is already connected to the pin marked D0 inside the board, with a small built-in helper part called a pull-up resistor. That just means when nothing is happening, the pin reads HIGH (1), and when you press the button it goes LOW (0). The code watches for that change. You do not have to wire anything for this - it just works.
**Step 3 - Spot the built-in blue LED.** Near the silver WiFi shield on the board there is a small blue LED. That one is wired straight to the pin marked D2 inside the board. When the stopwatch is running, the code blinks this LED about once a second so you can tell from across the room whether the timer is going. When the stopwatch is stopped, the LED is off. The red LED next to it is just the power light - ignore it. Why this matters: built-in LEDs already have their own current-limiting resistor (a tiny part on the board that stops too much electricity flowing through the LED and burning it out). If you ever wire your own LED to a pin later, you always need to add a resistor yourself - but for this project the board has already done that work for you.
**Step 4 - Open the Serial Monitor for the "screen".** The stopwatch has no screen of its own. Instead, all the times and laps print to the Arduino IDE Serial Monitor on your laptop. After you upload the code, click `Tools > Serial Monitor` at the top of the Arduino IDE (or hit Ctrl+Shift+M). Set the baud rate dropdown in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor to **115200** so the text comes through clearly. That window is your stopwatch display.
**One last warning.** While you are timing a run, do not bump the EN button and do not unplug the USB cable. Either one resets the chip and erases the lap memory. Only press BOOT. If something goes wrong, that is fine - just press EN to reset, reopen Serial Monitor, and start over. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. If there is already a URL in there, add a comma before pasting. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Type `esp32` in the search box, find "**esp32** by Espressif Systems", and click Install. It is a big download (a few hundred MB), so this is a good time to get a snack. 3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**. That tells the IDE which chip you are talking to. 4. No extra libraries are needed for this project. The sketch only uses ``, which comes built in with the ESP32 board package you just installed. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with the USB-C cable. The little red power LED on the board should light up. 2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that appeared when you plugged the board in. On Windows it looks like `COM5` (the number changes), on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`. If nothing new shows up, your USB cable might be a "charge only" cable - try a different one. 3. There are no passwords or placeholders to edit in this sketch. It is ready to upload as-is. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." for a few seconds, then "Connecting..." while it talks to the chip. **If it gets stuck on `Connecting........_____`**, hold down the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need that nudge on the very first upload; after that they usually behave on their own. 5. When you see "Hard resetting via RTS pin..." the upload is done. Now open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** (or press **Ctrl+Shift+M**). In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor, set the baud rate to **115200** to match `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code. 6. You should see a welcome message and then a `00:00` clock sitting there waiting. Tap the BOOT button once - the blue LED next to the WiFi shield starts blinking once per second and the clock starts counting `00:01`, `00:02`, `00:03`. Tap BOOT again to stop. Hold BOOT for about a second while it is running and you will see a `Lap 1` line print with hundredths of a second. That is the whole thing working. **Common gotchas:** - **Serial Monitor stuck on gibberish like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`.** The baud rate is wrong. Look at the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor and change it to **115200**. The default is often 9600, which makes everything come out garbled. - **Upload fails with `Failed to connect to ESP32: Timed out waiting for packet header`.** Hold the **BOOT** button on the board, click Upload again, and keep holding BOOT until you see "Writing..." in the output. Some boards need this every time, some only on the first flash. - **Blue LED never blinks even though the Serial Monitor says it is running.** A few NodeMCU-32S clones wire the built-in LED to GPIO 5 or GPIO 22 instead of GPIO 2. Open the sketch and change `const uint8_t PIN_LED = 2;` to `5` or `22`, then re-upload. The stopwatch itself still works either way - the LED is just a bonus. ## Talking points - **Why `millis()` instead of `delay()`.** `delay(1000)` would freeze the chip for a whole second, during which it cannot read the button or update the LED. `millis()` just asks "how many milliseconds since boot?" without stopping anything, so the same `loop()` can poll the button, blink the LED, and print the time all at once. - **One button, three actions, via a small state machine.** A short tap (< 600 ms) toggles start/stop. A long press (>= 600 ms while held) records a lap if running, or resets everything if stopped. The function `readButton()` measures how long the button was held and reports a `SHORT_PRESS` or `LONG_PRESS` event. The `loop()` then decides what that event means based on whether the stopwatch is currently running. That separation - "low-level: was it short or long?" vs. "high-level: what does that mean right now?" - is the core idea of a state machine, and it shows up in almost every embedded project later. - **Active-LOW buttons.** When BOOT is *pressed*, GPIO 0 reads `LOW` (0V), not `HIGH`. That is because the pin is pulled up to 3.3V by default, and pressing the button shorts it to ground. This is the single most common thing beginners get backwards, so it is worth re-reading: pressed = LOW. - **Debouncing.** Real metal contacts bounce for a few milliseconds when you press them - the pin flickers HIGH/LOW/HIGH/LOW before settling. `readButton()` ignores any change that happens within 25 ms of the last change, which filters that out so one press is one event. - **Why GPIO 0 is "free" to use as a button at runtime.** GPIO 0 is sampled at *boot* to decide between normal-run mode and flash-upload mode (that is why you sometimes have to hold BOOT during upload). Once the sketch is running, GPIO 0 is just a regular input - so we can re-use the BOOT button as our user button without any extra hardware. - **Why the built-in LED is GPIO 2 on this board.** A few clones put it on GPIO 5 or GPIO 22 instead. If the LED never blinks, change `PIN_LED` to 5 or 22 - the rest of the sketch will still work. ## Things to change once it works - **Upgrade to a real display.** When a TM1637 4-digit display arrives, replace the `Serial.print` calls in `showBigTime()` with `TM1637Display::setSegments()` and keep everything else identical. Add an SSD1306 OLED for the lap list. (That is the original "big stopwatch face + scrolling lap history" project, deferred until the parts are in hand.) - **Add a buzzer.** When the relay board is wired up to switch a piezo, beep once per lap so Andy's son can time himself without watching the screen. - **Persist the best-ever lap.** Use the `Preferences` library to save `bestLapMs` to ESP32 flash so it survives a power cycle. - **Push laps over WiFi.** Once the Orange Pi One is booted and running Mosquitto, publish each lap time over MQTT to the Pi for plotting in Grafana. That makes this the first project that talks to the future hub. - **Increase `MAX_LAPS`** from 20 to 100 - the ESP32 has plenty of RAM. ## Why this is interesting This project teaches the three skills that come up in nearly every later IoT project - **non-blocking timing with `millis()`**, **debounced button input with a state machine**, and **storing a short history in a fixed-size array** - using only the hardware that is already on the desk. There is nothing to wire wrong and nothing to fry. By the end, the same `loop()` that times your son's 100-metre sprint will be a working template for the next dozen projects, where the "display" becomes a TM1637 or an OLED and the "button" becomes any other GPIO input.

projects.name: Family Doorbell Web Page
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or USB wall charger into the ESP32's USB-C port (5V, the board's onboard regulator drops it to 3.3V for the chip)
projects.description:
**What it is**: Press the button on the breadboard. Every phone in the house that has the web page open goes "Ding!" and the counter jumps up by one. **Why it's fun**: It is a real doorbell you built yourself, and Dad's phone buzzes the second you push the button from the other room. Sneak up, mash it five times, and watch every screen in the house freak out at once. ## Parts list - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - hosts the web page and watches the button) - 1x push button (the doorbell itself) - 1x breadboard (holds the button without soldering) - 4x DuPont jumper wires (one to GPIO 4, one to GND, two spare) - 1x USB cable (powers the ESP32 from a laptop or USB wall charger) No resistor is needed for the button: we turn on the ESP32's internal pull-up resistor in code (`INPUT_PULLUP`). The LED that lights up on each press is the blue one already built into the NodeMCU board, so it has its own resistor on the PCB. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the pin that gives out 3.3V of power (don't use this one for the button project, just good to know). - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every circuit needs one of these to "come home" to. - **D4** - a pin marked D4 on the board. The number matches the GPIO number the code uses (pin / GPIO 4). - **USB-C** - the little oval socket where the cable plugs in. This brings in 5V from your laptop or wall charger, and the board quietly drops it to 3.3V for the chip. - **EN** - a reset button. If the board acts weird, tap this.
**Step 1 - Set the breadboard up.** - Lay the breadboard flat in front of you with the long red/blue strips (the long power strips that run down each side) at the top and bottom. - Push the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S into the breadboard so it straddles the gap down the middle, OR sit it next to the breadboard and use jumper wires to reach across. Either works for this build. This is a really small project, so you don't need much breadboard space. The only thing the breadboard does here is hold the button steady and give us a tidy place to land the wires.
**Step 2 - Plant the doorbell button.** - The tactile button has 4 little legs, but they are joined up in pairs inside. That means two of the legs are ALWAYS connected to each other, even before you press it. Tricky! - Sit the button across the middle gap of the breadboard so two legs are on the left side and two are on the right side. Push it down gently until it clicks in flat. - Place it at row 10, so one leg lands in hole E10 (and the leg on the opposite corner lands in hole F10... but we are going to use the leg further away). **Why this matters:** The trick to wiring this button is to ALWAYS use two legs that are diagonally across from each other. If you pick two legs on the same side of the button, those two are already connected together and pressing it will do nothing. Diagonal legs are the ones the switch actually opens and closes.
**Step 3 - Wire one leg of the button to ground (GND).** - Take a jumper wire (any colour, but black is the traditional "ground" colour - I'll use black). - Plug one end into hole E10 (the same row as one leg of the button). - Plug the other end into a hole on the blue long power strip - the GND rail running down the side. This gives one leg of the button a path back to 0V (ground) whenever the button is pressed.
**Step 4 - Connect the GND rail to the ESP32's GND pin.** - Take another jumper wire. - Plug one end into the blue long power strip (GND rail) you just used. - Plug the other end into the pin marked **GND** on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S. Now your breadboard's blue strip and the ESP32 share the same 0V ground. Without this, the button wouldn't have anywhere to "come home" to.
**Step 5 - Wire the other leg of the button to the pin marked D4.** - Take a third jumper wire (I'll use orange/yellow so it stands out). - The "other leg" of the button is the one diagonally opposite to the one you wired in Step 3. If you used the leg at E10, the diagonal partner is the one across the gap and on the other corner - it lands in hole H12 if the button is sitting at rows 10-12 of the breadboard. - Plug one end of the wire into H12. - Now we need to get from H12 to the ESP32's D4 pin. Run a short jumper from H12 over to a free row like J20. Then take a fourth jumper from J20 directly to the pin marked **D4** on the ESP32 (this is GPIO 4, which the code listens to). **Why this matters:** The ESP32 turns on a tiny built-in pull-up inside the chip when the code starts. That means the D4 pin sits quietly at 3.3V (HIGH) all the time. When you press the button, the two diagonal legs connect, and D4 gets yanked straight down to 0V (LOW) through the wire to GND. The code watches for that flip from HIGH to LOW and says "ding dong!"
**Step 6 - Power it up.** - Plug a USB-C cable into the ESP32's USB-C port. - Plug the other end into your laptop (for programming) or a USB wall charger (once it's already programmed). That's it. The cable brings in 5V, and the little chip on the ESP32 board quietly drops that to 3.3V for the brain. No batteries, no wall wart, no soldering. When everything is plugged in, a tiny red light on the ESP32 should come on, telling you it has power.
**One last check before you flash the code:** Press the button gently. You should feel a soft click. If it feels stuck or sideways, pop it back out and reseat it - tactile buttons only go in one way that sits flat. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open the IDE, go to **File -> Preferences**, and in the "Additional board manager URLs" box paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`. Click OK. 2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and install "**esp32 by Espressif Systems**" (it is a big download, give it a few minutes). 3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**. 4. No extra libraries to install. `WiFi.h` and `WebServer.h` both come built-in with the ESP32 board package you just installed. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with the USB-C cable. You should see a tiny red power LED come on near the USB port. 2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the COM port that just appeared (on Windows it will be something like `COM5`; on a Mac it will look like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`). If you are not sure which one is the ESP32, unplug it, look at the list, plug it back in, and pick the new one that showed up. 3. In the sketch, change `WIFI_SSID` to the name of your home WiFi (it is already set to `"GeeFam"` - leave it if that is right) and change `PASSWORD_HERE` to your actual WiFi password. Keep the quote marks around it. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling..." for a bit, then "Connecting....". If it sits on "Connecting" with lots of dots, hold down the small **BOOT** button on the ESP32 board until the upload starts, then let go. (After the first successful upload you usually don't have to do this again.) 5. Once it says "Done uploading", go to **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (drop-down in the top-right of the Serial Monitor window) to **115200**. 6. Press the small **EN** (reset) button on the ESP32. In the Serial Monitor you should see it connect to WiFi and print an IP address like `192.168.1.42`. Type that IP address into any phone or laptop on the same WiFi, hit go, and you should see the "Family Doorbell - All quiet." page. Press the button on the breadboard and the page should flash "Ding!" within a second. **Common gotchas:** - **WiFi band**: the ESP32 can only see **2.4 GHz** WiFi, not 5 GHz. If your router shows two networks (one ending in `-5G`), pick the one without `-5G` for `WIFI_SSID`. - **"Connecting...___" forever on upload**: hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 down while the dots are scrolling, and let go once it starts writing. This puts the chip into download mode by hand. - **Serial Monitor shows garbage characters**: the baud rate is wrong. The code calls `Serial.begin(115200)`, so the Serial Monitor drop-down must also say **115200**. ## Talking points - The button is just a switch. No "smartness" in it. The ESP32 is what turns "switch closed" into "tell every phone in the house". - The web page doesn't get pushed to; it asks the ESP32 every second "has the count gone up?". That's called polling. It's the simplest approach that works on every phone browser without extra libraries. - We count rings instead of just storing "is ringing". A counter means two phones loading the page at slightly different times still both notice the same press. - Debouncing: a physical button's metal contacts bounce when they touch, so one press can look like 3-5 presses electrically. The 400 ms timer in the code ignores those echoes. ## Things to change once it works - Make the page beep or vibrate the phone (a tiny bit of Web Audio API or `navigator.vibrate`). - Add a mDNS name (`ESP32.local`) so you don't have to memorise the IP. - Push instead of poll: switch to Server-Sent Events (`/events` endpoint) so the page updates instantly with no 1-second lag. - Log the last 10 rings with timestamps so you can see who rang while you were out. - Move from the breadboard button to a real doorbell button by the front door (still 2 wires). ## Why this is interesting This is the smallest possible "real" IoT loop: a thing in the physical world (a button) makes a thing on a screen change (a web page), with nothing in between except WiFi. Andy gets to feel the whole shape of an event-driven system in one afternoon - sensor -> microcontroller -> network -> UI - and his son gets immediate, obvious feedback (Dad's phone goes "Ding!" when he pushes the button). It's also the natural feeder project for the Orange Pi hub later: replace the polling page with an MQTT publish and the doorbell becomes one of many sensors on the home bus.

projects.name: Garage Light Web Switch (with Relay)
projects.power_supply: USB-A to USB-C cable into the NodeMCU-32S (5V, also feeds the relay coil via the JDVcc-bridged jumper), plus a separate 12V DC barrel-jack supply for the LED strip on the switched side of the relay.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Open a web page on your phone and tap a big button. CLICK - a light across the room turns on. Tap it again, CLICK, and the light turns off. **Why it's fun**: Your phone is now a magic wand for a real light, and you can hear the little click every time you tap. Show your friends - they will think you wired up the whole house. ## Parts list - ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brains and web server) - 2-ch Songle relay board (only channel 1 is used here) - 12V LED strip, short piece, or any 12V low-voltage lamp - 12V DC power supply for the LED strip (separate from the ESP32 USB power) - Breadboard (holds the ESP32 only) - DuPont jumper wires (M-F from ESP32 header to relay header, M-M for the 12V load side) - USB-A to USB-C cable (the NodeMCU-32S has a USB-C connector) Heads-up: only the ESP32 and the relay board are confirmed on hand from the kit list in CLAUDE.md. The 12V strip, 12V supply, breadboard, jumpers, and USB-C cable are not listed there. Confirm these are actually in the box before starting, or we will be stuck halfway through wiring. ## Wiring notes This project has two power worlds: a tiny safe 5V world for the brain (the ESP32) and a bigger 12V world for the light. The relay is the magic switch that lets the small brain turn the big light on and off without the two worlds ever touching. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **5V** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. We use it to feed the relay. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every circuit needs a GND to come home to. - **D26** - the pin marked D26 on the silkscreen. This is the "signal" wire we use to tell the relay to click. - **USB-C port** - where the USB cable plugs in. That is how the ESP32 gets its power and how you upload code to it.
**Step 1 - Park the ESP32 on the breadboard.** Push the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S gently down across the middle gap of the breadboard so its two rows of pins land in separate halves. The USB-C port should hang off one short edge so the cable can plug in without bumping anything. The breadboard is mostly just a comfy seat for the ESP32 here. We will only run three jumper wires off it to the relay board, so most of the holes will stay empty. That is okay.
**Step 2 - Meet the relay board.** The relay is a tiny mechanical switch. When the ESP32 sends it a signal, you will hear a click and an LED on the relay board will light up. That click is a metal contact closing inside, which lets the 12V power flow to your light. On one side of the relay board there is a little pin header. Look for three pins labeled **VCC** (power input, 5V in), **GND** (the 0V side - ground), and **IN1** (the signal pin for relay channel 1). We will hook these three to the ESP32. On the other side of the relay board there are big blue or green screw terminals. Channel 1 has three screws labeled **COM**, **NO**, and **NC**. We only use COM and NO. That side is where the 12V light wires will go later. There is also a small black jumper cap near the pins labeled **JDVcc** and **Vcc**. Leave it exactly how it came from the factory (bridging those two pins). That tells the relay to share the same 5V power as the ESP32, which is what we want for a small project like this.
**Step 3 - Power up the relay board.** Grab two jumper wires. A red one looks the part for power and a black one for ground, but any colors work. - ESP32 **5V** pin -> relay header **VCC** (power input) - ESP32 **GND** pin -> relay header **GND** (the 0V side) These two wires give the relay board the juice it needs to actually click. Without them, the relay would just sit there doing nothing.
**Step 4 - Send the click signal.** Grab one more jumper wire (yellow or orange is a nice "signal" color). - ESP32 pin marked **D26** -> relay header **IN1** D26 is just a normal pin the ESP32 can turn on and off in code. When the code flips that pin, the relay hears the change through IN1 and the little switch inside snaps over. That is the whole trick of the project. *Why this matters:* the IN1 pin on the relay board is connected to something called an optocoupler, which is a tiny light bulb sealed inside a tiny light sensor. The ESP32 lights up the bulb, the sensor sees the light, and the sensor flips the switch. The bulb and the sensor are in totally separate rooms with no wires between them. That is how the safe 5V world stays totally separate from the scary 12V world. You only need one signal wire to do this, which is why D26 is the only pin we use.
**Step 5 - Wire the light side (grown-up helps here).** The next three connections go on the screw-terminal side of the relay board. Use a small flat screwdriver. Strip a tiny bit of insulation off each wire and tighten the screw firmly on the bare copper. - 12V power supply **+** wire -> relay channel 1 **COM** screw - Relay channel 1 **NO** screw -> LED strip **+** wire - LED strip **-** wire -> 12V power supply **-** wire (these two just connect to each other - they do not touch the relay) That last line is important. The minus side of the LED strip goes straight back to the minus side of the 12V supply. It never touches the ESP32 or the relay board. Picture the relay as a drawbridge sitting in the middle of the plus wire only. When the bridge is down (relay clicked closed), power flows across to the light. When the bridge is up, the plus wire is broken and the light is off. *Why this matters:* notice that the 12V minus wire never connects to the ESP32 minus. That is the whole point of using a relay. The two worlds never share a wire, so even if something weird happens on the 12V side, it cannot zap the ESP32 (or the laptop the ESP32 is plugged into).
**Step 6 - Plug in the USB cable last.** Now plug the USB-A to USB-C cable into the ESP32's USB-C port and into a 5V USB charger or your laptop. The ESP32's little red power LED should light up. Do not plug in the 12V power supply yet. Get the code uploaded and make sure the relay clicks the way you expect first. The 12V supply only gets plugged in at the very end, once everything else looks good and a grown-up has double-checked the screw terminals.
**A small thing that can be tricky:** sometimes a Songle relay board really wants a strong 5V signal on IN1, but the ESP32 only sends 3.3V. Most of the time it works fine anyway. If your relay clicks sometimes but not always, or only after it warms up for a minute, that is the thing to suspect. Tell a grown-up and we can add one tiny extra part to fix it. It is rare though - try it the simple way first. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. File -> Preferences -> "Additional boards manager URLs". Paste in `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. (If there is already something in that box, add a comma first, then paste.) 2. Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager. Search for **esp32** and install "esp32 by Espressif Systems". This takes a few minutes - good time for a snack. 3. Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> **NodeMCU-32S**. 4. No extra libraries needed for this sketch. `WiFi.h` and `WebServer.h` both come with the ESP32 board package you just installed. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the NodeMCU-32S into the laptop with the **USB-A to USB-C** cable. A little red power LED on the board should light up. 2. Tools -> Port. Pick the one that just appeared (Windows: `COM3`, `COM4`, etc.; Mac: `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`; Linux: `/dev/ttyUSB0`). If nothing shows up, the cable might be charge-only - try a different USB-C cable. 3. In the sketch, find these two lines near the top and put in your real WiFi info: - `WIFI_SSID` - replace `"GeeFam"` if your network is named something else. - `WIFI_PASSWORD` - replace `"PASSWORD_HERE"` with your actual WiFi password (keep the quotes). 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." then "Connecting..." with little dots. If the dots keep going for more than 10 seconds, **hold the BOOT button** on the NodeMCU-32S until you see "Writing..." - that is the one weird trick most ESP32 boards need on the first flash. 5. When you see "Hard resetting via RTS pin... Done uploading," it worked. 6. Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. Set the baud rate (bottom-right dropdown) to **115200** - that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code. Tap the EN (reset) button on the NodeMCU-32S so it reboots and you catch the start-up messages. 7. You should see the ESP32 connect to WiFi and print an IP address like `192.168.1.42`. Type that address into a web browser on your phone (the phone has to be on the **same WiFi network**). The big circular button page loads - tap it, and you should hear the relay **CLICK** across the room. **Common gotchas:** - **5 GHz WiFi.** The ESP32 only speaks 2.4 GHz. Most home routers broadcast both - make sure the phone (and the ESP32) are on the 2.4 GHz network, not the 5 GHz one. If WiFi never connects, this is almost always why. - **BOOT button on first upload.** If "Connecting....." just dots forever and then fails, hold the BOOT button on the NodeMCU-32S the whole time it says "Connecting" and let go when "Writing" starts. After the first successful flash it usually does not need the trick again. - **Serial Monitor baud wrong.** If the Serial Monitor shows garbage characters like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`, the baud rate is wrong. Set it to **115200** in the bottom-right corner. - **Relay clicks once at power-up.** If you hear a CLICK the moment the ESP32 boots (before you tap the button), that is the active-LOW trap - the pin floats LOW briefly during reset. The code sets it HIGH first, so you should not see this; if you do, the IN1 wire is on the wrong GPIO or loose. ## Talking points - The relay is a remote-controlled light switch. The ESP32 cannot handle 12V directly, so it tells a tiny electromagnet (the relay coil) to physically push two metal contacts together. - Hear the click? That is the contacts closing. That click is also why you should not switch a relay thousands of times a second. - The web page is just HTML the ESP32 builds as a string and sends back when your phone asks for it. The big button is a link to `/on` or `/off`. The ESP32 sees the request, flips the pin, and redirects you back to `/` so the page updates. - `digitalWrite(pin, LOW)` turns the light ON here. That feels backwards, and it is. Most opto-isolated relay boards use "low-level trigger". - Because the button is a plain link with a 303 redirect, every tap reloads the whole page. That is fine for learning, but it will feel a little sluggish on a phone - half a second of white flash between taps. The first upgrade below fixes that. ## Things to change once it works - Replace the link-style buttons with a `fetch()` call so the page does not fully reload on every tap (the current 303-redirect design forces a full reload, which is why it feels slow). - Add channel 2 with a second button for a second light. - Add a `/status` endpoint that returns JSON so a phone app or Home Assistant can poll it. - Once the Orange Pi hub is up, switch from "web page" to MQTT: ESP32 subscribes to `home/garage/light/set`, publishes state to `home/garage/light/state`. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project where a tap on a phone moves a thing in the real world. Everything before this was the ESP32 talking to its own onboard LED. Now there is a 12V load, a separate power supply, and a mechanical click you can hear from across the room. That click is the bridge from "blinky tutorials" to "actually controlling the house".

"; html += "" + stateLabel + ""; html += ""; return html; } void handleRoot() { server.send(200, "text/html", renderPage()); } void handleOn() { lightOn = true; applyRelay(); server.sendHeader("Location", "/"); server.send(303); } void handleOff() { lightOn = false; applyRelay(); server.sendHeader("Location", "/"); server.send(303); } void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); delay(200); // Drive the pin HIGH (relay OFF) BEFORE setting pinMode, so the relay does not // click on briefly during boot. digitalWrite(RELAY_IN1, HIGH); pinMode(RELAY_IN1, OUTPUT); digitalWrite(RELAY_IN1, HIGH); Serial.print("Connecting to WiFi "); Serial.println(WIFI_SSID); WiFi.mode(WIFI_STA); WiFi.begin(WIFI_SSID, WIFI_PASSWORD); while (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED) { delay(500); Serial.print("."); } Serial.println(); Serial.print("Connected. Open this in your browser: http://"); Serial.println(WiFi.localIP()); server.on("/", handleRoot); server.on("/on", handleOn); server.on("/off", handleOff); server.begin(); Serial.println("Web server started on port 80."); } void loop() { server.handleClient(); // Auto-reconnect if WiFi drops. static unsigned long lastCheck = 0; if (millis() - lastCheck > 10000) { lastCheck = millis(); if (WiFi.status() != WL_CONNECTED) { Serial.println("WiFi lost, reconnecting..."); WiFi.reconnect(); } } } ]]>

projects.name: WiFi Signal Strength Meter on OLED
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from a power bank (user-supplied) to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S USB-C port (5V). The board powers the OLED off its 3.3V rail.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug it in and a tiny screen lights up with a bar that grows and shrinks as you walk around the house. The fatter the bar, the stronger the WiFi where you're standing. **Why it's fun**: You become the WiFi detective. Hunt down the dead zones, find the magic spot in the back bedroom where the signal finally comes back, and prove to your dad once and for all which room has the worst internet. ## Parts list From Andy's inventory: - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the "brain" - reads WiFi signal strength and drives the screen) - 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - SSD1306, 128x64 monochrome (the little screen that shows the bar graph) - 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) (for tidy wiring without solder) - 4x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc (we use 4 of the 40-pack: VCC, GND, SDA, SCL between ESP32 and OLED) Not in the inventory - grab from around the house: - USB power bank (any 5V "phone charger" pack with a USB output) - USB-C cable to go from the power bank to the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S's USB-C port These two are treated as user-supplied because they aren't catalogued in the electronics stock - any spare phone-charging gear will do. ## Wiring notes The ESP32 NodeMCU-32S is the brain of this project. It has WiFi built in, so it can listen for nearby networks and tell us how strong each signal is. The little screen will show the result. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - a pin that gives out 3.3 volts of power. Most small parts (like our screen) want 3.3V, not 5V. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs a GND connection to complete the loop. - **D21 / D22** - two pins marked on the board. These are the talking pins for I2C (more on that below). - **USB-C** - the port where you plug the cable from the power bank. - **EN** - a tiny reset button. If things freeze, press it to restart.
**About I2C (just two talking wires):** The screen uses something called I2C. That is a fancy way of saying "we only need two wires to talk, plus power and ground." One wire is the data wire (SDA), the other is the clock wire (SCL). Four wires total - that is it! **Step 1 - Put the ESP32 and the screen on the breadboard.** - Push the ESP32 down so it straddles the middle gap of the breadboard. Its USB-C port should hang off one end so you can plug a cable in. - Push the OLED screen pins into rows 20, 22, 24, and 26 on column E. The four pins are labeled VCC, GND, SCL, SDA. The long red and blue strips running down the side of the breadboard are called rails. We will use the red strip (called +5V_T in our layout) as the power strip for the screen, and the blue strip (GND_T) as the ground strip. Nothing should be dangling - both modules sit flat.
**Step 2 - Wire up power and ground for the screen.** - Red jumper wire: row A20 (the OLED VCC pin) to the red power strip on the side. - Black jumper wire: row A22 (the OLED GND pin) to the blue ground strip on the side. - Now jump from the ESP32 pin marked **3V3** to the red power strip. - And jump from the ESP32 pin marked **GND** to the blue ground strip. **Why this matters:** The OLED screen runs on 3.3 volts. The ESP32 has a special 3V3 pin that gives out exactly 3.3 volts. Do NOT use the 5V pin or the VIN pin - too much voltage can hurt the little screen. The red strip is just a handy way to share that 3.3V with the OLED's power input.
**Step 3 - Wire up the two I2C talking wires.** - Blue jumper wire: row A24 (OLED SCL, the clock pin) to row B5 on the breadboard. - Blue jumper wire: row A26 (OLED SDA, the data pin) to row B7 on the breadboard. - Now jump from the ESP32 pin marked **D22** to row B5. That hooks the clock wire to the ESP32. - Jump from the ESP32 pin marked **D21** to row B7. That hooks the data wire to the ESP32. **Why this matters:** D22 and D21 are the ESP32's built-in I2C pins. The code knows to use them automatically. If you swap SDA and SCL by mistake, the screen will stay blank - so double-check before powering up.
**Step 4 - Power it up.** - Plug the USB-C cable into the ESP32's USB-C port. - Plug the other end into your laptop while you upload the code, then move it to the power bank when you are done. The ESP32 is happy with any 5V USB source, so the power bank works just like the laptop. Once it boots, the screen should light up and start showing nearby WiFi names with bar graphs for signal strength. This is a tricky one if a wire is loose, so wiggle each jumper and make sure it is fully seated before you plug in power. **Before uploading the code:** open `WiFiRSSIMeter.ino` and find the line that says `PASSWORD_HERE`. Replace it with the real GeeFam WiFi password. Save the file, then upload. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open the Arduino IDE. Go to **File -> Preferences**. In the **Additional boards manager URLs** box, paste this URL and click OK: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` 2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Search for `esp32`, find **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"** and click **Install**. It downloads a few hundred megabytes, so give it a minute. 3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** (or "ESP32 Dev Module" if NodeMCU-32S isn't listed - both work). 4. Install the two screen libraries via **Tools -> Manage Libraries**. One at a time, search for and click **Install** on: - `Adafruit SSD1306` by Adafruit (the OLED driver) - `Adafruit GFX Library` by Adafruit (the drawing helper - the IDE may offer to install it as a dependency, say yes) **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB-C cable**. A red LED on the ESP32 should glow. 2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new port that appeared. On Windows it's something like `COM5`; on a Mac `/dev/cu.usbmodem...`; on Linux `/dev/ttyACM0`. If you can't tell which one, unplug the cable, peek at the menu, plug back in, and pick the entry that appeared. 3. Open the sketch and find `const char* WIFI_PASSWORD = "PASSWORD_HERE";`. Replace `PASSWORD_HERE` with the real GeeFam WiFi password (keep the quotes). 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the toolbar). The IDE compiles for a minute, then shows "Connecting...." while it flashes the board. If it sits there printing dots and underscores for more than 10 seconds, hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 down until the upload starts, then let go. 5. When the upload finishes you'll see "Hard resetting via RTS pin". The OLED should light up and say "Connecting to: GeeFam" with dots ticking across. 6. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** if you want to peek - this sketch doesn't call `Serial.begin()`, so the window will stay quiet. All the action is on the OLED. 7. **You'll know it worked when:** the OLED first shows "Connected!" with an IP address like `192.168.1.42`, then switches to the live meter - a number like `-58 dBm`, a word like `Good`, and a bar that wobbles as you tilt the board. Walk into the next room and watch the bar shrink. That's the whole game. Once it's running, unplug the USB-C cable from the laptop and plug it into the power bank instead. The sketch is stored in flash, so it boots back up and reconnects to GeeFam on its own. Now you're free to roam. **Common gotchas:** - **5 GHz WiFi won't work.** The ESP32 radio only speaks 2.4 GHz. If GeeFam has separate 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz network names, set `WIFI_SSID` to the 2.4 GHz one, otherwise the OLED sits on "Connecting..." forever. - **First upload needs the BOOT button.** If the IDE prints `Connecting......_____....` and gives up, hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until the upload bar starts moving, then release. After the first successful flash this usually isn't needed again. - **OLED stays black.** Almost always: VCC went to the 5V pin instead of 3V3 (don't do that - it can kill the screen), SDA and SCL got swapped (try swapping the two signal wires), or the address isn't `0x3C` (a few rare modules are `0x3D` - change `OLED_ADDR` in the sketch and re-upload). ## Talking points - **RSSI** (Received Signal Strength Indicator) is just a number in dBm that the WiFi chip reports for the access point it's connected to. -30 dBm is "I'm sitting on the router", -90 dBm is "I can barely hear it". -67 dBm or better is fine for streaming video, worse than -75 dBm is where things get flaky. - The bar graph is just a filled rectangle whose width is mapped from the RSSI range onto the screen width. It's the same idea as a volume bar in any music app. - "I2C" uses only two signal wires (SDA = data, SCL = clock) and an address to pick which device on the bus to talk to. The OLED's address is almost always `0x3C`. - Because the ESP32 reconnects to WiFi automatically, you can keep walking around even if the signal drops out briefly - the meter will recover on its own. ## Things to change once it works - Add a peak-hold marker: a thin vertical line that remembers the strongest reading you've seen in this room. - Show the SSID name and the IP address as small text above the bar, so the kids can confirm which network they're measuring. - Log readings to SD or send them over MQTT to the (future) Orange Pi hub so you can make a heat-map of the house. - Add a buzzer that beeps faster when signal gets weaker - a "Geiger counter" mode for finding the strongest spot. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project here that does something genuinely useful around the house: it answers the real question "why is the WiFi bad in the back bedroom?". It also introduces two big concepts in one go - reading a real-world radio measurement (RSSI) and driving a display over I2C - without needing any sensors or extra parts beyond a single screen. Once the OLED is working, every future project that needs a tiny readout (temperature, sensor values, MQTT status from the Pi) reuses exactly the same wiring and code pattern.

projects.name: Distance-Triggered Treat Dispenser
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a 5V/2A phone-style charger (or laptop port) into the ESP32 NodeMCU; VIN/5V feeds the HC-SR04 and SG90 with a 470 uF cap across the servo rail, and the HC-SR04 ECHO line is divided 1k/2k down to 3.3V before reaching the ESP32 GPIO.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Hold your hand over the box. A motor spins a little cardboard wheel and exactly one M&M drops into your palm. A small red display ticks up so you can see how many treats it has handed out today. **Why it's fun**: You built a candy machine that obeys your hand like magic, with no button to press. Set a daily limit, race your brother to trigger it the fastest, or aim it at the dog and watch his brain explode. ## Parts list - ESP32 NodeMCU (the brain - reads sensor, drives servo, updates display) - HC-SR04 ultrasonic distance module (looks straight up for your hand) - SG90 micro-servo (rotates the cardboard disk that drops one M&M) - TM1637 4-digit display (shows the running count of treats dispensed) - 1k and 2k resistors (voltage divider on the HC-SR04 ECHO line - see Wiring notes) - 470 uF electrolytic capacitor (across the servo's 5V/GND, prevents brownout resets) - Breadboard + male-to-male DuPont jumpers - USB cable from a 5V/2A phone-style charger (preferred) or a laptop port for power You will also build a tiny cardboard chassis: a tube (like an empty toilet-roll tube) holds the M&Ms, a flat cardboard disk on the servo horn has one M&M-sized slot cut out of it. As the servo turns from 0 deg to 90 deg the slot lines up with a hole in the chute and exactly one M&M drops out. This is the fun part - it will probably take three tries to get the disk geometry right. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **VIN** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. Good for powering 5V parts like the servo and the distance sensor. - **3V3** - a 3.3V power pin. Smaller voltage for the little display. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs a wire back here. - **Dx** (like D13, D18, D23) - the signal pins. On this board the number on the silver writing matches the number in the code. - **USB** - where the charger cable plugs in to power the whole thing.
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard power strips.** The breadboard has two long red/blue strips running down each side - the long red strip is for power (+5V) and the long blue strip is for 0V (ground). We will use the top strip for the sensor and the bottom strip for the servo, so both jobs each get their own clean area. - Run a short jumper from the ESP32 pin marked **VIN** to the top red strip. - Run another short jumper from one of the ESP32 pins marked **GND** to the top blue strip. - That gives the top half of the board 5V power and a 0V return.
**Step 2 - Plant the HC-SR04 distance sensor.** This is the part with two silver "eyes" - it sends out a chirp and listens for the echo to measure how far away the pet is. Push its 4 pins down into row 3 to row 6 on the breadboard (the pin marked VCC at row 3, then TRIG, ECHO, GND going down). - Jumper from the VCC row (A3) over to the top red strip (5V). - Jumper from the GND row (A6) over to the top blue strip (ground). - The TRIG row (row 4) and the ECHO row (row 5) we will connect to the ESP32 in the next two steps.
**Step 3 - Wire TRIG (the "send" pin) to the ESP32.** TRIG is the pin where the ESP32 tells the sensor "send a chirp now." - Jumper from the ESP32 pin marked **D23** straight over to row A4 (the TRIG row on the sensor). - That's it for this step - one wire. The sensor is happy to be tickled with a 3.3V signal even though it runs on 5V, so we can poke it directly.
**Step 4 - Wire ECHO (the "listen" pin) through two resistors.** This is a tricky one. The ECHO pin spits out a 5V signal, but the ESP32 only wants 3.3V on its pins. To shrink the 5V down to 3.3V we use two resistors as a little voltage step-down. Resistor colors: 1K is brown-black-red, 2.2K is red-red-red. - Plug the **1K resistor** between row B5 (the ECHO row on the sensor) and row B10 (an empty row further down the board). - Plug the **2.2K resistor** between row A10 (the same empty row) and the top blue strip (ground). - Jumper from row C10 (still that same empty row) over to the ESP32 pin marked **D18**. Why this matters: the sensor pushes out 5V on ECHO and the ESP32 chip can be damaged by 5V on its pins. The two resistors together split the voltage so only about 3.3V reaches D18 - exactly what the ESP32 likes. Without the resistors the ESP32 might stop working after a while.
**Step 5 - Hook up the 4-digit display.** This is the little red number screen that will show the distance in centimeters. It has 4 pins on the back: CLK, DIO, VCC (power input), and GND (ground). It lives off the breadboard - just run 4 jumper wires from the display straight to the ESP32. - Display **VCC** to the ESP32 pin marked **3V3**. - Display **GND** to any ESP32 pin marked **GND**. - Display **CLK** to the ESP32 pin marked **D4**. - Display **DIO** to the ESP32 pin marked **D5**. The display is fine running on the smaller 3.3V power, and bonus: that means CLK and DIO are already at the right voltage with no extra parts.
**Step 6 - Build the servo power area on the lower half of the breadboard.** The servo gets its own clean 5V area at the bottom of the board so its "kicks" do not upset the sensor. - Jumper from the ESP32 pin marked **VIN** to the bottom red strip. - Jumper from another ESP32 pin marked **GND** to the bottom blue strip. Now the bottom half also has 5V and ground available.
**Step 7 - Plant the 470uF capacitor near where the servo will sit.** A capacitor is a tiny battery that stores a little energy and releases it fast. This one has two metal legs, and it is polarized - it cares which way around it goes. - Look at the side of the capacitor: there is a stripe with a "-" sign printed on it. The leg under that stripe is the **short leg** and it must go to ground. - The other leg (the **long leg**, no stripe) goes to 5V. - Push the long leg into row F20 and the short leg into row F22. - Jumper from row J20 over to the bottom red strip (5V). - Jumper from row J22 over to the bottom blue strip (ground). Why this matters: when the servo first turns, it grabs a big gulp of power all at once. Without this capacitor that gulp can dip the voltage just enough to make the ESP32 restart in the middle of a treat drop. The capacitor sits there holding extra energy, ready to top up that gulp instantly. If you ever see your ESP32 reboot every time the servo moves, double-check this capacitor. Polarity warning: if you put the capacitor in backwards it can pop. Always check the stripe goes to ground before plugging in USB.
**Step 8 - Hook up the SG90 servo.** This is the little blue motor that swings the treat door open. Its cable has 3 wires: orange (signal), red (power), brown (ground). Push 3 male jumpers into the servo's plug, then push the other ends into rows 25, 26, 27 on the right side of the breadboard. - Orange signal wire into row F25. - Red power wire into row F26. - Brown ground wire into row F27. - Jumper from row J26 to the bottom red strip (5V). - Jumper from row J27 to the bottom blue strip (ground). - Jumper from row J25 over to the ESP32 pin marked **D13**. That carries the "swing to this angle" signal. The servo is now sharing its power strip with the 470uF capacitor we just placed - so when it kicks, the capacitor is right next door ready to help.
**Step 9 - Final ground check.** Every ground in the project must meet at one common 0V point or the distance numbers will be nonsense. - The top blue strip and the bottom blue strip should both be tied to an ESP32 GND pin (we did this in Step 1 and Step 6). - If you only have one GND wire going to one strip, add a short jumper between the two blue strips so they are joined. - The display's GND wire also goes to an ESP32 GND pin. Why this matters: the sensor measures very short time gaps (microseconds) to figure out distance. If the grounds are not all joined, the timing readings drift and your ESP32 will think your pet is 800 cm away when they are right in front of it.
**Step 10 - Power it up and tune.** Plug the USB cable from the 5V/2A charger into the ESP32. The 4-digit display should light up and start showing a number. Wave your hand 20 cm in front of the sensor and the number should drop. When it drops below the trigger distance in the code (try 15 cm to start), the servo should swing open for a couple of seconds, then close. If the servo twitches but the ESP32 keeps restarting, recheck the capacitor's stripe (short leg to ground) and use a proper 2A charger rather than a laptop USB port. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open the Arduino IDE, then go to **File -> Preferences**. In the box labelled "Additional boards manager URLs", paste this address and click OK: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` 2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download (a few hundred MB) so give it a minute. 3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** from the list. 4. Install two extra libraries. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** (or **Sketch -> Include Library -> Manage Libraries**), then one at a time: - Search for `ESP32Servo` and install the one by **Kevin Harrington / John K. Bennett**. - Search for `TM1637` and install **"TM1637Display"** by **Avishay Orpaz**. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with a **USB micro-B data cable**. Important: some cheap micro-B cables are charge-only and the IDE will not see the board. If no port shows up in step 2, try a different cable. 2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that just appeared. On Windows it looks like **COM4** or **COM5**, on a Mac it looks like **/dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX** or **/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART**. 3. Open the sketch. This project has no WiFi password or other placeholders to fill in - the only knobs you might want to tweak near the top of the file are `TRIGGER_CM` (how close your hand has to be, in cm) and `SERVO_DISPENSE` (how far the disk rotates, in degrees). Leave them alone for the first run. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top left). The IDE will compile for about 30 seconds, then start flashing. If you see `Connecting......_____....` and then a red error, hold down the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 board until you see `Writing at 0x...` scrolling, then let go. You only have to do this trick the first time, or after some other tools have grabbed the chip. 5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom right of the Serial Monitor window) to **115200**. 6. Press the small **EN** (or **RST**) button on the ESP32. You should see a startup line, the display should show `0000`, and the servo should jiggle to its rest position. Wave your hand about 10 cm above the HC-SR04 - the servo should snap to 90 deg, drop one M&M, snap back, and the display should tick up to `0001`. Pull your hand away past 20 cm and try again to see `0002`. If the display lights up but the count never goes up, the sensor is probably not seeing your hand - check the wiring of TRIG and ECHO before changing any code. **Common gotchas:** - **First-upload BOOT button trick.** On a fresh ESP32, the IDE often cannot put the chip into flash mode by itself. If Upload hangs at `Connecting......`, hold BOOT, tap EN once, keep holding BOOT until flashing starts, then let go. After the first successful flash this usually fixes itself. - **Capacitor polarity backwards.** The 470 uF electrolytic has a striped side - that is the negative leg and must go to GND. Wired backwards it can pop, get hot, or just refuse to smooth the servo dips so the ESP32 keeps rebooting every time the servo moves. If the display resets to `0000` every time you trigger a treat, check the cap before anything else. - **Serial Monitor baud rate wrong.** If the Serial Monitor shows a wall of garbage characters like `??????`, the baud rate is wrong. Set the dropdown in the bottom right of the Serial Monitor to **115200** to match the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch. ## Talking points - "What is an ultrasonic sensor?" It chirps a sound too high-pitched for us to hear, then times how long the echo takes to come back. Sound travels ~343 m/s, so the code multiplies microseconds by 0.0343 cm/us and divides by 2 (because the chirp goes there and back). - "Why does it only dispense one M&M, not a stream?" Look at the `armed` variable. We disarm as soon as a hand is detected and only re-arm once the hand has moved back past 20 cm. That hysteresis pattern shows up everywhere in electronics - thermostats, button debouncing, you name it. - "Why a slotted disk instead of just a flap?" A flap can let two M&Ms through if you're unlucky. A slot exactly one M&M deep is mechanically self-limiting - this is called a "rotary feeder" and is how real candy machines work. - "Why two resistors on the ECHO wire?" The sensor speaks at 5 V but the ESP32 listens at 3.3 V. The two resistors form a divider that quietly drops the loud 5 V down to a polite 3.3 V before it reaches the chip - cheap insurance against frying a GPIO. - "Why a fat capacitor next to the servo?" Motors are greedy in short bursts. The cap is a tiny local battery that hands current to the servo during those bursts so the ESP32 next door does not see its supply sag and reboot. ## Things to change once it works - Add a tiny buzzer (active-high) that beeps once per dispense. - Display the time-since-last-treat instead of the count, so you can compete with your son for "fastest reaction". - Publish the count over MQTT to the Orange Pi (once it's booted) so a Grafana dashboard tracks daily M&M consumption. - Replace the cardboard disk with a 3D-printed one - same code, much more reliable feed. - Add a long-press boot button check that resets the counter to zero. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project in the kit that combines a sensor (input), an actuator (output), and a display (feedback) into one closed loop. That is the basic shape of every IoT device. It also forces you to think about mechanical design as part of "the code working" - the firmware is the easy half, the cardboard is the hard half. That's a really useful lesson before moving on to the Orange Pi hub work where you'll be debugging across networks instead of across millimetres of cardboard.
