projects.name: Mailbox-Opened Pinger
projects.power_supply: 18650 cell, charged by a TP4056 charge-only module; cell B+ goes straight to the XIAO BAT pad (3.7V, no boost stage), B- to XIAO GND
projects.description:
**What it is**: Hide a tiny box inside your mailbox. The second the mail carrier lifts the flap, an LED inside your house blinks to tell you the mail just arrived. No more guessing, no more checking an empty mailbox five times a day. **Why it's fun**: You built a real-life notification, like a phone alert but made out of parts on your desk. The best part: the gadget sleeps for weeks on one battery and wakes up the instant something happens, like a little robot guard dog for your mail. A battery-powered XIAO ESP32-C3 sits inside the mailbox, asleep almost all the time. When the mail carrier lifts the flap, a tilt switch closes, pulls a GPIO pin HIGH, and the C3 wakes from deep sleep. It connects to WiFi, fires off an HTTP ping, blinks the indoor LED, then goes back to sleep. With the boost stage removed and the 18650 wired straight to the XIAO's battery pad, a single cell should run the project for a long time - though see the honest battery-life note below. ## Parts list - 1x XIAO ESP32-C3 (the sleeper) - 1x bare 2-pin Angle Tilt Switch (a tube with a metal ball that bridges two contacts when tilted - no electronics inside) - 1x 18650 cell + TP4056 charge-only module (power) - 1x 100k resistor - external pull-down on the wake pin AND the R of an RC debounce filter - 1x 100nF ceramic cap - the C of the same RC debounce filter - 1x Blue LED + 1x 100R resistor (visible "I woke up" indicator) - 1x Breadboard, ~8x M-M DuPont jumpers ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the XIAO ESP32-C3 board:** - **D0 ... D10** - the pins along the edge. On this little board the silkscreen number does NOT match the chip's GPIO number. We will always tell you the silkscreen label first. - **3V3** - the pin that gives out 3.3V of power. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. This is the "return" wire for everything. - **BAT** - a tiny pad on the underside of the board where you can feed in a battery directly. We use this so the battery lasts longer. - **The long red strip** on the side of the breadboard is the power strip. The long blue strip is the ground strip.
**Step 1 - Put the XIAO on the breadboard.** - Sit the XIAO across the gap in the middle of the breadboard so each row of pins lands in its own column. - We are NOT going to use the red and blue strips on the side this time. The wiring is short enough that we will run everything through the middle rows instead.
**Step 2 - Add the LED.**
- Push the LED's **long leg** into hole **E20** on the breadboard. - Push the LED's **short leg** into hole **E21**. - Take a 100R resistor (brown-black-black-black-brown stripes) and put one leg in **A20** (same row as the long leg) and the other leg in **A24**. - Run a short jumper wire from **A24** to **A27**. This is the wire we will later tie to the pin marked **D1 (GPIO3)** on the XIAO. - Run another jumper from **E21** (the short-leg row) to the ground row at the top of the breadboard (marked **GND_T** in the layout). Why this matters: an LED is hungry. If you connect it straight to a pin it will gulp too much electricity and burn out in a flash. The 100R resistor is a tiny speed bump that limits the current to a safe amount. The blue LED here only has about 0.1 to 0.3V of "headroom" to play with, so 100R is just right - any bigger and the LED would look dim.
**Step 3 - Add the tilt switch and its helper parts.** The tilt switch is a tiny tube with a metal ball inside. When the tube tips one way, the ball rolls to one end and connects the two legs together. When it tips the other way, the ball rolls away and the legs are not connected. We will mount this on the mailbox flap so it tilts when the flap opens. - Put one leg of the tilt switch on a wire going to the pin marked **3V3** on the XIAO. - The other leg of the tilt switch goes on a wire heading to hole **A10** on the breadboard. (Use long wires for this leg - this is the one that will actually sit on your mailbox flap.) - Put a **100K resistor** (brown-black-yellow stripes, or brown-black-black-orange) with one leg in **B10** and the other leg in the ground row **GND_T**. - Put a tiny **100nF capacitor** (a yellow or beige disc, often marked "104") with one leg in **D10** and the other leg in the ground row **GND_T**. This capacitor is not polarised so either leg can go either way. - Run a wire from hole **C10** to the pin marked **D0 (GPIO2)** on the XIAO. Why this matters: by itself, a bare switch is "noisy". When the metal ball lands, it actually bounces around for a few milliseconds and would make the pin look like the switch flipped on and off ten times in a row. The 100K resistor and the 100nF capacitor work together like a sponge that soaks up that bounce, so the XIAO only sees one clean signal. The 100K resistor also makes sure the pin stays at 0V whenever the switch is open - without it, the pin would just float, and the XIAO would see ghosts.
**Step 4 - Quick warning about the pin marked D0.** This is a tricky one. The pin marked **D0 (GPIO2)** on the XIAO is what's called a "boot mode" pin. The chip looks at this pin the instant you turn it on to decide what to do. If the pin is at 0V at power-on, the chip boots normally - which is what we want. If the pin is at 3.3V at power-on, the chip thinks you want to upload new code and just sits there waiting. This is why we have to mount the tilt switch so that **"mailbox flap closed" = "switch open"**. With the switch open, the 100K resistor pulls the pin to 0V, and your XIAO boots properly every time. If you accidentally wire it backwards, the XIAO will look broken whenever the mailbox is closed.
**Step 5 - Hook up the battery and charger.** The TP4056 is a tiny board with a USB-C socket on one end. It does two jobs: it safely charges the 18650 battery, and it protects the battery from being drained too far. - The **18650 battery** goes onto the pads marked **B+** and **B-** on the TP4056. B+ is the bumpy end (+), B- is the flat end (-). - The pad marked **OUT+** on the TP4056 goes to the **BAT** pad on the underside of the XIAO. Ask a parent to help you find the BAT pad - it is a small silver spot on the back of the board near the USB-C connector. - The pad marked **OUT-** on the TP4056 goes to the **GND** pin on the XIAO. - The USB-C cable only goes into the TP4056 when you want to charge. The rest of the time, the cable is unplugged and the battery runs the whole thing. Why this matters: the XIAO ESP32-C3 has a clever feature - the BAT pad lets you feed the battery in directly, and the XIAO's own little power regulator turns it into 3.3V for the chip. We are skipping the usual "5V" step entirely. That means a LOT less wasted electricity, so the battery can last for months instead of days while the XIAO sits and waits for the mailbox to open.
**Final check before powering on.** - Look at the LED row: long leg on **E20**, short leg on **E21**, with the resistor between **A20** and **A24**, and a jumper from **A24** going toward the pin marked **D1 (GPIO3)**. - Look at the tilt switch row: switch leg going to **3V3**, the other leg going to **A10**, with the 100K resistor (**B10** to ground) and the 100nF capacitor (**D10** to ground) all sharing row 10. - Wire from **C10** to the pin marked **D0 (GPIO2)**. - Battery on TP4056 B+ / B-, OUT+ to the BAT pad, OUT- to GND. Tip the tilt switch by hand. The blue LED should blink once and your phone should get a ping. If nothing happens, unplug the battery, double-check row 10 (that's the tricky row), and try again. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click OK. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type "esp32" in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download, so give it a few minutes. 3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"XIAO_ESP32C3"** from the long list. 4. No extra libraries needed for this sketch. WiFi, HTTPClient, esp_sleep, and driver/gpio all come bundled with the esp32 board package you just installed. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the XIAO into the laptop with a **USB-C cable that can carry data** (some cheap charging-only cables look identical but will not work - if the IDE never sees a port, that is usually why). For this first flash, leave the 18650 disconnected from the BAT pad so the board is powered only from USB. 2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged the XIAO in (something like `COM5` on Windows or `/dev/cu.usbmodem...` on a Mac). 3. In the sketch, find the line `const char* WIFI_PASSWORD = "PASSWORD_HERE";` and replace `PASSWORD_HERE` with your actual home WiFi password. Double-check `WIFI_SSID` matches your network name exactly (capitals matter). 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling", then "Connecting...", then start showing dots and percentages as it writes the program. If "Connecting..." sits there for more than 10 seconds without progress, **hold the tiny BOOT button on the XIAO, tap the RESET button next to it, then let go of BOOT**. The upload should start. (You usually only need this trick once; after the first successful flash the IDE can reset the board on its own.) 5. When the IDE says "Done uploading", open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of the Serial Monitor pane) to **115200** to match the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code. 6. To test it, gently tip the breadboard so the ball inside the tilt switch rolls to the other end. The blue LED should blink, and in the Serial Monitor you should see the boot count tick up and a line about WiFi connecting. **Two quick blinks** = the ping went out fine. **One long blink** = it woke up but could not reach the internet (check your WiFi name and password). Once that all works, unplug USB, connect the 18650 + TP4056 to the BAT pad as described above, and tuck the whole thing into the mailbox. **Common gotchas:** - **5 GHz WiFi will not work.** The ESP32-C3 only speaks 2.4 GHz. If your router broadcasts both bands under the same name and the C3 cannot connect, ask your dad to either turn off 5 GHz for a moment, or set up a separate 2.4 GHz network name and put that in `WIFI_SSID`. - **First upload hangs at "Connecting..."** Hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT. This puts the C3 into download mode by hand. After the first successful upload, the IDE can usually do this automatically. - **Serial Monitor shows garbage characters** (random symbols and boxes). The baud rate in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor is set wrong. Change it to **115200** to match the code. ## Talking points - **Deep sleep is the headline feature.** A XIAO running normally pulls ~80 mA with WiFi on. In deep sleep the chip itself drops to roughly 40-150 microamps. - **But "weeks to months" needs an honest asterisk.** The boost-converter round-trip in the earlier draft was leaking 1-10 mA all the time, which would have dominated the chip's own 43 uA and killed the cell in days. Going straight from the 18650 to the XIAO BAT pad removes that loss. The remaining drains are the TP4056 (~20 uA when idle, no USB plugged in), the chip itself in deep sleep (~40 uA), and the 100k pull-down (only conducts while the switch is closed). So the realistic budget is in the tens-of-microamps range - genuinely weeks of life - PROVIDED the tilt switch doesn't bounce back and forth all day. A single mail delivery that bounces 20 times is fine; a wind-rattled flap that wakes the chip every 30 seconds will flatten the cell in a day. - **The C3 needs a different deep-sleep wake API than the classic ESP32.** The classic ESP32 has an `ext1` wake source that uses the RTC_IO peripheral, but the C3 doesn't have that peripheral, so `esp_sleep_enable_ext1_wakeup` won't work as expected. On the C3 you use `gpio_wakeup_enable()` plus `esp_deep_sleep_enable_gpio_wakeup()`, and you check `ESP_SLEEP_WAKEUP_GPIO` (not `_EXT1`) for the wake cause. This is one of those quiet behavior differences between ESP32 family members that the part name doesn't telegraph. - **RTC_DATA_ATTR variables survive sleep.** The `bootCount` variable keeps its value across wake/sleep cycles because we put it in RTC memory, which stays powered. Regular variables get wiped. - **Why a brief LED pulse before WiFi?** So even if WiFi is down, you still get a visible confirmation that the wake actually happened. Debugging "did it wake?" vs "did the ping fail?" separately is much easier than debugging both at once. ## Things to change once it works 1. **Replace the demo HTTP endpoint** with something real: a Home Assistant webhook, an IFTTT trigger, a Pushover/ntfy notification, or your own MQTT publish to the Orange Pi once it's booted. 2. **Measure actual battery life.** Add a divider to read the battery voltage on an ADC pin and include it in the ping payload. Then graph it over a week and see how the cell is really discharging. 3. **Weatherproof the enclosure.** A small project box with a cable gland for the tilt-switch leads. The XIAO and battery stay inside the house; only the switch goes in the mailbox. 4. **Add a second debounce layer in software** if mailbox flap wind-rattle turns out to be a problem - e.g., require the line to stay HIGH for 100ms before treating it as a real event, otherwise sleep again. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project in the kit that isn't tethered to a USB cable. Up until now every sketch has assumed "plugged in, always on." Deep sleep + wake-on-GPIO is the technique behind every battery-powered IoT sensor on the market - door/window sensors, water leak detectors, motion sensors - and the pattern in `setup()` (wake, do one thing, sleep) is the same in every one of them. It's also the first project where the answer to "how do I make this last on a battery?" forced changes to the power topology (drop the boost stage), the wake pin (external pull-down because the internal one sleeps), and the input filtering (RC network because mechanical contacts bounce). Every one of those is a real-world IoT lesson that doesn't come up when the board is plugged into a laptop.

projects.name: OLED Spirit Level
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from laptop to the XIAO ESP32-C3 (5V in, 3.3V out on the 3V3 pin powers the IMU and OLED)
projects.description:
**What it is**: Tilt the breadboard and a little bubble slides around on the OLED screen, just like the bubble in a real spirit level at the hardware store. When the board is perfectly flat, the bubble lands in the center and a green LED lights up to tell you "you're level." **Why it's fun**: It is a real tool you can carry around the house and use to check if shelves, picture frames, or the kitchen table are crooked. Your dad probably owns the boring plastic version, but yours has a glowing screen and a light that congratulates you when you nail it. ## Parts list - XIAO ESP32-C3 (3.3 V logic, USB-C powered) - MPU-6500 IMU breakout (I2C, address 0x68) - 0.96" SSD1306 OLED, 128x64, I2C (address 0x3C) - Green LED + 220R current-limiting resistor - Breadboard and a handful of DuPont jumpers ## Wiring notes This is the first project where we put TWO devices on the same two wires. That's a trick called I2C - both the screen and the tilt sensor share one data wire and one clock wire, and each one has its own "name" (a number) so they don't talk over each other. The screen's name is 0x3C and the tilt sensor's name is 0x68, so they never get confused. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the XIAO ESP32-C3 board:** - **3V3** - a pin that gives back 3.3 volts. The screen and tilt sensor both run on this. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs a wire back to GND. - **D0 through D10** - the pins you can use in your code. On the XIAO, the silkscreen label (like "D4") is NOT the same as the GPIO number used in code. We'll remind you each time. - **SDA / SCL** - the two I2C wires. SDA carries the data, SCL is the clock that keeps both devices in step. - **USB-C** - the small port where the cable from your laptop plugs in.
**Step 1 - Power and ground rails from the XIAO.** The breadboard has two long strips at the top (we'll call them the top red rail and the top black rail) and two more at the bottom. We're going to feed 3.3V into the top red rail and GND into the top black rail, so every other part can just grab power from the closest hole. - XIAO **3V3 pin** -> top red rail (+3.3V everywhere along the top). - XIAO **GND pin** -> top black rail (0V everywhere along the top). Important: the screen and the tilt sensor want **3.3V, NOT 5V**. The XIAO's signal pins only like 3.3V, so giving the I2C parts 5V could slowly hurt the chip. Always use the 3V3 pin on the XIAO, never the 5V pin.
**Step 2 - Plug in the MPU-6500 tilt sensor.** Push the MPU-6500 board into the breadboard so its 4 pins land in rows 5, 6, 7, and 8 on the B column. Then run these short jumper wires from the A column (same rows): - **VCC** (power input, row 5) -> top red rail (3.3V). Use a red wire. - **GND** (0V side, row 6) -> top black rail. Use a black wire. - **SCL** (clock, row 7) -> row 16 column A (we'll share this with the screen in a moment). Use a blue wire. - **SDA** (data, row 8) -> row 17 column A (also shared with the screen). Use a blue wire. This little board has a tiny chip on it that feels which way is "down" using gravity. That's how the level knows when you've tilted it.
**Step 3 - Plug in the OLED screen.** Push the OLED screen into the breadboard so its 4 pins land in rows 14, 15, 16, and 17 on the B column. Notice that the screen's SCL row (16) and SDA row (17) line up with the wires we just brought over from the tilt sensor - that's how both devices end up sharing the same two I2C wires. - **GND** (0V side, row 14) -> top black rail. Black wire. - **VCC** (power input, row 15) -> top red rail (3.3V). Red wire. - **SCL** (clock, row 16) - already wired across to the tilt sensor's SCL. Now we need to bring this to the XIAO too: from row 16 column A -> the pin marked **D5** on the XIAO (that's GPIO7, the SCL pin in code). - **SDA** (data, row 17) - already wired across to the tilt sensor's SDA. Bring this to the XIAO: from row 17 column A -> the pin marked **D4** on the XIAO (that's GPIO6, the SDA pin in code). Why this matters: both little boards already have tiny resistors built in on the SDA and SCL lines (called pull-ups). That's why we don't have to add any extra resistors for the I2C - it would have been more work on a "raw" chip.
**Step 4 - The status LED with its safety resistor.**
We're adding a green LED that blinks when the level is, well, level. Push the 220R resistor into the breadboard so one leg is at row 22 column F and the other leg is at row 25 column F. Resistors don't care which way around they go, so either leg can be on either end. - Resistor leg 1: row 22 column F. - Resistor leg 2: row 25 column F. Then push the green LED in so its **long leg** (the positive side) is at row 25 column J, and its **short leg** (the flat-side, negative side) is at row 26 column J. The long and short leg are easy to tell apart: just look at the bottom of the LED before you bend the legs. - LED long leg -> row 25 column J (same row as the resistor's second leg). - LED short leg -> row 26 column J. Finish the LED with two jumpers: - From row 22 column J -> the pin marked **D2** on the XIAO (that's GPIO4 in code). This is the wire that turns the LED on. - From row 26 column J -> the bottom black rail (GND). Black wire. Why this matters: an LED is greedy - if you plug it straight into a pin, it tries to pull way too much electricity through itself and burns out in a second or two. The 220R resistor sits in line and politely says "slow down, you only get this much." That's why it's called a current-limit resistor.
**Step 5 - Plug in the USB-C cable and double-check.** Before you plug your laptop in, do a slow walk-around: - Every red wire goes to 3.3V on the top red rail. No red wire is anywhere near the 5V pin. - Every black wire ends up on a black rail (ground). - The two blue I2C wires (SDA and SCL) each touch THREE places: the tilt sensor, the OLED, and the XIAO. Both screens hearing the same wires is the whole point of I2C. - The LED's long leg goes through the resistor; the short leg goes to ground. When that all looks good, plug the USB-C cable from your laptop into the XIAO. The 5V from your laptop goes into the XIAO, the XIAO turns it into 3.3V on its 3V3 pin, and that 3.3V is what feeds the two I2C parts on the red rail. After upload, slowly tilt the breadboard - the screen should show a bubble drifting around like a real spirit level, and the green LED should light up when you hold it flat. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. This download is big (around 200 MB), so be patient. 3. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install these two, one at a time: - Search **"Adafruit SSD1306"** -> Install (when it asks about dependencies like Adafruit GFX and BusIO, click "Install all"). - Search **"Adafruit GFX Library"** -> make sure it is installed too (the SSD1306 install usually grabs it for you). 4. The MPU-6500 talks raw I2C through the built-in `Wire` library, so there is no library to install for the IMU. Nice. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the XIAO ESP32-C3 into your laptop with a **USB-C cable** (the same kind a lot of phones use). The tiny red power LED on the XIAO should light up. 2. **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> XIAO_ESP32C3** (it is in the long list, scroll until you see "XIAO_ESP32C3"). 3. **Tools -> Port** and pick the new one that appeared when you plugged in the XIAO (it will be `COM*` on Windows, `/dev/cu.usbmodem*` on a Mac, or `/dev/ttyACM0` on Linux). If you are not sure which one, unplug the XIAO, look at the list, plug it back in, and the new one that pops up is yours. 4. Nothing to fill in for this sketch - no WiFi password, no secret keys. The code is ready to go as is. 5. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the top-left of the IDE). The first line of the OLED should briefly show what the sketch wrote there, and the bottom of the IDE will say "Done uploading." 6. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the dropdown in the top-right of the Serial Monitor to **115200 baud** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` line in the sketch). You do not strictly need the Serial Monitor for the level to work - the OLED is the real display - but it is handy if something looks wrong. 7. **What you should see:** the OLED shows a circle (the "vial") with a small filled dot (the "bubble") inside it. Lay the breadboard flat on the table - the bubble should drift to the middle and the **green LED lights up**. Lift one corner of the breadboard a few degrees and the bubble slides toward the high corner, just like a real spirit level. The LED goes out as soon as you tilt past about 1.5 degrees. **Common gotchas:** - **First upload fails with "Failed to connect" or "Timed out waiting for packet header":** the XIAO sometimes needs to be put into flash mode by hand on the very first upload. Hold the tiny **BOOT** button on the XIAO, tap the **RESET** button while still holding BOOT, then let go of BOOT and click Upload again within a few seconds. - **OLED is blank but the LED still reacts to tilt:** the OLED's I2C address is usually `0x3C` but a few cheap ones ship as `0x3D`. If yours is dark, change the `OLED_ADDR` constant near the top of the sketch from `0x3C` to `0x3D` and re-upload. - **Bubble drifts off-center even when the breadboard is flat:** the IMU has not been calibrated yet, and every MPU-6500 chip has its own little zero-offset from the factory. That is normal - the "Things to change once it works" section below shows how to teach the sketch what "flat" means on your board. ## Talking points - **Why two addresses work on one bus:** I2C is like a party line. The XIAO shouts "0x3C, are you there?" and only the OLED answers. Then "0x68, what's your acceleration?" and only the IMU answers. The clock pin keeps everyone in step. - **Tilt from gravity:** when the board sits flat, gravity pulls straight down through the Z axis of the IMU and X / Y read ~0. Tip the breadboard and some of that 1 g leaks into X or Y. `atan2(ax, az)` and `atan2(ay, az)` give us the tilt angles in radians, which we convert to degrees. - **Why the bubble goes to the high side:** in a real spirit level the bubble floats to the high end because it is less dense than the liquid. We fake that by drawing the bubble offset in the same direction as the tilt (positive tilt -> bubble offset positive on screen). - **Why the LED has a deadband:** raw accel data jitters by a fraction of a degree even when still. If we lit the LED at "exactly 0.0 degrees" it would flicker. We light it only when both pitch and roll are within +/-1.0 degrees, and turn it off only above +/-1.5 degrees. That gap is called hysteresis. ## Things to change once it works - Add a calibration step: average 200 samples at boot and treat that as the new "zero" so the level reads true even if the IMU is glued in slightly crooked. - Show the numeric angles in the corners of the OLED. - Add a buzzer that beeps faster as you approach level (audible spirit level for when you can't see the screen). - Use the gyro as well as the accelerometer (complementary filter) so it stops jiggling when you tap the bench. - Make it battery-powered with a small LiPo on the XIAO's BAT pad and stick it in a 3D-printed case. ## Why this is interesting It is a real household tool you can hand to someone and they immediately understand what it does. Under the hood it teaches the three ideas you need for every future IMU project: sharing the I2C bus, turning raw accelerometer numbers into a physical angle, and smoothing noisy data so an output (the LED) doesn't chatter. From here, the same pattern scales up to a self-balancing robot, a step counter, or an orientation-aware game controller.

projects.name: Two-ESP32 Walkie-Talkie Lights
projects.power_supply: Two USB-C cables, one to each board (5V each) - the XIAO and the NodeMCU each get their own power from a laptop, phone charger, or USB hub.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Two tiny boards on opposite sides of the room, no wires between them. Push the button on one and the red LED on the other one blinks on. Push it again, it blinks off. **Why it's fun**: It feels like magic the first time. You stand in the kitchen, your dad's in the living room, you press the button, and his light flips on. That's the same trick every smart light switch in the world uses, and you just built one. ## Parts list - 1x Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 (the "remote" - has the button) - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the "lamp" - has the external LED) - 1x Tactile push-button (wired to the XIAO) - 1x Red LED (wired to the NodeMCU) - 1x 220R resistor (current-limit for the LED) - 1x Breadboard (everything plugs into this, no soldering) - Jumper wires (M-M for breadboard rails, F-M for board pins) - Two USB-C cables (one per board) - Existing GeeFam WiFi network ## Wiring notes This project uses **two** boards that talk to each other over WiFi. The little one (XIAO ESP32-C3) watches the button. The bigger one (NodeMCU-32S) blinks the LED. They never touch each other with wires - only with radio waves. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the boards:** - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every wire that goes "back home" ends here. - **5V / USB-C** - the power input from the USB cable plugged into your laptop or phone charger. - **D2 on the XIAO** - the pin marked D2 on the silkscreen. Inside the chip it is GPIO 4. We will say "D2" because that is what is printed on the board. - **D16 on the NodeMCU-32S** - the pin marked D16 on the silkscreen. On this board the silkscreen numbers match the GPIO numbers, so D16 is also GPIO 16. - **The long red and blue strips down the side of the breadboard** are for power and ground. We only use the ground strip in this build.
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard.** - Put the breadboard flat on your desk so the rows of numbers face you. - Pick one long blue strip running down the side - that strip will be our ground (GND). Every wire that needs to go to 0V will end on this strip. - We do not need the red strip for this build, because each board powers itself from its own USB-C cable.
**Step 2 - Plant the push-button on the XIAO side.** The button is the part we press to "talk" to the other board. - Push the tactile button into the breadboard so two of its legs land in row 3. The drawing shows one leg at hole E3. - The other leg of the button (the one across from E3) goes to the ground strip. Use one male-to-male jumper from F3 over to a hole in the blue GND strip. The button has four legs but they are joined in pairs inside. As long as one pair lands in row 3 and the other pair points across the middle gap, you are fine. If the button will not push in, rotate it 90 degrees and try again - that is a common gotcha.
**Step 3 - Hook the XIAO ESP32-C3 to the button.** The XIAO is the tiny board. It sits off to the side of the breadboard and we reach it with female-to-male jumper wires (the female end clips onto the XIAO's pin, the male end pokes into the breadboard). - Female-to-male jumper from **the pin marked D2** on the XIAO (that is GPIO 4 inside the chip) to hole **E5** on the breadboard. That same column (row 5) needs to connect to the free leg of the button - the easiest way is to add a short male-to-male jumper from a hole in row 5 across to row 3 where the button sits. - Female-to-male jumper from the XIAO's **GND** pin to the blue ground strip. - Plug the XIAO's USB-C cable into your laptop or a phone charger. That gives it 5V power. **Why this matters:** there is no extra resistor on the button. The XIAO has a tiny "pull-up" resistor hidden inside the chip that the code switches on. That means the pin reads as "high" when nothing is happening, and snaps to "low" when you press the button and connect it to ground. Fewer parts, same job.
**Step 4 - Build the LED side on the NodeMCU-32S board.**
Now we wire up the part that lights up. - Take the 220 ohm resistor (the small one with red-red-brown-gold stripes) and push one leg into hole **E22** and the other leg into hole **E25**. Resistors do not care which way around they go. - Take the red LED. Look at the legs - one is **longer** than the other. Push the **long leg** into hole **F25** (so it lines up with the far side of the resistor). Push the **short leg** into hole **F26**. - Add a male-to-male jumper from hole **F26** over to the blue ground strip. **Why this matters:** the 220 ohm resistor is the LED's seatbelt. The pin on the NodeMCU pushes out about 3.3 volts, which is way more than the LED wants. Without the resistor the LED would gulp too much current and burn out in a flash (sometimes a literal puff of smoke). The resistor slows the flow down to a safe sip. The long leg is the "+" side - it has to face the side that the resistor is feeding power in from. If you flip the LED around the wrong way it just stays dark - it will not break, so do not panic if your first try does not glow.
**Step 5 - Hook the NodeMCU-32S to the LED row.** The NodeMCU-32S is the bigger of the two boards. It can sit off to the side of the breadboard and reach it with female-to-male jumpers too, or you can plug it across the middle gap if there is room. - Female-to-male jumper from **the pin marked D16** on the NodeMCU-32S to hole **E22** on the breadboard. That is the pin that the code switches on and off to make the LED blink. - Female-to-male jumper from the NodeMCU-32S **GND** pin to the blue ground strip. - Plug the NodeMCU-32S's own USB-C cable into a laptop or phone charger. Now both boards are powered. **Why D16 and not some other pin?** A few of the pins on the NodeMCU-32S (like the one marked D5) wake up in a weird half-on state for a split second every time the board powers on. If you put the LED on one of those pins it flickers every time you plug in, which is annoying. The pin marked D16 wakes up nice and quiet, so the LED only does what your code tells it to.
**Step 6 - Final check before you flash.** - Trace the path with your finger: button leg -> XIAO D2. Other button leg -> GND. XIAO GND -> GND strip. That is the talker side done. - Trace the listener side: NodeMCU D16 -> resistor -> LED long leg -> LED short leg -> GND strip. NodeMCU GND -> GND strip. - Both USB-C cables are plugged in. Both boards have a tiny power LED glowing. - The two boards are **not** wired to each other. They do not need to be. They will find each other over WiFi once the code is flashed. This is the trickiest part of the whole build because there are two boards on the go at once - if something does not work, only touch one side at a time when you are checking. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). You will flash the *same* sketch twice - once to the NodeMCU, once to the XIAO - just changing which `ROLE_` line is uncommented. **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. File -> Preferences -> "Additional boards manager URLs": paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager. Search for `esp32` and install "esp32 by Espressif Systems" (it is a big download, give it a minute). 3. No extra libraries to install - `WiFi.h`, `HTTPClient.h`, `WebServer.h`, and `ESPmDNS.h` all come bundled with the esp32 board package you just installed. **Every time you flash (do the NodeMCU first, then the XIAO):** 1. Plug the board into the laptop with a USB-C cable. Use a cable you know carries data, not a charge-only one - if the board does not show up in step 2, that is the first thing to suspect. 2. Tools -> Board -> esp32. Pick the right one: - NodeMCU: choose "ESP32 Dev Module" (or "NodeMCU-32S" if you see it). - XIAO: choose "XIAO_ESP32C3". 3. Tools -> Port. On Windows it shows up as `COM3`, `COM4`, etc. On a Mac it is `/dev/cu.usbmodem*` or `/dev/cu.usbserial*`. Unplug the board, see which port disappears, plug it back in, and pick the one that came back. 4. Open the sketch. Make sure exactly one of these is uncommented and the other is commented out: - For the NodeMCU pass: `#define ROLE_NODEMCU` uncommented, `// #define ROLE_XIAO` commented. - For the XIAO pass: `#define ROLE_XIAO` uncommented, `// #define ROLE_NODEMCU` commented. 5. Find the line `const char* WIFI_PASS = "PASSWORD_HERE";` and replace `PASSWORD_HERE` with the real GeeFam WiFi password. Keep the quotes. 6. Click the Upload button (the right-arrow icon, top-left). On the **NodeMCU**, if you see `Connecting....._____....._____` and it gives up, hold down the BOOT button on the board, click Upload again, and let go of BOOT once you see the upload bar start filling. The XIAO usually does not need this trick. 7. Tools -> Serial Monitor. Set the baud rate (bottom-right of the Serial Monitor) to **115200**. 8. What you should see: - **NodeMCU**: a few dots while it connects, then `WiFi up, IP: 192.168.x.x`, then `mDNS up: http://nodemcu-lamp.local/`. Open that URL in any browser on the same WiFi - you should see `NodeMCU lamp. LED is OFF`. - **XIAO** (after you flash it second): `WiFi up, IP: 192.168.x.x` and `Will talk to http://nodemcu-lamp.local/led/toggle`. Push the button on the breadboard - the NodeMCU's red LED should flip on, and the XIAO's Serial Monitor should print `peer replied 200 : OK on`. Push again, LED goes off. **Common gotchas:** - **GeeFam is 2.4 GHz, right?** ESP32 chips cannot see 5 GHz networks at all. If your router broadcasts a separate 5 GHz SSID, make sure `WIFI_SSID` points at the 2.4 GHz one. - **BOOT button trick on the NodeMCU's first upload.** If Upload hangs on `Connecting...`, hold BOOT, click Upload, release BOOT when the progress bar starts. The XIAO ESP32-C3 has native USB and usually skips this dance. - **LED in backwards = no light, no damage.** The long leg is the anode and goes to the 220R resistor coming from GPIO16; the short leg goes to GND. If the LED stays dark even when the Serial Monitor says `LED ON`, pull it out and flip it around. ## Bring-up sequence (read before flashing) This project uses mDNS so we don't have to chase IP addresses. The NodeMCU advertises itself on the LAN as `nodemcu-lamp.local`, and the XIAO talks to that name. No hardcoded peer IP, no chicken-and-egg re-flash cycle. 1. Open the sketch. Replace `PASSWORD_HERE` with the GeeFam WiFi password (there's a `// TODO` comment marking the spot). 2. **Flash the NodeMCU first:** uncomment `#define ROLE_NODEMCU`, comment out `#define ROLE_XIAO`, upload. Open Serial Monitor (115200) and watch for `mDNS up: http://nodemcu-lamp.local/`. Optional sanity check: from any browser on the same WiFi, open `http://nodemcu-lamp.local/` and you should see the lamp's status text. 3. **Flash the XIAO second:** flip the `ROLE_` defines (XIAO on, NodeMCU off), upload. Open Serial Monitor and you should see it print `Will talk to http://nodemcu-lamp.local/led/toggle`. 4. Press the button on the XIAO. The NodeMCU's LED toggles. The XIAO's serial log shows `-> GET ...` and `peer replied 200 : OK on`. If mDNS resolution misbehaves on your network, the description for the "Things to change" section below explains how to drop back to hardcoded IPs. ## Talking points - "Press here, light there." This is the heart of every smart-home gadget: a sensor on one device, an actuator on another, glued together by a network. - The two boards have different jobs in this build: the XIAO is purely a **client** (it sends one HTTP request when the button is pressed) and the NodeMCU is purely a **server** (it listens for requests and toggles the LED). That asymmetry keeps the sketch small. The "make it bidirectional" version is in "Things to change" below. - We're using plain HTTP GET requests. When the XIAO sees a button press, it sends `GET /led/toggle` to `nodemcu-lamp.local`. The NodeMCU's web server hears that request, flips the LED, and replies with "OK". No cloud, no app - just two boards on the same WiFi. - mDNS is why we don't need to type IP addresses. It's a tiny "who is here" announcement system that lets devices on the same LAN find each other by name (`somename.local`). The NodeMCU shouts "I'm `nodemcu-lamp`", the XIAO listens, done. - This pattern (HTTP requests between devices) scales. Once the Orange Pi is running and hosting a real MQTT broker, you replace the direct HTTP call with "publish to topic" and "subscribe to topic" - same idea, less wiring. ## Things to change once it works - Make it bidirectional. Right now the XIAO is purely a remote: it has no web server and the NodeMCU never sends it anything. To go two-way, add a `WebServer` on the XIAO with a `/notify` route, and add a second button on the NodeMCU (a free GPIO like 17 or 18, wired the same way as the XIAO's button) that fires an HTTP GET to `xiao-remote.local/notify`. The XIAO has no onboard LED, so use the Serial Monitor as its "output" - or wire a second LED + 220R on a free XIAO pin. - Replace mDNS with a hardcoded IP if `*.local` resolution is flaky on your network (some routers strip mDNS). Read each board's IP from Serial Monitor at boot, paste the NodeMCU's IP into a `const char* PEER_IP` on the XIAO, and change the URL from `nodemcu-lamp.local` to that IP string. - Swap "toggle on press" for "pulse for 2 seconds and turn off" so the lamp acts more like a notification than a switch. - When the Orange Pi is alive, replace the direct board-to-board HTTP with both boards publishing to an MQTT broker on the Pi. This is the actual "hub and leaves" architecture from the kit notes. - Use the XIAO's deep sleep (wakes on a GPIO change) so a coin cell could power the remote for weeks. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project that uses BOTH ESP32 boards together, which is what the whole kit is structured around. It proves the "leaf endpoint" architecture: each board can independently sense, decide, and talk to peers over WiFi. The mental jump from "one board, one program" to "two boards cooperating" is the same jump you make from a desk calculator to the internet - and once it clicks, every distributed-system idea afterward (MQTT, Home Assistant, REST APIs, microservices) is just a refinement of what you built here.

projects.name: Hallway Weather Window
projects.power_supply: USB-A to Micro-USB from laptop or 5V/1A charger into the ESP32. 3.3V rail feeds the DHT11; 5V rail feeds LCD, relay coil, and (via COM/NO) the LED strip. Cap strip at ~200 mA on this rail; longer strips need a separate 5V/2A supply, GND tied.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Hang it in the hallway. A little screen shows the temperature inside your house and a one-word forecast pulled live from the internet (like SUNNY or RAINY). When rain is coming, a blue light strip flicks on so you see it on your way out the door. **Why it's fun**: It is basically a tiny weather robot that yells "TAKE A COAT!" at your family before school. Your friends have to check a phone to know if it will rain - you just glance at the wall. ## Parts list - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain, WiFi-capable) - 1x LCD 1602 with I2C Backpack (display) - 1x DHT11 Temperature & Humidity Sensor (indoor reading - 3-pin breakout preferred) - 1x 1-channel Relay Module (switches the LED strip) - 1x LED 5mm Blue (status indicator while talking to the internet) - 1x 220R resistor (current limit for the blue LED) - 1x Breadboard 830-point - DuPont jumper wires (M-M, M-F, F-F mix) - 1x USB-A to Micro-USB cable (power + programming) You also need (not in this allocation, supplied separately): - A short 5V LED strip (or single LED-on-leads). The relay switches its POSITIVE leg between the 5V rail and the strip - see the wiring diagram. Keep it short: about 200 mA max at 5V if you are powering everything from one USB port (see "Power budget" below). - A free Open-Meteo API endpoint (no key required) - the sketch already points at Andy's home grid square in northern England; change the lat/lon at the top to wherever your hallway is. - If your DHT11 is the bare 4-pin sensor (not the small breakout PCB), add a 4.7k-10k pull-up resistor from DATA to 3.3V. The blue 3-pin breakout has this on board already. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - a pin that gives you 3.3 volts of power (gentler than 5V). - **5V (or VIN)** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. - **GND** - the 0V side, ground. Every "minus" wire ends up here. - **D4, D2, D21, D22, D25** - the pins marked with those names on the board. The numbers match the GPIO numbers in the code, so "D4" in code and "D4" on the board are the same pin. - **EN** - reset button (we don't wire to this, but it's the button you press if the ESP32 acts weird).
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard power rails.** The breadboard has two long strips running down one side - the long red/blue strip running down the side is called a rail. The red one is for power, the blue one is for ground (the 0V side). - Run a jumper from the ESP32 pin marked **3V3** over to the red power rail. This rail will feed the DHT11 sensor. - Run a jumper from any **GND** pin on the ESP32 to the blue ground rail. This is your "common ground" - every minus wire in the project will end up touching this blue rail. If you skip this, the project will work once and then break, and you will spend hours trying to find out why. Trust me on this one.
**Step 2 - Plug in the DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor.** The DHT11 has 3 legs. Push it into the breadboard so each leg sits in its own row (rows 5, 6, and 7). - DHT11 **VCC** (power input, the leg marked + or VCC) goes to the red power rail (3.3V). Use a red jumper wire. - DHT11 **DAT** (the middle leg, data) goes to the ESP32 pin marked **D4**. Use any color jumper. - DHT11 **GND** (the leg marked - or GND) goes to the blue ground rail. Use a black jumper. **Why this matters:** the DHT11 talks back to the ESP32 using 3.3V signals. If we powered it from 5V, the data line would also push 5V into the ESP32's pin, which is only built for 3.3V. Over time that can hurt the chip. Sticking with 3.3V keeps everyone happy.
**Step 3 - Plug in the LCD screen.** The LCD has a small black board glued to the back called an I2C backpack. That backpack turns sixteen messy wires into just four neat ones. The four pins are usually labeled GND, VCC, SDA, SCL. - LCD **VCC** (power input) goes to the ESP32 pin marked **5V** (or **VIN**). The LCD needs 5V, not 3.3V, or the screen will be too dim to read. - LCD **GND** goes to the blue ground rail. - LCD **SDA** goes to the ESP32 pin marked **D21**. - LCD **SCL** goes to the ESP32 pin marked **D22**. **Why this matters:** SDA and SCL are the two wires that carry the message "show this text." The ESP32 is already set up to use D21 and D22 for this kind of chat, so we don't change anything in the code. Just plug them in.
**Step 4 - Build the blue status LED with its resistor.**
The blue LED has two legs. The **long leg** is plus (the side electricity comes in). The **short leg** is minus (the side electricity leaves). - Push the blue LED into the breadboard so the long leg sits in row 22 and the short leg sits in row 23. - Take the 220 ohm resistor (red-red-brown-gold stripes). It does not matter which end is which. Push one leg into row 22 (next to the LED's long leg) and the other leg into row 19. - Run a jumper from row 19 over to the ESP32 pin marked **D2**. - Run a black jumper from row 23 (the LED's short leg) over to the blue ground rail. **Why this matters:** LEDs are greedy. If you plug one straight to a pin, it tries to drink all the electricity at once and burns out in a flash (literally). The 220 ohm resistor is like a tiny straw - it slows the flow down to a safe sip. Every LED in your life should have a resistor friend. There is also a sneaky trick here: D2 has a rule that it must be low (not lit) for half a second at startup, otherwise the ESP32 gets confused about how to boot. Our LED-with-resistor-to-ground path keeps D2 nice and low at startup, so we are following the rule by accident. Just don't ever wire D2 up to 3.3V directly, or your ESP32 will refuse to start.
**Step 5 - Wire the relay module.** The relay is a tiny robot switch. The ESP32 tells it "click!" and a much bigger circuit (the LED strip) turns on. The relay has 3 pins on the small-signal side (VCC, GND, IN) and 3 big screw terminals on the high-power side (COM, NO, NC). - Relay **VCC** (power input) goes to the ESP32 pin marked **5V**. - Relay **GND** goes to the blue ground rail. - Relay **IN** goes to the ESP32 pin marked **D25**. Now the high-power side, where the LED strip lives. We do NOT use **NC** (normally closed). Leave that one empty. - Take the wire from your 5V LED-strip power supply (the plus wire) and screw it into the relay terminal marked **COM**. - Take the LED strip's plus wire and screw it into the relay terminal marked **NO** (normally open). - The LED strip's minus wire goes straight to the blue ground rail, the same one everything else uses. **Why this matters:** the relay clicks COM and NO together when it fires. That's why the strip only lights when the ESP32 says "go." The code also sets D25 to a "don't fire" state before turning the pin on, so the relay doesn't pop at boot and scare you.
**Step 6 - Double-check ground, then plug in USB.** Before you power up, walk through the build with a parent and trace every black wire with your finger. The ESP32 GND, the breadboard's blue rail, the LCD's GND, the relay's GND, and the LED strip's minus all need to end up at the same blue rail. If even one is floating, the project will act haunted (work for a second, then quit). When everything looks good, plug the USB-A to Micro-USB cable into the ESP32. The LCD backlight should glow, and the little blue LED on the ESP32 board (and your blue LED) should be ready to take orders. If you plan to drive a long LED strip (more than about a meter), give it its own 5V power supply rated at 2 amps. Just make sure that supply's GND is also tied to the blue rail. Same ground, always. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click OK. 2. **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Search `esp32` and install "**esp32 by Espressif Systems**" (it is a big download, give it a few minutes). 3. **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install these three: - "**LiquidCrystal I2C**" by Frank de Brabander (the screen) - "**DHT sensor library**" by Adafruit (the temp sensor). When it asks about "Adafruit Unified Sensor", click **Install all**. - "**ArduinoJson**" by Benoit Blanchon - pick a **6.x** version, not 7.x. 4. **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with the **Micro-USB cable**. The red power LED should come on. If nothing lights up, try a different cable - lots of Micro-USB cables are charge-only with no data wires. 2. **Tools -> Port**. Pick the new entry that appeared: on Windows it is **COM3 / COM4 / COM5...**, on a Mac **/dev/cu.usbserial-...** or **/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART**. If nothing new shows up, you need the USB-serial driver - search "CP210x driver" or "CH340 driver" depending on the chip next to the USB socket. 3. In the sketch, scroll to the "**user-edit area**" near the top: - Replace `PASSWORD_HERE` with your WiFi password (keep the quote marks). - Change `WIFI_SSID` from `GeeFam` if your network is called something else. - Change `LAT` and `LON` to your town. Google "lat lon " and copy the two numbers. 4. Click the **Upload** button (round right-arrow, top-left). It says "Compiling..." for ~30 seconds, then "Connecting....." while it flashes. **If "Connecting....." gets stuck with lots of dots**: hold down the little **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until you see "Writing at 0x..." appear, then let go. You usually only need this trick once. 5. When the bottom bar says "**Done uploading.**", open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. Bottom-right of that window, set baud to **115200** (it defaults to 9600 which shows gibberish). 6. Press the **EN** (reset) button on the ESP32. You should see: - "Connecting to WiFi..." then dots - "WiFi connected, IP: 192.168.x.x" - the ESP32 joined your network - "Indoor: 21.3 C, 47% RH" - the DHT11 reading - "Weather: SUNNY" (or CLOUDY/RAINY) once it talks to Open-Meteo Meanwhile the LCD lights up with the temperature on top and a scrolling weather word on the bottom. The blue LED blinks each time the board fetches weather. If rain is forecast, the relay goes *click* and the LED strip switches on. **Common gotchas:** - **ESP32s only see 2.4 GHz WiFi.** If your router or phone hotspot is 5 GHz only, the board sits forever printing dots and never gets an IP. Make sure the 2.4 GHz band is on, and the SSID matches the 2.4 GHz name exactly (some routers add "-5G" to the 5 GHz name). - **"Connecting....." that never finishes on first upload.** Hold the **BOOT** button the whole time the IDE says "Connecting", let go once "Writing at..." starts. - **LCD lights up but shows nothing, or shows black squares.** Turn the tiny blue contrast pot on the back of the I2C backpack with a small screwdriver until letters appear. If still totally blank, double-check SDA->GPIO 21 and SCL->GPIO 22 are not swapped. ## Power budget (read this before adding more LEDs) A laptop USB-A port supplies roughly 500 mA at 5V. From that the ESP32 itself takes 80-240 mA (bursty on WiFi TX), the LCD backlight 20-40 mA, and the relay coil ~70 mA when energised. That leaves a hard ceiling of around 150-200 mA for the LED strip if you want a stable system - call it 1-2 short WS2812-style segments or a couple of plain 5V LEDs in parallel with their own resistors. If you want a longer strip, switch to a **dedicated 5V/2A supply for the strip**, feed its + into the relay's COM via a separate wire, and **tie its GND to the ESP32 GND** (the relay only switches the + line; the grounds must stay common or nothing turns on). ## Talking points - The LCD is talked to over **I2C**, a 2-wire serial bus. The same two pins can address up to ~120 devices because each has a unique address (the backpack is usually `0x27` or `0x3F`). The sketch probes both at boot and constructs the LCD object once it knows which address answered. - The weather data comes from **Open-Meteo**, a free no-key API. We GET an **HTTPS** URL, the server replies with JSON, ArduinoJson plucks out the field we want. HTTPS on ESP32 needs a `WiFiClientSecure`; we call `setInsecure()` on it because we don't care about cert validation for a hobby weather widget. - **Why a relay for a 5V LED strip?** You don't strictly need one - a transistor would do. But (a) we have a relay in the kit and (b) the satisfying *click* is half the fun for a 10-year-old. It is also the right answer the moment you want to switch a 12V strip or a fan. - The forecast horizon is the next 12 hours. If the probability of precipitation in any of those hours exceeds 50%, the rain-warning light comes on. ## Things to change once it works - Add a second display mode (long-press a future button) showing tomorrow's high and low. - Replace the DHT11 with a DHT22 or BME280 - DHT11 is fine for whole degrees, but the BME280 also gives barometric pressure, which lets you predict weather changes a few hours ahead just from the trend. - Swap the polling loop for a deep-sleep-then-publish-then-sleep cycle if you ever want to run this on battery. - Send the indoor readings to Mosquitto on the Orange Pi One once that hub is online (see the kit-level CLAUDE.md - the Pi is the intended hub). - Add a buzzer that beeps once when the relay first switches on, then stays quiet. - Pin the Open-Meteo root CA instead of using `setInsecure()`, so a tampered DNS reply cannot feed you a bogus forecast. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project in the kit that **leaves the room**. Up to here, everything has been a closed loop: a button presses, an LED lights, a sensor reads, a relay clicks. Here, the ESP32 reaches out across the internet over TLS, asks a public weather service a question, parses the answer, and acts on it - all in about 250 lines of C++. Combining that internet data with a local sensor reading (the DHT11) is the entire essence of IoT in one project. After this, the rest of the kit's projects become variations on the same theme.

projects.name: MQTT Home: Pi broker + XIAO sensor publisher
projects.power_supply: Orange Pi One: 5V / 2A wall adapter via the 4.0/1.7mm barrel jack (NOT micro-USB). XIAO ESP32-C3: 5V over USB-C from a laptop or phone charger. DHT11 draws power from the XIAO's 3V3 rail. Router + WiFi assumed already powered.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A tiny sensor sits on your shelf and quietly sniffs the room's temperature and humidity. Every 30 seconds it whispers the numbers across WiFi to a little computer in another room, and you watch them pop up on your laptop screen. **Why it's fun**: This is your first project where two gadgets in different parts of the house actually talk to each other - one listens, one talks, and you're the puppet master in the middle. Unplug the sensor and a "I'm gone!" message shows up on the laptop a few seconds later, like the gadget left you a goodbye note. ## Parts list - Orange Pi One (H3) - the protagonist. Already booted into Armbian with `mosquitto` and `mosquitto-clients` installed (see the resume checklist in the OrangePi_One folder). - Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 - the leaf sensor node. - DHT11 temperature + humidity sensor (3-pin module variant has its own pull-up; bare 4-pin DHT11 needs a 10K resistor between DATA and 3V3). - 1x 10K resistor (1/8W) for the DHT11 pull-up. - Mini breadboard + a handful of M-M jumpers to hold the XIAO and DHT11. - Router / WiFi on `GeeFam` (2.4 GHz) - Pi on Ethernet, XIAO on WiFi, both on the same subnet. ## Wiring notes This project has two computers talking to each other over your home WiFi. The Orange Pi One is the "post office" (we call it the broker). The XIAO ESP32-C3 is a little weather reporter that mails temperature and humidity to the post office every 30 seconds. Most of the wiring is actually network plugs, not breadboard wires. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the XIAO ESP32-C3 board:** - **3V3** = the pin that gives out 3.3 volts of power (the XIAO's "small power" pin) - **GND** = the 0V side, also called ground (every circuit needs this) - **D0 to D10** = the pins along the edges where you plug in sensors. The number stamped on the board is NOT the same as the GPIO number the code uses (we will show both) - **USB-C** = the oval plug on the end where you connect the charging cable - **rail** = the long red or blue strip running down the side of the breadboard. Every hole in that strip is connected together
**Step 1 - Power up the Orange Pi One (the post office).** - Plug an Ethernet cable from the Pi's network port into a spare LAN port on your home router (the one that broadcasts the `GeeFam` WiFi). - Plug the 5V / 2A wall adapter into the small round barrel jack on the Pi. The plug has a 4.0mm outer and 1.7mm inner pin - it only fits one way. **Why this matters:** Do NOT power the Orange Pi from the micro-USB port, even if it looks like it would work. The micro-USB port on this board has a known problem where the Pi quietly browns out under load and reboots in the middle of a job. The barrel jack is the safe way.
**Step 2 - Find the Pi on your network.** Log in to your router's admin page (often `192.168.88.1` on a GeeFam network) and look in the list of connected devices for something called `orangepione`. Write down its IP address. It will look like `192.168.88.something`. We will call this number `PI_IP` from now on.
**Step 3 - Turn the Pi into a post office (install Mosquitto).** From your laptop, open a terminal and connect to the Pi over SSH: ```bash ssh root@PI_IP ``` (Replace `PI_IP` with the number you wrote down.) Once you are logged in, run these commands one at a time: ```bash apt update && apt install -y mosquitto mosquitto-clients cat > /etc/mosquitto/conf.d/lan.conf <<'EOF' listener 1883 0.0.0.0 allow_anonymous true EOF systemctl restart mosquitto systemctl enable mosquitto ``` Check it is working by typing `ss -tlnp | grep 1883`. You should see a line that mentions `mosquitto` and `0.0.0.0:1883`. That means the post office is open for letters from any computer on the home network. **Why this matters:** Mosquitto is the program that holds the mailbox. `listener 1883 0.0.0.0` tells it to accept letters from any computer on the home WiFi, not just from the Pi itself. `allow_anonymous true` means no password yet - that is OK for learning at home, but do not do this on a public network.
**Step 4 - Put the breadboard and XIAO together.** Sit your XIAO ESP32-C3 next to the breadboard. You do not need to push the XIAO into the breadboard for this project - the four wires can run straight from the XIAO pins to the breadboard holes. The USB-C plug on the XIAO faces away from the breadboard so you can plug a cable in without bumping anything.
**Step 5 - Plug in the DHT11 sensor.** The DHT11 is the blue brick with holes in the front. It has three pins sticking out of the bottom. Push the DHT11 into the breadboard so its pins land in column E: - DHT11 power pin (the one marked `+` or `VCC`) goes into hole **E10** - DHT11 data pin (the middle one, marked `DAT` or `OUT`) goes into hole **E12** - DHT11 ground pin (the one marked `-` or `GND`) goes into hole **E14**
**Step 6 - Add the 10K resistor (the helper).** The 10K resistor is a tiny tube with colored stripes (brown-black-orange-gold, or sometimes brown-black-black-red on the 1% kind). It does not have a long leg or short leg - either end can go in either way. - Bend the legs so one end goes into hole **B12** and the other end goes into hole **B18**. Hole B12 is on the same row as the DHT11 data pin. Hole B18 will be the row we pull up to 3.3V in the next step. **Why this matters:** The DHT11's data pin only knows how to pull the wire down to 0V - it cannot push the wire up to 3.3V by itself. The 10K resistor quietly pulls the wire up to 3.3V whenever the DHT11 is not talking, so the XIAO can see a clean signal. Without this resistor, the data wire floats around at random voltages and the readings come out as nonsense or just fail with a checksum error. If your DHT11 came pre-soldered onto a little blue board with three pins on a header (not the four-pin bare module), it already has this resistor built in and you can skip this step.
**Step 7 - Run the jumper wires from XIAO to breadboard.** Grab four male-male jumper wires. Try to use red for power, black for ground, and any other color for the signal so you can tell them apart later. From the XIAO ESP32-C3, run these wires: - **XIAO 3V3 pin** -> the long red strip on the top edge of the breadboard (the top "rail") - **XIAO GND pin** -> the long blue/black strip on the top edge of the breadboard (the top ground rail) - **XIAO pin marked D1** (this is GPIO 3 in the code) -> hole **C22** on the breadboard Now add two short jumper wires to finish connecting things up on the breadboard: - A red wire from **A10** (the DHT11 power row) to the top red rail - this powers the DHT11 - A black wire from **A14** (the DHT11 ground row) to the top blue rail - this grounds the DHT11 - A red wire from **A18** (the bottom of the resistor) to the top red rail - this pulls the data line up to 3.3V through the helper resistor - An orange or yellow wire from **C12** (the DHT11 data row) to **C22** (where D1 is) - this carries the temperature and humidity readings to the XIAO
**Step 8 - Plug the XIAO into your laptop.** Use a USB-C cable to plug the XIAO ESP32-C3 into your laptop or a phone charger. The XIAO's blue power LED should light up, and so should the DHT11's tiny power light if it has one. If nothing lights up, unplug right away and double-check that the red and black wires did not get swapped.
**Step 9 - Tell the code where the post office is.** Open the Arduino sketch and find the line that says `MQTT_HOST`. Change the value to the `PI_IP` number you wrote down in Step 2. Then upload the sketch to the XIAO (Tools -> Board -> XIAO_ESP32C3, then the Upload button).
**Step 10 - Watch the letters arrive.** On your laptop, open the Arduino Serial Monitor and set the speed to 115200 baud. You should see the XIAO connect to the `GeeFam` WiFi and then connect to the broker on the Pi. Now go back to the SSH window on the Pi and run: ```bash mosquitto_sub -h localhost -t 'home/livingroom/#' -v ``` Within a second or two you should see a line like `home/livingroom/status online`. Then every 30 seconds, two more lines will appear with the temperature and humidity. Try cupping your hand over the DHT11 and breathing on it - the humidity number will jump up. That is your weather reporter mailing live readings to the post office in your house. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). The XIAO ESP32-C3 is the only thing that needs flashing - the Pi side is just `mosquitto` running as a service (covered in Wiring notes above). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the box labelled "Additional boards manager URLs", paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click OK. 2. **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, search for `esp32`, install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"** (wait for the green "INSTALLED" tag - it is a big download). 3. **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> XIAO_ESP32C3**. 4. **Tools -> Manage Libraries**, install these three (search by name, click Install on each): - **PubSubClient** by Nick O'Leary - **DHT sensor library** by Adafruit - **Adafruit Unified Sensor** by Adafruit (the DHT library will nag for this one) **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the XIAO into the laptop with a **USB-C** cable. Make sure the cable can carry data - some charge-only cables look identical and the board just will not show up. 2. **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged in (looks like `COM5` on Windows or `/dev/cu.usbmodem*` on a Mac). If nothing new shows up, unplug and try a different cable. 3. Open the sketch and edit two lines near the top: - `WIFI_PASSWORD` - change `"PASSWORD_HERE"` to your real GeeFam WiFi password. - `MQTT_HOST` - change `"192.168.88.40"` to whatever IP the Orange Pi got from the router. 4. Click the **Upload** arrow (the round button with the right-pointing arrow, top-left). If the upload hangs on "Connecting....." for more than 10 seconds: hold the small **BOOT** button on the XIAO, tap **RESET** once while still holding BOOT, then let go of BOOT. Click Upload again. (Newer ESP32-C3 boards usually do this automatically, but the trick is the rescue if it does not.) 5. When it says "Done uploading", open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the dropdown in the bottom-right to **115200 baud** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch). 6. Within a few seconds you should see: ``` WiFi: connecting to GeeFam .... WiFi: IP=192.168.88.xx MQTT: connecting to 192.168.88.40:1883 ... ok ``` Then every 30 seconds a line with the temperature and humidity. On the Pi, the `mosquitto_sub` window from the Wiring step should print `home/livingroom/status online` first, then a temperature and humidity line every half minute. High-five your dad. **Common gotchas:** - **Wrong WiFi band.** The XIAO ESP32-C3 only sees **2.4 GHz** networks. If GeeFam shows up on your phone but the XIAO prints endless dots after "WiFi: connecting", your router is probably handing it the 5 GHz SSID - log into the router and either split the bands or make a 2.4 GHz-only guest network for the XIAO. - **Upload stuck on "Connecting....."**. First time only: do the BOOT-hold + RESET-tap trick from step 4. Almost every ESP32-C3 needs it once. - **Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `@$#@!`**. The baud rate dropdown is wrong - set it to **115200** (anything else turns the text into alien characters, but the sketch is fine). ## Talking points - **Pub/sub vs request/response.** The XIAO doesn't know or care who's listening. It pushes readings to a topic; anything that cares (a dashboard, Home Assistant, a Node-RED flow on the same Pi) subscribes. Adding a second display device later is zero changes to the publisher. - **Last-will testament.** `connect()` registers `home/livingroom/status = "offline"` as a "send this if I die". If the XIAO loses power or WiFi, the broker fires that message after the keepalive expires. That's how the Pi can know the node is gone without polling it. - **Retained messages.** Both readings are published with the retained flag. A subscriber that connects ten minutes later still gets the last known value immediately instead of waiting up to 30 seconds for the next one. - **The hub/leaf split is now real.** Up until now every project on the kit ran end-to-end on a single board. This one stops working unless both halves are alive on the network at the same time. That's the architectural shift that makes the rest of the kit's planned services (Home Assistant, Grafana) possible. ## Things to change once it works - **Add a second leaf.** Flash a similar sketch onto the NodeMCU-32S with topic `home/garage/temperature` and watch both streams in one `mosquitto_sub -t 'home/#' -v` window. - **Turn on auth.** Replace `allow_anonymous true` with a password file (`mosquitto_passwd -c /etc/mosquitto/passwd andy`), and pass the credentials into `mqtt.connect()`. - **Persist to disk.** `apt install sqlite3`, then run a tiny Python loop on the Pi that subscribes and inserts rows into a SQLite table. That's the foundation of the future InfluxDB + Grafana setup without committing to the heavy stack yet. - **Add the OLED.** Wire the 0.96" OLED to the NodeMCU-32S and have it subscribe to `home/livingroom/temperature` so it shows the XIAO's reading on its own screen. First "device A talks to device B via the Pi" moment. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project on the kit where the Orange Pi earns its place. Up to now it's been a powered-off board with a barrel-jack gotcha. After this, it's the always-on hub that every other ESP32 project can publish into, and every dashboard you ever add to the kit subscribes from. The DHT11 is intentionally boring - the point isn't the sensor, it's that the wiring diagram from now on is a network diagram, not a breadboard one.
