projects.name: Joystick Doodle Pad on OLED
projects.power_supply: ESP32 is powered from a laptop via USB; the joystick module and OLED both run off the ESP32's 3.3V rail through the breadboard.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Wiggle the joystick and a tiny blinking dot zips around a little screen. Click the stick down and the dot starts leaving a white trail behind it, so you can draw whatever you want one pixel at a time. **Why it's fun**: It's like having your own pocket Etch-A-Sketch that you actually built with your own hands. Draw your name, sketch a stick-figure dad, write a secret message, then hold the button for a second and watch the whole screen wipe clean so you can start over. ## Parts list - 1x Joystick Module (2-axis + button) - the star: two potentiometers (X and Y) and a push-button under the cap - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the joystick and drives the screen - 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - the 128x64 canvas you paint on - 1x Breadboard (~400 tie-points) - share 3.3V and GND between three things cleanly - 1x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc - power rails on the breadboard - 1x Jumper Wire F-M, 20pc - female ends plug into the joystick/OLED header pins ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the 3.3 volt power output. We treat this as our "power" pin for everything in this build. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs a wire back to GND. - **D21, D22** - pins for talking to the OLED screen. D21 sends data, D22 sends the clock tick. - **D32, D34, D35** - the pins we read the joystick from. D34 and D35 are input-only (they only listen, they cannot send). - **VIN / USB** - the pin connected to the USB cable's 5V. We are NOT using this today, only 3V3. - **The long red strip** on the side of the breadboard is the power strip. The long blue/black strip next to it is ground.
**Step 1 - Set up the power strips on the breadboard.** - Take a male-to-male jumper wire and run it from the pin marked **3V3** on the ESP32 to the long red strip on the breadboard. That whole red strip is now 3.3V. - Take another male-to-male jumper wire and run it from the pin marked **GND** on the ESP32 to the long blue/black strip. That whole strip is now ground. Every other part will grab its power and ground from these two strips. It saves a ton of wires going back to the ESP32.
**Step 2 - Plant the joystick on the breadboard.** Push the joystick module's 5 pins down into row 3 through row 7 of the breadboard (column A), so each pin sits in its own row. Then connect, using male-to-male jumper wires: - Joystick **GND** (row 3) -> ground strip (the blue/black one) - Joystick **+5V** (row 4) -> 3.3V strip (the red one). The label says +5V but ignore that - we are feeding it 3.3V on purpose. See the "Why this matters" note below. - Joystick **VRX** (row 5) -> pin marked **D34** on the ESP32 (X axis - left and right) - Joystick **VRY** (row 6) -> pin marked **D35** on the ESP32 (Y axis - up and down) - Joystick **SW** (row 7) -> pin marked **D32** on the ESP32 (the click button - push the stick straight down) **Why this matters (joystick on 3.3V even though it says +5V):** The joystick is really just two little knobs and a button inside. It doesn't actually care if you give it 5V or 3.3V - it works either way. But the ESP32's joystick pins (D34, D35, D32) can only safely handle 3.3V going in. If you accidentally wire the joystick to 5V and then press the button, 5V would hit the D32 pin and slowly hurt the ESP32. So we just feed the joystick 3.3V to keep everything matched and safe. Easy rule: on an ESP32, never put more than 3.3V into any pin.
**Step 3 - Plant the OLED screen on the breadboard.** Push the OLED's 4 pins down into rows 22 through 25 (column A), one pin per row. Then wire it up: - OLED **GND** (row 22) -> ground strip - OLED **VCC** (row 23, this means "power input") -> 3.3V strip - OLED **SCL** (row 24, the clock pin) -> pin marked **D22** on the ESP32 - OLED **SDA** (row 25, the data pin) -> pin marked **D21** on the ESP32 The OLED talks to the ESP32 using just two wires (SDA and SCL). It's like a tiny phone line - one wire sends a steady tick (SCL) and the other sends the message (SDA).
**Step 4 - Plug in the USB cable.** Plug the USB cable into the ESP32 and into your laptop. The little red power LED on the ESP32 should glow. If the OLED also wakes up with some fuzz or a glow, that's a great sign - it's getting power. If nothing lights up, unplug the USB right away and double-check that the red strip is going to **3V3** (not VIN or 5V) and that the joystick's +5V pin really is in the same red strip and not crossed over to the ground strip.
**Why we use the ESP32's built-in pull-up on the button:** The joystick button has only two states - pressed or not pressed - but a pin can't just float in space, it needs something gently holding it at a known voltage when nothing is happening. The ESP32 has a tiny built-in helper resistor that we turn on in the code (`INPUT_PULLUP`). It quietly pulls the pin up to 3.3V when the button is resting, and the button shorts it down to 0V when you press. So in the code, "not pressed" reads HIGH and "pressed" reads LOW. That feels backwards the first time you see it - totally normal.
## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open File -> Preferences. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Open Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager, type "esp32" in the search box, and install "esp32 by Espressif Systems". It is a chunky download, so let it finish. 3. Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> "NodeMCU-32S". 4. Install the two screen libraries: Tools -> Manage Libraries. Search for "Adafruit SSD1306" and install it - it will ask to also install "Adafruit GFX Library" and "Adafruit BusIO", say yes to both. These are what draw text, lines, and pixels on the OLED. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a USB cable (most NodeMCU-32S boards use a micro-USB cable - the same little trapezoid plug as older phones). Use a real data cable, not a charge-only one. 2. Tools -> Port, and pick the new entry that just appeared (on Windows it will be something like `COM4`, on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-XXXX`, on Linux `/dev/ttyUSB0`). If nothing shows up, unplug and try a different USB port or cable. 3. This sketch has no passwords or placeholders to fill in - it is ready to go as-is. 4. Click the Upload button (the right-arrow icon in the top-left). You will see "Connecting....." in the black box at the bottom. If it sits there for more than 5 seconds, press and hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until you see the upload progress percentage start counting up, then let go. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need that trick the first time. 5. When upload finishes, open Tools -> Serial Monitor and set the dropdown in the bottom-right to **115200 baud** (that matches `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). 6. Look at the OLED: you should see a tiny blinking dot near the middle of the screen. Wiggle the joystick - the dot follows. Push the joystick straight down (click) and wiggle again - now it draws a white line. Click once more to lift the pen. Hold the click for one full second and the screen wipes blank. That is how you know everything is working. **Common gotchas:** - **"Connecting......_____" forever on upload.** Hold the BOOT button on the ESP32 while the IDE is trying to connect, let go once you see the percentage count up. Very common on the first upload of the day. - **OLED stays completely black.** Some SSD1306 clones use I2C address `0x3D` instead of `0x3C`. If your screen is dark, change `OLED_ADDR` in the sketch from `0x3C` to `0x3D` and re-upload. - **Dot drifts on its own when you are not touching the joystick.** That means the joystick's center reading is not quite 2048. Wiggle the stick to the corners once after power-up, or bump `DEADZONE` in the code from 250 up to 400 so a tiny resting wobble gets ignored. ## Talking points - Move the stick: a blinking dot (the cursor) moves around the screen. - Click the button: the pen toggles between "up" and "down". With the pen down, the cursor leaves a trail of white pixels - that's the drawing. - Hold the button for one second: the screen wipes clean and the pen lifts. Good for "oops, start over". - The cursor blinks so you can see where you are even on a blank canvas. - The deadzone in the code (`DEADZONE = 250`) means the cursor only moves when you push the stick noticeably. Without it, ADC noise alone would make the cursor drift. - How the drawing survives the blinking cursor: the code keeps its own `canvas[128][64]` array of which pixels have been "painted". Every frame it wipes the OLED, redraws the whole canvas from that array, then stamps the cursor on top. The cursor is never stored in the canvas, so it can never leave phantom dots. ## Things to change once it works - Make the pen "thicker": draw a 2x2 or 3x3 block of canvas cells instead of a single one when the pen is down. - Diagonal-only mode for a 10-year-old's first maze drawing - only commit pixels when X or Y exceeds a threshold. - Add a small status line in the top corner showing PEN UP / PEN DOWN (just draw text after the canvas copy, before the cursor). - Speed-sensitive cursor: square the stick deflection so tiny pushes nudge gently and full deflection zooms. - Save the drawing to LittleFS so it survives a reboot, then add a "gallery" mode that cycles through saved drawings. - Two-player Etch-A-Sketch: one joystick controls X, a second joystick controls Y, and you have to cooperate. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project that asks the ESP32 to read TWO analog inputs at once and translate that into something visually obvious. The joystick teaches three ideas that show up everywhere later: an analog reading is a number from 0 to 4095, a "center" reading is rarely exactly half (so you need a deadzone), and a button without an external resistor needs the chip's internal pull-up to behave. Combining that with the OLED gives instant, satisfying feedback - the kind where a 10-year-old can sit down and start drawing within 10 seconds of plugging it in.

projects.name: Laser Tripwire Alarm
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the Arduino Uno; the Uno's 5V rail powers the laser, photoresistor, and alarm LED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A real red laser shoots a thin beam across the room to a little sensor on the other side. The second someone walks through and breaks the beam, an alarm LED snaps on - just like in spy movies. **Why it's fun**: Set it up across your bedroom doorway and you'll know the instant your sister sneaks in. It's the closest thing to a real museum security system you can build on a kitchen table, and the laser dot is honestly just cool to look at. ## Parts list - Arduino Uno R3 (the brain, 5V GPIO) - KY-008 Red Laser Module (the beam - the star of the show) - KY-018 Photoresistor Module (the beam catcher) - 5mm red LED + 330R resistor (the alarm indicator) - Breadboard, jumper wires ## Wiring notes This project uses a laser pointer and a light sensor to make an alarm. When you walk through the red beam, the LED lights up. It is like the lasers you see in spy movies, just smaller and friendlier. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the power output pin. It gives back 5 volts from the USB cable to power small parts. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every circuit needs a path back to ground or it will not work. - **D0 to D13** - digital pins. They can turn things on and off, like the laser. - **A0 to A5** - analog pins. They can read a value from 0 to 1023, like how bright a light is. - **USB-B** - the big square USB port where the cable from your laptop or phone charger plugs in.
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard and power rails.** - Look at the breadboard. The long red strip on the side is the +5V power rail (the long red strip running down the side). The long blue or black strip is the GND rail (the 0V side - ground). - With a male-to-male jumper wire, run a red wire from the Arduino's **5V** pin to the top of the red rail (+5V_T). - With another male-to-male jumper, run a black wire from the Arduino's **GND** pin to the top of the blue rail (GND_T). - Then run a red wire down the red rail (from +5V_T to +5V_B) and a black wire down the blue rail (from GND_T to GND_B). This makes sure both halves of the breadboard get power. This step gives the whole breadboard a "5V everywhere on red, ground everywhere on blue" setup. Now any part we plug in can grab power from the closest hole.
**Step 2 - Wire the alarm LED with its resistor.**
- Push the LED into the breadboard so the **long leg** is in hole **E15** and the **short leg** is in hole **E17**. - Take the 330R resistor (it has orange-orange-brown-gold stripes) and put one leg in hole **A15** (same row as the LED's long leg) and the other leg into the red +5V rail at the top. Wait - we are not connecting the LED to +5V directly. Instead, you will run a wire from Arduino pin **D9** to the same row as the LED's long leg later in the wiring. The resistor sits between the LED's long leg row and where D9 plugs in, so the current is limited. - Run a black male-to-male jumper from hole **A17** (the LED's short leg row) to the blue GND rail at the top. - Finally, plug a male-to-male jumper from Arduino **D9** to the breadboard row where the resistor meets the LED's long leg (row 15). Why this matters: the 330R resistor is a "speed bump" for electricity. LEDs are greedy - if you connect them straight to a pin, they gulp too much power and burn out in seconds. The resistor slows the current down to a safe amount so the LED can shine bright for years without dying.
**Step 3 - Wire the KY-008 red laser module.** The KY-008 has three pins: **S** (signal), a middle pin, and a **-** pin (ground). - Use a female-to-male jumper wire. Plug the female end onto the **S** pin of the laser module. Plug the male end into a row on the breadboard, then run a wire from that row to Arduino pin **D7**. Or, easier: just plug the male end straight into the Arduino's D7 hole. - Use another female-to-male jumper. Plug the female end onto the **-** pin of the laser. Plug the male end into the blue GND rail on the breadboard. - Leave the middle pin alone - do not connect anything to it. When D7 is turned on by the code, the laser shoots a red dot. When D7 is off, the laser is dark. Be careful: never look straight into the laser, and never point it at anyone's eyes. It is low power but still bright enough to hurt.
**Step 4 - Wire the KY-018 photoresistor module.** The KY-018 also has three pins: **S** (the sensor reading), a middle pin marked **+** (power input, 5V in), and **-** (the 0V side - ground). - Use a female-to-male jumper from the **S** pin to Arduino pin **A0**. - Use a female-to-male jumper from the **middle** pin to the red +5V rail on the breadboard. - Use a female-to-male jumper from the **-** pin to the blue GND rail. The black round bump on top of the KY-018 is the actual light sensor. When light hits it, the value at A0 goes up. When the laser beam gets blocked (because a hand or leg passes through it), the value drops fast - and that is what tells the Arduino to set off the alarm.
**Step 5 - Connect the jumper wires (a quick reminder).**
- The **female-to-male** (F-M) wires have a plastic plug on one end and a metal pin on the other. Use the plug end on the laser and photoresistor module pins, and the pin end on the breadboard or the Arduino. - The **male-to-male** (M-M) wires have metal pins on both ends. Use these to jump from the Arduino to the breadboard, and from rail to rail. Take a minute to make sure every wire color makes sense: red wires for 5V, black wires for ground, and any other color for signals. Future-you will thank present-you when you have to debug at 9pm.
**Step 6 - Plug in power and aim the laser.** - Plug the USB cable into the Arduino's USB-B port and into your laptop or a 5V phone charger. The little green LED on the Arduino should light up. - Now you have to aim the laser. Set the laser module on one side of a doorway and the photoresistor module on the other side. Wiggle the laser until the red dot lands right on the black sensor bump of the KY-018. - The closer the dot is to the center of the sensor, the better the alarm works. A wobbly aim equals a wobbly alarm. This is the trickiest part of the whole build. Tape, blu-tack, or a small lump of clay can help hold the laser steady. If your aim drifts after 5 minutes, the alarm will think someone walked through the beam when nothing happened.
**Final step - warmup and tune.** When the code first runs, it takes a quick reading of how bright the sensor sees the laser dot. That reading becomes the "beam is on" baseline. After that, any big drop in brightness means the beam was blocked - alarm time. If the alarm goes off for no reason, the room lights might be changing, or your aim might be slipping. Re-aim the laser and reset the Arduino (press the small button next to the USB port) to take a new baseline. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):** 1. Open the Arduino IDE. The Uno R3 board support is built in - nothing extra to install. 2. Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> **Arduino Uno**. 3. No extra libraries needed for this sketch. It only uses the standard `Serial` and `analogRead`/`digitalWrite` that ship with the IDE. 4. (CH340 clone note) This Uno is a CH340 clone. On Windows 10/11 the driver usually installs automatically when you plug it in. If the port never shows up, search "CH340 driver Windows" and install the one from wch.cn, then unplug and replug the Uno. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into the laptop with a **USB-A to USB-B** cable (the big square-ish printer-style plug). The green power LED on the Uno should light up. 2. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that looks like **COM3 / COM4 / COM5** on Windows, or **/dev/cu.usbserial-\*** on Mac, or **/dev/ttyUSB0** on Linux. If you see two ports, unplug the Uno, see which one disappears, and that is the right one. 3. No passwords or placeholders to change in this sketch - it works as-is. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the top-left). The TX and RX LEDs on the Uno will blink fast for a couple of seconds. The bottom of the IDE should say **"Done uploading."** 5. Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window, set the baud rate to **9600** (matches `Serial.begin(9600)` in the code). 6. You should see: ``` Laser Tripwire starting... Bright baseline (beam on target) = 850 Will trip if reading drops below 700 Aim the laser at the photoresistor and wave your hand through the beam. ``` The exact baseline number depends on your room lights and how well the laser is aimed - anywhere from about 600 to 1000 is normal. Now wave your hand between the laser and the sensor. The red alarm LED should snap on and the Serial Monitor should print `BEAM BROKEN! reading=...`. **Common gotchas:** - **Laser not aimed at the sensor.** If the baseline prints as something low like `120`, the red dot is missing the little black square on top of the KY-018. Move the laser until the dot lands dead center, then press the Uno's reset button (the small button next to the USB plug) to re-calibrate. - **Alarm LED in backwards.** No damage done - it just will not light. The long leg goes to pin 9 (through the 330R), the short leg goes to GND. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees, push it back in. - **Serial Monitor baud wrong.** If you see gibberish like `⸮⸮⸮⸮⸮` instead of words, the baud dropdown in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor is not on 9600. Change it. ## Talking points - "Why does the laser need GND?" Every circuit needs a complete loop. Electricity leaves the 5V/signal pin, does its work in the laser, and has to come back home through GND. Without GND, no loop, no light. - "Why doesn't the laser go through my hand?" Red 650nm laser light is visible, fairly low energy, and very directional. Your skin absorbs and scatters it, so almost none reaches the sensor on the other side - that's exactly why this works as a tripwire. - "Why calibrate at startup?" Different rooms have different ambient light. The sketch reads the photoresistor 20 times in the first second, averages those, and uses that as the "beam is hitting the target" baseline. Then any big drop from that baseline means something interrupted the beam. ## Things to change once it works - Add a buzzer or relay-driven siren in parallel with the alarm LED so it makes noise. - Replace `delay(50)` with a latch: once tripped, stay tripped until a button is pressed to re-arm. - Aim the laser at a mirror placed across the room and bounce the beam back into the photoresistor - turn a doorway into a long tripwire. - Log the time of each break to Serial and graph it later. ## Why this is interesting This is the project that makes a 10-year-old say "this is the coolest thing I've ever built." A real red laser, a real invisible tripwire across the kitchen, an alarm that goes off when someone walks through. It teaches three big ideas at once - digital output (turning the laser on), analog input (reading varying light levels), and calibration (the code adapts to whatever room you're in instead of using magic numbers). ## Eye-safety note The KY-008 is a low-power Class 2 (or similar) red laser, but **never aim it at anyone's eyes**, including pets. Aim it across a flat surface like a tabletop where the only thing that can break it is a hand or a toy car driving through.

projects.code:
<![CDATA[// Laser Tripwire Alarm
// Aim the KY-008 red laser at the KY-018 photoresistor.
// When something blocks the beam, the red alarm LED turns on
// and the Serial Monitor prints "BEAM BROKEN!".
//
// Board: Arduino Uno R3 (5V logic)
// Open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud to see readings.

const int PIN_LASER     = 7;   // KY-008 signal pin (S)
const int PIN_LDR       = A0;  // KY-018 analog out
const int PIN_ALARM_LED = 9;   // 5mm red LED through 330R to GND

// Tuning: higher number on A0 = MORE light hitting the photoresistor.
// We calibrate at startup, then trip if the reading falls well below
// the bright baseline.
int brightBaseline = 0;
const int TRIP_MARGIN = 150;   // how far below baseline counts as "blocked"

void setup() {
  pinMode(PIN_LASER, OUTPUT);
  pinMode(PIN_ALARM_LED, OUTPUT);

  Serial.begin(9600);
  delay(500);
  Serial.println(F("Laser Tripwire starting..."));

  // Turn the laser on and let the photoresistor settle.
  digitalWrite(PIN_LASER, HIGH);
  delay(800);

  // Take a few readings of the "beam clear" state and average them.
  long sum = 0;
  const int samples = 20;
  for (int i = 0; i < samples; i++) {
    sum += analogRead(PIN_LDR);
    delay(25);
  }
  brightBaseline = sum / samples;

  Serial.print(F("Bright baseline (beam on target) = "));
  Serial.println(brightBaseline);
  Serial.print(F("Will trip if reading drops below "));
  Serial.println(brightBaseline - TRIP_MARGIN);
  Serial.println(F("Aim the laser at the photoresistor and wave your hand through the beam."));
}

void loop() {
  int reading = analogRead(PIN_LDR);
  bool broken = (reading < brightBaseline - TRIP_MARGIN);

  if (broken) {
    digitalWrite(PIN_ALARM_LED, HIGH);
    Serial.print(F("BEAM BROKEN!  reading="));
    Serial.println(reading);
  } else {
    digitalWrite(PIN_ALARM_LED, LOW);
  }

  delay(50);
}
]]>

projects.name: Reaction-Time Game v2 (Proto PCB Edition)
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the Arduino Uno's USB-B socket - the Uno regulates and feeds the proto PCB's 5V/GND rails.
projects.description:
**What it is**: It is your old reaction-time game, but built for keeps. Instead of wires popping out of a breadboard, the buttons and LEDs sit on a real circuit board that you can drop in a drawer, pull out next week, and it still works. **Why it's fun**: This is the first time you get to use a soldering iron, and at the end you walk away with a finished gadget that looks store-bought, not "school project". Hand it to your little brother and watch him try (and fail) to beat your best time. **Soldering project - up front warning.** This is the one project in the kit that uses a soldering iron. Everything else has been solderless (breadboard + DuPont jumpers). The point of this build is to take a circuit Andy already knows works - the reaction-time game that was his first build - and make it *permanent* on a double-sided proto PCB so it lives on a shelf instead of occupying the breadboard. Treat it as Andy's intermediate solo project. His son can watch and read out reaction times, but the iron stays in adult hands. The Arduino itself is **not** soldered. We solder female header sockets onto the proto PCB and the Uno plugs into them, so the brain is reusable for the next thing. Only the buttons, LEDs, resistors, and short wire links get soldered. Workflow (this is half the lesson): 1. Rebuild the game on a breadboard one last time using these exact pins. Confirm green/red/buttons all behave. 2. Plan the layout on the PCB *before* heating the iron - a sharpie dot on each hole that gets a part. 3. Solder the lowest-profile parts first (resistors), then headers and buttons, LEDs last. 4. Flip the board, route point-to-point with the stripped insides of an M-M jumper wire. Keep wires short. 5. Inspect every joint under a lamp - should be shiny and concave, not a dull blob. Re-flow anything that looks like a "cold" joint. 6. Plug the Uno in *last*. Power up. If anything draws weird current, unplug fast. ## Parts list - 1x Double-Sided Prototype PCB (the star - the new home of the circuit) - 1x Arduino Uno R3 (sits in a socket on the PCB, not soldered in) - 2x Tactile push-button (START + PLAYER) - 1x Green 5mm LED (GO light) - 1x Red 5mm LED (WAIT / FAIL light) - 2x 330R resistor (LED current limit) - 2x 10K resistor (button pull-ups - belt-and-braces alongside `INPUT_PULLUP`) - 1x Female header strip, cut into two short rails to socket the Uno's D-pins - 1x Male header strip, cut for the PCB I/O block - Hookup wire (stripped from an M-M jumper) for point-to-point links on the underside - 1x Breadboard for the pre-solder dry run ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the power output pin. It gives you 5 volts to feed the breadboard. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every circuit needs a path back to GND. - **D2, D3, D9, D10** - pins marked with a D and a number. The code talks to these. - **USB-B** - the big square USB socket where the cable plugs in. - **The long red/blue strips on the breadboard** - power strips. The red one carries 5V, the blue one carries GND.
**Step 1 - Plug the Uno into power.** - Plug a USB cable from your laptop or a 5V phone charger into the Uno's USB-B socket. - The Uno turns that into clean 5V and shares it with the rest of the circuit. Leave the cable unplugged while you build. Only plug it in when you are ready to test.
**Step 2 - Wake up the breadboard power strips.** - Run one jumper wire from the Uno's **5V** pin to the top red strip (+5V_T) on the breadboard. - Run another jumper wire from the Uno's **GND** pin to the top blue strip (GND_T). Now the whole top edge of the board has power. Anything plugged into the red strip gets 5V. Anything in the blue strip is at 0V.
**Step 3 - Add the green "ready" LED.** - Put the green LED in the breadboard so the **long leg** is in hole E5 and the **short leg** is in hole E6. - Plug a 330R resistor (orange-orange-brown stripes) between hole A5 and the red 5V strip up top. - Run a short jumper wire from E6 to the blue GND strip. - Run a jumper from the pin marked **D9** on the Uno over to hole A5. Why this matters: an LED on its own would burn itself out the second you turn on the power. The 330R resistor sits in the path and slows the current down to a safe trickle. Always pair an LED with its resistor.
**Step 4 - Add the red "GO!" LED.** - Put the red LED in the breadboard so the **long leg** is in hole E10 and the **short leg** is in hole E11. - Plug another 330R resistor between hole A10 and the red 5V strip. - Run a short jumper wire from E11 to the blue GND strip. - Run a jumper from the pin marked **D10** on the Uno over to hole A10. Same idea as the green one. Green means "get ready", red means "tap NOW".
**Step 5 - Add the PLAYER button (the one you slap).** - Push a tactile button so its legs straddle the gap in the middle of the breadboard, with one corner sitting in hole F15. - Plug a 10K resistor (brown-black-orange stripes) between hole J15 and the red 5V strip. - Run a short jumper from J17 to the blue GND strip. - Run a jumper from the pin marked **D2** on the Uno over to hole F15. Why this matters: the 10K resistor is a "pull-up". When the button is just sitting there doing nothing, the resistor gently holds the pin at 5V so the Uno reads it as a clean HIGH. When you mash the button, it shorts the pin straight to GND and the Uno sees it drop to 0V. That's how the code knows you pressed it. Without the pull-up the pin would float around randomly and the game would trigger by itself.
**Step 6 - Add the START button.** - Push the second tactile button across the gap so one corner sits in hole F22. - Plug a 10K resistor between hole J22 and the red 5V strip. - Run a short jumper from J24 to the blue GND strip. - Run a jumper from the pin marked **D3** on the Uno over to hole F22. Same trick as the PLAYER button: 10K pull-up to 5V on one side, jumper to GND on the other side. When you press START the Uno sees the pin drop to 0V and kicks off a new round.
**Step 7 - Test on the breadboard first.** - Double-check every leg. Long legs on the LEDs go toward the resistor side. Short legs go to GND. - Plug the USB cable in. The green LED should come on. Press START, wait a moment, the red LED lights up, and you slap the PLAYER button as fast as you can. - If nothing happens, unplug the USB and check each wire one by one. A loose jumper is the #1 reason for a dead game.
**Step 8 - Move it to the proto PCB (parent helps, no soldering iron for the kid).** - Once the breadboard version works, a grown-up can move the same parts to the prototype PCB. The proto PCB has tiny holes in a grid - same idea as the breadboard, but the parts get held in place permanently. - Female header strips go on the PCB so the Uno can plug in and out (no soldering the Uno itself). - Male header pins poke out from the PCB so you can plug the LEDs and buttons into them with little wires. - Keep each LED's 330R resistor sitting right next to its LED on the PCB. That way if a resistor ever burns out you can spot it in two seconds. This step is a tricky one. There is real heat involved, so this is the parent's part. The breadboard is the kid's playground.
**Final check - tune the game.** - The code uses a random wait between "ready" (green) and "GO!" (red). If you find the wait too short or too long, adjust the numbers in the sketch. - If a button feels twitchy and triggers twice on one press, you can add a tiny delay in the code (called debouncing) instead of changing the wiring. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno on this laptop):** 1. Install the Arduino IDE and open it. The default install already includes the Uno board package, so there is no extra board manager URL to add. 2. This sketch only uses functions that ship with the IDE (`pinMode`, `digitalRead`, `digitalWrite`, `millis`, `random`, `Serial`). No extra libraries to install - you can skip Tools -> Manage Libraries entirely. 3. Tools -> Board -> **Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno**. 4. CH340 clone note: this Uno is a CH340 clone, not a "real" FTDI Uno. On Windows 10 the driver usually installs itself the moment you plug the board in. If after 30 seconds no new COM port shows up in Device Manager, grab the CH340 driver from `wch-ic.com`, install it, unplug, replug. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into the laptop with a **USB-A to USB-B** cable (the chunky printer-style square plug, not micro-USB). The green "ON" LED next to the barrel jack should light up. 2. Tools -> Port -> pick the new **COM\*** entry that appeared when you plugged in (on Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*`, on Linux `/dev/ttyUSB0`). If two ports are listed, unplug the Uno, see which one disappears, that is yours. 3. No passwords or placeholders to edit in this sketch - it is fully self-contained. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, second from the left in the top bar). The TX and RX LEDs on the Uno will flicker for a couple of seconds, then the IDE bottom panel says `avrdude done. Thank you.` 5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud dropdown at the bottom right to **115200** (this matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). 6. What you should see: the red LED stays off until you press **START**. Press START - red comes on for somewhere between 1.5 and 4.5 seconds, then it switches off and the green LED snaps on. Mash the **PLAYER** button. The Serial Monitor prints a line like `Reaction: 287 ms`. If you cheat and hit PLAYER while the red is still on, the red LED flashes a few times and the Serial Monitor scolds you with a false-start message. **Common gotchas:** - **Wrong COM port** - if Upload fails with `avrdude: stk500_getsync(): not in sync`, you almost certainly picked the wrong port (or none at all). Tools -> Port, pick the right COM, try again. - **LEDs in backwards** - if a press of START gives you nothing visible but the Serial Monitor is still alive, the red LED is probably flipped. No damage done, just pull it out, rotate 180 degrees, push back in. Long leg goes to the resistor side, short leg to GND. - **Serial Monitor baud wrong** - if the Monitor shows gibberish like `⸮⸮⸮d⸮@⸮` instead of readable text, the baud dropdown is set to 9600 (the default). Change it to **115200** to match the sketch. ## Talking points - "Why are we soldering this one?" Because a breadboard contact relies on a spring. Springs lose tension, and a circuit you want to keep deserves a real metal joint. - A *cold solder joint* looks like crumbly grey play-dough. A *good* joint looks shiny and pulled toward the pad - like a tiny silver volcano. Re-heat anything that looks crumbly. - The Arduino plugs into a socket, not directly into the board. That socket is the most expensive bit of foresight in the whole build - it means we can pull the Uno back out for the next project. - `INPUT_PULLUP` does the same job as the external 10K in software. We use both. On a breadboard, software alone is fine. On a permanent board that might sit near a noisy power supply, the physical resistor adds confidence. - The first sketch already debounced the buttons in code. On the soldered board that matters more, because a flaky button starts to look like a "ghost press". - Note on the debounce helper: the v2 sketch keys its per-button state by a small index (0 and 1) passed in by the caller, not by the raw GPIO pin number. That means swapping a button to a different Uno pin only changes one constant at the top of the file - the debounce arrays don't have to be re-sized or re-thought. ## Things to change once it works - Add the 4-digit 7-segment display module from the kit to show reaction time in milliseconds instead of using the Serial Monitor. - Add a third button for "two-player mode" - first one to hit GO wins. - Drill two small holes in a project box and mount the PCB inside, LEDs and buttons poking through the lid. - Power it from a 9V battery via the Uno's barrel jack so it doesn't need a laptop. - Log the last 10 reaction times in EEPROM so the leaderboard survives a power cycle. ## Why this is interesting The leap from "it works on a breadboard" to "it works on a board I keep in a drawer" is the leap from hobbyist tinkering to actually owning a thing you built. Soldering is the rite-of-passage skill that makes that leap possible, and a proto PCB is the friendliest place to learn it - the holes are pre-drilled, the pads are pre-tinned, and the spacing matches every through-hole part you own. Doing it on a circuit Andy already understands means the only new variable is the *technique*, not the *design*. If the soldered version misbehaves, he knows the bug is in the joints or the wiring, not in the code or the parts list. That's a very calm way to learn a slightly intimidating skill.

allocations.notes: Brains of the game. Plugs into the soldered proto PCB via female header sockets (so the Uno stays reusable).
Used as point-to-point wire on the PCB underside (strip jacket, tin tips) plus optional external test leads.
The GO light - lights up when the player should hit the button.
The WAIT / FAIL light - shows while waiting and flashes if the player jumps the gun.
Cut two short strips to make a socket on the PCB for the Uno's digital pins, so the Arduino is removable, not soldered.
Cut short strips to wire the PCB's I/O block - jumper leads from the Uno-socket area to the buttons/LEDs.
Used BEFORE soldering to rebuild and re-confirm the working circuit one last time, so Andy isn't debugging a soldered board.
The star of the project - the permanent home for the reaction-time game circuit. Pick a small size that fits the part count.
Pull-up resistors for the two buttons (we use INPUT_PULLUP in code too, but external 10K is good practice on a permanent build for noise immunity).
Current-limit resistors for the two LEDs.
PLAYER button (reacts to the LED) and RESET/START button. The 5mm tall ones poke through the proto PCB cleanly.

projects.name: Clap-O-Meter (Live Sound Bar Graph)
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the ESP32's onboard 3.3V regulator powers the KY-037 mic, the OLED, and the red LED through a 330R resistor.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Clap your hands. A bar shoots up across the little screen and a red light flashes. Whisper and the bar barely twitches. Yell and it pegs all the way to the edge. **Why it's fun**: You finally get to SEE how loud you are, like the bouncing bars on a music speaker. Have a shouting contest with your brother and watch the screen prove who actually won. A live loudness meter built around the KY-037 microphone. The ESP32 reads the mic, scales the result onto a bar across the OLED, and flashes a red LED whenever the sound crosses a "loud" threshold - so a clap, a shout or a slammed door becomes a thing you can see. ## Parts list - KY-037 Microphone Sensor (the protagonist) - analog audio input - ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the mic, drives the OLED, controls the LED - 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - the bar graph and the labels - 5mm red LED + 330R resistor - flashes on loud sound - 10uF electrolytic capacitor - decoupling across the mic VCC/GND for a cleaner signal - Breadboard, a pack of M-M jumpers, a pack of F-M jumpers ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the 3.3V power output pin. The ESP32 makes this from the USB cable for you. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs one wire going here. - **D21 / D22** - the two pins the ESP32 uses to talk to screens and sensors over a 2-wire chat called I2C. - **D34** - a pin marked D34. It can only listen, never speak. Perfect for reading the microphone. - **D23** - a normal pin we will use to switch the red light on and off. - **USB port** - the USB-C socket where you plug the cable from your laptop or a phone charger.
**Step 1 - Get the breadboard ready.** The breadboard has two long red/blue strips running down each side. Those are the long red/blue strips down the side of the breadboard - we will call the red one the "+5V strip" and the blue one the "ground strip" (the 0V side). - Take one red jumper wire and run it from the ESP32's pin marked **3V3** to the red **+5V strip** at the top of the breadboard. - Take one black jumper wire and run it from any ESP32 pin marked **GND** to the blue **ground strip** at the top. Now anything you plug into those long strips will have power and ground without needing more wires from the ESP32. Tip: even though the ESP32 sends out 3.3V here, the strip is still labeled "+5V" - just remember the actual voltage is 3.3V, which is exactly what every part in this build wants.
**Step 2 - Plug in the microphone.** The KY-037 is the little board with a silver mic can and a tiny blue knob on it. Push it into the breadboard so each of its 4 pins lands in row 3, 5, 7, and 9 on column B. - The pin marked **+** (row B7) gets a red wire to the **+5V strip** (power in for the mic). - The pin marked **G** (row B5) gets a black wire to the **ground strip** (the 0V side). - The pin marked **A0** (row B3) gets a jumper wire to the ESP32's pin marked **D34**. A0 is the "how loud is it right now" output. - Leave the **D0** pin on the mic empty. Do not connect it. We don't need it - our program decides when something is loud, not the little blue knob.
**Step 3 - Add the smoothing capacitor.** The 10uF capacitor is a small black cylinder with one long leg and one short leg. It has a white stripe down one side near the short leg. - Put the **long leg** into row E12 (which connects to the mic's + power pin). - Put the **short leg** (the side with the white stripe) into row E14 (which connects to the mic's G ground pin). **Why this matters:** When the WiFi radio or the screen turns on, they briefly pull a tiny bit of extra power and the voltage wobbles for a split second. The microphone is super sensitive and would see those wobbles as "noise." The capacitor is like a tiny water tank sitting right next to the mic - it fills up and tops the voltage back up the moment it dips. With this part in, your bar graph stays still when the room is quiet instead of jittering. It is polarized, which means it only works one way around. Long leg to power, short leg (white stripe) to ground. Backwards can make it pop, so double-check before plugging in USB.
**Step 4 - Plug in the OLED screen.** The OLED is the tiny glass screen with 4 pins. Push it into the breadboard so its pins land in rows 17, 19, 21, and 23 on column B. - **GND** (row B17) gets a black wire to the **ground strip**. - **VCC** (row B19, "power input") gets a red wire to the **+5V strip**. - **SCL** (row B21) gets a jumper wire to the ESP32's pin marked **D22**. - **SDA** (row B23) gets a jumper wire to the ESP32's pin marked **D21**. **Why this matters:** SDA and SCL are the two wires of a 2-wire chat called I2C. SDA carries the data (the bar graph picture), SCL is the clock that keeps both sides in step. D21 and D22 are the ESP32's normal I2C pins, so the code just works without setting anything special.
**Step 5 - Wire the red "loud!" light.** This is the LED that flashes when the room gets really noisy. The LED has a **long leg** (the side that gets power) and a **short leg** (the 0V side - ground). The short leg is also next to a tiny flat spot on the plastic rim, in case the legs got trimmed. - Push the 330R resistor into the breadboard so it goes from row E27 to row E29. A resistor is a tiny tube with colored stripes; it doesn't matter which way around it goes. - Push the **long leg** of the LED into row F29 (right next to one end of the resistor). - Push the **short leg** of the LED into row F30. - Take a jumper wire from the ESP32's pin marked **D23** to row B27. This sends the "turn on" signal into the resistor. - Take a black jumper wire from row F30 to the **ground strip** at the bottom of the board. **Why this matters:** LEDs are greedy - if you plug one straight into a pin it will gulp too much electricity, burn out in a flash, and might even damage the ESP32's pin. The 330R resistor is a tiny speed bump that limits the flow to a safe amount. Always put one in series with an LED. Never skip this step.
**Step 6 - Plug it all in and warm up.** Once you've checked every wire twice, plug the USB-C cable into the ESP32 and into your laptop or a 5V phone charger. The screen should light up showing a blank bar graph, and the red light should be off. Snap your fingers near the mic - the bar should jump. Clap hard - the red light should flash for a moment. If the bar graph is wiggly even when the room is quiet, gently push down on the capacitor to make sure both legs are seated. If the screen is blank, double-check that SDA and SCL aren't swapped - that's the most common mix-up on this build. If the red light stays on all the time, it might be in backwards (long leg and short leg swapped) - unplug USB, flip it, and try again. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open the Arduino IDE, then go to **File -> Preferences**. In the box labelled "Additional boards manager URLs", paste this address: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`. Click OK. 2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Type "esp32" in the search box, find the entry "esp32 by Espressif Systems", and click Install. It is a big download, so go grab a drink while it finishes. 3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **NodeMCU-32S** from the long list. 4. Now install the two screen libraries. Go to **Tools -> Manage Libraries** (or **Sketch -> Include Library -> Manage Libraries**). Search "Adafruit SSD1306" and click Install on the one by Adafruit. It will ask if you want to install dependencies too. Say "Install all" so it grabs the Adafruit GFX Library at the same time. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB-C cable** (or USB-A to micro-USB if your board has the older socket, depending on the exact NodeMCU-32S version). Use a real data cable, not a charge-only one - if the IDE never sees the board, the cable is the first thing to swap. 2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that just appeared. On Windows it looks like `COM5` or `COM7`, on Mac it is `cu.usbmodem...`, on Linux it is `/dev/ttyUSB0`. If you are not sure which is the right one, unplug the ESP32, look at the list, plug it back in, and the new line that pops up is yours. 3. There are no passwords or WiFi names in this sketch, so nothing to edit. (Optional: if you want to tweak the loud-clap threshold before flashing, scroll down to `LOUD_THRESHOLD` near the top of the code and change the number.) 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top left). The IDE will compile for a minute, then start flashing. If the upload stalls on a line like `Connecting......_____`, press and hold the small **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until you see dots turning into a percentage, then let go. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need that nudge the first time; after that they usually flash on their own. 5. When it says "Done uploading", open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window, set the baud rate to **115200** (that is what `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch expects). Anything else and you just see garbage. 6. Stay quiet for about a second after the board resets - that is when it measures the "quiet room" baseline. Then clap once. The bar on the OLED should leap to the right and the red LED should blink. Whisper and the bar barely twitches. If the Serial Monitor printed `OLED not found at 0x3C, halting.`, the screen is not wired right - check SDA/SCL and the 3.3V/GND pair before anything else. **Common gotchas:** - **Upload stuck on "Connecting..."**: hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 while the dots are scrolling, then release once flashing starts. Some boards need this every single upload, some only the first time. - **Serial Monitor shows weird symbols like `?z?$??`**: the baud rate in the bottom of the Serial Monitor is wrong. Set it to **115200** to match the `Serial.begin(115200)` line in the code. - **10uF capacitor in backwards**: the electrolytic cap has a "+" leg (longer) and a "-" leg (shorter, with a stripe on the can). Longer to mic VCC, shorter to GND. Backwards and it either does nothing useful, gets warm, or in the worst case pops - so double-check before powering up. - **Bar graph stuck pegged to the right and the LED is solid on**: you were probably clapping or talking during the first second after reset, so the baseline calibrated to a loud room. Unplug, replug, and stay quiet for one second while it boots. ## Talking points - The mic doesn't output "loudness" - it outputs the audio waveform, swinging above and below a quiet midpoint many hundreds of times a second. We sample on a steady 1 ms tick (~1000 Hz) and measure how far each sample is from the calibrated quiet baseline. That absolute swing is what we draw. - The bar uses a "peak with decay" trick: every new high pushes the bar up instantly, but a steady countdown drags it back down 20 ms at a time. That's why a clap shoots the bar up and then it slides back - matches how our ears feel loudness. - The calibration at boot is just a 1-second average of the quiet room. Cover the mic or shout at it during boot and the baseline will be wrong - reset and let the room be quiet for a second. ## Things to change once it works - Lower `LOUD_THRESHOLD` until a finger snap sets the LED off, or raise it so only a real clap counts. - Add a second LED at a higher threshold for "very loud" so you have a two-stage indicator. - Count claps in a 1-second window and use a double-clap as a "switch" - feed that into a relay to make a clap-on-clap-off lamp. - Log the peak loudness once a second over WiFi to a tiny web page and watch the room's noise level over an evening. ## Why this is interesting It turns something invisible (sound) into something visible and instantly playable. A 10-year-old can clap and see the bar move - no explanation needed. Underneath it's the same picture a real audio meter on a mixing desk is drawing, which makes it a great springboard into "how does a microphone actually work" without any math.

projects.name: Laser Posture Coach (desk slouch detector)
projects.power_supply: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S powered via its USB-C port from a laptop or 5 V phone charger; the VL53L0X, OLED, LEDs and button are fed from the ESP32's 3.3 V rail.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A tiny laser on your desk watches your chest while you work. Sit up straight and a green light says "GOOD." Hunch toward the screen and a red light flashes "SLOUCH!" until you straighten back up. **Why it's fun**: You built a robot hall monitor for your own posture - it catches you slouching before your mom does. Same kind of laser ranging that robot vacuums use to dodge furniture, except yours is yelling at you to sit up. A laser-based desk posture coach. The VL53L0X sits flat on the desk pointing straight up. When you sit upright, it sees your chest at (say) 500 mm. When you slouch forward toward the screen, that distance shrinks. A green LED + "GOOD" message means upright; a red LED + "SLOUCH!" warning means you've crept too close. A button lets you recalibrate the "upright" distance for your chair height. ## Parts list - ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (brain, drives I2C and LEDs) - VL53L0X ToF distance sensor (GY-VL53L0XV2 module) - the protagonist - 0.96" I2C OLED display - shows live distance and posture verdict - 1x green 5 mm LED + 330R resistor (good-posture light) - 1x red 5 mm LED + 330R resistor (slouch warning) - 1x tactile push-button (3x6x4.3 mm) - recalibrate - Breadboard + DuPont jumper wires ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the 3.3 volt power output. We feed the sensor, screen, LEDs and button from this pin. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs a GND wire back to the ESP32. - **VIN** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. We do not use it in this build. - **D21 / D22** - two special pins the ESP32 uses to "talk" to the sensor and screen. D21 is SDA (data), D22 is SCL (clock). - **D25, D26, D27** - normal output pins. We use them for the green LED, red LED, and the button. - **rail** - the long red and blue strip running down the side of the breadboard. Red rail = 3.3V power, blue rail = GND.
**Step 1 - Plug the ESP32 into the breadboard and feed the power rails.** - Push the ESP32 into the breadboard so it straddles the middle gap. The USB-C jack should hang off one end. - Run a red jumper wire from the pin marked **3V3** on the ESP32 to the **red (+) rail** at the top of the breadboard. - Run a black jumper wire from one **GND** pin on the ESP32 to the **blue (-) rail** at the top. - Run another black jumper from a **GND** pin on the ESP32 to the **blue (-) rail** at the bottom. This gives every part on the board easy access to 3.3V power and to GND. We power the ESP32 itself from a laptop or phone charger using the USB-C cable - that is all the power this whole project needs.
**Step 2 - Wire up the distance sensor (VL53L0X).** This is the eye of the project. It shoots a tiny invisible laser and times how long the light takes to bounce back, so it knows exactly how far away you are. - Push the sensor into the breadboard so its 4 pins land on rows **A3, A4, A5, A6**. - **VIN** (row A3) - red wire to the red (+) rail. - **GND** (row A4) - black wire to the blue (-) rail. - **SCL** (row A5) - this is the clock pin. Leave it for now; we wire it in Step 4. - **SDA** (row A6) - this is the data pin. Leave it for now; we wire it in Step 4. The sensor module has a tiny power chip on it that turns our 3.3V into the right voltage for the laser, so plugging it into 3.3V is safe.
**Step 3 - Wire up the OLED screen.** This is the little screen that will say "GOOD" or "SLOUCH!" and show your distance. - Push the OLED into the breadboard so its 4 pins land on rows **A10, A11, A12, A13**. - **GND** (row A10) - black wire to the blue (-) rail. - **VCC** (row A11, the power input pin) - red wire to the red (+) rail. - **SCL** (row A12) - blue jumper wire from **A12 to A5** (this ties the screen's clock pin to the sensor's clock pin). - **SDA** (row A13) - blue jumper wire from **A13 to A6** (this ties the screen's data pin to the sensor's data pin). **Why this matters:** the OLED and the sensor are both "I2C" parts. That just means they use a 2-wire language to chat with the ESP32. They share the same two wires (SDA and SCL) and take turns talking, because each one has its own address number (the OLED is 0x3C, the sensor is 0x29). That's why we can wire them in parallel without anything extra.
**Step 4 - Connect the I2C wires back to the ESP32.** - Run a wire from row **A5** (the shared SCL line) to the pin marked **D22** on the ESP32. - Run a wire from row **A6** (the shared SDA line) to the pin marked **D21** on the ESP32. Now the ESP32 can talk to both the sensor and the screen using just two pins.
**Step 5 - Place the green "good posture" LED with its resistor.** (The green LED looks just like the red one above, only green.) The green LED will glow when you are sitting nicely. - Put a **330 ohm resistor** between rows **E17 and E19**. Resistors don't care which way around - either end works. - Put the **green LED** with its **long leg** in row **F19** and its **short leg** in row **F20**. The long leg is the "+" side. - Run a black wire from row **F20** (the short leg) down to the blue (-) rail at the bottom. - Run a wire from row **E17** to the pin marked **D25** on the ESP32. **Why the resistor:** LEDs are greedy little parts. If you plug one straight into a pin, it will gulp too much current and burn out in a few seconds. The 330 ohm resistor is like a narrow straw - it limits how fast the electricity can flow through, so the LED lights up nicely without dying.
**Step 6 - Place the red "slouching!" LED with its resistor.** Same idea as Step 5, just one row over and using a different ESP32 pin. - Put a **330 ohm resistor** between rows **E22 and E24**. - Put the **red LED** with its **long leg** in row **F24** and its **short leg** in row **F25**. - Run a black wire from row **F25** (the short leg) down to the blue (-) rail. - Run a wire from row **E22** to the pin marked **D26** on the ESP32. When the sensor sees you slouch forward, the ESP32 will light this one up.
**Step 7 - Add the "Re-calibrate" push-button.** This little button lets you tell the project "this is what good posture looks like" whenever you sit down to work. - Push the **tactile push-button** into the breadboard so its legs land across the middle gap, with one corner in row **E27**. - Run a black wire from the **other side** of the button (row **G27**) to the blue (-) rail. - Run a wire from row **E27** to the pin marked **D27** on the ESP32. **Why no resistor on the button:** the ESP32 has a built-in "pull-up" trick we turn on in the code. That just means the pin sits at 3.3V by itself, and pressing the button drags it down to 0V (GND). So we save a part and the button fires the moment you press it.
**Step 8 - Aim and calibrate.** - Stand the breadboard up (or tape it) so the sensor's tiny black window points **straight up** from your desk, somewhere near the front edge. - Plug a USB-C cable from your laptop or a phone charger into the ESP32. The OLED should light up. - Sit at your desk in your best posture. Press the **RECAL** button once - the screen will save that distance as "good". - Now try slowly leaning forward over your keyboard. When your chest gets about 8 cm closer than your saved distance, the red LED will light up and the screen will yell "SLOUCH!". Sit back up and the green LED comes back. This is a tricky one to aim - if the LEDs flicker on and off, give the breadboard a more solid base or move the sensor a little so it's not looking at the edge of your shirt.
## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type "esp32" in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"** (it is a big download, give it a few minutes). 3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"**. 4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install these four, one at a time, by typing the name in the search box and clicking Install: - **Adafruit SSD1306** (for the OLED) - if it asks to also install Adafruit GFX and BusIO, say yes. - **Adafruit GFX Library** (the font / shape helper the OLED needs). - **Adafruit BusIO** (the I2C plumbing the two Adafruit libraries share). - **Adafruit VL53L0X** (for the laser distance sensor). **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with a **USB-C cable that can carry data** (some charging-only cables will not work - if the board does not show up, try another cable). 2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that appeared when you plugged in (Windows: `COM3`, `COM4`...; Mac: `/dev/cu.usbserial-...` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`; Linux: `/dev/ttyUSB0`). 3. There are no passwords or WiFi names to fill in for this sketch - it runs fully offline. You can leave the code alone. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). You will see "Connecting....." in the bottom panel. **If it gets stuck on dots,** hold the small **BOOT** button on the ESP32 down until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. You usually only need that trick on the very first upload. 5. When it says "Hard resetting via RTS pin," it is done. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of that window) to **115200** - the same number the sketch uses inside `Serial.begin()`. (If you do not see the Serial.begin line in this sketch, that is fine - the OLED is the main screen here.) 6. **What you should see:** the OLED lights up and shows "Posture Coach", a "Target: 500 mm" line, the live distance in big numbers, and "GOOD" in big letters at the bottom. The green LED is on. Wave your hand close to the sensor (within about 40 cm) and watch the number drop - when it gets ~8 cm under the target, "GOOD" flips to "SLOUCH!" and the red LED takes over. Sit at your normal typing position, press the button once, and the target updates to your actual chest distance. **Common gotchas:** - **Upload stuck on "Connecting....."?** Hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 while it tries to connect, and let go when you see "Writing..." start. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need this every time, others only on the first flash. - **OLED stays black or shows nothing?** It is almost always one of three things: SDA and SCL swapped (GPIO 21 = SDA, GPIO 22 = SCL), no power to the OLED's VCC pin, or the OLED's I2C address is 0x3D instead of 0x3C - some clones use the other one. If you suspect address, change `0x3C` to `0x3D` in the `display.begin(...)` line. - **"VL53L0X not found" on the screen, or distance never changes?** Both I2C devices share the same two wires, so a loose jumper on SDA or SCL kills both. Re-seat the four wires (SDA, SCL, 3V3, GND) and try again. Also check the sensor is the right way up - the tiny black square (the laser) needs a clear view, not blocked by a wire. - **LEDs do not light?** LEDs only work one way around - long leg (anode) goes through the 330R resistor to the GPIO pin, short leg (cathode) goes to GND. If yours is in backwards there is no damage, just flip it. ## Talking points - "Time of Flight" really does mean what it says: this chip fires a tiny invisible 940 nm laser pulse and measures how long the photons take to bounce back. Light moves about 30 cm in 1 nanosecond - the chip times that. - Unlike the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (which uses sound and gives ~1 cm resolution), the VL53L0X reports in millimeters and works fine at close range. That precision is what makes "you slouched 8 cm" detectable instead of "you moved, maybe." - Two different chips, one pair of wires. I2C lets multiple devices share SDA and SCL by giving each a unique address. The OLED answers at 0x3C; the ToF answers at 0x29. ## Things to change once it works - Add a buzzer (a piezo against a GPIO) that beeps after you've been slouching for more than 10 seconds. - Log slouch events to the serial monitor with timestamps, then graph "minutes slouched per hour." - Push posture stats to the Orange Pi (when it's booted) over WiFi/MQTT and build a daily report. - Use the second VL53L0X (we have two) mounted sideways to also detect when you lean too far back. ## Why this is interesting This sensor is the cheapest way an Andy-budget project can do real laser ranging - the same family of chips lives in robot vacuums and phone autofocus systems. Pairing it with an OLED on the same I2C bus is a clean first lesson in "multiple devices share two wires," which is the foundation for almost every more advanced sensor project that follows.

projects.name: Magnet Swipe Counter on OLED
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V USB charger into the ESP32's USB port; the ESP32's 3.3V rail powers the KY-003 and the OLED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Wave a magnet past the little sensor and the number on the tiny screen jumps up by one. A green LED blinks at the exact same moment, so every swipe gives you a flash and a fresh count. **Why it's fun**: It feels like a magic trick because nothing touches anything - the magnet just floats by and the screen reacts. Race your dad to 100 swipes, or stick the sensor on a door and turn it into a secret "who opened my room" detector. ## Parts list - 1x KY-003 Hall Switch Sensor (the protagonist - a tiny chip that snaps LOW when the south pole of a magnet gets close) - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (reads the sensor and drives the screen) - 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) (shows the live count) - 1x Green 5mm LED + 1x 330R resistor (flashes once per swipe for instant tactile feedback) - 1x breadboard - A handful of jumper wires - Any small magnet from around the house (fridge magnet, motor magnet, the round neodymium ones from old hard drives) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the 3.3V power output pin. We use it to feed power to the sensor and the screen. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs a GND connection. - **D14, D21, D22, D27** - pins along the edge of the ESP32. The number on the silkscreen matches the GPIO number in the code. - **USB** - the little socket where the cable from your laptop plugs in. That's how the board gets power and how the code gets loaded.
**Step 1 - Get the breadboard powered.** The long red and blue strips down the side of the breadboard are called the power strips. We feed them from the ESP32 so every part in the project can share the same power and ground. - ESP32 pin marked **3V3** to the red strip at the top of the breadboard. - ESP32 pin marked **GND** to the blue strip at the top of the breadboard. Now anywhere you push a wire into the red strip, it gets 3.3V. Anywhere you push a wire into the blue strip, it gets 0V (ground).
**Step 2 - Plug in the KY-003 magnet sensor.** The KY-003 has three pins. They are usually marked **S** (signal), middle (power input), and **-** (ground). This is a tricky one - the middle pin is power, not the data pin. Always check the tiny printed letters on the board before pushing it in. Push the KY-003 into the breadboard so the three pins land in row 3, 4, and 5 (column E). Then add these wires: - The pin marked **-** (row 5) to the blue ground strip. - The middle pin (row 4) to the red 3.3V strip. - The pin marked **S** (row 3) to the ESP32 pin marked **D14**. When you wave a magnet near the little black chip on the KY-003, the S pin tells the ESP32 about it. That's how the swipe counter knows you swiped.
**Step 3 - Add the green LED and its resistor.**
Look at the green LED. One leg is longer than the other. The long leg is the plus side, the short leg is the minus side. If you flip it the wrong way around, the LED just won't light up - it won't break, but nothing will happen. - Push the long leg of the green LED into row 12 (column F). - Push the short leg of the green LED into row 13 (column F). - Put one end of the 330R resistor in row 13 (column J), and the other end into the blue ground strip at the bottom of the breadboard. - Run a wire from the ESP32 pin marked **D27** to row 12 (column J), so it reaches the long leg of the LED. This little LED blinks every time a swipe is counted, so you can see it working even without looking at the screen. **Why this matters:** the 330R resistor is called a current-limit resistor. Without it, the LED would try to gulp down way too much electricity at once and burn itself out in a flash. The resistor is like a narrow drinking straw - it slows the flow down to a safe sip.
**Step 4 - Plug in the OLED screen.** The little 0.96" OLED screen has four pins: **GND**, **VCC**, **SCL**, and **SDA**. It talks to the ESP32 using just two data wires (SCL and SDA). That style of talking is called I2C, and the ESP32 already has the right pins ready for it. Push the OLED into the breadboard so its pins land in rows 22, 23, 24, and 25 (column E). Then: - OLED pin marked **GND** (row 22) to the blue ground strip. - OLED pin marked **VCC** (row 23, the power input) to the red 3.3V strip. - OLED pin marked **SCL** (row 24) to the ESP32 pin marked **D22**. - OLED pin marked **SDA** (row 25) to the ESP32 pin marked **D21**. Once the code is running, this screen will show a big swipe count that goes up by one each time the magnet passes the sensor.
**Step 5 - Plug in the USB cable and power up.** Plug a USB cable from your laptop (or a 5V phone charger) into the small port on the end of the ESP32. A little light should come on. The 3.3V strip on the breadboard now has power, and so does everything wired to it. **Why this matters (KY-003 pull-up note):** the KY-003 already has a tiny resistor on its own board that keeps the signal pin from "floating" when no magnet is near. We also turn on a backup pull-up inside the ESP32 in the code, just to be safe. You don't need to add any extra parts for this.
## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click OK. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type "esp32" in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download, so give it a minute. 3. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install these two, one at a time: - Search "Adafruit GFX" -> install **Adafruit GFX Library**. - Search "Adafruit SSD1306" -> install **Adafruit SSD1306**. If the IDE asks "install missing dependencies?", say **Install all**. 4. Pick the board: **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> ESP32 Dev Module** (that is the entry the NodeMCU-32S uses). **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB micro-B cable** (not micro-A, not USB-C). It must be a real data cable - some cheap "charge-only" cables will not show up. The red power LED on the ESP32 should light up. 2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged in (on Windows it looks like `COM5`, on Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-xxxx`, on Linux it looks like `/dev/ttyUSB0`). If nothing new appeared, the cable is charge-only - try a different one. 3. Open the sketch. This one has no WiFi password or other placeholders to fill in - it is ready to go as-is. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the toolbar). The IDE will compile for about 30 seconds, then start uploading. If you see `Connecting....____....` and it stalls, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see "Writing at 0x..." in the output, then let go. After the first successful upload you usually do not need to do the BOOT trick again. 5. When it says "Hard resetting via RTS pin" the code is running. The OLED should light up and show **"Magnet Swipe Counter"** with a big **0** underneath. 6. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom right of the Serial Monitor window) to **115200**. You should see `Ready. Wave a magnet near the KY-003.` Wave a magnet across the KY-003: the green LED flashes, the number on the OLED ticks up by one, and the bottom of the screen briefly shows `[ MAGNET DETECTED ]`. **Common gotchas:** - **Stuck on `Connecting....`**: hold the **BOOT** button while the upload starts, release once it begins writing. Some boards need this every time, most only the first time. - **OLED stays dark and the green LED blinks fast forever**: the sketch could not find the OLED on I2C. Double-check SDA is on GPIO 21 and SCL is on GPIO 22, and that the OLED is on 3V3 (not 5V on this build). - **Magnet does nothing**: the KY-003 only sees the **south pole**. Flip the magnet over and try again - that is the fix nine times out of ten. ## Talking points - Hall sensors are how your laptop knows the lid is closed and how your phone knows when the magnetic case is shut. They are everywhere and never wear out because nothing physically touches anything. - The KY-003 only reacts to one pole of the magnet (the south pole). If your magnet doesn't seem to trigger it, flip the magnet over - that is almost always the fix. - "Active LOW" means the signal pin is normally HIGH (3.3V) and drops to LOW (0V) when the sensor sees a magnet. This is backwards from how most people think about switches, so it's a great example of "the world doesn't always agree with you". - The 40 ms debounce window in the code is there because a magnet swept past quickly can make the digital line jitter for a millisecond or two. Without debouncing, one swipe could count as three. ## Things to change once it works - Try different magnets - a small ceramic fridge magnet vs. a tiny neodymium - and see how close you have to get for each. That distance is the sensor's effective range. - Change `PIN_HALL` to a different pin (e.g. `4` or `15`) and update the wiring to match. Get into the habit of changing both at once. - Add a "high score" reset by holding the magnet near the sensor for 3 seconds: detect a long LOW instead of a short pulse and zero the counter. - Replace the OLED with the LCD 1602 + I2C backpack and rewrite `drawScreen()` for the LCD - same data, different display. - Log each swipe out over WiFi (MQTT to the Orange Pi once it boots) so you have a "door opened" history. ## Why this is interesting Magnetic sensing is the cleanest "yes / no" the universe gives you in beginner electronics. There is no light to interfere with it, no sound to confuse it, no contact to wear out. Pair that with the OLED and you get a project where every action causes an immediate, satisfying visual change - which is the single most motivating thing when you are learning. It also sets up two real-world projects you will eventually want: a door/window open sensor, and a wheel-rotation speedometer.

<![CDATA[// Magnet Swipe Counter
// Wave a magnet past the KY-003 Hall switch. Each swipe increments a counter
// shown on the OLED, and the green LED flashes once per swipe.
//
// Board: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S
// Libraries (install via Library Manager):
//   - Adafruit GFX Library
//   - Adafruit SSD1306

#include <Wire.h>
#include <Adafruit_GFX.h>
#include <Adafruit_SSD1306.h>

// ---------- Pin assignments (match the wiring diagram) ----------
const int PIN_HALL = 14;  // KY-003 signal output (active LOW when magnet present)
const int PIN_LED  = 27;  // Green LED via 330R to GND

// ---------- OLED setup ----------
#define SCREEN_WIDTH 128
#define SCREEN_HEIGHT 64
#define OLED_RESET   -1
#define OLED_ADDR    0x3C
Adafruit_SSD1306 display(SCREEN_WIDTH, SCREEN_HEIGHT, &Wire, OLED_RESET);

// ---------- State ----------
unsigned long swipeCount = 0;
int lastHallState = HIGH;          // KY-003 idles HIGH (no magnet)
unsigned long lastEdgeMs = 0;
const unsigned long DEBOUNCE_MS = 40;
unsigned long ledOffAtMs = 0;
const unsigned long LED_FLASH_MS = 120;

void drawScreen(bool magnetNow) {
    display.clearDisplay();

    // Header
    display.setTextSize(1);
    display.setTextColor(SSD1306_WHITE);
    display.setCursor(0, 0);
    display.print("Magnet Swipe Counter");
    display.drawLine(0, 10, 127, 10, SSD1306_WHITE);

    // Big count
    display.setTextSize(3);
    display.setCursor(0, 18);
    display.print(swipeCount);

    // Status icon
    display.setTextSize(1);
    display.setCursor(0, 54);
    if (magnetNow) {
        display.print("[ MAGNET DETECTED ]");
    } else {
        display.print("Wave a magnet by...");
    }

    display.display();
}

void setup() {
    Serial.begin(115200);

    pinMode(PIN_HALL, INPUT_PULLUP); // KY-003 has its own pull-up, but belt-and-braces
    pinMode(PIN_LED, OUTPUT);
    digitalWrite(PIN_LED, LOW);

    Wire.begin();  // SDA=21, SCL=22 on ESP32 by default

    if (!display.begin(SSD1306_SWITCHCAPVCC, OLED_ADDR)) {
        Serial.println("OLED not found. Check wiring (SDA=21, SCL=22).");
        while (true) {
            digitalWrite(PIN_LED, HIGH);
            delay(200);
            digitalWrite(PIN_LED, LOW);
            delay(200);
        }
    }

    drawScreen(false);
    Serial.println("Ready. Wave a magnet near the KY-003.");
}

void loop() {
    int hallState = digitalRead(PIN_HALL);
    unsigned long now = millis();

    // Detect a falling edge (HIGH -> LOW = magnet just arrived) with debounce
    if (hallState != lastHallState && (now - lastEdgeMs) > DEBOUNCE_MS) {
        lastEdgeMs = now;
        if (hallState == LOW) {
            swipeCount++;
            digitalWrite(PIN_LED, HIGH);
            ledOffAtMs = now + LED_FLASH_MS;
            Serial.print("Swipe #");
            Serial.println(swipeCount);
            drawScreen(true);
        } else {
            drawScreen(false);
        }
        lastHallState = hallState;
    }

    // Turn the LED off after its flash window
    if (ledOffAtMs != 0 && now >= ledOffAtMs) {
        digitalWrite(PIN_LED, LOW);
        ledOffAtMs = 0;
    }
}
]]>
