projects.name: TV Remote LED Color Picker
projects.power_supply: USB cable from Andy's PC to the Arduino Uno - the Uno's onboard 5V rail powers the KY-022 and all four LEDs.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Point your TV remote at a little dark bubble on the breadboard and press a button. A red, green, blue, or yellow LED lights up, one color per button, like you just hacked the remote to control your own tiny stoplight. **Why it's fun**: You are teaching the Arduino to listen to a TV remote that already lives in your house, which feels a bit like wizardry. Once it works, hide the remote behind your back and make the lights change from across the room while your sister tries to figure out how you are doing it. ## Parts list - 1x KY-022 IR Receiver Module (the star - a tiny 38 kHz IR demodulator on a breakout board) - 1x Arduino Uno R3 (5V GPIO; the `IRremote` library is rock-solid on AVR) - 1x Breadboard (~400 tie-points) - 1x F-M jumper pack (for the 3-pin KY-022 header) - 1x M-M jumper pack (for the LEDs and resistors on the breadboard) - 1x Red, 1x Green, 1x Blue, 1x Yellow 5mm LED - 4x 330R resistors (one per LED) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the pin that gives you 5 volts of power for the parts on your breadboard. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs a path back to GND or it will not work. - **D2, D6, D7, D8, D9** - digital pins. The Uno's silkscreen labels match the numbers in the code exactly. - **USB jack** - where the USB-B cable from your PC plugs in. This is what powers the whole project. - **+ rail / - rail** - the long red and blue strips running down the side of the breadboard. + is for 5V, - is for GND.
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard power rails.** - Run a red M-M jumper from the Arduino **5V** pin to the **+ rail** at the top of the breadboard. - Run a black M-M jumper from an Arduino **GND** pin to the **- rail** at the top of the breadboard. - Run a second black M-M jumper from another Arduino **GND** pin to the **- rail** at the bottom of the breadboard. Why this matters: the long red and blue strips on the side of the breadboard let you share 5V and GND with lots of parts at once. The top rail will feed the IR receiver, and the bottom rail will be the "home" for all four LED short legs.
**Step 2 - Plug in the IR receiver.** The KY-022 is the little black bubble that "sees" the invisible light from a TV remote. It has 3 pins. Different clone boards label them slightly differently, but the pin marked **S** is the signal, and the pin marked **-** is GND. The middle one is the 5V power input. Look at the silkscreen on your board if you are not sure. - Push the KY-022 into the breadboard so its 3 pins land in rows 3, 4, and 5 (column E). - **S** (row 3) -> run a M-M jumper from **A3** to Arduino **D2**. - 5V power input (row 4) -> run a red M-M jumper from **A4** to the **+ rail** at the top. - **GND** (row 5) -> run a black M-M jumper from **A5** to the **- rail** at the top. This is a tricky one: if your KY-022 board has the pins in a different order, do not just copy the row numbers. Follow the letters **S**, middle, and **-** on the silkscreen.
**Step 3 - Wire up the red LED.**
Every LED has a long leg and a short leg. The long leg is the + side; the short leg is the - side. If you flip it, the LED just stays dark - it will not break, but it will not light up either. - Push a **330R resistor** so one end is at **B9** and the other end is at **E9**. - Push the red LED's **long leg** into **F9** (right next to the resistor). - Push the red LED's **short leg** into **F10**. - Run a black M-M jumper from **J10** to the **- rail** at the bottom. - Run a M-M jumper from Arduino **D6** to **A9**. Why this matters: the 330R resistor is called a "current-limit resistor". LEDs are greedy - if you wire one straight to 5V it will pull too much current and burn out in seconds. The resistor stands in the way and only lets a safe amount of electricity through, so the LED glows brightly without dying.
**Step 4 - Wire up the green LED.** Same pattern as the red one, just shifted down 5 rows. The green LED does not have a photo on file, but it looks just like the red one - long leg is +, short leg is -. - Push a **330R resistor** so one end is at **B14** and the other end is at **E14**. - Push the green LED's **long leg** into **F14**. - Push the green LED's **short leg** into **F15**. - Run a black M-M jumper from **J15** to the **- rail** at the bottom. - Run a M-M jumper from Arduino **D7** to **A14**.
**Step 5 - Wire up the blue LED.** - Push a **330R resistor** so one end is at **B19** and the other end is at **E19**. - Push the blue LED's **long leg** into **F19**. - Push the blue LED's **short leg** into **F20**. - Run a black M-M jumper from **J20** to the **- rail** at the bottom. - Run a M-M jumper from Arduino **D8** to **A19**.
**Step 6 - Wire up the yellow LED.** - Push a **330R resistor** so one end is at **B24** and the other end is at **E24**. - Push the yellow LED's **long leg** into **F24**. - Push the yellow LED's **short leg** into **F25**. - Run a black M-M jumper from **J25** to the **- rail** at the bottom. - Run a M-M jumper from Arduino **D9** to **A24**.
**Step 7 - Power up and watch the self-test.** Plug the USB-B cable from your PC into the Arduino's USB jack. The Uno will power up and feed 5V to the breadboard. When the sketch starts, it briefly flashes all four LEDs one after the other as a built-in wiring check. If one stays dark, that is the row to look at again - usually it is the LED plugged in backwards (try flipping the legs) or a resistor that did not push all the way in. Once all four flash, point a TV remote at the KY-022 and press buttons. The right LED will light up for the color you taught it. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):** 1. **First time only - USB driver.** Your Arduino Uno uses a **CH340** USB-to-serial chip (the dark rectangular chip near the USB jack on most clones). Plug it in: if a COM port appears in **Tools -> Port** within a few seconds, the driver is already installed and you can skip the rest of this step. If nothing shows up, install the CH340 driver from [sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers](https://sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers) (Windows / macOS / Linux all linked there), then unplug and replug the Uno. 2. Tools -> Board -> **Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno**. 3. Tools -> Manage Libraries. In the search box type **IRremote**, find the one by *shirriff, Armin Joachimsmeyer* (v3.x or v4.x), and click **Install**. This is the library that does all the hard work of decoding the remote. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into your laptop with the chunky **USB-B** cable (the squarish printer-style end goes into the Uno, the USB-A end into the laptop). The green **ON** LED on the Uno should light up straight away. 2. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that says **COM\*** on Windows, **/dev/cu.usbmodem\*** on Mac, or **/dev/ttyACM0** on Linux. If you only see one entry, that is the Uno. 3. No passwords or WiFi names to change in this sketch - it is offline. Just leave the code as it is. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, top-left of the IDE). The bottom of the IDE will say *Compiling sketch...* then *Uploading...*, and the **RX** and **TX** LEDs on the Uno will flicker for a couple of seconds. When you see **Done uploading.**, the sketch is running. 5. Open Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window, set the baud rate to **115200** - if it is on the wrong number you will just see garbage like `???????`. 6. What you should see: first, all four LEDs flash in order (red, green, blue, yellow) as the wiring self-test. Then the Serial Monitor prints something like `Press the button you want for RED`. Point any remote (TV, soundbar, old DVD player) at the dark bubble and press a button. The Serial Monitor prints a hex code like `0x20DF10EF` and moves on to GREEN, then BLUE, then YELLOW. After the fourth press it says it is ready, and from then on each learned button lights its matching LED for one second. Unknown buttons print a `?` - that is normal, it just means you pressed something the Uno does not have a colour for yet. **Common gotchas:** - **Serial Monitor shows gibberish.** The baud rate dropdown is on the wrong number. Set it to **115200** to match `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch. - **An LED stays dark during the self-test.** It is almost always the LED in backwards - the short leg (cathode) is the one that goes to the GND rail, the long leg (anode) is the one that meets the 330R resistor. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees, push it back in. No damage done. - **Remote presses do nothing and the Serial Monitor stays silent.** Either the KY-022's **S** pin is not on **D2** (check that wire first), or you are pressing a remote with a dead battery. The Uno's built-in pin 13 LED should blink every time *any* IR signal arrives - if it never blinks, the receiver is not seeing the remote at all. ## Talking points - **Why the dome is dark plastic.** That bubble on the KY-022 is a filter that lets infrared through and blocks visible light. Without it, sunlight or a desk lamp would drown out the remote. - **Why 38 kHz matters.** Remotes don't send a steady "on" - they send the signal as a 38,000-times-a-second flicker. The receiver is tuned to that flicker, so steady light sources don't fool it. - **Pressing the same button gives the same code.** That's the whole point of a remote protocol. The sketch learns four of those codes and reacts when it sees them again. - **Pin 13 blinks for free.** The `ENABLE_LED_FEEDBACK` flag makes the Uno's built-in LED blink every time *any* IR frame arrives. Even an unknown button proves the receiver is alive. ## Things to change once it works - Add a fifth "off" button that turns every LED off, by extending the learn sequence to five buttons. - Swap the LEDs for the 2-channel Songle relay (low-voltage DC only - the bedside lamp stays on its own switch) and turn this into a remote-controlled fan or LED strip switch. - Print the raw `0x...` codes for *every* button on your remote on the Serial Monitor and make a little reference table. You'll see the same prefix on every button - that's the remote's "address". - Wire up the LCD 1602 with I2C Backpack and have it show the name of the last colour pressed instead of just lighting an LED. ## Why this is interesting Most beginner sensor projects work in *one* direction: the world changes, the sensor responds. IR receivers flip that around - they give you a way to *send commands in* to the Arduino from across the room, using equipment (a TV remote) that's already in the house. Once you can decode a remote, an enormous chunk of consumer electronics suddenly stops being a black box. And because you're capturing real codes off a real remote, every household ends up with a slightly different demo, which keeps it fresh when Andy's son wants to show it off.

projects.name: Invisible Tripwire Alarm with OLED Face
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the ESP32's onboard regulator feeds the IR module, OLED, and LED from its 3.3V rail.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Set up an invisible beam across a doorway. When someone walks through it, a little face on the screen jumps from calm to shocked, a red light snaps on, and a counter ticks up by one. **Why it's fun**: Sneak it onto your bedroom door and catch your sister mid-snoop - the screen literally goes "!" when she crosses the line. It's the same trick museums use to know when you're getting too close to the dinosaur bones. A doorway "invisible tripwire" that watches a small patch of air in front of the IR Obstacle Avoidance Module. The moment your hand (or your son's hand) crosses the beam, the OLED face flips from calm "ARMED" to shocked "INTRUDER!", a red LED lights up, and a trip counter on the screen ticks up. Pull your hand away and everything snaps back. It's the same satisfying "did I really do that?" feedback as a museum motion sensor, built in an afternoon. ## Parts list - 1x IR Obstacle Avoidance Module (the protagonist - a digital "is something in front of me?" sensor) - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (reads the sensor, drives the OLED and LED) - 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) (for the ARMED / INTRUDER faces and trip counter) - 1x 5mm red LED (lights while the beam is broken) - 1x 330R resistor (current-limit for the red LED) - 1x breadboard, plus F-M and M-M jumper wires ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the power output pin that gives 3.3 volts. We use this to power the small parts. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs a wire back to GND to finish the circuit. - **D21, D22** - pins for talking to the OLED screen (these are the default I2C pins). - **D25, D32** - regular pins we use for the LED and the IR sensor. - **USB** - the silver port where you plug the cable from your laptop or phone charger. This powers the whole board.
**Step 1 - Put the breadboard and ESP32 ready.** - Place the breadboard flat in front of you. The little numbers and letters are your map. - Keep the ESP32 next to the breadboard for now - we will run wires from it into the breadboard holes. - Get out your jumper wires: the F-M ones (one end has a hole, the other end is a pin) and M-M ones (pin on both ends). The two long red and blue strips down the side of the breadboard are called the "rails" - the long strips that run all the way down the side. We will use the top rails as our power lanes: red for 3.3V, blue for ground.
**Step 2 - Power the rails from the ESP32.**
- Take an F-M jumper wire. Push the hole end onto the pin marked **3V3** on the ESP32. Push the pin end into the top red rail of the breadboard. - Take another F-M jumper wire. Push the hole end onto a pin marked **GND** on the ESP32. Push the pin end into the top blue rail. Now any part on the breadboard that needs power can grab it from the red rail, and any part that needs ground can grab it from the blue rail. Easy.
**Step 3 - Plug in the OLED screen.** The OLED has 4 little pins sticking out of one edge: GND, VCC (power input), SCL, SDA. Push the OLED straight down into the breadboard so its pins land in row 3 and row 4 area (holes A3, A4, A5, A6). - **GND** (at A3) - run a short M-M wire from row 3 over to the blue ground rail. - **VCC** (at A4) - run a short M-M wire from row 4 over to the red power rail. (VCC just means "power input" - it accepts 3.3V here.) - **SCL** (at A5) - run an F-M wire from row 5 to the pin marked **D22** on the ESP32. - **SDA** (at A6) - run an F-M wire from row 6 to the pin marked **D21** on the ESP32. **Why this matters:** SDA and SCL are the two wires the ESP32 uses to chat with the screen. D21 and D22 are the default chat pins on the ESP32, so we did not have to set anything special in the code.
**Step 4 - Plug in the IR tripwire sensor.** This little board has two clear bumps on the front (one sends invisible light, the other watches for it to bounce back). It has 3 pins on the back: OUT, GND, VCC. Push it into the breadboard with its pins in rows 11, 12, 13. - **OUT** (at A11) - run an F-M wire from row 11 to the pin marked **D32** on the ESP32. This is the wire that tells the ESP32 "someone broke the beam!" - **GND** (at A12) - run a short M-M wire from row 12 to the blue ground rail. - **VCC** (at A13) - run a short M-M wire from row 13 to the red power rail.
**Step 5 - Build the alarm LED.**
Look at your red LED. One leg is longer than the other - that long leg is the plus side. The short leg is the minus side. Also, the resistor is the little tan or blue tube with stripes; it does not matter which way around the resistor goes. - Push one leg of the **330R resistor** into hole **F20**. Push the other leg into hole **F23**. The resistor now bridges across row 20 to row 23. - Push the **long leg** of the LED into hole **J23** (same row as one end of the resistor). - Push the **short leg** of the LED into hole **J24**. - Run a short M-M wire from **J24** (short leg row) down to the blue ground rail. - Run an F-M wire from the pin marked **D25** on the ESP32 down to hole **J20** (the other end of the resistor). So the path the electricity takes is: D25 -> resistor -> long leg of LED -> short leg of LED -> ground. **Why this matters:** The resistor is there to slow down the electricity. If you connected the LED straight to the pin, too much current would rush through and burn the LED out in a flash. Putting the resistor in line is like adding a narrow doorway - it lets just enough current through to make the LED glow brightly without hurting it. Always put the resistor in before the LED, not after.
**Step 6 - Plug in the USB cable and tune the sensor.** - Plug the USB cable into the ESP32's silver USB port, and the other end into your laptop or a 5V phone charger. The little red power light on the ESP32 should turn on. - Look at the IR sensor board. On the back there is a tiny blue box with a screw slot - that is called a trimpot. Use a small screwdriver to turn it. This changes how far away the sensor can "see". Turn it one way for short range (a few centimetres), the other way for long range (about 30 cm). - The IR sensor also has two tiny LEDs on it. One shows it has power. The other one lights up whenever it sees something in the beam. That second LED is your best friend while tuning - wave your hand in front of the sensor and watch it blink. This is a tricky one to tune. Take your time, wave your hand at the distance you actually want the tripwire to trigger at, and turn the screw a little at a time until the "obstacle" LED clicks on at just the right spot.
## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click **OK**. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a chunky download, so give it a minute. 3. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install two libraries: - Search `Adafruit GFX` -> install **"Adafruit GFX Library"**. - Search `Adafruit SSD1306` -> install **"Adafruit SSD1306"**. (If it asks about installing extra dependencies, click **Install all**.) 4. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** (or **"ESP32 Dev Module"** if you don't see it). **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB micro-B cable that can carry data** (some cheap cables are charge-only - if the board never shows up, that is usually why). 2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged in. On Windows it looks like `COM4` or `COM7`; on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`. 3. This sketch has no WiFi password or other placeholder to fill in - the code is ready to go. Just double-check the pin numbers at the top (`PIN_IR_OUT = 32`, `PIN_LED = 25`) match your wiring. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top left). You will see "Connecting....." in the bottom panel. If it sits there for more than 5 seconds spamming dots, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need this trick on the first upload. 5. When it says **"Hard resetting via RTS pin"** the flash is done. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window) to **115200**. 6. The OLED should light up showing **ARMED** with a calm smiley face and `Trips: 0` at the bottom. Wave your hand about 10 cm in front of the IR module - the face should flip to **INTRUDER!** with wide eyes, the red LED should turn on, and the trip counter should tick up by one. Pull your hand away and it snaps back to ARMED. The little obstacle LED on the IR module itself lights up at the same time, which is a handy confirmation that the sensor is seeing your hand. **Common gotchas:** - *Upload sits on "Connecting....." forever.* That is the BOOT button trick - hold BOOT down on the ESP32 while the IDE is trying to connect, release once it starts writing. Once the sketch is running, future uploads usually work without it. - *OLED stays black.* Almost always either swapped SDA/SCL (SDA = GPIO 21, SCL = GPIO 22) or wrong I2C address. The sketch uses `0x3C`, which fits most 0.96" boards - if yours is `0x3D` the screen will just stay dark with no error. Also double-check the OLED's VCC goes to **3V3**, not 5V. - *Counter shoots up by 5 every time you wave.* The 40 ms debounce window should stop this, but if your IR module is extra twitchy, turn the little blue trimpot on the back a tiny bit anti-clockwise to make it less sensitive, or bump `DEBOUNCE_MS` from 40 to 80 in the sketch and re-upload. ## Talking points - *Active-LOW logic, again.* Just like the 2-ch relay board: the sensor's `OUT` line sits HIGH normally and pulls LOW when something is detected. Show your son `digitalRead(PIN_IR_OUT) == LOW` and ask him "so... does LOW mean nothing's there, or something IS there?" It's the classic beginner trap that's easier to learn once than to memorise forever. - *Why debounce?* The IR detector edge isn't perfectly clean - as a hand enters or leaves the beam you might get a few rapid HIGH/LOW flickers across a millisecond or two. Without the 40ms debounce window, one wave of the hand could log 5 trips. With it, you log exactly 1. - *Why a small built-in face on the OLED instead of just text?* Because feedback that feels like a reaction is more fun than feedback that looks like a log entry. Same information, completely different vibe. ## Things to change once it works - Add the small piezo buzzer (or a tiny servo arm that "slams" a paper door) so the alarm has audio or motion too. - Swap the IR Obstacle Avoidance Module for the HC-SR04 ultrasonic and compare: ultrasonic gives you a *distance number*, the IR module only gives you a *yes/no*. Same project shape, very different sensor character. - Add WiFi: have the ESP32 send a "tripped at HH:MM:SS" line to your laptop or to the Orange Pi (once it's booted) over MQTT, so you can see a log of every doorway crossing. - Mount the module sideways in a doorway with cardboard so it makes a real "laser-style" beam across the threshold. ## Why this is interesting Almost every "smart" presence sensor in the world - shop door chimes, automatic taps, elevator door re-open - is doing exactly what this circuit does: a beam, a detector, a digital edge, and a reaction. Building the toy version once makes the grown-up versions stop feeling like magic. It's also a near-zero-frustration project: no analog calibration, no flaky timing, no maths - just "something is here / something is not here" with instant visual payoff.

projects.name: Piggy Bank Coin Counter (TCRT5000 + OLED)
projects.power_supply: USB-C cable from a phone charger or laptop into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the ESP32's 3.3V rail powers the TCRT5000 module, the OLED, and the indicator LED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Drop a coin in the slot. The little screen bumps the count up by one, flashes a green LED, and shouts a cheer just for you. Unplug it, plug it back in tomorrow - your total is still there waiting. **Why it's fun**: It's a piggy bank that actually KNOWS how rich you are, and it celebrates every single coin like you just won a prize. Race your dad to see who can fill theirs first, or sneak up on it and try to drop a coin so fast the sensor misses it (spoiler: it won't). A real-world piggy bank that knows how much you've fed it. The TCRT5000 sits in the throat of the slot pointing across the gap; whenever a coin passes between the IR LED and the phototransistor, the module's digital output drops, the ESP32 counts it, the green LED blinks, and the OLED bumps the total along with a cheerful message. The count survives reboots because it is written to the ESP32's flash memory. ## Parts list - ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the brain - reads the sensor, drives the screen, stores the count) - TCRT5000 IR Reflective Tracking Module (the "eye" that catches each coin) - 0.96" OLED Display, I2C (the running tally and cheer board) - 5mm green LED + 330R resistor (an instant "I saw that" flash) - Breadboard + DuPont jumpers (no soldering) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - power output, 3.3 volts. We use this to power all our parts. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs to share this. - **D4, D17, D21, D22** - pins. The number after the D matches the GPIO number in the code. - **EN** - the reset button is right next to it. Press EN to restart the ESP32. - **USB port** - where the USB-C cable plugs in. This is how the board gets power.
**Step 1 - Get the breadboard ready.** A breadboard lets you plug parts in without any soldering. The long red and blue strips running down each side are called the power rails. Red is for power (the long red strip), blue is for ground (the long blue strip). The middle rows (A-E and F-J) are split down the middle, and each row of 5 holes is connected together inside.
**Step 2 - Power the rails from the ESP32.** Using jumper wires (the M-M kind), connect the ESP32 to the breadboard rails so every part can grab power and ground. - ESP32 **3V3** pin -> top red rail (+5V_T on the diagram, but we are sending 3.3V). - ESP32 **GND** pin -> top blue rail (GND_T). - ESP32 **3V3** pin -> bottom red rail (+5V_B). - ESP32 **GND** pin -> bottom blue rail (GND_B). This way both halves of the breadboard have power and ground waiting. Why this matters: all the parts need to share the same ground line so they can talk to each other. If the grounds are not connected, signals get confused.
**Step 3 - Plug in the OLED screen.** This little screen shows the coin count. Push it into the breadboard so each of its 4 pins lands in a different row. Look at the labels printed on the OLED itself. - OLED **GND** -> row E3. Then a short wire from A3 to the top blue rail (ground). - OLED **VCC** (power input) -> row E4. Then a short wire from A4 to the top red rail (3.3V). - OLED **SCL** -> row E5. Then a wire from A5 to the ESP32 pin marked **D22**. - OLED **SDA** -> row E6. Then a wire from A6 to the ESP32 pin marked **D21**. SCL and SDA are the two talking wires the screen uses (this is called I2C). D21 and D22 are the ESP32's default I2C pins, so the code just works.
**Step 4 - Plug in the TCRT5000 coin sensor.** This is the part that "sees" a coin drop. It has a little blue box with two clear bumps on top - one shines invisible infrared light down, the other catches it when something shiny bounces it back. Push the module into the board so its 4 pins land in separate rows. - TCRT5000 **VCC** (power input) -> row E12. Wire from A12 to the top red rail (3.3V). - TCRT5000 **GND** -> row E13. Wire from A13 to the top blue rail (ground). - TCRT5000 **DO** (digital out) -> row E14. Wire from A14 to the ESP32 pin marked **D4**. - TCRT5000 **AO** -> row E15. Leave this one unconnected. We don't use it. Why this matters: we power the sensor from 3.3V, not 5V. That way the DO signal coming back to the ESP32 is also 3.3V, which is exactly what the ESP32 wants. Powering it from 5V can hurt the ESP32 pin over time. The DO pin is normally HIGH and drops to LOW when a coin is right under the sensor. There is also a tiny screw (potentiometer) on the module - we will tune it later.
**Step 5 - Add the green "coin counted" LED with its resistor.** When a coin falls past the sensor, this LED will blink. The green LED has two legs of different lengths - the **long leg** is positive, the **short leg** is negative. The flat side of the LED's plastic dome is on the short-leg side. - Plug the **330R resistor** so one end is in F22 and the other end is in F25. - Plug the green LED's **long leg** into J25 (same row as the resistor end). - Plug the green LED's **short leg** into J26. - Run a wire from J26 to the bottom blue rail (ground). - Run a wire from the ESP32 pin marked **D17** to row J22 (the other end of the resistor). So the path is: ESP32 D17 -> 330R resistor -> LED long leg -> LED short leg -> ground. Why this matters - the resistor: LEDs are greedy. If you plug one straight into a pin with no resistor, it tries to grab way too much electricity and burns out in a flash (literally). The 330 ohm resistor is like a small road bump that slows the electricity down to a safe amount, so the LED glows nicely instead of dying.
**Step 6 - Plug in the USB-C cable.** Plug the small end into the ESP32's USB port and the big end into your laptop or a phone charger. The little red power LED on the ESP32 should light up right away. If it doesn't, unplug it and check your red and blue rail wires - one might be backwards.
**Step 7 - Tune the sensor.** The TCRT5000 has a tiny blue screw on it called a potentiometer. There is also a small indicator LED on the sensor module. Hold a coin about 1 cm (the width of your fingernail) under the sensor and gently turn the screw with a small screwdriver until the indicator LED just turns on. Move the coin away - the indicator LED should go off. Now your sensor is set to "see" a coin at the right distance. This is a tricky one, so go slow and only turn the screw a tiny bit at a time.
## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click OK. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type "esp32" in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"** (it is a big download, give it a few minutes). 3. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install these three, one at a time: - Search "Adafruit GFX" -> install **Adafruit GFX Library** - Search "Adafruit SSD1306" -> install **Adafruit SSD1306** - If it asks to also install dependencies (BusIO), say yes. 4. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** from the long list. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with a **USB-C cable** (or micro-USB, depending on which NodeMCU-32S you have - check the port on the board). Use a cable you know carries data, not a charge-only one. 2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that just showed up (on Windows it looks like **COM4** or **COM5**, on a Mac it looks like **cu.usbserial-XXXX**). If nothing new appears, try a different cable. 3. There are no passwords or placeholders to change in this sketch - it runs offline. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow at the top of the IDE). You will see "Connecting......" in the black box at the bottom. On the very first upload, if it gets stuck on dots, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see "Writing at 0x..." then let go. 5. When it finishes ("Hard resetting via RTS pin"), open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the dropdown on the right to **115200 baud**. 6. You should see `Loaded saved count: 0` in the Serial Monitor, and the OLED should light up with "PIGGY BANK", a big **0**, and "Ready - drop a coin!" along the bottom. Wave a coin (or your fingertip) about a centimetre over the TCRT5000 - the green LED flashes, the number jumps to 1, and a cheer appears. **Common gotchas:** - **Upload fails with "Failed to connect"**: this is the BOOT button trick. Hold BOOT on the ESP32, click Upload, and let go of BOOT when "Connecting..." turns into "Writing...". You only need this on stubborn first uploads. - **OLED stays dark and Serial Monitor says "OLED init failed"**: SDA and SCL are swapped, or the OLED's address is `0x3D` instead of `0x3C`. Try swapping the two yellow-ish wires first; if still nothing, change `OLED_ADDR` in the code from `0x3C` to `0x3D` and upload again. - **Counter races up to 50 the moment you power it on, with no coin**: the little blue pot on the TCRT5000 module is turned too sensitive. Turn it slowly with a small screwdriver until the on-board indicator LED goes OFF when nothing is over the sensor, then ON only when a coin sits above it. - **Serial Monitor shows garbled symbols like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`**: the baud rate dropdown is wrong. Set it to **115200** to match the `Serial.begin(115200)` line in the code. ## Talking points - The TCRT5000 is basically an IR flashlight and an IR camera sitting next to each other. The flashlight always shines forward; the camera only "sees" light if something in front bounces some of it back. A coin held a centimetre above the sensor is a great mirror for invisible IR. - Why "active LOW"? The comparator chip on the module is wired so that "lots of reflected light" pulls the output down to ground. It is the standard convention for these modules and is worth getting used to - it will come back on the IR obstacle modules and the PIR sensors. - The debounce timer (250 ms) is there because one coin passing through can briefly flicker the sensor twice as it tumbles. We treat anything inside 250 ms as the same coin. - `Preferences` is the ESP32's tiny built-in key/value store. We save the count every time it changes, so unplugging the bank does not reset the total. ## Things to change once it works - Build an actual slot: a cardboard tube or a 3D-printed funnel with the TCRT5000 staring across the throat. A short, narrow chute makes the detection rock-solid. - Add a "session" counter alongside the lifetime total - reset on a button press. - Switch the cheer text to count up the cash value if you only feed it one coin type ("$0.25", "$0.50"...). - Pipe the count to MQTT on the (eventually-booted) Orange Pi so the household can race each other to fill their banks. - Swap DO for AO (analog out) and look at how the reflected-light reading actually changes with coin distance - a great intro to ADCs. ## Why this is interesting It teaches the difference between a "raw" sensor reading and an "event". The TCRT5000 gives you a continuous on/off signal, but what you really want is one count per coin - which means edge detection, debouncing, and a tiny state machine. Those are the same three ideas that show up in every button, encoder, and motion sensor project, so once they click here they keep paying off.

projects.name: Porch Night-Light (KY-018 dusk-to-dawn fader)
projects.power_supply: Arduino Uno powered from a laptop USB cable; the KY-018 and the LED both run from the Uno's 5V rail.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Turn off the room lights and watch a little yellow LED slowly glow brighter, like a porch light waking up at sunset. Turn the lights back on and it fades away again, all by itself. **Why it's fun**: No button, no switch, no app - the light just KNOWS when it's dark. Cup your hand over the tiny sensor and you become the sunset. A pretend porch-light that turns on by itself when the room gets dark. The KY-018 photoresistor watches the ambient light; a yellow LED on the breadboard fades up as the room darkens and fades back down at sunrise - exactly how a real dusk-to-dawn porch bulb behaves, but built on the kitchen table. ## Parts list - KY-018 Photoresistor Module (the "eye" - an LDR on a little PCB) - Arduino Uno R3 (5V, 10-bit ADC - perfect for an analog sensor) - 1x yellow 5mm LED (stands in for a porch bulb; warm yellow looks the part) - 1x 220R resistor (current limit for the LED) - Breadboard + a handful of jumpers (3x F-M for the KY-018 module pins, the rest M-M for the LED side) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the power output pin. It gives you 5 volts to feed other parts. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs a wire going back here. - **A0** - an analog input pin. It can read a value from 0 to 1023 (not just on/off). - **D9** - a digital pin. The little `~` next to it means it can do a fast on-off signal that looks like dimming. We need that to fade the LED. - **USB-B** - the big square socket where the laptop cable plugs in. That cable also powers the board.
**Step 1 - Put the breadboard down next to the Uno.** The breadboard has rows of little holes. Inside the plastic, each row of 5 holes (A-B-C-D-E on the left side, and F-G-H-I-J on the right) is joined together by a hidden metal strip. So if you stick two leg ends into the same row, they are connected. Easy. We won't be using the long red and blue strips on the side this time. Everything will plug into the lettered rows.
**Step 2 - Plant the KY-018 light sensor into the breadboard.** The KY-018 is a small board with a round yellow light-sensing eye and three pins sticking out the bottom. Look at the side of those pins - you should see tiny letters. Most clones print them as: - **S** = signal (the pin that tells the Arduino how bright it is) - **+** = power input (the KY-018 wants 5V here) - **-** = the 0V side, ground Push the three pins into the breadboard like this: - **S** pin goes into hole **E5** - **+** pin goes into hole **E7** - **-** pin goes into hole **E9** The little yellow eye should be facing up so it can see the room.
**Step 3 - Wire the KY-018 to the Arduino.** Grab three male-to-male jumper wires (both ends look like a tiny metal pin). Pick a red one, a black one, and any other color for the signal - it makes mistakes way easier to spot later. - Red wire: from breadboard hole **E7** to the Arduino pin marked **5V**. That gives the sensor its power. - Black wire: from breadboard hole **E9** to any Arduino pin marked **GND**. That is the 0V side - ground. - Signal wire: from breadboard hole **E5** to the Arduino pin marked **A0**. That is how the Uno reads brightness. The KY-018 wants 5V power. Get used to checking this on every sensor before you plug it in - one day you will graduate to the ESP32 board, and that board's pins want 3.3V instead. Sending 5V into a 3.3V pin can fry it.
**Step 4 - Plant the resistor and the LED on the breadboard.**
The yellow LED has two legs. The **long leg** is the plus side. The **short leg** is the minus side. If you flip them, the LED just won't light - it won't break, but nothing will glow either. The 220R resistor is the little tan or blue tube with stripes. It does not have a plus or minus side - you can plug it in either way around. - Push one leg of the **resistor** into hole **F18** and its other leg into hole **F22**. - Push the **long leg** of the LED into hole **J22** (same row as one end of the resistor). - Push the **short leg** of the LED into hole **J23**. **Why the resistor matters:** An LED is a greedy little thing - if you plug it straight into 5V it will gulp too much electricity and burn out in about a second, with a tiny puff of smoke. The 220R resistor sits in the path and slows the flow down to a safe amount. Always put a resistor in front of an LED. Always.
**Step 5 - Wire the LED to the Arduino.** Two more male-to-male jumper wires: - Signal wire: from hole **F18** (the other end of the resistor) to the Arduino pin marked **D9**. Look closely - D9 has a little `~` symbol next to it. That symbol means the pin can do a fast on-off signal that looks like dimming. The code uses that to fade the light up and down. - Black wire: from hole **J23** (the LED's short leg) to any spare Arduino pin marked **GND**. **Why D9 matters:** Not every pin can fade. If you plug the LED into a pin without the `~` symbol (like D7), the LED can only go full bright or full off - it would flicker on and off instead of fading smoothly. Always check for the `~` when a sketch fades or dims.
**Step 6 - Power up.** Plug the USB cable from your laptop into the Arduino's USB-B socket (the big square one). The Uno should light up its little green power light. Nothing on the breadboard will do anything yet - that happens after you flash the code in the next section. Cover the yellow eye of the KY-018 with your finger to test it later. In the dark, the LED should glow brighter. In the light, it should dim. That's the whole job of a porch night-light. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):** 1. Open the Arduino IDE. 2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno**. (The Uno is built-in - no Boards Manager URL needed.) 3. No extra libraries to install for this sketch. Everything it uses (`analogRead`, `analogWrite`, `Serial`) is already baked into the IDE. 4. If Windows doesn't see your Uno at all, your board is a CH340 clone (ours is). Grab the CH340 driver from [sparks.gogo.co.nz/ch340.html](https://sparks.gogo.co.nz/ch340.html), install it, and unplug/replug the Uno. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into the laptop with a **USB-A to USB-B** cable (the big square plug, same as an old printer). The green `ON` LED on the Uno should light up straight away. 2. **Tools -> Port** -> pick the one that says `COM*` (Windows) or `/dev/cu.usbmodem*` (Mac) or `/dev/ttyACM0` (Linux). If you see more than one, unplug the Uno, look again, plug it back, and the new one that appeared is yours. 3. Open the sketch. Nothing to edit - there are no passwords or WiFi names in this one. (If the LED ends up ON in daylight and OFF in the dark, come back and flip `DARK_IS_HIGH` from `true` to `false` near the top, then re-upload.) 4. Click the **Upload** button (the round right-arrow at the top-left). The orange `TX` and `RX` LEDs on the Uno will flicker for a couple of seconds. When it says **"Done uploading"** at the bottom, the sketch is running. 5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window) to **9600** - that matches the `Serial.begin(9600)` in the sketch. 6. What you should see: a "Calibrating - cover then uncover the sensor" message, about 3 seconds of streaming raw numbers, then a steady stream of readings like `raw=812 dark%=64 led=140`. Cup your hand over the KY-018 and the `dark%` shoots up while the yellow LED fades on. Pull your hand away and watch it fade back down. That's success. **Common gotchas:** - **Serial Monitor shows gibberish** (random symbols, weird characters). The baud rate is wrong. Set it to **9600** in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor. - **LED never lights up, even when you cover the sensor.** The LED is in backwards. The long leg (anode) goes to the 220R resistor / pin D9 side; the short leg (cathode) goes to GND. No damage - just turn it around. - **LED is on in daylight and off in the dark** (backwards behaviour). Your KY-018 clone is wired the other way round. Open the sketch, change `const bool DARK_IS_HIGH = true;` to `false`, and click Upload again. ## Talking points - Why an analog pin (`A0`), not a digital one. The KY-018 doesn't say "dark / not dark"; it says "this much light", as a voltage from 0 to 5V. The Uno's ADC converts that voltage into a number from 0 to 1023, and that's the number we map into "how bright should the LED be". - Why smoothing. If the porch bulb just looked at the raw reading and turned on whenever it crossed a threshold, every passing shadow would flicker it. The sketch keeps a running average (an exponential moving average, or EMA) so it reacts to "the sun went down" but ignores "a hand briefly waved past". This is the single most advanced trick in the sketch - everything else is map/constrain/analogWrite. - Why two thresholds (`DARK_START_PERCENT` and `DARK_FULL_PERCENT`) instead of one. Two thresholds give a gentle fade-in region instead of a snap. This is what a real dusk-to-dawn sensor does inside, and it's also what makes the project feel polished instead of toy-like. - Calibration at startup. KY-018 clones vary - some give a high reading in the dark, some give a low one, and the absolute values depend on the room. Sampling for ~3 seconds at boot while you cover-then-uncover the sensor lets the sketch figure out what "normal" looks like in your room, so you don't have to hardcode magic numbers. If you miss the prompt entirely, the sketch falls back to sensible defaults (200/900) so it still works. - The polarity knob. Some KY-018 clones read higher as it gets darker; others read lower. The sketch has one constant near the top, `DARK_IS_HIGH`, that picks which. If the porch light is on in daylight and off in the dark, flip it from `true` to `false` and re-upload. One flag, one line - the rest of the code adapts. ## Things to change once it works - Swap the yellow LED for the blue or green one and watch the same logic work unchanged - the LED colour is "front-end", the logic is "back-end". - Cover the KY-018 with a cupped hand. The LED should fade up smoothly over half a second or so, not snap. If it snaps, increase `SMOOTHING` toward 0.2 (faster) or decrease it toward 0.01 (slower). - Add a second LED on `D10` (also PWM) that comes on only when it's *really* dark - call it the "burglar deterrent" porch flood. - Once Andy has soldered headers on a relay, the LED could be swapped for the 1-channel relay driving a real low-voltage lamp. (Project as written stays solder-free.) - The KY-018 vs the LM393 photoresistor module: the LM393 board has a comparator on it and gives you a *digital* dark / not-dark output (and a threshold knob). The KY-018 gives you the *analog* reading and lets you decide. That's why this project uses fading - you can't fade off a digital signal. ## Why this is interesting This is the cleanest possible example of "sensor in, actuator out, brain in the middle". Every home-automation project Andy will ever build is the same shape: read something about the world, decide what to do, change something in the world. Light -> Arduino -> LED is the smallest honest version of that loop, and once it works the same code structure scales straight up to "soil moisture -> ESP32 -> watering pump" or "motion -> ESP32 -> WiFi notification".

projects.name: Laser Tripwire Alarm (LDR + KY-008 pair)
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S; the board's onboard regulator feeds 3.3V to both the laser module and the photoresistor receiver.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A red laser shoots a thin beam across a doorway and lands on a tiny sensor on the other side. Walk through the beam and a red alarm light snaps ON and stays on until you press the button to reset it. **Why it's fun**: Set it up across your bedroom door and you instantly know when a sibling sneaks in, even hours later, because the light stays lit until you clear it. It is the closest you can get to building a real spy-movie laser tripwire with stuff that fits on a breadboard. ## Eye safety - read first The KY-008 is a real 650nm laser diode module (laser-pointer class, typically rated under 5mW but still hazardous). Even brief direct exposure or a glint off a shiny surface can damage the retina, and the damage is painless and permanent. Before powering the board: - Never look into the beam or the emitter aperture, not even "just to check it's on". If you need to confirm it works, look at the red dot on a matte surface (a piece of paper, a wall, the white face of the LDR module). - Never aim the laser at a person, a pet, a window, a mirror, polished metal, or any glossy surface that could bounce a specular reflection back at someone. - Aim it once with the receiver taped down, then leave it. Treat it like a loaded staple gun: it's pointed somewhere specific, and you don't pick it up to "see where it goes" while live. - The sketch turns the laser ON as soon as the board boots. Plug power in only after both modules are pointed at each other and taped in place. ## Parts list - 1x Photoresistor Module (LM393 comparator) - the receiver. It has a built-in pot to set the dark/light threshold and a clean digital DO output. - 1x KY-008 Red Laser Module (650nm) - the emitter. The narrow beam crosses the doorway and lands on the receiver. - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the receiver, controls the laser, latches the alarm. - 1x red 5mm LED + 220R resistor - "the wire's been tripped" indicator that stays on. - 1x tactile push-button - re-arm button to clear the latched alarm. - Breadboard + DuPont jumpers. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - this pin gives out 3.3 volts of power. Both parts in this project run on 3.3V. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs a wire back to GND or it won't work. - **D4, D21, D22, D23** - these are pins you can control from your code. On this board the "D" number matches the GPIO number, so the code that says GPIO 23 means the pin marked **D23**. - **USB** - the silver port at the end. This is where the laptop or phone charger plugs in to give the board power. - **EN** - a tiny button labeled EN. Pressing it restarts the board (handy if something looks stuck).
**Heads-up before you plug anything in:** the laser turns on the second the ESP32 wakes up. Build everything, aim the laser at the white window on the receiver, and tape both parts down BEFORE you plug in USB. Never look straight into the red dot.
**Step 1 - Put the breadboard and ESP32 in front of you.** - The breadboard has two long red strips and two long blue strips down the sides. The red one we will use is the **+ (power) strip on the top edge** - that's our "+5V" rail in the wiring map (even though we'll actually feed it 3.3V). - The blue one we will use is the **- (ground) strip on the top edge** - that's our "GND" rail. - Keep the ESP32 off the breadboard for now. Lay it next to the breadboard. We'll use the female-to-male jumper wires to reach from the ESP32 pins to the breadboard holes.
**Step 2 - Feed power from the ESP32 to the breadboard rails.**
- Use a red female-to-male jumper. Plug the female end onto the ESP32 pin marked **3V3**. Plug the male end into any hole on the red (+) strip along the top of the breadboard. - Use a black female-to-male jumper. Plug the female end onto a pin marked **GND** on the ESP32. Plug the male end into any hole on the blue (-) strip along the top of the breadboard. - Now the whole red strip is at 3.3V and the whole blue strip is at 0V. Every part we add can grab power from those two strips.
**Step 3 - Place the LM393 photoresistor receiver.** This is the little board with the white round window (the photoresistor) and a blue twisty knob (the trim-pot). - Push the 4 pins down into the breadboard so they land in row B, columns 3 to 6 (holes **B3, B4, B5, B6**). The pin order on the module is usually printed on the board. - **VCC** (power input) -> **B3**. Run a short red male-to-male wire from **B3** to the red (+) strip on top. This gives the module 3.3V. - **GND** (the 0V side) -> **B4**. Run a black male-to-male wire from **B4** to the blue (-) strip on top. - **DO** (digital out) -> **B5**. This is where the module tells the ESP32 "I see laser" or "I don't see laser". We'll hook this to the ESP32 in step 7. - **AO** (analog out) -> **B6**. We are not using this one. Just leave **B6** empty. **Why this matters:** the white round window is a photoresistor. It changes how much electricity flows through it depending on how bright the light shining on it is. The LM393 chip on the same little board reads that and squashes it into a clean "bright" or "dark" answer for the ESP32. The blue knob lets you decide where the line between "bright" and "dark" is. We'll set that knob in the last step.
**Step 4 - Add the re-arm button.** The button is a tiny silver square with 4 metal legs. - Push the button across the gap in the middle of the breadboard so its legs sit in row **B10** and row **I10** (or near there - the important thing is that its legs straddle the middle gap). - One leg of the button is now in **B10**. - Run a black male-to-male wire from **B12** (which connects to the same side of the button as B10 through the button's body when pressed) to the blue (-) strip. So one side of the button is wired to ground. - The other side of the button will go to the ESP32 in step 7. **Why this matters:** when you press the button, the two sides of it get connected. That pulls the ESP32 pin down to 0V, and the code sees the press. The ESP32 has a built-in "pull-up" that keeps the pin at 3.3V when the button is not pressed, so we don't need an extra resistor for the button.
**Step 5 - Add the red alarm LED and its resistor.**
The LED has two legs. The **long leg** is the + side. The **short leg** (and the flat spot on the rim) is the - side. - Put the LED's **long leg** into **B17**. - Put the LED's **short leg** into **B18**. - Take the 220R resistor. The body is small with red-red-brown-gold stripes. Resistors don't care which way around they go. - Bend the resistor's legs and plug one leg into **B18** (the same hole as the LED's short leg). Plug the other leg into the blue (-) strip on top. **Why this matters:** an LED is greedy - it will gulp down too much electricity and burn itself out in less than a second if you connect it straight across the pins. The 220 ohm resistor is the "speed bump" that slows the current down to a safe amount. Always put a resistor in series with an LED.
**Step 6 - Place the KY-008 laser module.** This is the small board with a red metal can on top - the can is the laser. Be careful: even small lasers can hurt eyes if you stare into them. - The module has 3 pins in a row, marked **S**, **middle (NC)**, and **-**. - Push the 3 pins into the breadboard so they land in **B23, B24, B25**. - **S** is in **B23** - this is the signal pin. The ESP32 will turn the laser on by sending 3.3V here. - The **middle pin (B24)** is "NC", which means **Not Connected**. Leave **B24** empty. Do NOT run a wire from here to power - it would damage the module. - **-** is in **B25**. Run a black male-to-male wire from **B25** to the blue (-) strip on top.
**Step 7 - Run the four signal wires back to the ESP32.** Now we connect the four "talking" wires to the ESP32. Use the female-to-male jumpers. The female end goes onto the ESP32 pin; the male end goes into the breadboard hole. - From the ESP32 pin marked **D21** -> breadboard hole **B5**. (This is the receiver's DO line - it tells the ESP32 whether the laser is hitting the window.) - From the ESP32 pin marked **D4** -> breadboard hole **B10**. (This is the re-arm button.) - From the ESP32 pin marked **D22** -> breadboard hole **B17**. (This drives the alarm LED's long leg.) - From the ESP32 pin marked **D23** -> breadboard hole **B23**. (This turns the laser on and off.) Take a moment and double-check each one. Wrong pins won't break anything here, but the code won't work until they match.
**Step 8 - Aim, tape, then plug in USB.** - Place the laser module and the receiver module across a doorway, on a shelf, or across a desk - whatever you want to guard. - Aim the red laser can at the white round window on the receiver. Get the dot dead-center on the white window. - Use masking tape or putty to lock both modules in place so they can't drift. If the dot wanders off the window, the alarm will think someone walked through. - NOW plug the USB cable into the ESP32 and into your laptop or phone charger. The laser turns on right away.
**Step 9 - Tune the blue knob on the receiver.** The receiver has a small blue twisty knob. It decides where the line is between "bright enough" and "too dark". - Look at the receiver's tiny onboard signal LED. With the laser hitting the white window, you want that LED to be **off** (meaning "bright"). Block the beam with your finger and that LED should turn **on** (meaning "dark"). - If the LED is always on, slowly turn the knob one way with a small screwdriver until it flips off. - If the LED is always off even when you block the beam, turn the knob the other way until it just barely turns on when blocked. - Aim for the spot where the LED is right on the edge - off when the laser is hitting, on the moment anything blocks it. That's the most sensitive setting.
**Step 10 - Test it.** Wave a finger (not your eye!) through the laser beam. The red alarm LED should latch on and stay on. Open the serial monitor on your computer and you should see `>>> TRIPWIRE BROKEN <<<`. Press the re-arm button to clear the alarm and start watching again. If nothing happens, check that the laser dot is actually landing on the white window and re-do the knob tuning in step 9. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). Before you plug anything in, double-check the laser is pointed at the white face of the LDR module and both modules are taped down. The sketch turns the laser ON the instant the board powers up, and you do not want a live beam swinging around the room while you fiddle with the IDE. **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open the IDE, go to **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click OK. 2. **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. In the search box type `esp32`. Find "esp32 by Espressif Systems" and click Install. It takes a few minutes - good time for a snack. 3. **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**. 4. No extra libraries needed for this sketch - it only uses the built-in `pinMode`, `digitalRead`, `digitalWrite`, and `Serial` stuff that comes with the ESP32 core. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a USB cable (make sure it is a **data** cable, not a charge-only one - if the board lights up but no COM port appears, that is usually the cable). 2. **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that just appeared (on Windows it looks like `COM5` or `COM7`; on a Mac it is `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`). 3. This sketch has no WiFi passwords or placeholders to fill in - leave the pin numbers alone unless you wired it differently. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). If you see "Connecting......_____" dots scrolling for more than 5 seconds, **hold the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. This is normal on the NodeMCU-32S the first time. 5. When upload finishes you should see "Hard resetting via RTS pin". The laser comes on right then. 6. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of the monitor window) to **115200**. You should see: ``` Laser Tripwire Alarm starting... Laser is ON. Aim it at the white dot on the LDR module and turn the blue trim-pot until the module's signal LED just barely turns OFF. Then block the beam to test. ``` Now use a small screwdriver on the blue trim-pot on the LDR module: turn it slowly until the tiny green "signal" LED on the module just barely switches off while the beam is hitting it. Wave your hand through the beam - the green LED on the module should pop on, and your red alarm LED should latch on with `>>> TRIPWIRE BROKEN <<<` printed in the Serial Monitor. Press the re-arm button to clear it. **Common gotchas:** - **"Connecting......_____" forever on upload.** The NodeMCU-32S often needs the **BOOT** button held down during the first upload. Press and hold BOOT, click Upload, and only release BOOT once you see "Writing..." appear. - **Alarm goes off the second you power up, even with the beam aimed correctly.** The trim-pot on the LDR module is set too sensitive. Turn it slowly while watching the green signal LED on the module - you want that LED OFF while the laser is hitting it, and ON when you block the beam. If it never changes, the laser is missing the white dot - re-aim it. - **Serial Monitor shows garbage characters like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`.** The baud rate is wrong. Set the dropdown in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor to **115200**, matching the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the sketch. ## Talking points - **A tripwire is just a "before vs after" test.** The laser doesn't measure anything fancy. It just gives the receiver one easy thing to see. When that one thing disappears, we know something passed through. - **Why latch the alarm?** A real intruder is only in the beam for a few milliseconds. If the LED only lit while the beam was broken, you'd never see it. Latching means: once tripped, stay tripped until a human acknowledges it. - **Two modules talking through air.** There are no wires between the laser and the receiver - the beam itself is the signal. That's the same idea as a TV remote, a barcode scanner, or fibre-optic internet, just slower. - **The LM393 comparator on the receiver.** The little chip on the module compares the LDR's voltage to whatever the pot is set to and gives a clean HIGH/LOW. Without it, you'd be reading a noisy analog value and writing your own threshold code. ## Things to change once it works - Add a piezo buzzer in parallel with the alarm LED for an audible siren. - Drive the laser through a transistor and **pulse** it at 1 kHz, then have the receiver only count the alarm if the pulse goes missing. That defeats someone shining a flashlight at the receiver to fool it. - Bounce the beam off a small mirror so the laser and receiver sit on the same side of the doorway. Easier to install, looks more like a spy movie. (Mirror placement still needs the eye-safety rules: don't aim it where a reflection could find a face.) - Have the ESP32 publish the trip event over MQTT to the Orange Pi (once the Pi is booted). - Add a 5-second arming countdown so you can leave the room before the tripwire goes hot. ## Why this is interesting It's the first project in the kit where two separate active components have to physically agree on something across empty space. The wiring on the breadboard is short and friendly, but the real "circuit" is invisible. That makes the debugging satisfying: nudge the laser, watch the latch hold, press re-arm, and you've built a tiny security system out of a 50-cent LDR module and a laser pointer.

projects.name: Coin Drop Counter (optical slot + OLED)
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or 5V phone charger into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S USB-C port; the ESP32's onboard regulator feeds 3.3V to the slot sensor and OLED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Drop a coin through a little slot. The number on the tiny screen jumps up by one, instantly, every single time. Drop ten coins fast and watch it climb to ten without missing a single one. **Why it's fun**: It feels like the screen is reading your mind because it counts faster than your eye can follow. Challenge your dad to drop five coins faster than you can, then point at the screen when it caught every single one. ## Parts list - 1x Optical Slot / Speed Sensor (the protagonist - an IR LED facing a phototransistor across a small gap) - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C, SSD1306) - 1x Breadboard - A handful of male-male and female-male jumpers - Coins, popsicle-stick wedges, or strips of paper to drop through the slot No resistors needed - the slot sensor module already has its own pull-up and current-limit resistors on board, and the OLED is I2C with internal pull-ups on the breakout. No LEDs in this build, so no current-limiting resistor either. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the power output pin that gives you 3.3 volts. We use this to power the OLED and the slot sensor. - **GND** - ground, the 0V side. Every part needs a wire back to GND or nothing works. - **VIN** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. We won't use it for the main wiring, but it's a backup if the sensor acts up. - **D21 / D22** - two special pins the ESP32 uses to talk to the OLED screen over a 2-wire chat called I2C. - **D4** - the pin we plug the slot sensor's signal into. The code watches this pin for coin drops. - **EN** - the reset button. Press it to restart the program.
**Step 1 - Put the ESP32 and the breadboard down.** The breadboard has two long strips down one side - those are the long red/blue strips running down the side of the breadboard. The red one is our "+5V" power line, the blue (or black) one is GND (0V). In the middle are short rows of 5 holes; everything in one row is connected under the plastic. - Plug a wire from the ESP32 **3V3** pin into the red strip on the breadboard. - Plug a wire from the ESP32 **GND** pin into the blue/black strip on the breadboard. That gives us power and ground anywhere along the breadboard. Even though the red strip is labeled "+5V," in this project it's actually carrying 3.3V from the ESP32, and that's fine - both the OLED and the slot sensor are happy on 3.3V.
**Step 2 - Wire up the OLED screen.** The little OLED screen has 4 pins along the top: GND, VCC, SCL, SDA. Push it into the breadboard so each pin is in its own row. Then run these wires: - OLED **GND** (the 0V side - ground) -> the blue/black strip on the breadboard. - OLED **VCC** (power input) -> the red strip on the breadboard. - OLED **SCL** -> the pin marked **D22** on the ESP32. - OLED **SDA** -> the pin marked **D21** on the ESP32. SDA and SCL are the two wires the ESP32 uses to chat with the screen. SDA carries the data and SCL is the timing beat. They have to go to D21 and D22 because those are the ESP32's special "I2C" pins.
**Step 3 - Wire up the optical slot sensor.** The slot sensor is the U-shaped part. One side of the U shines a tiny invisible light beam, and the other side watches for it. When nothing is in the slot, the beam gets through and the sensor reports "all clear." The moment a coin drops through and breaks the beam, the sensor reports "blocked!" - and that little blink is what we count. It has 4 pins, but we only use 3: VCC, GND, and D0. (There's also an A0 pin we ignore.) - Sensor **VCC** (power input) -> the red strip on the breadboard. - Sensor **GND** (the 0V side - ground) -> the blue/black strip on the breadboard. - Sensor **D0** (the signal pin) -> the pin marked **D4** on the ESP32.
**Step 4 - Use the right jumper wires.**
You have two kinds of jumper wires in this kit: - **M-M (male-to-male)** - pin on both ends. Use these between holes on the breadboard, for example to connect the slot sensor's row to the red or blue strip. - **F-M (female-to-male)** - one end has a little socket, the other end has a pin. Use the socket end to plug onto a sensor pin that's sticking up, and the pin end to push into the breadboard. If the OLED came with bendy header pins (not already in a row), an adult might need to wiggle them straight so all 4 plug into the breadboard at once.
**Step 5 - Set up the slot so coins can fall through it.** Stand the sensor up so the U-shape opening points **straight up**. Tape it to the edge of a hardback book, a shoebox, or a Lego tower so it can't wiggle. Coins need to fall down through the gap because of gravity - if the slot is sideways, the coin just sits there and nothing counts. A good test: hold the coin above the slot, let go, and listen. The coin should drop cleanly through. If it gets caught on the plastic edge, move the sensor a little or use a smaller coin first.
**Step 6 - Plug in power and check the screen.** Plug the USB cable from your laptop or a 5V phone charger into the ESP32's USB-C port. The little red light on the ESP32 should glow. After the code is flashed (next section), the OLED should show "Coins: 0" right away.
**Why this matters - the "I2C" chat (D21 + D22).** The OLED screen has its own tiny brain. The ESP32 doesn't draw each pixel one wire at a time - that would need 100+ wires. Instead, both chips agree to talk over just two wires: **SDA** for the message and **SCL** for the beat that says "now read it." This is called I2C ("eye-squared-see"). The ESP32 has these built in only on D21 and D22, so we have to use those exact pins. Plug them anywhere else and the screen stays blank. **Why this matters - the slot sensor's "fires when blocked" signal.** The D0 pin from the slot sensor stays at 3.3V (the "all clear" level) as long as the light beam gets through. When a coin drops in, the pin suddenly drops to 0V for a few milliseconds, then bounces back to 3.3V once the coin passes. The code watches for that quick dip and adds 1 to the counter every time it sees one. That's why a clean fall matters - if the coin bounces around in the slot, the sensor might dip twice and you'll count 2 coins for 1 drop. If that happens, the code adds a short "ignore for 50 milliseconds after each count" rule so it stops double-counting. **Tricky part - if drops sometimes don't count.** The slot sensor module is happy on either 3.3V or 5V. Most of the time 3.3V is fine. But if you drop 10 coins and only 7 or 8 show up on the screen, try moving the sensor's **VCC** wire from the red strip to the ESP32's **VIN** pin (the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable). The extra voltage often gives the sensor a stronger, cleaner "blocked!" pulse. Don't worry - the signal coming back into D4 is still safe for the ESP32 either way. **Final check before flashing.** - Both red and blue strips have a wire going to the ESP32 (3V3 and GND). - OLED has 4 wires: GND, VCC, SCL to D22, SDA to D21. - Slot sensor has 3 wires: VCC, GND, D0 to D4. - The slot opening points up so coins can fall through it. - No wire is touching a wire it shouldn't be touching. If all of that looks right, you're ready to load the code. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, search for `esp32`, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download (about 200 MB) so go grab a snack. 3. **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**. 4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** (or **Sketch -> Include Library -> Manage Libraries**) and install these two, one at a time: - Search `Adafruit GFX` -> install **Adafruit GFX Library**. - Search `Adafruit SSD1306` -> install **Adafruit SSD1306**. If the IDE asks "install missing dependencies?", click **Install All**. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB-C cable that can carry data** (a charge-only cable will look like nothing happens - if the board does not show up, swap the cable first). 2. **Tools -> Port** -> pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged in (on Windows it looks like `COM5`, on a Mac like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.wchusbserial-*`). If nothing new appears, your laptop may need the CP210x or CH340 USB-to-serial driver - ask your dad to help install it. 3. There are **no passwords or placeholders to fill in** for this sketch (it does not use WiFi). You can flash it as-is. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." for a while, then "Connecting....". If it gets stuck on `Connecting......_____......_____`, hold down the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. Some NodeMCU-32S clones need this on every upload, others never need it. 5. When it says **"Hard resetting via RTS pin..."** you are done flashing. 6. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor pane, set the baud rate to **115200** (this matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). You should see startup messages, and the OLED should light up showing `0` drops. Wave a finger through the slot and the count should jump to `1` on both the screen and the Serial Monitor. That's how you know it worked. **Common gotchas:** - **Stuck on "Connecting......":** hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 the moment it starts trying to connect, let go once "Writing..." appears. Charge-only USB-C cables also cause this - if BOOT does not help, try a different cable. - **OLED is black but the sketch uploaded fine:** the SSD1306 address is set to `0x3C` in the code. A few clone OLEDs are wired for `0x3D` instead - if the screen stays blank, change `#define OLED_ADDR 0x3C` to `0x3D` and re-upload. Also double-check `SDA -> GPIO 21` and `SCL -> GPIO 22` are not swapped. - **Count jumps by 2 or 3 on a single coin:** the coin is bouncing the beam on the way through. Bump the `DEBOUNCE_MS` value near the top of the sketch from `40` up to `60` or `80` and re-upload. If drops are being missed instead, move the sensor's `VCC` wire from `3V3` to `VIN` (the 5V rail) as the Wiring notes describe. ## Talking points - "What is an interrupt?" Most code in a loop is busy checking things. An interrupt is the chip dropping everything the moment a pin changes, running a tiny piece of code, then jumping back. For something as fast as a coin falling through a 5 mm gap, polling in `loop()` could miss it. An interrupt cannot. - "Why a `volatile` keyword?" The compiler usually assumes nothing else changes a variable behind its back. `volatile` tells it "no, this can change at any moment because an interrupt might touch it" so it always re-reads from memory. - "What's debounce?" A coin doesn't break the beam cleanly - it can flicker the signal a few times in a few milliseconds. We ignore any second trigger that comes within 40 ms of the previous one. - "What does `readSnapshot()` do?" An interrupt can fire halfway through `loop()` reading the shared variables, which would give us a torn, half-updated value. `readSnapshot()` briefly turns interrupts off, copies everything in one go, then turns interrupts back on. That's a "critical section". ## Things to change once it works - Tape a piece of card with evenly-spaced slits to the side of a spinning fan and you've turned the same sensor into a tachometer (RPM meter). Count slits per second, divide by slit count, multiply by 60. - Add the buzzer from the kit (or a piezo if you grab one) so each coin makes a beep. - Make a 10-second window: how many coins can you drop in 10 seconds? Reset on button press. - Log each drop's timestamp to the Serial Monitor and paste into a spreadsheet to graph drop intervals. ## Why this is interesting This is the first build in the kit where timing accuracy matters. Polling in `loop()` works fine for buttons and slow sensors, but the moment you start measuring fast physical events - a coin drop, a fan blade, a moving belt - you need interrupts. Once Andy sees the count tick up reliably even when he drops three coins in quick succession, the "why use an interrupt" lesson sticks. Same hardware later becomes the speedometer for a Lego car, the slot encoder on a robot wheel, or a beam-break alarm across a doorway.
