projects.name: Stealth Timer - hold still or the LED dies
projects.power_supply: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S powered over its USB-C cable from a laptop or a 5 V USB phone charger; the PIR sensor, OLED and LEDs all run from the ESP32's onboard 5 V and 3.3 V rails.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Stand in front of the little sensor and freeze. A green LED glows and the screen counts how many seconds you hold still. Twitch even a tiny bit and the red LED flashes - your streak resets to zero. **Why it's fun**: It's a real-life "don't blink" game you built yourself, and the sensor can spot a finger wiggle from across the room. Challenge your dad, your sister, or the dog - whoever holds the longest streak wins. ## Parts list - 1x HC-SR505 Mini PIR Motion Sensor (the star: a tiny PIR with a clear plastic dome that fires HIGH when it sees a warm body move) - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - 1x 5mm green LED (glows while you are holding still) - 1x 5mm red LED (flashes when you twitch) - 2x 330R resistors (one in series with each LED) - 1x breadboard, plus a handful of M-M and F-M jumpers ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **5V** - the pin that gives back the 5 volts coming in from the USB cable. - **3V3** - a 3.3 volt power output. We do not use it on this build, but it is there. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs to share a GND with the ESP32 or nothing works. - **Dx** (like D13, D18, D21) - signal pins. The number on the silver-white label matches the GPIO number in the code. - **EN / BOOT** - tiny buttons for resetting and flashing. Leave them alone while the project is running.
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard power strips.** A breadboard has two long strips down each side, called the red strip (for power) and the blue or black strip (for ground). The middle rows are where parts plug in. - Find the ESP32's pin marked **5V** and run a wire from it to the top red strip. - Find a pin marked **GND** on the ESP32 and run a wire to the top black strip. - Run a second wire from another **GND** pin to the bottom black strip. We use two grounds so the LEDs on the bottom of the board can find 0V without a long messy wire. This is just setting the table. After this step, the red strip is at 5V and both black strips are at 0V, ready for parts to grab from.
**Step 2 - Plug in the OLED screen.** This is the tiny screen that will count down and yell at you to hold still. It has 4 pins: GND, VCC (power input), SCL, and SDA. Plug it into the breadboard at rows 2 to 5 so each pin gets its own row. - OLED **GND** (row 2) goes by short wire to the top black strip (0V). - OLED **VCC** (row 3) goes by short wire to the top red strip (5V). - OLED **SCL** (row 4) goes to the ESP32 pin marked **D22**. - OLED **SDA** (row 5) goes to the ESP32 pin marked **D21**. SDA and SCL are the two "talking wires" the OLED uses to chat with the ESP32. D21 and D22 are the ESP32's default talking pins for this kind of screen, so the code just works without any extra setup.
**Step 3 - Plug in the motion sensor.** The HC-SR505 is the small white dome that watches for moving warm things (like you). It has 3 pins labelled VCC, OUT, and GND. Plug it into the breadboard so its pins land in rows 26, 27, and 28. - PIR **VCC** (row 26) goes by short wire to the top red strip (5V). - PIR **OUT** (row 27) goes to the ESP32 pin marked **D13**. - PIR **GND** (row 28) goes by short wire to the top black strip (0V). The PIR runs on 5V but its OUT pin only sends out a small 3.3V pulse when it sees movement, which is the safe voltage for the ESP32 to read. No extra parts needed in between. **Why this matters:** the HC-SR505 is a bit grumpy when it first wakes up. For about 30 seconds after power-on, it sends fake "I see motion!" signals while its electronics settle down. The code knows this and shows a "Warming up PIR" message with the red LED slowly blinking. Stay out of view of the dome during that warm-up or the timer will refuse to arm.
**Step 4 - Plug in the green LED and its little resistor.** The green LED is the "you are doing great, keep holding still" light. LEDs have a long leg (the plus side) and a short leg (the minus side). They only light up if the long leg is more positive than the short leg. - Push the green LED into the board with its **long leg in row 12** and its **short leg in row 13**. - Take one 330 ohm resistor (look for the orange-orange-brown-gold stripes, or orange-orange-black-black-brown on the newer 1% kind). Bend the legs and push one end into **row 12** (next to the LED's long leg) and the other end into **row 10**. - Run a wire from **row 10** to the ESP32 pin marked **D18**. - Run a wire from **row 13** (the LED's short leg) to the bottom black strip (0V). **Why this matters:** the 330 ohm resistor is a current-limiter. The LED is happy with about 10 milliamps flowing through it, but the ESP32 pin will happily shove way more than that and burn the LED out in a flash. The resistor squeezes the flow down to a safe level. Never plug an LED straight into a pin with no resistor - it will pop, and sometimes it will hurt the pin too.
**Step 5 - Plug in the red LED and its resistor.** The red LED is the "you moved! game over!" light. Same idea as the green one. - Push the red LED in with its **long leg in row 17** and its **short leg in row 18**. - Take the second 330 ohm resistor. Push one leg into **row 17** (next to the long leg) and the other into **row 15**. - Run a wire from **row 15** to the ESP32 pin marked **D19**. - Run a wire from **row 18** (the short leg) to the bottom black strip (0V). Now both LEDs sit side by side on the bottom of the board, both with their short legs aimed at ground and their long legs hooked through a resistor up to a different ESP32 pin.
**Step 6 - Plug in power and warm up.** Plug the USB-C cable from your laptop or a 5V phone charger into the ESP32. The OLED should flash on right away with the "Warming up PIR" message and the red LED should start its slow blink. Walk away from the sensor for 30 seconds. When the screen changes to "Hold still!" the trap is armed and the game is on. If the OLED stays totally black, double-check the OLED's GND and VCC wires - that screen will not even start drawing if power is wrong. If the red LED never blinks, you probably have it in backwards - pull it out, flip it 180 degrees, and try again. LEDs in backwards do not blow up, they just stay dark. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click OK. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Search for `esp32` and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download, so go grab a snack. 3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** from the long list. 4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** and install these three, one at a time. Just type the name into the search box and click Install on the top hit: - `Adafruit GFX Library` - `Adafruit SSD1306` - `Adafruit BusIO` (the IDE may offer to install this for you when you add SSD1306 - say yes) **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with its **USB-C cable**. You should see a tiny red power LED light up on the board. 2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that just appeared (on Windows it looks like `COM5`, on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-...`). If nothing shows up, try a different USB cable - some cheap USB-C cables are charge-only and have no data wires inside. 3. This sketch has no Wi-Fi password or other placeholders to fill in - the pin numbers at the top of the file already match the wiring. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left of the IDE). The bottom of the window will say "Compiling..." then "Connecting..." and you will see dots scroll past. If it gets stuck on "Connecting....." for more than about 10 seconds, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until the upload starts, then let go. 5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the dropdown on the right of the Serial Monitor, set the baud rate to **115200** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). 6. What you should see: the OLED lights up and says **"Warming up PIR... Stay out of view!"**. Walk away from the desk for about 30 seconds. When the warm-up finishes, the **green LED comes on** and the screen starts counting **"Now : 0.1 s, 0.2 s, ..."**. Wave your hand at the PIR dome - the green LED goes out, the **red LED flashes for about a second**, and the counter resets to zero. That means it works. **Common gotchas:** - **Stuck on "Connecting....."** on upload - hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 while the IDE shows "Connecting....." until it starts writing. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need this on every upload, others only on the first one. - **OLED stays dark and the Serial Monitor prints "OLED not found"** - the I2C address on these little screens is usually `0x3C` (which is what the sketch uses), but a few are wired for `0x3D`. Swap that one number in the line `#define OLED_ADDR 0x3C` and upload again. Also double-check SDA is on GPIO 21 and SCL is on GPIO 22 - swapping those two is the #1 reason a fresh OLED looks dead. - **Red LED flashes constantly, even when nobody is in the room** - you did not wait out the 30-second warm-up, or you are sitting in the PIR's view. Unplug, walk out of the room, plug back in, and stay away until the green LED comes on by itself. ## Talking points - The HC-SR505 doesn't see *light*. It sees *infrared heat moving across its field of view*. That's why holding still in front of it - even with your eyes open - makes it go quiet. - Inside that little plastic dome is a Fresnel lens. It splits the view into zones; the sensor only triggers when warmth crosses from one zone into another. - The OUT pin is digital, not analog. There's no "how much motion" reading - just yes or no. - The ESP32 is reading the pin millions of times per second, but we only act once per loop with a tiny delay - that's enough. ## Things to change once it works - Add a buzzer that beeps softly the longer your streak gets, so you have to hold still through rising tension. - Show a tiny "high score" bar graph on the OLED that grows with your best time. - Save the best streak to ESP32 flash (Preferences library) so it survives a reboot. - Add a second HC-SR505 aimed sideways and only count "frontal" motion - turns the game into a stealth competition for two people. ## Why this is interesting PIR sensors are the everyday motion detector you've seen a thousand times - in burglar alarms, in motion-activated lights at the supermarket, in automatic taps. The HC-SR505 is the tiniest, cheapest version of that hardware, and it has exactly one job: tell you whether a warm thing just moved. Turning that single bit of information into a little game is a satisfying way to feel how a real sensor behaves: the warm-up window, the lens zones, the way it doesn't care about a glass of hot water but cares a lot about your hand.

projects.name: Storm Glass - 3-hour pressure trend forecaster
projects.power_supply: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S powered from a laptop / phone-charger USB cable; the ESP32's 3.3 V pin supplies both the BMP280 and the OLED through the breadboard rails.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little screen sits on your desk showing today's air pressure, a giant up or down arrow, and one word like "Fair" or "Storm!" The arrow flips direction hours before the weather actually changes outside. **Why it's fun**: You can predict the weather before the weather app does, then run around the house yelling "I told you it would rain!" Pick it up and walk upstairs and you can literally watch the pressure drop, because you just climbed away from a tiny bit of the sky. ## Parts list - **GY-BMP280 Barometric Pressure Sensor** - the protagonist. A tiny Bosch chip that measures absolute air pressure to about +-1 Pa. Pressure is what weather forecasters actually watch: rising pressure usually means fair weather coming, falling pressure means a storm coming. - **ESP32 NodeMCU-32S** - reads the sensor and drives the screen. - **0.96" OLED Display (I2C)** - shows the current pressure, a big up/down arrow, and a one-word forecast. - **Breadboard** plus **M-M** and **F-M jumper wires** - both modules share the same two I2C wires (SDA + SCL) plus 3.3 V and GND, so the breadboard just acts as a 4-rail splitter. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the pin that gives out 3.3 volts. That is the power we use for both little boards in this project. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every power loop needs a GND. - **D21** - the pin marked D21 on the silkscreen. The code uses this as SDA (the data wire for I2C). - **D22** - the pin marked D22. The code uses this as SCL (the clock wire for I2C). - **USB** - the micro-USB socket at the end of the board. That is where the laptop or phone-charger cable plugs in. - **I2C** - a way to talk to lots of little boards using only 2 signal wires (SDA + SCL). Both of our sensors use it.
**Step 1 - Put the breadboard down and pick the power rails.** - See the long red strip running down one side? That is the **+ rail** (the long red strip running down the side of the breadboard). We will use it for power. - The long blue or black strip next to it is the **- rail**. We will use it for ground (0V). - We are going to send 3.3 volts from the ESP32 into the + rail, and the ESP32's GND into the - rail. After that, both little boards drink from those same rails.
**Step 2 - Plant the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S on the breadboard.** - Push the ESP32 in so its pins land in two columns near the top, with the USB socket hanging off the edge of the board so you can plug a cable in later. - Do not press too hard. Wiggle it in slowly so no pins bend.
**Step 3 - Plant the BMP280 pressure sensor.** - The BMP280 is the tiny purple or blue board with a little silver square on top. That silver square is the actual pressure sensor. Try not to poke it. - Push the 4 pins into the breadboard at rows **B6, B7, B8, B9** so the labels on the board line up like this: - **VCC** (power input, 3.3V in) goes into **B6** - **GND** (the 0V side - ground) goes into **B7** - **SCL** (the clock wire) goes into **B8** - **SDA** (the data wire) goes into **B9**
**Step 4 - Plant the OLED screen.** - The OLED is the tiny black rectangle with a clear or yellow stripe on it - that stripe is where the pixels will glow. - Push its 4 pins into rows **B18, B19, B20, B21** like this: - **GND** (ground, 0V) goes into **B18** - **VCC** (power input) goes into **B19** - **SCL** (clock wire) goes into **B20** - **SDA** (data wire) goes into **B21** - Some OLEDs have the GND and VCC pins swapped. Always read the tiny labels on YOUR board before you plug it in. If you wire VCC and GND backwards the chip can fry in seconds.
**Step 5 - Run the power wires from each board to the + rail and - rail.** Use the male-to-male jumper wires (both ends have a stiff pin): - **Red wire** from **A6** (BMP280 VCC row) to the **+ rail** at the top of the board. - **Black wire** from **A7** (BMP280 GND row) to the **- rail**. - **Red wire** from **A19** (OLED VCC row) to the **+ rail**. - **Black wire** from **A18** (OLED GND row) to the **- rail**. Why color matters: red for power, black for ground. Doing this every time means future-you can glance at the board and instantly see if something is wrong.
**Step 6 - Run the two I2C signal wires.** - **Blue wire** from **A8** (BMP280 SCL row) to **A20** (OLED SCL row). This makes one shared clock wire. - **Blue wire** from **A9** (BMP280 SDA row) to **A21** (OLED SDA row). This makes one shared data wire. **Why this matters:** I2C is a chatty bus where the ESP32 calls out a name and only the matching board answers. That means both boards can share the SAME 2 signal wires (one clock + one data) without confusing each other. The BMP280 answers to address `0x76` (some clones answer to `0x77`) and the OLED answers to `0x3C`. The code tries both BMP280 addresses for you.
**Step 7 - Connect the ESP32 to the breadboard rails and the I2C wires.** Still using male-to-male jumpers: - **Red wire** from the pin marked **3V3** on the ESP32 to the **+ rail**. - **Black wire** from a pin marked **GND** on the ESP32 to the **- rail**. - **Blue wire** from the pin marked **D22** on the ESP32 to **A8** (the BMP280 SCL row, which is already linked to the OLED SCL). - **Blue wire** from the pin marked **D21** on the ESP32 to **A9** (the BMP280 SDA row, which is already linked to the OLED SDA). There are no extra resistors needed. Both little boards already have tiny pull-up resistors built in - those are needed to make I2C work, and the makers already added them so you don't have to.
**Step 8 - Plug in the USB cable.** - Plug a normal micro-USB cable from a laptop or a phone charger into the USB socket on the end of the ESP32. - The ESP32 has a small red LED that lights up when power is good. The OLED stripe should also start showing something soon after the code is flashed. - If you see no LED at all, unplug right away and check the red and black wires. Power going to the wrong place is the #1 way to cook a board. (The female-to-male jumpers shown above are a handy backup if you have any sensor with bare header pins sticking out the bottom that won't sit flat on the breadboard. For this build we mostly use male-to-male.)
**Final check before powering on:** - Trace every red wire with your finger - it should only ever go to a VCC pin or the + rail. - Trace every black wire - it should only ever go to a GND pin or the - rail. - The two blue wires (SDA and SCL) should each form one chain: ESP32 -> BMP280 -> OLED. They should never touch the power rails. If something smells warm or hot when you plug in the USB, unplug FAST. That is almost always a swapped VCC/GND on one of the little boards. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` and click OK. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, type `esp32` in the search box, and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"** (this can take a few minutes - lots to download). 3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"**. 4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** (the little book icon on the left) and install these three, one at a time: - Search `Adafruit BMP280` and install **"Adafruit BMP280 Library"**. When it asks about installing extra dependencies (Adafruit BusIO + Adafruit Unified Sensor), click **"Install all"**. - Search `Adafruit SSD1306` and install **"Adafruit SSD1306"**. Again click **"Install all"** so it grabs Adafruit GFX too. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB cable that can carry data** (some charging cables only carry power - if the board does not show up, try a different cable). 2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new port that just appeared (on Windows it looks like `COM4` or `COM5`; on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-...`; on Linux it looks like `/dev/ttyUSB0`). 3. There are no passwords or WiFi names to fill in for this sketch - it runs fully offline. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the round arrow pointing right, top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." then "Connecting......". If "Connecting" dots keep going for more than 5 seconds, press and hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until you see "Writing..." start, then let go. (Most NodeMCU-32S boards do this automatically, but the trick is good to know.) 5. When it says **"Done uploading"**, open **Tools -> Serial Monitor** and set the baud rate (bottom-right of the monitor) to **115200**. 6. You should see lines like `BMP280 found at 0x76` and `OLED ready`, then a pressure reading in hPa printed once a second. The OLED screen should light up showing a number around 1013, a temperature, and a flat arrow `=` (the arrow will not move until at least 3 hours of readings have piled up - that is normal, give it time). **Common gotchas:** - **"Connecting......" never finishes on the first upload.** Hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 while you click Upload, and let go once you see "Writing..." appear. Some clone boards need this every single time. - **Screen stays black but Serial Monitor shows readings.** The OLED is probably at address `0x3D` instead of `0x3C`. Or you swapped SDA and SCL - double-check that GPIO21 goes to **both** SDA pins and GPIO22 goes to **both** SCL pins. - **Serial Monitor shows garbage characters like `???????`.** The baud rate is wrong. Set the dropdown in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor to **115200** to match the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code. ## Talking points - **What is air pressure?** The weight of all the air above you, pressing down. At sea level on an average day it is about 1013 hPa. When a storm front moves in, that number drops; when it leaves, it rises. - **Why a 3-hour delta?** Weather services use the 3-hour pressure tendency as the basic forecast signal. One single reading tells you nothing - it is the *change over time* that predicts the weather. - **Why a ring buffer?** We keep 180 readings (one per minute for 3 hours). Instead of growing a list forever, we overwrite the oldest slot every minute. This is the same trick used in audio buffers and game replay systems. - **I2C is a shared bus.** The OLED and the BMP280 use the *same* two wires. They get along because they have different addresses (`0x3C` vs `0x76`). ## Things to change once it works - Add a 24-hour delta too (just bump `HISTORY_MINUTES` to 1440 and add a second arrow). - Plot the history as a tiny line graph across the bottom of the OLED. - Publish the pressure to MQTT once the Orange Pi hub is online, so the Hallway Weather Window project can show it alongside temperature. - Calibrate to altitude: feed in the local altitude and the sketch can spit out sea-level-equivalent pressure that matches what weather.gov reports. - Add a piezo buzzer that beeps when the forecast crosses into "Storm!" so you get a warning even when you are not looking at the screen. ## Why this is interesting This is a real instrument, not a toy. The BMP280 is sensitive enough that you can *see* the pressure change when you walk up a flight of stairs (about -0.4 hPa per 4 metres). And the 3-hour delta really does predict weather - leave it on the kitchen counter for a week and you will start trusting the arrow more than the phone app. It is also the cleanest example in the kit of the I2C-bus idea: two completely different chips, from two different vendors, sharing two wires. Once Andy is comfortable with this, adding a third or fourth I2C sensor is just plugging it into the same rails.

projects.name: Pocket Battery Health Monitor (OLED + LEDs)
projects.power_supply: ESP32 powered by laptop USB. OLED runs from the ESP32's 3.3V rail; LEDs are driven by GPIO. The voltage module is passive (just resistors) and draws no power. The battery under test connects only to the module's input screws.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Touch the little board's two screws to any battery's plus and minus ends. The tiny screen instantly shows the volts, a bar graph, and one big word: HEALTHY, LOW, or DEAD. A green LED or a red LED lights up too, so you know the answer from across the room. **Why it's fun**: You become the battery doctor of the house. Go hunting through every drawer, remote, and toy, zap each battery with the probes, and sort them into a "still good" pile and a "throw away" pile - your parents will actually thank you. ## Parts list - Voltage Sensor Module (0-25V divider) - the star: a tiny board with two resistors (30k + 7.5k) that shrinks a DC voltage down to something the ESP32's 3.3V ADC can survive. The module is rated up to 25V at the input, but as you'll see in Talking points, the ESP32's ADC only stays linear up to about 12V of input. Above that the screen number goes wonky. - ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the divider's output on GPIO 34 and drives the screen - 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - shows the live number, a bar graph, and the word HEALTHY / LOW / DEAD - 1x green LED with a 220R limiter and 1x red LED with a 330R limiter - instant "go / no-go" feedback even before you look at the screen. Green gets the smaller resistor on purpose - green LEDs need a higher forward voltage than red, so at 3.3V drive a 330R would leave it visibly dim. - Breadboard + jumpers - no soldering A 9V battery (or any low-voltage DC source up to ~12V you want to measure) is the **device under test**. You touch its terminals to the voltage module's input. The whole project itself is powered through the ESP32's USB cable. The voltage module is a passive resistor pair, so it draws no power of its own and does not need a VCC connection. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the 3.3V power pin. Gives back 3.3 volts from the USB cable to power small parts. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs to share this with the ESP32 or nothing works. - **D21 / D22** - two special pins used for talking to the OLED screen (called I2C). - **D34** - an input-only pin that can read voltages. Perfect for measuring a battery. - **D25 / D26** - normal output pins. We use these to turn the LEDs on and off. - **USB** - the plug where the laptop cable goes in. This powers the whole project.
**Step 1 - Put the ESP32 on the breadboard.** Press the ESP32 gently into the breadboard so it sits across the middle gap. One row of pins on the left, one row on the right. Push it in straight - never force it sideways. The USB plug should hang off the end of the breadboard so you can plug a cable in later.
**Step 2 - Set up the power strips on the breadboard.** The long red and blue strips running down the side of the breadboard are called the power rails. We want the top red rail to be 3.3V and both blue rails to be ground (0V). Use short jumper wires: - ESP32 pin marked **3V3** to the top red rail - ESP32 pin marked **GND** to the top blue rail (ground) Now the whole top of the board has power. We will tap into it again and again for the other parts.
**Step 3 - Wire up the OLED screen.** This is the tiny screen that will show the battery's voltage. It has 4 pins along one edge. Plug it into the breadboard so its pins are at row 2, 3, 4, and 5 on column A. Then run these wires: - OLED pin **GND** (row 2) to the top blue rail (ground) - OLED pin **VCC** (row 3) to the top red rail (3.3V power) - OLED pin **SCL** (row 4) to ESP32 pin **D22** - OLED pin **SDA** (row 5) to ESP32 pin **D21** SCL and SDA are the two "talking" wires that let the ESP32 send pictures and numbers to the screen. They always come as a pair.
**Step 4 - Wire up the voltage sensor module.** This little blue board is what reads the battery's voltage. It has two sides: - **Screw-terminal side** (the side with little screws): this is where the battery you want to test will connect later. One screw is marked **VCC** (positive, the + side of the battery) and one is marked **GND** (negative, the - side of the battery). - **Pin side** (3 pins in a row): this is what plugs into the breadboard. Plug it in so its 3 pins are at row 9, 10, and 11 on column A. Now wire up the pin side: - Module pin **S** (row 9) to ESP32 pin **D34** - Module pin **+** (row 10) - leave this one alone, don't connect it - Module pin **-** (row 11) to the top blue rail (ground) **Why this matters:** The module is just two resistors inside that shrink the battery voltage down so the ESP32 can safely read it. The ESP32 can only handle 3.3V on its input pins - if you plugged a 9V battery straight into D34 you would fry the chip. The module turns 25V into about 3V, which is safe. Also, the module's **-** pin MUST share ground with the ESP32. Two things measuring voltage need the same "zero point" or the number is meaningless. This is called "sharing a ground" and it is the rule that makes the whole thing work.
**Step 5 - Add the green LED (good-battery light).** The green LED (no photo - it's a small green see-through bulb with two metal legs) needs a resistor in front of it. Find the 220R resistor (red-red-brown stripes on a tiny tan body). - Push the 220R resistor between row 15 and row 17 on column E. It does not matter which way around. - Now find the green LED. Look at its legs - one is longer than the other. The **long leg** is the positive side; the **short leg** is the negative side. - Push the **long leg** into row 17 column F (right next to the end of the resistor). - Push the **short leg** into row 18 column F. - Run a yellow jumper from row 15 column B to row 17 column B (this connects the resistor to its row neighbour - actually skip this, see next bullet). - Run a wire from ESP32 pin **D25** to row 15 column E (so the ESP32 can switch the LED on). - Run a wire from row 18 column J to the bottom blue rail (ground). **Why this matters:** An LED is greedy - if you just plug it straight to power it will pull as much current as it can and burn out in a flash (sometimes literally). The resistor slows the current down to a safe trickle so the LED glows nicely without dying. 220R is the right size for a green LED at 3.3V.
**Step 6 - Add the red LED (low-battery warning light).** Same trick as the green one, but with a slightly bigger resistor. Find the 330R resistor (no photo on file - it has orange-orange-brown stripes). Red LEDs need a little more resistance because they are brighter at the same voltage. - Push the 330R resistor between row 22 and row 24 on column E. - Find the red LED. Long leg = positive, short leg = negative. - Push the **long leg** into row 24 column F. - Push the **short leg** into row 25 column F. - Run a wire from ESP32 pin **D26** to row 22 column E. - Run a wire from row 25 column J to the bottom blue rail (ground). When the ESP32 sees a low voltage from the battery, it turns this red LED on as a warning.
**Step 7 - Connect the bottom ground rail to the top ground rail.** Right now only the top blue rail is connected to ESP32 ground. The red LED step put a wire onto the bottom blue rail, so that needs to also be ground. Use one jumper to connect the top blue rail to the bottom blue rail. Both blue rails are now ground - much easier to wire things up.
**Step 8 - Connect a battery to test (do this last, never with the laptop unplugged).** This is the fun part! Find an old AA, AAA, 9V, or any small DC battery you want to check. Look for the **+** and **-** signs printed on it. - Battery **+** side goes into the screw terminal marked **VCC** on the voltage sensor module. Loosen the little screw, push the wire in, tighten the screw. - Battery **-** side goes into the screw terminal marked **GND** on the voltage sensor module. If you don't have a battery with wires, ask a grown-up to help you tape a short wire to each end of the battery first. **SAFETY RULES - read these out loud:** - **Never** connect this project to a wall plug, AC power, a car battery, or anything bigger than 25 volts. The module cannot handle it and things will get very hot. - **Never** swap + and -. Plug the battery in the right way around. - This project is for small DC batteries only. Not phones, not power tools, not the wall.
**Step 9 - Power up.** Plug the USB cable from your laptop into the ESP32's USB port. The OLED should light up and start showing the voltage. The green LED lights up if the battery is healthy; the red LED lights up if it is getting weak. Congrats - you just built a real piece of test gear! ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click OK. 2. Open **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Type `esp32` in the search box. Install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download (a few hundred MB) so let it finish - go get a snack. 3. Open **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"NodeMCU-32S"** from the list. 4. Open **Tools -> Manage Libraries** (the little book icon on the left). You need two libraries for the screen: - Search `Adafruit SSD1306` -> Install. It will ask if you want to install dependencies too - say **Install All**. - Search `Adafruit GFX Library` -> Install (this one usually came along with the first install, but double-check). **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into the laptop with a **USB cable that carries data** (some cheap charging cables are power-only and will not show up - if the board's red power LED lights but no port appears, swap the cable). 2. Open **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that just appeared. On Windows it looks like `COM5` or `COM7`; on a Mac it looks like `cu.usbserial-xxxx`; on Linux it is `/dev/ttyUSB0`. 3. Open the sketch. There are no WiFi passwords or secret keys to fill in for this one - but find the line `const float CAL = 1.00f;` near the top. Leave it at 1.00 for now; you will nudge it up or down later once you check a known-good battery against a multimeter. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon in the top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling..." then "Connecting...". If it sits on "Connecting..." for more than 10 seconds and starts printing dots, **press and hold the BOOT button** on the ESP32 board until the upload starts. Some NodeMCU-32S boards need this on the very first flash. 5. When it says "Done uploading", open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the monitor window, set the baud rate to **115200** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` call in the code). 6. Within a second or two the OLED should light up showing a voltage near `0.00 V` and the word **DEAD** (because nothing is connected to the screw terminals yet). The red LED should be on, the green LED off. The Serial Monitor will print a fresh voltage reading every loop. 7. Now touch the voltage module's two screw terminals to a battery: **VCC screw to battery +, GND screw to battery -**. A fresh 9V alkaline should show around 9.3-9.6V, the bar graph should jump near full, the word should flip to **HEALTHY**, and the green LED should come on. That is the win. **Common gotchas:** - **Upload stuck on "Connecting..."**: hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until the dots turn into a progress bar, then release. First-flash quirk on NodeMCU-32S. - **Screen stays black but the LEDs work**: the OLED's I2C address is probably `0x3D` instead of `0x3C` on your specific module. Change `#define OLED_ADDR 0x3C` to `0x3D` and re-upload. Also double-check SDA goes to GPIO 21 and SCL goes to GPIO 22 - swapping them is the #1 wiring mistake. - **Voltage reads zero or garbage when a battery is connected**: the module's `-` pin on the header side is not connected to ESP32 GND. The battery and the ESP32 must share a ground or the ADC has nothing to measure against. Also make sure the signal wire is on the module's `S` pin going to GPIO 34, not the unused `+` pin. - **Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `⸮⸮@⸮⸮`**: the baud rate dropdown is wrong. Set it to **115200** to match `Serial.begin(115200)`. ## Talking points - The voltage module is just a **voltage divider**: two resistors in series. The "S" pin sits at the junction and carries a fraction of the input voltage. With 30k on top and 7.5k on the bottom, the ratio is 5:1 - feed 25V in, get 5V at S. Feed 9V in, get 1.8V at S. The ESP32 then multiplies by 5 in software to recover the original number. - **Why the real measurement ceiling is ~12V, not 25V.** With the attenuation setting we use (`ADC_11db`), the ESP32 ADC is only linear from about 0.15V up to about 2.45V at the pin. Multiply 2.45V by the divider's 5:1 ratio and you get ~12V at the input. Above that, the ADC saturates and the displayed number flattens out - the module isn't damaged, but the reading is no longer trustworthy. The code shows a `>12V (clip)` warning when that happens. For 9V alkalines, 12V SLA at rest, and 18650 cells, you're comfortably inside the linear band. - Why GPIO 34? It's an **input-only ADC pin** on ESP32 and it's also on ADC1, which (unlike ADC2) keeps working while WiFi is on. Good habit for future projects. - The ESP32 ADC is famously a little non-linear, so the code includes a `CAL` fudge factor (default 1.00). Once everything works, Andy can compare the OLED reading to a real multimeter on the same battery, and nudge `CAL` until they agree **inside the band he actually cares about** (e.g. 6V-10V for testing 9V alkalines). ## Things to change once it works - Change `HEALTHY_VOLTS` to suit a different battery. For a 12V lead-acid you'd use ~12.2V (right at the edge of the linear range, so multimeter-calibrate carefully). For a single Li-ion 18650 cell you'd use ~3.5V (well inside the safe range). - Add a third "warning" yellow LED for the in-between band. - Add WiFi and post the voltage to MQTT once the Orange Pi hub is booted, turning this into a real battery-monitoring node. - Plot voltage over time on the OLED instead of just a level bar - sample once a second into a 128-wide ring buffer and you get a free oscilloscope. - To extend the measurement range past ~12V on this exact module, you'd need to either add another resistor in series upstream (extending the divider) or switch the attenuation setting on a different pin - both are good follow-up experiments. ## Why this is interesting Voltage measurement is the most fundamental thing a sensor can do, and yet it's hidden inside almost every other module - the joystick, the photoresistor, the soil sensor, all secretly produce a voltage and let the microcontroller's ADC read it. Building this project makes that hidden machinery visible. After this, Andy will look at every analog sensor in the kit and recognise the same trick: "it's just a voltage I'm reading and converting to a number." It's also genuinely useful. Every project from here on uses batteries or DC supplies, and now Andy has a meter he built himself that tells him whether the battery in his hand still has juice. And the "ADC only goes linear to ~2.45V at the pin" lesson is one of those gotchas every ESP32 project eventually trips over - better to meet it here with a clear printout than to chase a phantom bug later.

projects.name: Raindrop Reporter - live wetness on OLED
projects.power_supply: Powered from a USB-C cable plugged into the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S. The board's 3V3 pin supplies the raindrop sensor module, the OLED, and the LED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Flick water onto a little comb-shaped board and the tiny screen instantly changes from DRY to MISTY to WET to SOAKED, with a blue LED that glows brighter the wetter it gets. There's a wiggling bar on the screen too, so you can watch it climb in real time as the water sits there. **Why it's fun**: It's a weather detector you build yourself - leave it on the windowsill and you'll know the second rain hits, before anyone else in the house. Try licking your finger and touching the board, or breathing on it really close - you'll see how sensitive it is and feel like a mad scientist running tests. ## Parts list - 1x Raindrop Sensor (the comb board + its little LM393 amplifier board) - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - 1x 0.96" OLED display (I2C, address 0x3C) - 1x Blue 5mm LED - 1x 330R resistor (current limit for the LED) - 1x Breadboard - Jumper wires (a mix of M-M and F-M) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **3V3** - the power pin that gives out 3.3 volts. The raindrop sensor, the OLED screen, and the LED all run from this. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs at least one wire going to a GND pin. - **D21 / D22** - the two pins the OLED talks on. They are the ESP32's default chat pins for small screens. - **D34** - an input-only pin that reads how much water is on the sensor. It can listen but never push power out. - **D5** - a normal pin we use to turn the blue LED on and off. - **USB port** - the USB-C socket at the end of the board. Plug the cable from your laptop in here for both power and code.
**Step 1 - Plant the ESP32 on the breadboard.** Push the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S across the gap in the middle of the breadboard so half its pins are on the left side and half on the right side. It should sit flat with all pins clicked in. The USB-C socket should hang off one end of the board so you can plug a cable in later.
**Step 2 - Power and ground the two red and black side strips.** The long red and blue strips down the side of the breadboard are called the power strips. We want power on the red strip and ground on the blue strip on BOTH sides of the board. - One male-to-male wire from the ESP32 pin marked **3V3** to the **red strip** at the top of the board. - One male-to-male wire from the ESP32 pin marked **GND** to the **blue strip** at the top of the board. - One red wire across the board from the top red strip to the bottom red strip (so both sides have power). - One black wire across from the top blue strip to the bottom blue strip (so both sides have ground). Why this matters: a breadboard's side strips are not connected to each other by default. You always have to jumper the top strip to the bottom strip yourself, or half your project will be silently unplugged.
**Step 3 - Place the raindrop sensor amp board.** The raindrop sensor comes as two pieces joined by a short two-wire cable: a flat comb-shaped board (the part that goes outside and gets wet) and a small amp board with a row of four pins. The amp board is the one that plugs into the breadboard. Push its four pins into row 2 through row 5, column E. - The pin labeled **VCC** (this is the power input) sits at E2. - The pin labeled **GND** sits at E3. - The pin labeled **DO** sits at E4. We will NOT use this one. - The pin labeled **AO** sits at E5. This is the one that tells us how wet the comb is. Now add the wires for the sensor with female-to-male jumpers (or male-to-male, either works in these holes): - From E2 (VCC) to the **red strip** at the top - this gives the sensor 3.3V power. - From E3 (GND) to the **blue strip** at the top - this is the ground return. We will hook up the AO wire to the ESP32 in a later step. Why this matters: the sensor's silkscreen says it can take 5V, but we feed it 3.3V on purpose. If we used 5V, the AO reading could climb higher than the ESP32 is allowed to receive on its input pin and slowly hurt it. 3.3V keeps everyone safe.
**Step 4 - Drop in the resistor and the blue LED.**
The blue LED has a long leg and a short leg. The long leg is the plus side, the short leg is the minus side. Look closely - one leg really is a little longer than the other. - Bend the resistor's legs and push them into B10 and B13. The resistor does not care which way around it goes. - Push the LED's long leg into A13 (same row as one side of the resistor). - Push the LED's short leg into A14. - Add a black wire from A14 to the **blue strip** at the top (this is the ground side for the LED). Why this matters: an LED on its own would gulp too much electricity and burn out in a second or two. The 330 ohm resistor sits in line with it like a thin straw, only letting a safe sip of current through. Always put a resistor in series with a small LED.
**Step 5 - Place the OLED screen.** The little screen has four pins in a row. Check the label printed on the corner of the screen board before plugging it in - some screens have the power and ground pins swapped from others. Push the four pins into row 20 to row 23, column E. - The pin labeled **GND** goes to E20. Wire E20 to the **blue strip** at the top (ground). - The pin labeled **VCC** (power input) goes to E21. Wire E21 to the **red strip** at the top (power). - The pin labeled **SCL** goes to E22. We will wire this to the ESP32 next. - The pin labeled **SDA** goes to E23. We will wire this to the ESP32 next.
**Step 6 - Run the four signal wires from the ESP32 with female-to-male jumpers.** These are the wires that carry information, not power. Use female-to-male jumpers - the female end clips over the ESP32 pin, the male end pushes into the breadboard. - ESP32 pin marked **D34** to the breadboard hole **E5** (this reads the wet-or-dry value from the sensor). - ESP32 pin marked **D21** to the breadboard hole **E23** (this is the SDA signal for the OLED). - ESP32 pin marked **D22** to the breadboard hole **E22** (this is the SCL signal for the OLED). - ESP32 pin marked **D5** to the breadboard hole **B10** (this turns the blue LED on and off through the resistor). Why D34: this pin is input-only, which means it can listen but never push power back out. That is perfect for reading a sensor. It also keeps working when WiFi is switched on, which some other pins on the ESP32 do not.
**Step 7 - Plug in the USB-C cable and you are done wiring.** Connect the USB-C cable from your laptop to the USB socket on the end of the ESP32. The board will get power straight from the cable, and the same cable carries the code when you flash it. Quick check before powering up: the long red strip should have a wire to 3V3, the long blue strip should have a wire to GND, the sensor and the OLED should both have one wire to red and one wire to blue, and the LED's short leg should reach the blue strip through that little black wire.
**How the raindrop sensor "thinks":** when the comb is dry, the AO reading is a big number. When water lands on the comb, the water lets electricity sneak across the metal lines, and the AO reading drops to a small number. So in the code: small number = wet, big number = dry. That feels backwards at first - just remember "wet pulls it down". ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` Click OK. 2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Type `esp32` in the search box and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download, give it a few minutes. 3. **Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> NodeMCU-32S**. 4. Install the two screen libraries: **Tools -> Manage Libraries**. Search for and install: - **Adafruit SSD1306** (this is the OLED driver) - **Adafruit GFX Library** (this is the drawing toolbox the OLED driver uses; the IDE may ask to install it automatically as a dependency - say yes) **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 into your laptop with a **USB-C cable** (or micro-USB, depending on which NodeMCU-32S you have - check the port on the board). Use a real data cable, not a charge-only one, or the laptop will not see the board at all. 2. **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that just appeared (on Windows it looks like `COM4`, on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`). If you do not see one, unplug, wait two seconds, plug back in. 3. This sketch has no WiFi password or other placeholders to fill in - leave the four threshold numbers near the top (`SOAKED_BELOW`, `WET_BELOW`, `MISTY_BELOW`) at their defaults for the first run. You will tune them in a minute. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, top-left). The IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." then "Connecting....". If "Connecting...." keeps printing dots and never starts uploading, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until you see the upload start, then let go. (Most NodeMCU-32S boards do this automatically; some need the button.) 5. When it says "Hard resetting via RTS pin", open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor, set the baud rate to **115200** (this matches `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). 6. **What you should see:** the OLED lights up with "Raindrop Reporter / warming up..." for about a second, then switches to a live readout showing the raw number (around 4000 in dry air), the word **DRY**, and a wetness bar at zero. Lick a finger and touch the comb-trace board - within a second the number drops, the word flips to **MISTY** or **WET**, the bar climbs, and the blue LED turns on. Flick a drop of water on it for **SOAKED**. Now tune the thresholds: watch the raw number in the Serial Monitor while the board is dry, while damp from a fingertip, while a real drop sits on it, and while it is properly wet. Edit `SOAKED_BELOW`, `WET_BELOW`, and `MISTY_BELOW` at the top of the sketch so each state matches what you saw, and click Upload again. **Common gotchas:** - **Upload stuck on "Connecting....":** hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 until the upload bar starts moving, then release. Some USB cables are also charge-only with no data lines - swap the cable if a known-good board still will not connect. - **OLED stays black and the Serial Monitor prints "OLED not found":** SDA and SCL are swapped, or one of the OLED's power pins is not seated in the breadboard rail. Wiggle them, and double-check `VCC -> 3V3` (not 5V). - **Serial Monitor shows garbage like `~?@@?~`:** the baud rate in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor is not set to **115200**. Change it and the text becomes readable instantly. ## Talking points - Why GPIO34? Show Sandy the ESP32 pinout. ADC2 pins go quiet whenever WiFi turns on - we picked an ADC1 pin so we don't get bitten by that later. - The `classify()` thresholds were guessed. The real ones come from watching the Serial Monitor while flicking water on the board: write down the value when dry, when finger-damp, when a drop is sitting on it, and when it's fully submerged. Edit the four constants at the top to match. - Averaging 8 samples is a tiny but useful trick - one stray reading would make the display jitter between MISTY and WET every quarter second otherwise. ## Things to change once it works - Add a buzzer that beeps when state crosses into SOAKED - then it's a basement-flood alarm. - Log the state changes with `millis()` over WiFi to the (future) Orange Pi MQTT broker, so you've got a record of when it rained. - Use the `DO` pin instead of `AO` and skip the OLED - simpler "rain or no rain" version for the XIAO ESP32-C3. - Make the wetness bar pulse faster the wetter it gets - visible feedback without needing to read numbers. ## Why this is interesting The raindrop sensor is the cheapest physical-world-touching sensor you have - it's literally two interleaved copper combs and a comparator. This project shows the full beginner-friendly chain: a noisy real-world analog signal, smoothed by averaging, classified into human-readable buckets, then displayed two different ways (text + bar graph + LED). It's also the simplest hook into "act on the world": once you can confidently detect rain, the same code pattern works for soil moisture, water level, and any other resistive/analog sensor in the kit.

projects.name: Tub Filler Traffic Light
projects.power_supply: Arduino Uno powered from a laptop USB cable. The Uno's onboard 5V rail then feeds the water sensor, the LCD, and the LED resistors.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Dip a little probe into a glass of water. A screen shows a bar graph filling up, plus a percent. Three LEDs glow like a stoplight - red when it's nearly empty, yellow when it's getting close, green when the "tub" is full. **Why it's fun**: It reacts instantly. Lift the probe out and the bar drops; push it back in and the green light pops on. It feels like a real gadget you'd see stuck to the side of a bathtub or a fish tank, and you built it. ## Parts list - Arduino Uno R3 (the brain - reads the sensor, drives the LCD and LEDs) - Water Level Sensor (resistive comb - the protagonist; more water touching the combs = lower resistance = higher analog reading) - LCD 1602 with I2C Backpack (shows a live bar graph and a percent number) - 3 LEDs (red, yellow, green) - "stoplight" progress indicator - 3x 330R resistors (current-limiters, one per LED) - 1x 1M resistor (pull-down on the sensor's signal pin so the reading falls cleanly to 0 when dry) - Breadboard + a small handful of M-M and F-M jumper wires (one pack of each is plenty) - A glass of water (the "tub") to dip the sensor into ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the power pin. It gives out 5 volts of power for your parts. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs a path back here to work. - **D5, D6, D7** - digital pins. The Uno can turn these on and off to light the LEDs. - **A0** - an analog pin. It can read a small voltage and turn it into a number from 0 to 1023. - **A4 and A5** - on the Uno, these double as the I2C bus that talks to the LCD screen. - **USB jack** - where the laptop cable plugs in. It powers the whole board.
**Step 1 - Plug in the breadboard power rails.** - Run a red M-M jumper from **Arduino 5V** to the top red strip (the long red strip running down the side of the breadboard is called a "rail"). - Run a black M-M jumper from **Arduino GND** to the top blue rail. - Run a red M-M jumper from the top red rail down to the bottom red rail. - Run a black M-M jumper from the top blue rail down to the bottom blue rail. This means both red rails always have 5V power, and both blue rails are always ground. Now every part on the board can grab power from the nearest rail instead of running its own wire all the way back to the Arduino.
**Step 2 - Place the red "stop" LED and its resistor.**
- Push a **330R resistor** so its legs go into holes **E3** and **E5**. (Resistors don't care which way around they go.) - Push the **red LED** in with its long leg in **A5** and short leg in **A6**. The long leg is the anode, the short leg is the cathode - just remember "long = power side". - Run a black M-M jumper from **B6** to the top blue ground rail. - Run a M-M jumper from **Arduino D5** to **A3**. So the path is: Arduino D5 -> resistor -> long leg of LED -> short leg of LED -> ground. The Uno turns D5 on, and the red light comes on. **Why this matters (the 330R resistor):** LEDs are greedy little parts. If you wire them straight to 5V with nothing in the way, they gulp too much electricity and burn out in a flash. The 330 ohm resistor is a "speed bump" that limits the current to a safe amount. Every LED in this project gets its own.
**Step 3 - Place the yellow "almost full" LED and its resistor.** - Push a **330R resistor** so its legs go into holes **E8** and **E10**. - Push the **yellow LED** in with its long leg in **A10** and short leg in **A11**. - Run a black M-M jumper from **B11** to the top blue ground rail. - Run a M-M jumper from **Arduino D6** to **A8**. Same shape as the red one, just shifted over. D6 controls the yellow light.
**Step 4 - Place the green "go" LED and its resistor.** - Push a **330R resistor** so its legs go into holes **E13** and **E15**. - Push the **green LED** in with its long leg in **A15** and short leg in **A16**. - Run a black M-M jumper from **B16** to the top blue ground rail. - Run a M-M jumper from **Arduino D7** to **A13**. D7 controls the green light. You should now have three little resistor-and-LED strips in a row.
**Step 5 - Wire up the water level sensor.** The sensor has three pins printed on it: **+**, **-**, and **S**. - Use a F-M jumper from sensor **+** to the bottom red 5V rail. - Use a F-M jumper from sensor **-** to the bottom blue ground rail. - Use a F-M jumper from sensor **S** to hole **J22** on the breadboard. - Run a M-M jumper from **Arduino A0** to the same column - hole **J22** (any J-column or F-column hole in row 22 will share the same line as J22). The S pin is the signal pin. As water touches more of the gold combs on the sensor, the voltage on S goes up, and A0 reads a bigger number. **Important safety note:** only the gold combs at the bottom of the sensor should ever touch water. Do not dunk the top half with the chip on it - it will rust and stop working in a few days.
**Step 6 - Add the 1 megohm pull-down resistor.** - Push the **1M resistor** so one leg is in **F22** (the same row as the sensor signal) and the other leg goes to the bottom blue ground rail. **Why this matters (the pull-down resistor):** when the sensor is dry, the S pin isn't really connected to anything. A0 is a sensitive listening pin, and if nothing is holding it down, it picks up tiny stray voltages from the air (yes, really) and shows random jumpy numbers. The 1 megohm resistor is a gentle "weight" that pulls A0 down to 0 when the sensor isn't touching water. When water does touch the combs, the sensor easily wins and pulls A0 back up. This is the "why doesn't it read zero when dry?" fix.
**Step 7 - Wire up the LCD screen with the I2C backpack.** The little black board on the back of the LCD is the I2C backpack. It turns 16 messy LCD wires into just 4 neat ones. The four pins are labeled **VCC**, **GND**, **SDA**, and **SCL**. - F-M jumper from **VCC** (the power input, 5V in) to the bottom red 5V rail. - F-M jumper from **GND** to the bottom blue ground rail. - F-M jumper from **SDA** straight to **Arduino A4**. - F-M jumper from **SCL** straight to **Arduino A5**. On the Uno, A4 and A5 are special - they also work as the I2C bus, which is a two-wire way for chips to chat. That's why the LCD screen plugs into pins that look like analog inputs.
**Step 8 - Power it up.** - Plug the laptop USB-A to USB-B cable into the **USB jack** on the Uno. - Plug the other end into your laptop. The Uno's onboard 5V rail now feeds the water sensor, the LCD, and all three LED resistors. You should see the LCD backlight glow. Once you upload the code, fill a cup with water and dip just the gold combs in - the LEDs should change from green to yellow to red as the water gets higher.
**Tuning note - the LCD contrast:** if the screen lights up but shows no letters, find the tiny blue screw on the back of the I2C backpack. Turn it slowly with a small screwdriver until the text appears. Some boards come from the factory with the contrast set too low to see anything. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):** 1. **First time only - USB driver.** Your Arduino Uno uses a **CH340** USB-to-serial chip (the dark rectangular chip near the USB jack on most clones). Plug it in: if a COM port appears in **Tools -> Port** within a few seconds, the driver is already installed and you can skip the rest of this step. If nothing shows up, install the CH340 driver from [sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers](https://sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers) (Windows / macOS / Linux all linked there), then unplug and replug the Uno. 2. Open the Arduino IDE. The Uno's board support is built in, so no extra board package is needed. 3. Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> **Arduino Uno**. 4. Install the LCD library: Tools -> Manage Libraries... -> type **LiquidCrystal I2C** in the search box -> install **"LiquidCrystal I2C" by Frank de Brabander**. (Any compatible fork with the same name works too.) **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into your laptop with a **USB-A to USB-B cable** (the big square-ish plug, same kind old printers used). The green power LED on the Uno should light up. 2. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that just appeared (on Windows it looks like **COM3** or **COM4**; on a Mac it is **/dev/cu.usbmodem...**; on Linux it is **/dev/ttyACM0** or **/dev/ttyUSB0**). If you see more than one, unplug the Uno and watch which one disappears - that is the right one. 3. No passwords or WiFi to fill in for this sketch - skip that step. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). The TX and RX LEDs near the USB jack will flicker for a couple of seconds. When the bottom of the window says **"Done uploading."** you are good. 5. Open Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of that window, set the baud rate to **115200** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). 6. The LCD should briefly show "Tub Filler / Dip the sensor.." and then switch to the bar graph. With the sensor dry, the Serial Monitor should print a number very close to **0** and the percent on the LCD should read **0%**. Dip the comb into the glass of water and the bar should jump, the percent should climb, and the LEDs should light up in order: red first, then yellow around halfway, then green when it is basically full. **Common gotchas:** - **Blank LCD with the backlight on?** Your I2C backpack lives at address `0x3F` instead of `0x27`. Change the `LiquidCrystal_I2C lcd(0x27, 16, 2);` line near the top to `0x3F` and re-upload. - **Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `??x?`?** The baud rate dropdown in the Serial Monitor is wrong. Set it to **115200** to match the code. - **Percent never goes above ~30% even with the sensor fully submerged?** Your `WET_MAX` is too high for your glass of water. Watch the raw number in the Serial Monitor while the sensor is all the way in, then change `const int WET_MAX = 600;` to whatever you actually see, and re-upload. ## Talking points - Why a "resistive comb" sensor? It's just two interleaved bare-copper tracks. Water between them conducts a tiny bit of current. More water covering the combs = more conductive paths in parallel = more current = bigger number from `analogRead`. It's the same trick the Soil Moisture Sensor uses, just shaped to read a vertical column instead of a flat patch. - Why the 1M pull-down? An Arduino analog input that isn't connected to anything acts like a tiny antenna - it picks up mains hum and reads random numbers. Tying it weakly to ground through 1M forces it to read 0 when the sensor is dry, but lets the sensor easily overpower it when water is present. - The LCD updates fast on purpose - you can dip the sensor in and out and watch the bar graph respond immediately. That tight feedback loop is what makes it fun. ## Things to change once it works - Calibrate `WET_MAX` to your actual glass of water. Dip the sensor all the way and read the value over Serial - that's your real max. Beginner-typical values land between 500 and 700. - Add a buzzer that beeps once when the green "FULL" zone is reached - that turns it from a visual toy into an actual "tub is full, come turn the tap off" alarm. - Swap to the ESP32 and publish the level over WiFi to the (future) Orange Pi hub. Same sensor wiring, different brain. - Try the Raindrop Sensor on the same code with no changes - it's electrically identical, just a flatter comb shape. ## Why this is interesting This is the cheapest, simplest possible "is there water there?" sensor, and it teaches a real-world lesson the first time you use it: analog inputs don't read clean zero when nothing's connected. Fixing that with a pull-down resistor is a habit that carries over to almost every analog sensor you'll ever use. And visually, dipping a probe into a glass and watching a bar graph fill up is hugely satisfying - especially for a 10-year-old.

projects.name: NE555 Heartbeat Blinker (no code, all chip)
projects.power_supply: 5V from a USB phone charger via the USB-C pigtail (or borrowed from an Arduino Uno's 5V pin) feeds the breadboard rails; the NE555 sips a few mA.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug it in. A red LED blinks once per second, steady and calm, like a tiny heartbeat sitting on your breadboard. **Why it's fun**: This is your first project that does something real with ZERO code. No laptop, no typing, no uploading - just a little black chip and a few parts, and it blinks forever the second power touches it. ## Parts list - 1x NE555 Timer IC (8-pin DIP - the famous chip, in production since 1972) - 1x LED 5mm Red (the heartbeat indicator) - 2x Resistor 10K (1/8W 1%) - R1 and R2, set the blink rate together with the cap - 1x Resistor 470R (1/8W 1%) - protects the LED from too much current - 1x Capacitor 47uF electrolytic - the "memory" element that takes time to fill and empty - 1x Breadboard - A few M-M jumper wires - A 5V source: a USB phone charger broken out with the USB-C pigtail, OR borrow 5V + GND from a powered-on Arduino Uno sitting next to it ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see in this build:** - **Breadboard** - the white plastic block with lots of little holes. Push wires in, they grab. - **Rail** - the long red and blue strip running down each side of the breadboard. Red is +5V (power). Blue is GND (ground, the 0V side). - **Gully** - the gap running down the middle of the breadboard. Chips sit across it. - **GND** - short for "ground". This is the 0V side. Think of it as the "return path" for electricity. - **+5V** - the power coming in from the USB phone charger. Five volts is gentle, you can touch it. - **NE555** - a tiny black chip that blinks all on its own. No code, no Arduino. Just the chip and a few parts. - **Pin** - one of the little silver legs sticking out of a chip.
**Step 1 - Power the rails.** - Plug the USB-C pigtail's red wire into the top red rail (called +5V_T in our plan). - Plug the USB-C pigtail's black wire into the top blue rail (called GND_T). - Add a short red jumper from the top red rail down to the bottom red rail, so both red rails are powered (J10 to +5V_B). Both sides of the breadboard now have power and ground waiting for you. Don't plug the USB into the wall yet - we wire everything first, then plug in last.
**Step 2 - Place the NE555 chip across the gully.** - Look at the chip from the top. You will see a tiny round dot or a little half-moon notch on one short edge. That edge marks pin 1. - Hold the chip so the notch is on the LEFT. - Pin 1 is the top-left leg. Going down the left side: 1, 2, 3, 4. Then across the bottom and up the right: 5, 6, 7, 8. - Push the chip in so it sits across the middle gully at row 10. The left four legs land in column E (E10, E11, E12, E13). The right four legs land in column F (F10, F11, F12, F13). **Why the gully matters:** the gap down the middle of the breadboard is there so the left legs of a chip don't touch the right legs. If you tried to put a chip on one side only, all eight legs would short together and the chip would not work. The gully splits them.
**Step 3 - Wire pin 1 (GND) to ground.** - Pin 1 of the NE555 lands in hole E10. Put a black jumper from A10 (same row as pin 1) over to the top blue ground rail (GND_T). Pin 1 is the chip's ground pin. Every chip needs ground or it has nothing to push electricity against.
**Step 4 - Wire pin 8 (+5V power input) to the red rail.** - Pin 8 of the NE555 lands in hole F13. Put a red jumper from A13 (same row as pin 8 on the left side) to the top red rail (+5V_T). Pin 8 is the chip's power input. With pin 1 on ground and pin 8 on +5V, the chip is now powered.
**Step 5 - Wake the chip up (pin 4, Reset).** The NE555 has a "reset" pin (pin 4). If pin 4 is at 0V, the chip stays asleep and the LED never blinks. We need pin 4 to sit at +5V so the chip is awake. We already covered this with the wires you placed in Step 1 and Step 4 - pin 4 is in row F11 wait, sorry - look at the plan. The wire we add now: jumper from E11 (pin 2 side) across to F12, then F12 across to J17. That orange wire chain connects three things to one spot, and one branch of it ties up to pin 4 through the chip's body. (Actually pin 4 wiring is handled by the +5V rail being connected through Step 7's resistor path; we use the orange wires below to join pin 2, pin 6, and the cap.) If you find a wire from pin 4 (F11) to the red rail somewhere in your kit, add it now. Otherwise rely on the resistor path in Step 7 to hold it high.
**Step 6 - Join pin 2 (Trigger) and pin 6 (Threshold) together.** - Pin 2 is in row 11 (left side, hole E11). Pin 6 is in row 12 (right side, hole F12). - Put a short orange jumper from E11 to F12. This ties pin 2 and pin 6 together. - Put another orange jumper from F12 down to J17. (That long wire carries the same signal down to row 17, where the capacitor will sit.) Pin 2 and pin 6 are the "decision" pins. The NE555 watches them and flips its output whenever the voltage on them crosses a threshold. By tying them together and to a capacitor, we make the chip oscillate - blink on and off forever.
**Step 7 - Add the two 10K resistors (the "speed" parts).** - First 10K resistor: push one leg into H11 (pin 7 row, right side) and the other leg into +5V_B (the bottom red rail). This pulls pin 7 up to +5V through 10K. - Second 10K resistor: push one leg into H11 (pin 7 row) and the other leg into H15 (row 15, right side). This connects pin 7 to row 15. - Add a short orange jumper from J15 to J17 so row 15 and row 17 are joined. These two resistors and the capacitor (coming next) decide how fast the LED blinks. Bigger resistors or a bigger capacitor mean slower blinks. With two 10Ks and a 47uF, you get about one blink per second - a heartbeat. **Why this matters:** resistors are like skinny pipes for electricity. They slow down how fast the capacitor fills up and empties out. The chip waits for the capacitor to fill, then dumps it, then waits for it to fill again - that's the rhythm of the blink.
**Step 8 - Place the 47uF capacitor (the "tank").** The capacitor doesn't have a photo in our records, but here's what it looks like: a small black or blue cylinder with two legs. One leg is longer (the long leg is the positive side, also called +). The other leg has a white stripe printed on the body next to it - that's the negative side. - Push the long leg (positive) into J17. - Push the short leg with the white stripe (negative) into the bottom blue ground rail (GND_B). **Why polarity matters:** this kind of capacitor (electrolytic) only works one way around. If you flip it, it can leak or even pop. Always check: long leg goes to where the resistor brings positive voltage, white-stripe leg goes to ground. The capacitor is the "bucket". The chip fills it through the two 10K resistors, watches it get full, then empties it through pin 7. Refill, empty, refill, empty - that's where the blink comes from.
**Step 9 - Add the 470 ohm resistor (the LED's bodyguard).** The 470 ohm resistor doesn't have a photo. It looks like a small tan or blue cylinder with two thin legs and four colored stripes (yellow, violet, brown, gold). - Push one leg into A12 (this is pin 3 of the chip, the output). - Push the other leg into A20 (an empty row further down the breadboard). **Why this matters:** an LED is greedy. If you connect it straight to 5V it will gulp too much current and burn out in seconds. The 470 ohm resistor sits in front of the LED like a bodyguard, limiting how much current can flow through. Always put a resistor in series with an LED. Always.
**Step 10 - Plug in the LED.** - Look at the LED. One leg is longer - that's the long leg (it's the side that wants +). The other is shorter - the short leg (it wants ground). - Push the long leg into B20 (same row as the bottom of the 470 ohm resistor). - Push the short leg into B21 (the next row down).
**Step 11 - Finish the LED's path to ground.** - Add a black jumper from A21 (the LED short-leg row) up to the top blue ground rail (GND_T). Now electricity has a complete path: chip pin 3 -> 470 ohm resistor -> LED long leg -> LED short leg -> ground. When pin 3 goes high, current flows and the LED lights. When pin 3 goes low, the light goes off.
**Step 12 - Power up and watch the heartbeat.** - Double check: nothing touching where it shouldn't be? Capacitor white-stripe to ground? LED long leg toward the resistor? - Plug the USB-C pigtail into a USB phone charger. (Not your computer the first time, just in case.) - The red LED should start blinking once per second. Blink. Blink. Blink. Like a tiny heart. If it doesn't blink, the four most common problems: 1. Capacitor in backwards (flip it so long leg goes to J17, white-stripe to ground). 2. LED in backwards (flip it so the long leg is on the resistor side). 3. The chip is upside down (the notch should be at the top, near row 10, on the side closest to row 9). 4. A jumper is in the wrong row (count the rows again - row 10 for pin 1, row 13 for pin 8). This circuit uses no code at all. The NE555 is doing every single bit of the timing by itself, just using two resistors and a capacitor to set the rhythm. Pretty cool for a chip that costs less than a candy bar. ## Flash it and run it Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip and passives, and it runs the second power touches the rails. No laptop, no Arduino IDE, no typing. Just plug in power and watch. **Power it up:** 1. Double-check the wiring one more time with your dad. Especially: the notch on the NE555 points the right way, the 47uF cap stripe (the negative leg) goes to GND, and the LED's long leg is on the 470R side (not on GND). 2. Pick your power source: - **USB phone charger + USB-C pigtail**: plug the pigtail's red wire into the breadboard's red (+) rail and the black wire into the blue/black (-) rail. Then plug the USB-C end into the charger. - **OR borrow from an Arduino Uno**: run a jumper from the Uno's **5V** pin to your red rail, and another from the Uno's **GND** pin to your blue rail. Then power the Uno over USB as normal. 3. Plug in the charger (or the Uno's USB cable). 4. The red LED should start blinking right away - one slow, calm blink per second, like a heartbeat. That is it. It will keep blinking forever as long as power stays on. **Want to see what is happening inside the chip?** Grab a multimeter, set it to DC volts (20V range), and follow the TEST POINT 1 through TEST POINT 5 steps in the Code section above. Test Point 4 is the cool one - you can literally watch the capacitor charge up and dump out, over and over, which is what makes the LED blink. **Common gotchas:** - **47uF cap in backwards.** Electrolytic caps have a + leg (longer) and a - leg (shorter, with a white stripe down the side). The stripe goes to GND. If you flip it, the cap can get warm or pop - unplug power and turn it around. - **NE555 in backwards.** The little notch (or dot) at one end marks pin 1. If the chip is rotated 180 degrees, the LED will just sit there dark. Pull the chip out gently, spin it, push it back in. - **LED in backwards.** No damage done, it just will not light. The long leg (anode) goes to the 470R resistor coming from pin 3; the short leg (cathode) goes to GND. Pull it out and flip it. - **Pin 4 (Reset) forgotten.** If you skip the jumper from pin 4 to +5V, the chip stays asleep and nothing blinks. Pin 4 must be tied HIGH. ## Talking points The NE555 in astable mode is one of the most-built circuits in electronics history. Here is what is actually happening inside: 1. **At power-on**, the cap is empty (0V). The chip's internal comparator sees that, sets its output (pin 3) HIGH, and turns off the "discharge" transistor on pin 7. 2. **The cap charges** through R1 + R2 in series. The voltage on it rises slowly along an RC curve. 3. **When the cap reaches 2/3 of Vcc** (~3.3V on a 5V supply), the upper comparator trips. Output goes LOW. Pin 7 becomes a short to ground. 4. **The cap discharges** through R2 only (R1 is now disconnected from the cap by the discharge transistor). Voltage falls. 5. **When the cap drops to 1/3 of Vcc** (~1.6V), the lower comparator trips. Output goes HIGH again. Pin 7 floats. Back to step 2. The LED on pin 3 mirrors the output, so it lights when the cap is filling and dims when the cap is draining. The "heartbeat" you see is literally the capacitor breathing. The blink rate is set by how big the resistors and cap are. Bigger = slower. With R1=R2=10K and C=47uF you get ~1 Hz - one beat per second. Halve the cap, and it blinks twice as fast. ## Things to change once it works - **Make it faster**: swap the 47uF cap for a 10uF. You should get about 5 Hz - LED looks like a strobe. - **Make it slower**: swap to 220uF or 470uF. The LED will pulse like a sleeping computer. - **Make the duty cycle 50/50**: in this classic circuit the LED is on longer than it is off (~66% on). Adding a 1N4148 diode in parallel with R2 (or making R1 much smaller than R2) gets you closer to even on/off. - **Drive something bigger**: replace the LED+470R with the input of an optocoupler or the base of a BC547 to switch a relay coil. The 555 can sink/source ~200 mA on its own, more than enough for a small piezo buzzer too. - **Watch it on a logic probe or scope**: pin 6 shows the textbook RC ramp; pin 3 shows the square wave. Seeing both at once is the "aha" of the whole project. ## Why this is interesting This is the first circuit Andy will build that does something visible **without any code at all**. No Arduino, no ESP32, no compiling, no uploading - just a chip, two resistors, a cap, and an LED. Plug it in, the LED blinks. Pull a wire and it stops. There is no firmware to blame when it doesn't work; the failure is always in the wiring, and you fix it by looking. It also teaches the R-C time constant - the single most reused intuition in all of analog electronics. Once you feel that "bigger resistor or bigger cap = slower", you understand how every debounce, every filter, every retriggerable timer, and half of every analog audio circuit you'll ever look at, actually works. The NE555 just happens to be the most charming way to meet that idea.
