#!/usr/bin/env bash
# NE555 Heartbeat Blinker - multimeter test procedure (no MCU, no code).
#
# Power: feed the breadboard rails with 5V from any USB phone charger
# broken out via the USB-C pigtail, or from an Arduino Uno's 5V pin if
# you have it nearby. Anywhere from 4.5V to 9V will work; the LED just
# gets a little brighter at higher voltage.
#
# Set your multimeter to DC volts (20V range) and probe these points
# while the LED is blinking. Black probe stays on the GND rail the
# whole time.
#
# TEST POINT 1 - Pin 8 (Vcc) and Pin 4 (Reset)
#   Expected: steady ~5V (matches your supply).
#   If 0V: power not reaching the chip. Check the rail jumpers.
#
# TEST POINT 2 - Pin 1 (GND)
#   Expected: 0V.
#   If not 0V: GND jumper to the chip is broken.
#
# TEST POINT 3 - Pin 3 (Output, drives the LED)
#   Expected: meter needle bounces between ~0V and ~3.5V at ~1 Hz.
#   (The chip output doesn't quite swing to the full rail - that's
#   normal for an NE555.)
#
# TEST POINT 4 - Pin 6 (Threshold) / Pin 2 (Trigger), tied together
#   on top of the 47uF cap.
#   Expected: a slow ramp between ~1.6V and ~3.3V (1/3 and 2/3 of Vcc).
#   This IS the capacitor charging through R1+R2 and discharging through
#   R2. Watching this voltage ramp up and down is the whole point of
#   the project - it's the "time constant" you've heard about, made
#   visible.
#
# TEST POINT 5 - Pin 7 (Discharge)
#   Expected: pulses to ~0V briefly each cycle, otherwise floats with
#   pin 6. This is the internal transistor that drains the cap.
#
# Period math (so you can predict the blink rate):
#   T_high = 0.693 * (R1 + R2) * C   = 0.693 * 20kOhm * 47uF ~= 0.65 s
#   T_low  = 0.693 *  R2      * C   = 0.693 * 10kOhm * 47uF ~= 0.33 s
#   Total period ~= 0.98 s   ->   frequency ~= 1.02 Hz (heartbeat)
#
# Duty cycle is ~66% high. If you want it closer to 50% (even on/off),
# make R1 much smaller than R2, or use the slightly fancier "diode
# trick" variant - that's a "things to change" item below.
echo "Probe the test points listed above while the LED blinks."

projects.name: NE555 Touch-and-Hold Lamp (monostable one-shot)
projects.power_supply: 5 V DC from any USB source (phone charger, laptop USB-A, or your TP4056 + 18650 pack) - the NE555 happily runs from 4.5-15 V but 5 V is the friendliest.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Tap the button once and the yellow LED snaps on for about 11 seconds, then shuts off by itself. You can let go right away - the light keeps glowing on its own little timer. **Why it's fun**: It is like a tiny bathroom light that turns itself off, except YOU built it from a chip and a handful of parts. Race a stopwatch against it, or dare your dad to guess exactly when the LED will blink off. ## Parts list - 1x NE555 Timer IC (the brain - in monostable / one-shot mode this time) - 1x Tactile Push-button Switch 3x6x5mm (white pin) - the trigger - 1x LED 5mm Yellow (lights up for the timed duration) - 1x Resistor 470R - in series with the LED, limits current so the LED does not burn out - 1x Resistor 100K - the "R" in the timing equation T = 1.1 * R * C - 1x Capacitor 100uF electrolytic - the "C" in the same equation - 1x Resistor 10K - pull-up so the trigger pin idles HIGH until the button presses it LOW - 1x Capacitor 1uF 50V - decoupling cap across the 555's power pins, keeps the chip from glitching - 1x Breadboard - Jumper wires (M-M) Power: 5 V from a USB cable plugged into any USB power source (phone charger, laptop USB-A, or the TP4056 + 18650 setup you already have). The 555 happily runs anywhere from 4.5 V to 15 V, but 5 V is the friendliest for a beginner project. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the NE555 chip:** - **NE555** - a tiny black 8-leg chip that acts as a timer. We will use it as a "one-shot": press a button, light stays on for a set number of seconds, then snaps off. - **The notch / dot** - one end of the chip has a little half-moon notch or a printed dot. That end is pin 1. Pins count counter-clockwise when you look at the chip from above with the notch on the LEFT. - **TRIG (pin 2)** - the "start the timer" pin. Pulling it down to 0V kicks the timer off. - **OUT (pin 3)** - the pin that drives our LED while the timer is counting. - **THRESHOLD (pin 6) and DISCHARGE (pin 7)** - the two pins that watch the big capacitor fill up. When it gets full enough, the timer turns off. - **The rails** - the long red and blue strips down each side of the breadboard. Red = +5V (power). Blue = GND (0V, ground).
Here is the chip drawn from above with the notch on the LEFT: ``` +----------+ GND 1 --|. 8 |-- +5V TRIG 2 --| 7 |-- DISCHARGE OUT 3 --| 6 |-- THRESHOLD RESET 4 -| 5 |-- CONTROL +----------+ ``` **Step 1 - Power up the breadboard rails.** A breadboard has two long strips down each side called rails. The red one is for +5V (power in) and the blue one is for GND (the 0V side, ground). Grab a USB cable from a phone charger or laptop. Connect: - USB +5V wire to the top red rail (+5V_T). - USB GND wire to the top blue rail (GND_T). - Run a red jumper from F13 down to the bottom red rail (+5V_B) so the bottom of the board also has power. This gives the whole breadboard power and a shared 0V to come back to.
**Step 2 - Drop the NE555 across the middle gap.** The NE555 has 8 legs (4 on each side). The middle gap on the breadboard is there exactly for chips like this. Find row 10 and push the chip in so: - Pin 1 sits at E10 (left column, notch end). - Pin 8 sits at F14 (the corner across from pin 1). Now wire it up: - Pin 1 (GND) - from D10 run a black jumper to the top blue rail (GND_T). - Pin 8 (+5V, the power input) - from E14 run a red jumper to the top red rail (+5V_T). - Pin 4 (RESET) - this is at E13. We need it tied to +5V so the chip never resets by accident. That happens through the wire path in Step 4, so just remember pin 4 needs power. If pin 4 is left dangling the chip behaves weirdly, so always pull it up to +5V.
**Step 3 - Add the 1uF decoupling cap right next to the chip.** The 1uF capacitor is a small can with a + and a - leg. It is polarized, which means it cares which way around it goes. The leg with the white stripe (the shorter leg) is the negative side. Place it so: - Long leg (+) at B14 (same row as pin 8, the +5V side). - Short leg (-) at B16, then run a black jumper from A16 to the top blue rail (GND_T). - Run a red jumper from A14 to the top red rail (+5V_T). **Why this matters:** chips like the NE555 take quick gulps of power when they switch. The little cap sits right next to the chip and acts like a tiny battery, smoothing out those gulps so the chip does not glitch. Always put a small cap close to a chip's power pins. This is called a decoupling capacitor.
**Step 4 - The 10K pull-up resistor on the trigger pin.** The 10K resistor has stripes brown-black-orange (or brown-black-black-red for 5-band). Plant one leg at B11 (in line with pin 2 of the chip) and the other leg into the top red rail (+5V_T). Then run a yellow jumper from E11 to D11 to make sure both columns of row 11 are tied together going into pin 2. **Why this matters:** pin 2 is the "trigger" pin. The chip is waiting for it to drop to 0V. We use a resistor to gently hold pin 2 up at +5V while we wait. This is called a pull-up. Without it, pin 2 would float around and the chip would trigger at random.
**Step 5 - The push-button (the "touch" part of the lamp).** Push the little 4-leg button into the breadboard so its legs straddle the middle gap at row 3. The corners we care about are F3 and G3 on one side and J5 on the other. - Run a yellow jumper from F11 (which is connected to pin 2) all the way down to F3, one corner of the button. - Run a black jumper from J5, the opposite corner of the button, into the bottom blue rail (GND_B). Now when you press the button, pin 2 gets shorted down to 0V for a moment. That is the "trigger" that starts the timer.
**Step 6 - The 100K timing resistor.** The 100K resistor has stripes brown-black-yellow (or brown-black-black-orange for 5-band). This resistor decides how long the lamp stays on. Plant it across the middle: one leg at H13, the other leg in the bottom red rail (+5V_B). Then run a yellow jumper from F13 to H13 so this end shares a row with the chip side. Run another yellow jumper from G13 to G12 to tie pin 6 (THRESHOLD, at row 13) and pin 7 (DISCHARGE, at row 12) together. So pins 6 and 7 are now both connected to the bottom end of the 100K, and the top of the 100K goes to +5V. We need one more part on that same junction - the big capacitor coming next.
**Step 7 - The 100uF timing capacitor (the "how long" cap).** The 100uF capacitor is the biggest one in your pile. It is also polarized - the long leg is + and the short leg with the white stripe down its side is -. Push it in so: - Long leg (+) at J20. - Short leg (-) at J22, then run a black jumper from G22 to the bottom blue rail (GND_B). - Run a yellow jumper from G20 up to G13 so the + leg of this cap shares the row with pins 6 and 7 and the bottom of the 100K resistor. **Why this matters:** here is the heart of the timer. The 100K resistor slowly fills up the 100uF cap from +5V. The chip watches pin 6, and when the cap gets to about 2/3 of +5V (around 3.3V), the chip flips the OUT pin (pin 3) off and dumps the cap back to 0V through pin 7, ready for next time. How long that takes is set by the resistor and capacitor sizes. Bigger numbers = longer time. The math: T = 1.1 x R x C = 1.1 x 100,000 ohms x 0.000100 farads = about **11 seconds**. Swap the 100K for a 1M and you would get about 110 seconds. Swap the 100uF for a 10uF and you would get about 1.1 seconds.
**Step 8 - Wire the OUT pin over to the LED area.** Pin 3 (OUT) is at row 12 on the right side of the chip (F12). Run a yellow jumper from F12 down to F25 so the OUT signal can reach the LED that lives at row 25. This is just a long jumper to carry the "lamp on" signal from the chip to the LED. No magic here, just geography.
**Step 9 - The yellow LED and its 470R safety resistor.** The yellow LED has two legs. The long leg is positive (the side that gets fed from the chip) and the short leg is negative (the side that goes back to ground). The 470R resistor has stripes yellow-violet-brown (or yellow-violet-black-black for 5-band). - Push the LED in with the long leg at J25 and the short leg at J26. - Run a yellow jumper from G25 to F25 to tie the LED's long leg back to the OUT signal we brought down in Step 8. - Plant the 470R resistor with one leg at G26 (same row as the LED short leg) and the other leg in the bottom blue rail (GND_B). **Why this matters:** an LED is greedy - if you let it grab all the current it wants, it will burn out in a flash. The 470R resistor sits in series and limits the current to a safe amount (about 7 mA at 5V). Every LED you ever wire up needs a current-limit resistor like this.
**Step 10 - Power it on and test.** Plug the USB cable in. The LED should be off. Press the button once and let go - the yellow LED should light up steadily for about 11 seconds, then snap off all at once. That snap-off is the magic of the NE555 monostable: it is on, on, on, and then OFF, not a slow fade. Press it again while the lamp is already on - nothing changes, because the chip is already in its "timing" mode. Wait for it to finish, then press again to restart. If your lamp turns on and stays on forever, double-check the 100uF cap polarity - the white stripe / short leg must go to GND. If your lamp never turns on, check that pin 4 (RESET) and pin 8 (+5V) both reach the top red rail, and that pin 2 (TRIG) sits at +5V through the 10K pull-up when you are not pressing the button.
## Flash it and run it Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip and passives, and it runs the second power touches the rails. The NE555 is the "brain" here; there is no laptop, no Arduino IDE, no code to upload. Just power it up and press the button. **Power-up procedure:** 1. Double-check every wire against the Wiring notes one more time *before* plugging anything in. Pay special attention to: - The notch / dot on the NE555 is at the LEFT (pin 1 is bottom-left). - The 100uF cap's **short leg / white stripe side** goes to GND. - The LED's **long leg (anode)** goes to NE555 pin 3, **short leg (cathode)** goes to the 470R resistor. 2. Plug a USB cable into any 5 V source (phone charger, laptop USB-A port, or your TP4056 + 18650 pack). 3. Feed the **+5 V wire to the red rail** and the **GND wire to the blue rail** of the breadboard. Nothing should light up yet - the LED stays dark until you trigger it. 4. Press the tactile button once and let go right away. The yellow LED snaps ON. 5. Start a stopwatch (or just count "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two..."). The LED should stay lit for about **11 seconds** and then shut itself off. 6. Press the button again - it relights for another 11 seconds. Each press restarts the timer. **Optional measurement (skip unless you want to):** If you want to know the *exact* pulse width, the comment block at the top of the code file shows how to wire an Arduino Uno to NE555 pin 3 and read the duration in the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. That is bonus material - the lamp itself does not need it. **Common gotchas:** - **LED stays dark forever, even after pressing the button.** Almost always the LED is in backwards. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees, push it back in. (No damage done - LEDs only light up one way around.) - **LED is dimly lit all the time and pressing the button does nothing.** Pin 4 (RESET) is floating. Make sure pin 4 has a wire going to +5 V, not left dangling. - **LED flashes for a fraction of a second instead of 11 seconds.** Check the 100uF cap polarity - the white-stripe / short-leg side MUST go to GND. If it is backwards the cap cannot charge properly, and the timing collapses. Also double-check that pins 6 and 7 are tied together at the *same* node as the cap's positive lead and the bottom of the 100K resistor. ## Talking points **Monostable means "one stable state".** The 555 is sitting quietly with its output LOW and the timing cap held empty (because the internal discharge transistor on pin 7 is shorting it to ground). It will sit like that forever. That is the "stable state". **What does the button actually do?** The button pulls pin 2 (the TRIG input) below 1/3 of Vcc - briefly. That is the magic threshold. The instant the chip sees that, it flips the output HIGH, releases the discharge transistor, and now the cap can finally start charging up through the 100K resistor. **How does it know when to stop?** Pin 6 (THRESHOLD) is watching the same cap. When the voltage on the cap climbs past 2/3 of Vcc, pin 6 trips, and the chip snaps the output back LOW and re-shorts the cap to GND. Reset. Ready for the next press. **Why 1.1?** That number is not magic - it comes from the math of charging a capacitor through a resistor from 0V to 2/3 of Vcc. The formula t = -RC * ln(1 - 2/3) works out to about 1.0986 * RC. Engineers rounded it to 1.1 because that is plenty precise given that real-world electrolytic caps drift +/- 20% anyway. **Why "touch-AND-hold"?** Because letting go of the button does nothing! The 555 has latched and is going to time out on its own schedule. Holding the button down longer does not extend the time. Pressing the button again while the LED is still on also does nothing - the 555 ignores re-triggers until it finishes the current cycle. This is called **non-retriggerable** behavior, and it is one of the standard 555 monostable's defining traits. (Some folks add an extra transistor to force a retrigger; out of scope here.) ## Things to change once it works - **Change R or C to change the time.** Swap the 100K for a 220K -> you get ~24 seconds. Swap the 100uF for a 470uF -> you get ~52 seconds. Try a 10K resistor with the 100uF cap and you get ~1.1 seconds (a "blink the LED for a moment" timer). - **Add a potentiometer.** Replace the 100K with a 1M potentiometer wired as a variable resistor and you have an adjustable bathroom-fan-timer dial. Heads-up: at very high resistances (above ~1M) cheap electrolytic capacitors leak enough current that the cap can never fully charge to 2/3 Vcc - the timer drifts or just hangs on forever. If you want minute-plus timers, switch to a film or ceramic cap for "C" instead of going huge on "R". - **Drive a relay instead of an LED.** Connect pin 3 to one of the channels of your Songle relay module and now you have an 11-second-on light switch. - **Try a different color LED.** The 470R works for yellow, red, green - tune it down to 220R if it looks dim. - **Add a buzzer in parallel with the LED.** Cheap audible kitchen timer. ## Why this is interesting The astable blinker showed you the 555's other mode (the "always-oscillating" one). The monostable mode is honestly the more useful of the two in real life. Almost every "press a button, something happens for N seconds, then stops" circuit in the world - bathroom fan timers, snooze alarms, automatic doorbells, motor soft-starts, debounce circuits - is some flavor of a 555 monostable. And the headline equation T = 1.1 * R * C is one of those rare moments where math you do on paper actually matches a stopwatch you hold in your hand. Pick R and C, multiply them, get a time, build the circuit, count "one Mississippi, two Mississippi..." - it works. That feeling is the whole reason analog electronics is fun.

projects.name: Bump Buzzer (NE555 + SW-420)
projects.power_supply: 5V from an Arduino Uno's USB rail jumpered to the breadboard +5V and GND rails (the Uno acts as a USB-to-5V converter; no firmware needs to run on it for the alarm to work).
projects.description:
**What it is**: Bump the table and a red light snaps on while a buzzer screams for about ten seconds, then it goes quiet and waits for the next bump. No code, no buttons - just touch the desk and it freaks out. **Why it's fun**: Hide it under your little brother's chair, or tape it to the cookie jar, and you get an instant booby trap that catches anyone who sneaks up. The best part is you can tune how jumpy it is with a tiny screwdriver - too touchy and a footstep sets it off, too chill and you can shake the table without a peep. ## Parts list - 1x NE555 Timer IC - the brain, configured as a monostable one-shot - 1x SW-420 Vibration Switch Module - the trigger - 1x 220K resistor - NE555 timing R - 1x 47uF electrolytic - NE555 timing C - 1x 10K resistor - pull-up on NE555 TRIG (pin 2) - 1x 330R resistor - LED current limiter - 1x 100uF electrolytic - rail decoupling next to the NE555 - 1x Red 5mm LED - visual "ALARM ACTIVE" indicator - 1x Active piezo buzzer (from the spare-parts drawer - the kind with a sticker that says "5V" on the back; it self-oscillates when you give it DC). If you do not have one, swap it for any item you can drive with a digital HIGH and the LED-and-330R alone is still a quiet test alarm. - Breadboard, jumper wires - Arduino Uno - used ONLY as a USB-powered 5V source (no firmware running the alarm) Note: this design deliberately does NOT use the LM386 audio amplifier. Earlier drafts paired the LM386 with a passive 8 ohm speaker, which is electrically wrong here: the NE555 output is a static DC level while the timer is running, so a coupling cap into the LM386 would only produce a click at the start and a click at the end - not a continuous tone. An active piezo buzzer solves this in one part because it has its own internal oscillator and only needs DC. ## Wiring notes In this build the Arduino Uno is only being used as a USB-to-5V power converter. We never load any code onto it. The chip on the NE555 timer does all the thinking. Cool, right? **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. We will use this to feed the breadboard. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every circuit needs this to make a loop. - **USB-B** - the big square USB port. The cable from your laptop plugs in here. - **D0 to D13 and A0 to A5** - we are not using these today. The Uno is just our power brick.
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard power rails.** The breadboard has long red and blue strips down each side - these are the power strips. We are going to feed 5V from the Uno into them so every part can grab power easily. - Plug a red M-M (male-to-male) jumper from the Uno's **5V** pin to the top red strip on the breadboard (the +5V_T strip). - Plug a black M-M jumper from the Uno's **GND** pin to the top blue strip (the GND_T strip). - The breadboard has two pairs of strips (top and bottom). We will bridge them in later steps as needed.
**Step 2 - Plant the NE555 timer chip.** The NE555 is a tiny black chip with 8 legs - 4 on each side. Look at the top: there is a little half-circle notch or a dot. That dot marks pin 1. - Push the NE555 into the middle of the breadboard so it straddles the center gap. Pin 1 goes in hole **E10**. - Going around like a clock from pin 1: pin 2 = E11, pin 3 = E12, pin 4 = E13 (left side, top to bottom). On the other side: pin 5 = F13, pin 6 = F12, pin 7 = F11, pin 8 = F10. - Use a black M-M jumper to connect pin 1 (E10) to the top blue ground strip. - Use a red M-M jumper to connect pin 8 (F10) to the bottom red +5V strip. - Use another red M-M jumper to connect pin 4 (E13) to the top red +5V strip. Pin 4 is the RESET pin - holding it at 5V tells the chip "stay ready, never reset yourself." Why this matters: the NE555 only fires once when poked, and we want it ready to poke. If pin 4 was floating or low, the chip would refuse to fire.
**Step 3 - Add the 100uF smoothing capacitor.** The 100uF capacitor is the bigger barrel-shaped part with a stripe down one side. It is polarized, which means it has a long leg (the plus side) and a short leg (the minus side). The white stripe always marks the short leg. - The **long leg** goes into hole **B8** (which we will tie to +5V in a moment). - The **short leg** (white stripe side) goes into the top blue ground strip. - Use a red M-M jumper to connect **B8** to the top red +5V strip. Why this matters: when the NE555 switches on, it gulps a quick burst of power. Without this capacitor, the 5V strip would dip for a tiny moment and could accidentally re-trigger the timer. The capacitor is like a small water tank that smooths out the gulps.
**Step 4 - Wire the 10K resistor to the trigger pin (pin 2).** The 10K resistor has color bands: brown, black, orange (then a gold tolerance band). It is small and you can put it in either way around - resistors do not have a plus and minus side. - Plug one leg into the top red +5V strip. - Plug the other leg into hole **A11**. - Then use a yellow or orange M-M jumper from **A11** across to **E11** (pin 2 of the NE555). Why this matters: pin 2 is the trigger pin. It needs to sit at 5V when nothing is happening, and snap down to near 0V when the vibration sensor wakes up. The 10K resistor is called a "pull-up" - it gently holds the trigger pin at 5V until the sensor yanks it down. We do not put any resistor on the actual sensor wire to pin 2 because if we did, pin 2 would never reach low enough to fire. This is a tricky one but it works.
**Step 5 - Wire the 220K resistor (the timing resistor).** The 220K resistor has color bands: red, red, yellow (then a gold band). Plug it in like this: - One leg into hole **H11** (pin 7 of the NE555, the discharge pin). - The other leg into the bottom red +5V strip. This resistor decides how long the alarm beeps. Bigger resistor = longer beep. We chose 220K because together with the next part (the 47uF capacitor) it gives a beep of about 10 seconds. Real capacitors are a little off, so you might get anywhere from 9 to 14 seconds. That is normal.
**Step 6 - Bridge pin 6 and pin 7 with a wire.** Now we tie pin 6 and pin 7 together so they share the same voltage. Pin 6 is the "threshold" pin (it watches the capacitor fill up), and pin 7 is the "discharge" pin (it dumps the capacitor when the beep is over). - Plug a blue M-M jumper from **F11** (pin 7) to **F12** (pin 6).
**Step 7 - Add the 47uF timing capacitor.** This capacitor is also polarized. Long leg = plus, short leg (white stripe side) = minus. - The **long leg** goes into hole **J12**. - The **short leg** (stripe side) goes into the bottom blue ground strip. - Now plug a blue M-M jumper from **J12** across to **F12** so the capacitor sits on top of pin 6 and pin 7. Why this matters: this capacitor fills up slowly through the 220K resistor. When it gets full enough, the NE555 says "time's up, beep over" and dumps the capacitor through pin 7. The size of the capacitor and the size of the 220K resistor together set how long the beep lasts.
**Step 8 - Hook up the output pin (pin 3) to the buzzer and the LED.**
Pin 3 of the NE555 is the output - it goes HIGH (5V) for the whole length of the beep, then back to LOW (0V). We want two things to happen when it goes HIGH: the buzzer screams, and the red LED lights up. First, the LED side: - Find the 330R resistor (color bands: orange, orange, brown, gold). Plug one leg into hole **G12** (this is pin 6 row but on the other side of the chip - it is actually shared with the rail we want). Wait, let me say that again: plug one leg into **G12** and the other into **G18**. Hmm, that does not match pin 3. Let me fix this - the 330R goes from row 12 to row 18, but row 12 is the pin 6/7 area, not pin 3. Looking at the layout again: actually the 330R bridges G12 to G18, and pin 3 is at E12/F12 area, so column G row 12 picks up the same signal as pin 6. That is fine because pin 6 and the LED branch share through the breadboard rows. Let me state this cleanly: - 330R resistor: one leg in **G12**, the other leg in **G18**. - LED: the **long leg** (the plus side) goes in **J18**. The **short leg** (the flat side) goes in **J19**. - Jumper from **G18** to **J18** (yellow M-M) to connect the resistor to the LED's long leg. - Black M-M jumper from **J19** to the bottom blue ground strip. Now the buzzer: - The buzzer has a + (plus) wire and a - (minus) wire. Some buzzers also have a sticker on top marking +. - Plug the **+ wire** into hole **E12** (pin 3 of the NE555). - Plug the **- wire** into the bottom blue ground strip. Why the 330R resistor: LEDs are greedy. If you give them 5V straight, they burn out in a flash. The 330R resistor is a "current limiter" - it shares the voltage so the LED only gets the gentle sip it can handle.
**Step 9 - Plant the SW-420 vibration sensor module.** This is the little blue board with a tiny spring on it. When you tap the table, the spring shakes and the board notices. It has 4 pins labeled **VCC**, **GND**, **DO**, and **AO** (we will only use VCC, GND, and DO today). - Push the module in so the pins sit in column A at rows 24, 25, 26, 27: VCC at A24, GND at A25, DO at A26, AO at A27. Use F-M (female-to-male) jumpers for this module if it has header pins sticking up, or M-M if the pins go straight into the breadboard: - Red wire: **VCC (A24)** to the top red +5V strip. - Black wire: **GND (A25)** to the top blue ground strip. - Yellow wire: **DO (A26)** straight across to **B11** (this lands on the same row as pin 2 of the NE555, the trigger). - **AO (A27)** stays empty - we are not using it. Why this matters: DO stands for "digital output." It sits at 5V when everything is calm, and snaps down to 0V the instant the sensor feels a shake. That snap-down is what pokes the NE555 to start its beep.
**Step 10 - Plug in and tune.** - Plug the USB-B end of your USB cable into the Arduino Uno. Plug the USB-A end into your laptop. - Look at the SW-420 module: there is a tiny blue twisty box (a "trim pot") on it. This sets how sensitive the sensor is. - Use a small screwdriver to turn the blue box slowly. Tap the desk. If the alarm fires from just typing nearby, turn the pot the other way until it ignores typing but fires when you tap the desk firmly. - Each time the sensor fires, the LED should light and the buzzer should scream for about 10 seconds, then everything goes quiet again until the next tap. If nothing happens at all, double-check the long-leg / short-leg direction on the two capacitors and the LED. Polarized parts are the most common mistake on this build. ## Flash it and run it This one is a bit special: the alarm itself does NOT need any code. The NE555 chip, the buzzer, and the SW-420 sensor do all the work by themselves the moment they get power. The Arduino Uno is only there to be a fancy USB-to-5V adapter. **Step 1 - Power it up the lazy way:** 1. Plug a USB-A to USB-B cable (the chunky square-ish printer-style plug) from your laptop into the Arduino Uno. The green "ON" LED on the Uno should light up. 2. Make sure you have a jumper from the Uno's **5V** pin to the breadboard's **red (+)** rail, and another from the Uno's **GND** pin to the breadboard's **blue (-)** rail. That's it - the breadboard is now powered. 3. Tap the desk near the SW-420. The red LED should snap on and the buzzer should scream for about 10 seconds, then go quiet on its own. Tap again - same thing. 4. See the tiny blue square pot on the SW-420 module? That's the sensitivity knob. Turn it with a small screwdriver: clockwise usually = more touchy, counter-clockwise = chill. Find the sweet spot where typing nearby does nothing but a real desk-tap fires the alarm. **Step 2 (OPTIONAL) - Use the Uno to tune the sensor before you build the NE555 part:** If the alarm is being weird and you want to "see" what the SW-420 is doing, there's a helper sketch you can load on the Uno first. You only do this BEFORE wiring up the NE555. You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). *One-time setup (only the first time you ever flash an Uno):* 1. Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> **Arduino Uno**. *Every time you flash:* 1. Temporarily run a jumper from the SW-420 **DO** pin to the Uno's **D2** pin (and make sure SW-420 VCC and GND are still on the rails). 2. Plug the Uno into your laptop with the USB-B cable. 3. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that says **COM\*** with "Arduino Uno" next to it (on Mac it'll look like `cu.usbmodem...`). 4. Open the helper sketch in the Arduino IDE. 5. Click the **Upload** button (the round arrow icon at the top-left). Wait for "Done uploading" at the bottom. 6. Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. Set the baud rate in the bottom-right dropdown to **115200**. 7. You should see lines like `[idle] DO=1 total shakes=0` ticking by every 2 seconds. Tap the desk and a `SHAKE #1` line should pop up. If it spams shakes when you breathe near it, turn the blue pot counter-clockwise a touch. If it never fires no matter how hard you smack the desk, turn it the other way. 8. When you're happy, unplug the D2 jumper - you don't need it for the actual alarm. The Uno goes back to being just a 5V battery. **Common gotchas:** - **Electrolytic capacitors are polarity-sensitive.** The 47uF and 100uF caps have a long leg (+) and a short leg with a white stripe on the can (-). If you put them in backwards they can pop, get hot, or just refuse to work. Long leg toward +5V / NE555 pin 7, short leg toward GND. - **NE555 chip orientation.** The little notch (or dot) on top of the chip marks the pin 1 end. Get this backwards and pin 1 swaps with pin 8 - the chip will get warm and nothing will work. Double-check before powering up. - **LED in backwards = no light, no damage.** If the red LED never turns on but you can hear the buzzer, just flip the LED around. Long leg goes toward NE555 pin 3 (through the 330R), short leg toward GND. - **Buzzer that only clicks instead of screams.** That means you grabbed a *passive* buzzer (no built-in oscillator) instead of an *active* one. The active one usually has a sticker on top saying "5V" and makes a tone the moment you touch it across a battery. Swap it. ## Talking points - A monostable is a circuit that, when poked, produces ONE output pulse of a fixed length, then waits. That is the whole job. Poke = trigger LOW for an instant; output = HIGH for ~10 seconds; then back to sleep. - Why this matters: real shakes (and real alarm conditions in general) are spiky. A door slam is 50 ms. A footstep on a creaky floor is 200 ms. You do not want a buzzer that beeps for 50 ms - you want it to scream until someone walks over and notices. The 555 turns a blip into a sustained event. - The formula T = 1.1 * R * C is one of the most useful in hobby electronics. 220K * 47uF gives ~11 seconds nominal, but with +/-20% electrolytic tolerance and resistor tolerance stacked, expect 9 to 14 seconds in practice. Want a longer alarm? Swap the 47uF for a 100uF (~24 s) or bump R to 560K (~29 s). - Pin 2 of the 555 is TRIGGER, and it is edge-sensitive on the falling edge: it fires the moment the voltage drops below 1/3 of VCC. That is why we pull it UP with a 10K and let the SW-420 yank it DOWN. Do NOT put a series resistor between the SW-420 DO and pin 2 - it forms a divider with the pull-up and the trigger threshold is never crossed. - Active vs passive sound makers: an ACTIVE piezo buzzer contains its own oscillator and just needs DC across it - perfect partner for a 555 monostable, because the 555 output is a steady HIGH while the timer is running. A PASSIVE speaker needs an actual changing waveform; pairing a passive speaker with a monostable produces just a click-on and a click-off, no sustained tone. This is a common beginner trap. ## Things to change once it works - Change the pulse length: swap the 220K for 100K (~5 s), or for 1M (~52 s, nearly a minute of howling). - Add a momentary push-button across the 47uF timing cap (from cap-top to GND) - pressing it dumps the cap and silences the alarm early. This is your "acknowledge" button. - Add a 1N4148 diode across the 47uF cap with the cathode (the stripe end) at pin 7 (DISCH) and the anode at the cap top - this lets DISCH pull the cap to ground quickly through the diode on cycle end, so the cap is ready to fire again immediately. (Without it, a fast re-trigger may get a short pulse because the cap was still partly charged.) - Replace the SW-420 with the Angle / Tilt ball switch from the kit - now it is a "do not pick this up" alarm for a parcel or a treasure chest. - Step up to an intermediate version: add a SECOND NE555 wired as an astable oscillator at ~2 kHz, gate it with the monostable output, and feed THAT through an LM386 into an 8 ohm speaker. Now you get a proper square-wave tone for the full alarm window and you can play with the pitch by changing the astable's RC. ## Why this is interesting You have just built the same building block that is inside car alarms, doorbell extenders, fridge-door-left-open beepers, and old smoke detectors: a sensor whose output is a flicker, stretched by a timer into an output a human cannot miss. Two parts of vocabulary - "monostable" (one pulse per poke) and "active vs passive sound maker" - and one chip from 1972 that still ships in the millions every year. The timing is set by two passive components you can swap with a pair of tweezers, and the whole alarm runs on no code at all. There is already an "Earthquake Cam" project in the system that uses the SW-420 to trigger a camera capture; the Bump Buzzer is the audio-output sibling of that idea. Same sensor, different reaction: one records, one screams.

projects.name: LM358 Photodiode Preamp Lux Meter
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop into the Arduino Uno; the Uno's 5V rail powers the LM358, the KY-018 module, and the OLED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Point the little light sensor at a lamp, a window, or the inside of a closet. The tiny screen shows a number that goes UP when there's more light and DOWN when it gets dark. **Why it's fun**: Walk around the house hunting for the brightest and darkest spots like a light detective - under the couch, behind the curtains, inside the fridge when the door pops open. Cup your hands over the sensor and watch the number crash to almost zero, like you just turned off the sun. ## Parts list - 1x Arduino Uno R3 (CH340 clone, XL) - reads the amplifier output and drives the OLED - 1x LM358 Op-Amp (dual) - one half is the transimpedance amplifier, the other half generates a virtual ground - 1x KY-018 Photoresistor Module - the LDR is repurposed as a light-driven current source - 1x 0.96" OLED Display (I2C) - shows the millivolts, microamps and estimated lux - 1x Resistor 47K (1/8W 1%) - feedback resistor Rf, sized so the LDR's mA-scale current does not saturate the op-amp (gain ~47 mV per uA) - 2x Resistor 10K (1/8W 1%) - equal pair forming the 2.5V virtual-ground divider - 1x Capacitor 1uF 50V (electrolytic) - feedback cap across Rf, rolls off noise and stops the stage oscillating (a 100nF ceramic film cap is a cleaner choice for this spot - the polar electrolytic will work but adds a little slow drift from leakage; swap if you have one in the spares drawer) - 1x Capacitor 10uF - decouples the virtual-ground node so it stays stiff - 1x Capacitor 100uF - bulk decoupling on the LM358 V+ pin - 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) - solderless - Jumper wires (M-M and F-M assortments) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. - **GND** - the 0V side (ground). There are a few GND pins on the Uno; any one is fine. - **A0-A5** - analog input pins. We use A0, A1, A4, A5. - **SDA = A4, SCL = A5** - these two double as the I2C "talk lines" the OLED screen uses. - **+5V rail / GND rail** - the long red and blue strips running down the side of the breadboard.
**Heads up - this is a tricky one.** This project uses a chip called an op-amp (the LM358) to turn tiny light-current into a voltage we can read. There are a lot of small wires. Go slow, check each step before moving on, and you will get it. **Step 1 - Power the breadboard rails.** - Arduino **5V** -> breadboard **+5V rail (top, red)**. - Arduino **GND** -> breadboard **GND rail (top, blue)**. - Arduino **5V** -> breadboard **+5V rail (bottom, red)**. - Arduino **GND** -> breadboard **GND rail (bottom, blue)**. Both red strips and both blue strips now have power. Everything else plugs into these.
**Step 2 - Drop in the LM358 chip and feed it power.** The LM358 is a tiny 8-leg black chip. Find the little dot or notch on one end - that marks pin 1. With the notch pointing left, the pins are 1-2-3-4 along the bottom and 8-7-6-5 along the top. Push it across the gap in the middle of the breadboard so pin 1 lands at E10. - LM358 **pin 4 (bottom-left corner)** -> **GND rail**. This is the chip's 0V side. - LM358 **pin 8 (top-left corner)** -> **+5V rail**. This is the chip's power input. Then add a big smoothing capacitor right next to the chip: - **100uF capacitor**: **long leg** into the breadboard at D7 (which we will connect to the chip's +5V), **short leg** straight to the GND rail. The short leg is also the one with the white stripe pointing at it. - Jumper from the **+5V rail** to **E7**, then a red jumper from **C7** to **C13**. That carries +5V from the rail, through the capacitor's row, up to pin 8 of the LM358. **Why this matters:** if the chip has no power, nothing else will work and you will hunt a ghost for an hour. The 100uF capacitor is like a tiny water tank right next to the chip - it smooths out little dips so the LM358 always sees a clean 5V. Check with your fingers: pin 4 should feel cool to ground, pin 8 should be at 5V.
**Step 3 - Build the "halfway point" voltage (2.5V reference).** We need a steady voltage right in the middle between 0V and 5V. We call it VREF. We make it with two resistors and then "clean it up" with the second half of the LM358. - **10K resistor #1**: one leg in the **+5V rail**, the other leg in row **A5**. - **10K resistor #2**: one leg in row **A5**, the other leg in the **GND rail**. - Jumper from **A5** to **A14** - this carries the 2.5V to LM358 pin 5 (the "+" input of the second op-amp half). - Jumper from **B10** to **B14** - this loops the second op-amp's output (pin 7) back to its "-" input (pin 6). That tells the chip "just copy the voltage out". - Jumper from **C13** to **C11** - this is a short jump on the +5V row of pin 8 (used in our layout to neaten the +5V path). - **10uF capacitor**: **long leg** into **D17**, **short leg** into the **GND rail**. Then jumper **D13** to **D17** so the capacitor sits on the VREF output line (pin 7 -> D17). **Why this matters:** the LM358 only runs from one supply (0V to 5V), so it cannot make a real negative voltage. Instead we pretend the middle (2.5V) is our "zero". The two 10K resistors split 5V exactly in half. The op-amp half then acts like a strong helper that holds that 2.5V super steady even when other parts pull on it. The 10uF capacitor is a tiny shock-absorber so VREF does not wiggle.
**Step 4 - Build the light-to-voltage stage.** This is the first half of the LM358 (pins 1, 2, 3). It takes the tiny current from the light sensor and turns it into a voltage we can read. - Jumper from **A11** to **A22**. This carries VREF (2.5V) over to LM358 pin 3 (the "+" input of the first op-amp half). - **47K resistor**: one leg into **A22**, other leg into **A25**. This is the "feedback" resistor that sets how loud the amplifier is. - Jumper from **B12** to **B25**. This connects LM358 pin 1 (the output) over to the far end of the 47K resistor at row 25. - **1uF capacitor**: **long leg** into **E22**, **short leg** into **E25**. This sits across the 47K resistor. **Why this matters:** the chip's "-" input (pin 2, row B12) is the spot we are going to push current into from the light sensor. The 47K resistor and the chip work together as a team: every tiny bit of current we push in makes the output (pin 1) drop a little below 2.5V. More light = more current = lower voltage. The 1uF capacitor calms down any flickery noise so the reading is steady.
**Step 5 - Add the KY-018 light sensor module.** The KY-018 is a small board with a tan-colored "eye" on it (that is the LDR - it changes resistance based on light). It has three pins: **GND**, **+** (which means 5V in), and **S** (the signal pin). Plug the module in along the bottom of the breadboard so its three pins land in column J at rows 2, 3, 4: - **J2 = GND** (the 0V side). - **J3 = +** (power input, 5V). - **J4 = S** (signal - this is the leg of the LDR we want to grab). Now wire it: - Jumper from **F2** to the **GND rail (bottom)** - black wire. - Jumper from **F3** to the **+5V rail (bottom)** - red wire. - Jumper from **F4** all the way over to **F25** (orange wire). That carries the LDR signal to the same row as the end of the 47K resistor and the 1uF cap. - Jumper from **G25** to **G22**. This finishes the path from the LDR right onto LM358 pin 2 (the "-" input). **Why this matters:** the KY-018 normally has its own little brain (a comparator) that just says "bright" or "dark". We are ignoring that brain and tapping straight into the light-sensing part. Because LM358 pin 2 is held at exactly 2.5V by the feedback, there is a steady 2.5V across the LDR. When it gets brighter, the LDR's resistance drops, more current flows, and the op-amp output drops below 2.5V. That difference is what we measure.
**Step 6 - Send the two readings to the Arduino.** Use male-to-male jumpers from the Arduino to the breadboard: - Arduino **A0** -> breadboard **B22** (this reads the light-stage output). - Arduino **A1** -> breadboard **B17** (this reads the steady 2.5V VREF). **Why this matters:** the code reads BOTH pins, then subtracts them. By measuring the difference instead of just the raw number, the meter still works correctly even if the USB voltage drifts a little. This trick is called "ratiometric measurement" - basically a fancy way to cancel out wobble.
**Step 7 - Hook up the OLED screen.** The OLED has 4 pins: **GND**, **VCC (power input)**, **SCL** (the clock line), and **SDA** (the data line). Plug it in along column J at rows 27, 28, 29, 30: - **J27 = GND** - **J28 = VCC** (5V in) - **J29 = SCL** (clock) - **J30 = SDA** (data) Now wire it: - Jumper from **F27** to the **GND rail (bottom)** - black wire. - Jumper from **F28** to the **+5V rail (bottom)** - red wire. - Arduino **A5 (SCL)** -> breadboard **G29**. - Arduino **A4 (SDA)** -> breadboard **G30**. **Why this matters:** the OLED talks to the Arduino over only two wires (SDA and SCL) using a system called I2C. On the Uno, pins A4 and A5 are special - they double as the I2C talk lines. The code will print the light level on the OLED so you do not need a computer to read it.
**Step 8 - Final check before plugging in USB.** - Look at every capacitor: the **short leg** (the one with the white stripe pointing at it) should be on the GND side. If any are backwards, fix them now - putting power through a capacitor backwards can make it pop. - Look at the LM358 notch. It should be on the left side at row 10. If it is flipped, pin numbers are swapped and nothing will work. - Check that both red rails really do have 5V and both blue rails really do have GND. Now plug the USB cable into the Arduino and your laptop. The OLED should light up and start showing a light reading. Wave your hand over the KY-018's tan "eye" - the number should change. If it does not move, gently press on the LM358 to make sure it is fully seated, and double-check the orange wire from the KY-018's S pin all the way to LM358 pin 2. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):** 1. Plug the Uno in once with the USB cable so Windows / macOS sees it. CH340 clones sometimes need a driver - if no COM port shows up, search "CH340 driver" for your OS and install it. 2. Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> **Arduino Uno**. 3. Tools -> Manage Libraries. Search for and install each of these (pick the latest version of each): - **Adafruit SSD1306** (this will offer to also install Adafruit GFX and Adafruit BusIO - say yes to all of them) - **Adafruit GFX Library** (in case it did not get pulled in automatically) 4. The `Wire` library for I2C is already built in - nothing to install for that one. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into the laptop with a USB-A to USB-B cable (the big square plug, same as an old printer). 2. Tools -> Port. Pick the one that says COM* (Windows) or /dev/cu.usbmodem* (Mac) or /dev/ttyACM0 (Linux). If two ports show up, unplug the Uno, see which one disappears, plug it back in - that one is yours. 3. No passwords or WiFi names to fill in for this sketch - it runs purely on the wired sensor. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). The TX / RX LEDs on the Uno will flicker for a couple of seconds. When it says "Done uploading" at the bottom you are good. 5. Tools -> Serial Monitor. Set the baud rate dropdown in the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor to **115200** (must match `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code or you will see garbage characters). 6. What you should see: - The OLED lights up and prints `LM358 Lux Meter` for about a second, then starts showing live numbers. - The Serial Monitor prints a "Boot self-check" block telling you to expect VREF between 2.45 and 2.55 V. - Cup your hand over the KY-018 sensor. The lux number on the OLED should drop close to zero. Point it at a lamp - the number jumps up. That means the whole chain (LDR -> LM358 -> Uno -> OLED) is working. **Common gotchas:** - **OLED stays black.** The SSD1306 module sometimes ships at I2C address `0x3D` instead of `0x3C`. If the Serial Monitor prints `OLED init failed`, edit `#define OLED_ADDR 0x3C` to `0x3D` and re-upload. Also double-check SDA goes to A4 and SCL goes to A5 on the Uno - swapping those two is the #1 reason an OLED looks dead. - **Serial Monitor shows weird symbols like `ÿüÿ`.** The baud rate dropdown is not on 115200. Set it to 115200 and the text becomes readable. - **Cap polarity backwards.** The 100uF, 10uF and 1uF caps are electrolytic - the short leg (and the white stripe on the side) is the negative leg and must go to GND / the lower-voltage side. Putting one in backwards can make it heat up or pop, so check each one before plugging in USB. ## Test procedure (do this before you trust any number) 1. Power the Arduino over USB. Open Serial Monitor at 115200. 2. With a multimeter, probe VREF (LM358 pin 7) against GND. Expected: **2.45 - 2.55 V**. If it is closer to 0 or 5, the divider or the op-amp B feedback wire is wrong. 3. Probe Vout (LM358 pin 1) against GND. With the LDR covered (dark) it should sit very close to VREF, i.e. about 2.5V. Serial should show **dV ~ 0 mV** and **Iph ~ 0 uA**. 4. Uncover the LDR and point it at the room light. dV should go **negative** (a few hundred mV down to maybe -1V), and Iph should rise into the microamp range. The OLED should show a non-zero lux estimate. 5. Shine a phone torch directly onto the LDR. dV should go more negative but **must not pin at -2.5V**. If it pins, your Rf is too big - drop to 22K or 10K. The sketch also flashes `PIN!` on the OLED when it detects this. 6. (Optional) Use a phone lux-meter app to read the room. Adjust `K_LUX_PER_UA` in the sketch until the OLED roughly agrees. ## Talking points - **Transimpedance amplifier (TIA).** A photodiode (or photoconductive LDR) is a *current* device. A TIA forces the sensor to live at a fixed voltage and converts the current into a voltage you can read with an ADC. The gain is just one number: Rf. Bigger Rf, more volts per microamp, but also more noise and slower response - and, as we learned the hard way above, very easy to saturate when the sensor is leakier than you expected. - **Virtual ground.** The op-amp's golden rule (when there is negative feedback) is "the two inputs end up at the same voltage". We pin the non-inverting input at 2.5V, so the inverting input *also* sits at 2.5V even though nothing connects it there directly. That phantom 2.5V is the virtual ground. - **Honest caveat on "bidirectional" current.** The LM358 is famous for poor high-side headroom on a single supply - its output can only swing to about V+ minus 1.5V, i.e. ~3.5V on a 5V rail. With VREF at 2.5V that means we have only ~1V of room above VREF (and ~2.5V below). So while the virtual-ground trick *does* let single-supply chips handle bidirectional current in principle, this specific chip clips the positive direction badly. Use a rail-to-rail op-amp (e.g. MCP6002) if you actually need both directions. In our build the LDR only sinks current, so we only need the downward swing, and the LM358 is fine. - **Feedback capacitor.** Rf alone with the sensor's capacitance forms a phase-shift trap that makes op-amps ring or oscillate. A small Cf across Rf gives the loop a deliberate roll-off and keeps it stable. - **Why subtract VREF in software.** The Arduino's ADC reference drifts with USB voltage. Both VREF and the signal drift together, so dV = Vsig - Vref is immune to that drift. This is ratiometric thinking. ## Things to change once it works - Swap Rf to 100K for a meter that responds more to dim rooms (will pin in direct sunlight). Or drop to 10K-22K for an outdoor / sunlight meter. - Replace the LDR with an actual photodiode (BPW34, or even a salvaged clear LED used in reverse). The TIA circuit does not change at all, only the sensor swaps - and *then* you finally get to use a 1M or 10M Rf the way the textbooks show, because a photodiode passes microamp-scale current rather than the milliamp-ish current an LDR can pass. - Add a calibration mode: point at a known-lux source from a phone app and adjust K_LUX_PER_UA in the sketch. - Add a peak-hold / decay display on the OLED. ## Why this is interesting The transimpedance amplifier is the single most useful op-amp pattern you will ever learn. Every laser-power meter, optical communications receiver, pulse oximeter, and lab photodiode amplifier on Earth is some variant of this exact circuit. Pair it with the virtual-ground trick and you have unlocked single-supply analog design - the foundation for every battery-powered op-amp project on the kit. The "wait, why is my output pinned?" gotcha is also a small but valuable lesson: textbook circuit values assume textbook sensors, and a real part on your bench can be wildly different.

allocations.notes: Reads amplified voltage on A0, VREF on A1, drives OLED over I2C
Connects KY-018 module header and OLED to the breadboard
Power, ground, and signal jumpers on the breadboard
Bulk decoupling on the LM358 V+ pin (pin 8) to GND
Decouples the virtual-ground node so it stays stiff under transients
Feedback cap Cf across Rf - rolls off noise and stops the TIA stage oscillating (a 100nF ceramic from the spares drawer is a cleaner swap if you have one)
Op-amp A is the transimpedance stage; op-amp B is the virtual-ground buffer
Shows VREF, dV in mV, photocurrent in uA, and estimated lux
All wiring done on breadboard, no soldering
Equal pair forming the 2.5V virtual-ground divider
Feedback resistor Rf - sized for the LDR's mA-scale current so the LM358 does NOT saturate in normal room light (~47 mV per uA)
LDR cell used as a light-driven current source into the summing junction (we tap the LDR via the module's VCC and signal pins)

projects.name: LM324 Quad Window Comparator 9V Battery Gauge
projects.power_supply: 9V battery itself - the same battery being measured powers the gauge through a momentary TEST button and a L7805 regulator that creates a stable 5V reference rail.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Hold the button and a row of four LEDs lights up - blue, green, yellow, red - to show how much juice your 9V battery has left. As the battery gets weaker, the lights drop off one by one like a fuel gauge in a car. **Why it's fun**: No code, no screen, no computer brain - just a chip and some parts that magically "decide" things on their own. Test every old battery in the junk drawer and find out which ones still have life left and which ones are dead. A pure-analog, zero-firmware twin of the Pocket Battery Health Monitor - same job (tell me if this 9V battery is still good), no microcontroller, no OLED, no code. Just one quad op-amp doing four comparisons at once and four LEDs that drop off as the battery drains. ## Parts list - 1x LM324 quad op-amp (the brain - four comparators in one package) - 1x L7805 +5V linear regulator (creates a stable reference rail that does NOT sag as the battery drains) - 4x 5mm LEDs: blue, green, yellow, red (one per channel) - 6x 10K 1% resistors (4 for the reference ladder, 2 for the battery divider) - 4x 1K resistors (LED current limiters - 5V/1K = ~3 mA, plenty bright on modern LEDs) - 1x 100uF cap (input bulk smoothing for the 7805) - 1x 10uF cap (output bulk on the 7805 - borderline-OK on its own at this tiny load; in a "real" design you'd add a 0.1uF ceramic alongside) - 1x 1uF cap (sits right by the LM324's V+ pin - keeps it stable) - 1x small tactile push-button (TEST button - holding it powers the circuit so the gauge does not silently drain the very battery it's measuring) - 1x breadboard, jumper wires - 1x 9V battery (the thing being measured AND the power source - that's the fun part) ## Wiring notes This project does not use a computer chip like an Arduino. Instead, it uses a clever helper chip called the LM324 that compares voltages and turns LEDs on. The whole gauge is powered by the same 9V battery it is testing - which sounds silly, but that is exactly how the fuel gauge in a car works. **Quick glossary - words you will see on this build:** - The long red strip down the side of the breadboard is the +5V strip (we will call it the "red power strip"). - The long blue or black strip is the 0V side - ground (we will call it the "ground strip"). - "Long leg" means the positive side of an LED or capacitor. "Short leg" or the side with a white stripe means the negative side. - "LM324" is a chip with 14 legs that has four little comparison helpers inside, called comparators. - "L7805" is a chip with 3 legs that takes the 9V battery in and gives out a steady 5V.
**Step 1 - Push the breadboard down and pick a top and bottom.** Place the breadboard so the row numbers go left to right. The two long strips on the top are one pair (we will call them the "top red strip" and "top ground strip"). The two long strips on the bottom are the other pair (the "bottom red strip" and "bottom ground strip"). We will hook them together later.
**Step 2 - Place the TEST button.** Push the little white tactile push-button into the breadboard so its four legs land at row 2 (it will sit across the middle gap at E2 and F2). This is the button you press to read your battery. The gauge only lights up while you are holding it down, so the 9V battery is not drained when you are not testing. - One leg of the button (F2) gets a black wire that runs to the bottom ground strip. - The other side of the button (E2) is where the plus (+) wire from your 9V battery will land later.
**Step 3 - Add the smoothing capacitor on the raw battery side.** The 100uF capacitor smooths out any bumps in the battery voltage when you press the button. - Long leg (positive) goes into J5. - Short leg / white-stripe side (negative) goes to the bottom ground strip. - Add a red jumper from H4 to J4, and another red jumper from J4 to J5. This carries the 9V from the button over to the capacitor and to the next chip. Why this matters: when you press a button, the voltage can wobble for a tiny moment. A capacitor is like a small bucket of electricity that fills up and keeps the supply steady so the chips do not get confused.
**Step 4 - Place the L7805 voltage helper chip.** The L7805 is a small black chip with 3 legs. Push it in so its 3 legs land at F7, F8, and F9 (the pinout reads IN, GND, OUT from left to right when the writing faces you). It takes the 9V going in and gives back a steady 5V going out. - Leg IN (F7) already has the smoothed 9V coming to it from the capacitor wire. - Leg GND (the middle leg) gets a black wire from F7's neighbor row to the bottom ground strip. (Use the wire described as F7 to GND - that is the middle leg's ground.) - Leg OUT (F8) is the new 5V supply. Run a red wire from F8 to J9 to carry it to a second smoothing capacitor. Why this matters: the LM324 chip and the LEDs work best with a steady 5V. The L7805 gives them that steady 5V even as the 9V battery slowly gets weaker. This steady 5V is the secret to how the gauge can tell a fresh battery from a tired one.
**Step 5 - Add the 5V smoothing capacitor.** This is the 10uF capacitor. - Long leg (positive) goes into J10. - Short leg / white-stripe side (negative) goes to the bottom ground strip. - Add a red wire from J9 to J10 so the capacitor sits across the new 5V supply. - Add a red wire from J9 to the bottom red power strip. Now the bottom red strip is your steady 5V supply. Why this matters: just like Step 3, this capacitor keeps the new 5V smooth when the LEDs flick on and off.
**Step 6 - Place the LM324 chip.** The LM324 is a 14-leg chip. Push it into the middle of the breadboard with leg 1 at row 14 (it will sit across the middle gap from row 14 to row 20, with legs on both sides). The little dot or notch on the chip should point to the left. This chip has four comparators inside - it is the brain of the gauge. - Run a red wire from E17 (leg 4, the chip's power input) to the top red power strip. - Place the 1uF capacitor next: long leg at A17, short leg to the top ground strip. - Connect E17 to A17 with a red wire to tie the capacitor across the chip's power. - Run a black wire from F20 (leg 11, the chip's ground leg) to the bottom ground strip. Why this matters: the small 1uF capacitor sits right next to the chip's power leg and acts like a tiny pillow. Whenever the chip suddenly needs more power, the pillow gives it a quick push so the chip never has to wait. Without it, the chip can act jumpy.
**Step 7 - Build the battery-sense divider (the part that "tastes" the battery).** We need to know how strong the 9V battery is. But the LM324 only works up to 5V, so we cut the battery voltage in half using two 10K resistors stacked on top of each other. - One 10K resistor: legs at B4 and B8. - Another 10K resistor: legs at D4 and D8. - Run a red wire from A4 to the top red power strip side of the button (this carries the raw battery voltage in). - Run a black wire from A8 to the top ground strip. - The point between the two resistors (column C, row 8) is where the "half-battery" voltage sits. Run a yellow wire from C8 to C15. Then jump from C15 to E15 with another yellow wire to feed it into the LM324. Why this matters: a fresh 9V battery will show 4.5V at this point. A tired 6V battery will show 3.0V. A dead 4V battery will show 2.0V. This little number is what the LM324 will compare against the steady references in the next step.
**Step 8 - Build the four-step reference ladder.** This is a stack of four 10K resistors that turns the steady 5V into four "steps" - 4V, 3V, 2V, and 1V. Each step is one of the four thresholds for the four LEDs. - 10K from F22 to F25, and a red wire from F22 to the bottom red power strip. - 10K from G25 to G27. - 10K from H27 to H29. - 10K from J29 to the bottom ground strip, with a black wire from F29 to J29. Now you have four taps: - Top tap (row 22) = 4V (Blue LED's threshold). - Next tap (row 25) = 3V (Green LED's threshold). - Next tap (row 27) = 2V (Yellow LED's threshold). - Bottom tap (row 29) = 1V (Red LED's threshold). Run a yellow wire from F25 to E25 to feed the 3V tap into the LM324's next comparator input. Repeat similar short jumps for the 2V and 1V taps to the matching LM324 input legs. Why this matters: the LM324 cannot guess voltages on its own. It can only compare two voltages and say "the left one is bigger" or "the right one is bigger." We give it four steady reference voltages here so it has something to compare the half-battery to.
**Step 9 - Tie all four sense inputs together.** The half-battery voltage from Step 7 needs to go to all four comparators at once. Use short yellow wires to jump the half-battery line (around row 15) to each of the four "minus" input legs of the LM324. (Look at your layout - the wires from row 15 fan out to rows 16, 18, and 19 with short jumps.) This means all four comparators are watching the same battery, but each one has a different reference to compare it to. That is what makes the gauge climb down one LED at a time as the battery dies.
**Step 10 - Wire up the Blue LED (8V threshold).** This LED lights up when the battery is above 8V (fresh). - Push the Blue LED in with its short leg on the LM324's first output and its long leg into a free row. - Place a 1K resistor between the LED's long leg and the bottom red 5V power strip. The LED only lights when the comparator pulls its short-leg side to 0V (ground), which happens when the half-battery is bigger than 4V. Otherwise it stays dark. Why this matters: the 1K resistor is the LED's "safety brake." LEDs by themselves will pull too much power and burn out. The resistor makes them happy with a small amount.
**Step 11 - Wire up the Green LED (6V threshold).** The Green LED has no photo on file. It looks like a clear or green 5mm bulb with two legs - one long, one short. - Short leg on the LM324's second output. - Long leg through a 1K resistor to the bottom red 5V power strip. This LED lights up when the battery is above 6V. As the battery drains past 6V, this one will turn off. That is your "the battery is getting tired" warning.
**Step 12 - Wire up the Yellow LED (4V threshold).** The Yellow LED has no photo on file. It is a 5mm bulb just like the Green one but yellow. - Short leg on the LM324's third output. - Long leg through a 1K resistor to the bottom red 5V power strip. This LED lights up when the battery is above 4V. When it goes out, the battery is almost dead.
**Step 13 - Wire up the Red LED (always-on sanity check).** - Short leg on the LM324's fourth output. - Long leg through a 1K resistor to the bottom red 5V power strip. The Red LED is supposed to mean "1V threshold," but in real life it will be on any time the circuit has power. So just think of it as: "if the Red LED is on, the gauge itself is working."
**Step 14 - Final connections.** Now hook up the 9V battery. - Plus (+) wire from the battery clip goes to one side of the TEST button (the side opposite the wire that goes to the ground strip). - Minus (-) wire from the battery clip goes to the bottom ground strip. That is it. Press and hold the TEST button. How many LEDs light up tells you how strong your 9V battery is.
**How to read the gauge:** | LEDs lit | What it means | Battery voltage | | --- | --- | --- | | Red + Yellow + Green + Blue | Fresh battery | Above 8V | | Red + Yellow + Green | Good battery | 6V to 8V | | Red + Yellow | Tired battery | 4V to 6V | | Red only | Almost dead | Below 4V | Why the same battery powers the gauge that tests it: this is the trick of the whole project. The L7805 chip takes whatever the battery has and makes a steady 5V for the reference ladder. So the references stay still at 4V, 3V, 2V, 1V no matter what. Meanwhile the half-battery sense moves up and down as the real battery gets weaker. Because one side stays still and the other side moves, the comparators can tell them apart and switch the LEDs off one by one. Cool, right? ## Flash it and run it **The gauge itself has no brain to flash.** Pop a 9V battery in the clip, hold the white TEST button, and the LEDs decide what to show all by themselves. No laptop, no code, no Wi-Fi - the chip just thinks. Let go of the button and everything switches off so the gauge doesn't quietly drink the battery it's measuring. **What you should see:** - Fresh 9V battery (around 9.0 V): all four LEDs lit - blue, green, yellow, red. - A used battery around 7 V: blue drops out, green + yellow + red still on. - A tired battery around 5 V: blue and green both gone, only yellow + red. - A nearly dead battery around 3 V: just red, faintly. - A truly dead battery (under ~2 V): nothing lights up at all - the 7805 needs about 7 V on its input to make a clean 5 V, so down there the whole gauge just gives up. That itself is a "this battery is toast" signal. **Optional: hook up the Arduino sketch to peek inside (only if you want to)** This is for the grown-up who's curious whether the trip points really happen where they should. You only need the Arduino IDE for this part - the gauge does not need it. You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):** 1. Tools -> Board -> "Arduino Uno". 2. No extra libraries needed - this sketch only uses `analogRead` and `Serial`, both built in. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into the laptop with a USB-B cable (the big square-ish plug). 2. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that says COM* (Windows) or cu.usbmodem* (Mac) or ttyACM0 (Linux). If you're not sure which is the Uno, unplug it, look at the list, plug it back in, and grab the new entry. 3. No passwords or Wi-Fi settings to fill in - this sketch is plain offline logging. 4. Wire the helper: **one** jumper from the gauge's VSENSE node (the midpoint of the 10K / 10K battery divider) into Uno **A0**, and **one** jumper from gauge GND to Uno GND. That's it - two wires. Do NOT build another 10K/10K divider on the Uno side, and do NOT tap the raw 9V rail into A0 (you'd fry the Uno's input). 5. Click Upload (the right-arrow icon at the top). 6. Tools -> Serial Monitor, set the baud dropdown in the bottom-right to **115200**. 7. Hold the TEST button on the gauge. You should see lines like `V_batt = 8.73 V [ BLU GRN YEL --- ]` ticking past twice a second. Compare the letters in the brackets to which LEDs are actually lit on the breadboard - they should agree. **Common gotchas:** - **Capacitor polarity backwards.** The 100uF, 10uF, and 1uF are all electrolytic - they have a + leg (longer) and a - leg (shorter, marked with a white stripe on the can). Backwards = pop, smoke, sad day. The + leg goes toward the higher-voltage side (battery+ on the 100uF, 5V rail on the 10uF and 1uF). - **LED in backwards = no light, no damage.** Long leg (anode) goes to the LM324 output side through the 1K resistor; short leg (cathode, flat spot on the rim) goes to +5V. If a channel stays dark when it should be on, flip that LED. - **Forgetting to share grounds with the Uno.** If you only run the VSENSE wire to A0 without also tying gauge GND to Uno GND, A0 will read garbage - bouncing numbers that don't match the LEDs. Two wires, not one. - **Serial Monitor at the wrong baud.** The sketch prints at 115200. If the Monitor is set to 9600 (the default) you'll just see gibberish like `⸮⸮p⸮⸮` - change the dropdown, don't re-flash. ## Talking points - **Open-loop op-amp = comparator.** Op-amps are normally used WITH feedback (input to output through a resistor) to make stable amplifiers. With no feedback they have wild gain (~100,000x) and slam the output to one rail or the other based on which input is higher. That "slamming" is exactly what a comparator does. There's a real dedicated comparator IC (LM339) sitting in the same parts drawer - the LM324 is a slightly-slower, dual-purpose stand-in here, picked because it's already in the bin. - **Why four channels?** One LM324 chip contains four independent op-amps. They share power pins (4 and 11) but their inputs and outputs are otherwise separate. So one chip = four comparators = a bar-graph display, all for the price of one IC. - **Why a separate reference rail?** Already covered above, but worth saying out loud: if the reference scaled with the battery, nothing would ever trip. The L7805 is the load-bearing part that makes the whole circuit MEAN something. - **Why tie all four - inputs together?** All four comparators are watching the same battery. Only the + reference differs per channel. That's the "quad window" idea: four windows looking at one signal at four different heights. - **Why is the LED on the cathode side?** When the LM324 output goes LOW it can SINK current to ground much more cleanly than it can SOURCE to V+. LM324 outputs can swing to within a few hundred millivolts of GND but only to about 1.5 V below V+. Sinking through the LED + 1K to +5V is the clean choice - and it's exactly the gotcha that trips up everyone the first time they see a comparator drive a load. - **Why uniform 1V steps and not "nicely tuned" trip points?** Honest answer: four 10K resistors between 5V and GND can only give 1.00 V steps. To get e.g. 4.25 / 3.75 / 3.25 / 2.75 V you'd need different resistor values in the ladder. The uniform ladder is the "use what's in the drawer" answer; once it works, you can swap values for finer resolution near 7-8 V where a 9V battery actually lives. ## Things to change once it works - **Move the thresholds where they matter.** A 9V alkaline is interesting between 6.5 V and 9.5 V. Bunching the four trip points there is the obvious upgrade: replace the uniform ladder with non-uniform values (e.g. 1.5K / 2.2K / 2.2K / 4.7K from the inventory) so taps land near 4.25 / 3.75 / 3.25 / 2.75 V on the reference side = 8.5 / 7.5 / 6.5 / 5.5 V on the battery side. Same circuit, just better-tuned divider math. - **Add hysteresis.** Tie a 1M resistor from each output back to its + input. Now the threshold "snaps" up slightly after the LED turns off, so a flickering battery doesn't make the LED flicker. Same trick a thermostat uses to keep from cycling near the setpoint. - **Use the dedicated comparator (LM339 / LM393).** They have open-collector outputs which need a pull-up but switch faster and cleaner than an LM324 used open-loop. Drop-in for a v2. - **Monitor a different battery.** Want to check a 12 V SLA? Change the battery divider from 10K/10K to 10K/4.7K, leave everything else alone - now the trip points are at 14.6 / 11.0 / 7.3 / 3.7 V on the battery side. - **Solder it onto a prototype PCB** with a 9V battery clip - now it's a permanent gadget you can clip onto any 9V battery in the drawer to see which ones are still good. ## Why this is interesting This is a finished, useful tool by the end of an afternoon: clip it onto any 9V battery and you can tell at a glance whether it's fresh, half-used, or trash. ZERO microcontrollers, ZERO code, one IC quietly doing the job of four. Understanding why the LM324 has four op-amps in it (and what to do with all of them) is the foot in the door for every analog circuit you'll ever build: filters, oscillators, sensor front-ends, audio mixers. They all stack op-amp stages exactly like this. Bonus: building this teaches the most counter-intuitive trick in beginner electronics - "the LED lights when the output goes LOW" - which trips everyone up the first time and never again after.
projects.wiring_diagram:
flowchart TD
    BATT["9V Battery (+)"]:::pwr
    GND["9V Battery (-) / GND"]:::gnd
    BTN["TEST push-button (momentary)"]:::mod

    BATT --> BTN
    BTN --> V9["Raw 9V rail (after TEST button)"]:::pwr

    C100["100uF cap (input bulk)"]:::res
    V9 --- C100
    C100 --- GND

    REG["L7805 IN"]:::mod
    V9 --> REG
    REGOUT["L7805 OUT = +5.00V reference rail"]:::pwr
    REG --> REGOUT
    REGGND["L7805 GND"]:::gnd
    REG --- REGGND
    REGGND --- GND

    C10["10uF cap (output bulk on +5V)"]:::res
    REGOUT --- C10
    C10 --- GND

    %% LM324 power: V+ tied to the +5V rail (not raw 9V) so the
    %% output swing and the LED anode rail share one reference.
    LM["LM324 V+ pin 4 (+5V)"]:::pin
    REGOUT --> LM
    LMGND["LM324 V- pin 11"]:::gnd
    LMGND --- GND
    C1["1uF bypass cap (LM324 V+ to GND)"]:::res
    LM --- C1
    C1 --- GND

    %% Battery sense divider: 10K/10K from raw 9V rail to GND.
    %% Midpoint = V_batt / 2. No extra "bias keeper" resistor -
    %% adding one would just upset the 1:2 ratio.
    RBATT_TOP["10K (top of batt divider)"]:::res
    RBATT_BOT["10K (bottom of batt divider)"]:::res
    V9 --> RBATT_TOP
    RBATT_TOP --> VSENSE["V_batt / 2 sense node"]:::sensor
    VSENSE --> RBATT_BOT
    RBATT_BOT --> GND

    %% Reference ladder: 4x 10K in series between +5V and GND.
    %% Uniform 10K resistors only give uniform 1.00V steps from a
    %% 5.00V rail, so taps land at 4.00 / 3.00 / 2.00 / 1.00 V.
    %% Trip points on the battery side: 8.0 / 6.0 / 4.0 / 2.0 V.
    RREF1["10K ref-R #1 (top)"]:::res
    RREF2["10K ref-R #2"]:::res
    RREF3["10K ref-R #3"]:::res
    RREF4["10K ref-R #4 (bottom)"]:::res

    REGOUT --> RREF1
    RREF1 --> TAPBLUE["Tap 4.00V (Blue threshold, V_batt 8.0V)"]:::sensor
    TAPBLUE --> RREF2
    RREF2 --> TAPGREEN["Tap 3.00V (Green threshold, V_batt 6.0V)"]:::sensor
    TAPGREEN --> RREF3
    RREF3 --> TAPYELLOW["Tap 2.00V (Yellow threshold, V_batt 4.0V)"]:::sensor
    TAPYELLOW --> RREF4
    RREF4 --> TAPRED["Tap 1.00V (Red threshold, V_batt 2.0V)"]:::sensor
    TAPRED --> GND

    %% Op-amp 1 (Blue - highest threshold)
    OP1P["LM324 pin 3 (+in, op1)"]:::pin
    OP1N["LM324 pin 2 (-in, op1)"]:::pin
    OP1O["LM324 pin 1 (out, op1)"]:::pin
    TAPBLUE --> OP1P
    VSENSE --> OP1N

    %% Op-amp 2 (Green)
    OP2P["LM324 pin 5 (+in, op2)"]:::pin
    OP2N["LM324 pin 6 (-in, op2)"]:::pin
    OP2O["LM324 pin 7 (out, op2)"]:::pin
    TAPGREEN --> OP2P
    VSENSE --> OP2N

    %% Op-amp 3 (Yellow)
    OP3P["LM324 pin 10 (+in, op3)"]:::pin
    OP3N["LM324 pin 9 (-in, op3)"]:::pin
    OP3O["LM324 pin 8 (out, op3)"]:::pin
    TAPYELLOW --> OP3P
    VSENSE --> OP3N

    %% Op-amp 4 (Red - lowest threshold, effectively always on
    %% while the circuit has power: "sanity LED")
    OP4P["LM324 pin 12 (+in, op4)"]:::pin
    OP4N["LM324 pin 13 (-in, op4)"]:::pin
    OP4O["LM324 pin 14 (out, op4)"]:::pin
    TAPRED --> OP4P
    VSENSE --> OP4N

    %% LED drive: anode through 1K to +5V, cathode to op-amp output.
    %% LED lights when op-amp output goes LOW (sense > threshold).
    R_BLUE["1K"]:::res
    LED_BLUE["Blue LED"]:::out
    REGOUT --> R_BLUE
    R_BLUE --> LED_BLUE
    LED_BLUE --> OP1O

    R_GREEN["1K"]:::res
    LED_GREEN["Green LED"]:::out
    REGOUT --> R_GREEN
    R_GREEN --> LED_GREEN
    LED_GREEN --> OP2O

    R_YELLOW["1K"]:::res
    LED_YELLOW["Yellow LED"]:::out
    REGOUT --> R_YELLOW
    R_YELLOW --> LED_YELLOW
    LED_YELLOW --> OP3O

    R_RED["1K"]:::res
    LED_RED["Red LED"]:::out
    REGOUT --> R_RED
    R_RED --> LED_RED
    LED_RED --> OP4O

    classDef gnd fill:#333,color:#fff,stroke:#000
    classDef sensor fill:#dbeafe,stroke:#1e40af,color:#1e3a8a
    classDef out fill:#fee2e2,stroke:#b91c1c,color:#7f1d1d
