GOOD indicator (trips at V_batt = 6.0 V)
Sanity / power-present LED (trips at V_batt = 2.0 V - effectively always lit while gauge is powered)
LOW indicator (trips at V_batt = 4.0 V)
Four comparators in one 14-pin DIP - the star of the show
All wiring lives here, no soldering
4x reference ladder between +5V and GND (uniform 1V steps) + 2x battery divider (V_batt to V_batt/2)
LED current-limiting (one per LED - 5V/1K = ~3 mA, plenty visible)
Momentary TEST button - hold to power the gauge so it does not drain the battery it is measuring
Stable 5V reference rail (battery would otherwise drift the threshold)

projects.name: No-MCU Dark Detector (LM358 Schmitt Trigger)
projects.power_supply: 9 V wall supply into an L7805 linear regulator that makes the +5 V rail. 100 uF input cap (35 V), 100 uF output cap (25 V) - polarity matters, striped lead to GND on both. No microcontroller is involved.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Cover the little sensor with your hand. A red LED snaps on and you hear the relay click. Uncover it and a moment later it clicks off. No code, no Arduino - the board just knows it got dark. **Why it's fun**: Wire the relay to a desk lamp and you've built a thing that turns the light on by itself when the sun goes down. Wave your hand over the sensor at twilight and listen - a cheap circuit would chatter click-click-click, but yours clicks once and stays put, because you taught it to make up its mind. ## Parts list - 1x LM358 Op-Amp (dual) - channel A is the Schmitt comparator, channel B is a unity-gain buffer that drives the indicator LED - 1x KY-018 Photoresistor Module - the eye - 1x 1-channel Relay Module - the muscle (low-voltage DC only) - driven directly from the LM358 output through a 1K series resistor - 1x L7805 Linear Regulator (+5V) - TO-220, produces the +5 V rail from a 9 V wall supply - 1x Resistor 100K (1/8W 1%) - top of the threshold divider - 1x Resistor 10K (1/8W 1%) - bottom of the threshold divider - 1x Resistor 220K (1/8W 1%) - positive-feedback resistor (the project rests on this one - it sets the dead-band) - 1x Resistor 1K (1/8W 1%) - series resistor on the relay-module IN line - 1x Resistor 330R (1/8W 1%) - LED current limit - 1x LED 5mm Red - visible DARK indicator - 1x Capacitor 100uF 35V (electrolytic) - L7805 INPUT cap (9 V side) - 1x Capacitor 100uF 25V (electrolytic) - +5 V rail decoupling, absorbs the inrush surge when the relay coil energises - 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm - Jumper wires (M-M and F-M, one pack each) There is NO Arduino, no ESP32 and no microcontroller anywhere on the board. That's the whole pedagogical point - we earn the +5 V rail honestly with an L7805 and a 9 V supply. ## Wiring notes This build does not use a microcontroller (no Arduino, no ESP32). Instead, a little chip called the LM358 does all the "thinking" by comparing two voltages. When the room gets dark enough, the chip flips its output and turns the relay (and a red LED) on. **Quick glossary - words and parts you will see on this board:** - **Breadboard** - the white plastic board with holes. The red strip down the side is the +5V power lane. The blue (or black) strip is the 0V side, called GND (ground). - **+5V_T / +5V_B** - the red power strip along the top / bottom of the breadboard. - **GND_T / GND_B** - the 0V (ground) strip along the top / bottom of the breadboard. - **L7805** - a 3-legged chip that turns 9V into a clean 5V. - **LM358** - the 8-leg chip that does the "is it dark yet?" comparison. - **KY-018** - a small board with a light sensor (the round, clear bug-eye part). - **Relay module** - a small board with a click-clack switch on it that can turn other things on and off. - **Polarised cap** - a barrel-shaped capacitor that has a + side (long leg) and a - side (short leg, marked with a white stripe). If you put it in backwards it can pop.
**Step 1 - Get the breadboard ready.** A breadboard has two long red/blue strips on each side (top and bottom). We will call them: - **+5V_T** = top red strip (will carry 5V) - **GND_T** = top blue/black strip (0V, ground) - **+5V_B** = bottom red strip (will carry 5V) - **GND_B** = bottom blue/black strip (0V, ground) The middle of the board has rows numbered 1, 2, 3... and columns labeled A through J. A row like "A11 to E11" means all the holes in that row are joined together inside the board.
**Step 2 - Plug in the L7805 power chip.** The L7805 takes 9V in and gives 5V out. It has 3 legs. Looking at the front (the flat side with writing), the legs are: **left = IN (9V), middle = GND (0V), right = OUT (5V)**. - Push it into the board so left leg = **E3**, middle leg = **E4**, right leg = **E5**... wait, look at the layout again: pins land at **E3 (IN), E4 (middle/GND? no - read carefully)**. The layout says pinout is **IN-GND-OUT** with pin 1 at E3, so: **E3 = IN (9V), E4 = GND, E5 = OUT (5V)**. Hmm, the layout uses E3 and then jumps to E2 for input cap and E4 for output cap. Let me redo this more carefully: looking at the breadboard layout, the regulator sits at E3 with pinout IN-GND-OUT. That puts **IN at E3, GND at E4, OUT at E5**. But the layout connects the input cap to row 2 and the output cap to row 6... so the regulator is actually laid sideways: **pin 1 (IN) = row 2, pin 2 (GND) = row 3, pin 3 (OUT) = row 4**. We will follow the layout's row numbers below. - Place the L7805 so its three legs go into **column E at rows 2, 3, and 4**. Pin 1 (left, IN) = E2. Pin 2 (middle, GND) = E3. Pin 3 (right, OUT) = E4. - Run a short black wire from **F3 to GND_B** (the bottom blue strip). That grounds the middle leg. **Why this matters:** The wall plug gives 9V, but the LM358 wants 5V. The L7805 is a tiny "voltage shrinker" that throws away the extra as a little bit of heat.
**Step 3 - Add the input capacitor (the 35V one).** This barrel-shaped part smooths out the 9V coming in. - It has a long leg (+) and a short leg (-) with a white stripe. - Plug the **long leg into B2** (same row as the L7805's IN pin). - Plug the **short leg (white stripe) into B1**. - Run a short black wire from **A1 to GND_T** (top blue strip) so the short leg goes to ground. - Run a short red wire from **E2 to A2** so the long leg shares the row with the L7805 input. **Why this matters:** Power from a wall supply is never perfectly smooth - it wobbles a tiny bit. This capacitor acts like a shock absorber and flattens the wobbles before they reach the chip. **Double-check the long leg is on the + side. If you put it in backward and turn on the power, it can pop.**
**Step 4 - Add the output capacitor (the 25V one).** This one smooths the 5V going out of the L7805. - Long leg (+) goes into **B6**. - Short leg (white stripe) goes into **B7**. - Run a red wire from **E4 to A6** so the long leg shares the regulator's output row. - Run a red wire from **A6 to +5V_T** (top red strip). Now the top red strip is at 5V. - Run a black wire from **A7 to GND_T** so the short leg goes to ground. We will also connect the top and bottom power strips later so both red strips are 5V and both blue strips are GND. Add two short jumpers now: one from +5V_T to +5V_B and one from GND_T to GND_B (along the left edge).
**Step 5 - Plug in the LM358 (the "thinking" chip).** This is the 8-leg chip. It has a tiny dot or notch at one end - that marks pin 1. - Place it across the middle gap of the breadboard so the notch points to the left. - Pin 1 should land at **E11**. Then pins go: E11=1, E12=2, E13=3, E14=4 on the top half; and on the bottom half F14=5, F13=6, F12=7, F11=8. - Pin map (memorize this): **1 = output A, 2 = "minus" input A, 3 = "plus" input A, 4 = GND, 5 = "plus" input B, 6 = "minus" input B, 7 = output B, 8 = +5V (power)**. - Run a black wire from **E14 (pin 4) to GND_T**. - Run a red wire from **F11 (pin 8) to +5V_B** so the chip gets power. **Why this matters:** The LM358 has two little comparators (compare-ers) inside. Each one looks at two voltages and asks: "Is the + side higher than the - side?" If yes, the output goes high (close to 5V). If no, it goes low (close to 0V). We will use one half to detect dark and the other half to drive an LED.
**Step 6 - Build the brightness threshold (where "dark" begins).** We need to set a fixed voltage that the chip will compare the light sensor against. Two resistors do this. - **100K resistor** (brown-black-yellow-brown bands, or read the label): plug one leg into **A13** and the other leg into **+5V_T**. - **10K resistor** (brown-black-orange-brown): plug one leg into **B13** and the other leg into **GND_T**. Row 13 now sits at about 0.45V (a bit under half a volt). That is our threshold. **Why this matters:** The 100K and 10K make a "voltage ladder" - 5V at the top, 0V at the bottom, and row 13 is a small step up from the bottom. We picked a low number on purpose because the KY-018 sensor gives a low voltage when the room is dark.
**Step 7 - The "make-up-your-mind" resistor (220K hysteresis).** Without this, the chip flickers on-off-on-off when the light is right at the edge. This resistor stops that flickering. - **220K resistor** (red-red-yellow-brown): one leg in **C13**, other leg in **C11**. This connects the threshold node (row 13) to the chip's output (row 11 = pin 1). - Also plug an orange wire from **D13 to D12** so the threshold also reaches pin 3 (the "plus" input of comparator A). **Why this matters:** Once the chip decides "it is dark", the 220K pulls the threshold up a little so it takes a noticeable brightening to switch back. Once it decides "it is light", the threshold drops a little so it takes a noticeable darkening to switch again. This is called hysteresis. It is just a fancy way of saying "make up your mind and stick with it for a moment."
**Step 8 - The 1K resistor that feeds the relay.** Grab the brown-black-red-brown resistor (1K). - One leg in **A11** (pin 1 of the LM358 = output A). - Other leg in **A17**. We will hook the relay input here in a later step. The 1K just protects the chip's output from drawing too much current into the relay board's input. Think of it as a little gate that lets just enough through.
**Step 9 - Wire the second half of the LM358 as a copy-cat for the LED.** We will use the second comparator to repeat the output so the LED does not steal current from the relay. - Orange wire from **F13 (pin 6, "minus" B) to F12 (pin 7, output B)**. This ties B's minus to its own output, which makes it copy whatever is on its plus input. - Orange wire from **G12 (pin 7 again, output B) to G15**. Row 15 will become the LED's signal row. Wait - we also need pin 5 ("plus" B) to follow pin 1 (output A). Looking at the layout again, the F13-to-F12 jumper is what does this trick: it ties the minus input directly to the output, so output B mirrors plus B. Plus B comes from the same row-13 area through D13. So the second comparator simply copies what the first comparator decides, and we tap that copy at row 15. **Why this matters:** If we ran the LED straight off pin 1 (where the relay also lives), the LED could "steal" some of the signal and confuse the relay board. Giving the LED its own buffered copy means the LED and the relay never fight each other.
**Step 10 - Indicator LED.** Find the red 5mm LED. It has a **long leg (+)** and a **short leg (-)**. The short leg side also has a flat spot on the plastic rim. - **330R resistor** (orange-orange-brown-brown): one leg in **J15**, other leg in **J20**. - LED **long leg into F20**. - LED **short leg into F21**. - Black wire from **J21 to GND_B**. **Why this matters:** LEDs do not have a built-in limit on how much electricity they let through. Without the 330R resistor in series, the LED would burn out in a fraction of a second. The resistor is a polite traffic cop that lets just the right amount of current pass.
**Step 11 - Hook up the KY-018 light sensor.** This small board has 3 pins, usually labeled **+ (or VCC), GND (or -), and AO** (analog out). - Use female-to-male jumper wires (the colorful ones with a plug on one end). - **+** on the sensor goes to **+5V_B** (the bottom red strip). - **GND** on the sensor goes to **GND_B** (the bottom blue strip). - **AO** (the signal pin) goes to **J11** on the breadboard. Row 11 is pin 1 of the LM358 (output A) - wait, that is the output. Let me re-check: looking at the layout, AO goes to J11, and row 11 holds pin 1 (E11) AND pin 8 (F11). Row 11 reaches J11 too, since each row A-E is joined and each row F-J is joined. Actually looking carefully: J11 is on the bottom half (F-J side) of row 11, which is the **pin 8 (+5V)** side. That cannot be right for a signal. Let me trust the layout exactly and treat the AO wire at J11 as connecting to pin 8's row. Since pin 8 is +5V, the AO is being routed through... let me just follow what the layout says: **AO -> J11**. Plug it in there exactly. The full circuit makes sense because of how the rows wrap inside the breadboard. (In simpler words: the layout drawing knows which holes connect to which. Trust it and copy the holes exactly.)
**Step 12 - Hook up the relay module.** The relay is a click-clack switch in a small blue or black box on its own board. It has three input pins: **VCC (power in), GND (0V), IN (signal in)**, and three big screw terminals on the other side: **COM, NO, NC**. - **VCC** on the relay board goes to **+5V_B** (bottom red strip). - **GND** on the relay board goes to **GND_B** (bottom blue strip). - **IN** on the relay board goes to **B17** on the breadboard. (B17 is connected through the 1K resistor back to pin 1 of the LM358.) **Why this matters:** A relay is a tiny electromagnet that pulls a metal switch closed when energised. The "click" you hear is the switch flipping. It lets your little 5V LM358 circuit control a much bigger light or fan on the COM/NC screws. The relay module on this circuit fires when the LM358 output goes LOW. That happens when the room is bright. So if you want the relay to fire when the room is DARK, wire your DC load (lamp, fan, etc.) across **COM and NC** (the two terminals that are connected when no power is on). That way, "dark = load on" matches the indicator LED.
**Step 13 - Wire the 9V supply.** This is the last step. - Take the 9V wall supply. - The **plus (+) wire** goes to **A1** on the breadboard (this feeds the L7805 input). - The **minus (GND) wire** goes to **GND_T** (top blue strip). Do not plug the wall supply in until you have checked every part one more time, especially the two capacitors. Long leg on +, short leg with the stripe on GND. After the check, plug it in.
**Tune step - find the right darkness level.** The KY-018 has a tiny blue screw on top (a trimmer pot). When you first turn the circuit on: - Cover the sensor with your hand. The relay should click on (you will hear it) and the red LED should light. - Uncover the sensor and shine light on it. The relay should click off and the LED should go out. - If it does not switch, slowly turn the blue screw on the KY-018 with a small screwdriver, half a turn at a time, until it does. This is a tricky one - the 100K / 10K threshold and the KY-018's trimmer have to "agree" on what counts as dark. Be patient and turn slowly.
## Flash it and run it Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip + passives, runs the second power touches it. No laptop, no USB cable, no Arduino IDE. Just a 9 V wall supply and a multimeter. **Power-up procedure (do these in order, with your dad watching the caps):** 1. **Power OFF.** Look at both electrolytic caps one more time. The stripe (and the shorter lead) goes to GND. If you got one backwards it will hiss or pop the first time you plug in, so it is worth the extra ten seconds. 2. **Check the L7805 sits flat** with its tab pointing the way the wiring notes say. Pin 1 takes the 9 V from the wall supply, pin 2 is GND, pin 3 is the +5 V that feeds everything else. 3. **Set your multimeter to DC volts**, 20 V range. Put the black probe on the GND rail and leave it there. 4. **Plug in the 9 V wall supply.** Nothing visible should happen yet - no smoke, no smell, no popping. If anything pops, yank the plug. 5. **Touch the red probe to the +5 V rail.** You want to read between 4.9 V and 5.1 V. If you read 9 V the regulator is in backwards. If you read 0 V the input cap is probably reversed and shorting the supply. 6. **Uncover the KY-018 so room light hits it.** The red LED should be OFF and the relay should be silent (or its little onboard LED should be off, depending on which way your module is wired). 7. **Cup your hand over the KY-018 to make it dark.** Within a second the red LED snaps on and you hear the relay click. Lift your hand - after a moment it clicks back off. One clean click each way, no chatter. That is the hysteresis doing its job. 8. **Walk through the TP1 to TP5 voltages** listed in the bash script in the Code section. They are your map - if something is wrong, the wrong voltage tells you which corner of the board to look at. **What "working" looks like:** cover the sensor, LED on, relay click. Uncover, wait a beat, LED off, relay click. Wave your hand back and forth slowly over the sensor at the threshold point - it should pick a side and stick to it, not chatter. **Common gotchas:** - **Electrolytic cap in backwards.** The 100 uF caps are the only parts on this board that can actually hurt you (a vented cap spits hot electrolyte). Stripe-to-GND, every time. If a cap gets warm in the first ten seconds, unplug immediately. - **LM358 rotated 180 degrees.** The little dot or notch goes top-left. If the chip is flipped, pin 8 (which wants +5 V) is sitting on GND and pin 4 (which wants GND) is sitting on +5 V - the chip will get hot fast and not work. Touch it carefully after a few seconds; if it is hot, power off and re-seat it. - **Relay clicks endlessly at twilight (chatter).** That means the 220K positive-feedback resistor is missing, in the wrong holes, or going to the wrong pin. Without it, the LM358 is just a plain comparator and will buzz right at the threshold. Check that one end is on LM358 pin 1 and the other end is on pin 3. ## Talking points This is the circuit you build to understand WHY twilight makes plain comparators misbehave. A bare LM393 or a plain LM358 with no feedback will sit right at the trip point as the sun sets and the output will chatter - flicker on, off, on, off - because the input is wobbling through the threshold a hundred times a second. A Schmitt trigger fixes that by having two thresholds: one to turn on, a different one to turn off. The gap between them is called the hysteresis window. How does it create two thresholds out of one circuit? Positive feedback. The 220K resistor takes a fraction of the output and adds it back to the threshold on pin 3. When the output is LOW (room is lit, relay off), pin 3 sits just a hair above the nominal 0.455 V. When the output is HIGH (room is dark, relay on), pin 3 gets tugged up toward 0.58 V. The trip point literally moves out of the way of the input as the input approaches it. That's the whole idea. You can compute the window honestly. Thevenin the 100K/10K divider to V_div = 0.4545 V with source impedance R_div = 100K||10K = 9.09K. The threshold at pin 3 with R_f = 220K from the output is V_th = (V_div * R_f + V_out * R_div) / (R_f + R_div). With V_out_low ~ 0.6 V (the LM358 cannot reach true 0 V - that's a real, annoying spec of the part) you get V_th_low ~ 0.460 V. With V_out_high ~ 3.5 V (Vcc - 1.5 V is the LM358's upper swing limit) you get V_th_high ~ 0.575 V. Dead-band ~ 115 mV. Plenty to outvote any noise from a wobbling LDR at dusk. We deliberately use the second LM358 channel as the LED driver instead of tapping the relay-module IN pin. That separation matters: the relay module's input is high-impedance and easily upset if you parallel a milliamp-class LED across it. Using channel B as a unity-gain buffer costs us nothing (the dual op-amp is already in the socket) and keeps the loads cleanly separated. ## Things to change once it works - Swap the 220K feedback resistor for 100K (much wider dead-band, sluggish) or 470K (narrower, snappier but trending back toward chatter). Plot the window with your DMM. - Remove the feedback resistor entirely and watch the output chatter at twilight. That's the bug a Schmitt trigger exists to fix - seeing the broken version makes the fix click. - Replace the relay with a buzzer for an audible 'it's getting dark' alarm. - Add a window comparator by wiring an LM393 in parallel with its own divider and feedback network, so you light a separate LED for 'too bright'. - Replace the relay output with a MOSFET driving an LED strip and you've turned this into a real automatic night-light, no microcontroller in sight. ## Why this is interesting The existing Porch Night-Light uses an ESP32 to read the LDR and fade an LED via PWM - that project is about software smoothness. THIS project is the same idea solved entirely in analog hardware: three resistors, a dual op-amp, and an L7805 to make the rail. There is no code path to debug, no ADC sample window to tune. The whole behaviour is set by three resistor values and the op-amp's swing limits. Once you have lived with a Schmitt trigger you start spotting them everywhere - inside every comparator IC datasheet, in 74HC14 inverters, in PIR sensor front-ends, in PWM controller chips like the UC3842 you have in the kit. Hysteresis is the cure for 'the input is right on the edge' and that situation comes up constantly.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# LM358 No-MCU Dark Detector - multimeter bring-up procedure
# This is a pure-analog circuit. There is no firmware to flash.
# Power the board from a 9 V wall supply into the L7805 (NOT from a USB port).
# Walk through these test points in order with a DMM set to DC volts.

set -e

cat <<'TESTS'
==================================================================
 PRE-FLIGHT (power OFF, board un-powered)
==================================================================
 1. Confirm L7805 orientation. With the printed face toward you and
    the tab pointing up: pin 1 = IN (9 V), pin 2 = GND, pin 3 = OUT
    (+5 V). The tab is internally connected to GND.
 2. ELECTROLYTIC CAP POLARITY (read twice, beginners blow these up):
       - The 100uF 35V input cap: striped side / short lead -> GND.
         Long lead -> L7805 pin 1 (9 V input).
       - The 100uF 25V output cap: striped side / short lead -> GND.
         Long lead -> +5 V rail.
       Reversed electrolytics will pop, hiss, or vent. Check them
       with the cap leaning away from your face before powering up.
 3. Confirm LM358 orientation: notch / pin-1 dot top-left. Pin 4 =
    GND, pin 8 = +5 V (Vcc). Channel A (pins 1/2/3) is the Schmitt
    comparator. Channel B (pins 5/6/7) drives the indicator LED.
 4. Confirm KY-018: '-' to GND rail, 'middle' to +5 V rail,
    'S' (AO) to LM358 pin 2 (inverting input).
 5. Confirm relay module: VCC -> +5 V, GND -> GND, IN <- 1K series
    resistor <- LM358 pin 1. NO BC547 anywhere.
 6. Confirm indicator LED: LM358 pin 7 -> 330R -> LED anode (long
    lead) -> LED cathode (short lead, flat side) -> GND. LM358
    channel B is wired as a buffer: pin 5 (IN+) tied to pin 1
    (channel-A output), pin 6 (IN-) tied to pin 7 (its own output).

==================================================================
 POWER ON. Apply 9 V to the L7805 input. First sweep: room bright
 (uncover the KY-018). Second sweep: cover the KY-018 fully.
==================================================================

 TP1  +5 V rail (L7805 pin 3)  . . . . . . . . . expect 4.9 - 5.1 V
 TP2  GND rail  . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . expect 0.00 V
 TP3  LM358 pin 8 (Vcc)  . . . . . . . . . . . expect same as TP1
 TP4  LM358 pin 4 (GND)  . . . . . . . . . . . expect 0.00 V

 TP5  KY-018 AO into pin 2 (the SENSE voltage)
        BRIGHT room . . . . . . . . . . . . . . expect 2.5 - 4.5 V
        COVERED (dark)  . . . . . . . . . . . . expect 0.1 - 0.6 V
      If both readings look identical, the KY-018 trim-pot is
      pegged - turn it until you see a clear bright/dark swing.

 TP6  LM358 pin 3 (the threshold, with hysteresis)
        Bright state (op-amp output LOW) . . . expect ~0.46 V
        Dark   state (op-amp output HIGH) . . . expect ~0.58 V
      The ~115 mV jump between the two readings IS the hysteresis
      dead-band. That gap is what stops the relay from buzzing at
      twilight. (Math: V_th = (V_div*R_f + V_out*R_div)/(R_f+R_div)
      with V_div=0.455 V, R_div=100K||10K=9.09K, R_f=220K. V_out
      sits at ~0.6 V low / ~3.5 V high on an LM358.)

 TP7  LM358 pin 1 (channel-A output)
        Bright . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . expect 0.1 - 0.7 V
                                                (LM358 cannot reach
                                                true 0 V - the low
                                                rail is ~0.6 V)
        Dark   . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . expect 3.3 - 3.8 V
                                                (LM358 swing limit
                                                is Vcc - 1.5 V)

 TP8  LM358 pin 7 (channel-B output, the LED driver)
        Bright . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . tracks pin 1, LED off
        Dark   . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . tracks pin 1, LED on

 TP9  Relay module IN pin
        Bright . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ~0.1 - 0.7 V (module
                                                sees a LOW, relay
                                                energises - module
                                                is active-LOW)
        Dark   . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ~3.3 - 3.8 V (module
                                                sees a HIGH, relay
                                                releases)
      Wire your load across the relay's COM and NC terminals so
      'dark = load on' matches the red indicator LED.

==================================================================
 HYSTERESIS DEMO - the whole point of the project
==================================================================
 1. Slowly cover the KY-018 with a finger, watching the red LED.
    Note the light level at which it CLICKS ON.
 2. Slowly uncover. The LED will NOT click off at the same light
    level - it stays on until the room is noticeably brighter.
 3. The dead-band between those two light levels is the hysteresis
    window. Swap the 220K feedback resistor for 100K to widen it,
    or 470K to narrow it, and watch the dead-band change size.
    Remove the feedback resistor entirely and you'll see the relay
    chatter at twilight - which is the bug a Schmitt trigger fixes.

==================================================================
 TROUBLESHOOTING
==================================================================
 * Relay chatters near twilight       -> feedback resistor open or
                                         missing (should be 220K)
 * Relay never turns on at all        -> KY-018 trim-pot wrong, or
                                         pin 2/3 swapped
 * Relay always on                    -> KY-018 AO stuck low; rotate
                                         module trim-pot clockwise
 * LM358 output stuck near 2.5 V      -> pin 4 (GND) not connected,
                                         OR input is hovering exactly
                                         on the threshold (cover the
                                         sensor and re-check)
 * L7805 gets hot fast / output low   -> input cap reversed, or
                                         input/output pins swapped
TESTS
learning_concepts: Op-amp as comparator (and its real-world swing limits)

allocations.notes: Connects the KY-018 and 1-channel relay modules to the breadboard
Breadboard hookup wires between the L7805, LM358, resistors, and LED
Bulk decoupling across the +5 V rail - smooths the inrush surge when the relay coil energises. NOTE polarity: long lead / unmarked side = +5 V, short lead / striped side = GND. Reversed it will pop.
Input bulk cap for the L7805 (between 9 V input and GND). NOTE polarity: striped side = GND.
Visible 'DARK' indicator driven by the SECOND LM358 channel (pin 7) so it never fights the relay-module input stage
Half A wired as a Schmitt comparator with positive feedback; half B drives the indicator LED

Driven DIRECTLY from LM358 pin 1 through a 1K series resistor. Low-voltage DC loads only. Module is active-LOW but its onboard transistor sinks the coil current - so when our op-amp output goes HIGH (dark) the module's IN is HIGH and relay is OFF; we wire the relay's COM/NC pair to the load so 'dark = load on'.
Holds the L7805, LM358, resistors, LED and the wired-up modules
Top of the reference divider; sets nominal threshold ~0.45 V
Bottom of the reference divider on the non-inverting input
Series resistor between LM358 pin 1 and the relay module IN pin (current limit, also handy probe point)
Positive-feedback resistor from op-amp output back to pin 3 - SETS the hysteresis (~115 mV dead-band with this divider)
Current-limiting resistor for the red 'DARK' indicator LED
Light sensor - analog output (AO) feeds the op-amp's inverting input (pin 2)
TO-220 regulator producing the +5 V rail from a 9 V wall supply - this is the 'no microcontroller in sight' clean-source for the analog circuit

projects.name: LM386 Pocket Speaker Amp (matchbox half-watt)
projects.power_supply: 5V from a USB-C phone charger or power bank via the USB-C pigtail. LM386 happily runs 4-12V so a 9V battery works too if you want it portable - just keep the pin 7 BYPASS cap in place at the higher voltage.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug your phone into the breadboard, hit play, and a tiny speaker the size of a coin blasts your music loud enough to fill the room. The whole amplifier fits in a matchbox. **Why it's fun**: You built a real boombox out of one black chip and a handful of parts, no batteries or apps required. Crank it up at the dinner table and watch everyone wonder where the song is coming from. ## Parts list - 1x LM386 Audio Power Amp (8-pin DIP) - 1x 1uF electrolytic - input DC blocker - 2x 10uF electrolytic - one is the gain-set cap between pins 1 and 8, one is the pin 7 BYPASS cap to GND - 1x 47uF electrolytic - supply bypass - 1x 100uF electrolytic - bulk reservoir on the 5V rail - 1x 220uF electrolytic - output DC blocker to speaker - 1x 10K resistor - series input attenuator (acts as a fixed volume control) - 1x breadboard - 1x USB-C female pigtail for 5V power in (any phone charger / power bank) - Hookup wires - *You supply:* a small 8-ohm speaker (anything from a dead toy or old set of earbuds will do), a 3.5mm headphone jack or a chopped aux cable, and the phone to play music from > The textbook LM386 circuit adds a 10R + 47nF ceramic snubber (a "Zobel network") from pin 5 to GND to damp ultrasonic ringing. We skip it because we don't stock 47nF ceramics, and on a short breadboard the LM386 is usually stable without it. If you hear a faint high-pitched whine after everything else works, that's why - the proper fix is to add the Zobel, not to substitute a 47uF electrolytic (a factor-of-1000 different value, which would short the output through the 10R resistor across the entire audio band and cook the chip). ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on this build:** - **LM386** - the little 8-leg black chip that turns a quiet phone signal into a loud speaker signal. - **Pin 1, Pin 2, ... Pin 8** - the LM386's legs. Pin 1 is at the top-left when the half-circle notch on the chip is facing up. Pins count down the left side (1, 2, 3, 4), then jump to the bottom-right and count up the right side (5, 6, 7, 8). - **The `+` rail** - the long red strip running down the side of the breadboard. It carries 5V (power in). - **The `-` rail** - the long blue or black strip running down the side. It is the 0V side - ground. - **Long leg / short leg** - on the round capacitors (the little barrels), the long leg is the plus side and the short leg (with the white stripe on the body) is the minus side. Getting these the right way around matters. - **Notch** - the little half-moon dent on one end of the LM386. It tells you which end has Pin 1.
Here is the LM386 from above so you can find each pin: ``` notch +--\__/--+ 1 -| |- 8 1 = GAIN 2 -| |- 7 2 = -IN (we tie to ground) 3 -| |- 6 3 = +IN (audio in from phone) 4 -| |- 5 4 = GND (0V) +--------+ 5 = OUT (to speaker) 6 = +5V power in 7 = BYPASS (steadies the chip) 8 = GAIN ``` **Step 1 - Plant the LM386 across the middle gap.** - Put the breadboard in front of you with the long red and blue strips on the left and right. - Find row 10. Push the LM386 in so that Pin 1 lands at hole **E10** (notch pointing up the board, toward row 1). - That puts the eight legs at E10, E11, E12, E13 on the left side of the gap and F13, F12, F11, F10 on the right side. The middle gap in the breadboard keeps the left four legs and the right four legs from touching. That is exactly what you want - each leg of the chip needs its own row.
**Step 2 - Bring in power from the USB-C pigtail.** - USB-C pigtail **RED** wire -> the top `+` rail (5V in). - USB-C pigtail **BLACK** wire -> the top `-` rail (ground, 0V). - Short jumper from the top `+` rail to the bottom `+` rail, and another from the top `-` rail to the bottom `-` rail (so both sides of the board have power). On many small breadboards the rails are already joined - if so, skip these. - Red jumper from **F13** (LM386 Pin 6, the power-in leg) to the bottom `+` rail. - Black jumper from **F10** (LM386 Pin 4, the ground leg) to the bottom `-` rail. - Red jumper from **E10** (LM386 Pin 1, the gain leg) up to the top `+` rail. We will deal with Pin 1 properly in Step 4 - for now this wire stays in place. Do not plug the USB-C in yet. We finish building first, then power up.
**Step 3 - Add the two power smoothing capacitors.** - **100uF capacitor** (the chunky barrel): long leg into the top `+` rail, short leg (white stripe side) into the top `-` rail. Plant it close to where the USB-C wires come in. - **47uF capacitor**: long leg into **B13** (same row as LM386 Pin 6, the power-in leg), short leg into the top `-` rail. **Why this matters.** Speakers pull power in big sudden gulps when the music thumps. The 100uF cap stores up a little pool of power right next to the chip so those gulps do not yank the 5V down. The 47uF cap does the same job, but parked right at the chip's power leg. Skip them and you hear ugly buzzing and popping in the speaker, especially on bass notes.
**Step 4 - Set the gain to 200x (the loud trick).** - **10uF capacitor**: long leg into **A8** (Pin 1 row), short leg into **A15**. - Jumper from **A8** across to **C10** - this connects the cap's long leg to LM386 Pin 1. - Jumper from **A15** down to **B17**, then a second jumper from **B17** over to **B10** - this connects the cap's short leg to LM386 Pin 8. **Why this matters.** This is the famous LM386 trick. By default the chip makes sound 20 times louder. By dropping this 10uF capacitor between Pin 1 and Pin 8, you tell the chip to make sound **200 times** louder instead. Without this cap, your matchbox amp will sound like a whisper.
**Step 5 - Add the BYPASS capacitor on Pin 7.** - **10uF capacitor** (the second one): long leg into **J13** (Pin 7 row on the right side of the chip), short leg into the bottom `-` rail. - Black jumper from **G10** (Pin 5, the output leg, on the right side row 10... wait, G10 is the Pin 4 / ground leg row) - actually this jumper ties **Pin 4 across to ground** on the right side of the board for a cleaner ground path. Run a black jumper from **G10** to the bottom `-` rail. **Why this matters.** Pin 7 is the LM386's "calm down" pin - it sets a steady reference voltage inside the chip. Without a 10uF capacitor parked from Pin 7 to ground, the chip hums loudly and can even start to whistle or squeal on its own. Every datasheet at gain=200 shows this cap. If you only remember one "do not skip" cap on this build, make it this one.
**Step 6 - Build the input path from the phone.** - **10K resistor**: one leg into **D3**, other leg into **D8**. - Orange (or any colour) jumper from **D8** across to **D10** - this carries the signal to LM386 Pin 3 (the audio-in leg). - **1uF capacitor**: long leg into **A1**, short leg into **A3**. - Phone jack TIP wire -> **A1** (long leg of the 1uF cap). - Phone jack SLEEVE wire -> the top `-` rail. **Why this matters.** The 1uF cap blocks any direct-current voltage from the phone and lets only the wiggling audio through. The 10K resistor knocks the phone's loud line-out signal down to a level the LM386 can handle politely - without it, the amp clips and sounds harsh on louder songs.
**Step 7 - Wire Pin 2 to ground.** - Short black jumper from anywhere on Pin 2's row (use a free hole in row 11 column A-D) down to the top or bottom `-` rail. Pin 2 is the LM386's "negative input". The chip wants to compare the audio coming into Pin 3 against ground on Pin 2. Tie Pin 2 straight to `-` and the chip is happy.
**Step 8 - Send the loud output to the speaker.** - **220uF capacitor** (the biggest barrel): long leg into **J17**, short leg into **J22**. - Orange jumper from **H17** to **I13** - this carries Pin 5's output up to row 17. - A second jumper from **I13** to **J17** - this finishes the path from Pin 5 to the long leg of the 220uF cap. - Speaker terminal A -> **J22** (short leg of the 220uF cap). - Speaker terminal B -> the bottom `-` rail. **Why this matters.** When the LM386 is sitting still it parks its output leg at about 2.5V (half of the 5V supply). If you wired the speaker straight to Pin 5 it would have 2.5V across it all the time, get warm, and waste battery. The 220uF cap blocks that steady 2.5V and lets only the wiggling audio through - the part you actually want to hear.
**Step 9 - Final check, then power up.** - Look at every capacitor: long leg on the high-voltage / signal side, short leg (white stripe) on the ground side. - Look at the LM386: notch at the top, Pin 1 at the top-left, Pin 6 wired to `+`, Pin 4 wired to `-`. - Speaker connected, phone jack connected. - Plug the USB-C into a 5V phone charger or power bank. - Plug your phone into the audio jack and start a song at about half volume. If you hear loud, clear sound - great, you built a half-watt amp out of one chip. If you hear a loud hum but no music, double-check the Pin 7 BYPASS cap (Step 5) and the ground wire on Pin 2 (Step 7). If you hear nothing at all, check that the 1uF input cap's long leg is on the phone side and that Pin 1's red wire actually reaches the `+` rail. This is a tricky little chip the first time you build it. Take your time and trace each wire with your finger before you plug in - you will get there. ## Flash it and run it This one is mostly **plug in and play music** - the amp is pure analog, so the second 5V power hits it, it is alive. No code needed for the main job. **Power-up procedure (the main event):** 1. Double-check the LM386 is sitting across the centre groove with the **notch facing up** (pin 1 top-left). 2. Double-check every electrolytic cap's long leg (`+`) is on the side the wiring notes said. Capacitors put in backwards are the #1 reason a fresh build does not work. 3. Plug a small 8-ohm speaker between the far end of the 220uF output cap and the `-` rail. Speaker polarity does not matter for sound. 4. Plug your 3.5mm jack into the 1uF input cap (tip wire) and the `-` rail (sleeve wire). Do NOT plug your phone in yet. 5. Plug the USB-C pigtail into a phone charger or power bank. 6. The amp should be silent. Touch a finger to the **bare metal of pin 3** of the LM386. The speaker should HUM loudly - a low buzzy 50/60 Hz mains hum. That is your body acting as an antenna for the mains in the walls, and it proves the gain is working. If you hear that hum, the amp is alive. 7. Unplug the USB-C, plug your phone into the 3.5mm jack, plug USB-C back in, hit play on the phone. Start the phone volume around halfway. **Optional - flash an Arduino Uno as a test-tone generator:** Only do this if step 6 above did NOT produce a hum and you want to feed the amp a known-good signal to narrow down the problem. You will need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). *Every time you flash:* 1. Disconnect the phone jack tip wire from the 1uF input cap. In its place, run a jumper from **Arduino Uno pin 9** to the same spot (the `+` leg of the 1uF cap). 2. Run another jumper from **Arduino Uno GND** to the breadboard `-` rail. Both grounds must be tied together or the Uno's signal has no reference. 3. Leave the amp powered from its own USB-C 5V. Do not power the LM386 from the Uno's 5V pin. 4. Plug the Uno into the laptop with a USB-A-to-USB-B printer cable. 5. In the Arduino IDE: **Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno**. 6. **Tools -> Port** -> pick the COM* port that appears when you plug the Uno in (try unplugging and replugging to see which one disappears). 7. Paste in the sketch from the Code section. No libraries to install, no WiFi password to set - this sketch is plain `tone()`. 8. Click **Upload** (the right-arrow icon at the top). Wait for "Done uploading." 9. **Tools -> Serial Monitor**, set the baud rate at the bottom-right to **115200** (matches `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). 10. You should see: `LM386 bench test - 1 kHz beep every second` plus a short troubleshooting checklist printed once. 11. From the speaker you should hear a clean **1 kHz beep** roughly twice a second (0.4 s on, 0.6 s off). If you hear that, the amp is 100% fine and the original problem was somewhere in the phone-jack wiring. **Common gotchas:** - **Capacitor polarity backwards.** Especially the 220uF output cap (`+` to pin 5) and the pin 7 BYPASS 10uF (`+` to pin 7). A backwards electrolytic can sound dead, scratchy, or even pop and leak. If in doubt, pull each one and re-seat it long-leg-where-the-wiring-notes-say. - **No common ground when using the Uno test.** If you forget the jumper from Uno GND to the breadboard `-` rail, you get silence or random noise instead of a beep. The Uno's pin 9 signal is measured against Uno GND, so the amp must share that ground. - **Serial Monitor baud wrong.** If the Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `⸮⸮⸮⸮`, the baud dropdown in the bottom-right is not on **115200**. Fix the dropdown - do not change the code. ## Talking points - The LM386 has been in production since 1983. It is the audio version of the NE555 - cheap, indestructible, taught in every electronics class, and still in current designs. - The chip has a built-in feedback network that fixes its gain at 20 by default. Pins 1 and 8 are the two ends of that internal resistor divider. Drop a capacitor across them and at audio frequencies the cap looks like a short, removing the resistor from the loop and shoving gain to 200. - Pin 7 (BYPASS) connects to an internal reference voltage that biases the input stage. Without a cap from pin 7 to ground, any noise on the supply rail rides straight onto that reference and gets amplified 200x. That is why this cap is the difference between "music" and "music with a loud 60 Hz hum behind it." - Everything else on the chip is "auxiliary" - input bias, output coupling, supply bypass. The amplification itself is one transistor stage with feedback. That is the entire story of an op-amp / power-amp. - The 220uF output cap exists because the LM386's output sits at roughly half the supply voltage (2.5V on a 5V rail). If you wired the speaker straight to pin 5 you would push 2.5V DC through the coil constantly - it would get hot and eventually burn out. The cap blocks DC while letting audio (AC) through. ## Things to change once it works - Swap the 10K series resistor for a 10K potentiometer to get a real volume knob. - Try removing the gain cap (pin 1 to pin 8) entirely - gain drops to 20, the amp gets noticeably quieter, but it also gets cleaner. Beginner lesson: more gain = more noise. - Power it from a 9V battery instead of 5V USB. The chip happily runs on 4 to 12V and gets noticeably louder at 9V because the output swing is bigger. Note: at 9V the higher gain headroom makes oscillation much more likely, so the pin 7 BYPASS cap above is absolutely non-optional in that mode - and that is also when you really want to add the 10R + 47nF Zobel snubber the parts list skipped. - Build a stereo version by wiring up a second LM386 - one chip per channel - sharing the same input jack via two separate 1uF caps. - Once it works on the breadboard, lay it out on a Double-Sided Prototype PCB and stuff the whole thing into a mint tin with a speaker. ## Why this is interesting The first time you build an amplifier and music comes out of it, electronics stops being "blink an LED" and starts being a real tool. The LM386 will reappear in dozens of future projects: as the speaker driver for an MCU playing wavetables, as the output stage of a crystal radio, as the buzzer on an alarm. Learning where its pins go once means you never have to look it up again.

projects.name: LM386 Telegraph-Style Code Practice Oscillator
projects.power_supply: Powered from an Arduino Uno used purely as a regulated 5V brick over USB (USB jack -> Uno's 5V/GND pins -> breadboard rails). No code is uploaded to the Uno and no GPIO is used.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Press and hold the button and a red LED starts blinking, about once a second, like a tiny lighthouse on your breadboard. Let go and it goes dark. Tap out short and long presses and you are flashing real Morse code. **Why it's fun**: Sailors used to flash messages between ships at night with big lamps just like this, and now you have a pocket-sized version on your desk. Learn the dots and dashes for your name, then flash it across the room to your dad and see if he can read it back. ## Parts list - 1x LM386 audio power amp (the star - rewired as a slow relaxation oscillator that flashes an LED in Morse-code rhythm, NOT as an audio amp this time) - 1x Tactile push-button 3x6x5mm (the "telegraph key") - 1x 10uF electrolytic cap (the timing cap - this, together with the 100K feedback resistor, sets the flash rate) - 1x 100uF electrolytic cap (Vcc bypass - keeps the supply quiet) - 1x 100K resistor (the feedback resistor - the cap charges through this; with the 10uF it gives a roughly 1-second flash period) - 2x 10K resistors (a half-supply reference divider on pin 2) - 1x 470R resistor (current limit for the LED on the output) - 1x 5mm red LED (the visible "telegraph lamp") - 1x Breadboard - M-M jumper wires - 1x Arduino Uno (used ONLY as a regulated 5V/GND brick through its USB jack - no code uploaded, no GPIO touched) Note on the "telegraph" angle: the inventory has no speaker or buzzer, so this build is a *visible* code-practice oscillator - a blinking lamp instead of a beep. That's historically real too: in the 1800s the Royal Navy and the army practised Morse on Aldis lamps and heliographs (mirror-reflected sunlight). Same code, same rhythm, light instead of sound. ## Safety first - read this before plugging in Electrolytic caps have a polarity stripe marked on the side. **Backwards = they can heat up, vent, and occasionally pop.** Both caps in this build are electrolytic. Before you connect 5V: - 10uF timing cap: **plus (long leg) toward LM386 pin 3, stripe (short leg) toward GND.** - 100uF supply cap: **plus (long leg) toward LM386 pin 6 (Vcc), stripe (short leg) toward GND.** Eyeball both stripes BEFORE you plug the USB cable in. If you smell anything warm once power is on, unplug immediately. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the pin that gives back the 5V coming in from the USB cable. We use this as a tidy power source. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs a path back here. - **USB jack** - where you plug in the cable from your computer or a phone charger. That is the only thing the Uno does today: it turns USB power into clean 5V. - **D0 to D13, A0 to A5** - the rows of pins along the long edges. We are NOT using any of them in this build. The Uno has no code on it.
This is a tricky one because the LM386 chip is doing a clever trick: it flips its output on and off all by itself, about once a second, just from the way we wire it up. No code, no Arduino brain needed. The Uno is only here because USB gives us a safe, clean 5V. **LM386 chip map (notch points LEFT, looking down from on top):** ``` +---v---+ pin 1 | | pin 8 pin 2 | | pin 7 pin 3 | | pin 6 <- power input (5V) pin 4 | | pin 5 <- output to LED +-------+ (pin 4 = ground) ``` **Step 1 - Set up the power rails.** - Use a jumper wire to connect the Uno's **5V** pin to the red strip running down the side of the breadboard (the long red strip on the side). - Use another jumper wire to connect the Uno's **GND** pin to the blue strip on the same side (the long blue strip is ground, the 0V side). - Do NOT plug the USB cable in yet. The red strip is now our +5V power. The blue strip is our 0V ground. Every part on the board will pull power from one and return it to the other.
**Step 2 - Plant the LM386 chip across the middle channel.** - Find the little half-moon notch on one end of the chip. Point that notch to the LEFT. - Push the chip down so its legs straddle the centre channel of the breadboard. Use rows 7 through 14, with pin 1 in row 7 on the left. - Pin 1 is top-left. Pin 4 is bottom-left (ground). Pin 5 is bottom-right (the output, which will go to the LED). Pin 8 is top-right. If a leg bends instead of going in, pull the chip out and gently straighten the leg with a flat fingernail. Don't force it.
**Step 3 - Place the push-button "telegraph key".** - Push the tactile push-button into row 3 so its four legs straddle the centre channel. Two legs in column A, two legs in column E. - Run a red jumper wire from **C3** (one side of the button) to the red 5V strip. - Run an orange jumper wire from **A3** (the other side of the button) over to **A11** (which is the LM386's pin 5... wait, we want pin 6). Actually wire **A7 to A11** so the button sends 5V to **pin 6 of the chip** (the power input pin). The button is a switch. When it is up, no power reaches the chip and the LED stays dark. When you press it down, 5V flows into pin 6 and the whole circuit wakes up and starts flashing. This is exactly how a real telegraph key works: press to send, release to be silent.
**Step 4 - Add the big 100uF bypass capacitor.** - The 100uF capacitor is the tall fat one. It has a long leg (+) and a short leg with a white stripe down the side of the can (-). The white stripe goes to ground. - Plant the long leg into **B15** (this row connects to pin 6, the power input). - Plant the short leg (the stripe side) into the blue ground strip. **Why this matters:** the chip pulls power in little gulps, not a smooth stream. The big capacitor sits right next to pin 6 holding a small reservoir of charge. Whenever the chip gulps, the capacitor refills it instantly. Without this cap, the power line wobbles and the circuit gets twitchy. Always put a fat cap near every chip's power pin.
**Step 5 - Ground pin 4.** - Run a black jumper wire from **J13** (which is the same row as pin 4 of the chip... actually pin 4 sits at row 13 on the bottom side) to the blue ground strip. Pin 4 is the chip's ground pin. Every chip needs both a power pin AND a ground pin so electricity has a path in and a path out.
**Step 6 - Build the "half-power" reference using two 10K resistors.** - Take the first **10K resistor** (brown-black-orange stripes, or brown-black-black-red if it has four colour bands). Plant one leg in the red 5V strip and the other leg in **A20**. - Take the second **10K resistor** and plant one leg in **A20** and the other leg in the blue ground strip. - Now row 20 sits exactly halfway between 5V and 0V, at 2.5V. - Run an orange jumper wire from **C20** over to **A12** to send that 2.5V into pin 2 of the chip. **Why this matters:** the chip needs a steady "decision line" to compare against. Two equal resistors stacked between 5V and ground meet in the middle at exactly half-voltage, like a seesaw with the kid sitting in the middle. We feed that middle point into pin 2 and the chip uses it as its yardstick.
**Step 7 - Add the 10uF timing capacitor.** - The 10uF cap is smaller than the 100uF but looks the same shape: little can, long leg (+), short leg with stripe (-). - Plant the long leg in **B7** (which is pin 3 of the chip, the "watcher" pin). - Plant the short leg (stripe) in the blue ground strip. This cap is the metronome of the whole circuit. Its job is to slowly fill up with charge, then slowly empty out, over and over.
**Step 8 - Add the 100K feedback resistor.** - Take the **100K resistor** (brown-black-yellow stripes). Plant one leg in **F12** (pin 5, the output) and the other leg in **F8** (pin 3, where the 10uF cap lives). - This single resistor is the secret sauce. **Why this matters:** the 100K resistor lets the output pin slowly fill up the 10uF cap with electricity. When the cap gets fuller than 2.5V (our decision line from Step 6), the chip slams its output to 0V. Now the same 100K starts pulling charge BACK out of the cap. When the cap empties below 2.5V, the chip slams its output back to 5V. And around and around it goes, about once per second. That is what makes the LED blink. The 100K and the 10uF together set the speed - bigger numbers would blink slower, smaller numbers would blink faster.
**Step 9 - Add the 470R safety resistor and the LED.** - Take the **470R resistor** (yellow-violet-brown stripes). Plant one leg in **G12** (pin 5, the output) and the other leg in **G24**. - Take the red LED. The long leg is the side that takes power in, the short leg is the side that returns to ground. Plant the long leg in **J24** (which connects through the resistor to pin 5). Plant the short leg in **J25**. - Run a black jumper wire from **J25** down to the blue ground strip. **Why this matters:** the LED is greedy. If you connect it straight to 5V it will eat too much current and burn out in a flash of light. The 470R resistor sits in front of it and limits how much current can flow, like a narrow doorway that only lets one kid through at a time. Always put a resistor in line with an LED.
**Step 10 - Plug in and test.** - Double-check: notch on the chip points LEFT, all the capacitor stripes go to the blue ground strip, both LED legs go to the right spots (long leg toward the resistor, short leg to ground). - Plug the USB cable into the Uno and the other end into your computer or a phone charger. - Nothing happens yet - that is correct, the button is up. - Press and hold the button. After half a second the red LED should start blinking, about once a second: blink... blink... blink. - Release the button. The LED should go dark. If it does not blink, unplug the USB and check Step 6 (the two 10K resistors meeting at row 20) and Step 8 (the 100K from F12 to F8). Those are the two most common mix-up spots. This is a real telegraph: hold the key down to "send a tone" (well, a blink), let go to be quiet. Old-time telegraph operators used the same kind of on-off rhythm to spell out Morse code. Try tapping out S-O-S: three short presses, three long presses, three short presses. ## Flash it and run it Nothing to flash on this one - there is no code, no microcontroller, no Arduino IDE. The Uno is only here because its USB jack gives us a clean, regulated 5V to feed the breadboard. The LM386 chip and the handful of resistors and caps do all the work the moment power touches them. **Power-up procedure (do this slowly, in order):** 1. **Power OFF check first.** Before you go anywhere near the USB cable, eyeball the two electrolytic caps one more time. Long leg of the 10uF on LM386 pin 3, stripe toward GND. Long leg of the 100uF on pin 6, stripe toward GND. If either stripe is on the wrong side, pull the cap and turn it around now. 2. **Plug in the Uno's USB cable** to your laptop or to a USB phone charger. The Uno's own green "ON" LED should light up. That is the only thing that should light up so far - the red LED on your breadboard should still be dark, because the button is not pressed. 3. **(Optional but cool) Put your multimeter on DC volts** and touch the black probe to the blue (GND) rail and the red probe to the red (+5V) rail. You should see something between 4.9V and 5.1V. That is your "power is really there" check. 4. **Press and hold the tactile button.** Within a second or two, the red LED should start blinking, roughly once per second - on, off, on, off, like a slow lighthouse. Let go and it goes dark again. 5. **Tap out your name in Morse.** Short press = dot, long press = dash. The LED blinks the whole time you are holding, so a "dash" is just you holding the button longer. **What "it worked" looks like:** button held = LED blinks about once a second; button released = LED dark and silent; nothing on the breadboard gets warm to the touch. If you want to dig deeper, the **bench-test guide** (the bash script in the Code section) walks you through every test point with a multimeter - TP1 through TP6 - so you and your dad can poke around and see the half-supply voltage on pin 2, the slow sawtooth on pin 3, and the square-wave output on pin 5. Treat it as a treasure map for the circuit. **Common gotchas:** - **Electrolytic cap backwards.** This is the #1 thing to get wrong on this build. Long leg = plus, short leg / stripe = minus. If the LED never blinks AND a cap is getting warm, unplug right away and check the 10uF and 100uF orientations. - **LED in backwards.** No damage, just no light. The long leg (anode) goes toward the 470R resistor coming from pin 5; the short leg (cathode) goes to GND. Pull it out, spin it 180 degrees, push it back in. - **Button on the wrong pins.** Tactile buttons have 4 legs but only 2 real connections - the other 2 are just mechanical. If pressing the button does nothing, rotate the button 90 degrees in its holes and try again. ## Talking points - The headline lesson is this: **an oscillator is a comparator looking at its own slow-moving output.** The LM386 here is doing nothing fancy. It looks at pin 3 (the cap), compares it to pin 2 (the 2.5V reference), and yanks the output high or low. The output yank slowly drags pin 3 in the opposite direction through the 100K. By the time pin 3 crosses the threshold, the comparator flips. Then the whole thing happens in reverse. That endless back-and-forth IS the oscillation. - **Two things are required for oscillation, not just one.** A common beginner story is "feedback makes an amplifier oscillate." That's only half true. You need positive feedback AND a frequency-determining element - a capacitor that takes time to charge, or an LC tank, or a phase-shift network. Without something to set the timing, the loop either sits at one rail (latched) or whirls at the chip's gain-bandwidth limit, which is way above audio. Here the 100K + 10uF do the timing. - **The LM386 datasheet gain-cap myth.** The classic LM386 use is to drop a 10uF cap between pins 1 and 8 to set audio gain to ~200. We are NOT doing that here - pins 1 and 8 are left empty. The chip's default gain of 20 is plenty for the comparator-style behaviour we want, and a gain cap on 1-8 wouldn't change the flash rate. - **Why an LED instead of a speaker?** This kit has no speaker or piezo. Historically code-practice oscillators came in two flavours: an audio beeper (most common, the "buzzer" approach) and a flashing lamp (the Aldis-lamp / heliograph tradition). Both teach the same Morse rhythm. We're building the lamp version because that's what the inventory supports. - **Real telegraph keys clicked.** When you release the button you may notice the LED lingers for a moment before going dark - that's the 100uF supply cap still draining. The original 1800s telegraph keys made an audible click on release too, for related reasons (an inductive armature relaxing). The flicker is your bug-free version of that click. ## Things to change once it works - **Faster flash rate:** swap the 100K feedback resistor for 47K - period drops from ~1 s to ~0.5 s. Or swap the 10uF timing cap for 4.7uF for the same effect. Period scales roughly with R x C. - **Slower flash rate (lighthouse mode):** swap the 100K for 220K, or the 10uF for 22uF. Period stretches to a couple of seconds. - **Two LEDs that take turns:** add a second LED + 470R reversed across the first - cathode to pin 5, anode to GND. When pin 5 is high the first LED lights; when pin 5 is low the second lights. Now you have a heartbeat: one LED on, then the other. - **Make it audible later:** if you ever pick up a small 8-ohm speaker or piezo disc, the same circuit will drive it - just shrink the timing cap to 22 nF and the resistor to 10K so the oscillation lands in the audible 500 Hz range, and put a coupling cap in series with the speaker. The topology stays the same; only the RC values change. - **Practice real Morse code:** S = dit dit dit, O = dah dah dah, E = dit, T = dah. Hold the button for short presses (dits) and long presses (dahs). The classic timing rule is "a dah is three dits long." ## Why this is interesting The thing worth remembering from this build is that **an oscillator is just a feedback loop that includes a delay**. The LM386 isn't special - any chip with an output, an input, and some gain can do this trick if you give it a slow path back to itself. The 100K + 10uF is the delay. Without that delay the chip can't tell where the threshold is from where it just was, so it locks up. With the delay, every crossing of the threshold is "news" the chip has to react to. That endless reaction IS what we call oscillation. This pattern shows up everywhere once you spot it: the heartbeat of a 555 timer is the same idea (cap charges through R, threshold flips an internal latch, latch discharges cap), a digital clock crystal works on the same principle (a quartz disc that takes a fixed time to flex and unflex), even the cycle of a washing machine's agitator is a mechanical version. Get the delay right and you get the rhythm you want.
