#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Telegraph-style code practice oscillator - bench-test guide.
# No microcontroller. Use a multimeter (DMM) to confirm the circuit
# before you start tapping. The whole thing should draw < 15 mA.
# If you smell anything hot, pull power IMMEDIATELY.
#
# CRITICAL POLARITY CHECK (do this BEFORE plugging in 5V):
#   - 10uF cap:  + (long leg) toward LM386 pin 3,
#                stripe / short leg toward GND.
#   - 100uF cap: + (long leg) toward LM386 pin 6 (Vcc),
#                stripe / short leg toward GND.
#
# Reversed electrolytics can heat up, vent, or pop. Always eyeball
# both stripes before powering up.
#
# Test points are labelled in the wiring_diagram. Probe with the
# black DMM lead on GND and the red lead on each test point.

set -e

cat <<'TESTS'
==============================================
LM386 Telegraph-Style CPO - bench-test guide
==============================================

Step 0: Eyeball check, power OFF
  - LM386 notch faces LEFT (pin 1 top-left, pin 8 top-right).
  - 10uF cap: + leg on pin 3, stripe on GND rail.
  - 100uF cap: + leg on pin 6 (Vcc side of the button), stripe on GND.
  - Two 10K resistors form a divider from +5V to GND; their midpoint
    goes to pin 2.
  - 100K resistor links pin 5 (output) to pin 3.
  - 470R + LED: pin 5 -> 470R -> LED anode (long leg) -> LED cathode
    -> GND.

Step 1: Power ON, button NOT pressed
  Plug the USB cable into the Uno. Do not press the button yet.
  TP1 (+5V rail)             -> expect  +4.9 to +5.1 V DC
  TP6 (LM386 pin 6, Vcc)     -> expect  ~0 V DC (rises briefly if the
                                100uF still holds charge from a
                                previous run - wait ~30 s for it to
                                drain through leakage, then re-probe)
  TP5 (LM386 pin 2, -IN)     -> expect  ~2.5 V DC (half-supply, set by
                                the 10K + 10K divider, present even
                                with the chip unpowered)
  LED                        -> dark

Step 2: Press and HOLD the tactile button
  TP6 (LM386 pin 6, Vcc)     -> expect  +4.8 to +5.0 V DC
  TP5 (LM386 pin 2, -IN)     -> still   ~2.5 V DC
  TP3 (LM386 pin 3, +IN)     -> expect  a slow sawtooth between
                                roughly 1 V and 3 V, swinging once
                                per second. A DMM in DC mode will
                                bounce; AC mode shows ~0.5 V AC.
  TP2 (LM386 pin 5, output)  -> expect  square wave between ~0 V and
                                ~4 V at about 1 Hz. DMM in DC mode
                                will average around 2 V.
  LED                        -> flashes about once per second

Step 3: Tap dits and dahs
  Short press (~0.5 s)  = dit  (LED gives a brief flash)
  Long  press (~1.5 s)  = dah  (LED gives a longer flash)
  SOS = dit dit dit  ...  dah dah dah  ...  dit dit dit

  Note: because the oscillator starts fresh each time you press, the
  very first flash of each press may be slightly off-rhythm. Real
  1800s lamp operators dealt with the same thing.

Step 4: Troubleshooting
  LED never lights:
    - Probe TP2 (pin 5) with DMM in DC mode while holding the button.
      If pin 5 reads a steady value near 0 V or near 4 V (not flipping),
      the feedback loop is broken - re-check the 100K from pin 5 to
      pin 3 and the 10uF from pin 3 to GND.
    - Confirm the LED is the right way round (long leg toward the
      470R / pin 5 side).
  LED on but does not blink:
    - Check the 100K wire. Without it pin 3 floats and the output
      latches.
    - Check the divider: pin 2 must sit at ~2.5 V. If pin 2 is at 0 V
      or 5 V, one of the 10K resistors is open or in the wrong row.
  Flashes way too fast (looks like a dim steady glow):
    - The timing cap or feedback resistor is wrong. Confirm 10uF
      (not 100 nF) and 100K (not 100R).
  LED stays lit dimly even with button released:
    - The button is wired across the wrong rows. It should break the
      +5V line between the rail and pin 6, not bridge pin 5 to GND.

TESTS
learning_concepts: Oscillation needs positive feedback AND a frequency-determining RC
Using a chip as a comparator with hysteresis
Electrolytic capacitor polarity and why reversed caps fail
Reading the LM386 datasheet beyond its 'audio amp' role

allocations.notes: Used ONLY as a tidy regulated 5V/GND source via its USB jack. No code uploaded, no GPIO touched.
Hookup wire between rows on the breadboard.
Vcc bypass. Plus leg to pin 6, stripe to GND. Keeps the supply quiet during output transitions.
Timing cap. Plus leg to LM386 pin 3, stripe to GND. With the 100K feedback resistor this sets the ~1 second flash period.
The visible telegraph lamp. Anode (long leg) to the 470R, cathode (short leg) to GND.
Used as a comparator-with-hysteresis, not as an audio amp. Positive feedback through the 100K plus the 10uF timing cap makes pin 5 flip at ~1 Hz.
Holds the LM386, button, caps, resistors, and LED.
Feedback resistor from pin 5 (output) to pin 3 (+IN). Together with the 10uF timing cap this sets the oscillation rate.
Two of them, in series from +5V to GND, form a half-supply divider. Their midpoint feeds pin 2 (-IN) with a fixed 2.5V reference.
Current-limit resistor in series with the LED on pin 5 output.
The telegraph key - breaks the +5V line between the rail and LM386 pin 6 (Vcc). Press = chip powered = LED blinks.

projects.name: TDA2822D Stereo Earbud Amp
projects.power_supply: Single 9V PP3 battery via a snap clip feeds Vcc (pin 5) and GND (pin 4) of the TDA2822D, with a 100uF 16V bulk decoupling cap across the rails close to the chip.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug your phone into one end and your earbuds into the other. Hit play and the music comes out loud and clear in both ears, left and right, powered by a tiny 9V battery. **Why it's fun**: This is the first thing you build that turns into a real piece of audio gear you can actually use. Pull out a battery-powered headphone amp you made yourself at the kitchen table, plug in, and listen to your own music through it. ## Parts list Allocations below are the canonical parts list. A few items are NOT in the kit inventory and you'll need to bring your own: - **Bring-your-own (not in kit inventory):** - 9V PP3 battery with snap clip (the power source). - 3.5mm stereo input jack or a sacrificial 3.5mm cable (tip = L, ring = R, sleeve = GND). - A pair of earbuds (32 ohm typical). Do NOT plug in big 4 ohm bookshelf speakers - the TDA2822D is a small-signal chip. - **From the kit (see allocations):** - 1x TDA2822D dual audio power amp. - 1x breadboard. - 1x 100uF 16V cap (bulk supply decoupling). - 2x 10uF caps (input DC blocking). - 2x 100uF 16V caps (AC bypass at IN-). - 2x 470uF 16V caps (output DC blocking). - 2x 4.7R resistors (output series damping). - 1x Arduino Uno + 2x 10K resistors - ONLY for the optional test-tone procedure. Skip them if you go straight to a phone as the audio source. ## Wiring notes This project uses a tiny 8-leg chip called the TDA2822D. It is a stereo amplifier, which means it makes quiet music from a phone or laptop loud enough for earbuds. Think of it as two little amps in one chip - one for the left ear, one for the right ear. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the TDA2822D chip:** - **Pin 1 (OUT1)** - the left earbud sound comes out here. - **Pin 8 (OUT2)** - the right earbud sound comes out here. - **Pin 3 (IN1+)** and **Pin 6 (IN2+)** - this is where the music goes IN (left and right). - **Pin 2 (IN1-)** and **Pin 7 (IN2-)** - these "gain" pins tell the chip how loud to make the music. - **Pin 4 (GND)** - the 0V side, called ground. - **Pin 5 (VCC)** - the power input, the +9V from the battery. The chip has a little half-moon notch at one end. With the notch pointing up, pin 1 is the top-left leg and the pins count down the left side (1, 2, 3, 4), then jump across to the bottom-right (5) and count back up the right side (5, 6, 7, 8).
**Step 1 - Put the chip on the breadboard.** - Push the TDA2822D chip into the breadboard so it sits across the middle gap (the trench down the middle). - Pin 1 (the leg next to the notch) goes in hole **E13**. - That means pin 4 (GND) is in **E16**, pin 5 (VCC) is in **F16**, and pin 8 (OUT2) is in **F13**. - The two long red and blue strips on the side of the breadboard are the "rails". The top red strip is our +9V power, and the top blue strip is GND (0V). Why a breadboard? It lets you push parts in and pull them out without any soldering. Every short row of 5 holes (like A13, B13, C13, D13, E13) is joined inside the board, so anything you push into those holes is connected.
**Step 2 - Power the chip.** - Run a short red wire from **E13** (pin 1's row - wait, careful - actually we use row 16 for power on this build) to the top red rail (+9V). Specifically: connect **E13 to +5V_T** with a red wire (this jumpers chip pin 1's row to the +9V rail so the chip body can be powered through pin 5 via the rail). - Run a black wire from **F13** (pin 8's row) to the bottom blue rail (GND). This grounds pin 8's row. - Actually for the power pins: connect pin 5 (VCC, at **F16**) to the top red rail (+9V), and pin 4 (GND, at **E16**) to the top blue GND rail. Tip: keep the wires short and tidy so it is easy to spot mistakes.
**Step 3 - Add the big 100uF power smoothing cap.** - Take one **100uF 16V electrolytic capacitor**. It is a small black cylinder with two legs. The long leg is "+" and the short leg (the one with a white stripe down the side) is "-". - Push the long leg (+) into **B17** and the short leg (-) into the top blue GND rail. - Add a short red wire from **B16 to +5V_T** (top red rail) and a short red wire from **A17 to +5V_T** (so both sides of pin 5's row and the cap's + pin meet at +9V). - Add a short black wire from **A16 to GND_T** so pin 4 (GND) is firmly tied to the 0V rail. **Why this matters:** When the amp suddenly plays a loud drum hit, it grabs a quick gulp of current from the battery. This big cap acts like a tiny water tank right next to the chip, ready to release power instantly so the sound stays clean. Without it, you would hear pops and the chip would behave oddly.
**Step 4 - Build the LEFT channel input cap (10uF).** - Grab one **10uF electrolytic capacitor**. Same rules: long leg is +, short leg with the white stripe is -. - Push the long leg (+) into **B11** and the short leg (-) into **B9**. - Add a yellow (or any color) wire from **A11 to A13**. This carries the music from the cap straight to pin 3 (IN1+) of the chip. **Why this matters:** Music coming out of a phone is a wiggling voltage on top of a small DC offset. The chip only wants the wiggle, not the DC. This cap "blocks the DC and lets the music through". Long leg toward the chip side because the chip's input sits at a small positive voltage and the phone side sits at about 0V.
**Step 5 - Add the LEFT gain-setting cap (100uF).** - Grab another **100uF 16V capacitor**. - Push the long leg (+) into **D11** and the short leg (-) into **D9**. - Add a wire from **C11 to C14**. This jumpers the cap's + leg over to pin 2 (IN1-) of the chip (row 14, column on the left side). - Add a black wire from **C9 to GND_T** so the - side of this cap reaches GND. **Why this matters:** This cap is the "loudness setting". By connecting pin 2 (IN1-) to GND for music frequencies, it tells the chip "turn the volume all the way up - about 39 dB of gain". The chip's own DC voltage is still kept correct through internal resistors, but for the music, pin 2 looks like it is tied straight to GND. Note: old tutorials may call pins 2 and 7 "bootstrap" pins - they are not. On this chip they are the inverting inputs. The job is the same idea (gain control) but the wiring trick is different.
**Step 6 - Add the LEFT output resistor (4.7 ohm) and big output cap (470uF).** - Take one **4.7 ohm resistor** (color bands: yellow-violet-gold-brown for 4.7R 1%). Push it between **A20** and **A13**. One end is now at pin 1 (OUT1) of the chip; the other end is at row 20. - Take one **470uF 16V electrolytic capacitor**. Push the long leg (+) into **B20** (next to where the resistor ends) and the short leg (-) into **B23**. - **B23** is where the LEFT earbud's positive wire will connect later. **Why this matters:** The 4.7 ohm resistor is a tiny safety brake - it stops the chip from "whistling" (oscillating) at radio frequencies. The 470uF cap blocks the chip's DC level (about 4.5V) so only the music wiggle reaches the earbud. Earbuds hate DC and would burn out without this cap. Long leg toward the chip side (the side with 4.5V), short leg toward the earbud side (which sits at 0V).
**Step 7 - Now mirror everything for the RIGHT channel.** The right side uses pin 6 (IN2+), pin 7 (IN2-), and pin 8 (OUT2). Use the matching holes on the J/I/H side of the breadboard, just like the left side mirror image. - **10uF input cap (right):** long leg (+) into **I11**, short leg (-) into **I9**. Wire from **J11 to J13** (carries music to pin 6, IN2+). - **100uF gain cap (right):** long leg (+) into **G11**, short leg (-) into **G9**. Wire from **H11 to H14** (jumpers to pin 7, IN2-). Black wire from **H9 to GND_B** (the bottom blue GND rail). - **4.7 ohm resistor (right):** between **J20** and **J13** (connects to pin 8, OUT2). - **470uF output cap (right):** long leg (+) into **I20**, short leg (-) into **I23**. **I23** will go to the RIGHT earbud's positive wire. Also add: a black wire from **F13 to GND_B**. This grounds pin 8's row to the bottom GND rail. (Pin 8 itself is the output, but its row neighbor needs to reach GND so the bottom rail is alive for the right earbud return.) Actually note: the bottom GND rail and the top GND rail are two separate strips. To use them together, run a "jumper wire" between them - a black wire from the top blue rail to the bottom blue rail at any convenient point. This makes both rails act as one big ground.
**Step 8 - Add the 10K resistors for the test-tone input (optional, only if using Arduino).** - Take two **10K resistors** (color bands: brown-black-black-red-brown or brown-black-orange-gold). - Push one between **A9 and A5** (left input side). - Push the other between **J9 and J5** (right input side). **Why this matters:** The Arduino Uno (if you connect it) puts out a 0V-to-5V fast on-off signal that is way too loud for an amp input. The 10K resistors turn the volume way down so it sounds like a normal music level. The cap at row 9-11 still blocks the DC, so the chip only hears the test tone wiggle.
**Step 9 - Plug in the audio source (3.5mm jack from a phone/laptop).** A 3.5mm headphone plug has three parts: - **TIP** = the very end metal point = LEFT audio. Wire this to **A9** on the breadboard. - **RING** = the middle metal ring = RIGHT audio. Wire this to **J9** on the breadboard. - **SLEEVE** = the long metal part nearest the wire = audio ground. Wire this to the top GND rail. If you have a 3.5mm jack breakout board, those three terminals will be labeled TIP, RING, SLEEVE (or L, R, GND). If you cut up an old earphone cable, the colored wires (usually red=right, white or green=left, bare or black=ground) are the same three signals.
**Step 10 - Plug in the earbuds.** Earbuds also have three contacts on their plug, just like the input. But this amp drives them through two separate output caps, so: - LEFT earbud (+) wire goes to **B23** (the short leg side of the left 470uF cap). - RIGHT earbud (+) wire goes to **I23** (the short leg side of the right 470uF cap). - Both earbuds (-) wires go to the bottom blue GND rail (GND_B). The easiest way: get a 3.5mm jack socket too (so you can plug normal earbuds in). Wire TIP to **B23**, RING to **I23**, and SLEEVE to GND_B.
**Step 11 - Connect the 9V battery LAST.** - 9V battery (+) (red wire from the PP3 snap clip) goes to the top red +9V rail. - 9V battery (-) (black wire from the PP3 snap clip) goes to the top blue GND rail. Always plug in the battery last, after every other wire is checked. That way if there is a mistake, no smoke. If a cap gets warm fast, unplug the battery and check that every electrolytic has the long leg in the spot marked "+" on the wiring list.
**Step 12 (optional) - Add the Arduino Uno for a built-in test tone.** If you want the amp to play a beep without needing a phone: - Arduino **D9** -> breadboard **A5** (this is the left test signal, before the 10K resistor). - Arduino **D10** -> breadboard **J5** (this is the right test signal). - Arduino **GND** -> the top blue GND rail. The Arduino code will use the `tone()` function on D9 and D10 to play short beeps. The 10K resistors quiet the signal down, the 10uF caps block the DC offset, and the amp does the rest. Power the Arduino from USB (not the 9V battery - the Uno can take 9V on its barrel jack, but it is simpler to just use USB for testing).
**Final check before you press play:** - Every electrolytic cap has the long leg in the "+" hole on the wiring list (or the white-stripe leg in the "-" hole). - The chip is sitting in the breadboard with the half-moon notch pointing up (pin 1 at E13). - The 9V battery is the LAST thing connected. - Volume on your phone or laptop should start at about 25% the first time - this amp is louder than a phone alone. If the earbuds buzz instead of play music, check that the SLEEVE wire from the jack reaches GND. If only one ear works, double check that channel's 10uF input cap is the right way around. If the chip gets hot, unplug the battery immediately and check the 100uF bulk cap polarity at row 17. ## Flash it and run it This project is a real analog amplifier - the **TDA2822D chip plus a handful of caps and resistors** do all the work the moment power touches them. But there is an **optional** test-tone helper sketch you can run on an Arduino Uno that plays a 440 Hz tone in the left earbud and an 880 Hz tone in the right, swapping every 2 seconds, so you can confirm left and right are not crossed before you plug in a phone. The "Power-up procedure" further down shows how to run the amp on its own without any code at all. **Option A - Skip the Uno and just play music.** Jump to the **Power-up procedure** below. Wire a 3.5mm jack to the input caps (tip = LEFT, ring = RIGHT, sleeve = battery GND), snap on the 9V battery, plug in your earbuds, hit play on your phone. Done. **Option B - Run the test-tone helper first.** This needs the Arduino IDE and takes about 5 minutes. **Software you need:** - **Arduino IDE 2.x** - free download from [arduino.cc/en/software](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software). Install it, open it once, let it finish setting itself up. **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):** 1. **USB driver.** Your Uno is a CH340 clone (the dark rectangular chip next to the USB jack). Plug it in: if a COM port shows up in **Tools -> Port** within a few seconds, you are already set. If nothing shows up, install the CH340 driver from [sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers](https://sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers), then unplug and replug. 2. **Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno.** 3. No extra libraries needed - `tone()`, `pinMode`, `Serial`, and `delay` are all built in. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno in with the chunky **USB-A to USB-B** cable (the printer-style one). The green ON LED on the Uno lights up. 2. **Tools -> Port -> COM*** (Windows) or **/dev/cu.usbmodem*** (macOS) or **/dev/ttyACM0** (Linux). If you only see one port, that is it. 3. Paste the sketch from the **Code** section into a new IDE window. Nothing to edit - no WiFi passwords, no pin numbers to change. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon up top). The TX and RX LEDs on the Uno will blink for a couple of seconds, then the IDE says **Done uploading**. 5. **Tools -> Serial Monitor** at **115200 baud** (bottom-right dropdown). **What "it worked" looks like:** - Serial Monitor prints `TDA2822D test: 440 Hz LEFT, 880 Hz RIGHT.` followed by a `Swapped: ...` line every 2 seconds. - With the test wiring connected (D9 -> 10K -> LEFT input cap, D10 -> 10K -> RIGHT input cap, Uno GND -> battery GND) **and the 9V battery snapped on the amp**, you hear a **low buzz in the left earbud and a high buzz in the right** for 2 seconds, then they swap, then they swap back. If the tones are reversed, your earbud wiring (tip vs ring) is swapped. - Once you have confirmed the channels, **unplug the Uno entirely**, pull the test wires off, and continue with the regular audio source. **Common gotchas:** - **Earbuds going into the OUTPUT, not the INPUT.** The 470uF caps go on the *output* side (pins 1 and 8 of the TDA2822D) and feed the earbuds. The 10uF caps go on the *input* side (pins 3 and 6) and feed the audio source. Swapping these will make the amp silent and may pop the earbud. - **9V battery on the wrong terminal.** The snap clip is keyed but it is easy to twist the wires on later. Red lead = battery + = chip pin 5. Black = battery - = chip pin 4 and breadboard GND rail. - **Electrolytic cap polarity.** Every electrolytic on this board (10uF, 100uF, 470uF) has a stripe pointing to its negative leg. Get any of them backwards and at best the amp is silent, at worst the cap pops. Long leg = +, short leg / stripe = -. - **Serial Monitor at 9600.** The sketch uses 115200. If the Serial Monitor shows garbage, fix the baud dropdown. ## Talking points - **This is your first stereo amp.** Up to now you've only built mono amps (LM386). Stereo is just "do it twice in one package." - **What you actually save with a dual chip.** The TDA2822D is two complete amplifiers sharing one Vcc/GND pair. The savings aren't the transistors inside (those still doubled) - it's that the package, the supply pins, and the ground pin are shared. You go from two chips plus two sets of supply wiring to one chip plus one set. - **DC blocking caps everywhere.** Audio is AC riding on top of a DC level. The chip biases its outputs to mid-supply (~4.5V) so the signal has room to swing both up and down. But your earbud coil doesn't want 4.5V DC pushing constant current through it - that wastes battery and heats the coil. The 470uF cap on each output blocks the DC and only lets the AC swing through. Same idea on the input: your phone's audio output sits near 0V already, but you cap-block in case the source has any DC offset. - **Why 470uF on the output specifically?** At low frequencies the output cap and the earbud impedance form a high-pass filter. With a 32 ohm earbud and 470uF, the cutoff is around f = 1 / (2 * pi * R * C) ~ 10 Hz, well below anything you can hear. If you used 10uF here, the cutoff would be ~500 Hz and the project would sound tinny because all the bass would be filtered out. - **What the IN- bypass caps actually do.** This is the part that beginner tutorials get wrong (and that an earlier draft of this project got wrong too). The TDA2822 has internal resistors that set a closed-loop gain when IN- is left to its internal bias point. When you AC-couple IN- to GND through a big cap, you're saying "for audio frequencies, hold IN- at ground." That makes the chip run at its maximum gain (~39 dB, around 90x). Remove the cap and gain drops a lot. So these caps are gain-set caps, NOT bootstrap caps - bootstrap is a different trick used on different chips (like the TDA2003). - **The 4.7R series resistor on each output is mostly defensive.** If you short an earbud lead by accident, this tiny resistor limits the current spike enough to give the chip's internal protection time to react. ## Things to change once it works - **Add a volume pot:** replace the wire between the audio source and each 10uF input cap with a 10K log-taper pot wired as a voltage divider. Ganged stereo pots give you a single volume knob. - **Add a real Zobel network on each output** (~10R in series with 100nF to GND, right at the OUT pin) to suppress any HF oscillation if you upgrade to longer speaker leads. - **Try 4 ohm or 8 ohm small speakers** (still low power - this chip is rated to about 650 mW per channel at 4 ohm, 9V). With 32 ohm earbuds it's much quieter, which is what you want for hearing safety. - **Swap the 9V battery for a USB-C 5V supply:** the chip works down to 3V. You'll get less volume but it'll run for hours off a power bank. The 9V PP3 also sags fast under load - dropping to 5V regulated will actually be more consistent. - **Bridge mode:** if you only need mono but want more volume into a single 8 ohm speaker, the TDA2822 can be wired in BTL (bridge) mode. That's a different schematic - worth building as a follow-up project. ## Why this is interesting You now have three audio amps in the kit (LM386 mono low-power, TDA2822D stereo low-power, TDA2030A mono high-power) and they all solve "make audio louder" but with different trade-offs. Building this one teaches you that "stereo" is not a special technology - it's just two independent mono amps that happen to live in the same package and share a power rail. That mental model carries over to almost everything multi-channel in electronics: stereo ADCs are two ADCs in one package, dual op-amps are two op-amps sharing pins 4 and 8, quad comparators are four of the same thing on one die. It also teaches a very practical lesson about copying tutorials from the internet: a common mistake (one this project's first draft made) is to confuse the TDA2822's IN- pins with the bootstrap pins on a TDA2003. Same DIP-8 outline, different chip family, different pin functions. Always check the datasheet pinout for the exact part number.

projects.name: NE5532 Hi-Fi Headphone Preamp
projects.power_supply: 9V battery (or 9V DC wall-wart, centre-positive) feeding the breadboard rails directly. The op-amp draws under 10 mA, so a single 9V will last many hours of listening. If the rail sags below ~6.5V the NE5532 starts to clip - swap the battery.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug your phone or laptop into one end and your headphones into the other. Music goes in, music comes out, but cleaner and louder, with no static or hiss in the quiet parts. **Why it's fun**: You built the same kind of audio booster that lives inside real recording studio gear, from a handful of parts on a breadboard. Hand the headphones to your dad, play his favourite song, and watch his face when he realises YOU made the thing the sound is coming through. ## Parts list - 1x NE5532 Op-Amp (audio dual) - the "U1" in the schematic; both halves used (one per stereo channel) - 4x Capacitor 1uF 50V (electrolytic) - AC coupling caps (2 input, 2 output) - 4x Resistor 10K (1/8W 1%) - 2 input bias resistors to virtual ground, 2 feedback path resistors - 2x Resistor 100R (1/8W 1%) - output build-out resistors to protect against headphone-cable capacitance - 2x Resistor 22K (1/8W 1%) - virtual-ground bias divider - 1x Capacitor 100uF 25V (electrolytic) - power-rail bulk decoupling - 1x Capacitor 100uF 16V (electrolytic) - virtual-ground filter cap (kills supply hum on the mid-rail) - 1x LED 5mm Red + 1x Resistor 470R (1/8W 1%) - power-on indicator (470R picks the dim end of the inventory's 220R-470R LED range) - 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm - build surface - Jumper wires M-M You also supply: a 9V battery (or 9V wall-wart with the centre pin positive), a 3.5mm stereo audio input (e.g. a cut-up old aux cable), a 3.5mm stereo headphone jack for the output, and a pair of headphones (32-ohm or higher impedance is happiest - see talking points for why). ## Wiring notes This build has no computer chip and no code to upload. It is a pure audio amplifier that makes the music from your phone or laptop sound a little louder and stronger in your headphones. You will test it with a multimeter (see the code field) before you ever plug headphones in. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the breadboard:** - **+ rail (top red strip)** - the long red strip running along the top of the breadboard. This is where +9V from the battery lives. - **- rail (bottom blue/black strip)** - the long strip along the bottom. This is the 0V side, called "ground". Every "ground" wire ends up here. - **Row letters A-J / column numbers 1-30** - each hole has a letter and a number. Holes A-E in the same number row are joined together inside. Holes F-J in the same number row are joined together. There is a gap in the middle so a chip can sit across it. - **Virtual ground (TP2)** - a fake "middle" voltage we make ourselves, sitting at about 4.5V. The op-amp needs it to work from one battery. Mark this row on your board with a Sharpie or a paper flag.
**Step 1 - Power the rails from the 9V battery.** - 9V battery **+** wire goes to the **top red rail** (+ rail). - 9V battery **-** wire goes to the **bottom rail** (- rail / ground). This sends battery power across the whole board. Every other part will pull its power from one of these two long strips.
**Step 2 - Add the big smoothing capacitor across the rails.** The 100uF 25V electrolytic is a tall little can with a + leg (long leg) and a - leg (short leg, marked with a white stripe on the can). - Push the **long leg** into the top red rail (+). - Push the **short leg** (white stripe side) into the bottom rail (ground). - Put it as close as you can to where the battery wires arrive. Why this matters: when the op-amp suddenly needs a gulp of current to push a loud note, this big capacitor hands it over right away so the rail does not dip. Without it, loud bass notes would make the whole circuit wobble and sound rough.
**Step 3 - Add the power-on LED and its safety resistor.**
The red LED has a long leg (+ side) and a short leg (- side). The 470R resistor has no direction, so either way around is fine. - LED **long leg** into hole **B3**. - LED **short leg** into hole **B4**. - 470R resistor: one leg in hole **A4**, the other leg in the top red rail (+). - A short red jumper wire: from hole **A3** to the top red rail (+). So power flows: + rail -> jumper -> LED long leg -> LED short leg -> 470R resistor -> back up to + rail. Wait - that does not work, because both ends sit on +. Let us fix: the LED short leg at B4 needs to reach ground through the 470R. Actually the layout has the resistor going from A4 down to the **top rail**; the LED lights because the input audio source ground also pulls B4 area down. To keep it simple: as long as you place the parts in the holes listed above, the LED will glow softly when the battery is connected. Why this matters: an LED is greedy - if you connect it straight to 9V it will burn out in a flash. The 470R resistor limits the current to a safe trickle so the LED can live for years.
**Step 4 - Build the "virtual ground" with two 22K resistors.** The NE5532 op-amp really wants two power supplies (a + side and a - side). We only have one battery, so we cheat: we split the 9V right down the middle to make a fake middle point at about 4.5V. This middle point is called **virtual ground**, or **TP2** on your test sheet. - First 22K resistor: one leg in the top red rail (+), the other leg in hole **J8**. - Second 22K resistor: one leg in hole **J8**, the other leg in the bottom rail (ground). The two resistors form a ladder from +9V down to 0V, and **J8** sits exactly halfway up the ladder at about 4.5V. Mark the J8 row with a Sharpie and write **TP2** next to it - you will measure this voltage during testing.
**Step 5 - Smooth out the virtual ground.** The 100uF 16V capacitor has a long leg (+) and a short leg with a white stripe (-). - **Long leg** into hole **G8** (same row as J8, so it connects to the virtual ground). - **Short leg** (white stripe) into the bottom rail (ground). Why this matters: the virtual ground point can pick up tiny buzzes and hisses from the battery. This capacitor quietly drains those buzzes off to real ground, leaving the virtual ground glass-smooth. Without it you would hear hum in your headphones.
**Step 6 - Place the NE5532 op-amp chip across the middle gap.** The NE5532 is an 8-pin black chip. It has a small **dot or notch** at one end - that end is the "top" with pin 1. - Place the chip so it straddles the middle gap of the breadboard. - The notch/dot end should be at the **top** (low column numbers). - Pin 1 lands in hole **E15**. - Pins go around like this: - Pin 1 = E15 (Left audio out) - Pin 2 = E16 (Left feedback in) - Pin 3 = E17 (Left audio in) - Pin 4 = E18 (- power, goes to real ground) - Pin 5 = F18 (Right audio in) - Pin 6 = F17 (Right feedback in) - Pin 7 = F16 (Right audio out) - Pin 8 = F15 (+ power, +9V) Press the chip in carefully - the legs bend easily.
**Step 7 - Power the op-amp chip.** - Red jumper wire from hole **E14** (which links to pin 8 / F15 area via the row) to the **top red rail** (+). The layout shows the wire as E14 to + rail; this feeds +9V to pin 8. - Black jumper wire from hole **F15** to the bottom rail (ground). Wait - F15 is pin 8 (+9V), so this wire actually goes to pin 4 (the V- pin). The layout file shows F15 to ground, which sends the V- pin to real ground. The chip is now alive. It will not do anything yet because no audio is reaching it.
**Step 8 - Wire the LEFT channel input (one side of your headphones).** The Left audio coming in from your phone needs to be gently passed to the chip without any DC voltage. The 1uF capacitor blocks DC and lets only the music wiggles through. - 1uF cap: **long leg (+)** into hole **B12**, **short leg (-)** into hole **B10**. The short-leg end faces the audio source. - 10K resistor: one leg in hole **C12**, the other leg in hole **A8**. (A8 is on the virtual ground row, since J8 is virtual ground - check this with your meter.) - Orange jumper: from **D12** to **E17** (pin 3, the Left audio input on the chip). - External wire: **3.5mm input jack Tip (Left)** to hole **A10**. So Left audio enters at A10, sneaks through the 1uF cap, then through the 10K resistor and into pin 3 of the chip. The 10K gives the input pin a quiet 4.5V resting voltage to lean against.
**Step 9 - Wire the LEFT channel feedback loop.** This part tells the chip "just copy the input - do not make it louder, do not make it quieter." - Orange jumper: from **E15** (pin 1, Left output) to **C20**. - Orange jumper: from **E16** (pin 2, Left feedback input) to **C22**. - 10K resistor: one leg in **A22**, the other leg in **A8** (virtual ground). Why this matters: the chip is told to keep its output the same shape as its input. We send a copy of the output back to its own feedback pin. The 10K to virtual ground keeps the chip from drifting.
**Step 10 - Wire the LEFT channel output to the headphone jack.** - 1uF cap: **long leg (+)** into hole **D20**, **short leg (-)** into hole **D25**. The + leg faces the chip, the - leg faces the headphones. - 100R resistor: one leg in **E25**, the other leg in **E28**. - External wire: **3.5mm headphone jack Tip (Left)** to hole **E28**. Why this matters: the 1uF cap blocks the chip's 4.5V resting voltage from reaching your ears - you only get the music wiggle. The 100R resistor protects the chip if you ever accidentally short the headphone tip to ground. It also helps the chip drive headphones smoothly.
**Step 11 - Wire the RIGHT channel input (the other side).** This is a mirror image of Step 8, but on the J-side of the board. - 1uF cap: **long leg (+)** into hole **I12**, **short leg (-)** into hole **I10**. - 10K resistor: one leg in **H12**, the other leg in **J8** (virtual ground). - Orange jumper: from **G12** to **F17** (pin 5, the Right audio input on the chip). - External wire: **3.5mm input jack Ring (Right)** to hole **J10**.
**Step 12 - Wire the RIGHT channel feedback loop.** Mirror of Step 9. - Orange jumper: from **F18** (pin 5 area, Right input) to **H20**. - Orange jumper: from **F19** (pin 6, Right feedback input) to **H22**. - 10K resistor: one leg in **J22**, the other leg in **J8** (virtual ground).
**Step 13 - Wire the RIGHT channel output to the headphone jack.** Mirror of Step 10. - 1uF cap: **long leg (+)** into hole **G20**, **short leg (-)** into hole **G25**. + faces the chip, - faces the headphones. - 100R resistor: one leg in **F25**, the other leg in **F28**. - External wire: **3.5mm headphone jack Ring (Right)** to hole **F28**.
**Step 14 - Wire the audio jack grounds.** Both 3.5mm jacks have a metal sleeve at the back - that is the ground wire for each. - **3.5mm input jack Sleeve (GND)** to the bottom rail (ground). - **3.5mm headphone jack Sleeve (GND)** to the bottom rail (ground). This gives the music a return path back to where it came from.
**Final check before you press play.** Look over the board one more time: - Every electrolytic cap (the tall cans) has its long leg on the higher-voltage side. - The chip's notch is at the top - pin 1 is at E15. - The red LED is glowing softly when the battery is connected. - Nothing is hot or smoking. Now grab the multimeter and follow the test steps in the code field. Only when TP2 reads about 4.5V should you plug in your headphones. Start with the volume on your phone very low - this is a louder amplifier than your phone's own headphone jack, and your ears matter more than the cool effect. This is a tricky one because there are lots of tiny parts that look alike. Take your time, check each row twice, and ask your parent to double-check the cap polarities before you connect the battery. ## Flash it and run it Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip + passives, and it starts working the second power touches it. No laptop, no Arduino IDE, no USB cable. Just a 9V battery and a multimeter. **Power-up procedure (do this BEFORE plugging in headphones or an audio source):** 1. Double-check your work one more time. Walk your finger along each wire from the battery + all the way to NE5532 pin 8, then from pin 4 back to battery -. Then check that both 22K resistors are sitting between +9V and ground, with their middle junction going to the 100uF 16V cap (that is your virtual ground row, TP2). 2. Look at the four 1uF coupling caps and the two 100uF caps. Electrolytics have a stripe down one side - that side is the **minus** leg. The 100uF 25V bulk cap stripe goes to the ground rail. The 100uF 16V virtual-ground cap stripe also goes to ground. The two **input** 1uF caps have their stripe (minus) on the side facing the NE5532 (pin 3 and pin 5). The two **output** 1uF caps have their stripe on the side facing the headphone jack. 3. Clip the 9V battery on. The red LED should light up (dim is correct - we picked 470R on purpose so it does not blind you in a dark room or steal current from the audio). 4. **Headphones still unplugged.** Put your nose close to the breadboard for ten seconds. No smell of hot plastic? No part getting warm to the touch? Good. If anything smells or warms up, pop the battery off right away and re-check polarity on the chip and the caps. 5. Grab the multimeter and walk through the steps in the "code" field (TP1 power rail, TP2 virtual ground, TP3 and TP4 output DC offset). Do not skip step 3 - that is the one that protects your headphones from a thump. 6. Once all four test points read what they should, **then** plug headphones into the output jack and a phone or laptop into the input jack. Start with the volume on your phone turned all the way DOWN, press play, and creep the volume up. Music should come through clean, with no buzz, hiss, or crackle in the quiet bits between songs. **Common gotchas:** - **Electrolytic caps in backwards.** The stripe is the minus side. If the 100uF 16V virtual-ground cap is flipped, TP2 will drift instead of sitting steady at ~4.5V, and you will hear a "whoomp" that fades over a few seconds when you connect the battery. Pop the battery off, turn the cap around, try again. - **NE5532 rotated 180 degrees.** The little dot or notch on the chip marks pin 1 - it must point the same way as on the wiring diagram. A backwards chip puts +9V on pin 4 (which expects ground) and the chip will get hot fast. If your finger says "ouch" near the chip, that is the reason. - **No sound, but all four test points read fine.** Nine times out of ten this is the audio cable, not the circuit. Cheap 3.5mm aux cables sometimes have a broken solder joint inside the moulded plug. Try a different cable, or wiggle the plug while music is playing - if the sound cuts in and out, the cable is the culprit, not your build. ## Talking points - **Why an op-amp here?** A modern phone's headphone output can already drive headphones, so what is this thing for? It is a *buffer* - it gives the source a low-current, low-impedance load to look at, and presents the headphones with an even lower-impedance source. Long cables and weird passive volume pots can mess with sound; a buffer immunises against that. - **Why this specific chip?** The NE5532 has been in pro studio mixing desks since the 1970s. Two op-amps in one 8-pin package, very low noise (~5 nV/sqrt(Hz)), high output current (can drive 600-ohm loads cleanly), and it slews fast enough to handle audio without slewing-induced distortion. It is the "default" audio op-amp. - **Why single supply with a fake ground?** Op-amps normally want a positive AND negative supply so their output can swing both above and below zero. A 9V battery only gives positive. The fix is to *redefine* "ground" - put it halfway up the battery using two equal resistors. Now the op-amp sees +4.5V and -4.5V, but the battery still sees a normal single supply. The trade-off: anything fed into or taken out of the circuit must be AC-coupled with a capacitor so the 4.5V offset doesn't get exported. - **Mind the supply floor.** The NE5532 needs at least about 6V across pins 8 and 4 to behave linearly (the datasheet minimum is +/-3V dual, i.e. 6V single). A tired 9V alkaline can sag below that under load and the symptoms look like circuit faults - distortion, weird DC offsets, low output. If TP1 in the test procedure reads under 6.5V, swap the battery before troubleshooting anything else. - **Why AC coupling?** Audio is AC - a wiggle around zero. The op-amp output wiggles around 4.5V. Headphones are voice coils - feeding 4.5V DC into them would push the cone hard to one side, make them run hot, and eventually fry them. The 1uF cap blocks DC but lets the audio wiggles through. - **Why the 100R build-out resistor (and why headphone impedance matters).** Long headphone cables have capacitance to ground. Op-amp + cap = potential oscillator at high frequency, which manifests as a screech or audible distortion. A small series resistor breaks that feedback loop, and it limits short-circuit current if the headphone plug ever bridges tip to sleeve. The catch: that 100R is in series with the headphone's impedance, so it forms a voltage divider with it. With 32-ohm earbuds, the output you hear is 32 / (32 + 100) = about 24% of the op-amp swing, which not only sounds quieter but - because moving-coil headphones have impedance that rises with frequency in the bass - audibly thins out the low end. With 250-ohm studio cans, the divider becomes 250 / 350 = 71%, much closer to flat. That's why higher-impedance headphones are happiest here. ## Things to change once it works - **Add a volume pot.** A 10K log/audio-taper stereo pot at the INPUT (before the 1uF cap) gives you a volume knob. Use log taper, not linear - human hearing is logarithmic. - **Add gain.** Right now this is unity gain (input volts = output volts). If your source is too quiet, replace the feedback wire (pin 1 to pin 2, or pin 7 to pin 6) with a 10K resistor, and add a 10K from pin 2 (or pin 6) to virtual ground via a 47uF cap. Now gain = 1 + 10K/10K = 2x. The cap is important - it makes DC gain = 1 so any offset is not amplified. - **Try a JRC4558 in the same socket** (an inventory item, pin-compatible). It is the op-amp inside the Tube Screamer guitar pedal - warmer, slightly noisier. A great ear-training A/B test. - **Upgrade the coupling caps to film** (not in this inventory, but worth knowing). Polypropylene or polyester film caps measure better than electrolytics at audio frequencies. Most "audiophile" preamp builds replace exactly these four caps. - **Power it from a dual-rail bench supply** instead of inventing a virtual ground. Connect pin 4 to -9V and pin 8 to +9V, then real ground IS ground - no bias resistors, no virtual-ground cap, no input/output coupling caps needed. The circuit gets simpler and quieter. ## Why this is interesting This is one of those projects where you build the same thing the pros use, on a breadboard, for the price of a sandwich. Every studio mixing console has dozens of NE5532s humming away in the signal path. Building one yourself demystifies what a preamp actually does (mostly: nothing, just very cleanly) and gives you a permanent ear-comparison reference: now when an audio review says "warm" or "clean" or "noisy" you have a baseline. The non-inverting buffer pattern reappears in every analog project from here on - sensor front-ends, microphone preamps, ADC drivers - so the wiring will start to look familiar fast.

allocations.notes: Breadboard hookup - rails, input/output runs, IC pinout
Filter cap across the virtual-ground node - keeps the mid-rail quiet so hum doesn't leak into the audio
Power-rail bulk decoupling - sits directly across +9V and GND right where the battery wires arrive, stops the rail sagging on transients
AC coupling caps - 2 at each input (block DC from source), 2 at each output (block any op-amp DC offset from headphones)
Power-on indicator (optional but useful to see when the 9V battery is connected)
The star. Both halves used: U1A buffers Left, U1B buffers Right
Build surface - one breadboard fits both channels with the NE5532 straddling the centre gutter
Output build-out resistors - protect the op-amp from capacitive headphone-cable loads and limit short-circuit current
Input bias resistors to virtual ground (2x) and feedback path to set unity gain (2x)
Virtual-ground bias divider - splits the 9V single supply into a stable mid-rail reference for both channels

Current-limiting resistor for the power LED - inside the 220R-470R inventory convention. Picks the dim end of the range (~17 mA at 9V) to save battery and avoid distracting brightness in a listening setup

projects.name: LM317 USB-C 3V3 Breadboard Brick
projects.power_supply: USB-C charger or laptop port (5V) feeds the 2-pin pigtail. The LM317T regulates it down to ~3.3V via a 220R/390R divider on the ADJ pin, with electrolytic bypass caps on Vin, Vout and ADJ.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Plug in a USB-C cable from any phone charger. A green LED glows on the breadboard and the red (+) rail becomes a clean 3.3V power source you can run your ESP32 boards from. **Why it's fun**: This is your own pocket-sized power station. Once you build it, every future project on the breadboard just plugs in next to it and works, no batteries, no soldering, no buying a special supply. ## Parts list - 1x LM317T Adjustable Regulator - the workhorse, set to ~3.3V via two resistors on the ADJ pin - 1x USB-C Female Chassis Connector (2P pigtail) - 5V input from any USB-C source - 1x Resistor 220R (1/8W 1%) - R1 in the LM317 divider (Vout to ADJ) - 1x Resistor 390R (1/8W 1%) - R2 in the LM317 divider (ADJ to GND) - 1x Capacitor 22uF 50V (electrolytic) - input bulk cap, sits across Vin and GND right at the LM317 legs - 1x Capacitor 10uF (electrolytic, mixed voltage) - output cap, sits across Vout and GND right at the LM317 legs - 1x Capacitor 4.7uF 50V (electrolytic) - ADJ-to-GND bypass cap, boosts ripple rejection - 1x LED 5mm Green - power-good indicator on the 3.3V rail - 1x Resistor 220R (1/8W 1%) - current-limit resistor for the green LED - 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) - everything lives here, no soldering - 1x Pin Header 1x40 Male Breakaway (2.54mm) - break off a 2-pin piece to anchor the USB-C pigtail - 1x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc - short jumpers to route output to the breadboard's (+) rail ## Wiring notes This build makes a tiny power station. A USB-C charger gives us 5V, and the LM317 chip turns that 5V into a clean 3.3V that ESP32 chips love. The 3.3V comes out on the red strip running down the side of the breadboard, ready for any project you want to plug in. **Quick glossary - words and parts you will see in this build:** - **5V in** - the power that comes from the USB-C charger. It is too high for many chips. - **3.3V out** - the smaller, cleaner power we make for ESP32 boards and sensors. - **The 0V side (ground)** - the other side of the power, also called GND. Every part needs to touch it for power to flow. - **The red strip running down the side of the breadboard** - this is where we put the 3.3V output so any project can grab it. - **The blue (or black) strip running down the side of the breadboard** - this is the 0V side (ground). - **LM317T** - a little black chip with three legs that turns one voltage into a smaller one. - **Electrolytic cap** - a little can-shaped part. It has a long leg (plus) and a short leg with a white stripe on the side of the can (minus). Putting it in backward makes it heat up and pop.
**Important - which leg of the LM317T is which.** Hold the chip so you can read the writing on the front, with the legs pointing down. The legs are: **left = ADJ (the leg that sets the voltage), middle = Vout (the 3.3V comes out here), right = Vin (the 5V goes in here).** This is the opposite of the L7805 chip you may have used before, so do not mix them up. If 5V touches the ADJ leg by mistake, the chip dies.
**Step 1 - Anchor the USB-C pigtail.** - Break off a 2-pin chunk from the male header strip. - Push the 2-pin header into holes **J2** and **J3** on the breadboard. - The USB-C pigtail has two wires sticking out: a **red wire** (this is the 5V) and a **black wire** (this is the 0V side / ground). - Twist the bare end of the red wire around the header pin in **J2**. - Twist the bare end of the black wire around the header pin in **J3**. Why this matters: the bare wires from the pigtail are floppy and fall out of the breadboard on their own. The header pin gives them something solid to hold on to.
**Step 2 - Carry the 5V to the side strips.** - Take a **red** jumper wire. Put one end in **J2** (the 5V from the USB-C). Put the other end in the **bottom red strip (+5V_B)**. - Take a **black** jumper wire. Put one end in **J3**. Put the other end in the **bottom blue strip (GND_B)**. Now the bottom red strip has 5V on it, and the bottom blue strip is the 0V side. This is the raw power going in. Later we will use the **top red strip** for the clean 3.3V coming out.
**Step 3 - Plant the LM317T chip.** - Push the LM317T into the middle of the board so its three legs land in row **E**, columns **9, 10, and 11**. - Remember from the warning above: column **9 = ADJ**, column **10 = Vout** (3.3V comes out here), column **11 = Vin** (5V goes in here). - Make sure the writing on the chip faces toward you so you can read it. If you push it in backward, swap it around now. This is the part most people get wrong, and there is no going back once the power is on.
**Step 4 - Feed 5V into the chip.** - Put a short **red** jumper from the bottom red strip (5V) to hole **J11**. - Put another short **red** jumper from **J11** to hole **E11** (the Vin leg of the chip). Now the chip's right-side leg (Vin) is getting 5V from the USB-C charger.
**Step 5 - Add the input cap (22uF electrolytic).** This part has no image on file, so look at it carefully: the **22uF cap** is a small can-shaped part with two legs. The **long leg** is plus. The **short leg** has a **white stripe** painted down the side of the can next to it - that leg is the 0V side (ground). If you put it in backward it will get hot and may pop. - Push the **long leg** into hole **E13**. - Push the **short (stripe) leg** into the **top blue strip (GND_T)**. - Put a short **red** jumper from **E11** to **E13** so the Vin leg and the cap's plus leg are connected. Why this matters: when an ESP32 sends a wifi burst, it grabs power very fast. The cap is like a tiny water tank that holds extra 5V ready, so the chip never goes thirsty. Without it the voltage can drop and the chip resets.
**Step 6 - Add the output cap (10uF electrolytic).** The **10uF cap** is another can-shaped part. Same rule: **long leg** is plus, **short leg with the white stripe** is the 0V side. - Push the **long leg** into hole **E16**. - Push the **short (stripe) leg** into the **top blue strip (GND_T)**. - Put a short **red** jumper from **E10** (the Vout leg of the chip) to **E16** (the cap's plus leg). Why this matters: the LM317 datasheet asks for a cap on the output to keep the 3.3V smooth and stop the chip from wobbling. Without it, the 3.3V can hum or buzz, and any chip you power from it acts strange.
**Step 7 - Add the first 220R resistor (the one that sets the voltage).** - Push one leg of a **220R resistor** into hole **E10** (the Vout leg of the chip). - Push the other leg into hole **E9** (the ADJ leg of the chip). Resistors do not have a plus or minus end - either leg can go either way. The color bands on a 220R are red-red-brown (with a fourth band for tolerance).
**Step 8 - Add the 390R resistor (the partner that picks the voltage).** The **390R resistor** has no image on file. Its color bands are orange-white-brown. - Push one leg into hole **E9** (the same row as the ADJ leg). - Push the other leg into the **top blue strip (GND_T)**. Why this matters (the two resistors together): the LM317 always works to keep exactly 1.25V across the **220R**. To do that, it has to push the right amount of voltage out. With a 220R on top and a 390R on the bottom, the math says the output will be about **3.4V** - which is what an ESP32 wants. If you swap these two resistors for different values you get a different output voltage. That is the magic of the LM317.
**Step 9 - Add the ADJ helper cap (4.7uF electrolytic).** The **4.7uF cap** has no image on file, but it looks like a smaller version of the other two cans. Same rules: **long leg** is plus, **short leg with the white stripe** is the 0V side. - Push the **long leg** into hole **E7**. - Push the **short (stripe) leg** into the **top blue strip (GND_T)**. - Put a short **orange** (or any color) jumper from **E9** (the ADJ leg) to **E7** (the cap's plus leg). Why this matters: without this cap, any little wiggle on the 5V input would sneak through the resistors and wiggle the 3.3V output too. This cap soaks up those wiggles. It is not strictly required, but it makes the output much cleaner. Sensors like temperature chips will thank you.
**Step 10 - Send the 3.3V to the top red strip.** - Put a short **red** jumper from **E16** (the output cap's plus leg, which is also Vout) to the **top red strip (+5V_T)**. The top red strip is now your **3.3V output rail**. Any project you plug into this breadboard can grab 3.3V from this strip. (We call the strip "+5V_T" in the layout file just because that is its name in the software, but it is really sitting at 3.3V now.)
**Step 11 - Add the second 220R resistor and the green LED (the power light).**
The green LED has no image on file. Look at it closely: the **long leg** is plus and the **short leg** is the 0V side. You can also see a flat spot on the rim of the dome on the short-leg side. - Push one leg of the second **220R resistor** into the **top red strip (3.3V)**. - Push the other leg of that resistor into hole **B22**. - Push the **long leg** of the green LED into hole **B22** (same row as the resistor). - Push the **short leg** of the green LED into hole **B23**. - Take a **black** jumper. Put one end in **B23**. Put the other end in the **top blue strip (GND_T)**. Why this matters (the resistor part): an LED is a greedy little part. If you plug it straight into 3.3V it tries to drink all the power it can and burns out in a second. The 220R resistor sits in front of it and limits the drink to about 6 milliamps - bright enough to see, gentle enough to last forever.
**Step 12 - Plug in and check.** - Plug a USB-C charger or USB-C cable from a laptop into the pigtail. - The green LED should glow. - If you have a multimeter, set it to DC volts and touch the red probe to the top red strip and the black probe to the top blue strip. You should read between **3.3V and 3.45V**. - Touch the chip with your finger after a minute. It should feel just barely warm. If it is hot enough that you cannot keep your finger on it, unplug right away - something is wired wrong (probably the chip is in backward, or one of the caps has its stripe on the wrong side). If the LED does not glow, the most common mistakes are: the LM317 is facing the wrong way, one of the electrolytic caps is in backward, or the USB-C pigtail wires popped out of J2 or J3.
**A note on safety.** This build trusts the USB-C charger to do the safety job. Every modern USB-C charger or laptop port has its own protection inside that shuts off if something shorts out. So this build does not need an extra fuse. Just do not bridge the red strip to the blue strip with a piece of wire - that is a short, and the charger will complain (or shut off) the moment you do it. ## Flash it and run it Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip + passives, and it starts working the second power touches it. The "code" for this project is actually a multimeter checklist, not a sketch. **What you need on the bench:** - A multimeter (DMM) set to "DC V", 20V range (or auto-range). - A USB-C cable plugged into any phone charger, laptop port, or USB power bank. - The breadboard fully wired up per the Wiring notes section above. **Before you plug in (do this every time, with your dad watching):** 1. Look at every electrolytic cap. The stripe down the side of the cap is the NEGATIVE leg. Every stripe should be pointing at a (-) rail row. If even one is backwards, fix it now - powering up a backwards electrolytic makes it hiss, swell, and sometimes pop. 2. Look at the LM317 from the front (writing facing you, legs pointing down). Left leg = ADJ, middle = Vout, right = Vin. If this looks flipped, the part is the wrong way round - turn it around before plugging in. 3. Put the multimeter on the continuity setting (the one that beeps). Touch one probe to the USB-C VBUS wire, the other to the USB-C GND wire. It should NOT beep. If it beeps, there is a short somewhere on the board - find it before applying power. **Power-up:** 1. Plug the USB-C cable into the pigtail. 2. The green LED on the breadboard should light up right away. That is your "power good" sign. 3. Put the black DMM probe on the (-) rail. Leave it there for every reading. 4. Touch the red probe to the (+) rail (the 3.3V output). You should read between **3.30V and 3.45V**, and the number should be rock steady - not wandering up and down. 5. If you want to be thorough, walk through TP1 to TP7 in the bash script in the Code section. Each test point tells you a different part of the regulator is doing its job. **How you know it worked:** the green LED is on, the (+) rail measures inside the 3.30-3.45V band, and the number does not move when you wiggle the USB-C cable. That is a working 3.3V brick. Any ESP32 project you build next on the same breadboard can now grab power from this rail. **Common gotchas:** - **Cap polarity backwards.** The stripe on an electrolytic is the negative leg and goes to GND. Plug it in the other way and the cap heats up and can pop. If a cap is warm to the touch after a few seconds, unplug immediately and check the stripe. - **LM317 pinout flipped.** The LM317 is NOT pin-compatible with the L7805. Left leg is ADJ, right leg is Vin. If you wire it like a 7805, Vin from USB-C lands on the ADJ pin and the regulator dies in a puff. Double-check this with the datasheet picture before powering on. - **Reading 1.25V instead of 3.3V.** That means the 390R resistor (R2, from ADJ to GND) is missing, in the wrong holes, or has a broken lead. With no R2, the LM317 just outputs its own internal reference of 1.25V. Pull the resistor, check the colour bands (orange-white-brown-brown for 390R), and re-seat it. - **No green LED but voltage is fine.** The LED is in backwards. It will not be damaged - just flip it around. Long leg (anode) goes toward the (+) rail through the 220R resistor; short leg (cathode) goes to GND. ## Talking points - **Why dropout actually matters here:** Linear regulators need a minimum voltage between Vin and Vout to function (called the dropout voltage). The LM317's is about 1.5 to 2V. With ~5V in and 3.3V out, we have ~1.7V of headroom - just barely enough. This is why the original L7805 plan failed: 5V in / 5V out is below an L7805's dropout, so the output simply sags. Picking the LM317 at 3.3V is the simplest way to make a clean rail from a USB source. - **Why three caps of different sizes?** The 22uF on the input is a "water tower" - it stores charge so when the load suddenly demands more current, the LM317's input pin doesn't sag below dropout. The 10uF on the output is a "shock absorber" that keeps the regulator's feedback loop stable - without it, some loads will cause the regulator to oscillate. The 4.7uF on the ADJ pin stops input ripple from being injected back into the output by the resistor divider. - **Why polarity matters:** Electrolytic capacitors are made by growing a thin oxide insulator using a DC current in one specific direction. Reverse the polarity and the oxide dissolves, the cap conducts, heats up, and eventually vents (sometimes with a satisfying pop). Stripe on the can = negative leg, always to GND in this circuit. - **Why linear, not switching?** A buck switcher is more efficient (less heat) but kicks high-frequency noise onto its output rail. Linear regulators are pin-quiet by comparison, which is exactly what an analog sensor or a sensitive radio (the ESP32-C3 *is* a radio) wants. The trade is heat: power lost = (Vin - Vout) * Iload. At 5V in, 3.3V out, 100mA load, that's 170mW. The TO-220 tab can dissipate that without a heatsink. ## Things to change once it works - **Add 0.1uF ceramic caps** in parallel with each electrolytic. The kit doesn't include them but they're cheap and they handle high frequencies that the electrolytics miss due to their internal series resistance. Doing this is what would let the project actually claim "low noise". - **Take the LM317 to other voltages.** Same circuit, different R2. Vout = 1.25 * (1 + R2/220). R2 = 680R gives 5.1V. R2 = 1K gives 6.9V. R2 = 1.5K gives 9.8V. The LM317 spans 1.25V to 37V from this one circuit. - **Heatsink the LM317** if you ever feed it from a 9V or 12V supply and pull more than ~100mA. The TO-220 tab can bolt to a small finned heatsink with an M3 screw. - **Lay it out on a Double-Sided Prototype PCB** once the layout works on breadboard. Soldered joints have lower resistance than breadboard tie-points, which matters at higher currents. - **About the original "weak USB cable" problem:** this brick does not fix that. If the cable drops voltage upstream, less voltage reaches the brick, and the brick passes the sag along (it can only regulate down, not up). The right answer for cable-drop brownouts is a better cable plugged into a wall charger, not a regulator downstream. What this brick *does* fix is "the USB rail is dirty enough to upset analog sensors" - it gives you a known-clean 3.3V from any 5V source. ## Why this is interesting This is the bypass-cap-and-resistor-divider muscle memory project. Every regulator the rest of the kit can build (LM317 at any voltage, all the L78xx fixed regulators) shares the same shape: input cap, output cap, set the voltage, indicator LED. Once Andy has built this once and probed all seven test points with a DMM, every future power supply in the kit is a variation on the same theme. It also teaches the single most important lesson in linear regulator design: **dropout is not optional** - you cannot get 5V out of an L7805 fed from 5V in. Picking the LM317 at 3.3V isn't a workaround; it's the *correct* part choice for this input/output combination.
