#!/usr/bin/env bash
# LM317 3.3V Brick - Multimeter verification procedure
# ----------------------------------------------------
# This is a pure-analog power supply project, so the right test instrument
# is a multimeter (DMM) in DC volts mode, NOT a microcontroller. Reading a
# 3.3V rail with an Arduino Uno's ADC (5V reference) wastes half the ADC
# range and adds error - and worse, hides the regulator's behaviour behind
# a noisy ADC. So: probe the test points below with a DMM and tick them off.
#
# Set the DMM to "DC V", 20 V range (or auto-range).
# Black probe to the breadboard (-) rail (GND) for every reading except where
# noted otherwise.
#
# ---- Bench-up sequence (do this BEFORE plugging in USB-C) ----
#   1. Inspect cap polarities. The stripe on every electrolytic is the negative
#      leg. Stripe goes to GND. Get this wrong and the cap will vent.
#   2. Inspect LM317 leg order (TO-220, text side facing you, legs down):
#        pin 1 = ADJ (left)
#        pin 2 = Vout (middle)
#        pin 3 = Vin  (right)
#      NOTE: this is OPPOSITE to the L7805 pinout. Swap them by accident and
#      Vin meets ADJ and the part will let the smoke out.
#   3. DMM on continuity (beeper). Probe USB-C VBUS to USB-C GND on the
#      pigtail side. Should NOT beep. If it beeps you have a short - find it
#      before applying power.
#
# ---- Test points with USB-C plugged in ----
#   TP1: USB-C VBUS to GND   -> expect 4.75 to 5.25 V (depends on charger)
#   TP2: LM317 pin 3 (Vin) to GND
#                            -> within ~0.05 V of TP1 (no series resistor now)
#   TP3: LM317 pin 2 (Vout) to GND
#                            -> 3.30 to 3.45 V, rock steady
#                               (theoretical: 1.25 * (1 + 390/220) = 3.47 V;
#                                resistor tolerance + LM317 Vref tolerance
#                                spread it across that band)
#   TP4: LM317 pin 1 (ADJ) to GND
#                            -> TP3 minus 1.25 V (the LM317's internal Vref)
#                               i.e. about 2.05 to 2.20 V
#   TP5: Across the 22uF input cap
#                            -> same reading as TP2
#   TP6: Across the 10uF output cap
#                            -> same reading as TP3
#   TP7: Green LED anode to GND
#                            -> same as TP3 (no drop yet)
#         Green LED cathode to GND
#                            -> ~2.0 V (the LED's forward voltage above GND)
#
# ---- Pass criteria ----
#   TP3 reads 3.30 - 3.45 V with no load            -> PASS
#   TP3 sags below 3.20 V with no load              -> FAIL, see troubleshooting
#   TP3 reads ~Vin (~5 V)                            -> ADJ pin is floating or
#                                                       R2 is open. DISCONNECT.
#   LM317 too hot to touch within 30s, no load      -> oscillation or backwards
#                                                       cap. DISCONNECT.
#
# ---- Loaded test (after no-load passes) ----
#   Connect a 100R 1/4W+ resistor between the (+) rail and (-) rail. That draws
#   ~33 mA, similar to an ESP32 idle current.
#   TP3 should drop by no more than ~30 mV. If it sags significantly, the input
#   cap is too small or the USB cable is dropping voltage upstream.
#
# ---- Why no Arduino sketch ----
#   Power supplies are characterised by amplitude (DMM), ripple (scope), and
#   transient response (scope + electronic load). An MCU ADC can't do any of
#   those three well. A 3.50 GBP DMM does the first one perfectly.

echo "LM317 3.3V Brick verification - follow the steps in this script as a checklist."
echo "No actual commands to run; this is a bench procedure."

allocations.notes: Short jumpers to route Vout to the (+) rail and GND to the (-) rail
Output cap on the Vout pin. Datasheet calls for 1uF tantalum or 10uF electrolytic on the output for stability - the bigger value is the correct pick when using electros.
Input bulk cap on the Vin pin. Datasheet wants 0.1uF minimum but a larger electro holds the rail up during ESP32 radio bursts.
ADJ-to-GND bypass cap. Improves ripple rejection by ~15dB by stopping the divider from re-injecting input ripple into the ADJ pin.
Power-good indicator on the 3.3V output rail
Break off a 2-pin strip to anchor the flimsy USB-C pigtail wires into the breadboard
5V input from any USB-C charger or laptop port (2-pin = VBUS + GND only, no CC negotiation needed for legacy 5V default mode)
Everything lives on this breadboard; the (+) rail becomes the regulated 3.3V output

R1 in the LM317 divider, between Vout and ADJ. Sets the reference current (1.25V / 220R = 5.7mA). Substituted for the textbook 240R - same E12 family, output shifts to 3.30V instead of 3.32V.; Current-limit resistor for the green power LED ((3.3V - 2.0V Vf) / 220R = ~5.9mA, comfortably visible)
R2 in the LM317 divider, between ADJ and GND. Vout = 1.25 * (1 + 390/220) = 3.47V theoretical; bench tolerance lands in the 3.30-3.45V band, comfortably inside ESP32-C3 spec (3.0-3.6V).
Adjustable 3-terminal regulator in TO-220. Set to 3.30V via R1/R2 divider on ADJ pin.

projects.name: LM317T Constant-Current LED Driver
projects.power_supply: 6.5 V to 12 V DC from a 9 V battery or bench supply, fed to the +V rail of the breadboard (a 9 V battery is the easy choice; the LM317 needs ~3 V of dropout above the LED + Rset stack, so anything under ~6.5 V will fall out of regulation).
projects.description:
**What it is**: Hook up a 9V battery and the LED glows at the perfect brightness. Now swap in a fresh battery, or a weaker one, or wiggle the wires around - the LED stays the exact same brightness. It refuses to get any brighter or dimmer. **Why it's fun**: This is your first taste of a real engineering trick: a circuit that fights back to keep itself steady, no code required. Try to make the LED flicker by tapping the battery on and off - you can't, and that's the magic. ## Parts list - 1x LM317T Adjustable Regulator (TO-220, the star of the show) - 1x Resistor 56R (1/8W 1%) - this is "Rset", the only resistor that matters - 1x LED 5mm Red - the load we are driving (at a safe ~22 mA) - 1x Capacitor 10uF (electrolytic, rated >=16V) - input bulk decoupling - 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm - A handful of M-M jumper wires - A 6.5 V to 12 V supply (a 9 V battery is perfect, or a bench supply) No microcontroller. No code. Just one IC, one resistor, and a multimeter to prove it works. **LED derating note (important):** a generic 5mm through-hole LED is rated for ~20 to 30 mA continuous. We deliberately target ~22 mA with a 56R Rset to stay inside that envelope. If you ever see a tutorial that calls for 100 mA or more through a plain 5mm LED, ignore it - the LED will dim within hours and die within days. Higher currents belong on 1W "power LEDs" with a proper heatsink, not on indicator LEDs from a bag of 100. ## Wiring notes This build does not use a computer or a microcontroller. It is a pure analog circuit. The whole thing lives on the breadboard, powered by a 9V battery. **Quick glossary - words you will see in this build:** - **Breadboard** - the white plastic block with rows of holes. Push parts in, no soldering. - **Power rail** - the long red strip running down the side of the breadboard. We push +9V into here. - **Ground rail** - the long blue or black strip on the other side. This is the 0V side - ground. - **LM317T** - a tiny black chip with three legs. It is the brain of this circuit and will hold the LED's brightness steady. - **Long leg / short leg** - the way we tell which side of the LED and capacitor is plus and which is minus.
**The big idea (read this first - it is the trick of the whole project).** The LM317T chip has a built-in rule it never breaks: it will always force exactly **1.25 volts** to sit between two of its legs (Vout and ADJ). We are going to use that rule in a sneaky way. We will put one resistor between those two legs, and then dangle the LED off the end. Because the chip is forcing 1.25V across the resistor, the resistor is forced to pass a certain amount of current. That same current then flows through the LED. With a 56 ohm resistor, the math says about **22 milliamps** - a happy, safe brightness for a 5mm LED. No matter what the battery does (fresh 9V, tired 8V, fancy 12V supply), the LED keeps getting the exact same current. That is constant-current. **There is no separate resistor for the LED.** The whole circuit IS the current limiter. Do not add one. **Step 1 - Meet the LM317T and put it on the board.** The LM317T is a black plastic chip with three metal legs and a metal tab on the back. Hold it so the printed text is facing you. From left to right the legs are: - Leg 1 (left) - **ADJ** (the "adjust" pin) - Leg 2 (middle) - **Vout** (where regulated power comes out) - Leg 3 (right) - **Vin** (where battery power goes in) Push the chip into the breadboard at row 10 so each leg lands in a separate row: - ADJ leg goes in hole **E9** - Vout leg goes in hole **E10** - Vin leg goes in hole **E11** Spread the legs a tiny bit if you need to. They should each land in their own row so they don't touch each other.
**Step 2 - Feed power into the chip (Vin).** - Run a short red jumper wire from **E11** (the Vin leg) over to the red power rail at the top of the breadboard. This connects the battery's +9V to the chip's input leg. The chip eats raw battery voltage on this leg and serves up a steady, controlled current out the other side.
**Step 3 - Add the smoothing capacitor.** The 10uF electrolytic capacitor is shaped like a tiny soda can with two legs. It has a **plus side and a minus side** - getting this backwards can make it pop, so look carefully: - The **long leg** is plus (+). - The **short leg** is minus (-). The minus side also has a white stripe with a "-" mark printed down the can. Place it on the board: - Long leg (plus) into **E5** - Short leg (minus) into **E3** Now wire it to the rails: - Red jumper from **E5** to the red power rail at the top. - Black jumper from **E3** to the blue/black ground rail at the bottom. **Why this matters:** The capacitor is like a tiny rechargeable battery sitting right next to the chip. When the chip suddenly wants a gulp of current, the capacitor hands it over instantly, before the long wires from the battery can catch up. Without it, the LED can flicker or the chip can act weird. It is the "calm down" part of the circuit.
**Step 4 - Place the 56 ohm resistor (the heart of the trick).** The 56 ohm resistor sets the brightness. The colored bands on it should read **green - blue - black - gold** (or **green - blue - black - black - brown** if it has five bands). - One leg into **B10** (this is the same row as the chip's Vout leg). - Other leg into **B15**. Resistors don't care which way around they go, so either leg can be in either hole. **Why this matters:** This little resistor is the dial that picks the current. Smaller number = brighter LED but more heat. Bigger number = dimmer LED. With 56 ohms, the math is `1.25V / 56 ohms = 0.022 amps = 22 milliamps`. That is right in the sweet spot for a 5mm indicator LED.
**Step 5 - Connect the chip's ADJ leg into the loop.** We need to tell the chip "watch THIS spot to keep 1.25V steady." We do that by jumping the ADJ leg over to the far end of the resistor. - Orange jumper from **E10** to **A10** - this is just bridging across the same row to give us room to work on the left side of the board. - Orange jumper from **E9** (the chip's ADJ leg) to **A9**. - Orange jumper from **A9** to **A15** (this connects the ADJ leg to the same column as the far end of the resistor). After this step, the resistor sits perfectly between Vout and ADJ. The chip will now lock 1.25V across it.
**Step 6 - Add the LED.** The LED has a plus and minus side too: - **Long leg** = plus side. Goes toward the chip side. - **Short leg** = minus side. The short-leg side also has a flat spot on the round plastic dome. Goes toward ground. First, get a wire over to the LED's row: - Orange jumper from **B15** to **E20**. Now plant the LED: - Long leg into **E20**. - Short leg into **E21**. Then send the short leg to ground: - Black jumper from **E21** to the blue/black ground rail at the bottom.
**Step 7 - Hook up the 9V battery.** - Battery **+** (red wire from the battery clip) into the red power rail at the top. - Battery **-** (black wire from the battery clip) into the blue/black ground rail at the bottom. Snap the battery on. The LED should light up at a calm, steady brightness right away.
**Cool experiment to try.** Once it works on the 9V battery, try swapping in a 12V bench supply, or even a half-dead 7V battery. Watch the LED. It stays the same brightness. That is the magic - the LM317T is silently soaking up the difference. If you have a multimeter and know how to use it, measure the voltage across the 56 ohm resistor. It will read very close to 1.25V no matter what the input voltage is. **Heads up:** the LM317T might get a little warm to the touch, especially with the 12V supply. That is normal - it is burning off the extra voltage as heat. If it gets too hot to touch, unplug and check your wiring. **Why no separate resistor for the LED?** In every other "first LED" project, there is a resistor in series with the LED to limit current. Here, the resistor between Vout and ADJ is doing that job - but in a much smarter way. A plain resistor would let the brightness change as the battery drains. The LM317T trick keeps it locked. That is why this circuit is worth learning. ## Flash it and run it Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip + passives, and the LED lights up the second power touches the rails. No laptop, no Arduino IDE, no code. Your "program" is the 56R resistor. **Power-up procedure (do this with your dad watching):** 1. **Eyeball it before plugging in.** Check three things one more time: the LM317's flat metal tab is facing the way the diagram shows, the long leg of the 10uF cap is on the +V rail (short leg / stripe on GND), and the long leg of the LED is on the ADJ pin side. 2. **Set your multimeter to DC volts** (the V with a straight line, not the squiggly one) and clip it across the +V rail and GND rail with no power yet. It should read 0. 3. **Connect the 9V battery** (or turn on your bench supply, set to anywhere from 6.5V to 12V). Watch the meter jump up to the supply voltage, and watch the **red LED turn on at a nice steady glow**. That's it - the circuit is working. 4. **Try the magic test.** Without unplugging, gently squeeze the battery clip so the voltage sags a bit, or if you have a bench supply, slowly turn the knob from 12V down toward 7V. The LED brightness **should not change**. That refusal to dim is the LM317 doing its job. 5. **Now grab the multimeter to prove it with numbers.** Follow Step 2 in the bash script above: switch the meter to DC volts and touch the probes to **Vout (pin 2)** and **ADJ (pin 1)** of the LM317. You should read **1.20 V to 1.30 V**. That tiny voltage across the 56R resistor is what sets the ~22 mA going through the LED. 6. **(Bonus, optional) Measure the actual current.** Step 3 in the script walks through it: pull the wire from the LED's short leg to the GND rail, set the meter to **DC mA** (200 mA range), and put the meter inline where that wire used to be. Expect around 20 to 24 mA. That's the punchline of the whole project - the LM317 is holding that current rock-steady. **Common gotchas:** - **LM317 pinout backwards.** The legs are ADJ-Vout-Vin (1-2-3) reading left to right with the text facing you. Get this wrong and the LED simply will not light - no damage, just no glow. Pull power, rotate the chip, try again. - **LED in backwards.** Long leg goes to the ADJ pin, short leg (flat side of the plastic) goes to GND. Backwards = no light, no damage. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees, push it back in. - **Electrolytic cap polarity backwards.** The long leg is + and goes to the +V rail; the side with the stripe is - and goes to GND. Backwards on a 10uF cap at 9V usually just gets warm, but on a bad day it can pop with a little puff of smoke. Double-check before you connect the battery. - **Supply voltage too low.** A tired 9V battery that reads 6V under load will drop the LM317 out of regulation, and you'll see the LED go dim or flicker. Swap in a fresh battery or bump the bench supply up to 9V. ## Talking points - The LM317 has a tiny internal reference, about 1.25 V, that it works very hard to hold across two of its pins (Vout and ADJ). Everything else in the LM317 - the pass transistor, the error amp, the protection - is in service of that one number. - In the textbook hookup (two resistors making a divider on ADJ) you trick that 1.25 V into becoming a higher output voltage. Here we skip the divider entirely. With only a resistor across the reference, the LM317 has no choice but to push exactly `1.25 V / R` amps through it. That current then flows through whatever you stick in series with it - in our case, an LED. - Why is this better than a plain resistor in series with an LED? Because LED forward voltage changes. It changes with temperature (around -2 mV/degC), it changes between parts in the same bag, and it changes as the LED ages. With a plain resistor driver, those Vf shifts become current shifts, and current is what determines LED brightness and lifespan. With a current source, the LM317 absorbs the Vf shifts in its own dropout headroom and the LED keeps the same current. That is the whole game. - Headroom matters: the LM317 needs Vin to be at least about 3 V above its own Vout pin to stay in regulation. With a red LED (Vf ~2 V) and 1.25 V across Rset, the LM317's Vout pin sits at ~3.25 V above ground, so Vin needs to be at least ~6.25 V. A 9 V supply gives comfortable headroom. The difference between Vin and Vout is dissipated as heat in the LM317. - This is the same trick used inside cheap LED bulbs and LED strip drivers, just scaled up. Real designs swap the LM317 for a switch-mode controller for efficiency, but the topology - "current sense resistor across a fixed reference voltage" - is identical. ## Things to change once it works - **Change the current (safely).** Swap the 56R for a different value: 120R gives ~10 mA (a gentler glow), 27R gives ~46 mA (right at the edge of what a generic 5mm LED can tolerate - run it briefly only). The math is always `I = 1.25 / R`. - **DO NOT use 10R (~125 mA) with a generic 5mm LED.** That current is 4-6x the LED's continuous rating - it will degrade in minutes and fail. If you genuinely want 125 mA from this circuit, you need either a 1W power LED on a small heatsink, or a series chain of several LEDs so each one's brightness can be moderated through better thermal mass (and you will need a higher Vin to cover the chain plus dropout). The LM317 itself is happy to source that current; it is the indicator LED that is not. - **Drive a different LED color.** Blue and white LEDs need ~3.3 V Vf - you may need to bump Vin to 12 V to stay in headroom. - **Watch it self-regulate.** Run a stiff supply at 9 V and confirm ~22 mA. Drop the supply to 7 V. The current should stay locked until you fall below dropout, at which point the LED goes dark suddenly rather than fading. - **Mind the heat.** At 22 mA with 9 V in and ~3.25 V out, the LM317 burns about (9 - 3.25) x 0.022 = 0.13 W. The TO-220 will be only slightly warm. For sustained higher currents, bolt it to a small heatsink. - **Series more LEDs.** As long as Vin is high enough to cover Vf_total + 3 V of dropout + 1.25 V across Rset, you can stack LEDs in series on the ADJ pin and every one gets the same current. This is exactly how multi-LED panels are wired. ## Why this is interesting Most people meet the LM317 once, as the "adjustable 5 V supply" demo, and never look at it again. But it has a secret second job that is arguably more useful: **it is a near-ideal precision current source with a one-resistor BOM**. That is a remarkable feat for a 1970s-era three-terminal chip. The same circuit topology - "force a known reference across a sense resistor" - shows up everywhere, from real LED drivers to laser diode controllers to bench-supply current limit circuits. Build this once and the rest of analog regulator design starts to look familiar.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# ============================================================
# LM317T Constant-Current LED Driver - bench test procedure
# ============================================================
# This is a pure-analog project. There is no MCU and no code.
# Instead, follow this multimeter procedure to prove the circuit
# is doing what the datasheet says: holding a fixed current
# regardless of LED forward voltage drift.
#
# Tools needed:
#   - Digital multimeter (DMM) set to DC volts, then to DC mA
#   - 9V battery OR bench supply set to 9V (anything 6.5V to 12V works)
#
# Test point map (matches the wiring diagram):
#   TP1 = LM317 Vin pin (pin 3, the input)
#   TP2 = LM317 Vout pin (pin 2, the output, top of Rset)
#   TP3 = LM317 ADJ pin (pin 1) = bottom of Rset = LED anode
#   TP4 = LED cathode = where the cathode wire meets the GND rail
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 1: Power-off sanity check
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# With power disconnected, measure resistance from TP2 to TP3.
# Expected: ~56 ohms (your Rset). If you read kilohms or open,
# the resistor is wrong or not seated. Fix before powering on.
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 2: Verify the reference voltage (the LM317 magic number)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Power the circuit. LED should be glowing steadily.
# DMM in DC volts, measure between TP2 (Vout) and TP3 (ADJ).
# Expected: 1.20 V to 1.30 V (datasheet says 1.25V nominal).
# This is the LM317 holding its internal reference across Rset.
# If you see this, the regulator is in regulation. Done.
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 3: Verify the current (Ohm's law in action)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Compute I = V(TP2,TP3) / 56 ohms.
# Example: 1.25 V / 56 R = 0.0223 A = ~22 mA.
# Now confirm by measurement: open the LED-cathode-to-GND
# connection (pull the wire that runs from the LED's short leg
# to the GND rail) and insert the meter inline there. Set DMM
# to DC mA (start on the 200 mA or higher range to be safe).
# Expected: within ~5 percent of the computed value above.
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 4: Prove it is a CURRENT source, not a voltage source
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# This is the cool part. While running:
#   a) Change Vin. Drop it from 9V to 7V (or swap to a different
#      supply in the 6.5-12V range). Re-measure the LED current.
#      It should barely move. A voltage source would change the
#      current a lot - this does not, because the LM317 fights
#      to keep 1.25V across Rset.
#   b) Touch the LED gently with a finger to warm it. Its forward
#      voltage drifts down ~2 mV/degC. A plain resistor driver
#      would let the current creep up. Here the current stays put.
#
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# Step 5: Headroom check (why Vin must be > Vled + Vrset + ~3V)
# ------------------------------------------------------------
# The LM317 needs about 3V of dropout between its own Vin and
# Vout pins to regulate. Measure Vin - Vout (TP1 - TP2). It
# must be at least ~3 V for the chip to stay in regulation.
#
# Now slowly drop Vin from 9V toward 5V and watch the LED.
# At some point (around 5.5-6V for a red LED) it will go DARK,
# not just dim - that is the regulator falling out of compliance,
# the chip can no longer hold 1.25V across Rset because there
# is not enough voltage left in the budget. That sudden cliff
# is the experiment working as intended.
#
# That is the whole circuit. One IC, one resistor, no math
# beyond I = 1.25 / R. Same trick lives inside cheap LED bulbs.
echo "Run the steps above with your multimeter. Nothing to execute."

All the wiring lives here - no soldering on this build
Rset - sets the current at I = 1.25V / 56R = ~22 mA, safe for a generic 5mm LED

projects.name: ULN2803 Knight Rider Light Bar
projects.power_supply: Arduino Uno powered from laptop USB (5V). The 5V rail also feeds the ULN2803 COM pin (10) and the LED anodes through 220R resistors; the chip sinks each LED cathode to GND when its input pin goes HIGH.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Eight LEDs in a row light up one at a time, with a glowing dot that zooms left, then right, then left again, forever. It looks exactly like the front of KITT, the talking car from Knight Rider. **Why it's fun**: You built the same effect that 80s TV used on a real car prop, and once it works you can crank the speed dial in the code to make the dot bounce slow and lazy or so fast it almost blurs into a solid line. Show it to your friends with the lights off and watch them lean in. ## Parts list - 1x Arduino Uno R3 (the brain - sends the "which LED" pattern) - 1x ULN2803APG Darlington Array - the star of the show: eight transistor pairs in one chip - 1x Breadboard (~400 tie-points) - everything lives here, no soldering - 8x 5mm LEDs - 5 Red + 3 Yellow (we only have 5 red in stock, the yellows finish the bar) - 8x 220R resistors - one per LED to keep them from burning out - Jumper wires (M-M for the breadboard, F-M from Uno to breadboard) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - power output pin. Gives 5 volts when the USB cable is plugged in. Good for lighting up small things like LEDs. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every wire that goes "down" the circuit ends here. There are three GND pins on the Uno; any of them work. - **D0 to D13** - the digital pins. You can turn each one ON (HIGH, about 5V) or OFF (LOW, 0V) from code. We use D2 through D9 for this project. - **USB-B** - the big square USB jack. Your laptop plugs in here to give power and to send the code.
**Step 1 - Plant the breadboard and power the rails.** - Put the breadboard flat on the table. The long red strip down the side is the "+" rail (the power strip). The long blue or black strip is the "-" rail (the ground strip). - Plug a jumper wire from the Arduino pin marked **5V** into the top red rail (we call that **+5V_T**). - Plug another jumper from any Arduino pin marked **GND** into the bottom blue rail (we call that **GND_B**). Now the whole red strip carries 5 volts and the whole blue strip is at 0 volts. Every other part will tap into these two strips.
**Step 2 - Drop in the ULN2803 chip.** The ULN2803 is the brain helper for this build. It is a black bug-shaped chip with 18 legs (9 on each side). It has a small notch or dot at one end - that end is the **top**. - Find row 2 on the breadboard. Sit the chip across the middle gully so its legs go into rows 2 through 10 on the left side and rows 2 through 10 on the right side. The notch should point toward row 2. - This means pin 1 is at **E2** (top-left leg) and pin 18 is at **F2** (top-right leg). Pin 9 is at **E10** (bottom-left leg) and pin 10 is at **F10** (bottom-right leg). Here is the secret: the chip has 8 "switches" inside. You poke an input pin with a HIGH signal from the Arduino, and the matching output pin on the other side gets pulled down to ground. That is what turns each LED on.
**Step 3 - Power the ULN2803 chip itself.** - Run a short jumper from **F2** (pin 9 of the chip, which is GND) down to the **blue ground rail (GND_B)**. - Run a short jumper from **E10** (pin 10 of the chip, which the datasheet calls COM) up to the **red 5V rail (+5V_T)**. Pin 9 ties the chip to ground so it has a "0V side" to dump current into. Pin 10 ties to 5V because of a special part inside the chip called a flyback diode - it protects against voltage spikes. For LEDs we do not really need that protection, but tying pin 10 to 5V is safe and standard, so do it.
**Step 4 - Wire the 8 control pins from the Arduino to the chip inputs.** The inputs are pins 1 through 8 on the left side of the chip. They sit at breadboard holes E2, E3, E4, E5, E6, E7, E8, and E9. Use eight jumper wires: - Arduino **D2** to breadboard **E2** (chip input 1) - Arduino **D3** to breadboard **E3** (chip input 2) - Arduino **D4** to breadboard **E4** (chip input 3) - Arduino **D5** to breadboard **E5** (chip input 4) - Arduino **D6** to breadboard **E6** (chip input 5) - Arduino **D7** to breadboard **E7** (chip input 6) - Arduino **D8** to breadboard **E8** (chip input 7) - Arduino **D9** to breadboard **E9** (chip input 8) When the code makes D2 go HIGH, chip input 1 wakes up and chip output 1 turns on its LED. Same idea for the other seven.
**Step 5 - Plant the 8 LEDs in a row.**
Each LED has a **long leg** (this is the "+" side, where power comes in) and a **short leg** (this is the "-" side, where current leaves). The short-leg side also has a tiny flat spot on the plastic rim - that helps you double-check. Push each LED across two breadboard rows. The long leg goes in the row that is closer to the top of the board. - LED 1 (red): long leg at **B13**, short leg at **B14** - LED 2 (red): long leg at **B15**, short leg at **B16** - LED 3 (red): long leg at **B17**, short leg at **B18** - LED 4 (red): long leg at **B19**, short leg at **B20** - LED 5 (red): long leg at **B21**, short leg at **B22** - LED 6 (yellow): long leg at **B23**, short leg at **B24** - LED 7 (yellow): long leg at **B25**, short leg at **B26** - LED 8 (yellow): long leg at **B27**, short leg at **B28** Lining them up in a tidy row is what makes the "chase" effect look like a moving dot. The 5 reds in the middle with yellows on the ends gives it that classic Knight Rider look.
**Step 6 - Add a 220R resistor in front of every LED.** A resistor has two legs and a tiny tube body. The color bands on a 220R are red-red-brown-gold. Resistors do not care which way they face, so you can put either leg in either hole. For each LED, bend one resistor into a little arch. One leg goes into the red 5V rail at the top of the board. The other leg goes into the **A** row directly across from the LED's long leg: - Resistor for LED 1: from **+5V_T** to **A13** - Resistor for LED 2: from **+5V_T** to **A15** - Resistor for LED 3: from **+5V_T** to **A17** - Resistor for LED 4: from **+5V_T** to **A19** - Resistor for LED 5: from **+5V_T** to **A21** - Resistor for LED 6: from **+5V_T** to **A23** - Resistor for LED 7: from **+5V_T** to **A25** - Resistor for LED 8: from **+5V_T** to **A27** Why this matters: an LED is a greedy drinker. If you connect it straight to 5V it will gulp too much current and burn out in seconds, like a balloon over-inflated. The resistor is a tiny "drinking straw" that limits how much current can flow. 220 ohms gives a bright but safe glow. Never skip these.
**Step 7 - Connect each LED's short leg to the chip's output pin.** Use eight more jumper wires. The chip outputs are on the right side: pin 11 is at hole **F9**, pin 12 at **F8**, pin 13 at **F7**, pin 14 at **F6**, pin 15 at **F5**, pin 16 at **F4**, pin 17 at **F3**, and pin 18 at **F2**... wait, pin 18 is at F2 but pin 11 is at F9? Yes - because the chip is sitting upside-down (notch at top), output 1 is the bottom-right leg. The wiring below is the right one to copy: - **F10** (chip output 1) to **C14** (LED 1 short leg row) - **F9** (chip output 2) to **C16** (LED 2 short leg row) - **F8** (chip output 3) to **C18** (LED 3 short leg row) - **F7** (chip output 4) to **C20** (LED 4 short leg row) - **F6** (chip output 5) to **C22** (LED 5 short leg row) - **F5** (chip output 6) to **C24** (LED 6 short leg row) - **F4** (chip output 7) to **C26** (LED 7 short leg row) - **F3** (chip output 8) to **C28** (LED 8 short leg row) When the chip turns on an output, that output gets yanked down to 0V. Current then flows: from the 5V rail, down through the resistor, down through the LED, into the chip output, and out to ground. The LED lights up. When the chip turns the output off, the path is broken and the LED goes dark.
**Step 8 - Plug in the USB cable and you are done.** Plug the USB-B end into the Arduino and the other end into your laptop. The Arduino's little green power LED should glow. After you upload the code, the eight LEDs will start their bouncing dot dance.
**If nothing lights up, check these first:** - Is the chip notch pointing the right way (toward row 2)? Putting it in backwards is the most common mistake. - Are all 8 LEDs facing the same way - long legs at the top, short legs at the bottom? One LED flipped around will stay dark while the others work. - Is the red rail really getting 5V? Touch the resistor leg that is in the red rail - if you have a multimeter, it should read about 5V to ground. - Are pins 9 and 10 of the chip wired the right way around? Pin 9 to blue ground, pin 10 to red 5V. Swapping these can stop the chip from working. This is a tricky one because there are a lot of wires, but once it lights up you will never forget how the ULN2803 works - it is one of the most useful chips you will meet. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):** 1. **First time only - USB driver.** Your Arduino Uno uses a **CH340** USB-to-serial chip (the dark rectangular chip near the USB jack on most clones). Plug it in: if a COM port appears in **Tools -> Port** within a few seconds, the driver is already installed and you can skip the rest of this step. If nothing shows up, install the CH340 driver from [sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers](https://sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers) (Windows / macOS / Linux all linked there), then unplug and replug the Uno. 2. Install the Arduino IDE and open it once so it finishes setting itself up. 3. Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> **Arduino Uno**. 4. No extra libraries needed for this sketch. The `pinMode`, `digitalWrite`, and `delay` functions are all built in. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into your laptop with a **USB-A to USB-B** cable (the big square-ish printer-style plug goes into the Uno). You should see a little green LED on the Uno light up. 2. Tools -> Port -> pick the one that says **COM*** on Windows, or **/dev/cu.usbmodem*** on a Mac, or **/dev/ttyACM0** on Linux. If you see more than one, unplug the Uno, look again, plug it back in, and grab the one that just reappeared - that is the Uno. 3. Open the sketch in the IDE. Nothing to edit - there are no passwords or placeholders in this one. (If you want to change the chase speed later, find `STEP_MS = 80` near the top and try `30` for blazing fast or `200` for lazy.) 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, second from the left at the top). The bottom of the IDE will say "Compiling sketch..." then "Uploading...". The two tiny LEDs on the Uno labeled **TX** and **RX** will flicker while the code transfers. 5. When the bottom of the IDE says "Done uploading", look at the breadboard. The dot should already be bouncing left -> right -> left across the eight LEDs. There is no Serial Monitor needed for this project - the LEDs themselves are the output. **You know it worked when** the lit LED slides smoothly from one end of the row to the other, bounces off the end, and slides back. If only one LED ever lights up and never moves, see the gotchas below. **Common gotchas:** - **An LED is dark and never lights up.** It is probably in backwards. LEDs only work one way. Pull it out, flip it 180 degrees so the long leg (anode) is on the +5V/resistor side and the short leg (flat side, cathode) is on the ULN2803 output side, push it back in. No damage done - LEDs just refuse to light when reversed. - **The dot jumps over a gap (LED 3 stays dark while the others chase).** That LED's wire is in the wrong row on the breadboard. Trace from Arduino D4 -> ULN2803 IN3 (pin 3) -> ULN2803 OUT3 (pin 16) -> LED 3's short leg. One of those four hops is in the wrong hole. - **All eight LEDs are off, nothing happens.** Either the ULN2803 is upside down (the little notch or dot must point toward pin 1, which is the IN1 side wired to Arduino D2), or pin 9 (GND) and pin 10 (+5V COM) are swapped. Swapping those two will not blow the chip up immediately, but nothing will light. Double-check: pin 9 to the blue rail, pin 10 to the red rail. ## Talking points - The whole point of the ULN2803 is replacement of eight separate transistor circuits. If you wanted to drive eight LEDs with discrete BC547s, you would need 8 transistors plus 8 base resistors - sixteen extra parts and a maze of wires. Here it is one chip. - "Darlington" means two transistors in a row inside the chip, which gives huge current gain - a tiny 5V signal from the Arduino can switch loads up to 500 mA per channel. - The chip is a SINK driver, not a source driver. It pulls outputs DOWN to ground, it does not push UP to +5V. That is why the LED anodes go to +5V and the cathodes go to the chip. This is "current sinking" or "low-side switching" and it is the most common way driver ICs work. - Pin 10 (COM) has internal flyback diodes built in. We do not need them for LEDs, but they exist so the same chip can drive relays and motors without exploding from coil kickback. Free feature. - The "Knight Rider" scan pattern - dot moves left, then right, then left - is one of the first 80s TV special effects done with simple electronics. Same trick was used for the actual car prop, just with more LEDs. ## Things to change once it works - Change the scan speed. Lower `STEP_MS` from 80 to 30 - lightning fast. Raise to 200 - lazy bouncing ball. - Add a fade trail. Instead of just on/off, PWM the LEDs so the previously-lit ones glow dimly for a frame or two. (The Uno only has 6 PWM pins, so this needs software PWM - good intermediate challenge.) - Swap to a different pattern: all-on/all-off blink, alternating odd/even, random sparkle. - Build the same circuit with eight discrete BC547 transistors instead of the ULN2803 to feel why driver ICs were invented. - Drive a real load. The ULN2803 can handle ~500 mA per channel - swap LEDs for small 5V relays, small DC motors, or solenoids (one per channel) and you have an 8-output controller. ## Why this is interesting This is the "one chip swallows eight transistors" moment. You wire it once and suddenly your breadboard is uncluttered, your code is clean, and the same circuit pattern scales to relays, motors, stepper coils, and segment displays. The ULN2803 is one of those parts that has been in continuous production since 1980 because nothing replaced its sweet spot: lots of cheap medium-current low-side switches in one DIP package. Knowing how to use it unlocks a huge category of projects with almost no effort.

projects.name: PC817 Optoisolated Relay Trigger Board
projects.power_supply: ESP32 NodeMCU-32S powered from USB; load-side 5V tapped from the ESP32 Vin rail for the first build (shared ground, no real isolation yet - cut later for a separate brick).
projects.description:
**What it is**: Tell the ESP32 to flip a tiny switch, and CLICK - a real relay snaps shut and a green LED lights up. You hear the click, you see the light, and the chip in the middle controls it all without ever touching the LED's wires. **Why it's fun**: That click sound is the same one in dishwashers, garage doors, and old arcade machines - now you can make it happen on command. Even cooler: the two halves of the circuit never touch each other, they only talk through a flash of invisible light inside a little black chip. ## Parts list - ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the controller side - 3.3V logic) - PC817 optocoupler (the isolation barrier - an LED facing a phototransistor in a 4-pin DIP) - BC337 NPN BJT in TO-92 (the muscle that switches the relay-module input) - 1-channel Relay Module (active-LOW; we treat it as the "load" stage) - 1K resistor (limits current into the PC817 input LED) - 10K resistor (base pull-down so the BC337 stays off when the opto is dark) - 330R resistor + green 5mm LED (a visible "load" the relay switches so you can see the result) - Breadboard, M-M and F-M jumper wires ## Wiring notes This project has two "sides" that are supposed to live in different worlds: a tiny brain side (the ESP32) and a louder load side (the relay and a light). A little black chip called a PC817 sits in the middle and passes the message across using a beam of invisible light, so no copper wire ever has to connect the two sides. For our first build we cheat a little and share the same 5V from one USB cable so it is easier to test. Later you can snip one wire to make the isolation real. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **D23** - the pin marked D23. This is the one pin that talks to the relay. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. The ESP32 has several GND pins and they are all the same. - **VIN** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. We will use it to power the relay. - **3V3** - a 3.3V power pin. We do not need it for this build. - **EN** - a reset-style button pin. Ignore it for this project. - **USB** - the little square port where the USB cable goes in to power the board and load code.
**Step 1 - Plant the ESP32 and set up two power strips on the breadboard.** - Push the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S across the middle gap of the breadboard so each row of pins sits in its own column. - The two long strips down the side of the breadboard (the red and blue stripes) are called power strips. We will use the TOP pair as the "brain side" power strips, and the BOTTOM pair as the "load side" power strips. - Even though both sides will share the same 5V for now, treat them like two separate strips in your head. It will make the next steps make sense. This little trick of pretending two strips are separate is what makes the rest of the wiring feel clean. Pros call this "controller side" and "load side". You can call it "brain side" and "muscle side".
**Step 2 - Wire the ESP32 to both sets of power strips.** - ESP32 **VIN** -> the bottom red strip (load-side 5V). - ESP32 **GND** -> the bottom blue strip (load-side ground). - ESP32 **GND** -> the top blue strip (brain-side ground). - The top red strip is special: it is not really a 5V strip. It is a "signal entry" strip where the GPIO will come in through a resistor in Step 4. Leave it empty for now. VIN is the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable, so plugging it into the bottom red strip is how we power everything from one USB cord.
**Step 3 - Place the PC817 optocoupler.** The PC817 is a black plastic chip with 4 legs. It has a tiny dot or a notch at one end - that end is **pin 1**. Hold the chip so the dot is at the top-left. - Pin 1 (top-left) is the long leg of a tiny invisible LED inside the chip. - Pin 2 (bottom-left) is the short leg of that LED. - Pin 3 (bottom-right) is the emitter of a tiny light-sensor transistor inside. - Pin 4 (top-right) is the collector of that same sensor. Push the chip into the board so it straddles the middle gap, with pin 1 at row E column 10. That puts pin 2 at A10, pin 3 at A11, and pin 4 at E11. (Counting goes around the chip, not straight across.) **Why this matters:** Inside the PC817 there is a tiny light bulb glued right next to a tiny light sensor, sealed up in the black plastic. When the brain side switches the light bulb on, the load side sensor sees the glow and turns on - but no copper wire ever crosses between the two halves. That is what "optical isolation" means. It is a clever, simple idea and you can build a thousand things on top of it.
**Step 4 - Brain side: GPIO into the PC817 LED through a 1K resistor.** - Take the 1K resistor (brown-black-red color bands). Push one leg into the top red strip and the other into hole **B10** (which connects to PC817 pin 1). - Now run a jumper from ESP32 **D23** down to the top red strip. The top red strip is now acting as a one-stop "signal in" lane. - Run a short black jumper from **A10** (PC817 pin 2) over to the top blue strip (brain-side ground). When D23 turns on, current flows out of the pin, through the 1K resistor, through the tiny LED inside the PC817, and back to ground. The resistor is there to keep the current small and safe. Without it the LED inside the chip would burn out very fast.
**Step 5 - Load side: place the BC337 transistor.** The BC337 is a tiny black plastic transistor with a flat front and 3 legs. Hold it with the flat side facing you. The legs in order from left to right are **C, B, E** (collector, base, emitter). - Stick it in upright at column 20 so the legs go into holes **F20** (C), **G20** (B), and **H20** (E). The pin layout is "CBE". - The collector (C) at F20 is what will pull the relay's input pin down. - The base (B) at G20 is what gets the signal from the PC817. - The emitter (E) at H20 goes to ground. This transistor is a tiny switch. A small wiggle on the base leg turns on a much bigger flow between collector and emitter.
**Step 6 - Connect PC817 output to the BC337 base.** - Use an orange jumper from **F11** (PC817 pin 3, emitter of the light sensor) over to **F20** (BC337 collector). Wait - that is the wrong leg. Look again: the orange wire should land on the BC337 **base**. In the board layout the orange wire goes from F11 to F20 because the transistor's middle pin sits at G20, and F11/F20 are linked through a short slide. Just push the orange jumper into F11 and F20 and the breadboard does the rest. - Now connect PC817 pin 4 (at hole F11... wait, pin 4 is at E11, so use a separate orange wire from **J11** to the bottom red strip, which is load-side 5V). That feeds the light sensor's collector with power. So the path is: load-side 5V -> PC817 pin 4 -> through the light sensor -> PC817 pin 3 -> into the BC337 base. When the brain side lights up the LED inside the PC817, the sensor turns on, and a little current trickles into the BC337 base.
**Step 7 - Add the 10K pull-down resistor on the BC337 base.** - Put a 10K resistor (brown-black-orange) from **J20** (the same row as the BC337 base) down to the bottom blue strip (load-side ground). **Why this matters:** if the PC817's light sensor is dark (no signal), the BC337 base is just hanging in midair. Hanging legs are bad - even a stray bit of light leaking into the chip or static in the air can make the relay click on by accident. The 10K resistor gently pulls the base down to ground when nothing else is talking to it, like holding a kite string so it does not blow away. We use 10K because it is gentle enough not to fight the real signal but firm enough to keep things quiet.
**Step 8 - BC337 emitter to ground.** - A short black jumper from **J21** (BC337 emitter row) to the bottom blue strip (load-side ground). Now the transistor can do its job: when the base goes up a little, current flows from collector to emitter (which is on ground), and the collector pin gets yanked down low.
**Step 9 - Run the relay trigger jumper.** - Orange jumper from **J19** (BC337 collector row) over to **F25**. F25 is just a parking spot where the relay's IN wire will land in the next step. When the BC337 turns on, F25 gets pulled close to ground. That is the signal the relay module is waiting to hear.
**Step 10 - Hook up the 1-channel relay module.** Use female-to-male jumpers - the female end clips onto the relay module's header pins, the male end pushes into the breadboard. - Relay **VCC** (power input, 5V in) -> bottom red strip (load-side 5V). - Relay **GND** (the 0V side, ground) -> bottom blue strip (load-side ground). - Relay **IN** -> hole **F25** (the parking spot from Step 9). The relay module is a small board with a blue plastic cube on it (the relay itself) and three screw terminals on the end labeled **COM**, **NO**, and **NC**. We will use COM and NO in the next step. The relay fires when the IN pin is pulled close to ground - exactly what the BC337 does when our signal arrives. When the brain side is quiet, IN sits high all on its own and the relay stays open.
**Step 11 - Wire the LED that the relay will switch.** - Find the green 5mm LED. The longer leg is the long leg (+) and the shorter leg is the short leg (-). There is also a small flat spot on the side of the LED right next to the short leg. - Push the long leg into **F5** and the short leg into **F6**. - Add a 330R resistor (orange-orange-brown) from **J5** (same row as the short leg) down to the bottom blue strip (load-side ground). - Now the relay screw terminals: connect **NO** (Normally Open) to the bottom red strip (load-side 5V). Connect **COM** (Common) to a wire that lands at **A5** (same row as the LED's long leg). When the relay is asleep, COM and NO are not touching, so no power reaches the LED. When D23 fires and the relay clicks closed, COM and NO touch, 5V flows through COM, through the LED's long leg, out the short leg, through the 330R resistor, and back to ground. The LED turns on. **Why the 330R?** A bare LED across 5V would gulp too much current and burn out in a flash. The 330R resistor is a flow limiter - it slows the current down to a safe sip so the LED glows happily for years.
**Step 12 - Final check before plugging in the USB.** Trace the path with your finger before you power it up: - ESP32 D23 -> 1K resistor -> top red strip -> PC817 pin 1. - PC817 pin 2 -> top blue strip -> ESP32 GND. - Bottom red strip -> PC817 pin 4 -> through the chip -> pin 3 -> BC337 base (with a 10K leash to ground). - BC337 emitter -> bottom blue strip (ground). - BC337 collector -> relay IN. - Relay COM -> green LED long leg -> short leg -> 330R -> ground. Relay NO -> bottom red strip. - ESP32 VIN -> bottom red strip. ESP32 GND -> bottom blue strip. If all of that looks right, plug the USB cable in. You should hear a click from the relay and see the green LED blink on and off when the code runs. **One last thing - this is a tricky one to wrap your head around:** most cheap relay modules already have their own little PC817 hidden on the green board. So we are kind of doubling up. We are doing the discrete PC817 + BC337 build by hand anyway, because the whole point of this project is to **see and touch** the parts that make isolation work, not just trust a hidden chip on someone else's board. You learn way more by building it the hard way once. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open File -> Preferences. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` then click OK. 2. Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager. Type "esp32" in the search box and install "esp32 by Espressif Systems". It is a big download, so go grab a snack. 3. Tools -> Board -> esp32 -> "NodeMCU-32S". (If you do not see it, scroll - the list is long.) 4. No extra libraries are needed for this sketch. It only uses the built-in Arduino functions (`pinMode`, `digitalWrite`, `Serial`, `delay`). **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S into your laptop with a **USB micro-B data cable** (the same shape as old phone chargers). Make sure it is a data cable, not a charge-only one - if your laptop does not see the board at all, that is the first thing to swap. 2. Tools -> Port -> pick the new entry that appeared when you plugged the board in. On Windows it looks like `COM5` or `COM7`; on Mac it is `/dev/cu.usbserial-*` or `/dev/cu.SLAB_USBtoUART`; on Linux it is `/dev/ttyUSB0`. 3. No passwords or placeholders in this sketch - nothing to fill in. Just open the `.ino` file. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon at the top-left). You will see "Connecting....." dots scroll in the bottom panel. If the dots keep going for more than about 10 seconds, **hold down the BOOT button** on the ESP32 until the upload starts, then let go. (Most NodeMCU-32S boards auto-reset and you will not need this, but the first flash on a new board sometimes needs the nudge.) 5. When you see "Hard resetting via RTS pin..." and a green "Done uploading" bar, the code is on the chip. 6. Tools -> Serial Monitor. Set the baud rate dropdown in the bottom-right of that window to **115200** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). You should immediately see: ``` PC817 Optoisolated Relay Trigger - boot Toggling GPIO 23 every 2 seconds. Listen for the relay click. Watch the green LED. OPTO ON -> relay CLOSED (LED should be lit) OPTO OFF -> relay OPEN (LED should be dark) OPTO ON -> relay CLOSED (LED should be lit) ... ``` At the same time you should hear a soft **click... click... click...** from the relay module every 2 seconds, and the green LED should flash on and off in time with the clicks. That is the moment it all comes together: the chip is talking, the relay is snapping, the LED is winking. High-five your dad. **Common gotchas:** - **No COM port shows up when you plug the board in.** Nine times out of ten this is a charge-only USB cable. Swap it for one you know carries data (try the cable that came with a phone, not the one that came with a battery pack). On Windows you may also need the CP210x or CH340 USB-serial driver - the Arduino IDE will usually warn you if it is missing. - **"Connecting....._____....._____" forever during Upload.** Hold the **BOOT** button on the ESP32 down while clicking Upload, and let go once you see the percentage start counting up. The board is just stubborn about entering flash mode on the first try. - **Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `?@@?N??$??`.** The baud rate in the Serial Monitor window does not match the code. Click the dropdown in the bottom-right corner and pick **115200**. - **You hear the click but the green LED never lights (or it stays lit all the time).** The LED is probably in backwards - it only lights one way around. Flip it 180 degrees in the breadboard (long leg = anode = the 330R side, short leg = cathode = GND side). No damage, just no glow until you flip it. ## Talking points - A PC817 is just an LED pointed at a phototransistor inside a black 4-pin package. There is no wire between them - the only connection is light. That is what "galvanic" means: no shared metal. - This matters because the load side can be at a totally different voltage, polarity, or ground reference, and nothing bad can flow back into the ESP32. - The BC337 is here because the PC817 phototransistor, at the low LED current we are driving (2.1 mA), is operating well below its rated test point (typically 5 mA) - so the available collector current is modest, maybe a few mA. The BC337 amplifies that into the tens of mA the relay module's IN pin can pull cleanly. (The PC817 phototransistor's absolute max collector current is 50 mA, so the part is not the limit - the operating point is.) - Three switching stages in series: MCU pin (small signal) -> PC817 LED + phototransistor (isolated signal) -> BC337 (boosted signal) -> relay coil (mechanical contact). Each stage takes a weaker signal and produces a stronger one with the right characteristics for the next stage. - The "active-LOW" relay quirk is worth pointing out: counterintuitively, the BC337 turning ON makes the relay's IN pin go LOW, and LOW is what the module wants to energize. Trace it carefully so you do not get inverted logic in software. ## Things to change once it works 1. **Make the isolation real.** Right now the load-side +5V rail comes from the ESP32's Vin (USB 5V) pin, so both grounds are tied together and there is no actual isolation - the PC817 is just relaying a signal. Cut that single jumper between ESP32 Vin and the load-side +5V rail, and feed the load side from a separate USB charger or bench supply. The green LED keeps blinking. The ESP32 still drives it. But now there is no copper path between the two sides - that is the entire reason this circuit exists. 2. **Drive a real load.** Replace the green LED + 330R with a 12V DC fan or LED strip wired through COM/NO. (Keep the load-side supply matched to the load, and remember the relay rating is for DC switching here - no mains AC.) 3. **Tune the LED current.** At 3.3V GPIO and a 1.2V LED drop inside the PC817, 1K gives about 2.1 mA forward current. That is on the low end of the PC817's useful range - if turn-on feels sluggish or unreliable with a particular part, drop the resistor to 470R for ~4.5 mA and you will get crisper transitions. (The PC817 LED can take 50 mA absolute max, so there is plenty of headroom.) 4. **Add a freewheel diode if you wire a coil directly.** The relay module already has one onboard, but if you ever drive a bare relay coil with the BC337 collector, you need a 1N4007 across the coil cathode-to-collector or the BC337 will die from coil kickback. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project in the kit where you can honestly say "the microcontroller and the load do not share any copper" - once you cut the jumper in step 1, anyway. That is the principle behind every safe mains-switching board, every industrial PLC input, and every USB-isolator dongle. The schematic is small, but the idea scales: every time you see a black 4-pin IC near a relay or a SCR or an SSR, that is an optocoupler doing exactly what this circuit does. Building it from discrete parts - rather than just buying a pre-made isolated relay board and trusting the chip you cannot probe - means you can see each stage, measure it, and break it. That is the fastest way to internalize why the topology exists at all.

projects.name: BC327 High-Side Load Switch for the Laser
projects.power_supply: USB-C into the XIAO ESP32-C3; the board's 5 V rail powers the laser and the 3.3 V GPIO drives the BC547 inverter.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Type a command on your laptop and a real red laser beam clicks on. Type another and it clicks off. Wave your hand through it in a dusty room and you can see the line cutting through the air. **Why it's fun**: It is your first actual laser, and YOU are the switch. Stick it in a cardboard box with a mirror and you have the start of a spy-movie tripwire for your bedroom door. ## Parts list - Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 (3.3 V GPIO control signal) - BC327 PNP BJT in TO-92 (high-side pass transistor for the 5 V rail) - BC547 NPN BJT in TO-92 (small inverter that pulls the BC327 base down) - KY-008 red laser module (the load being switched) - 1x 10K resistor (base pull-up keeping BC327 off by default) - 2x 1K resistor (one for the XIAO -> BC547 base, one for BC547 collector -> BC327 base) - Breadboard, jumper wires (USB cable powers everything off the XIAO's 5 V rail) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the XIAO ESP32-C3 board:** - **5V** - the pin that gives back 5 volts from the USB-C cable. We use this to power the red laser. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every circuit needs a ground to come back to. - **D0 to D10** - the small pins printed on the silver edges of the board. The code talks about GPIO numbers, but the printed labels are different! For this project, the silkscreen pin marked **D2** is GPIO4 in the code. - **USB-C port** - where you plug in the cable from your laptop. This is both power and how you upload the code.
**Heads up - this is a tricky one.** We are building a "high-side switch". That just means the on/off button (made out of two transistors) sits between the +5V power and the laser, not between the laser and ground. It keeps the laser's ground side glued to true 0V the whole time, which is friendlier for other parts sharing the same ground. **Step 1 - Put the XIAO ESP32-C3 on the breadboard and bring power across.** - Push the XIAO ESP32-C3 across the middle gap of the breadboard so the USB-C port hangs off one end. - Use a red M-M jumper wire from the XIAO **5V** pin to the long red strip running down the side of the breadboard (we will call that the "+5V rail"). - Use a black M-M jumper wire from the XIAO **GND** pin to the long blue strip running down the other side ("GND rail"). The two long strips on the sides of the breadboard are like little highways for power. Anything that needs +5V or GND can just grab from the highway instead of running a wire all the way back to the XIAO.
**Step 2 - Place the BC547 transistor (the helper).** The BC547 is a tiny black plastic part with three legs. It looks like a little flat half-circle. The flat side has writing on it: "BC547". With the flat side facing you and the legs pointing down, the legs from left to right are **C, B, E** (collector, base, emitter). - Plant the BC547 with its legs in row 8 of the breadboard: leg C in C8, leg B in D8, leg E in E8. - Run a black M-M wire from D8 (the same row as the base leg... wait, that is actually the row where the E leg sits in our layout) to the GND rail. Look at the picture: the wire goes from **D8 to GND rail** so that the emitter leg (in column E, row 8) ties to ground through the breadboard row. The BC547 is an NPN transistor. Think of it like a small water valve: when you trickle a tiny bit of current into the middle leg (base), it lets a much bigger flow run from the top leg (collector) down to the bottom leg (emitter, which we just tied to ground).
**Step 3 - Add the 1K resistor from the XIAO pin to the BC547 base.** - Take one of the 1K resistors (color bands: brown, black, red, then a tolerance band). Resistors are not picky about direction, so either way is fine. - Push one leg into row 5 (B5) and the other into row 8 (B8). That puts the resistor between the XIAO control pin and the base of the BC547. - Now run a M-M jumper from the pin marked **D2** (GPIO4) on the XIAO across to A5 on the breadboard. The code calls this pin `CTRL_PIN = 4`, and the silkscreen calls it D2. They are the same pin. **Why this matters:** The 1K resistor keeps the XIAO pin safe. If we hooked the pin straight to the transistor base with no resistor, too much current would try to flow and could damage the XIAO. The resistor is a friendly speed bump.
**Step 4 - Place the BC327 transistor (the main switch) and the second 1K resistor.** The BC327 looks almost identical to the BC547 - same little black half-circle - but it is a different kind of transistor (PNP instead of NPN). Check the writing on the flat side: it should say **BC327**. With the flat side facing you and the legs pointing down, the legs from left to right are **E, B, C** (emitter, base, collector). That is the OPPOSITE order from the BC547, so go slow here. - Plant the BC327 with its legs in row 18: leg E in E18, leg B in D18, leg C in C18. - Take the second 1K resistor and plug one leg into A7 and the other into A18. This builds a path from the BC547's collector area over to the BC327's base. - Run an orange or yellow M-M jumper from A9 to A19. This jumper ties the BC547's collector row (row 7-9, all connected by the breadboard) into the chain that drives the BC327's base. This second 1K resistor does the same safety job as the first one: it limits how much current squeezes into the BC327's base when the BC547 pulls hard.
**Step 5 - Add the 10K resistor as the "default off" pull-up.** The 10K resistor has color bands brown, black, orange. It is the most important safety part in the whole build. - One leg of the 10K goes into C18 (the BC327 base row). The other leg goes into the +5V rail. **Why this matters:** This is the part that keeps the laser OFF when the XIAO first powers up. The instant you plug in USB-C, the XIAO is still booting and its pins are not driving anything yet. Without the 10K, the BC327's base would be floating and could turn the laser on by accident. The 10K gently holds the BC327's base at +5V, which is the "off" position for a PNP transistor. So the laser starts off and stays off until your code tells it otherwise.
**Step 6 - Connect the BC327's emitter to +5V.** - Run a red M-M jumper from D17 to the +5V rail. This carries +5V across to row 17, which the BC327's emitter leg shares. The emitter of the BC327 is the part that the power flows IN from. The collector (the other outside leg) is where the power flows OUT to the laser.
**Step 7 - Place the KY-008 red laser module.** The KY-008 has three pins sticking out of a little black plastic base. Flip it over and look at the writing next to each pin. You should see the letters **S**, something in the middle (often blank or marked with a + or a dash, this varies), and **-**. - Plug the **S** pin into E24. - Plug the middle pin into E25 - and leave it there with nothing else attached. - Plug the **-** pin into E26. **Important - read this twice.** KY-008 modules are made by lots of different factories, and they do not all agree on what the middle pin does. Some say it is +5V power, some say "not connected", some lie completely. We are playing it safe and only using **S** (signal) and **-** (ground). The middle pin stays disconnected. Do NOT try to wire the middle pin to +5V, because if your specific module already has a current-limiting resistor on S, adding a second power feed will burn out the laser diode.
**Step 8 - Connect the BC327 collector to the laser's S pin.** - Run a red M-M jumper from D19 across to D24. That sends the switched +5V from the BC327's collector over to the laser's signal pin.
**Step 9 - Connect the laser's ground pin to the GND rail.** - Run a black M-M jumper from D26 to the GND rail. Now the laser has a complete loop: power comes from +5V, gets switched on/off by the BC327, runs through the laser, and goes back to GND.
**How the on/off actually works (the cool part).** You have two transistors stacked together. Here is what happens when your code writes the pin marked D2 HIGH: 1. The XIAO sends 3.3V through the first 1K resistor into the BC547's base. 2. The BC547 turns ON. Its collector gets pulled near 0V. 3. That pulls the BC327's base low (through the second 1K resistor), beating the 10K pull-up. 4. The BC327 turns ON. Power flows from +5V through the BC327 to the laser. Laser lights up. When the code writes D2 LOW, the BC547 turns off, the 10K resistor pulls the BC327's base back up to +5V, and the BC327 turns off. Laser dark. We need two transistors (the BC547 and the BC327) because the XIAO only puts out 3.3V on its pins, but the BC327 needs its base pulled close to 0V to turn on. The XIAO cannot do that on its own, so the BC547 is the little helper that does the pulling.
**Final check before plugging in USB-C.** - Look at both transistors one more time. The BC547 is in row 8 with legs C-B-E left to right. The BC327 is in row 18 with legs E-B-C left to right. These are OPPOSITE orders. If you swap them, nothing will work and one of them might get hot. - Make sure no exposed transistor legs are touching each other. - Make sure the laser's middle pin truly is not connected to anything. - Aim the laser at a wall, not at anyone's face or any pet, before you plug in. Now plug the USB-C cable into the XIAO and into your laptop. The laser should stay OFF when the board powers up. That is the 10K resistor doing its job. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any ESP32):** 1. Open **File -> Preferences**. In the "Additional boards manager URLs" box, paste this link: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json`. Click OK. 2. Go to **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**. Type `esp32` in the search box and install **"esp32 by Espressif Systems"**. It is a big download, so go grab a snack. 3. Go to **Tools -> Board -> esp32** and pick **"XIAO_ESP32C3"** from the list. 4. No extra libraries needed for this sketch. Everything it uses (`Serial`, `digitalWrite`, `pinMode`) is built in. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the XIAO into your laptop with a **USB-C cable** (the same kind that charges most newer phones). The little orange LED on the XIAO should light up. 2. Go to **Tools -> Port** and pick the new one that appeared when you plugged it in. On Windows it looks like `COM4` or `COM5`; on a Mac it looks like `/dev/cu.usbmodem...`; on Linux it looks like `/dev/ttyACM0`. If you are not sure which is new, unplug the XIAO, look at the list, plug it back in, and pick the one that just showed up. 3. There are no passwords or placeholders to change in this sketch. It runs as-is. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the round arrow pointing right at the top-left). You will see "Compiling" then "Uploading" at the bottom. The XIAO ESP32-C3 has a built-in USB-serial bridge, so you should NOT have to hold any BOOT button. If it gets stuck on "Connecting...", unplug, plug back in, and click Upload again. 5. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window, make sure the baud rate dropdown is set to **115200** (that matches the `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code). 6. You should see: ``` BC327 high-side switch demo HIGH on D2/GPIO4 = laser ON, LOW = laser OFF ON (1 s) OFF (1 s) ``` And at the same time, the **red laser dot** on the KY-008 should be blinking on and off, once per second. Point it at a piece of white paper on the bench (NOT at anyone's face, and NOT at the cat). If the room is a little dusty you can wave your hand near the module and see the red line cutting through the air for a split second. **Common gotchas:** - **Laser stays on forever, no blinking.** You almost certainly wired the BC327 base directly to GPIO4 instead of going through the BC547 inverter. Without the inverter, the base is never pulled down to "off", so the PNP stays on. Double-check that the BC547 collector (not the GPIO) is what feeds the 1K resistor going into the BC327 base. - **Laser stays off forever, even with serial showing "ON".** Check the BC327 orientation. TO-92 transistors are easy to flip 180 degrees on the breadboard. With the flat side facing you and legs pointing down, the BC327 pinout is **Emitter - Collector - Base** (left to right). The BC547 is the opposite: **Collector - Base - Emitter**. Mixing them up is the #1 cause of "circuit does nothing". - **Upload fails with "Failed to connect" or "No serial port".** Some USB-C cables are charge-only and have no data wires. Try a different cable (the one that came with your phone is usually fine). Also make sure you picked the right port under Tools -> Port - if no new port appears when you plug the XIAO in, that is the cable's fault, not the board's. ## Talking points - High-side vs low-side switching: where in the load loop you put the switch matters. Mains-AC light switches are high-side for a reason - the lamp socket and bulb threads stay at neutral when the switch is off, which is the safe state. - PNP turn-on: V_BE for a PNP is positive when the emitter is more positive than the base. "Pull the base down to turn it on" is the mental model. - Why two transistors instead of one MOSFET: a logic-level P-channel MOSFET would do the same job in one part, but BJTs are cheap, forgiving of static, and the two-transistor pattern shows up everywhere (motor drivers, totem-pole outputs, level shifters). Worth seeing once. - Default-off pull-up: the 10 K is doing real work. Without it, the BC327 base would float when the BC547 is off, and the laser would do whatever it felt like at boot and on every reset. ## Things to change once it works - Replace the BC327 with an AO3401 or IRLML6402 P-channel MOSFET on a SOT-23 breakout. The 10 K stays the same; the 1 K from BC547 collector becomes optional. You'll see the laser turn on more crisply because the MOSFET has no V_BE drop. - Drive the GPIO with `analogWrite()` / LEDC PWM and dim the laser. The switch is fast enough for kHz PWM. - Add a 100 nF ceramic cap right at the KY-008 power pins to swallow switching noise (useful when you later switch something inductive like a small motor instead of a laser). - Move the load to a separate 5 V wall supply, keep grounds tied together, and watch the same circuit work unchanged - that's the high-side switch's superpower. ## Why this is interesting Every beginner trips over one of two things: "my LED is on when it should be off" (because they wired an NPN low-side switch and forgot the load floats high when off) or "my PNP won't turn on" (because they tied the base to a 3.3 V GPIO and expected it to behave like an NPN). This project makes both problems visible in one cheap circuit, and the two-BJT inverter pattern is the same shape you'll find inside half-bridge drivers, level shifters, and totem-pole logic outputs.
