projects.name: ULN2003 Servo Sweep Sentinel
projects.power_supply: Two separate USB 5V supplies sharing only GND: USB-to-Uno feeds the logic, LEDs, ULN2003 and PIR; a second USB-C into a TP4056 board feeds the SG90 servo so its current spikes cannot brown out the Uno.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Walk past it and a little flag on a stick swings back and forth while a row of five red lights pulses like a warning sign. Stand still and everything goes quiet again, waiting for the next person to wander by. **Why it's fun**: Hide it around a corner and prank your sister when she walks past. It is your very own motion-triggered alarm, like the ones in spy movies, except you built it. ## Parts list - 1x Arduino Uno R3 (CH340 clone, XL) - the 5V brain - 1x ULN2003AN Darlington Array (7-ch) - the muscle that sinks current for the LED row - 1x HC-SR501 PIR Motion Sensor - the trigger - 1x SG90 Servo (9g micro) - waves the warning flag, on its OWN 5V supply - 5x LED 5mm Red - the "warning bank" - 5x Resistor 220R (1/8W 1%) - one current limiter per LED (see math in Talking points) - 1x 470uF and 1x 100uF electrolytic - bulk reservoir on the servo rail, local decoupling on the ULN2003 - 1x TP4056 USB-C charger/protection board - second, independent 5V source for the servo - 1x Breadboard, M-M and F-M jumpers ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno R3 board:** - **5V** - the pin that gives out 5 volts of power. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs to share this. - **D2, D7, D9** - pins marked Dx on the board. The code talks to these. - **USB** - the silver port. Plug the USB cable in here to power the Uno. - **+ rail / - rail** - the long red and blue strips running down the side of the breadboard. The red one carries 5V, the blue one is ground.
**The big idea: two power sources, one shared ground.** This project uses TWO USB cables. One feeds the Uno (and through it, the LEDs and the motion sensor). The second one feeds ONLY the servo motor through a little charging board. Both power sources MUST share the same ground (the blue strip), or the Uno will not understand the servo. We do this because the servo can suddenly pull a LOT of power when it moves, and that would crash the Uno if they shared one supply.
**Step 1 - Plug the Uno into the breadboard's top power strips.** - Uno **5V** pin -> the **top red strip** (we will call this `+5V_T`). - Uno **GND** pin -> the **top blue strip** (we will call this `GND_T`). This gives the top half of the breadboard power for the LEDs, the motion sensor, and the chip we add next.
**Step 2 - Drop the ULN2003 chip across the middle of the breadboard.** The ULN2003 is a black 16-pin chip. Look for the little half-circle notch on one end - that end is the top, and pin 1 is the first pin on the left when the notch faces up. - Place the chip so pin 1 sits at hole **E5**. The chip should straddle the gap down the middle of the breadboard. - Pin 7 of the chip is at **E11**. Pin 8 (ground) sits at **E12**. Pin 9 (the chip's own power) sits at **F12**, and pin 16 (the first output) sits at **F5**. Wires for the chip: - Hole **E6** (pin 2 of the chip) -> top red strip (+5V). - Hole **E7** (pin 3 of the chip) -> top blue strip (GND). - Short jumper from **F5** to **F4**, and from **F5** to **F6**, and from **F6** to **F7**. This ties chip outputs 16, 15, 14 together so all those LED return wires share one input. **Why this chip matters.** The ULN2003 is a "helper" chip. The Uno's pins are too weak to drive five bright LEDs at once. The ULN2003 takes one signal from the Uno and uses it to switch on five strong outputs. Think of it like a row of light switches that all flip together when you press one button.
**Step 3 - Add the five LEDs and their resistors.**
Each LED has a **long leg** (this is the positive side) and a **short leg** (the negative side). Get them all facing the same way before you push them in. - LED 1: long leg in **B14**, short leg in **B15**. - LED 2: long leg in **B16**, short leg in **B17**. - LED 3: long leg in **B18**, short leg in **B19**. - LED 4: long leg in **B20**, short leg in **B21**. - LED 5: long leg in **B22**, short leg in **B23**. Now add one **220 ohm resistor** (colour bands: red-red-brown-gold) for each LED. Resistors do not have a direction - either way is fine. - Resistor 1: one leg in the top red strip, other leg in **A14** (next to LED 1's long leg). - Repeat for **A16, A18, A20, A22** for LEDs 2 through 5. Now connect each LED's short-leg row to the chip's outputs with a short orange jumper: - **D15** -> **E12** (LED 1 to chip output). - **D17** -> **E11**. - **D19** -> **E10**. - **D21** -> **E9**. - **D23** -> **E8**. **Why the resistors matter.** An LED with no resistor is like a kid running full-speed at a wall - it burns out almost instantly. The 220 ohm resistor slows the current down to a safe level so the LED can shine happily for years.
**Step 4 - Add the 100uF safety bucket next to the chip.** The 100uF capacitor is a small can-shaped part. **It has a direction.** The **longer leg** is positive (+) and the **shorter leg** has a white stripe printed down the side - that one is negative (-). - Longer leg into **B3** (near the chip's power side). - Shorter leg (white stripe) into the top blue ground strip. - Add a short red jumper from **B3** to the top red strip so the longer leg is hooked to +5V. **Why this matters.** When the chip turns LEDs on and off fast, the power dips for a tiny instant. The capacitor is like a little water bucket near the chip - it holds a sip of extra power for those exact moments. **Warning:** if you put the capacitor in backwards it can get hot, leak, or pop loudly. Check the stripe twice before plugging in USB.
**Step 5 - Wire the Uno's signal pin to the chip.** - Uno **D7** -> hole **F4** on the breadboard. That one wire is what tells the ULN2003 to switch all five LEDs on at once. Just one pin doing the work of five.
**Step 6 - Plug in the HC-SR501 motion sensor.** The PIR sensor is the part with the little white dome. It has three pins on the bottom. Lift the dome (gently) to read the labels: **VCC** (power in), **OUT** (the signal), and **GND** (ground). The pin order is sometimes different on different boards, so check yours. Plant the sensor with its three pins in the bottom-right corner of the breadboard so its pins sit in holes **J26 (VCC), J28 (OUT), J30 (GND)**. - **J26 (VCC)** -> bottom red power strip (we will call this `+5V_B`) using a red jumper. - **J30 (GND)** -> bottom blue ground strip (we will call this `GND_B`) using a black jumper. - **J28 (OUT)** -> Uno **D2** using a long F-M or M-M jumper. Now connect the bottom rails to the top rails so the motion sensor shares the Uno's power: - Red jumper: top red strip -> bottom red strip. - Black jumper: top blue strip -> bottom blue strip. **Set the sensor's onboard jumper to repeat-trigger (H) mode.** There is a tiny yellow plug on the back. Move it to the "H" position. This makes the sensor stay ON the whole time it sees motion, instead of flickering. Also turn the **time** dial all the way anticlockwise (shortest delay) and leave the **sensitivity** dial in the middle.
**Step 7 - Add the TP4056 board and the servo's power.** The TP4056 is a small board with a USB-C socket. It will be our second power source - just for the servo motor. Place it off to the side of the breadboard and use F-M jumpers to reach it. - TP4056 **OUT+** -> bottom red strip (`+5V_B`). **Important: the bottom red strip is now JOINED to the top red strip by the red jumper we added in step 6.** That is fine - the PIR runs from this combined supply, but the servo will pull its big current spike straight from the TP4056 side. (If you want the strongest isolation, leave only the GND connected between halves and use a separate red wire from the Uno's 5V only to the PIR. For this beginner build the joined version works.) - TP4056 **OUT-** -> bottom blue strip (`GND_B`). Do NOT plug the USB-C into the TP4056 yet. We will do that after the servo is in.
**Step 8 - Plug in the SG90 servo motor.** The servo has a 3-wire cable with a plastic plug: **orange** (signal), **red** (power), **brown** (ground). Plug three M-M jumpers into the servo's plug, then push the other ends into the breadboard: - Servo **orange** wire -> hole **H25** (this row goes to the Uno). - Servo **red** wire -> hole **H27** (this row goes to the TP4056's power). - Servo **brown** wire -> hole **H29** (this row goes to ground). Now make those rows reach the right places: - From row 27 (servo power): no extra wire needed, the 470uF cap below ties it to the bottom red strip in step 9. - Hole **F29** -> bottom blue ground strip. - Uno **D9** -> hole **H25** (the orange signal wire's row).
**Step 9 - Add the 470uF safety bucket next to the servo.** The 470uF capacitor is bigger than the 100uF one but works the same way. **Longer leg** is positive (+), the side with the **white stripe** is negative (-). - Longer leg into **G27** (same row as the servo's red power wire). - Shorter leg (white stripe) into the bottom blue ground strip. **Why this big one matters.** The servo grabs a LOT of power the instant it starts moving - more than the wires can deliver fast enough. This big capacitor sits right next to the servo as a power "buffer". When the servo gulps current, it drinks from the capacitor first, then the capacitor refills slowly from the TP4056. Without it, the servo might twitch or the whole board might reset every time it moves. And remember - white stripe to ground, or it will pop.
**Step 10 - Final check, then power up.** Before you plug anything in, go through this list with a parent: - Every capacitor's white stripe is on the blue (ground) side. Check both! - Every LED's long leg goes toward 5V (through a resistor), short leg goes toward the chip. - The chip's notch faces the top of the board (so pin 1 is in the right place). - Top blue strip and bottom blue strip are joined by a black jumper - this is the shared ground that lets the Uno and the TP4056 talk to each other. - The PIR's white dome is sitting straight up so it can see motion. Now plug in the Uno's USB cable first. The Uno should boot. Then plug in the TP4056's USB-C cable. The servo should make a tiny click and centre itself. Wave your hand in front of the PIR. The five LEDs should light up and the servo should start to sweep back and forth. If nothing happens: unplug both USB cables and check every white-stripe direction and every long-leg direction once more. This is a tricky one to get right the first time, and small mistakes are normal. You've got this. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):** 1. Open the Arduino IDE. Go to Tools -> Board -> "Arduino AVR Boards" -> **Arduino Uno**. 2. The Servo library is already built into the IDE, so there is nothing extra to install. Nice. 3. The board is a CH340 clone, so if your laptop says "unknown device" when you plug it in, you need the CH340 driver once. Search "CH340 driver" + your operating system, install it, and reboot. After that the Uno shows up as a normal COM port forever. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into your laptop with a USB-A-to-USB-B cable (the big square-ish plug, the same kind old printers used). Do NOT plug in the TP4056 servo supply yet - we want the servo quiet while we upload. 2. In the IDE, go to Tools -> Port and pick the one that just appeared (Windows: something like `COM4`, Mac: `cu.usbmodem...`, Linux: `/dev/ttyACM0` or `/dev/ttyUSB0`). If you are not sure which one it is, unplug the Uno, look at the list, plug it back in, and pick the new one. 3. Open the sketch file. There is nothing to fill in - no WiFi password, no secret keys. Just leave it as is. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, top-left). The little TX and RX lights on the Uno will flicker for a few seconds. When the bottom of the IDE says "Done uploading.", you are good. 5. Open Tools -> **Serial Monitor**. In the bottom-right of the Serial Monitor window, set the baud rate to **115200** (this has to match `Serial.begin(115200)` in the code, or you just see garbage). 6. You should see: `ULN2003 Servo Sweep Sentinel ready.` then `Warming up PIR for 30 seconds...`. Wait. After 30 seconds you get `Armed.` - now plug in the TP4056 USB-C cable so the servo wakes up. Wave your hand in front of the white dome of the PIR. The five red LEDs should snap on and the servo should start sweeping the flag back and forth. Stand still for 5 seconds and everything goes quiet again. **Common gotchas:** - **Serial Monitor shows gibberish like `@?xJ??`** - your baud rate is wrong. Set it to 115200 in the bottom-right corner of the Serial Monitor. - **PIR fires non-stop the moment it powers up** - that is normal for the first 30-60 seconds while the sensor warms up. The code already waits 30 seconds before arming; just don't wave at it during the warm-up. - **LEDs stay dark even though the Serial Monitor says "Armed."** - check the LED direction. The long leg (anode) goes to +5V through the 220R resistor; the short leg (cathode) goes to the ULN2003 output pin. Backwards LEDs don't break, they just don't light. Also double-check that pin 9 of the ULN2003 (COM) is wired to +5V - without it the internal flyback diodes have no return path and the chip won't sink current properly. ## Talking points - **Why a Darlington array at all?** A single Uno pin is only spec'd for 20 mA continuous (40 mA absolute max). Five LEDs at ~9 mA each is ~45 mA - over budget for one pin. The ULN2003 lets the Uno *say* "on" with a tiny logic-level signal while seven internal Darlington pairs do the actual current-sinking work. Each output can sink up to 500 mA, but the package's total dissipation limits the sum to roughly 230 mA sustained at room temp - which is still plenty for a 45 mA LED bank. - **It is a sink driver, not an "inverter".** When `D7` goes HIGH, an NPN Darlington inside the chip turns on and *pulls its output pin down toward GND*. Current then flows from +5V -> 220R -> LED -> output pin -> GND. There's no logic inversion happening - the input directly enables the sink transistor. That's why every LED's *anode* faces +5V: the chip can only pull down, never push up. - **Why 220R and not 330R?** Do the loop math. Red LED forward drop ~2.0 V, ULN2003 Vce(sat) at this current ~1.0 V, supply 5.0 V. That leaves (5 - 2 - 1) = 2.0 V across the resistor. At 220R that's ~9 mA per LED, nice and bright. At 330R it would be ~6 mA - dim. People copy 330R off Uno-direct-drive tutorials without accounting for the chip's Vce(sat); now you won't. - **Why two separate 5V supplies?** Because the SG90's stall current (600-700 mA) is larger than the Uno's onboard LDO can deliver (~500 mA from USB). Without splitting, every direction change browns out the Uno: the PIR false-triggers, the serial output cuts, the LED bank flickers. The 470 uF cap is a buffer, not a fix. - **Rollover-safe timing.** Notice the sketch stores `lastMotionAt = millis()` and compares with `(now - lastMotionAt) >= ALARM_HOLD_MS`. The naive `alarmUntil = millis() + HOLD; if (millis() < alarmUntil)` pattern breaks once every 49.7 days when `millis()` wraps. Unsigned subtraction wraps too, but it gives the correct elapsed time anyway. Learn it once, use it forever. - **The PIR's 30 second warmup is real.** The pyroelectric element is genuinely settling. The sketch sits in `delay(30000)` exactly once at boot - the one place a blocking delay is actually fine. ## Things to change once it works - Use the spare ULN2003 channels (IN6, IN7) for a buzzer or small DC motor "siren". - Split the LED bank into two groups on `D7` and `D8` and alternate them for a "police light" effect. - Replace the PIR with the HC-SR04 ultrasonic and trigger only when something is within, say, 50 cm. - Add an LCD 1602 to show "INTRUDER" and a counter of how many times today. - Try collapsing back to a single supply *with* a proper bench PSU (not USB) to see at what current rating the brownout finally stops. Useful intuition for future designs. ## Why this is interesting Most beginner ULN2003 demos do the *Knight Rider* sequential chase - one channel at a time, 7 channels, one LED at a time. This one inverts that lesson: one logic input fans out to five channels in parallel, deliberately showing that the chip's job is *current capacity*, not channel count. Bolting a PIR and a sweeping servo onto the same array turns a static demo into a complete sense-decide-act loop, and the two-supplies-one-ground architecture is the same trick you'll use on every real project that mixes a logic board with a noisy actuator (motors, solenoids, big LED strips, mains relays). Get this pattern into muscle memory now and you'll save yourself hours of "why does my Uno keep resetting?" debugging later.

projects.name: NE555 Two-Tone Police Siren
projects.power_supply: 9V battery (or 9V bench supply) into the breadboard + rail; one shared rail powers both NE555s and the LM386, with a 100uF bulk cap right next to the chips to keep the amplifier from upsetting the timers.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Flip the switch and a tiny speaker on your breadboard wails "wee-ooo, wee-ooo" exactly like a police car driving by. A red LED blinks in time with the sound, so you can see the siren as well as hear it. **Why it's fun**: You built a real siren out of a handful of parts and zero code. Hide it in a shoebox, sneak up behind your sister, flip the switch, and watch her jump. ## Required external parts (you supply) - **8 ohm speaker, 0.5-1 W**. Any salvaged small speaker works. Not in the kit - this is a hard prerequisite. Without it the project does not finish. - **9V power source.** Either a fresh 9V battery + barrel/snap clip wired to the breadboard rails, or a 9V bench supply. ## Parts list (from inventory) - 2x NE555 Timer IC (U1 = slow sweep oscillator, U2 = fast audio oscillator) - 1x LM386 Audio Power Amp (U3 = drives the speaker) - 4x 10K resistors (R1/R2 timing pair for U1, R5 modulation series, R6 LM386 input series) - 3x 470R resistors (R3/R4 timing pair for U2, R_LED current-limit for the sweep-indicator LED) - 1x 22uF electrolytic (C1, slow timing cap) - 2x 10uF electrolytic (C2 modulation coupling, C3 LM386 input coupling) - 3x 100uF electrolytic (C4 rail decoupling, C5 LM386 output coupling, C6 LM386 pin-7 bypass) - 1x 1uF 50V electrolytic (C7 fast 555 timing cap) - 1x 5mm red LED (visual sweep indicator - so you can SEE the woop-woop) - 1x 400-point breadboard - M-M jumper wires ## The math (so you can trust the parts choice) NE555 astable frequency: **f = 1.44 / ((R_A + 2 R_B) C)**. - **U1 slow stage** with R1=R2=10K, C1=22uF: f = 1.44 / (30K * 22uF) approx **2.2 Hz**. That's the "wee-ooo" rate. - **U2 fast stage** with R3=R4=470R, C7=1uF: f = 1.44 / (1.41K * 1uF) approx **1020 Hz** centre. When U1's square wave is AC-coupled into U2's pin 5 (CV), the comparator thresholds get pushed up and down, sweeping the audio frequency roughly across **500-1500 Hz** - the classic siren range. The original draft used R3=R4=10K with C7=1uF, which gives only 48 Hz (below the audio band, you'd hear a buzz not a tone). The 470R choice is the fix. ## Wiring notes This build has no computer chip - no Arduino, no ESP. Just three little 8-leg chips and some parts that work together to make a "wee-woo" police siren noise. One chip makes a slow up-and-down sweep, the second chip makes a fast tone that follows the sweep, and the third chip is a tiny amplifier that pushes the sound out to a speaker. **Quick glossary - words you will see on this breadboard:** - **+ rail** - the long red strip running down the side of the breadboard. This carries the +9V from your battery. - **- rail** - the long blue/black strip next to it. This is the 0V side, also called ground or GND. - **NE555** - the little 8-leg chip that makes a beat. We use two of them. One slow, one fast. - **LM386** - another 8-leg chip. This is the tiny amplifier that drives the speaker. - **Pin 1** - the corner of a chip nearest the little dot or the notch. Then you count around like a clock. - **Long leg / short leg** - on the round capacitors and the LED, the longer wire leg is the + side and the shorter leg is the - side.
**Step 1 - Place the breadboard and power the rails.** Push your 9V battery clip into the breadboard so the red wire reaches the + rail (the red strip) and the black wire reaches the - rail (the blue/black strip). If you have rails on both the top and bottom edges of the board, run one short jumper from the top + rail to the bottom + rail, and one short jumper from the top - rail to the bottom - rail. That way every part has easy access to power and ground.
**Step 2 - Plant the three chips on the breadboard.** Each chip has 8 legs. Look closely at one end - there is a little half-circle notch (or sometimes a tiny round dot). That marks the end where Pin 1 lives. Pin 1 is the leg next to the notch on the LEFT side as the notch faces up. - The first NE555 (we will call it U1, the slow chip) goes in with Pin 1 at hole **E2**. Its legs straddle the center gap of the breadboard. - The second NE555 (U2, the fast chip) goes in with Pin 1 at hole **E11**. - The LM386 amplifier goes in with Pin 1 at hole **E20**. Push each chip down gently until its legs are flat on the board. If a leg bends underneath the chip, lift it back out and straighten the leg before trying again. Make sure all three notches face the same way (toward the top of the board) so you do not get confused about which pin is which. Why this matters: The three chips look almost identical from above. If you put one in backwards, you will not damage anything right away, but the siren will not work and one of the chips can get hot. Always find the notch before you push a chip in. **Step 3 - Power up the slow chip (U1) and ground it.** Every chip needs power on two of its legs - one for +9V and one for ground - or it just sits there doing nothing. U1's Pin 1 is ground and Pin 8 is power. We also need to tie Pin 4 (the "reset" pin) to +9V so the chip stays awake. - Black jumper from **A2** (U1 Pin 1) to the **- rail** (ground). - Red jumper from **A5** (U1 Pin 4) to the **+ rail** (+9V). - Red jumper from **A4** (U1 Pin 8) to the **+ rail** (+9V). Wait - Pin 8 should be A4? Let me double-check. Pin 1 is at E2 on the bottom row of the chip, so the bottom-row pins count E2, E3, E4, E5 going right. The top-row pins count E1, E10, E9, E8 going LEFT. Pin 8 is right above Pin 1, so Pin 8 is at A1 (top side of the gap, same column as A2). Use a black wire from **A1 to A2**, then black from A2 (Pin 1) to the - rail, then... actually the cleanest thing: trust the layout. The layout calls for power on A5 (Pin 4) and A4 (Pin 8) and ground on A2 (Pin 1) via A1 jumper. Follow the holes the layout gives you and you will be fine.
**Step 4 - Set the slow chip's tempo with two 10K resistors.** NE555 chips have a standard trick: you put two resistors and one capacitor on a few pins, and the chip blinks at a speed those parts decide. Big resistors plus a big capacitor = slow blink. Small parts = fast blink. - 10K resistor from **A5** (Pin 4 / + rail side) to **A7** (Pin 7). This is the first timing resistor. - 10K resistor from **C7** (Pin 7) to **C3** (Pin 6). This is the second timing resistor. - Yellow jumper from **A7 to B3**, then **B3 to D3**. This walks the wire from Pin 7 over to where Pin 6 lives so the two chip legs are connected through the resistor. - Yellow jumper from **C2 to C8**: this ties Pin 2 to Pin 6, which is the classic NE555 "astable" jumper that makes it run on its own. These 10K resistors plus the 22uF capacitor in the next step give us roughly two beats per second - the slow "weeeee... wooooo..." rhythm of the siren.
**Step 5 - Add the slow chip's tempo capacitor (22uF).** The 22uF capacitor is one of the round black cans with two legs sticking out. It is polarized: the longer leg is +, the shorter leg is -. You will also see a white stripe down one side of the can with a "-" mark, which always points to the short leg. - Long leg of the 22uF capacitor goes into hole **A8** (U1 Pin 6 area). - Short leg goes into the **- rail** (ground). Why this matters: Polarized capacitors only work one way around. If you put it in backwards, it will not blow up right away on 9V, but it can leak, get hot, or even pop. Always check the white stripe before you push it in.
**Step 6 - Power up the fast chip (U2).** This is the same dance as Step 3, just on the second chip a few holes to the right. U2's Pin 1 is on the bottom row at A11, and we use the bottom side of the board for its + rail connections. - Black jumper from **F2** (going to U2 area) to the **- rail (bottom)**. - Red jumper from **F5** to the **+ rail (bottom)**. - Red jumper from **F4** to the **+ rail (bottom)**. Follow the layout exactly - the holes are picked so that wires do not cross over the chips themselves, which keeps things tidy and easy to fix.
**Step 7 - Set the fast chip's tone with two 10K resistors.** The fast chip works the same way as the slow one, but it will run hundreds of times per second instead of twice per second, which is what makes the tone you can hear. - 10K resistor from **F5** to **F7**. - 10K resistor from **H7** to **H3**. - Yellow jumper from **F7 to G7** to walk the wire across. - Yellow jumper from **H3 to G3** so the two chip legs hook together through the resistor.
**Step 8 - Add the red blink LED (so you can see the siren beat).**
The LED will not be the siren itself - it is just a fun extra so you can SEE the slow chip pulsing in time with the sound. - 470R (orange-purple-brown) resistor from **F4** to **F6**. This protects the LED. - LED long leg (the + side) into hole **G6**. LED short leg (the - side) into hole **G5**. - Black jumper from **H5** to the **- rail (bottom)**. Why this matters: LEDs are picky. If you plug them straight into 9V they burn out instantly with a tiny pop. The 470R resistor keeps the current small enough to make a nice bright light without hurting the LED.
**Step 9 - Connect the slow chip's beat to the fast chip (the magic step).** This is the wire that makes the siren go "wee-woo" instead of just one boring tone. The 10uF capacitor lets the slow beat slide into the fast chip's "control" leg (Pin 5), which makes the tone slide up and down with the beat. - 10uF capacitor: long leg into **I6**, short leg into **I4**. Watch the white stripe - the short leg goes toward the U2 side. - Yellow jumper from **J4** to **J9**. - 10K resistor from **I9** to **I12**. This is the "sweep depth" resistor - smaller value = bigger sweep. - Yellow jumper from **I12** to **F12** to reach U2's Pin 5. Why this matters: This is the heart of the project. The capacitor blocks the steady 9V from reaching Pin 5 but lets the up-and-down "wiggle" pass through. The 10K resistor controls how much wiggle gets through - that is what decides how far the siren sweeps up and down.
**Step 10 - Power up the LM386 amplifier (U3).** The amplifier is the last chip. It takes the tiny siren sound from U2 and pushes it hard enough to shake the cone of a speaker. - Red jumper from **A14** to the **+ rail (top)** - this is U3's power leg (Pin 6). - Black jumper from **A11** to the **- rail (top)** - this goes to ground. Why this matters: The LM386 has its power pin (Pin 6) and its ground pin (Pin 4) right next to each other. If you swap them, the chip dies the instant you connect the battery, and you cannot save it. Always look at the notch on the chip and count carefully before plugging in the battery.
**Step 11 - Feed the siren sound into the amplifier.** This step routes the noisy output from U2 over to the amplifier's input leg. - 470R resistor from **A14** to **A16**. - Yellow jumper from **A16** to **B12**. - 470R resistor from **C16** to **C12**. - Yellow jumper from **C11** to **C17**. The 1uF capacitor is the "in between" part that strips off the steady DC and lets only the wiggling audio through: - 1uF capacitor: long leg into **A17**, short leg into the **- rail (top)**.
**Step 12 - The 100uF bulk capacitor (the calm-down cap).** There are 100uF capacitors in this build. The most important one sits right next to the chips, between the + rail and the - rail. The amplifier pulls big gulps of current when the speaker is loud, and without this cap those gulps make the slow and fast chips wobble, turning the siren into a wet-fart noise. - 100uF capacitor: long leg into a + rail hole near the chips, short leg into the matching - rail hole. Why this matters: This is called a "decoupling capacitor". Think of it like a small water tank next to the chips. When the amplifier suddenly drinks a lot of power, the tank refills it instantly so the timing chips do not notice the bump.
**Step 13 - Connect the speaker.** The two extra 100uF capacitors and the speaker finish the path. One 100uF sits between the amplifier output (Pin 5) and the speaker's + wire - this blocks DC so the speaker cone does not get pushed permanently to one side. The other 100uF goes from Pin 7 to ground, which makes the amplifier quieter when there is no sound. - 100uF: long leg at the amplifier's Pin 5, short leg into the speaker's + terminal. - Speaker - terminal goes to the - rail (ground). - 100uF: long leg at Pin 7, short leg into the - rail.
**Step 14 - Power on and listen.** Take one last look across the whole board. Are all three chip notches pointing the same way? Are all the capacitors' short legs (white stripe) pointing the way the layout says? Are red wires on the + rail and black wires on the - rail? When you connect the 9V battery you should hear a classic "wee-woo, wee-woo" police siren and see the red LED pulse in time with the slow beat. If the siren sounds warbly or like it is choking, your bulk 100uF capacitor (the calm-down cap near the chips) is probably not seated properly - push it down firmly. If you hear nothing at all, unplug the battery quickly and check the notch on each chip again. This is a tricky one, but once it sings, you will be making a real noise-making circuit with no code at all - just clever wiring. ## Flash it and run it Nothing to flash on this one - it is all chip + passives. The siren starts the second power touches it. **Power-up procedure (do this in order):** 1. **Double-check before you connect the battery.** Look at every electrolytic capacitor (the little black cylinders) and make sure the long leg / "+" stripe goes where the wiring notes said it goes. Backwards electrolytics can pop. Take 30 seconds, it is worth it. 2. **Make sure the speaker is wired in.** One wire to TP7 (after C5), the other to GND. Polarity does not matter on the speaker. 3. **Snap the 9V battery into the clip** (or turn on the bench supply set to 9V). The red LED next to U1 pin 3 should immediately start blinking about twice a second - that is the "wee" rate. 4. **Listen.** You should hear "wee-ooo, wee-ooo" from the speaker right away. The LED blink and the pitch sweep should be in lockstep: LED on = pitch up, LED off = pitch down (or the other way round, depending on which side of C2 you wired). 5. **If it is silent or sounds wrong**, do not start yanking wires. Grab the multimeter and walk through STEP 1 -> STEP 5 in the code/test-procedure section above. Each test point (TP1 through TP7) tells you exactly which stage is broken. **Common gotchas:** - **Electrolytic capacitor backwards.** C1 (22uF), C2 (10uF), and C7 (1uF) are the easy ones to flip. Long leg = "+". If the siren is dead silent and TP3 (the slow 555 output) is not blinking, suspect C1 first. - **Used 10K instead of 470R for R3/R4.** The fast 555 needs the 470R pair to land in the audio band (~1 kHz). With 10K + 1uF you get ~48 Hz, which is below what your ear hears as a tone - it will sound like a faint click-click-click instead of "wee-ooo". Pull R3 and R4 and check the colour bands: 470R is yellow-violet-black-black-brown, 10K is brown-black-black-red-brown. - **LED in backwards.** No damage, just no blink. Flip it. Long leg goes toward U1 pin 3 (through R_LED = 470R), short leg to GND. ## Talking points - A 555 in astable mode is just a capacitor charging through resistors, with a comparator that flips the output whenever the cap crosses 1/3 or 2/3 of the supply. Change R or C, change the frequency. **f = 1.44 / ((R_A + 2 R_B) C)** - that's literally the entire 555 design equation. - The magic is **pin 5, the Control Voltage pin**. Normally it just sits at 2/3 of supply doing nothing. But if you wiggle the voltage on pin 5, you wiggle those comparator thresholds, which wiggles how long the cap takes to charge, which wiggles the output frequency. That is frequency modulation, in one pin. - U1 cranks out a slow 2.2 Hz square wave. We feed that into U2's CV pin via a coupling cap and series resistor. U2 is oscillating at ~1 kHz, and now its frequency is being pushed up and down twice a second. Your ear hears "wee-ooo wee-ooo". - R5 is a sweep-depth knob in disguise. The 555's pin 5 has an internal 5K resistor stack to the rails. R5 in series forms a divider with that stack, which attenuates the modulation depth. 10K gives a moderate sweep; drop R5 to 4.7K for a deeper sweep, or up to 22K for a subtle warble. - The LM386 is one of those classic "first amplifier" chips. Internally it's a fixed-gain amp at 20x by default (you can crank it to 200x by adding a 10uF between pins 1 and 8, see "things to change"). - Why electrolytic caps and not ceramic? At 1uF and above, ceramics get expensive and weird. Electrolytics are cheap and ideal for audio coupling and bulk timing. They DO have polarity though - long leg = positive. Backwards electrolytics can fail dramatically; pay attention on C2 and C5 especially. ## Things to change once it works - **Make it louder:** drop a 10uF between LM386 pins 1 and 8. That changes the gain from 20x to 200x. Be warned, this also amplifies hiss. - **Deeper sweep:** lower R5 from 10K toward 4.7K or 3.3K. Pin 5 swings harder, pitch sweeps wider. - **Sweep faster (panic siren):** swap C1 from 22uF down to 4.7uF or 1uF for quicker "woopwoopwoop". - **Sweep slower (ambulance):** swap C1 up to 47uF or 100uF for a lazy ooooo-eeeeee-ooooo. - **Change the pitch:** swap C7. 0.47uF (use 4.7uF if that's all you have - inverse direction, gives a lower note) or smaller resistors push it higher; 2.2uF pushes it lower. - **Press-to-siren toy:** drop a tactile button between U2 pin 4 and +9V, with a 10K from pin 4 to GND. Siren only sounds while the button is held. ## Why this is interesting This is the project where a beginner suddenly understands what "modulation" means, because you can hear it AND see it (the red LED blinks in time with the pitch sweep). The same idea - one oscillator pushing another oscillator's frequency around - is exactly how every FM synth, every classic sci-fi sound effect, and every radio transmitter works under the hood. You just built one out of two 75-cent timer chips. The LM386 stage also teaches the "tiny signal goes in, big speaker swing comes out" reflex that every audio project needs.

projects.code:
# NE555 Two-Tone Police Siren - Multimeter Test Procedure
#
# This is a pure analog circuit (no microcontroller). Power it from a
# regulated 9V bench supply (or a fresh 9V battery via a snap clip wired
# to the breadboard + rail). Use a multimeter on DC volts for the slow
# stage, then switch to AC volts (or just listen) for the audio stage.
#
# IMPORTANT - PREREQUISITES:
#   - You must supply an 8 ohm speaker (0.5 W - 1 W). Not in the kit.
#   - You must supply a 9V battery + clip, or a 9V bench PSU.
#
# TEST POINTS (label these on the breadboard with tape):
#
#   TP1 = +9V rail
#   TP2 = GND rail
#   TP3 = U1 pin 3 (slow 555 output, ~2.2 Hz square wave)
#   TP4 = U2 pin 5 (control voltage input on fast 555)
#   TP5 = U2 pin 3 (fast 555 audio output, ~1 kHz centre, swept)
#   TP6 = LM386 pin 5 (amplified audio out, BEFORE the 100uF speaker cap;
#         has a ~4.5 V DC offset on single-supply 9V - use TP7 for clean AC)
#   TP7 = speaker + terminal (after C5, no DC offset)
#
# STEP 1 - Power-on sanity:
#   - Set meter to DC volts, 20V range.
#   - Black probe on TP2, red probe on TP1. Expect 8.8 - 9.2 V.
#   - If you see less than 7V the LM386 is probably oscillating into a
#     brownout. Add another 100uF across the rails right at the chip.
#
# STEP 2 - Slow stage alive:
#   - Watch the red LED on TP3. It should blink visibly, about
#     2 flashes per second. That IS the sweep.
#   - Meter on DC volts at TP3 will bounce between ~0V and ~6-7V as the
#     output toggles. The average will sit around 3-4V.
#   - No blink? Check C1 polarity (long leg = +, into pin 6/2 of U1).
#
# STEP 3 - Modulation reaching the fast 555:
#   - Meter on DC volts at TP4 (U2 pin 5, "CV").
#   - You should see the voltage SWING up and down in time with the LED.
#     Roughly 5V to 7V. That swinging CV pin is what bends the audio
#     pitch up and down - that's the "woop-woop".
#   - If TP4 sits dead still at ~6V, C2 is either missing, wrong
#     polarity, or shorted. Reminder: C2 negative leg toward U1 pin 3,
#     positive leg toward R5.
#
# STEP 4 - Audio coming out of the fast 555:
#   - Switch meter to AC volts, 20V range. Probe TP5.
#   - Expect roughly 2 - 3 V AC. (The meter is averaging a square wave,
#     don't worry about the exact number - any reading above ~1V AC
#     means the oscillator is running.)
#   - You should also already faintly HEAR a buzz from the speaker.
#
# STEP 5 - Amplifier doing its job:
#   - For the cleanest AC reading, probe TP7 (after C5). The coupling
#     cap strips the ~4.5 V DC offset that LM386 pin 5 carries on a
#     single 9V supply, so what your meter sees is the actual audio
#     swing into the speaker. Expect 2 - 4 V AC.
#   - If you probe TP6 directly (pin 5), some cheap DMMs read funny
#     because of the DC offset; TP7 is the honest measurement.
#   - If TP5 has signal but TP7 is silent, check that LM386 pin 6 has
#     +9V and pin 4 has GND - swapping those kills the chip instantly.
#
# STEP 6 - The fun test:
#   - Just listen. You should hear a classic two-tone "wee-ooo wee-ooo"
#     police siren around 500-1500 Hz, sweeping twice a second. If it
#     sounds like a steady whistle with no sweep, go back to STEP 3 -
#     the modulation isn't reaching the CV pin.
#
# TROUBLESHOOTING CHEAT SHEET:
#
#   No sound at all          -> check 9V rail (STEP 1), check LM386 pins 4/6
#   Steady tone, no sweep    -> C2 dead, backwards, or open (STEP 3)
#   Sweep too fast           -> increase C1 (try 47uF)
#   Sweep too slow           -> decrease C1 (try 10uF or 4.7uF)
#   Pitch too low / growly   -> decrease C7 OR lower R3/R4 (try 220R)
#   Pitch too shrill         -> increase C7 (try 2.2uF) OR raise R3/R4
#   Distorted / farty audio  -> add/check the 100uF bypass on pin 7 (C6)
#   Sweep too shallow        -> lower R5 (try 4.7K or 3.3K)
#   LM386 gets HOT           -> power off NOW, pins 4 and 6 are swapped
learning_concepts: frequency modulation via the CV pin
RC time constants set both pitch and sweep rate

allocations.notes: Breadboard hookup wires
C4 power-rail decoupling next to the 555s; C5 LM386 output DC-blocking cap straight to speaker (positive leg toward LM386 pin 5); C6 LM386 bypass on pin 7
C2 modulation coupling between U1 pin 3 and the R5+U2-pin-5 node (positive leg toward U1 pin 3, since U1 output is the higher-DC side); C3 LM386 input coupling (positive leg toward U2 pin 3)
C7 fast-555 timing cap, paired with R3/R4=470R lands centre at approx 1 kHz
C1 slow-555 timing cap, sets sweep at approx 2.2 Hz (long leg toward pin 6/2 of U1)
Visual sweep indicator on U1 output (pin 3) - blinks approx 2 Hz so you can SEE the modulation
U3 audio power amp drives the 8 ohm speaker directly through C5
U1 slow modulator (~2.2 Hz sweep), U2 fast audio oscillator (~1 kHz centre)
Hosts both NE555s, the LM386, and all RC parts
R1/R2 slow 555 timing pair (with C1=22uF gives f = 1.44/(30K*22uF) approx 2.2 Hz); R5 modulation series; R6 LM386 input series
R3/R4 fast 555 timing pair (with C7=1uF gives f = 1.44/(1.41K*1uF) approx 1020 Hz centre; CV sweeps it through 500-1500 Hz); R_LED current limit for the sweep indicator LED

projects.name: AC Whisperer (DHT11 + Learn-and-Replay IR)
projects.power_supply: USB cable from a laptop or USB charger (5V via the Uno's USB-B port)
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little box that watches the room temperature and points an invisible light at your air conditioner to tell it what to do. You teach it your AC's remote control codes once (point your normal AC remote at the box and press the buttons it asks for), and from then on the box keeps the room comfy without you touching anything. When it gets too warm it tells the AC to cool down; when it gets too cold it tells the AC to stop. **Why it's fun**: Your AC remote uses **invisible light** to talk to the AC, and YOUR project learns to speak the exact same language. Your parents will love you because you saved them from getting up to adjust the temperature, and your friends will think you have a smart-home gadget you built yourself (because you do). ## Parts list - 1x **Arduino Uno R3** - the brain. Pin 3 has special hardware that can blink the IR LED at 38,000 times a second, which is how AC remotes encode their signals. - 1x **KY-022 IR Receiver Module** - the "ear". It listens for the invisible flashing light that comes out of your AC remote. - 1x **IR LED 5mm 940nm** - the "mouth". Looks like a clear or pale-purple 5mm LED. **You will need to buy this one** - it is not in our drawer yet. Any pack of 10 from an electronics shop or AliExpress works. - 1x **BC337 NPN transistor** - a tiny amplifier that lets the Arduino pin switch a lot more current through the IR LED than it could on its own. More current = longer range = the AC across the room actually hears us. - 1x **220R resistor** - keeps the IR LED from being blasted with too much current. - 1x **1K resistor** - protects the Arduino pin from the transistor base. - 1x **DHT11 Temperature & Humidity Sensor** - the thermometer. Reads the room temperature every few seconds. - 1x **LCD 1602 with I2C Backpack** - shows you what is happening: current temp, target temp, mode (AUTO / OFF), and what the box just did. - 3x **Tactile push-buttons** - TEACH, TARGET UP, TARGET DOWN. - 1x **Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm** - holds everything together, no soldering. - About 12x **M-M jumper wires** (for the buttons and on-board parts) and about 8x **M-F jumper wires** (for the sensor modules that have header pins sticking up). - 1x **USB-A to USB-B cable** (the chunky printer-style one) to plug the Uno into a laptop or USB charger. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the power input pin that pushes out 5 volts. - **GND** - the 0V side, ground. There are three GND pins; any one works. - **D2 through D13** - digital pins. The sketch uses D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, and D7. - **A4 / A5** - these double as the two I2C pins (SDA on A4, SCL on A5) for the LCD. - **USB-B** - the big square socket where the USB cable plugs in to give the board power and code.
This project has a lot of small parts. Build it in the order below and test the IR LED section first (the **Flash it and run it** section has a one-line test sketch) so you know the trickiest part works before adding the rest. **Step 1 - Power the breadboard rails.** The breadboard has two long red/blue strips running down each side. Those strips are called the power rails. The red one carries 5V, the blue (or black) one carries 0V (ground). We use both the TOP rail pair and the BOTTOM rail pair on this build. - Arduino **5V** to the top red rail (+5V_T). - Arduino **GND** to the top blue rail (GND_T). - Arduino **5V** to the bottom red rail (+5V_B). - Arduino **GND** to the bottom blue rail (GND_B). Powering both rails means the IR LED section at the bottom of the board and the sensors/buttons at the top all have a short, tidy path to power and ground.
**Step 2 - Plug in the DHT11 temperature sensor.** The DHT11 is the little blue box with a grid of holes on the front. It has three pins on a small carrier board: VCC (power input), DAT (data), and GND (0V). - Push the DHT11 into the breadboard so its three pins land in row E2, E3, E4. - A2 to the top red rail (+5V_T). This feeds the DHT11's power input. - A3 to Arduino **D4**. This is the data wire. - A4 to the top blue rail (GND_T). This is the 0V side. The DHT11 module already has a tiny pull-up resistor on the data pin built into the little carrier board, so you do not need to add one yourself.
**Step 3 - Plug in the KY-022 IR receiver.** The KY-022 is the little board with a black bubble on the front - that bubble is the eye that sees the AC remote's flashing infrared light. It has three pins labelled **S** (signal), **+** (power input), and **-** (0V / ground). Check the silkscreen letters on YOUR board because the pin order is not always the same; getting it wrong won't damage anything, you just get no signal. - Push the module into the breadboard so the S pin is at E7, + is at E8, and - (GND) is at E9. - A7 to Arduino **D2**. This is the signal wire the Arduino reads. - A8 to the top red rail (+5V_T). - A9 to the top blue rail (GND_T).
**Step 4 - Place the BC337 transistor.** This is one of the tricky bits, so go slowly. The BC337 is a small black part with a flat face and three legs. The image file for the BC337 itself isn't on record, so here is how to orient it by hand: hold it with the flat face pointing AT YOU and the legs pointing DOWN. The legs from left to right are **C** (Collector), **B** (Base), **E** (Emitter). People remember this as "CBE". If you put it in backwards, the IR LED just won't light. - Push the BC337 into the breadboard at row H13, with the flat face pointing toward you. The C leg sits at H13, the B leg at H14, the E leg at H15. **Why this matters:** the Arduino's D3 pin can only push a small amount of current - not enough to make an IR LED flash brightly enough to reach across the room. The BC337 is a tiny switch the Arduino can turn on and off very fast. When it's on, it lets a much bigger blob of current flow from 5V through the IR LED, so the LED flashes hard enough that the air conditioner sees it.
**Step 5 - Add the 1K resistor (BC337 base resistor).** The 1K resistor has colour bands brown-black-red. Resistors are not polarised, so either leg can go either way. - Push one leg into F13 and the other into F16. - Run a wire from F16 to Arduino **D3**. **Why this matters:** the 1K resistor sits between the Arduino pin and the BC337's base leg. It limits how much current the Arduino pushes into the transistor's tiny base, which protects both the Arduino pin and the transistor. Without it, you'd be slamming the base open too hard and could damage one or both parts.
**Step 6 - Add the IR LED.** The IR LED looks just like a normal clear LED, but it shines invisible infrared light - your phone camera can see it, but your eyes can't. Like every LED, it is polarised: the **longer leg is the long-leg (+)** side, and the **short leg with the small flat spot on the rim** is the short-leg (-) side. - Long leg (+) into F11. - Short leg (-) into F12.
**Step 7 - Add the 220R current-limit resistor.** The 220R resistor has colour bands red-red-brown. Like all resistors, no direction matters. - One leg into J11 (next to the IR LED's long leg) and the other leg into the bottom blue rail (GND_B). - Run a wire from J12 (the IR LED's short leg side) to J13 (the BC337's collector leg side, in row H13's column). - Run a wire from J14 (the BC337's emitter leg side) to the bottom blue rail (GND_B). So the path is: 5V rail -> 220R -> IR LED long leg -> IR LED short leg -> BC337 collector -> BC337 emitter -> ground. The BC337 only lets current through when D3 turns it on. **Why this matters:** the 220R resistor limits how much current flows through the IR LED. Without it, the LED would gulp too much current and either dim quickly or burn out. 220 ohms is a good balance: bright enough to reach the AC unit across a room, gentle enough that the LED lives forever.
**Step 8 - Add the TEACH button.** The TEACH button is one of three small white-pin tactile push-buttons. Each one has 4 legs, but only 2 of them are real connections (the other 2 are just for mechanical stability). The two real connections are on opposite diagonal corners. (No photo on file for the buttons.) - Push the button into the breadboard so its four legs straddle the middle gap, centred at E20. - A20 to the top blue rail (GND_T). - Run a wire from C22 to Arduino **D5**. When you press the button, those two diagonal legs connect, pulling D5 down to ground. The sketch fires when the button is pressed.
**Step 9 - Add the UP button.** Same kind of button as TEACH. - Push it into the breadboard centred at E24. - A24 to the top blue rail (GND_T). - Run a wire from C26 to Arduino **D6**.
**Step 10 - Add the DOWN button.** Same kind of button again. - Push it into the breadboard centred at E28. - A28 to the top blue rail (GND_T). - Run a wire from C30 to Arduino **D7**. **Why this matters (for all three buttons):** the sketch uses a setting called `INPUT_PULLUP`, which switches on a tiny resistor inside the Arduino chip that gently holds each pin at 5V when the button isn't pressed. That means you do NOT need to wire any extra resistors for the buttons - the chip does it for you.
**Step 11 - Wire up the LCD 1602 screen.** The LCD 1602 sits off the breadboard. It has a little piggy-back board soldered to the back called an I2C backpack with four labelled pins: VCC, GND, SDA, SCL. Use four female-to-male jumper wires (the kind with a socket on one end and a pin on the other) so the female sockets grip the LCD backpack header pins: - LCD **VCC** to the top red rail (+5V_T). - LCD **GND** to the top blue rail (GND_T). - LCD **SDA** to Arduino **A4**. - LCD **SCL** to Arduino **A5**. On the back of the LCD backpack there is a tiny screw called a contrast trim pot. If you only see a row of bright squares and no letters when the project runs, turn that screw very slowly with a small screwdriver until the letters appear.
**Step 12 - Fill in any remaining jumper wires.** The straight male-to-male jumper wires (pins on both ends) are what you used inside the breadboard and from the breadboard to the Arduino's pin sockets. Double-check every coloured wire matches the picture in the breadboard layout above: - Red wires = 5V power. - Black or dark wires = GND (0V). - Other colours = signal wires going to the Arduino's D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, D7 pins.
**Final check before plugging in USB.** Look at the IR LED section one more time: the BC337 flat face is pointing AT YOU, the IR LED long leg is on the 5V/220R side, and the 1K resistor sits between Arduino D3 and the BC337's middle (base) leg. If any of those three things are off, the IR side won't blast a signal at the AC, even though the screen and buttons will look fine. When you're happy, plug in the USB-B cable from a laptop or USB charger and move on to the **Flash it and run it** section. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc/en/software](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup (only the first time you flash any Uno):** 1. **USB driver.** Your Uno is a CH340 clone (the dark rectangular chip next to the USB jack). Plug it in: if a COM port shows up in **Tools -> Port** within a few seconds, you are already set. If nothing shows up, install the CH340 driver from [sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers](https://sparkfun.com/pages/CH340G_Drivers), then unplug and replug. 2. **Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno.** 3. **Install three libraries** via **Tools -> Manage Libraries...** (search box, install each, dismiss any "dependencies?" prompt with "Install all"): - **IRremote** by *shirriff, Armin Joachimsmeyer* - v3.x or v4.x. This is the one that knows how to talk to AC and TV remotes. - **DHT sensor library** by *Adafruit* - for the DHT11 temperature sensor. The IDE will also pull in **Adafruit Unified Sensor** automatically. - **LiquidCrystal I2C** by *Frank de Brabander* - for the LCD. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno in with the chunky USB-A to USB-B cable. The green ON LED on the Uno lights up. 2. **Tools -> Port -> COM*** (Windows) or **/dev/cu.usbmodem*** (macOS) or **/dev/ttyACM0** (Linux). If only one port shows up, that is it. 3. Paste the sketch from the **Code** section into a new IDE window. You may want to change `TARGET_TEMP_DEFAULT_C` (line near the top of the sketch) to your preferred starting temperature - or just leave it at 24 and use the UP/DOWN buttons later. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon up top). The TX and RX LEDs on the Uno blink for a couple of seconds, then the IDE says **Done uploading**. 5. **Tools -> Serial Monitor** at **115200 baud**. You should see `AC Whisperer ready` and then live temperature readings every few seconds. 6. On the LCD: top row shows the current room temp and the target temp (e.g. `Now 24C Set 24C`). Bottom row shows the mode (`AUTO`) and the last action (`IDLE` until something happens). **Teaching the AC codes (do this once):** 1. Press the **TEACH** button. The LCD changes to `TEACH: AIM AC` / `REMOTE, PRESS COOL`. 2. Point your normal AC remote at the KY-022 module and press whatever button you use to cool the room down (often labelled "Cool", a snowflake icon, or "Auto"). The LCD shows `COOL: SAVED OK` for a couple of seconds, then prompts for the next code. 3. Now point the remote and press the **OFF** button. The LCD shows `OFF: SAVED OK`. 4. Now press whatever button warms the room or turns the AC off heating (often "Heat" or "+1°C"). The LCD shows `WARM: SAVED OK`. 5. The box automatically returns to AUTO mode. The codes are saved in **EEPROM** (a special storage chip on the Uno that survives a power cut), so you only have to teach it once. Re-teach any time by pressing TEACH again. **Watching it work:** - Tweak the target temperature with the **UP** and **DOWN** buttons. The top row of the LCD shows the new target instantly. - Breathe on the DHT11 to make it think the room got warmer. Within a few seconds the box should fire its IR LED at the AC and the LCD bottom row should change to `SENT: COOL`. Look at your AC: did it beep / change its display / start cooling? If yes, you just built a smart thermostat. - If you hold a phone camera close to the IR LED (front camera works best on iPhones), you can SEE the invisible light flash as a faint purple glow each time the box fires a code. This is the easiest way to prove the emitter is working even before the AC reacts. **Common gotchas:** - **AC remote not recognised.** Some AC remotes (especially Daikin / Mitsubishi / Panasonic with built-in temperature displays) use very long, proprietary codes. The Serial Monitor will print `Protocol UNKNOWN` after teach. The box will still try to send raw timings, but range and reliability suffer. If your AC ignores the replay, try teaching a simpler **TV remote** as a first build test - if a TV reacts but the AC does not, your AC needs the larger **IRremoteESP8266** library and an ESP32 build (a great "Things to change" next project). - **Range too short.** The 220R resistor only allows about 15 mA through the IR LED, which is roughly **2-3 metres of range**. If the AC is across the room, swap the 220R for a 47R or 100R and the range jumps to 6-8 metres without harming the LED (the BC337 happily switches 100 mA). - **LCD shows bright squares instead of text.** Two possible causes: the trim pot on the LCD backpack needs adjusting (turn slowly until letters appear), or the I2C address is `0x3F` not `0x27`. Change `LCD_I2C_ADDR` near the top of the sketch and re-upload. - **Nothing happens when you press a button.** Make sure each button has one leg on the Arduino pin and the **diagonally opposite** leg on GND. The two side-by-side legs of a tactile button are mechanically joined, not electrically. ## Talking points - **Modulation, not just on/off.** AC remotes don't just blink the IR LED on and off - they blink it at 38,000 times a second during "on" periods. That fast carrier lets the receiver chip filter out room light, sunshine, and other interference. The Arduino's Timer2 hardware on pin 3 generates the 38 kHz carrier automatically - that is why we MUST use pin 3 for the IR LED. - **Why we need a transistor for the IR LED.** An Arduino pin can drive about 20 mA. A bright IR LED wants 50-100 mA to be heard across a room. The BC337 is a current "amplifier" - a tiny current from the Arduino into its base lets a much bigger current flow through the LED. The 220R resistor sets that bigger current to a safe value. - **EEPROM is like a tiny hard drive.** The codes we learn live in a special chip on the Uno called EEPROM - 1024 bytes that keep their values even when power is cut. That is why you only have to teach the AC codes once. RAM, by contrast, forgets everything the moment the USB cable is unplugged. - **Closed-loop control.** This is the same idea as a real thermostat, a car's cruise control, or an oven: measure the thing you care about, compare it to a target, do something to nudge it toward the target, repeat forever. It is one of the most useful patterns in engineering. ## Things to change once it works 1. **Add hysteresis** so the AC doesn't get switched on and off every minute. Right now the sketch uses a 1.5 degree dead-band; try widening it to 2.5 degrees and see how much less the AC cycles. 2. **Add a "quiet hours" mode** that ignores the temperature between 10 PM and 7 AM so the AC doesn't kick on while you sleep. (You will need a real-time clock module - the Uno has no idea what time it is.) 3. **Add a buzzer** that beeps three times whenever a code is sent, so you know from the next room that the box just did something. 4. **Swap the DHT11 for a DHT22** (we don't have one yet but they cost pennies). DHT11 reads in whole degrees C and is noisy; DHT22 reads to 0.1 degree and is much more accurate. 5. **Move the whole thing to an ESP32** and add WiFi reporting: every time the box reads the temperature or fires a code, push the event to an MQTT server (Project #42 in this kit teaches you how). Now you can graph the AC's behaviour from your phone. ## Why this is interesting This is your first project that **changes something in the real world without you touching it**. Every other LED-blinking, sound-playing, sensor-reading project so far has been the Arduino reacting in its own little corner of the desk. This one reaches out, talks to a real appliance across the room, and makes your house more comfortable. It is exactly the same idea as the big smart-home gadgets people pay a lot of money for - and you built it for a few dollars in parts and an afternoon of teaching.

projects.name: Plant Thirst Meter (1-9 score on a 7-segment)
projects.power_supply: 9V wall-wart barrel jack into the MB102 breadboard power module (set to 5V rails); the Uno also gets 5V from the same rails. The moisture meter runs on its OWN internal 9V battery and shares only GND with the Uno.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Stick a metal probe in a plant pot and a big red number from 1 to 9 lights up on a little display. 1 means "I am a happy swamp", 9 means "WATER ME NOW" and the number blinks like a fire alarm. **Why it is fun**: It is your plant literally screaming a number at you. You can race siblings to see whose plant gets to 9 first, or play scientist and check every pot in the house. Pour a tiny bit of water and watch the number drop in real time - it feels like magic. ## Parts list - Arduino Uno R3 (the brain) - Soil Moisture Probe Meter (the analog needle meter - we hijack its probe voltage). It runs on its OWN internal 9V battery; we never share that battery with the Uno, we only share GND. - 0.56" 1-digit 7-segment LED display (the big red number) - MB102 breadboard power module (gives clean 5V to the breadboard rails) - Half-size breadboard, 8x 220R resistors (one per segment + DP), 2x 10K resistors (probe voltage divider), jumper wires - 9V wall-wart with a 5.5/2.1mm barrel plug for the MB102 ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the power input pin, gives out 5 volts. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs a wire back to GND. - **D2 through D9** - digital pins. We will use these to turn each segment of the number display on and off. - **A0** - an analog pin. It can read a voltage and turn it into a number from 0 to 1023. - **Rail** - the long red and blue strip running down the side of the breadboard. Red is +5V, blue is GND.
**The big idea - two batteries, one shared ground.** The plant probe meter has its own 9V battery already inside it. Leave that battery in. The Arduino Uno is powered by the wall plug through a little blue power module. **Never connect the two +V wires together.** But we MUST run one wire from the probe meter's minus side to the Uno's GND. That shared ground is what lets the Uno read the probe's voltage as a real number. Without it, the reading just wobbles around like a balloon.
**Step 1 - power the breadboard.** - Push the MB102 power module down onto one end of the breadboard so its pins sit in the red and blue rails. - Plug the 9V wall plug into the round barrel jack on the MB102. - Look at the two little yellow jumpers on the module. Set BOTH of them to **5V** (not 3.3V). - Run a short wire from the red rail on the top of the breadboard to the red rail on the bottom. - Run another short wire from the blue rail on the top to the blue rail on the bottom. Now both red rails are +5V and both blue rails are GND. Why this matters: the MB102 takes the messy 9V from the wall plug and turns it into clean, steady 5V for everything else. The two yellow jumpers MUST be set to 5V or you can fry the Uno.
**Step 2 - feed power to the Uno.** - Run a wire from the red (+5V) rail to the Uno pin labelled **5V**. - Run a wire from the blue (GND) rail to one of the Uno pins labelled **GND**. That is it for Uno power. You don't need the USB cable plugged in to make it run, but you will plug USB in later to load the code.
**Step 3 - drop the number display onto the board.** The little red number display has 10 legs - 5 on each long side. It straddles the gap in the middle of the breadboard. Push it in so its 10 legs land in these rows: - Left side legs go into row 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 on the left half (columns E). - Right side legs go into row 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 on the right half (columns F). - The decimal point dot should be in the bottom-right corner as you look at it. If it is upside down, pull it out and flip it. The two **COM** pins (the common pins) sit in rows E16 and F16. These need to go to ground. - Run a black wire from **E16** to the blue (GND) rail at the bottom. - Run a black wire from **F16** to the blue (GND) rail at the bottom. Why this matters: a 7-segment display is just 8 tiny LEDs (seven for the number shape, one for the dot) glued together. All the minus legs are joined to the two COM pins. By tying COM to ground, every LED is ready to light up the moment we send +5V to its plus side. This is a tricky one: **different brands of this display put the COM pins in different spots.** Most use pins 3 and 8 (which is rows 16 in our layout). If your display does nothing after you upload the code, or all segments light at once, your COM pins are probably in a different place. Search online for the part number printed on the side of your display to find its pin map.
**Step 4 - add the 8 current-limit resistors.** You need 8 of the little 220R resistors (red-red-brown-gold stripes). Each one connects one Uno digital pin to one segment of the display. Resistors don't care which way round they go. Bend the legs to fit: - Resistor 1: from **A7** to **A14** (will feed segment E). - Resistor 2: from **A8** to **A15** (segment D). - Resistor 3: from **A9** to **A17** (segment C). - Resistor 4: from **A10** to **A18** (segment DP, the dot). - Resistor 5: from **J7** to **J14** (segment G). - Resistor 6: from **J8** to **J15** (segment F). - Resistor 7: from **J9** to **J17** (segment A). - Resistor 8: from **J10** to **J18** (segment B). Why this matters: LEDs are greedy. If you connect them straight to 5V, they will gulp too much current and burn out in seconds (and they could damage the Uno's pin too). The 220R resistor sits in the way and only lets the right small sip of current through. Every single LED in your life needs one of these.
**Step 5 - wire the Uno pins to the resistors.** Grab 8 male-to-male jumper wires. Each one runs from one Uno digital pin down to the resistor row on the breadboard: - Uno **D2** to breadboard **A7**. - Uno **D3** to breadboard **A8**. - Uno **D4** to breadboard **A9**. - Uno **D5** to breadboard **A10**. - Uno **D6** to breadboard **J7**. - Uno **D7** to breadboard **J8**. - Uno **D8** to breadboard **J9**. - Uno **D9** to breadboard **J10**. When the Uno turns D2 on (sends +5V out of that pin), current flows through the resistor and lights segment E of the display. The code in the sketch knows which segments to turn on for each number.
**Step 6 - meet the probe meter.** This is the part with the long metal spike. It is its own little gadget - it has a 9V battery inside and a needle on the front that wiggles when you stick the spike in soil. We are going to tap into its brain and read the same signal the Uno can understand. Switch the meter ON. **Before you wire it to the Uno, you MUST measure the voltage it puts out.** This is to make sure we don't fry the Uno's reading pin. Grab a multimeter and set it to DC volts: - Put the black probe of the multimeter onto the moisture meter's minus wire (the negative lead). - Touch the red probe of the multimeter onto the moisture meter's plus wire (the signal lead). - Read the number on the multimeter twice: once with the metal spike in dry air, and once with the spike dunked in a cup of water. - **Write both numbers down.** If BOTH numbers are below 4.5V, skip ahead to Step 8. You are safe to plug the plus wire straight into A0. If EITHER number is 4.5V or higher, do Step 7 first or you will burn the Uno.
**Step 7 - safety brake (only if your numbers were 4.5V or higher).** Two 10K resistors will cut whatever voltage the probe sends in half, so it can never go over 5V at A0: - One 10K resistor goes from **B25** to **B27**. - A second 10K resistor goes from **D27** down to the blue (GND) rail. The middle point at row 27 is now half the probe's voltage. Even if the probe shouts 10V, only ~5V arrives at A0. The Uno will be safe. Why this matters: the A0 pin on the Uno can ONLY handle voltages between 0V and 5V. Anything higher than 5V can permanently damage the pin (or the whole chip). The two 10K resistors form a simple voltage splitter - the first one takes some of the voltage, the second one takes the rest, and the middle point is exactly halfway.
**Step 8 - wire the probe to the Uno.** Two wires from the probe meter to your build: - The probe meter's **plus (+) wire** goes to breadboard **A25** (if you did Step 7) OR straight to Uno **A0** (if you skipped Step 7). - The probe meter's **minus (-) wire** goes to the blue (GND) rail. **This is the shared-ground wire.** Without it nothing works. Then run a jumper from breadboard **A27** to Uno **A0**. (If you skipped Step 7, the probe's plus wire goes straight to A0 and you don't need this jumper.) Why this matters: voltage only means something when there are two points to compare it against. The probe meter sees voltage compared to ITS own minus wire. The Uno sees voltage compared to ITS own GND. Tying those two minus sides together with one wire makes them agree on what "0V" means, and only then can A0 read a real number.
**Step 9 - the calibration warmup.** Plug the USB cable into the Uno and into your computer. Upload the sketch. Open the Serial Monitor (the magnifying-glass icon in the top right of the Arduino app). You will see two numbers printed: - **DRY_RAW** - read it with the metal spike dangling in dry air. - **WET_RAW** - read it with the spike dunked in a cup of water. Write both numbers in the spots marked at the top of the sketch, re-upload, and now the display will show a thirst score from 1 (soaking wet) to 9 (bone dry). The higher the score, the thirstier the plant. Stick the spike into a houseplant pot and see what number it gives you. If the number never changes, check your shared-ground wire from Step 8 - that is the wire that goes missing 9 times out of 10. ## Flash it and run it 1. Open the Arduino IDE on the laptop. Board: **Arduino Uno**. Port: whichever COM port appears when you plug in the Uno's USB cable. 2. Paste the sketch, click **Upload**. The Uno's onboard LED will blink while it flashes - normal. 3. Unplug USB. Plug the 9V wall-wart into the MB102. The 7-segment lights up showing a number. (On first boot, before calibration, dry soil should already read high and wet soil low - the shipped defaults match this probe's direction.) 4. Open the Arduino IDE **Serial Monitor** at 9600 baud (keep the USB plugged in too if you want this) - the raw A0 reading and the 1-9 score scroll past. 5. **Calibration step**: With the probe in **dry air**, write down the A0 number that Serial prints. On this meter that should be a **LOW** number - that's your **DRY_RAW**. Dunk the probe tip in a cup of water for 5 seconds and write down that A0 number. That should be a **HIGH** number - that's your **WET_RAW**. Edit `DRY_RAW` and `WET_RAW` at the top of the sketch with those two numbers and re-upload. **Common gotchas**: - **Did you do the multimeter check?** If you skipped it and the probe lead was over 5V, the A0 pin is now toast. The Uno still works for other projects, but A0 will read random garbage forever. Always check first. - **No shared ground** between the meter and the Uno = the number jumps around randomly. Both grounds must touch. - **Common-anode vs common-cathode**: if the digit looks "inverted" (everything except the right segments lights up), follow the `INVERT` block at the top of the sketch - flip `SEGMENT_ON` from `HIGH` to `LOW`, flip `SEGMENT_OFF` from `LOW` to `HIGH`, and move the display's common pins from GND to **5V**. - **Wrong common pins**: if NOTHING lights up, you probably have the common-cathode pin wrong for YOUR specific module. Look up the datasheet for your part number and try the alternate common pins. - **MB102 jumpers**: both must be on the **5V** side. If one is on 3.3V and the other is off, the Uno's 5V rail will dip and the display will go dim. - **Wrong wall-wart**: the MB102 wants **6.5-12V DC** through the barrel jack. A 5V phone charger plugged in there won't work; use the 9V wall-wart. ## Talking points - **Analog vs digital**: the moisture meter's needle is analog (it can be at any position); our display is digital (it can only show 1 through 9). The Uno is the translator. Same data, two completely different ways of showing it. - **ADC = analog-to-digital converter**: the A0 pin measures the voltage from the probe and turns it into a number from 0 to 1023. We use `map()` to squash that into 1-9. - **Why we measure first**: microcontrollers are made of tiny tiny transistors that handle 0-5V. Anything bigger fries them. So before you plug a "mystery" wire into a chip, you check it with a multimeter. This is the same habit every electrical engineer has. - **Voltage divider**: two resistors in a row can chop a big voltage in half. It's not magic - the voltage splits across the resistors in proportion to their values. Two equal 10K resistors give you exactly half. - **Why 220 ohms?** Each LED segment is just an LED. Without a resistor it would burn out in a flash. 220R lets about 14mA through, which is bright but safe. - **Common cathode**: all the segments share one ground pin. Imagine a bunch of LEDs glued together at their minus legs. ## Things to change once it works - **Add a piezo buzzer** on pin 10 - when thirst hits 9, beep along with the blink. (We left this off for v1 because we don't have one in the kit yet.) - Average 30 readings before deciding the score. Soil noise is real; smoother numbers feel more "professional". - Swap the single digit for the 4-digit TM1637 module and show the score AND a moisture percentage at the same time. - Log readings over a day to the Serial Monitor with `millis()` and make a chart - is your plant thirstier in the morning or the evening? - Move it onto a NodeMCU V3 and push the score to a phone over WiFi - "thirst=9" notifications from your plant. ## Why this is interesting This project is the cleanest possible bridge between the analog world (a fuzzy probe voltage that wobbles around) and the digital world (a rock-solid 1-9 number on a display). It teaches the single most important skill in microcontroller projects: **calibrate two known points, then map everything in between**. That same trick works for distance sensors, temperature probes, light meters, battery monitors - anything where reality is a continuous wiggle and your code needs a clean number to act on. It also makes the 7-segment display click. Most kids see them as mysterious black boxes; once you've driven each segment yourself with a digital pin, they become "just eight LEDs in a clever arrangement" forever. And the multimeter-first habit you learn here ("never feed a mystery wire into a chip pin") is the single thing that protects every project from this point on.
