projects.name: One-Digit Dice Roller
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the Uno (5V via USB-B); the Uno's 5V pin feeds the breadboard +5V rail
projects.description:
**What it is**: A tiny dice you can hold in your hand. Push the button and a bright red number on the display flickers really fast - 4, 2, 6, 1 - then slows down and stops on one number between 1 and 6, just like a real dice landing. **Why it is fun**: It is a real, working game piece you built yourself. You can use it for board games, for picking who goes first, or for daring your sister to "roll higher than me." Every press feels different because the answer is genuinely random. ## Parts list - Arduino Uno R3 (the brain) - 0.56" red 7-segment LED display (one digit, the "screen") - Tactile push button (the roll button) - 7 x 220 ohm resistors (one for each segment of the display) - Half-size breadboard and a 40-piece pack of M-M jumper wires - The Uno's stock USB-A to USB-B cable (whatever you used to flash it - that is also the power) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the power output pin. It gives back 5 volts to power your parts. - **GND** - the 0V side, called "ground." Every circuit needs a path back to here. - **D2 through D13** - the digital pins. We will use D2 to D9 in this build. Just say "the pin marked D9" - the number on the board matches the number in the code. - **USB-B** - the big square USB jack. The cable from your laptop plugs in here and does two jobs: it uploads the code AND powers the whole project. - **Rail** - the long red or blue strip running down the side of the breadboard. Red = power (+5V). Blue = ground (0V).
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard power rails.** - Run a **red** jumper from the Arduino's **5V** pin to the red rail at the top of the breadboard. - Run a **black** jumper from the Arduino's **GND** pin to the blue rail at the top of the breadboard. - Run a **red** jumper from the top red rail down to the bottom red rail. - Run a **black** jumper from the top blue rail down to the bottom blue rail. This gives you power and ground on both sides of the board, so you can grab 5V or GND from anywhere. Think of it like running an extension cord around the whole workspace before you start plugging things in.
**Step 2 - Plant the 7-segment display.** A 7-segment display is really just seven tiny LEDs glued into a figure-8 shape, plus a shared pin called the "common." Each LED is a segment, and each segment has a letter: - **a** = top bar - **b** = upper-right bar - **c** = lower-right bar - **d** = bottom bar - **e** = lower-left bar - **f** = upper-left bar - **g** = middle bar Push the display into the breadboard so its pins straddle the center gap. The pins on the top row (with the little decimal dot) sit in row E columns 5 through 9. The pins on the bottom row sit in row F columns 5 through 9. The decimal dot should be at the bottom-right when you look at the display from the front. Most of the red displays in our kit are **common cathode** style - the shared pin (called COM) needs to go to ground. If yours is the other kind (common anode), the shared pin goes to 5V instead and you flip one line in the code (`COMMON_ANODE = true`).
**Step 3 - Wire the COM pins to ground.** The display has TWO common pins (one on the top row at column 7, one on the bottom row at column 7). They are connected to each other inside the display, but we will tie both to ground just to be safe. - Run a **black** wire from **E7** (top COM pin) to the blue rail (GND) at the top. - Run a **black** wire from **F7** (bottom COM pin) to the blue rail (GND) at the bottom. This is the "return path" for all seven LEDs. Without it, no segment will light up at all.
**Step 4 - Add the seven current-limit resistors.** You need seven 220 ohm resistors, one for each segment. The color bands on a 220 ohm resistor are red-red-brown-gold. Resistors do not care which way around they go, so bend the legs into a U and push them in. Place them like this (each resistor stretches between two holes): - Resistor 1: from **A8** to **A14** (segment a) - Resistor 2: from **A9** to **A15** (segment b) - Resistor 3: from **J8** to **J14** (segment c) - Resistor 4: from **J6** to **J16** (segment d) - Resistor 5: from **J5** to **J17** (segment e) - Resistor 6: from **A6** to **A18** (segment f) - Resistor 7: from **A5** to **A19** (segment g) **Why this matters:** LEDs are greedy. If you connect them straight to 5V they will gulp too much electricity and burn out in seconds, like a balloon popping. A resistor is a polite traffic cop - it slows the flow down to a safe level (about 15 milliamps per segment). One resistor per LED is the rule.
**Step 5 - Connect the Arduino pins to the segments.** Now run jumper wires from the Arduino digital pins to the OTHER end of each resistor (the end that is NOT touching the display): - **D2** -> **A19** (segment a, top bar) - **D3** -> **A15** (segment b, upper-right) - **D4** -> **J14** (segment c, lower-right) - **D5** -> **J16** (segment d, bottom bar) - **D6** -> **J17** (segment e, lower-left) - **D7** -> **A18** (segment f, upper-left) - **D8** -> **A14** (segment g, middle bar) When the code wants to light up segment a, it switches D2 ON (sends out 5V). Electricity flows from D2, through the resistor, through that segment LED, out the COM pin, and back to ground. Seven pins, seven segments, total control.
**Step 6 - Add the roll button.** The push button (a tiny white square with four legs) goes across the center gap of the breadboard near column 24. Push it in so its legs sit firmly. The button is wired internally so that two pairs of legs are always connected, and pressing the button bridges all four together. - Push the button in so one leg lands at **E24** and the diagonal leg lands at **F26**. - Run a **black** wire from **F26** down to the blue rail (GND) at the bottom. - Run a jumper wire from **D9** on the Arduino to **E24**. **Why this matters:** You might be wondering "where is the resistor for the button?" Good catch. The Arduino has a built-in resistor we can switch on using `INPUT_PULLUP` in the code. It quietly holds D9 at 5V whenever the button is NOT pressed. When you mash the button, it pulls D9 down to ground, and the code sees the change and rolls the dice. One less part to wire - thank you, Arduino.
**Step 7 - Plug in the USB cable.** There is no extra power supply for this build. The Arduino Uno gets 5V from the USB cable you used to upload the code, and the Uno's own **5V** pin feeds the red rail of the breadboard. The Uno's **GND** pin feeds the blue rail. That is it - one cable, one board. A single 7-segment digit lit up with 220 ohm resistors only sips about 100 to 140 milliamps total, which the little chip on the Uno can handle without breaking a sweat.
**Final check before powering on.** - Count your resistors: there should be seven, one for each segment. - All seven segment wires go through a resistor BEFORE reaching D2 through D8. - The COM pins on the display go to GND (blue rail). - The button has one leg on D9 and the opposite-corner leg on GND. - The red rail has 5V from the Arduino. The blue rail has GND from the Arduino. If your display shows nothing when you press the button, the most common mistake is having the display in upside down - try flipping it 180 degrees. If only some segments light up, double-check that each Arduino pin (D2 to D8) is wired to the right segment letter. ## Flash it and run it 1. Plug the Arduino Uno into your laptop with the USB-B cable. 2. Open the Arduino IDE. Choose **Tools -> Board -> Arduino Uno**. 3. Choose **Tools -> Port** and pick the COM port that appeared when you plugged in the Uno. 4. Paste the sketch in, click the round Upload arrow at the top. 5. Once you see "Done uploading," the display should light up showing a steady "0". Press the button and watch the digit dance, then land on a number from 1 to 6. **Common gotchas** - If the display lights up but shows weird patterns (like every segment glowing when it should be off, and going dark when it should be on), your display is probably common-anode, not common-cathode. Open the sketch, change `const bool COMMON_ANODE = false;` to `true`, and re-upload. You will also need to move the display's common pin from GND to the +5V rail. - If only some segments work, one of the 220 ohm resistors is probably not making contact, or a jumper popped out of the breadboard. Wiggle each wire and check the resistors are firmly seated. - If pressing the button does nothing, the button might be rotated 90 degrees on the breadboard. Tactile buttons have four legs - two pairs that are always connected to each other. Rotate the button 90 degrees and try again. - If the digit looks dim, double-check that the Uno's 5V pin (not 3.3V) is feeding the breadboard red rail, and that the display's common pin actually reaches the blue (GND) rail. ## Talking points - A 7-segment display is just seven LEDs in a special shape. The number you see is a "code" - which segments are on and which are off. - The `random()` function in Arduino is not really random - it follows a pattern. We use `randomSeed(micros())` so the starting point changes based on exactly when you pressed the button, which makes it feel real. - "Debouncing" is the trick we use so one press equals one roll. When you press a button, the metal contacts bounce a few times in a millisecond. The small `delay(20)` after the press, plus waiting for the release, smooths that out. - The slow-down at the end is just maths: we add a little more delay between flashes near the end of the loop. That tiny detail is what makes the dice feel alive. ## Things to change once it works - Make it a 20-sided dice. Hook up a second display and have the code count to 20. - Make a "shake to roll" version with an accelerometer instead of a button. - Add a piezo buzzer that ticks during the roll and beeps when it lands. - Change `random(1, 7)` to `random(1, 11)` for a 1-10 dice for math homework. - Build a "rock-paper-scissors" version: 1=rock, 2=paper, 3=scissors, with two buttons (one per player). ## Why this is interesting This project is the gateway to almost everything else with displays. Once you understand "set segment a high, set segment b high, that draws the top half of an 8," you can drive a four-digit clock, a scoreboard, a thermometer readout, anything. It is also one of the cleanest places to learn that "random" in a computer needs a little help to actually feel random - the same lesson you will use later when you build a game on a phone or a website.

projects.name: Finger-Freezer Cold Spot
projects.power_supply: A 12V wall-wart you already own feeds the buck converter's barrel jack; the buck's USB 5V output runs the Peltier directly via DuPont jumpers, and also feeds the MB102 which distributes 5V onto the small breadboard rails as multimeter probe points.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little metal square that gets cold the moment you plug it in - cold enough to press the back of your finger against and feel a tiny shiver. There is no code and no computer; it is pure science. **Why it is fun**: You are making cold out of electricity. There is no ice, no fridge, no freezer - just a flat chip the size of a sugar cube that turns one side cold and the other side hot the second the power comes on. Flip the wires and the cold side becomes hot. It feels like a magic trick that you built with your own hands. ## Parts list From your inventory: - TEC1-4905 Peltier thermoelectric cooler (the magic tile) - 6-24V to 5V 3A USB buck converter - MB102 breadboard power supply module (used here as a rail-distribution board only) - Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) - small board, used only for multimeter probe points - Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc - Jumper Wire F-M, 20pc Things you already own (NOT stocked in this inventory, supply your own): - Any 12V 1A-or-more wall-wart with a standard 5.5/2.1mm barrel plug to feed the buck converter - A small aluminium heatsink (CPU heatsink, a finned aluminium block, anything with fins) AND a small tube of thermal paste - the Peltier hot side MUST be stuck to it before power-on - A digital multimeter (any cheap DMM with DC volts and DC amps ranges) ## Wiring notes This build has no microcontroller - it is a pure "power and a part" project. The job is to turn 12V from a wall plug into a gentle cool spot you can touch with your finger. Read every step before you plug the wall plug in - especially the heatsink rule. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the parts in this build:** - **+5V** - the 5V power wire (red). - **GND** - the 0V side, also called "ground" (black). - **IN+ / IN-** - the screw holes on the MB102 where power comes IN (+ is red, - is black). - **VIN** - "voltage in", another way of saying "power coming in". - **Rail** - the long red and blue strips running down the side of the breadboard. Every hole in a red strip is connected together. Same for the blue. - **Buck converter** - a little board that takes a bigger voltage in and gives a smaller voltage out. Ours takes 12V in and gives 5V out. - **Peltier** - a flat square that gets cold on one side and hot on the other when you put power through it. Like magic, but real.
**Step 1 - Get the heatsink ready FIRST. This is the most important rule of the whole build.** - Look at the Peltier square. One side has writing on it - that side is the HOT side. The blank side is the COLD side (the finger side). - Squeeze a pea-sized blob of thermal paste onto the HOT side and press the aluminium heatsink (parent supplies this) flat onto it. A rubber band or a small clamp keeps it stuck while you work. - The cold (blank) side faces UP. That is the side your finger will touch later. **Why this matters:** the Peltier does not destroy heat - it just moves heat from one side to the other. If the hot side has nowhere to dump that heat, the whole thing cooks itself in under a minute and dies forever. The heatsink is the dump truck for the heat. No heatsink = no Peltier. We mean it. Do this step before any wires get connected.
**Step 2 - Plug 12V into the buck converter.** - Find your 12V wall plug (the kind with a round barrel tip). Do NOT put it in the wall yet. - Push the barrel tip into the round hole on the buck converter. - That is it for this step. Leave the wall plug unplugged until everything else is done. **Why this matters:** the buck converter is the safety lid on this project. The Peltier is rated for 12V but at 12V it gets so cold so fast that it grows frost and is uncomfortable to touch. We feed the buck 12V and it hands us a friendly 5V out the other side. That makes a "cool plate" instead of a "freezer plate". Much nicer for fingers.
**Step 3 - Run two thick wires from the buck STRAIGHT to the Peltier. Skip the breadboard.**
- The Peltier has TWO wires sticking out: one RED, one BLACK. - Take a male-to-female jumper (or two male-to-male jumpers twisted together) and connect the buck's +5V output to the Peltier's RED wire. - Take another jumper and connect the buck's GND output to the Peltier's BLACK wire. - These two wires do NOT go through the breadboard. They go from the buck DIRECTLY to the Peltier. **Why this matters:** the Peltier drinks a LOT of power - about 1 to 2 amps. The little holes in the breadboard are not built for that much current. They get warm, they sag the voltage, and over time they melt or burn. So we keep the high-current path short and direct, and use the breadboard only as a place to clip a multimeter later. Tip: if you mix up red and black, it still works - but the cold and hot sides swap places. Cool experiment, but not what we want for the finger demo.
**Step 4 - Wire the buck's USB 5V into the MB102 power module.** - Find the buck converter's USB output (the 5V coming out the USB end). - Run a red male-to-female jumper from the buck's USB +5V to the MB102's IN+ screw hole (the + side). - Run a black male-to-female jumper from the buck's USB GND to the MB102's IN- screw hole (the - side). - Look at the MB102: there are two small black jumpers (called "selectors"). Make sure BOTH of them are set to the 5V position, not 3.3V. Both jumpers = 5V. **Why this matters:** the MB102 normally turns 7-12V into a clean 5V or 3.3V for breadboards. Here we are tricking it - feeding it 5V and asking for 5V back. It just passes the power straight through. We use it because it has nice clean screw terminals and gives us a tidy place to clip the multimeter. It is not "regulating" anything - the buck is doing all the real work.
**Step 5 - Drop the MB102 onto the breadboard.** - The MB102 has two rows of pins underneath. Push it down into the breadboard so its pins land in rows A2, A4 (one side) and J2, J4 (the other side). - Run a short red wire from the breadboard hole at A2 over to the red rail at the top of the breadboard (the +5V rail). - Run a short black wire from A4 to the blue rail at the top (the GND rail). - Run another red wire from J2 to the red rail at the bottom. - Run another black wire from J4 to the blue rail at the bottom. **Why this matters:** the MB102 only puts power into 4 little holes. By running wires from those 4 holes out to the long red and blue strips, every hole along those strips now has 5V or GND in it. That makes the breadboard ready to use as multimeter probe points.
**Step 6 - Add two probe points and link the top and bottom rails together.** - Run a red wire from the top +5V rail down into hole E10. That gives a "+5V probe point" in the middle of the board. - Run a black wire from the top GND rail down into hole E12. That is the "GND probe point" next to it. - Run a red wire from the bottom +5V rail up into hole F18, and a black wire from the bottom GND rail up into hole F20. Now you have probe points on both halves. - Last, run one red wire from the top red rail across to the bottom red rail, and one black wire from the top blue rail across to the bottom blue rail. This makes both halves of the board share the same 5V and GND. **Why this matters:** breadboards have a split down the middle - the top rails do not connect to the bottom rails on their own. The two crossover wires bridge them so the whole board has 5V everywhere it should. The probe points at E10, E12, F18, F20 are just easy spots to clip a multimeter on without poking around near the power module.
**Step 7 - Check everything, THEN plug the wall plug into the wall.** - Heatsink stuck to the hot side of the Peltier? Yes? Good. - Red Peltier wire to buck +5V? Black Peltier wire to buck GND? Yes? Good. - MB102 selectors both on 5V? Yes? Good. - Now plug the 12V wall plug into the wall. - Within 10-20 seconds, the cold (blank) side of the Peltier should feel cool to the touch. Press your finger gently on it. The hot side / heatsink will feel warm or hot - that is normal and means it is working.
**Step 8 - Use the multimeter as a "see the electricity" tool.** - Set the multimeter to DC Volts (the symbol with a straight line and dashes, often labeled "V" with a "---"). - Touch the red probe to hole E10 or F18 (the +5V probe points). Touch the black probe to E12 or F20 (the GND probe points). - You should see about 5.0V on the screen. If it reads way lower than that, the buck might be sagging because the Peltier is pulling more current than it likes - unplug, let it rest, and try again. **Why this matters:** the multimeter is your X-ray vision. You cannot see electricity, but the meter shows it. Reading 5V on the rails means the buck is doing its job. If the Peltier is cold AND the meter reads 5V, the whole circuit is happy.
**Safety reminders before you call it done:** - Do not run this for more than 5-10 minutes at a time on the first try. Keep an eye (and a finger) on the heatsink. If it ever feels too hot to keep your finger on for 2 seconds, unplug right away and let it cool. - Never run the Peltier without the heatsink, even for "just a second to test". It really does kill them fast. - The cold side can get cold enough to make water droplets appear (condensation). That is normal, just wipe them off and keep electronics dry. ## Flash it and run it There is nothing to flash - this is a pure analog build. Instead, the "program" is a multimeter procedure that proves the cold is real: 1. Stick the heatsink to the Peltier's hot side with a thin layer of thermal paste. Let it set for a minute. **Do not skip this step.** 2. Set the buck converter to 5V output (most boards are fixed at 5V; if yours has a trim pot, adjust with the multimeter dial on DC Volts 20V range, red probe in the V/Ohm socket). 3. Snap the MB102 onto the small 400-point breadboard, set BOTH jumpers to 5V, feed it from the buck converter USB output, and press its power button. (Remember: it is just distributing rails for the meter, not regulating.) 4. Multimeter on DC Volts: red probe on red rail, black probe on blue rail. Should read ~5 V. 5. Peltier RED wire DIRECTLY from buck +5V (not through the breadboard). Peltier BLACK wire DIRECTLY from buck GND. 6. Wait 30 seconds. Touch the top of the Peltier with the back of your finger. It is cool! 7. After 1 minute, touch the heatsink (carefully). It is warm. Heat MOVED from one side to the other. 8. **Current measurement (do this LAST and be careful)**: power off. Move the RED probe from V/Ohm to the 10A socket. Turn the dial to DC current (10A range). Break the +5V line to the Peltier and put the meter in-line. Power on. Should be 1-2 A. Power off. **Move the red probe BACK to the V/Ohm socket immediately.** Never leave the probe in 10A while switching the dial back to Volts - it makes the meter a dead short. **Common gotchas** - Forgot the heatsink: the Peltier will fail within a minute and the hot side gets too hot to touch. - Wires swapped: hot side becomes cold side. Not broken - just flipped. Swap back. - No noticeable cold: check the multimeter actually reads 5V at the buck output, and that thermal paste is between the Peltier and the heatsink (not just dry contact). - Tried to push the Peltier leads through the breadboard tie-points: rails warm up and the cold side feels weak. Use direct DuPont jumpers from the buck output for the high-current path. - Probe left in the 10A socket when switching back to Volts: blows the meter's 10A fuse. - Buck converter set too high (if adjustable): at 9-12V the cold side goes below freezing and forms frost - fun, but uncomfortable to touch and wet. ## Talking points - A Peltier is "solid state" - no moving parts, no liquid, no gas. Just a flat chip that pumps heat when you push electricity through it. - It does not CREATE cold. Cold is just the absence of heat. The Peltier MOVES heat from one face to the other. The hot face has to dump that heat somewhere - that is what the heatsink is for. - This is exactly how cup-cooler car gadgets and small wine fridges work. The big fridge in the kitchen uses a different trick (compressed gas) because Peltiers waste a lot of energy. - Look at the multimeter: 5V x 1.5A = about 7 watts of electricity. That is roughly how much heat is moving from the top face to the bottom face every second. - Why TWO power boards (buck AND MB102)? The buck does the real work - drops 12V down to 5V. The MB102 is just a polite way to clip the multimeter onto rails without crocodile-clipping the buck's USB connector. In a "minimum parts" build you could skip the MB102 entirely. ## Things to change once it works - Bump the buck converter to 9V (if adjustable) and watch frost form on the cold side. Wipe it dry before touching. - Add the W1209 temperature controller (in your bumped inventory) and use its NTC probe to log the cold-side temperature live on the W1209 display. - Put a drop of water on the cold side and watch it freeze. - Stick a thin coin on the cold side and watch it become a "cold coin" that stays cool for a minute after you take it off. - Once Sandy is comfortable with this build, the next step is software control: put a NodeMCU + transistor in the circuit so a phone can switch the cold spot on and off. ## Why this is interesting This is Sandy's first encounter with the **Peltier effect** - a real piece of solid-state physics discovered in 1834 that turns electricity directly into a temperature difference with no moving parts. It is also his first lesson in **thermal management**: every powerful electronic part dumps heat somewhere, and ignoring that heat is how you kill a component. The "must have a heatsink" rule he learns here applies to every future TEC project, every motor driver, every power transistor, and every CPU. He also gets a real-world taste of **current path design** - the realisation that a small breadboard's tie-points are not magic wires and that 1-2 A wants a direct route. Doing it right at the absolute-beginner level builds the habit before the stakes get higher.

projects.name: Two-Player Dual-Gang Score Knob
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the Arduino Uno (5V via the Uno USB-B port)
projects.description:
**What it is**: One knob, two players, one glowing red number that flips back and forth between Player 1's digit and Player 2's digit. The trick is that the two digits ALWAYS add up to 9 - if P1 shows 3, P2 shows 6; if P1 shows 7, P2 shows 2. Each player has a secret target digit (e.g. P1 wants to land on 4, P2 wants to land on 5), and a red LED lights up the moment one of them hits it. **Why it is fun**: You and your sibling argue over one knob. Every twist helps one of you and hurts the other - there's exactly ONE shaft position on the whole dial where you BOTH win at the same time, and when somebody finds it the red LED flashes like crazy. It's a tabletop tug-of-war controlled by a single piece of plastic, and the secret is that the knob has TWO sliders hidden inside one shaft, wired in opposite directions. ## Parts list - **Arduino Uno R3** - the brain. Reads both pot layers and drives the display. - **WH148 10K Stereo Potentiometer (B10K)** - the shared knob. Two independent resistor tracks ("gangs") stacked on one shaft. The shaft turns both at once, but because we wire them in opposite directions, one reading goes up while the other goes down. - **0.56" Red 7-Segment LED Display (1 digit)** - the single glowing number. We flip it between P1 and P2 every half-second so it looks like both numbers are there. - **LED 5mm Red** - the "on target" warning flash. - **Tactile Push-button Switch (3x6x4.3mm, white pin)** - "new round": picks new secret targets for both players. - **8x 220R resistors** - one in series with each of the 7 segments + 1 with the decimal point, so the display does not burn. - **1x 220R resistor** - in series with the alert LED. - **Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm** + jumper wires. - USB cable from laptop to the Uno (also how power gets in). ## Wiring notes The brain of this project is the Arduino Uno R3. It gets all of its power from the USB cable plugged into your laptop, so you don't need a wall plug or batteries. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Uno board:** - **5V** - the power input pin, 5 volts coming back out of the USB cable. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. This is the "return path" for electricity. - **D2 through D13** - digital pins. We turn these on and off in code. Just say "D9", "D12", etc. - **A0, A1** - analog input pins. They can read in-between voltages (not just on/off), which is how we read a knob. - **D13 LED** - a tiny yellow LED already built into the board. We will NOT use D13 in this project because that built-in LED would confuse us.
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard power strips.** A breadboard has two long red and blue strips running down the side. The red strip is for 5V power, the blue strip is for ground. These long strips are called rails. Use two male-to-male jumper wires: - Uno **5V** pin -> the long red strip (5V rail). - Uno **GND** pin -> the long blue strip (ground rail). Now every part on the breadboard can grab power from the red strip and ground from the blue strip. Tip: bridge the red strip at the top of the board to the red strip at the bottom with a short wire, and do the same for the blue strip. That way both sides of the board have power.
**Step 2 - Plant the 7-segment display.** The 7-segment display is the chunky red number screen. It has 10 little metal legs (5 on top, 5 on bottom). The dot in the corner of the screen tells you which way is "up" - keep that dot on the bottom-right when you push it into the board. - Push the display into the breadboard so it straddles the center gap. The top row of legs goes in row E (pins E5 through E9) and the bottom row goes in row F (F5 through F9). - Take a male-to-male wire and connect **B7** -> the blue ground strip. - Take another male-to-male wire and connect **I7** -> the blue ground strip. The two middle pins (the ones now in E7 and F7) are called the "common cathode" pins. They are the shared return path for all the little LEDs inside the display, so both need to go to ground. *Why this matters:* The display is really just 8 tiny LEDs glued into the shape of a number (7 sticks plus a dot). To light up the digit "3", the Arduino lights segments a, b, c, d, and g all at once. Each segment LED needs its own current-limit resistor coming next, or it would burn out.
**Step 3 - Add the 8 current-limit resistors for the display.** You need eight 220 ohm resistors (the little tubes with red-red-brown-gold stripes). Bend the legs in a U shape and push them across empty rows on the breadboard. Resistors don't have a direction, so it doesn't matter which way around you put them. - Resistor 1: **A5 to A11** (this is for segment a). - Resistor 2: **A6 to A12** (segment f). - Resistor 3: **A8 to A13** (decimal point - the dot). - Resistor 4: **A9 to A14** (segment c). - Resistor 5: **J5 to J11** (segment g). - Resistor 6: **J6 to J12** (segment b). - Resistor 7: **J8 to J13** (segment e). - Resistor 8: **J9 to J14** (segment d). *Why this matters:* Each tiny LED inside the display would happily eat too much electricity and burn out in seconds if connected straight to the Uno. The 220 ohm resistor squeezes the flow down to a safe amount - like a narrow straw on a milkshake.
**Step 4 - Wire the display segments to the Arduino.** Now use female-to-male wires. The female end goes on the Arduino pin headers, the male end pushes into the breadboard on the OTHER side of each resistor. - Uno **D2** -> breadboard **A11** (segment a). - Uno **D3** -> breadboard **J12** (segment b). - Uno **D4** -> breadboard **A14** (segment c). - Uno **D5** -> breadboard **J14** (segment d). - Uno **D6** -> breadboard **J13** (segment e). - Uno **D7** -> breadboard **A12** (segment f). - Uno **D8** -> breadboard **J11** (segment g). - Uno **D9** -> breadboard **A13** (the decimal point, dp). Double-check that each Arduino pin lands on the resistor side of the row, not the display side. If the digit comes out scrambled later, this is the first place to look.
**Step 5 - Push in the "New Round" button.** The tactile push-button has 4 little metal legs sticking out in a square pattern. Two pairs are joined inside: left-top is joined to left-bottom, and right-top is joined to right-bottom. So you really only have two electrical "sides" to worry about. - Push the button so it straddles the center gap with one leg in **E18** and a leg diagonally opposite (the F-row leg on the other side of the gap). - Connect a wire from **A18** -> the blue ground strip. - Female-to-male wire: Uno **D12** -> breadboard **E20** (E20 is on the same row as one of the button's other legs). *Why this matters:* In the code, we turn on a feature called INPUT_PULLUP on D12. That makes the Uno keep D12 at 5V all by itself. When you press the button, you connect the pin straight to ground, the voltage drops, and the Uno notices. The button "fires when it is pressed" - the rest of the time, the pin sits quietly at 5V.
**Step 6 - The stereo knob (this is the cool trick).** A stereo pot is like two knobs glued onto one shaft. It has 6 pins in two rows of three. Each row of three is one "gang" (one layer). On each row: the two outer pins are the ends of a tiny built-in resistor, and the middle pin is the wiper - that's the part that slides as you turn the knob. The shaft turns BOTH gangs at the same time. You can't turn one gang on its own. That's normal: a real stereo volume knob does the same thing so the left and right speakers stay matched. So how can two players play on one shaft? **We wire the two gangs facing opposite directions.** Twist the shaft clockwise, and Gang A's wiper voltage goes UP while Gang B's wiper voltage goes DOWN at the same time. Player 1's number climbs and Player 2's number drops together. The game becomes a tug-of-war over the same knob. Push the pot in so Gang A lands across row C (around C24) and Gang B lands across row H (around H24). **Gang A (Player 1, the normal way around):** - Wire from **A23** (the left outer pin of Gang A) -> the blue ground strip. - Wire from **A25** (the right outer pin of Gang A) -> the red 5V strip. - Female-to-male: Uno **A0** -> breadboard **C24** (the middle wiper pin). **Gang B (Player 2, the REVERSED way around):** - Wire from **J23** (the left outer pin of Gang B) -> the red 5V strip. - Wire from **J25** (the right outer pin of Gang B) -> the blue ground strip. - Female-to-male: Uno **A1** -> breadboard **H24** (the middle wiper pin). Notice how Gang A has ground on the left and 5V on the right, but Gang B is flipped: 5V on the left and ground on the right. That swap is the whole secret. If you accidentally wire both gangs the same way around, both players will always show the same number, because both wipers will be at the same voltage. That's the dead giveaway you forgot the swap.
**Step 7 - The alert LED.**
The 5mm red LED has two legs. The long leg is the positive side (it goes to the Arduino pin through the resistor) and the short leg (next to the flat spot on the side of the plastic) is the negative side (it goes to ground). LEDs only work one way around - if you flip it, nothing lights up. - Use the 9th 220 ohm resistor. Place it across **F28 to F30**. - Push the LED into the board so the long leg goes in **J28** and the short leg (flat-side leg) goes in **J29**. - Wire from **J30** -> the blue ground strip. - Female-to-male: Uno **D11** -> breadboard **F28** (the resistor side, NOT the LED side). *Why this matters:* We use D11 and not the famous D13 because the Uno already has a tiny yellow LED soldered onto the board next to D13. That built-in LED blinks every time the board powers up or you upload code, and it would also light up our alert LED at the same time. Using D11 keeps our alert LED quiet until the code says "fire!". And the 220 ohm resistor is here for the same reason as on the display: without it, the LED would gulp too much current and pop.
**Final check before plugging in:** - Red rail = 5V. Blue rail = ground. Never swap them. - All eight display resistors are in place, plus the ninth one for the LED. - The LED's long leg points toward the resistor (toward the Arduino side), short leg toward the ground rail. - Gang A has ground on the left, 5V on the right. Gang B is flipped: 5V on the left, ground on the right. - Nothing is touching the metal USB port on the Arduino. If the digit shows up scrambled (like an "8" that looks like a squiggly shape), one of the segment wires from Step 4 is in the wrong spot. Trace D2 through D9 one at a time and match them against the list. If both players' scores always match each other, you forgot to flip Gang B in Step 6. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup:** 1. Open Arduino IDE. The Uno is the default-supported board - no extra board manager URL needed. 2. **Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno**. 3. No extra libraries needed. The sketch only uses `Arduino.h` (built in). **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into the laptop with a **USB-B data cable** (the chunky printer-style cable). The Uno's green `ON` LED will light. 2. **Tools -> Port** and pick the new entry that appeared (looks like `COM4` on Windows, `/dev/cu.usbmodemXXXX` on Mac, `/dev/ttyACM0` on Linux). 3. Nothing to edit in the sketch - no WiFi, no passwords. 4. Click the **Upload** button (the right-arrow icon, top-left). Bottom of the IDE will say "Compiling..." then "Uploading..." and the orange RX/TX LEDs on the Uno will blink during the upload. 5. When you see "Done uploading", the display will boot up showing P1's digit alternating with P2's digit (with the decimal point ON), and the Serial Monitor will print both players' secret target digits. 6. Press the button to roll a new pair of targets. Then twist the knob until one (or both!) of you hits the secret digit on your turn - the red LED will tell you. 7. (Optional) **Tools -> Serial Monitor**, baud **9600**, to watch `P1=3 (target 4) P2=6 (target 5) showing=P1` print out. **Common gotchas:** - **Display shows the wrong shape for each digit.** A segment wire is in the wrong pin. Light one segment at a time by editing the `setup()` to manually `digitalWrite(2, HIGH)` etc, and label each pin with what segment it actually turns on. Then fix the constant array at the top of the sketch. - **Both scores read the same no matter how you turn the knob.** You forgot to swap 5V and GND on Gang B. On Gang A, 5V should be on one outer pin and GND on the other; on Gang B, those two wires need to be the OTHER way around. With both gangs wired identically, the two wipers on one shaft always read the same value - that's just how a stereo pot works. - **P1 and P2 do not always sum to 9, they are off by 1.** That is normal at the edges - the analog reading at "fully clockwise" might be 1022 not 1023, so the bucket math sometimes rounds to 8/0 instead of 9/0. Fine for the game. - **Score jumps around even when the knob is still.** The analog reading is noisy at the edges. The sketch already averages 8 reads and snaps to the nearest 0-9 step, but if it is still jittery, increase `SAMPLES` from 8 to 16. - **"avrdude: stk500_getsync()" error on upload.** A cable problem 9 times out of 10. Try a different USB cable - many "charge only" cables look identical to data cables. - **Display is on but very dim.** Make sure each segment has its own 220R - sharing one resistor for the whole display makes each lit segment fight for current, so 8 lit segments are 8x dimmer than 1. ## Talking points - **What a "stereo" pot really is.** A normal potentiometer is one resistor strip with one wiper. A stereo pot is *two* of those, stacked on the same shaft, glued so they spin together. In a real stereo amplifier this is exactly how the volume knob turns up the left and right speakers in lockstep - you do NOT want one ear getting louder than the other. The point is *mechanical synchronisation*, not independence. - **Then how is this a 2-player game?** We cheat with the wiring. If both gangs are wired the same way, both wipers report the same voltage and P1 == P2 always. But if we **flip 5V and GND on one gang**, that gang's voltage runs *backwards* as the shaft turns. Now spinning clockwise pushes P1 up AND P2 down at the same time - one knob, two opposite outputs. That's why every legal pair sums to 9. - **Reading an analog voltage.** `analogRead(A0)` gives a number from 0 (0V) to 1023 (5V). To get a score from 0 to 9 we divide that range into 10 buckets: roughly `score = analogRead(A0) / 102`. The `map()` function does exactly that for us. - **Why we average 8 reads.** The voltage on the wiper wiggles slightly because of electrical noise. A single read might say 511 then 514 then 509. Averaging smooths it out so the score does not flicker between 4 and 5 right at the boundary. - **How the bit pattern thing works.** Each digit (0-9) is stored as one byte like `0b01101111`. The byte has 8 bits, one per segment. Bit 0 (rightmost) is segment a. Bit 1 is segment b. And so on. To find out if segment 3 (which is segment d) should be lit, we do `(pattern >> 3) & 0x01`. The `>> 3` *slides* the byte 3 places to the right so the bit we care about is at the very end, and `& 0x01` *masks* away everything except that last bit - giving us either 1 (light it) or 0 (leave it off). Storing 8 yes/no decisions in one byte is a very common trick. - **Multiplexing in time.** We have ONE physical digit but TWO scores to show. Every half-second we wipe the segments and redraw them with the other player's number. Your eye sees the slow blink, but the multiplex trick (sharing one display by switching fast in time) is the same idea used to drive 4-digit and 8-digit displays - just much, much faster. - **The decimal point as a name tag.** Lighting the dp tells you which player you are currently looking at. It is the cheapest possible 1-bit "label". ## Things to change once it works - Speed up the multiplex from 500 ms per side to 5 ms per side. You will see *both* numbers at once (sort of - the human eye blends them), like a 2-digit display made from one digit. - Add a "first to 5 wins" round counter: every time someone lands on their target, increment their win count, show it on the display for a beat, then roll new targets. - Replace the alert LED with the passive buzzer (once we get one) so target hits chirp instead of flash. - Swap the single 1-digit display for the 4-digit module and show both scores side by side as `P1.X-Y.P2` for no more multiplex trickery. - Pick a different game where sum-to-9 still matters: e.g. "P1 wants ODD, P2 wants EVEN" - LED on whenever the right person's digit is odd/even. ## Why this is interesting This project teaches one really important idea - **time-domain multiplexing** - without any new chips or libraries. The display is the simplest possible kind (just 8 LEDs in a box), the analog read is the simplest possible kind (`analogRead`), and yet the *behaviour* (one display showing two things, one knob controlling two opposite things) feels much fancier than the parts. The dual-gang pot is the perfect physical metaphor: two resistor tracks stacked into one shaft, mechanically locked together but **electrically wired any way you like**. That last part is the lightbulb moment - the same piece of hardware can be a synchroniser (in a stereo amp) or a tug-of-war (in this game) depending entirely on how you connect the four outer pins. Once a kid sees that, potentiometers stop being mysterious and become a building block.

projects.name: Garden Bed Soil Snitch
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop while flashing/testing; for handheld use a 9V wall-wart or battery pack (not in kit) into the 6-24V to 5V buck converter, USB output to the NodeMCU
projects.description:
Imagine you are a soil detective stalking around the house with a wand that BEEPS out a number whenever you stab it into a pot. The thirstier the plant, the bigger the number. **What it is**: A handheld garden gadget you stab into a pot of soil. The little needle on the front of the probe meter wiggles to show wetness like an old-fashioned dial, AND a big red number from 0 to 9 lights up on a tiny screen - 0 means "soaking wet" and 9 means "this plant is dying of thirst". **Why it is fun**: You can run around the yard ranking every pot in the house from happiest to thirstiest. Bring it to grandma's place and announce that her fern is a 7 and needs water RIGHT NOW. Bonus: it runs off a small wall-wart or USB pack, so you can wander cable-free for short rounds. ## Parts list - Soil Moisture Probe Meter (standalone) - the gun-shaped one with the metal blade and the needle dial - NodeMCU V3 (ESP8266) snapped onto its I/O Shield (the green screw-terminal board) - 1-digit 0.56" red 7-segment LED display (common cathode) - 7 x 220R resistors (one for each segment) - Small breadboard for the display and resistors - 6-24V to 5V 3A USB buck converter (only if you want to run it off a 9V wall-wart / battery pack) - DuPont jumpers (M-M and F-M) You will ALSO need (not in the kit): - A USB cable to flash the NodeMCU from the laptop. Easiest "power source" while you're learning is just to keep that USB cable plugged in. - If you really want it cable-free: a 9V wall-wart or a 9V battery + battery snap, fed into the buck converter. Those bits aren't in the inventory - source them separately. ## Wiring notes The brain of the Snitch is a NodeMCU V3. It sits on top of an "I/O Shield" that turns each pin into a tidy 3-hole column you can plug jumper wires straight into. No soldering. Heads up: the labels printed on the NodeMCU (D0, D1, D2, ...) do NOT match the GPIO numbers in the code. We will always say "the pin marked Dx" so you do not have to do any math. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the NodeMCU board:** - **D0 through D8** - the pins you can use for signals (each Dx column on the shield has three holes: outer = signal, middle = +5V, inner = 0V ground) - **A0** - the one analog input pin; the only pin that can read "how wet is the soil?" as a number - **G** - ground; the 0V side that every part must share so the chip understands what 0 means - **VU / VIN** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable (we will not use it in this project) - **TX** - this pin also talks to your laptop over USB. We will use it as segment "g" later, which means you cannot use Serial.print at the same time. The code already handles this. - **USB port** - power and code come in here from your laptop
**Step 1 - Park the breadboard and the shield next to each other.** - Slide the NodeMCU V3 down onto the I/O Shield so all the pins line up. It only fits one way. - Set the breadboard right next to the shield with the lettered rows (A, B, C, D, E and F, G, H, I, J) facing you. Numbers run 1, 2, 3, ... down the side. - Inside the breadboard, every row of 5 holes labelled A-E is one little wire underneath. Same for F-J on the other side. So poking something into A10 and E10 connects them automatically. We will NOT use the long red/blue strips down the side of the breadboard for power - the shield already gives us power and 0V (ground) right where we need them.
**Step 2 - Plant the 7-segment display.** The 7-segment display is the little red number digit. It has 10 short metal legs underneath, 5 on each side. - Hold the display so the decimal-point dot is in the bottom-right corner. That is the "right way up." - Push it into the breadboard so one row of 5 legs lands in column E (rows 10, 11, 12, 13, 14) and the other row of 5 legs lands in column F (rows 10, 11, 12, 13, 14). The display straddles the middle gap. Press it down gently and evenly. - Two of those 10 legs are the "common" legs - they are both joined to the 0V (ground) side inside the part. We will deal with them in the next step. The other 7 legs are the seven little stripes (a, b, c, d, e, f, g) that draw the number, plus one for the dot which we leave alone.
**Step 3 - Send the two common legs to ground (0V).** This display is "common cathode" style, which is fancy talk for "the two common pins must go to 0V." - Black M-M (male-to-male) jumper from **E12** to **A12** (this just hops the signal over to the other side of the breadboard's middle gap). - Black M-M jumper from **A12** down off the breadboard and into the inner (ground) hole of the I/O Shield's **G** column. - Black M-M jumper from **F12** to **J12**. - Black M-M jumper from **J12** off to another **G** (ground) hole on the shield. Why this matters: every LED segment is going to need a path back to 0V to light up. If the common legs are not grounded, the display will just stay dark no matter what code we run.
**Step 4 - Add the 7 current-limit resistors (one per segment).** You have seven little 220R resistors. They look the same from both ends - resistors do not care which way round they go. Each one acts like a tiny squeeze on the wire so the LED gets just the right gulp of electricity. Without these, the LEDs would blast for a second and then die forever. Bend the legs of each resistor at 90 degrees so it can straddle two breadboard rows. Push each one in like this: - Resistor 1: legs into **A10** and **A4** - Resistor 2: legs into **A11** and **A5** - Resistor 3: legs into **A13** and **A19** - Resistor 4: legs into **A14** and **A20** - Resistor 5: legs into **J10** and **J4** - Resistor 6: legs into **J11** and **J5** - Resistor 7: legs into **J13** and **J19** Take a quick look: you should have 4 resistors on the A side and 3 on the J side. The far-side row (4, 5, 19, 20) is where the NodeMCU wires will come in. The near-side row (10, 11, 13, 14) is where the display legs already are. Why this matters: each segment of the display is its own little LED. LEDs are greedy - if you do not put a resistor in series they pull too much current and burn out. 220 ohms is a friendly value for 3.3V signals into a red LED.
**Step 5 - Bridge the inside display legs over to the outside row.** The display legs are in column E or column F. The resistors are sitting in column A or column J (across the gap). We need 6 yellow jumper wires to hop across: - Yellow M-M jumper: **E10** to **A10** - Yellow M-M jumper: **E11** to **A11** - Yellow M-M jumper: **E13** to **A13** - Yellow M-M jumper: **E14** to **A14** - Yellow M-M jumper: **F10** to **J10** - Yellow M-M jumper: **F11** to **J11** - Yellow M-M jumper: **F13** to **J13** - Yellow M-M jumper: **F14** to **J14** Now each display leg has a yellow wire reaching across to a resistor, and the other end of that resistor is sitting on row 4, 5, 19, or 20, waiting for a signal from the NodeMCU.
**Step 6 - Wire each segment to its NodeMCU pin.** Grab seven F-M (female-to-male) jumper wires. The female (cup) end plugs into the outer (signal) hole of a Dx column on the I/O Shield. The male (pin) end plugs into the breadboard. The pins below are carefully chosen to skip the NodeMCU's "scary at boot" pins (D3, D4, and D8) - those pins are picky during startup, and connecting an LED to them can stop the chip from turning on. - Segment **a**: shield **D1** signal hole -> breadboard **A4** - Segment **b**: shield **D2** signal hole -> breadboard **A5** - Segment **c**: shield **D5** signal hole -> breadboard **J5** - Segment **d**: shield **D6** signal hole -> breadboard **J4** - Segment **e**: shield **D7** signal hole -> breadboard **A19** - Segment **f**: shield **D0** signal hole -> breadboard **J19** - Segment **g**: shield **TX** (also marked D10) signal hole -> breadboard **J20** Tricky one: segment **g** shares the pin that talks to your laptop over USB. While that wire is plugged in, your code cannot use Serial.print to log messages. The sketch already knows this - it turns off serial logging once it starts driving the display.
**Step 7 - Tap the soil moisture meter.** This is the gadget with the long metal spike that you stab into the dirt. It has its own little battery and its own ON / OFF switch. We are not opening it up - we are just gently borrowing its signal. - Flip the meter ON and leave it ON the whole time you use the Snitch. If you switch it off, the number on the display will go wild. - Look at the meter's small circuit board (you can usually see it through a window in the back). Find a tiny metal pad labelled **OUT**, **TP**, or **SIG**. That pad is the meter's brain talking. Sometimes it is just a bare solder dot next to the main chip - ask your parent if you cannot find it. - Grab an F-M jumper. The female end clips onto that OUT pad (or you can hold it there with a small clothes peg / sticky tack). The male end plugs into the outer (signal) hole of the shield's **A0** column. - Grab a second F-M jumper. Clip the female end onto the negative end of the meter's battery clip (the spring side). The male end plugs into the inner (ground) hole of any **G** column on the shield. Why this matters: A0 is the one pin on the NodeMCU that can read a number from 0 (super dry) up to a big number (super wet). The second wire to G is just as important - if the meter's "0V" and the NodeMCU's "0V" are not joined, the NodeMCU has no idea what number it is reading. They MUST share ground. If you really cannot find an OUT pad on your meter, no problem - swap to a dedicated soil moisture sensor module from the kit and skip this step.
**Step 8 - Power it up the easy way (laptop USB).** For testing indoors, just plug a USB cable from your laptop into the NodeMCU. That powers the board AND lets you flash the code at the same time. The blue LED on the NodeMCU should light up.
**Step 9 - Power it up the handheld way (buck converter).** When you want to carry the Snitch out to the garden, you need a battery instead of a laptop. The buck converter is a tiny brick that takes a fat 9V input and makes a clean 5V USB output the NodeMCU can drink. - Hook a 9V battery snap or 9V wall-wart to the converter's **IN+** and **IN-** screw terminals. The red wire goes to IN+ (the "plus" side). The black wire goes to IN- (the "minus" side). Getting these swapped will kill the converter, so double-check before turning anything on. - Plug a short USB cable from the converter's USB OUTPUT into the NodeMCU's USB port. - The little LED on the buck converter should light up, and so should the blue LED on the NodeMCU. If neither lights up, the polarity is probably swapped - unplug fast and check. Why this matters: the NodeMCU only wants 5V on its USB port. A 9V battery would fry it. The buck converter politely drops the 9V down to a steady 5V for us.
**Final check before flashing.** Walk your eye over the board once more: - 7 resistors? Check. - 8 yellow jumpers from the display to the resistor rows? Check. - 7 F-M signal jumpers from the shield's Dx columns to rows 4, 5, 19, 20 on the breadboard? Check. - 2 black ground jumpers from the display commons to the shield's G column? Check. - 2 F-M jumpers to the soil meter (one to A0, one to G)? Check. - Meter switched ON? Check. If you can say yes to all six, you are ready to flash the code. ## Flash it and run it 1. Install the Arduino IDE (free, from arduino.cc). 2. File -> Preferences -> Additional Boards Manager URLs - add: `http://arduino.esp8266.com/stable/package_esp8266com_index.json` 3. Tools -> Boards Manager - install "esp8266 by ESP8266 Community". 4. Plug the NodeMCU into your laptop with a USB cable. Windows installs the CH340G driver automatically (give it 30 seconds). 5. Tools -> Board -> "NodeMCU 1.0 (ESP-12E Module)". 6. Tools -> Port -> pick the new COM port (COM3, COM4, etc). 7. Tools -> Upload Speed -> 115200 (slower is more reliable for first-time uploads). 8. Paste the sketch in, press the Upload arrow. If the IDE sits on "Connecting........_____........_____" for more than 10 seconds, hold down the FLASH button on the NodeMCU and tap RESET once, then release FLASH a second after the upload starts. CH340G boards need this nudge surprisingly often on the first flash of a session. 9. To watch the calibration numbers, first set `#define SERIAL_DEBUG 1` at the top of the sketch, re-upload, and open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. You'll see `raw=... score=...` lines (segment g will flicker because it shares the TX pin - that's expected during debug mode). 10. Watch the display do a 0..9 countup at boot - that proves every segment works. Calibration (this is where the magic numbers happen): - With `SERIAL_DEBUG 1`, push the probe into a full glass of water. Note the `raw=` number. Put that into `RAW_WET` at the top of the sketch. - Hold the probe in dry air, away from your hand. Note the `raw=` number. Put that into `RAW_DRY`. - The sketch's convention is: RAW_WET is the HIGH reading, RAW_DRY is the LOW reading. (More water -> more conductive -> bigger op-amp output -> bigger ADC number.) If your particular meter is wired the opposite way and dry-air reads HIGH, just swap the two values - the rest of the code will still work. - Re-upload. Now 0 means "wet like the glass" and 9 means "dry like air". - Set `SERIAL_DEBUG` back to 0 for normal use so segment g stops flickering. Once it works, unplug from the laptop, plug the buck converter's USB output into the NodeMCU, and you're handheld. Common gotchas: - "Chip won't boot - just resets forever" - one of your segment resistors landed on D3 or D4 instead of the listed pins. Both are boot-strap pins that must be HIGH at reset and a resistor + LED to ground pulls them LOW. Move that segment to D0, D5, D6 or D7. - "All segments lit, won't change" - the common pin is connected to 3.3V instead of GND. This is a common-cathode display, so common = GND. - "Nothing lights up" - missing the resistors, OR you wired a common-anode display (some 7-segs are anode). Flip the polarity by changing HIGH to LOW inside `showDigit`. - "Number is upside down" - the display is in the breadboard the wrong way round. Pull it out, rotate 180 degrees, push back in. - "Score jumps around like crazy" - bump `SAMPLES` from 16 to 64, OR add the 100k + 100nF filter on A0 described in Wiring notes. - "9 in water, 0 in air" - your probe reads opposite to the convention. Swap the values of `RAW_WET` and `RAW_DRY`. - "Digit goes garbage suddenly" - you switched the soil-meter's own power switch OFF. Its op-amp output then floats and A0 reads noise. Switch the meter back ON. - "Upload won't connect" - hold FLASH, tap RESET, release FLASH after a second. Some CH340G boards need this every cold boot. ## Talking points - Why does the analog needle work AND the digital number work at the same time? Because the probe is just a sensor whose voltage changes with moisture. The needle is one "listener" and the ESP8266 is a second "listener". They share a ground so they agree on what zero volts means. - The buck converter is a voltage shrink-ray. 9V goes in, 5V comes out, and the leftover energy becomes a tiny bit of heat - that's why it has a coil and a chip on it. - Common-cathode means all the LED minus-sides are bonded together inside the part. Common-anode is the opposite. Either kind exists - check the datasheet. - The 220R resistor stops the GPIO pin from shoving too much current into the LED segment. Without it the LED burns dim-then-dark in a few minutes. - Why are some pins "off limits"? On the ESP8266, GPIO0, GPIO2 and GPIO15 are read at power-up to decide if it should boot normally or wait for a new program. If a part is holding them at the wrong level, the chip just won't start. That's why we picked D0/D1/D2/D5/D6/D7/D10 instead. ## Things to change once it works - Add a tiny buzzer that beeps three times when the score hits 9 - "WATER ME" alarm. - Tap a button into a spare GPIO to remember the last 10 readings; press the button to scroll through them on the display (recall mode). - Turn the WiFi back on (delete the `WiFi.forceSleepBegin()` line, set mode WIFI_STA, SSID "GeeFam", password "PASSWORD_HERE") and POST the reading to a Google Sheet via IFTTT - garden history graph for free. - Add a 74HC595 shift register and run a 2-digit display from just 3 GPIOs, so you can show 00-99 for finer detail. - 3D-print a stick-shaped case so the whole thing looks like a magic wand instead of a breadboard. ## Why this is interesting This is a real-world example of two systems sharing one sensor: an analog meter and a microcontroller both reading the SAME voltage. That's how almost all modern instruments work - the dashboard gauge AND the OBD-II computer in a car both read the same temperature sensor at the same time. Once you see that pattern here, you'll see it everywhere. The other big lesson hiding in this build is that microcontroller pins are not all equal: some are "strapping pins" that decide what the chip does at boot, and you have to plan your wiring around them - that's a habit that will save you hours on every future ESP8266 / ESP32 project.

projects.name: Tasmota Plant Nightlight
projects.power_supply: 12V/2A wall-wart into the 6-24V-to-5V buck; buck USB powers the NodeMCU and a 5V tap feeds the ESP-01S relay Vcc. The 12V runs through the relay's dry contacts to the LED strip. Soil meter stays on its own battery (no MCU power into it).
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little houseplant gets its own glowing nightlight that turns itself on when the soil is dry. You stick the meter's probe in the pot, and when the plant gets thirsty the LED strip lights up like the plant is asking for a drink. You can also tap a button on your phone to turn the light on or off any time. **Why it is fun**: Your plant tells YOU what it needs instead of the other way around. Your friends will think the plant is alive and glowing on purpose, and you can secretly water it before anyone notices the light came on. Plus the phone control feels like real grown-up smart-home magic. ## Parts list - NodeMCU V3 (ESP8266) on its screw-terminal I/O Shield - the brain that reads the soil signal and talks to the relay over WiFi. - ESP-01S 5V Relay Module (Tasmota-ready) - pre-flashed WiFi switch; you control it from a phone or from the NodeMCU over WiFi. - Soil Moisture Probe Meter (standalone) - the battery-powered dial meter with the metal prong. It stays a standalone meter; we only TAP its probe lead so the NodeMCU can see the same voltage the meter sees. - 6-24V to 5V 3A USB Buck Converter - turns the 12V wall-wart into clean 5V USB for both boards. - 12V LED strip (a short ~30cm piece, brought by the builder; under 500mA so the 12V/2A wall-wart has plenty of headroom) - the "glow" that the relay switches on. - A red and a green LED with 220R resistors - dashboard lights on the breadboard to show "dry" and "wet" while you tune it. - Breadboard and DuPont jumper wires - the playground we build on. ## Wiring notes The brain of this build is a **NodeMCU V3** (an ESP8266 chip on a blue board with a silver USB plug on one end). It already has Wi-Fi built in, so it can talk to your phone over your home network. We will plug it into a helper board called the **I/O Shield** so we never have to fight skinny single wires. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the NodeMCU V3 board:** - **D0 through D8** - the pins you can use to turn things on and off. The numbers printed on the board do NOT match the GPIO numbers in code (e.g. D5 is GPIO14). Always go by the silkscreen label "Dx". - **A0** - the one pin that can measure how "in-between" a voltage is (not just on or off). We use this to read the soil. - **3V3** - a pin that gives out 3.3V of power. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs a wire here so the circuit completes a loop. - **VIN** - the pin that gives back the 5V from the USB cable. We do not use it in this build; we power from USB instead.
**Heads up about the soil meter (read this before you start).** The soil meter in our bin is the kind with a little needle that runs on its own battery. It does NOT have a wire that says "signal out" like fancier soil sensors do. That is fine - we have a trick. We will clip an extra wire onto the metal prong that goes in the soil, and let the NodeMCU "listen in" on the prong. Wet soil lets electricity flow easier, so the voltage at A0 drops. Dry soil makes it climb back up. The meter still works the normal way for your eyes. (If this feels too tricky, you can skip the prong-listening trick: just watch the needle yourself, and in the code set DRY_THRESHOLD and WET_THRESHOLD to the same number so the relay never flips by itself. You can still turn the light on and off from your phone.)
**Step 1 - Snap the NodeMCU onto the I/O Shield.** - Line up the two rows of pins under the NodeMCU with the two rows of holes on the I/O Shield. The USB plug should be on the same end as the USB hole in the shield. - Press straight down until it seats. No tools, no soldering. The shield turns every NodeMCU pin into a row of three holes: the outer hole is the **signal** (the actual Dx pin), the middle hole is **+5V**, and the inner hole is **GND**. That means you can grab a 3-wire jumper cable and plug a sensor straight in without juggling separate wires.
**Step 2 - Set up the breadboard power rails.** The breadboard has two long red/blue strips running down each side - those are the **power rails**. The red one we will call "+", the blue one we will call "GND" (0V). - Use a short red M-M jumper to connect the top red rail to the bottom red rail (so both red rails carry the same power). - Use a short black M-M jumper to connect the top blue rail to the bottom blue rail (so both grounds match). Now anywhere you plug into a red rail gets power, and anywhere you plug into a blue rail is ground. Easy.
**Step 3 - Wire up the buck converter (the power box).** The buck converter takes the 12V coming from the wall-wart and squeezes it down to a tidy 5V. It has two input screw terminals (marked IN+ and IN-) and a USB-A socket on the side. - Cut or unscrew the barrel jack off your 12V wall-wart, or use a barrel-to-screw adapter. The **+** wire goes into IN+ and the **-** wire goes into IN-. Get this the right way around or the buck dies. - Plug a short USB cable from the buck's USB-A socket into the NodeMCU's micro-USB jack (the one poking out of the I/O Shield). That powers the brain. - Find the buck's 5V output pads (right next to the USB socket) and run one F-M jumper from 5V to a red rail hole on the breadboard, and one F-M jumper from GND to a blue rail hole. Now the breadboard has 5V too. **Why this matters:** the NodeMCU needs 5V, the relay module needs 5V, and the LEDs need ground. One buck feeds all three from a single 12V wall-wart so we never have two power supplies fighting.
**Step 4 - Plant the red "dry" LED.**
- Take the red LED. The **long leg** goes into hole **E5**, the **short leg** goes into hole **E6**. - Take one 220R resistor (red-red-brown-gold stripes). Put one end in hole **A6** (same row as the short leg) and the other end in the blue **GND** rail at the top. - Take an M-M jumper. Plug one end into hole **A5** (same row as the long leg) and the other end into hole **B10**. - Take a 3-wire F-F jumper or a single F-M jumper. Plug it into the **D5** signal hole on the I/O Shield (silkscreen "D5", which is GPIO14 in code), and the other end into hole **B10** on the breadboard. **Why the resistor:** an LED is greedy - if you just hand it 3.3V straight, it gulps too much current and burns out in a second. The 220R resistor sits in line and politely slows the current down to a safe amount. Always pair an LED with a resistor.
**Step 5 - Plant the green "wet" LED.** (The green LED in our bin doesn't have a stock photo - it looks like the red one but glows green.) - Take the green LED. The **long leg** goes into hole **E14**, the **short leg** goes into hole **E15**. - Take the second 220R resistor. One end in hole **A15** (same row as the short leg), other end in the blue **GND** rail. - Take an M-M jumper. One end in hole **A14** (same row as the long leg), other end in hole **B19**. - Run a wire from the **D6** signal hole on the I/O Shield (silkscreen "D6", GPIO12 in code) to hole **B19**. Now you have two little status LEDs sitting on the breadboard, ready to glow red when the plant is dry and green when it's happy.
**Step 6 - Build the soil-listening corner.** (The 1M-ohm resistor has no stock photo - it's a tiny part with brown-black-green color bands.) - Take the 1M-ohm resistor. Put one end into hole **E23**. Put the other end into the **red +** rail at the top of the breadboard (we will feed this rail with 3.3V from the NodeMCU, not the buck's 5V - read on). - Take an M-M jumper from hole **A23** over to hole **B25**. - From the I/O Shield, run a wire from **A0** (the one analog pin) to hole **B25**. - Important swap: also run a wire from the I/O Shield **3V3** pin to the **red +** rail near where the 1M resistor lives. (Yes, this rail will have 3.3V on it, not 5V. The reason: A0 on the NodeMCU can only handle up to about 3.3V, so we feed the divider with 3.3V to stay safe.) - Run a wire from the I/O Shield **GND** to the blue **GND** rail. **Why this matters:** the 1M resistor and the prong-in-soil together form a tiny "voltage seesaw". The 1M tries to pull A0 up to 3.3V. The wet soil tries to pull A0 down to ground through the meter's own internals. Drier soil = less pulling-down = A0 reads higher. Wetter soil = more pulling-down = A0 reads lower. We have to use 1M (a million ohms) because anything smaller would mess up the meter's own needle reading.
**Step 7 - Clip the alligator to the soil meter prong.** - Put the soil meter's battery in and clip its two stock wires onto the metal prong like normal (one clip per labeled spot - follow the meter's instructions). - Take an extra alligator-to-jumper lead. Clip the alligator end onto any bare metal part of the prong (above the soil line, so it doesn't fall in). Push the jumper end into hole **E23** on the breadboard. Stick the prong into a pot of dirt. The meter's needle will still wiggle for your eyes, and the NodeMCU will quietly listen in at A0.
**Step 8 - Set up the ESP-01S relay module (the radio-controlled switch).** This little board is its own tiny Wi-Fi computer with a relay strapped on. The relay is just a switch you turn on or off by sending it a message over Wi-Fi. It has four pins on the bottom edge: **VCC** (power input, 5V in), **GND** (0V ground), and two skinny pins we don't need to touch. It also has three big screw terminals on the green block: **COM**, **NO**, and **NC**. - Plug the module so the VCC pin lands in hole **F2** and the GND pin lands in hole **F3**. - Take an M-M jumper. One end in hole **J2** (same row as VCC), the other in the red **+5V** rail. This sends 5V power into the relay board. - Take another M-M jumper. One end in hole **J3** (same row as GND), the other in the blue **GND** rail. **Why the relay is separate:** the relay has its own little brain and its own Wi-Fi. The NodeMCU does not control it through a wire - it sends it a phone message over the network, just like you would. That keeps the dangerous 12V wiring on its own island, away from your fingers.
**Step 9 - The 12V switching side (this part needs a grown-up).** This is the only place 12V shows up, and the only part you must NOT touch while the wall-wart is plugged in. - Take a short solid-core wire. Strip both ends. Put one end into the relay's **COM** screw terminal and tighten the screw. Put the other end onto the **+ wire from the 12V wall-wart**. - Take another short wire. One end into the relay's **NO** screw terminal (NO means Normally Open - so the switch is off until the relay closes it). The other end goes to the **+ wire of the 12V LED strip**. - Connect the LED strip's **-** wire straight back to the wall-wart's **-** wire. When the relay clicks "on" over Wi-Fi, it joins COM and NO inside, which lets 12V flow from the wall-wart through the strip and back. When it clicks "off", that path opens up and the strip goes dark. The relay's logic side (the VCC/GND pins) is completely walled off from the screw terminals - they cannot zap each other, which is why we get to use it safely.
**Final check before plugging in.** - Every red rail is wired to a red rail and a 5V source. Every blue rail is wired to a blue rail and the GND of the buck. There are no loose ends. - The buck's IN+ has the 12V wall-wart's + wire and IN- has the - wire. Not swapped. - The 12V on the screw terminals does not touch any breadboard hole - only the relay screws and the LED strip. - The soil prong has the alligator clip above the dirt, not in it. Plug in the 12V wall-wart. The NodeMCU's blue light should blink. The ESP-01S relay should boot up too. The needle on the soil meter should swing as you push the prong into wet or dry soil. The first time everything lights up calmly with nothing smoking is a great feeling - this is a tricky one, well done. ## Flash it and run it The ESP-01S Tasmota relay arrives PRE-FLASHED. You do NOT need to flash it. On first power-up it broadcasts a WiFi access point called something like `tasmota-XXXX-1234`. Join it from your phone, then enter SSID `GeeFam` and the password. After it reboots it shows up on your home WiFi and you control it from its built-in web page at http:/// or by pressing the on-board button. Note the IP address - you'll paste it into the sketch below. If you ever DO need to re-flash the ESP-01S relay yourself, that takes a CP2102 USB-to-TTL UART Module, a 3.3V supply (NOT 5V on the ESP-01S header pins - it'll cook the chip), and you have to hold GPIO0 to GND while powering up to enter flash mode. For the NodeMCU V3, open the Arduino IDE. 1. File -> Preferences -> Additional Board Manager URLs: add `http://arduino.esp8266.com/stable/package_esp8266com_index.json` 2. Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager -> install "esp8266" by ESP8266 Community. 3. Tools -> Board -> NodeMCU 1.0 (ESP-12E Module). 4. Tools -> Port -> pick the COM port that appears when you plug the USB cable in. 5. In the sketch: SSID is already set to `GeeFam`, replace `PASSWORD_HERE` with the real WiFi password, and set `TASMOTA_IP` to the IP your relay got from the router. 6. Sketch -> Upload. Calibration: open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud after upload. Stick the probe in a glass of water, watch the "Soil raw:" number for ~10 seconds - that's your WET_THRESHOLD. Pull it out and let it dry on a paper towel - that's your DRY_THRESHOLD. Edit the two constants and re-upload. Common gotchas: - No COM port showing up? The CH340 driver is missing. Install it from wch.cn and re-plug the USB cable. - Soil readings stuck at 0 or 1023? You wired the probe tap to a digital pin. It has to go to A0 (the only analog pin on the NodeMCU). - Soil readings always the same number? You forgot the 1M pull-up to 3.3V on the A0 line, so the pin is floating instead of being pulled down by the soil-meter path. - Relay clicks but the strip does not light? You swapped + and - on the 12V LED strip - it only conducts one way. - Relay never clicks AND the serial log shows "HTTP code: 401"? Your Tasmota WebUI has a username/password set. Either disable WebUI auth in the Tasmota Configuration page, or set TASMOTA_USER and TASMOTA_PASS in the sketch (the URL builder appends `&user=...&password=...` automatically). - Relay never clicks AND the serial log shows "HTTP code: -1"? The TASMOTA_IP in the sketch is wrong or the relay is off the network. Open its web page in a browser first to confirm. ## Talking points - Why does wet soil pull our A0 reading LOWER, not higher? Water lets electricity flow more easily, so it drains charge from A0 through the soil to the meter's ground faster than the 1M resistor can re-fill it. Dry soil = pin floats high; wet soil = pin gets pulled down. - Why does the relay click? There's a tiny electromagnet inside that pulls a metal bar across two contacts. That's why old phones used to "ring" - same mechanism, just faster. - Why two separate boards instead of one? The Tasmota relay is a complete WiFi switch the grown-up world already trusts; the NodeMCU is our "decision maker." Splitting the job is how big smart-home systems work too: cheap sensors send messages, separate actuators do the heavy switching. - Why didn't we feed 3.3V into the soil meter? The meter has its own button-cell battery and its own little circuit inside. Pushing power INTO an output pin can fight the meter's internals and damage either side. ## Things to change once it works - Add a buzzer that beeps once when the light first turns on, so you hear the plant ask before you see it. - Swap the dry/wet LED dashboard for the 0.96" OLED Display and show the moisture as a percentage. - Add a second probe tap and a second Tasmota relay so each plant gets its own light. - Have the NodeMCU log every reading to a Google Sheet through IFTTT - watch the moisture drop over a week. - Replace the LED strip with the W1209-controlled fan to "blow" cool air on a thirsty plant instead. ## Why this is interesting This is your first taste of a real smart-home pattern: one device measures the world, another device acts on it, and they talk over WiFi instead of wires. That same pattern runs giant warehouses, greenhouses, and factory floors. You also got your first "no-code" device (the Tasmota relay) and your first "code-it-yourself" device (the NodeMCU) cooperating on the same network - which is exactly how grown-up automation projects are built. Bonus lesson: tapping a signal off an existing meter (without powering it from your MCU) is a real-world technique for reading something a sensor module doesn't exist for.
