projects.name: Screw-Terminal Weather Card
projects.power_supply: Micro-USB cable from laptop to the NodeMCU on the I/O Shield (5V in, 3.3V regulated on board for the BMP280)
projects.description:
**What it is**: A tiny weather station you can read from any phone. Plug it in, walk away, then open a web page that shows the temperature, the air pressure right now, and a big arrow telling you if the weather is getting better or worse. **Why it is fun**: It's a real instrument - the same kind of barometer that pilots and sailors use. You can predict if tomorrow will be sunny or rainy before the weather app does, and shout "I told you so" when you're right. ## Parts list - 1x NodeMCU V3 (ESP8266) - the WiFi brain - 1x NodeMCU V3 I/O Shield - screw-terminal jacket so we don't need a breadboard - 1x GY-BMP280 pressure/temperature sensor - the actual barometer - 4x M-M jumper wires (from the 40pc pack) - sensor to shield terminals - 1x micro-USB cable - power and programming (the one that came with the NodeMCU) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the NodeMCU and I/O Shield:** - **Dx (D1, D2, etc.)** - the pin labels printed on the board. The code uses different numbers (GPIOs) for the same pins, but you only need to look at the Dx label. - **3V3** - the 3.3V power output. The BMP280 sensor runs on this. - **5V** or **VIN** - 5V power (the same voltage that comes in from the USB cable). - **G** or **GND** - ground, the 0V side. Every circuit needs a ground connection. - **SDA / SCL** - the two data wires for I2C, which is how the sensor talks to the NodeMCU. - **Screw terminal** - the little hole on the I/O Shield where you push a wire in and tighten a tiny screw to hold it.
**Step 1 - Push the NodeMCU into the I/O Shield.** - Hold the I/O Shield so the screw terminals point up. - Line up the two rows of pins on the bottom of the NodeMCU with the two black sockets on the shield. - Push down gently and evenly. The USB port on the NodeMCU should stick out over the edge of the shield (so a cable can plug in later). - Check that no pin is bent or missed - every pin needs to sit in a hole. The shield turns every NodeMCU pin into a screw-down hole with a clear label next to it. That means no breadboard and no soldering for this project - just a tiny flat screwdriver.
**Step 2 - Connect the BMP280 sensor with 4 jumper wires.**
The BMP280 is a tiny blue or purple board with 4 (or 6) pins along one edge. It uses a chat method called I2C, which only needs two data wires plus power and ground. Make 4 wire connections like this: | BMP280 pin | I/O Shield screw terminal | | ---------- | ------------------------- | | VCC (power input) | 3V3 | | GND (the 0V side - ground) | G (any of the G screws) | | SDA (data line) | the pin marked D2 (GPIO 4 in code) | | SCL (clock line) | the pin marked D1 (GPIO 5 in code) | How to use each screw terminal: - Pick a male-to-male jumper wire. - Unscrew the tiny screw on the terminal about half a turn. - Push the bare metal end of the wire into the hole on the side. - Tighten the screw until the wire is held firmly. Give the wire a soft tug - it should not come out. - Plug the other end of the wire into the matching pin on the BMP280. Important: the BMP280 needs 3.3V power, not 5V. Use the **3V3** screw terminal, not 5V or VIN. Plugging it into 5V can damage the sensor.
**Why this matters - I2C and the missing resistors.** I2C needs two small pull-up resistors on the SDA and SCL wires for the sensor and the NodeMCU to hear each other clearly. Good news: the GY-BMP280 board you have already has those two resistors soldered onto it. You do not have to add any. (If you ever buy a bare BMP280 chip without a breakout board, you would need to add two 4.7K resistors yourself, but not today.)
**Step 3 - Plug in the USB cable and power up.** - Plug a Micro-USB cable into the NodeMCU's USB port. - Plug the other end into your laptop. - A small blue LED on the NodeMCU should blink once when power arrives. - The BMP280 does not have an LED, so it will look the same whether it is working or not. We will check it from the code in the next step. The USB cable does two things at once: it sends 5V power into the NodeMCU, and it lets your laptop talk to the chip to upload code.
**Final check before flashing.** - All 4 wires to the BMP280 are tight (gentle tug test). - BMP280 VCC goes to **3V3**, not 5V. - SDA is on **D2**, SCL is on **D1**. If you swap these two, the sensor will not answer. - No bare wire ends are touching each other. - USB cable plugged in, blue power LED visible. If anything looks off, unplug the USB first, fix the wire, then plug back in. Never move wires around while the board is powered. ## Flash it and run it 1. Open Arduino IDE. **File -> Preferences -> Additional Board URLs** and add `http://arduino.esp8266.com/stable/package_esp8266com_index.json`. 2. **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, install "esp8266 by ESP8266 Community". 3. Pick board **NodeMCU 1.0 (ESP-12E Module)**. Upload speed 115200. 4. **Sketch -> Include Library -> Manage Libraries**: install "Adafruit BMP280 Library" (it will offer to install "Adafruit Unified Sensor" and "Adafruit BusIO" too - say yes). 5. Plug the NodeMCU's micro-USB cable into your laptop. The first time Windows may install a CH340 driver - wait for it. 6. Pick the new COM port under **Tools -> Port**. 7. Paste the sketch, hit Upload, then open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. You'll see "IP: 192.168.x.x" once it joins WiFi. 8. Open that IP in your phone browser (same WiFi). Boom - weather card. **Common gotchas**: - "BMP280 not found" almost always means SDA/SCL are swapped, or the sensor is on the 5V rail instead of 3V3. - Some BMP280 boards live at I2C address 0x77 instead of 0x76; the sketch tries 0x76 first, then 0x77. - No COM port? You're missing the CH340G driver - search "CH340 driver win10" and install. - WiFi never connects? Double-check the SSID and password strings are spelled exactly right. ## Talking points - Air pressure is measured in hectopascals (hPa). Normal sea-level pressure is about 1013 hPa. - When pressure rises, the atmosphere is "pushing down" harder - usually clear skies. Falling pressure means storms are coming. - I2C is just two wires (data + clock) that lots of sensors share. You could add more sensors on the same SDA/SCL. - The NodeMCU is its own little web server - your phone is literally talking to this matchbox-sized board. ## Things to change once it works - Add a `/json` endpoint and have a second project poll it. - Log every sample to a CSV via Serial and graph a week of data. - Display pressure in inHg (inches of mercury) for the Americans in the family. - Add a buzzer that beeps if pressure drops fast (storm alarm). - Swap the BMP280 for a BME280 to also get humidity. ## Why this is interesting This is your first real WiFi project. You learn three big ideas at once: I2C (how chips chat), HTTP (how phones talk to servers), and meteorology (why the air pressure matters). Everything you build later that uses a web page builds on this exact pattern.

projects.name: Mini Ice-Cube Maker (W1209 + Peltier auto-stop)
projects.power_supply: 12V 6A wall-wart (centre-positive) into the MB102 barrel jack. MB102 12V rail splits to three branches: W1209 controller, heatsink fan (always on), and W1209 relay COM (which switches the Peltier). No DC-DC converter in the path.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little machine that actually freezes a real (tiny) ice cube right in front of you, using a bottle cap full of water sitting on a metal plate. A small display shows the temperature counting down, and when the plate hits minus two degrees, the machine clicks and shuts itself off so the cube stays frozen but the parts do not keep getting colder. **Why it is fun**: You are making ICE with electricity. No freezer. No moving parts inside the plate. You touch one side and it is hot enough to feel; you touch the other side and it is so cold it stings. Drop one drop of water into the bottle cap, watch the display count down like a rocket - "12... 8... 3... -1... CLICK!" - and pop out a real ice disc to show your sister. ## Parts list - 1x TEC1-4905 Peltier Thermoelectric Cooler (the magic plate - 12V 5A nominal, hot on one side, cold on the other) - 1x W1209 Temperature Controller (NTC probe + 7-seg display + 10A relay all on one tiny board - no microcontroller, no code to upload) - 1x MB102 Breadboard Power Supply Module (used here as a tidy clamp-style distribution block: the 12V wall-wart goes into its barrel jack, and the three 12V branches - W1209, fan, relay COM - tap off its labelled rails) - 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) - the MB102 snaps onto one end and gives us the shared 12V/GND rails - 1x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc - for the breadboard rail hops - 1x Jumper Wire F-M, 20pc - to reach the W1209 screw terminals and the Peltier flying leads - A bottle cap (any clean plastic soda-bottle cap) - this is the ice mold - A big CPU heatsink with a 12V fan strapped to the hot side of the Peltier (recycled PC heatsink works great) - Thermal paste smear between the Peltier hot side and the heatsink - 12V wall-wart, centre-positive, **at least 6A** (this is the project's only power input - the TEC1-4905 alone pulls about 5A at 12V, the fan adds another 0.3A, and we want headroom so the supply does not sag or thermally trip) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on this build:** - **W1209** - the little red board with the glowing red number screen. It is a thermostat: it watches a temperature and flips a switch when the temperature gets cold enough. - **Peltier** - a flat square chip that gets cold on one side and hot on the other side when you put 12V across it. - **NTC probe** - the silver bullet-shaped tip on the end of the W1209's two-wire cable. This is the thermometer. - **Relay** - a tiny mechanical switch inside the W1209 that you can hear click. It turns the Peltier on and off. - **COM and NO** - two of the relay's screw holes. COM means "common" (one side of the switch). NO means "normally open" (the other side, which only joins COM when the relay clicks closed). - **MB102 rail** - the long red strip running down the side of the breadboard, fed by the MB102 power board. The whole strip is 12V.
**THE BIGGEST RULE, READ THIS FIRST.** The Peltier has a cold side and a hot side. The hot side MUST be pressed flat against a big metal heatsink with a running fan on it. If you forget the fan, the hot side cooks the cold side from behind and the whole chip can burn in under a minute. Before you plug anything in, do a dry test: feel the chip. Whichever side ends up against the heatsink is the hot side. The other side, facing up, is where the little bottle cap of water sits.
**Step 1 - Plant the breadboard and the power board.**
- Put the breadboard flat on the table with row 1 at the top. - Press the MB102 power board down so its two long rows of pins sit in rows 2 and 3 (top half) and rows 2 and 3 on the other side too. The board straddles the middle gap. - Look at the MB102. It has two little black jumper caps near the output pins. Pull them off and set them aside. Those switches choose 3.3V or 5V; we do NOT want either of those. We want raw 12V. The MB102 is just being used as a tidy splitter today. The wall-wart plugs into its barrel jack, and the MB102 shares that 12V out to several wires at once.
**Step 2 - Send the MB102's 12V out to the side rails of the breadboard.** - Red jumper wire from **A2** to the red **+ rail** at the top of the breadboard. - Black jumper wire from **A3** to the blue **- rail** at the top. - Red jumper from **J2** to the red **+ rail** at the bottom. - Black jumper from **J3** to the blue **- rail** at the bottom. This makes both red side-strips carry 12V and both blue side-strips be the 0V (ground) side. Now anywhere on the board, you can grab 12V from the red strip and ground from the blue strip. WARNING: the red strips on this build are 12V, NOT the usual 5V you see in beginner kits. Do not poke any 5V-only parts into them.
**Step 3 - Power the W1209 thermostat.** The W1209 has six screw terminals along one edge. From one end you will see them labeled something like **12V+**, **12V-**, **probe**, **probe**, **K0/COM**, **K1/NO**. - Red jumper from the red 12V rail (top) to **A12**, which is the W1209's **12V+** input. - Black jumper from the blue 0V rail (top) to **A13**, which is the W1209's **12V-** input. When you plug the wall-wart in, the little red number screen on the W1209 should light up. That means the controller is awake.
**Step 4 - Give the W1209 its thermometer (the NTC probe).** The W1209 comes with a thin two-wire cable ending in a small silver bullet. That bullet is the thermometer. Its two bare wires go into the two **probe** screw terminals (positions A15 and A16 on the layout). The probe is not polarized, so either wire can go in either screw. - Lay the silver bullet flat on the COLD side of the Peltier, right next to where the water bottle cap will sit. - Hold it down with a tiny dab of thermal paste and a strip of foil tape over the top to lock it in place. - The silver bullet is waterproof. The bare copper at the screw terminals is NOT waterproof - keep those ends dry and away from the cold plate, or condensation will short them out. **Why this matters:** the whole job of the W1209 is to ask "is the cold plate cold enough yet?" If the probe is loose, or sitting in the air, or wrapped in dry cloth, the W1209 will see a warm reading and never turn the Peltier off. Good contact between the silver bullet and the metal of the cold plate is what makes this project safe.
**Step 5 - Wire the Peltier's red lead through the W1209's relay.** The relay is a tiny switch inside the W1209. It has two screw holes that matter for us: **COM** (at A18) and **NO** (at A19). We are going to send the Peltier's positive wire through that switch so the W1209 can turn the Peltier on and off. - Red jumper from the red 12V rail (top) to **A18** (the W1209's **COM** screw). - The W1209's **NO** screw is at A19. Take the Peltier's RED wire and clamp it into the A19 screw (this is an "external" wire that leaves the breadboard area and runs to the Peltier). - Take the Peltier's BLACK wire and run it straight to the blue 0V rail at the bottom of the breadboard (the **GND_B** spot). Now follow the chain in your head: 12V wall-wart -> MB102 -> red 12V rail -> COM -> [the relay switch] -> NO -> Peltier red. When the W1209 closes its relay (you hear a click), the chain is complete and the Peltier gets full 12V. When the W1209 opens the relay, the chain breaks and the Peltier stops cooling.
**Step 6 - Wire the heatsink fan straight to 12V (always on).** The fan that sits on top of the heatsink has two wires, usually red and black. - Fan RED -> the red 12V rail (top). - Fan BLACK -> the blue 0V rail (top). Notice the fan is NOT going through the relay. That is on purpose. We want the fan running the whole time, even after the W1209 turns the Peltier off, so the heatsink can keep dumping leftover heat for a minute or two after. If the fan stopped at the same time as the Peltier, all that stored heat would creep back through to the cold side.
**Step 7 - Stack the cold side, the hot side, and the heatsink.** This is the order from top to bottom: 1. A clean plastic bottle cap with a teaspoon of water in it. (The future ice cube.) 2. The Peltier's COLD face, with the silver thermometer bullet held against it. 3. The Peltier's HOT face, pressed flat against... 4. The heatsink, with a thin smear of thermal paste between them. 5. The fan, screwed or clipped to the top of the heatsink, blowing AWAY from the Peltier. Squeeze it all together with a rubber band or a small clamp. The tighter the hot side is to the heatsink, the better.
**Step 8 - Set the W1209's target temperature.** The W1209 has three little buttons under its red number screen: **SET**, **+**, and **-**. Hold **SET** for about 3 seconds. The display will start blinking. Use **+** and **-** to dial the target to **-2** (minus two degrees Celsius). Press **SET** again to save. From now on the W1209 will keep the relay closed (Peltier ON) whenever the probe reads warmer than -2 C, and open the relay (Peltier OFF) when it gets to -2 C or colder.
**Step 9 - First power-up checklist.** Before you plug the wall-wart in, walk through these four checks with a parent: 1. Hot side of the Peltier is clamped to the heatsink, and the heatsink is clean. 2. The fan wires are on the 12V rail, not on the relay output. 3. The Peltier's black wire goes straight to the blue 0V rail, NOT through the relay. 4. The silver thermometer bullet is touching the cold plate, not flapping in the air. Now plug in. The fan should start spinning right away. The W1209 screen should light up. Within a few seconds you should hear a soft "click" - that is the relay closing - and the cold plate should start to fog up and then frost over. Roughly 8 to 15 minutes later you will hear another "click" as the W1209 hits -2 C and turns the Peltier off. That is your ice cube ready. **Heads-up on the relay clicking:** the relay is rated for 10 amps and the Peltier only pulls about 5 amps, so we are well inside the limit. But after a few hundred on-off cycles you may eventually hear the click sound get a little louder or rougher. That is normal wear on a tiny mechanical switch. It is not dangerous, it just means the relay has earned its retirement someday.
## Flash it and run it There is no code to upload - the W1209 is a self-contained controller with a tiny menu you set with three buttons. Here is the multimeter + button procedure. Do the stages **in order** and do not skip Stage 2.5. **Stage 1 - bench-test the wall-wart and the MB102 splitter (Peltier disconnected).** Plug the 12V wall-wart into the MB102 barrel jack. Set your multimeter to DC volts (20V range). Probe the MB102's 12V output rail. You should read between 11.8V and 12.3V. If you read 5V you flipped the MB102 voltage-select jumpers; set them back to "OFF / 12V passthrough" per the silkscreen. **Stage 2 - power the W1209 alone (Peltier disconnected).** Connect ONLY the W1209 12V+ and 12V- terminals to the MB102 12V rail. Plug in. The 3-digit display should light up showing room temperature (e.g. "22"). If it shows "LLL" the NTC probe is open (re-seat the two NTC wires). If it shows "HHH" the NTC probe is shorted (check for stripped insulation). If the display is dark, polarity is wrong. **Stage 2.5 - lower the setpoint floor (P3) BEFORE setting the trip point.** Many W1209 firmware revisions clamp the user setpoint to the P3 (lower-limit) parameter. Out of the box P3 is often 0 or -9 - if you skip this step and try to dial the setpoint to -2 in Stage 3 the display will silently refuse and stop at 0. To fix: press and hold **SET** for about 5 seconds to enter the parameter menu. Press SET to step until the display shows **P3**. Use - to drop it to **-10** (the display reads "-10"). Press and hold SET to save and exit. **Stage 3 - set the cooling trip point to -2 C.** From the home screen, press and hold SET for about 3 seconds. The display starts FLASHING - that is the setpoint. Use + and - to set it to **-2** (display reads "-02"). Press SET once to save. The display goes back to live temperature. **Stage 4 - set the mode to COOLING and hysteresis to 2 C.** Press and hold SET for about 5 seconds (the longer press) to enter the parameter menu. Press SET to step through. Use + and - to change values. - **P0** = mode. Set to **C** (Cooling). In Cooling mode the relay is CLOSED (Peltier ON) when measured temp is ABOVE setpoint, and OPENS (Peltier OFF) when measured temp is BELOW. - **P1** = hysteresis. Set to **2**. After the relay opens at -2 C, it will not re-close until the plate climbs back to 0 C. Prevents rapid clicking at the setpoint. - **P2** = upper-limit (safety ceiling for the setpoint). Leave default. - **P3** = lower-limit. You already set this to -10 in Stage 2.5. - **P4** = calibration offset. Leave at 0. - **P5** = relay-engage delay on power-up. Leave at 0. - **P6** = high-temp alarm. Leave default. Press and hold SET to save and exit. **Stage 5 - connect the Peltier and run it.** Power off. Wire the Peltier as described in Wiring notes. Tape the NTC bead to the cold side of the Peltier, right next to (NOT inside) the bottle cap. Drop one or two drops of water into the bottle cap. Plug in. With a 12V 6A supply feeding the Peltier directly through the relay, the display counts down: 22, 18, 12, 6, 1, -1, -2... CLICK! Relay opens, Peltier stops, fan keeps running. Wait 30 seconds, pop the bottle cap off, and a real ice disc comes out. Real-world time from room temperature to first ice is roughly 2-3 minutes; below 2 minutes is unusual, above 4 minutes means your thermal paste contact between Peltier and heatsink is poor. **Common gotchas:** - **Display shows "LLL" or "HHH"**: NTC probe disconnected or shorted. Re-seat the probe wires. - **Setpoint refuses to go below 0**: you skipped Stage 2.5. Set P3 to -10 first. - **Plate gets warm not cold**: Peltier wired backwards. Swap the red and black leads at the MB102 / relay output. - **Relay never clicks open**: P0 is set to H (heating). Redo Stage 4. - **It freezes the cap fine but then the cap thaws fast**: that is normal - the cold side warms the second the Peltier turns off. Pop the ice out within 30 seconds. - **Hot side gets scary hot**: stop. Unplug. Fan is not running, or thermal paste is missing. Fix before re-powering. - **Wall-wart gets noticeably warm and the plate barely cools**: your supply cannot deliver the current. Confirm the wall-wart label says at least 12V 6A. ## Talking points - The Peltier is a **solid-state heat pump**. There are no moving parts inside it - just a stack of tiny semiconductor pillars. Electricity goes in, and one side gets cold while the other side gets hot. Reverse the wires and the hot and cold sides swap. This is called the *Peltier effect* and was discovered in 1834. - **Heat has to go somewhere.** A Peltier does not destroy heat - it MOVES heat from the cold side to the hot side. If the hot side cannot get rid of the heat fast enough (no heatsink, no fan), the whole plate ends up warm and the cold side stops getting cold. The fan is not a luxury, it is required. - The W1209 is a **closed-loop controller** - it reads the temperature, compares it to your setpoint, and switches the relay accordingly. The **hysteresis** value (P1) keeps the relay from clicking on and off rapidly when the temperature is right at the setpoint. - **Why we run the Peltier at the full 12V here even though we are "just doing a kid demo".** The thermostat is the safety net, not the voltage. With the W1209 cutting power at -2 C, running at 12V just gets us to that cutoff faster. Trying to "be gentle" with a half-rated buck converter actually made the project worse in an earlier draft - the buck would overheat trying to deliver 5A from a 3A-rated chip. - A real fridge does the same thing your project does, just much bigger and using a compressor and refrigerant gas instead of a semiconductor stack. ## Things to change once it works - **Use a piece of aluminium foil instead of a bottle cap** to make a thinner sheet of ice that freezes in 30 seconds. - Set the W1209 setpoint to **+4 C** instead of -2 and call it a tiny soda chiller - the relay will keep a small can of juice near fridge temperature, and the Peltier will cycle less, which is easier on the relay contacts. - Add an **LED + 220R resistor** wired across the relay output - it lights up while the Peltier is running, goes dark when the cube is ready, giving you a "done!" indicator without staring at the display. - Swap the cold-side bottle cap for a **drop of food colouring in water** - watch it crystallise into a coloured ice star. - Insulate around the bottle cap with a ring of foam so less heat sneaks in from the sides - your cube freezes twice as fast. ## Why this is interesting Making ice with no moving parts feels like magic the first time. This project also teaches the single most important idea in control engineering: a **setpoint + a sensor + a switch** is enough to keep almost anything at the temperature you want - fridges, ovens, 3D printer hot ends, fish tanks, beer fermenters, server rooms. You have just built the same control loop they all use, in miniature, with one little blue board. And you have learned a quieter but equally important lesson: **size the wires for the current you actually need**, not for the current you wish you needed.

projects.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Mini Ice-Cube Maker - W1209 setup + multimeter test procedure.
# There is NO microcontroller and NO sketch to upload. The W1209 is a
# self-contained controller; you configure it with three buttons on
# the board itself. This file documents the menu walk and the
# multimeter checkpoints to verify wiring before the Peltier runs.
#
# Power path (final, no buck converter):
#   12V 6A wall-wart  ->  MB102 (used as a 12V splitter, NOT as a
#                         5V/3.3V regulator - leave those switches OFF)
#   MB102 12V rail    ->  three branches:
#                           (a) W1209 12V in
#                           (b) Heatsink fan (always on)
#                           (c) W1209 relay COM
#   W1209 relay NO    ->  Peltier RED
#   MB102 GND rail    ->  Peltier BLACK
#
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# SAFETY FIRST - DO THESE EVERY TIME BEFORE PLUGGING IN
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
#   1. Is the hot side of the Peltier pressed FLAT against the heatsink
#      with thermal paste in between? If you cannot see paste squish
#      around the edges, STOP and re-seat it.
#   2. Is the heatsink fan spinning the SECOND the 12V comes on? Put
#      your hand near it. No spin = unplug immediately.
#   3. Is the NTC probe taped to the COLD plate (the side facing UP,
#      with the bottle cap on it), NOT dunked in the water?
#   4. Is the W1209 board mounted ABOVE the cold plate, off to the
#      side, so any condensation drips DOWN onto the bench and not
#      onto the screw terminals? Run a slack loop in the NTC wires.
#   5. Does the wall-wart label say at least 12V 6A?  A 3A wall-wart
#      will sag under the Peltier's ~5A load and may thermally trip.
#
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# STAGE 1 - BENCH-TEST THE WALL-WART AND THE MB102 SPLITTER
#           (Peltier still disconnected)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Plug the 12V 6A wall-wart into the MB102 barrel jack.
# Confirm the MB102 voltage-select switches/jumpers are NOT set to
# 3.3V or 5V on either rail - we want raw 12V passthrough.
# Set your multimeter to DC volts, 20V range.
# Probe the MB102 12V output rail (red) vs the GND rail (black).
#
# Expected: 11.8 V to 12.3 V on the 12V rail.
# If you read 5V: the MB102 regulator is enabled. Switch it off.
# If you read 0V: barrel jack polarity is wrong, or wall-wart is dead.
#
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# STAGE 2 - POWER THE W1209 ALONE (Peltier still disconnected)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Connect ONLY the W1209 12V+ and 12V- terminals to the MB102 12V rail.
# Plug in. The 3-digit display should light up showing room temp,
# e.g. "22" (Celsius).
#
# Expected: display shows a sensible room temperature (15 to 30).
# If display shows "LLL": NTC probe is open - re-seat the two
#                          NTC wires in the screw terminals.
# If display shows "HHH": NTC probe is shorted - check for a pinched
#                          wire or stripped insulation.
# If display is dark:      12V is not reaching the board. Check polarity.
#
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# STAGE 2.5 - LOWER P3 (SETPOINT FLOOR) BEFORE TRYING TO DIAL TO -2
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Many W1209 firmware revisions clamp the user setpoint to the P3
# (lower-limit) parameter. The factory default is often 0 or -9, which
# means trying to set the setpoint to -2 in Stage 3 will silently
# refuse and stop at the floor. Fix this BEFORE Stage 3.
#
#   a) Press and hold SET for ~5 seconds to enter the parameter menu.
#   b) Press SET to step through P0, P1, P2, P3...
#   c) When P3 is shown, use - to dial the value down to -10.
#   d) Press and hold SET to save and exit.
#
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# STAGE 3 - SET THE COOLING TRIP POINT (-2 C)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# From the home screen:
#
#   a) Press and hold SET for ~3 seconds. The display starts FLASHING -
#      that is the setpoint value.
#   b) Use + and - buttons to dial it down to -2. The display reads
#      "-02". (If it refuses to go below 0, you skipped Stage 2.5.)
#   c) Press SET once to confirm. The display stops flashing.
#
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# STAGE 4 - SET THE MODE TO COOLING + HYSTERESIS = 2 C
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Press and hold SET for ~5 seconds (the longer press) to enter the
# parameter menu again. Press SET to step through. Use + and - to
# change values.
#
#   P0 = mode. Set to "C" (Cooling). In Cooling mode the relay is
#        CLOSED (Peltier ON) when measured temp is ABOVE the setpoint,
#        and OPENS (Peltier OFF) when measured temp is BELOW it.
#   P1 = hysteresis. Set to "2". After the relay opens at -2 C, it
#        will not re-close until the plate climbs back to 0 C.
#   P2 = upper-limit (setpoint ceiling). Leave default.
#   P3 = lower-limit. Already set to -10 in Stage 2.5.
#   P4 = calibration offset. Leave at 0.
#   P5 = delay before relay engages on power-up. Leave at 0.
#   P6 = high-temp alarm. Leave default.
#
# Press and hold SET to save and exit.
#
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# STAGE 5 - CONNECT THE PELTIER AND RUN IT
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Power off. Wire the Peltier as shown in the diagram:
#
#   MB102 12V rail (+)  -->  W1209 Relay COM
#   W1209 Relay NO      -->  Peltier RED lead
#   Peltier BLACK lead  -->  MB102 GND rail
#
# Tape the NTC bead to the cold side of the Peltier, right next to
# (NOT inside) the bottle cap. Drop ONE drop of water into the cap.
# Make sure the W1209 board is mounted ABOVE the cold plate, off to
# the side - condensation will drip and the screw terminals must stay
# dry.
#
# Power on. Expected behaviour with a healthy 12V 6A supply:
#
#   t=0s    Display "22", relay clicks closed, fan spins, Peltier on.
#   t=20s   Display "12", cold plate already cold to touch.
#   t=60s   Display "2", you can see frost forming around the cap.
#   t=120s  Display "-2", RELAY CLICKS OPEN, Peltier off, fan still on.
#   t=150s  Pop the bottle cap off - tiny ice disc falls out.
#
# Real-world is 2-3 minutes to first ice. If you are still at +5 C
# after 4 minutes, your hot-side thermal contact is poor (re-paste)
# or your wall-wart cannot sustain the current (check the rating).
#
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# MULTIMETER CHECKPOINTS WHILE RUNNING
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# (Set meter to DC volts, 20V range.)
#
#   CP1: Across MB102 12V rail  -> ~12V steady, both when Peltier is
#                                  on AND after the relay opens. Should
#                                  NOT sag below 11V under load. If it
#                                  does, the wall-wart is undersized.
#   CP2: Across W1209 12V in    -> ~12V steady.
#   CP3: Across Peltier leads   -> ~12V while relay is closed, drops
#                                  to ~0V the instant the relay opens.
#   CP4: Across fan leads       -> ~12V the whole time. Fan never stops.
#
# If CP3 stays at 0V from the start: the relay never closed. Check
# P0 = C, not H.
# If CP3 stays at 12V even when display reads -5 C: the relay contacts
# are stuck. Tap the W1209 gently; if still stuck, replace it (the
# contacts pit over time from switching the Peltier's resistive inrush
# - normal end-of-life, not a defect).

echo "Mini Ice-Cube Maker - follow the staged procedure in this file."
echo "Setpoint: -2 C    Mode: C (cooling)    Hysteresis: 2 C    P3: -10"
echo "Power on, watch the display count down, listen for the click."

Used as a 12V splitter: wall-wart into barrel jack, 12V/GND rails feed W1209, fan, and relay COM. Onboard 3.3V/5V regulator switches left OFF - we want raw 12V passthrough
Standalone thermostat: P3=-10, setpoint -2 C, mode C, hysteresis 2; switches the Peltier via its onboard 10A relay (well above the Peltier's ~5A draw)

projects.name: Fog-the-Window Cloud Demo
projects.power_supply: 12V wall-wart powers the TEC1-4905 via the W1209 relay; the same 12V also feeds the 6-24V-to-5V USB buck whose 5V USB output powers the Arduino Uno and the LCD/DHT11 rail.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A jam-jar that grows its own tiny cloud. You breathe into the jar, screw the lid back on, and a cold metal lid (made cold by a black square called a Peltier) makes the warm wet air inside fog up and even drip little dew drops back down. A small screen on the side tells you how warm and wet the air is, and a blue light blinks when the air in the jar is humid enough that fog WOULD form against the cold lid. **Why it is fun**: You are literally building weather in a jar. Clouds happen because warm wet air bumps into cold stuff up in the sky, and you just made that happen on the kitchen table. Race your sibling: who can fog the lid the fastest by huffing into the jar? ## Parts list - 1x Arduino Uno R3 (the brain that reads the DHT11, drives the LCD and blinks the LED) - 1x DHT11 Temperature & Humidity Sensor (taped high on the inside jar wall) - 1x TEC1-4905 Peltier Thermoelectric Cooler (the black cold-plate against the lid) - 1x W1209 Temperature Controller (standalone thermostat that pulses the Peltier ON/OFF) - 1x LCD 1602 with I2C Backpack (shows jar temp, humidity and dew point) - 1x 6-24V to 5V 3A USB Buck Converter (drops 12V to a clean 5V USB for the Arduino) - 1x Breadboard, M-M and F-M jumpers, blue LED, 220R resistor, 10K resistor - 1x 12V 5A wall-wart (must comfortably supply the Peltier's ~3-4A plus the buck's draw) - 1x glass jar with a flat metal lid (household item) - 1x CPU heatsink + 40mm 12V fan (clamped to the HOT side of the Peltier - non-negotiable) - 1x small tube of thermal paste (between Peltier hot side and heatsink) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the power input pin (gives out 5 volts when the Uno is powered) - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. All the "minus" wires meet here - **D2, D8** - digital pins (the ones marked Dx); we use D2 for the temperature sensor and D8 for the LED - **A4, A5** - the two pins used for talking to the LCD screen over a tiny 2-wire chat called I2C - **USB-B** - the big square USB socket where power and code come in
**Heads up: this is a tricky one.** It uses a Peltier cooler that gets cold on one face and hot on the other. The hot side gets REALLY hot. Always have a grown-up nearby, and never touch the hot side. Build it on the bench first, then mount it on the jar.
**Step 1 - Set up the two power paths.** One 12V wall plug does two jobs at once: - 12V wall-wart **+** -> Buck Converter **IN+** AND W1209 **+12V** pin (both at the same time) - 12V wall-wart **-** -> Buck Converter **IN-** AND W1209 **GND** pin (both at the same time) - Buck Converter **USB OUT** -> short USB-A-to-USB-B cable -> Arduino Uno **USB-B** socket The little buck converter is a voltage shrinker. It takes the 12V from the wall and squeezes it down to 5V so the Arduino is happy. The same 12V (full strength) feeds the W1209 cooler controller, because the cooler needs the big voltage. **Why this matters:** the cooler pulls a lot of current. We do NOT want all that current sneaking through the Arduino. Keep the cooler power and the Arduino power on separate wires that only meet at ground.
**Step 2 - Plug in the breadboard.** The breadboard has two long strips down each side - the long red strip and the long blue strip. We will call these the power strips. - Arduino **5V** pin -> top red power strip (the +5V line) - Arduino **GND** pin -> top blue power strip (the 0V line) - Use one short jumper to link the top red strip to the bottom red strip - Use one short jumper to link the top blue strip to the bottom blue strip Now both sides of the breadboard have 5V and 0V everywhere. That makes it easy to grab power for any part.
**Step 3 - Add the DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor.**
Push the DHT11 into the breadboard so its three pins land in rows 3, 4, and 5 on column E. - DHT11 **VCC** (power input) at E3 -> red strip with a short male-male wire - DHT11 **DATA** at E4 -> Arduino **D2** with a male-male wire - DHT11 **GND** (0V) at E5 -> blue strip with a short male-male wire This little blue brick measures the air temperature and how wet the air feels (humidity). The code uses both to work out the dew point - the temperature at which the air gives up its water and makes fog.
**Step 4 - Add the 10K pull-up resistor (most likely you can skip this).** The plan says to add a 10K resistor between the DHT11 DATA pin and 5V (row B4 to the red strip). BUT - most 3-pin DHT11 boards already have this resistor built in. Look at the back: if you see a tiny black part marked "103" or "10K" near the pins, you already have it. Skip the extra one. **Why this matters:** the DATA wire needs to be gently held at 5V when nothing is talking. The 10K resistor is the gentle hand. Without it the Arduino sees random nonsense.
**Step 5 - Add the LCD 1602 screen with I2C backpack.** The screen has a little board glued to the back with only 4 pins. That little board is the I2C backpack - it lets the Arduino talk to the screen using just 2 wires instead of 16. Use female-to-male wires (the colored ones with a sock on one end and a pin on the other). Plug the sock onto the screen pins and the pin into the breadboard at rows 10 to 13. - LCD **GND** (0V) at E10 -> blue strip - LCD **VCC** (power input, 5V) at E11 -> red strip - LCD **SDA** at E12 -> Arduino **A4** - LCD **SCL** at E13 -> Arduino **A5** Turn the little blue screw on the back of the backpack if the screen looks blank when powered - it sets how bright the letters look.
**Step 6 - Add the blue LED with its 220R resistor.**
The LED has a long leg and a short leg. The long leg is the + side. The short leg is the - side. - Arduino **D8** -> row J20 on the breadboard (use a male-male jumper) - 220R resistor: one end at F20, the other end at F23 - LED long leg at F24 - LED short leg at F25 - Short wire from J25 to the blue power strip (0V) So the current flows: D8 -> resistor -> LED long leg -> LED short leg -> ground. **Why this matters:** an LED is greedy. If you plug it straight into 5V it drinks too much electricity and burns out in a flash. The 220R resistor is a tiny speed bump that slows the current down to a safe sip. When the code thinks the air is sticky enough to make fog (dew point at or above 10C AND humidity at or above 70%) the LED blinks. That is your "we should be making fog" signal.
**Step 7 - Wire up the W1209 cooler controller.** The W1209 is a tiny thermostat with a built-in switch (called a relay). It checks the temperature of its little probe wire, and clicks the switch on or off to keep things in a target range. This step is not on the breadboard - the W1209 sits beside it with its own wires. - W1209 **+12V** -> 12V wall-wart + (already done in Step 1) - W1209 **GND** -> 12V wall-wart - (already done in Step 1) - W1209 **NTC** probe (the little metal bead on a wire) -> taped to the cold side of the Peltier, or to the metal jar lid - W1209 **K0** and **K1** screw terminals -> these are the relay switch. The Peltier's + power wire goes through these (see next step) After you power it up, hold the SET button to set the target. Set "ON at 5C" and "OFF at 8C". The W1209 will click the cooler on and off to hold the lid in that sweet spot where fog forms.
**Step 8 - Wire up the Peltier cooler. STOP and read before you do this one.** The Peltier is a flat white square with two wires. One face gets cold, the other face gets hot. **Before you connect any wires:** 1. Smear a thin layer of thermal paste on the HOT face 2. Press a metal heatsink (the finned aluminium block) onto the hot face 3. Stick the 40mm fan onto the heatsink with the air blowing AWAY from the jar 4. The cold face will press against the metal lid of the jar (a bit of paste here too is good) If you skip the heatsink and fan, the Peltier cooks itself in under a minute and can burn a finger. No heatsink = no power, ever. Now the wiring: - 12V wall-wart **+** -> W1209 **K1** screw terminal - W1209 **K0** screw terminal -> Peltier **+** wire (red) - Peltier **-** wire (black) -> 12V wall-wart **-** - 40mm fan **+** -> 12V wall-wart **+** (fan runs all the time, that is fine) - 40mm fan **-** -> 12V wall-wart **-** The Peltier's red wire only sees power when the W1209 clicks its relay closed. That keeps the lid from getting too cold.
**Step 9 - The one-spot ground rule.** The Peltier pulls a fat slug of electricity. If that current sneaks through the Arduino's wires it makes the temperature readings jump around like crazy. So all the "minus" wires (Arduino GND, buck converter GND, W1209 GND, wall-wart minus) should meet at ONE single spot - the blue power strip on the breadboard or a single screw point. Do not run ground in a chain. This is called a star ground. Think of it like a family meeting: everyone walks to the same spot to chat, instead of whispering through a long line of people.
**Final check before plugging in the 12V:** - Heatsink and fan on the HOT side of the Peltier? Yes. - W1209 probe touching the lid or cold side? Yes. - Star ground at one point? Yes. - LCD wires at A4 and A5? Yes. - DHT11 DATA at D2? Yes. - LED long leg toward D8 (through the resistor), short leg toward ground? Yes. Now plug in the 12V. The LCD should glow, the fan should spin, and within a minute the lid should feel cool. Breathe gently on the jar - fog forms when your warm wet breath hits the cold lid. The blue LED will blink when the conditions are right. ## Flash it and run it 1. With the 12V wall-wart UNPLUGGED, build the Arduino-side wiring (DHT11, LCD, LED) on the breadboard. 2. Plug the Arduino Uno into your laptop USB. Open Arduino IDE. 3. Tools -> Board -> "Arduino Uno". Tools -> Port -> the new COM port. 4. Sketch -> Include Library -> Manage Libraries. Install "DHT sensor library" by Adafruit and "LiquidCrystal I2C" by Frank de Brabander. 5. Paste the sketch, click Upload. The LCD should immediately show "Cloud Demo" then start printing temp / humidity / dew point. 6. Unplug the laptop USB. Wire the 12V rail to the W1209 +12V and the buck IN+. Wire the buck's USB OUT to the Arduino USB-B. Wire the W1209 relay contacts into the Peltier's + lead. 7. Apply thermal paste between the Peltier HOT side and the heatsink, clamp the fan on, wire the fan to the 12V rail. Put the COLD side flat against the metal jar lid. 8. Plug in the 12V wall-wart. Buck powers the Arduino (LCD lights up). W1209 powers on, shows the lid temperature. 9. Set the W1209 setpoint: press SET, dial down to about 5C, press SET again. Now the lid will get cold and you should see frost / dew start to form. 10. Breathe a big warm breath into the jar, screw the lid on. Watch the inside of the lid fog up and drops form. Blue LED blinks when dew point + humidity say fog is likely. Common gotchas: - HOT side gets HOT fast. If no heatsink + fan, stop immediately. - DHT11 hates condensation directly on the sensor. Tape it high up on the jar wall, not on the lid. - If the wall-wart sags when the Peltier kicks in, the buck's 5V will dip and the Arduino can brown-out and reboot. Use at least a 5A 12V supply. - If the W1209 shows "LLL" or "HHH", its NTC probe is not connected. - If the LCD stays blank, try I2C address 0x3F in the sketch instead of 0x27. ## Talking points - "What is humidity?" Tiny invisible water in the air. Your breath has a LOT of it. - "Why does breath fog the lid?" Warm air can carry lots of invisible water. When that warm air touches the cold lid, it can no longer hold all the water, so the water becomes visible droplets - fog. - "That same thing makes real clouds!" Warm air rises, hits cold high-up air, and the water it was carrying turns into a cloud. - "What is the dew point?" The exact temperature at which the air gives up its water. We can see ours on the LCD. - "Why does the LED not actually know the lid is cold?" Good catch. The Arduino can only read the air. The lid is read by the W1209's own probe. The LED is really saying: 'IF the lid is around 5-8C like the W1209 is trying to hold it, fog should form RIGHT NOW.' ## Things to change once it works - Add a thermistor on an Arduino analog pin reading the lid directly, so the LED only blinks when both the air is wet AND the lid is actually cold. - Add a second LED that lights only when humidity is above 80% AND dew point is above 12C - "perfect cloud" indicator. - Log temp / humidity / dew point to the serial monitor over time and plot it. - Try a colored LED ring around the jar so the cloud is lit dramatically. - Use a piece of black card behind the jar - the cloud is way more visible against black. - Swap the DHT11 for a BMP280 + DHT22 combo to add pressure and chase real dew-point math. ## Why this is interesting You just built a working model of how clouds form. The same physics happens in every thunderstorm: warm wet air rises, meets cold air, and condenses into water droplets. The Peltier is doing the job that altitude does in real weather. And you got to read live numbers off the air with the DHT11 and watch a relay (the W1209) act like an automatic thermostat - the same kind of feedback control that keeps your fridge cold. Notice the build has TWO power domains that share only ground: the noisy high-current Peltier loop sits on 12V, and the quiet Arduino logic sits on 5V from the buck. Splitting them like this is how grown-up electronics keep their sensors from being lied to by their own motors and heaters.

projects.name: Twin-Knob Web Mixer
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the NodeMCU V3 (5V via the micro-USB port on the I/O Shield carrier)
projects.description:
**What it is**: A double-stacked knob that controls coloured LEDs on the breadboard AND a live web page on your phone. Turn the LEFT half of the knob and the LEDs smoothly get brighter or dimmer (and a bar on the phone follows it). Turn the RIGHT half of the knob past the middle and the LEDs jump to the next colour - Red, Green, Blue, White, and back to Red again. **Why it is fun**: Your phone becomes the dashboard, the breadboard is the disco. Hand the phone to a sister, twist one knob, and watch her chase the brightness bar while the LEDs change colour on command. No app to install - the chip itself serves the web page. ## Parts list - NodeMCU V3 (ESP8266, CH340G) - the WiFi brain - NodeMCU V3 I/O Shield - screw-terminal breakout (no soldering) - WH148 10K Stereo Potentiometer (B10K) - the twin-knob; one shaft, two pots inside (we call them "Left gang" and "Right gang") - 3 x 5mm LEDs (Red, Green, Blue) acting as a DIY RGB cluster - 3 x 220R resistors (one per LED leg) - Breadboard, M-M and F-M jumper wires - A USB cable to the laptop ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the NodeMCU V3 board and its I/O Shield:** - **NodeMCU V3** - the little blue board with the silver metal box (that is the WiFi chip). It has a micro-USB port on one end. - **I/O Shield** - the bigger board the NodeMCU plugs into. It turns each pin into a 3-screw column you can clamp wires into. No soldering needed. - **D0 to D8** - the labels printed on the board for the digital pins. Heads up: the names do NOT match the GPIO numbers in the code. We will tell you exactly which D-label to use for each wire. - **A0** - the only analog input pin. It reads a voltage between 0V and about 3.3V and turns it into a number. We use it to read one knob. - **3V3** - the "power input" for things that must run on 3.3 volts (like our knobs). - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every wire that goes out has to come back here.
**Step 1 - Plug the NodeMCU into the I/O Shield, then plug in USB.** - Push the NodeMCU V3 down onto the I/O Shield. The micro-USB port on the NodeMCU should face out off the edge of the shield, not into it. - Plug a USB cable from your laptop into the micro-USB port on the NodeMCU (not into the shield). That is how the board gets its 5V power and how the code gets uploaded. This is the only power the project needs. The shield then makes the 3.3V we will use for the knobs.
**Step 2 - Set up the breadboard power strips.** The long red and blue strips running down each side of the breadboard are called the power strips. We use the bottom strips for 3.3V and ground for the knobs, and the top blue strip for ground for the LEDs. Use female-to-male jumper wires (one end has a hole, the other end is a pin) to connect the I/O Shield screw terminals to the breadboard: - I/O Shield **3V3** screw terminal -> the bottom red strip on the breadboard. - I/O Shield **GND** screw terminal -> the bottom blue strip on the breadboard. - I/O Shield **GND** screw terminal (a second wire from the same GND) -> the top blue strip on the breadboard. The pin end goes into the breadboard. The hole end clamps under the screw terminal on the shield - loosen the screw, push the wire in, tighten the screw. **Why this matters:** the knobs need 3.3V, not 5V. The chip inside the NodeMCU can only handle 3.3V on its pins. If we used 5V, we could damage A0. Always pull from the **3V3** terminal for anything that touches a pin.
**Step 3 - Plant the red LED and its resistor.**
LEDs have two legs. The **long leg** is the plus side. The **short leg** is the minus side (you can also feel a flat spot on that side of the plastic dome). - Red LED long leg -> hole **E3**. - Red LED short leg -> hole **E4**. - 220R resistor (the small striped one) -> one leg in **A3**, other leg in **A7**. Resistors do not have a plus or minus side, so either way is fine. - Male-to-male jumper wire from **E4** -> the top blue strip (ground). - Male-to-male jumper wire from **A7** -> the I/O Shield **D1** screw terminal. **Why the resistor:** the LED is greedy. Without a resistor it would try to pull too much current and burn itself out in a flash. The 220R resistor slows that current down to a safe amount. Always pair every LED with a resistor.
**Step 4 - Plant the green LED and its resistor.** The green LED has no photo on file, but it looks the same as the red one with a green dome. Same long leg / short leg rule. - Green LED long leg -> hole **E9**. - Green LED short leg -> hole **E10**. - 220R resistor -> one leg in **A9**, other leg in **A13**. - Male-to-male jumper wire from **E10** -> the top blue strip (ground). - Male-to-male jumper wire from **A13** -> the I/O Shield **D2** screw terminal.
**Step 5 - Plant the blue LED and its resistor.** The blue LED also has no photo on file - same shape, blue dome. - Blue LED long leg -> hole **E15**. - Blue LED short leg -> hole **E16**. - 220R resistor -> one leg in **A15**, other leg in **A19**. - Male-to-male jumper wire from **E16** -> the top blue strip (ground). - Male-to-male jumper wire from **A19** -> the I/O Shield **D5** screw terminal. **Why D5 and not D3 for blue:** the pin marked **D3** on this board is a special "boot pin." If anything pulls it low when the board turns on, the board gets stuck and will not start your sketch. **D5** has none of that drama, so it is the safer choice for our third LED.
**Step 6 - Plant the twin-knob potentiometer.** This part is one shaft with two knobs inside it. It has 6 pins in two rows of 3. The front row of 3 is the "left knob" and the back row of 3 is the "right knob." They turn at the same time because they share the same shaft, but they each give their own signal. Push the part into the breadboard so the pins land like this (one row in column G, around rows 22-28): Front row (left knob): - One outer pin in **G22**. - Middle pin (the wiper, the part that moves) in **G23**. - Other outer pin in **G24**. Back row (right knob): - One outer pin in **G26**. - Middle pin (the wiper) in **G27**. - Other outer pin in **G28**. Now connect the knob power and signals with male-to-male jumper wires: - **G22** -> the bottom red strip (3.3V). - **G24** -> the bottom blue strip (ground). - **G26** -> the bottom red strip (3.3V). - **G28** -> the bottom blue strip (ground). - **H23** -> the I/O Shield **A0** screw terminal. (This is the LEFT knob's signal.) - **H27** -> the I/O Shield **D7** screw terminal. (This is the RIGHT knob's signal.) **Why both knobs are not on A0:** the NodeMCU only has ONE analog input pin (A0), so only one knob can give a smooth range of numbers. The left knob gets that smooth job. The right knob's signal goes to a regular digital pin (**D7**), which can only tell us "high" or "low." So we use it like a step switch: each time you turn past the middle, the code jumps to the next colour mode.
**Step 7 - Power on and tune.** Once everything is wired, plug the USB cable into your laptop. The NodeMCU's blue light should blink, and the I/O Shield should feel warm but not hot. Open the web page from the sketch, then turn the left knob - the LEFT bar on the page should follow it smoothly, and the brightness of the active LED should change. Turn the right knob past its middle a few times - the RIGHT bar should jump between Red, Green, Blue, and White modes. If a wire pops out of a screw terminal, that is the most common bug. Wiggle each wire gently. If it slides, loosen the screw, push it back in firmly, and tighten again. ## Flash it and run it 1. Plug the NodeMCU V3 into the I/O Shield. Plug the micro-USB into your laptop. 2. Open Arduino IDE. File -> Preferences -> Additional Board Manager URLs: `http://arduino.esp8266.com/stable/package_esp8266com_index.json` 3. Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager -> install "esp8266 by ESP8266 Community". 4. Tools -> Board -> "NodeMCU 1.0 (ESP-12E Module)". Tools -> Port -> the new COM port that appeared. 5. Edit the sketch: SSID is already "GeeFam", set the password where it says `PASSWORD_HERE`. 6. Click Upload. When you see "Done uploading", open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud and watch for the IP address it prints. 7. Open that IP address in your phone's browser (must be on GeeFam WiFi). You should see a brightness bar that follows the left knob, a step indicator that shows the colour name, and a colour swatch. **Common gotchas** - Wrong port? Install the CH340G driver - the V3 uses that chip, not the original CP2102. - LEFT bar stuck at 0 or 1023, never moves? The LEFT pot wiper isn't wired to A0. Triple-check the middle pin of the left row. - RIGHT bar / colour name never changes? Right pot wiper isn't on D7, OR the right gang's outer pins are not connected to 3V3 AND GND (you need both - if only one is wired, the wiper voltage will be stuck and never cross the threshold). Note that the RIGHT bar is a step indicator, not a smooth reading - it only moves when you turn the right knob past its middle. - LEDs glow dim with knob fully on? Resistor too high - you used 470R or 1K instead of 220R. Swap them. - All three LEDs come on at once and stay on - you wired the LED short legs to 3V3 by mistake. Flip them so the short legs go to GND. - Board refuses to boot - just blinks, or Serial Monitor keeps resetting? Unplug whatever you have on D3 and try again. D3 is a boot-strap pin and it does not like extra circuitry at power-on. ## Talking points - "One shaft, two pots" - that's what stereo means. Same idea in old hi-fi amplifiers where one knob controlled both speakers at once. - PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) is how we dim LEDs without a dimmer chip - we blink them too fast to see and just change how long they're on for. - The ESP8266 has just ONE real analog input. Real engineers hit this wall and solve it with a multiplexer chip (like a CD4051) that lets one ADC pin read many sources in turn. We picked a simpler honest workaround instead: read the second gang as a digital signal that crosses HIGH past the middle. - The web page is served from the chip itself - no Internet needed once you're on the WiFi. The chip is the web server. ## Things to change once it works - Replace the digital-step right-knob trick with a CD4051 8-channel analog multiplexer. That lets you read both gangs as smooth analog values from the same A0 pin, and the RIGHT bar becomes a smooth reading instead of a step indicator. - Replace the three LEDs with a real common-cathode RGB LED and only use three resistors total - same wiring, tidier breadboard. - Make the web page remember the last colour mode in the browser's localStorage so it reloads where you left off. - Stream the values out as MQTT instead of a web page so Home Assistant can react. - Or simplify the whole thing: ditch the stereo pot, use a single 10K pot on A0 for hue, and add a momentary tactile button on D6 for "next mode". You get smooth-turn behaviour with one ADC and no boot-strap gotchas. ## Why this is interesting This is the smallest possible "phone is the display" project. You stop needing an LCD or an OLED - the phone every kid already has becomes the dashboard. You also meet a real engineering wall (one ADC, two things you want to read) and pick a deliberate workaround instead of pretending the problem isn't there. Once you've seen a knob update a bar on a phone in real time, every WiFi-MCU project after this feels obvious.

projects.name: VU Meter Stereo Volume Display
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the Uno (5V); the Uno's 5V pin feeds the breadboard rails for the pot and LCD - single supply, ratiometric ADC.
projects.description:
**What it is**: One knob, two bars. You twist a single chunky knob and two glowing bars on a little screen - one labelled L and one labelled R - grow longer or shorter together. It looks exactly like the volume meters on a big stereo. **Why it is fun**: Here is the magic trick: the two bars almost never match perfectly. As you turn the knob slowly you can see the L bar leap ahead of the R bar by a tiny bit, then R catches up, then they drift apart again. You just caught a real factory imperfection live on screen. Bet your sibling they cannot make both bars line up exactly - they will be twisting forever. ## Parts list - Arduino Uno R3 (the brain that reads the knob and writes to the screen, powered from your laptop's USB cable) - WH148 10K Stereo Potentiometer B10K (one shaft, two wipers inside - that is the whole trick) - LCD 1602 with I2C backpack (the 16-character, 2-line screen that draws the bars) - 400-point breadboard - M-M jumper wires for the pot legs and rails, F-M jumpers for the LCD backpack header - USB-B cable from the Uno to your laptop (powers everything, flashes the sketch, runs the serial monitor) ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the pin that gives back 5 volts of power from the USB cable. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. The "return" path for electricity. - **A0, A1, A4, A5** - analog input pins. A0 and A1 measure voltage (good for reading a knob). A4 is SDA and A5 is SCL - those two are the talk-and-listen wires for the LCD. - **D0-D13** - digital pins. We do not use these in this project, but you will see them along the top edge. - **USB-B port** - the big square socket the laptop cable plugs into.
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard power strips.** The breadboard has two long red and blue strips down the sides. Those long strips are called the power strips (one strip is for 5V, the other is for ground/0V). - Take one male-to-male jumper wire (red is nice for power) and run it from the Arduino pin marked **5V** to the red strip at the top of the breadboard. - Take another male-to-male jumper (black or blue for ground) and run it from the Arduino pin marked **GND** to the blue strip at the top of the breadboard. - Also run a red wire from the top red strip down to the bottom red strip, and a black wire from the top blue strip down to the bottom blue strip. Now both halves of the board have power. This gives you 5V and 0V available all along both sides of the board. It is way easier than running a separate wire from the Arduino for every part.
**Step 2 - Plug in the stereo knob (potentiometer).** The WH148 is one knob that has TWO sets of three pins underneath (six total in two rows of three). One row controls the left channel, the other row controls the right channel. That is what "stereo" means - one knob, two outputs. For each row of three pins: - The outer two pins are the ends of the resistor track. - The middle pin is the wiper - it moves as you turn the knob and is what we read. Push the knob into the breadboard so the pins land in rows 8, 10, and 12. Left row (the L gang): - Pin in hole A8 (one end) - this is the 5V end. - Pin in hole A10 (the middle/wiper) - this is the signal we read. - Pin in hole A12 (the other end) - this is the ground end. Right row (the R gang): - Pin in hole E8 - 5V end. - Pin in hole E10 - wiper. - Pin in hole E12 - ground end. Now wire each row: - Red male-to-male jumper from the top red strip to hole **A8** (left gang, 5V end). - Black male-to-male jumper from the top blue strip to hole **A12** (left gang, ground end). - Red male-to-male jumper from the top red strip to hole **E8** (right gang, 5V end). - Black male-to-male jumper from the top blue strip to hole **E12** (right gang, ground end). - Male-to-male jumper from hole **A10** to the Arduino pin marked **A0** (left wiper goes to A0). - Male-to-male jumper from hole **E10** to the Arduino pin marked **A1** (right wiper goes to A1). **Important:** wire BOTH rows the same way around - both with 5V on the same side. If you flip one row backwards, that channel will go DOWN when you turn the knob up, and the other channel will go up. Same direction = both bars climb together. **Why this matters:** the potentiometer is a tiny adjustable voltage maker. Turn the knob and the voltage on the middle (wiper) pin slides smoothly from 0V to 5V. The Arduino measures that voltage and turns it into a number from 0 to 1023, which we use to draw the bar height on the LCD.
**Step 3 - Plug in the LCD screen.** This LCD has a little black board soldered to the back of it called an I2C backpack. Without it, the LCD would need 16 wires. With it, only 4. Big win. The four pins on the backpack are labelled **VCC**, **GND**, **SDA**, **SCL**. Use four female-to-male (F-M) jumpers - the female end clips onto the LCD pin, the male end pushes into the breadboard or the Arduino. - LCD **VCC** (power input, 5V) -> top red power strip on the breadboard. We picked hole J20 for tidiness, but any red-strip hole works. - LCD **GND** (the 0V side, ground) -> top blue power strip. We used hole J22. - LCD **SDA** (the "data" wire) -> Arduino pin **A4**. We used hole J24 as a stopover, then a male-to-male from J24 over to A4. - LCD **SCL** (the "clock" wire) -> Arduino pin **A5**. We used hole J26 as a stopover, then a male-to-male from J26 over to A5. **Why this matters:** SDA and SCL are a special pair of wires called I2C. The Arduino sends out a steady tick-tock on SCL while squirting message bits down SDA. The backpack listens for those messages and figures out which dots to light up on the screen. That is how 4 wires can drive a 16-letters-by-2-rows display.
**Step 4 - Plug in the USB cable and power up.** Connect the USB-B end of the cable to the Arduino's big square socket, and the other end to your laptop. The Arduino's "ON" LED should light up, and after a second the LCD backlight should glow. That is it. One USB cable powers everything - the Arduino, the LCD, and the knob - so the voltage the Arduino is measuring (5V from USB) is the same voltage feeding the knob. That matters because it keeps the readings steady: if the supply wobbles a little, the knob's output wobbles with it, and the math cancels out.
**Step 5 - First-power check.** - Look at the LCD. If you see two rows of faint white squares, the screen has power but the code is not running yet - that is normal before you upload. - If the screen is totally blank but the backlight is on, twist the tiny blue screw on the back of the backpack (the contrast pot) with a small screwdriver until the squares appear. - If nothing lights up at all, unplug fast and check that 5V and GND are not swapped - this is a tricky one because the LCD will tolerate a quick reverse but the knob and Arduino do not love it. Once the squares show up, you are ready to upload the code and turn the knob. ## Flash it and run it 1. Open the Arduino IDE. **Tools -> Board -> Arduino Uno**. **Tools -> Port -> the COM port the Uno is on.** 2. **Sketch -> Include Library -> Manage Libraries...** and install **LiquidCrystal I2C** by Frank de Brabander (or marcoschwartz). This is the one that uses the LiquidCrystal_I2C constructor. 3. Paste in the sketch, hit Upload. 4. The LCD backlight should turn on and you should see L: and R: with two bars. 5. Twist the knob. Both bars should grow together. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor at 115200** and watch the `diff` value: that is the live channel mismatch in ADC counts. Common gotchas: - **Blank screen with backlight on**: the LCD I2C address is wrong. The two common addresses are 0x27 and 0x3F. Change the `0x27` in the sketch to `0x3F` and re-upload. - **One bar moves backwards**: you wired one gang of the pot the opposite way round. Swap the two outer pins on that gang. - **One bar pegs at full and never moves**: a wiper pin is shorted to 5V (or GND) instead of the A0 / A1 input. Check that the MIDDLE pin of each gang goes to the analog pin, not an outer pin. - **Screen shows weird characters**: you forgot to install the LiquidCrystal I2C library, or you installed a different one. Make sure the constructor in the sketch matches the library. - **Both bars wiggle at rest**: very long jumpers between Uno 5V and the pot can pick up noise. Keep those leads short, or print the raw values on the serial monitor to see how much wiggle there really is - usually a count or two, which the moving-average filter in the sketch already hides. ## Talking points - One knob, two signals. Inside the WH148 are two completely separate resistor tracks stacked back to back, sharing the same shaft. That is what "stereo pot" means. - Why audiophiles care: in a real amplifier this same knob sets your left and right speaker volume. If the two gangs mismatch, one ear gets louder than the other and the music feels lopsided. - The Uno's ADC reads 0 to 1023 (10 bits). At any one instant the L and R readings are usually within a few counts of each other - but not zero. - Ratiometric reading: by powering the pot's outer pins from the same 5V the Uno measures against, the answer stays correct even if that 5V wobbles a bit. The pot just divides whatever voltage you give it, and the ADC compares against that same voltage. - The diff value on the serial monitor will jump much higher near the very ends of the travel. That is because the pot's track is hand-deposited carbon and it is not perfectly uniform. ## Things to change once it works - Hold a "balance" mode: press a button to freeze the current reading and show the mismatch as a number in the middle of the screen. - Make the LCD beep (add a small piezo) when the two channels are within 1 count of each other - a "matched!" tone. - Add a piezo buzzer and play a tone whose pitch follows the L channel - now you have a theremin you can SEE. - Swap the pot for two single-gang pots side-by-side and you have a stereo balance control - now you have to keep two knobs matched by hand. - Plot the diff value live: open the Arduino IDE's **Serial Plotter** instead of Serial Monitor to see the mismatch as a wiggly line. ## Why this is interesting This project makes an invisible analogue imperfection visible. The "channel mismatch" you can see on the LCD is the same physical reason expensive hi-fi amplifiers use stepped attenuators (precision resistor networks) instead of a normal pot - the matching matters when the bars are music levels going to your ears. It is also a tidy demo of how a microcontroller turns a continuous voltage into a discrete number (a ratiometric ADC reading), and how custom LCD characters let a 16x2 character display act as a 65-pixel-wide graphics canvas.
