projects.name: Tempo + Pitch Twin-Track Visual Sequencer
projects.power_supply: USB cable from laptop to the Arduino Uno (5V via USB-B); the Uno's onboard 5V rail feeds the breadboard, pot, LED, and 7-seg display.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little light show you control with one knob. Twist the knob and a red light flashes faster AND brighter at the same time. A glowing red number next to it counts the flashes 0, 1, 2, 3... up to 7, then starts over. **Why it is fun**: It feels like magic that one twist changes two things at once - how OFTEN the light blinks AND how BRIGHT it gets when it blinks. You can spin it slowly for a sleepy heartbeat glow, or crank it all the way up for a strobe-light dance party. Show your sister, then race her to match the flash speed to a song on the radio. ## Parts list - Arduino Uno R3 (CH340 clone, XL) - WH148 10K Stereo Potentiometer (B10K) (the special twin-gang one) - LED 5mm Red (the "drumbeat" indicator) - 0.56" red 7-segment display (one digit, counts the beats) - 9x 220 ohm resistors (one for each segment line including the dot, plus one for the LED) - Half-size breadboard + jumper wires - USB cable from a laptop to power the Uno ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the power-out pin. It gives back the 5 volts that came in from the USB cable. - **GND** - the 0V side, called "ground". Every part needs a wire back to GND or it will not work. - **A0 to A5** - "analog in" pins. These can read a knob and tell the code a number from 0 to 1023. - **D0 to D13** - "digital" pins. They can be on (5V) or off (0V). The ones with a little squiggle (~) like D3, D5, D6, D9, D10, D11 can also do a fast on-off signal that looks like dimming. - **USB-B** - the big square USB socket. The cable from the laptop plugs in here and powers the whole project.
**Step 0 - Test the 7-segment display BEFORE you wire it. This is the tricky one.** The little red number display can be one of two types: "common cathode" (CC) or "common anode" (CA). The bag does not say which. They look the same but they need opposite wiring AND opposite code. Five-minute test with a 3V coin cell (CR2032) and one 220R resistor: 1. Pick any two pins on the display. Touch the + side of the coin cell through the 220R to one pin, and the - side of the coin cell to the other pin. 2. If a little glow-stripe lights up: the pin on the + side is a segment pin, and the pin on the - side is the COMMON pin. You have a **common cathode (CC)** display. The wiring below is for this type. Good news - keep going. 3. If nothing lights up no matter which two pins you try, flip the cell so the - side goes through the 220R. If a stripe now lights, you have a **common anode (CA)** display. You will need to (a) wire both COM pins to 5V instead of GND, and (b) flip every HIGH and LOW inside the showDigit() and blankDigit() parts of the code. Write "CC" or "CA" on a sticky note and press it onto the display so you do not forget.
**Step 1 - Plant the breadboard and feed it power.** The breadboard has two long red and blue strips down the sides - those are the power strips. The red strip will be 5V (power), the blue strip will be GND (0V). - Jumper wire from the Arduino pin marked **5V** to the top red strip. - Jumper wire from any Arduino pin marked **GND** to the top blue strip. - Plug the USB cable from your laptop into the Arduino's big square USB socket. A green light on the board should come on. This gives the whole breadboard power so every other part has somewhere to grab 5V and GND from.
**Step 2 - Plug in the twin knob (the stereo potentiometer).** This knob has **six** legs on the bottom, not three. It is really two knobs stacked inside one shaft, called Gang A and Gang B. When you turn the shaft, both gangs turn at the same time. That is the whole magic of this project - one knob does two things. Push the knob into row A so the six legs land in holes A2, A3, A4 (Gang A) and A6, A7, A8 (Gang B). - Jumper wire from **B2** to the top red strip (this gives Gang A its 5V end). - Jumper wire from **B4** to the top blue strip (this gives Gang A its GND end). - Jumper wire from **B3** to the Arduino pin marked **A0** (this is the wiper - it reads the knob position for tempo). - Jumper wire from **B6** to the top red strip (this gives Gang B its 5V end). - Jumper wire from **B8** to the top blue strip (this gives Gang B its GND end). - Jumper wire from **B7** to the Arduino pin marked **A1** (this is the wiper - it reads the knob position for brightness). **Why this matters:** Each gang is a little voltage slider. One end is at 5V, the other end is at 0V, and the wiper in the middle picks somewhere in between depending on where the knob is pointed. That in-between voltage is what A0 and A1 read.
**Step 3 - Wire the red LED with its safety resistor.**
Look at the LED. One leg is **longer** than the other - that is the plus side. The shorter leg is the minus side. There is also a tiny flat edge on the plastic rim next to the short leg. - Push the LED's **long leg** into **F11** and the **short leg** into **F12**. - One 220R resistor: bend the legs and push one end into **J11** (same row as the long leg) and the other end into **J14**. - Jumper wire from **F12** (the LED's short leg row) to the bottom blue strip (GND). - Jumper wire from **J14** (the far end of the resistor) to the Arduino pin marked **D10**. **Why this matters:** An LED is greedy - if you connect it straight to 5V it will gulp too much current and pop in a flash of smoke. The 220R resistor sits in front of it like a bouncer and only lets a safe amount through. We chose D10 because it is one of the pins that can do a fast on-off signal, which the eye sees as dimming. That is how the brightness knob fades the LED smoothly.
**Step 4 - Plant the 7-segment display across the gap in the breadboard.** The display has two rows of 5 pins each. Plant it so it straddles the middle gap, with the bottom row of pins in row F (holes F17 to F21) and the top row of pins in row A (holes A17 to A21). The decimal-point dot should be at the bottom-right. The pin map ends up like this: - F17 = segment **e** - F18 = segment **d** - F19 = **COM** (one of the two common pins) - F20 = segment **c** - F21 = segment **dp** (decimal point) - A17 = segment **b** - A18 = segment **a** - A19 = **COM** (the other common pin) - A20 = segment **f** - A21 = segment **g** Now wire the two common pins to GND (because you proved it is CC in Step 0): - Jumper wire from **J19** to the bottom blue strip (GND). - Jumper wire from **B19** to the top blue strip (GND).
**Step 5 - Add one 220R safety resistor in front of every segment.** Each glowing stripe in the display is its own little LED, so each one needs its own 220R bouncer. Plant eight resistors like little arches: - 220R from **C18** to **C25** (this is the resistor for segment a) - 220R from **C17** to **C26** (for segment b) - 220R from **H20** to **H25** (for segment c) - 220R from **H18** to **H26** (for segment d) - 220R from **H17** to **H27** (for segment e) - 220R from **C20** to **C27** (for segment f) - 220R from **C21** to **C28** (for segment g) - 220R from **H21** to **H28** (for the decimal point dp) **Why this matters:** Without these eight resistors, each segment would gulp too much current and either burn out or hurt the Arduino pin behind it. One resistor per segment keeps things safe and even-brightness.
**Step 6 - Connect each segment to its Arduino pin.** Now run a jumper wire from the far end of each resistor (the end away from the display) over to the Arduino: - **C26** to the pin marked **D2** (segment a) - **C25** to the pin marked **D3** (segment b) - **H25** to the pin marked **D4** (segment c) - **H26** to the pin marked **D5** (segment d) - **H27** to the pin marked **D6** (segment e) - **C27** to the pin marked **D7** (segment f) - **C28** to the pin marked **D8** (segment g) - **H28** to the pin marked **D9** (segment dp) Eight wires for eight stripes. Take it slow and check off each one as you go.
**Step 7 - Last check before power on.** Eyes-on check before you push code: - Both power strips fed? (Red strip to Arduino 5V, blue strip to Arduino GND.) - LED long leg goes through a resistor to D10? Short leg goes to GND? - Display's two COM pins both go to GND? (Or both to 5V if your test said CA.) - All eight segment wires land on D2 through D9 in order a, b, c, d, e, f, g, dp? - Knob has six legs in, and each gang has one wire to 5V, one wire to GND, and a wiper wire to A0 or A1? If all yes, plug in the USB cable. The Arduino's green power light should come on. You are ready to flash the code.
## Flash it and run it 1. Open the Arduino IDE. 2. Tools - Board - Arduino AVR Boards - Arduino Uno. 3. Tools - Port - the COM port the Uno shows up on (CH340 clones may need the CH340 driver installed first). 4. Paste in the sketch, click the right-arrow Upload button. 5. Open Tools - Serial Monitor at 9600 baud to see live BPM / brightness / beat numbers. Common gotchas: - LED stays dark? Long leg is the + side and goes to the resistor and D10; short leg goes to GND. Swap if you have it backwards. - 7-segment shows wrong digits or weird patterns? You probably wired common-anode but the code expects common-cathode. Re-do the coin-cell test, move both COM pins to 5V, and swap HIGH for LOW (and LOW for HIGH) inside showDigit() and blankDigit(). - Knob only changes one thing? You wired only one gang of the WH148. Confirm BOTH wiper legs are landing on A0 and A1, and that each gang has its OWN pair of outer legs reaching 5V and GND. - Pot is jumpy at the ends? That is normal for a WH148 - the values 60 BPM and 300 BPM are at the very edges of the rotation. ## Talking points - Why does turning a single shaft change two things? Because inside the WH148 there are TWO totally separate carbon tracks stacked on top of each other - your fingers move both wipers at once. - BPM means "beats per minute". 60 BPM is one beat every second (like a slow heartbeat). 240 BPM is four beats every second (like a fast techno song). - PWM ("pulse-width modulation") is how the Arduino fakes a "half-bright" LED. It actually flicks the LED fully on and off hundreds of times a second; the longer it stays on each cycle, the brighter it looks to your eyes. - analogWrite(pin, 0) is fully off, analogWrite(pin, 255) is full brightness - everything in between is a PWM duty cycle. ## Things to change once it works - Make beat 0 (the downbeat) flash a different LED or twice as bright, so it sounds-er, LOOKS-like a backbeat. - Change the BPM range to 30-600 for crazy speeds. - Skip every other beat (only flash when beatCount is even) to play half-time. - Add a second LED on D11 through its own 220R that flashes on the OFF beats - now you have a stereo light pair. - Read the pots more smoothly by averaging the last 4 readings, so the brightness does not jitter. ## Why this is interesting This is your first taste of "multi-dimensional control" - one physical input driving two independent things. It is the same idea as a video game joystick (one stick = X and Y) or a DJ filter knob (one twist = cutoff frequency and resonance). Once you see how a stereo pot works, you suddenly understand how a guitar's tone-and-volume stacked knob works too.

projects.name: Pocket Peltier Chill Coaster
projects.power_supply: 12V SLA pack (preferred) or fused/BMS-protected 3S LiPo to the W1209 V+ and to the TEC1-4905 + 80mm fan via the W1209's onboard relay; the same 12V also feeds a 6-24V to 5V 3A buck converter that powers a logic-side green status LED only.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little cold plate the size of a drinks coaster. You sit a soda can on top, switch the battery pack on, and the metal under the can gets really cold so the drink stays chilly even on a hot day. **Why it is fun**: Touch it after one minute and it feels like a tiny patch of winter inside the workshop. You can frost up the surface, watch ice crystals form on your finger, and brag that you built a portable fridge that runs from a battery you can carry around. ## Parts list From this inventory (allocated): - TEC1-4905 Peltier Thermoelectric Cooler (the cold/hot square) - W1209 Temperature Controller (thermostat brain with display, 10A onboard relay) - 6-24V to 5V 3A USB Buck Converter (drops 12V to 5V for a status LED only - NOT for the Peltier rail) - LED 5mm Green + 220R resistor (a "5V rail is alive" indicator) - Breadboard + jumper wires for the low-current control wiring User-supplied hardware (NOT in the inventory - source these separately): - 12V SLA pack (recommended) OR a 3S LiPo pack WITH integrated BMS and a 5A inline fuse - An extruded finned aluminium heatsink at least 50 x 50 x 20 mm - An 80 mm or 120 mm 12V case fan (a 40 mm fan is TOO SMALL - see "Wiring notes" below) - A small tube of thermal paste - A pair of 18 AWG (or thicker) hookup wires for the Peltier + fan loop - A 5A inline fuse holder + 5A fast-blow fuse if running from LiPo - A metal saucer (the cold plate will sweat) ## Wiring notes This build has no Arduino or ESP32. The brain is a little blue board called the **W1209 Temperature Controller**. It already knows how to read a temperature probe, show a number on its red display, and switch a relay on and off. You just have to wire it up and tell it what temperature you want. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the W1209 board:** - **V+ / V-** - the two power-input screw terminals. V+ is 12V in, V- is the 0V side (also called GND, short for "ground"). - **NTC** - the little waterproof temperature probe with two wires that plugs into the small 2-pin socket. - **COM / NO / NC** - the three relay screw terminals. COM is "common" (always connected). NO is "normally open" - it joins to COM only when the relay clicks on. NC is "normally closed" - we do not use it here. - **SET button** - the only programming button. Hold it down to enter the menu. - **Relay** - the little black box on the board that clicks. Think of it as a remote-controlled switch the W1209 flips when it is too warm.
**Step 1 - Bolt the Peltier to its heatsink BEFORE you wire anything.** The **TEC1-4905 Peltier** is a flat white ceramic tile with a red wire and a black wire. One side gets cold, the other side gets HOT - really hot. If the hot side cannot get rid of its heat, the Peltier will cook itself in under a minute and be ruined. So before you plug in any battery: - Put a thin smear of thermal paste on the hot side of the Peltier (the side with the writing usually faces cold; if unsure, test briefly at low voltage and feel which side warms up). - Press the hot side flat against a chunky aluminium heatsink, at least 50 x 50 x 20 mm with fins. - Bolt or clamp them tight. - Mount an **80 mm 12V fan** blowing onto those fins. A small 40 mm fan is NOT enough - the Peltier dumps about 50-60 W of waste heat and a tiny fan cannot move that much air. - On the COLD side, press a small flat aluminium plate that your drink can will sit on. Slip the W1209's NTC probe between the Peltier cold side and that plate so it can feel how cold things are getting. Why this matters: a Peltier is not like a normal cooler. It pumps heat from one side to the other. If the hot side cannot let go of its heat, both sides just get hotter and hotter until the tile dies. The heatsink and fan are not optional - they are the whole reason the cold side stays cold.
**Step 2 - Wire 12V into the W1209's power terminals.** The W1209 has three screw terminals on one edge for power. Find the ones marked **V+** and **V-**. - Battery **12V+** -> W1209 **V+** screw terminal. - Battery **GND** (0V) -> W1209 **V-** screw terminal. Now the W1209 has power and its little red display will light up the moment you connect the battery (do not connect the battery yet - we are still wiring).
**Step 3 - Send 12V into the relay's COM terminal too.** The other three screw terminals on the W1209 (usually on the opposite side) are the relay terminals: **COM**, **NO**, **NC**. We are using COM and NO. NC stays empty. - Battery **12V+** -> W1209 relay **COM** screw terminal. So the same battery 12V+ wire actually goes to TWO places on the W1209: V+ (to power the brain) AND COM (so the relay has 12V ready to switch). Use a Y-splice or a small terminal block - do not push two thick wires into one screw. Why this matters: the relay is just a switch. COM is the "input" side of the switch. We give it 12V so that whenever the W1209 closes the relay, that 12V can flow out through NO to the Peltier and fan.
**Step 4 - Wire the relay output to the Peltier and fan.** When the W1209 decides it is too warm, it clicks the relay, and 12V flows from COM out through NO. That output needs to feed both the Peltier and the 80mm fan in parallel. - W1209 relay **NO** screw terminal -> TEC1-4905 **red** (+) wire AND 80mm fan **red** (+) wire (joined together). - Battery **GND** -> TEC1-4905 **black** (-) wire AND 80mm fan **black** (-) wire (joined together). Two important rules for this loop: - Use **thick wire** (18 AWG hookup wire is good). This loop carries about 4 amps, which is a lot. - This loop does NOT go on the breadboard. Wire it directly between the battery, the W1209 screw terminals, the Peltier, and the fan - either screwed into terminal blocks or twisted firmly together. A breadboard or DuPont jumper cannot safely carry 4 amps and will get warm and unreliable. Why this matters: the fan must turn on at the exact same time as the Peltier. If the Peltier turns on without the fan, the hot side has nowhere to dump its heat. Wiring them to the same NO terminal guarantees they always run together.
**Step 5 - Place the NTC temperature probe.** The little black probe on the end of the W1209's NTC cable is what tells the W1209 how cold things are. Where you put it matters a lot. - Sandwich the probe **between the Peltier cold side and the aluminium top plate** that the can sits on. - A dab of thermal paste here helps too. - Tape or clamp it so it cannot slip out. If the probe dangles in the air, the W1209 will read room temperature and never turn off, and your Peltier will freeze solid and waste battery.
**Step 6 - Add the buck converter for the 5V status light.** The **6-24V to 5V buck converter** is a tiny board with an input side (IN+ / IN-) and a USB-A socket on the output side. It takes our 12V battery and turns it into a clean 5V to power a small status LED on the breadboard. - Battery **12V+** -> Buck converter **IN+**. - Battery **GND** -> Buck converter **IN-**. The buck converter's 5V comes out of its USB-A socket. Grab a short USB cable you do not mind cutting, snip the small end off, and find the **red** wire (that is 5V) and the **black** wire (that is GND, the 0V side). The other two wires (white and green) you can ignore - tape them off so nothing shorts.
**Step 7 - Set up the breadboard for the green status LED.** The **breadboard** is the white plastic block with lots of little holes. Down each long side runs a red strip and a blue strip - we call these the long red/blue strips that run down the side of the breadboard (the "power strips"). The red one will be our 5V, the blue one will be our 0V (GND). - Cut the USB cable from Step 6. Push the **red** (5V) wire from the buck converter into the **top red strip** of the breadboard. - Push the **black** (GND) wire from the buck converter into the **top blue strip** of the breadboard. - Add a jumper wire from the top red strip to the bottom red strip (so both red strips have 5V). - Add a jumper wire from the top blue strip to the bottom blue strip (so both blue strips have GND).
**Step 8 - Plug in the green LED and its resistor.**
We have no photo of the green LED, but you know it - the small clear/green plastic lens with two metal legs sticking out the bottom. One leg is **long** (that is the + side) and one leg is **short** (that is the - side, the GND side). The **220 ohm resistor** is the little tube with four colour bands (red-red-brown-gold). - Put the LED into the breadboard with the **long leg** in hole **E10** and the **short leg** in hole **E11**. - Put the 220 ohm resistor with one leg in hole **B11** and the other leg in hole **B15**. (Resistors do not have a + or - end - either way is fine.) - Add a short red jumper from hole **A10** to the **red strip** (5V). - Add a short black jumper from hole **A15** to the **blue strip** (GND).
Why this matters: an LED is greedy. If you plug it straight into 5V, it will draw too much current and burn out instantly. The 220 ohm resistor sits in the way like a narrow gate, slowing the current down to a safe amount. The current flows 5V -> resistor -> LED long leg -> LED short leg -> GND, and the LED glows softly the whole time the battery is on. It is your "the system is awake" light.
**Step 9 - About those jumper wires.**
You will use the **male-to-male (M-M) jumpers** for everything on the breadboard - they have a stiff metal pin on both ends. The **female-to-male (F-M) jumpers** (with a plastic socket on one end) are handy if you want to clip onto something that has a pin sticking out, but this project mostly uses M-M. Remember: jumper wires are tiny and thin. Use them ONLY on the 5V LED side. The big 12V Peltier-and-fan loop needs thick 18 AWG wire, not jumpers.
**Step 10 - Set up the W1209 (one-time menu).** After you connect the battery and the W1209 wakes up, you have to teach it what to do. Hold down the **SET button** for about 3 seconds until the display shows **P0**. - **P0** is the setpoint. Set it to **8** (degrees C). This is the temperature you want your can to be. - **P1** is the hysteresis (the gap before the relay turns back on). Leave it at **2**. - **P4** must be set to **C** (cooling), not H (heating). This is the most important one - if you leave it on H, the relay will fire when things get COLD instead of when they get warm, which is the opposite of what you want. Press SET briefly to step through each menu item. Hold SET to save and exit. How the cooling cycle then works (with P0=8 and P1=2): - When the temperature climbs to **10 C** (setpoint 8 + hysteresis 2), the relay CLOSES. The Peltier and fan turn ON and start cooling. - When the temperature drops back to **8 C**, the relay OPENS. The Peltier and fan turn OFF. - It will cycle between 10 C and 8 C. The 2 C gap stops the relay from clicking on and off every second.
**Step 11 - One last warning: the cold side will sweat.** When the cold plate goes below room temperature, water from the air will condense on it - just like a cold glass of lemonade on a hot day. That water can drip onto the breadboard and short things out. Sit the whole project on a saucer or a plastic tray so the puddle goes somewhere safe, and keep the breadboard raised up or off to the side so drips do not land on it. If you want to make the Peltier work less hard (so it does not dump as much heat, does not need such a big fan, and runs longer on the battery), use a **smaller battery pack** - like a 2S LiPo (about 7.4V) or a 9V sealed lead-acid. Do NOT try to "tap a lower voltage" from the buck converter; the buck is 5V output only and is not built to push the 4 amps the Peltier needs. Pick the supply voltage at the battery, not in the middle of the circuit. ## Flash it and run it There is no microcontroller code to flash here - the W1209 is a stand-alone thermostat with its own firmware. Instead, this is a multimeter check + thermostat-config procedure. Multimeter procedure: 1. Build the wiring with the battery DISCONNECTED. Confirm with the multimeter that the lead labelled "+12V" actually goes to the W1209 V+ terminal and to the relay COM terminal. Reverse polarity on V+ / V- will destroy the W1209 - this is the moment to catch it. 2. Confirm the heatsink is mechanically clamped to the Peltier hot side and the fan can spin freely. 3. Put your multimeter on the 20V DC range. Probe across the Peltier red and black wires - it should read 0V (relay is open until the W1209 boots and reads the temperature). 4. Connect the battery. The W1209 display lights up showing room temperature (around 22 C). 5. Because room temperature is way above the 10 C cut-in threshold (8 C setpoint + 2 C hysteresis), the relay should click closed and the display dot should light up - meaning "cooling on". The Peltier voltage should now read close to battery voltage. 6. Hold an ice cube against the NTC probe for 10 seconds. The number drops, and at 8 C the relay should click off again. That click is the project working - hysteresis in action. 7. Re-mount the probe on the cold plate, sit the soda can on top, and let it run. Common gotchas: - Hot side not on a properly-sized heatsink with a properly-sized fan -> Peltier dies in seconds. Spec the cooling first, power second. - Battery polarity reversed -> the W1209 has NO reverse-polarity protection. Reversed 12V across V+ / V- will likely destroy the board (and may damage the relay). Verify polarity with a multimeter BEFORE plugging in. - W1209 set to H (heating) instead of C (cooling) -> the relay turns ON when warm and OFF when cold, exactly the wrong way around. - NTC probe dangling in the air -> it reads room temp forever and the Peltier never stops. Tape it to the cold plate. - Trying to route 4A through breadboard jumpers -> jumpers heat up and voltage sags. Use 18 AWG direct wires for the Peltier + fan loop. - LiPo with no BMS and no fuse -> a shorted Peltier wire can dump huge current from a LiPo. Always BMS + fuse, or just use a 12V SLA for the beginner build. ## Talking points - A Peltier is a thermoelectric heat pump - one side gets cold by pushing the heat to the other side. No moving parts, no refrigerant. - The W1209 is a tiny computer too, but you do not write code for it - you tell it the rules through three buttons. That is called "configuring firmware". - Hysteresis means there is a gap between "turn on" and "turn off" so the relay does not chatter. In cooling mode the relay turns ON when the cold plate drifts UP past (setpoint + hysteresis) and OFF when it comes back DOWN to setpoint. Same idea as the thermostat in a house. - A buck converter steps a higher voltage down efficiently without wasting it as heat - much better than a 7805 for battery-powered builds. But buck converters have a fixed output voltage (this one is 5V), so you cannot "dial in" 9V from a 5V module - you would need a different module entirely. - Battery + buck is the recipe for almost every portable electronics gadget you own. ## Things to change once it works - Add a second probe on the hot-side heatsink and a second W1209 to shut everything down if the hot side gets above 60 C - safety upgrade. - Replace the green status LED with an OLED that shows battery volts, current temp, and minutes-since-on. - Swap the W1209 for an ESP32 and a DS18B20 so the chill coaster can publish its setpoint to your phone over WiFi. - Insulate around the cold plate with foam so the cold does not leak out into the air. - Add a proper buck-boost module (NOT this 5V buck) rated for 4A at 9V if you want to run the Peltier gentler without changing the battery pack. - Reverse the W1209 mode to H and slap the same build under a mug to make a warm-coffee coaster instead. ## Why this is interesting Almost every cool gadget you carry is a battery, a buck converter, and a sensor-driven switch glued together. The Chill Coaster strips that recipe down to its absolute minimum so you can SEE each block: the battery is the brick on the desk, the buck converter is the green LED that says "5V is alive", the sensor is the NTC probe taped to the cold plate, and the switch is the W1209's clicky relay. Once you grok this loop you can build anything portable: a cooler bag, a hand-warmer, a plant waterer, a kid-built fridge.

projects.code:
# Pocket Peltier Chill Coaster - W1209 Configuration Card

This project has **NO microcontroller**. The W1209 Temperature Controller is a
stand-alone thermostat - it runs its own firmware that you configure through
the SET button on the board. There is therefore no Arduino sketch to upload.

This card is a one-page reference you can print and tape inside the project
box. It documents the W1209 setpoints used by this build and the expected
behaviour, so anyone (including future-you) can re-configure the thermostat
without digging through documentation.

To use: open this file, read the steps, then walk to the W1209 and press
the buttons in the order shown. No compile, no upload.

---

## Hardware summary

- Power in   : 12V SLA (preferred for beginners) or 3S LiPo with BMS + 5A fuse
- Brain      : W1209 Temperature Controller (stand-alone, no MCU)
- Cold maker : TEC1-4905 Peltier (cold side -> aluminium plate under can)
- Hot dump   : Large finned heatsink (>= 50x50x20 mm) + 80 mm 12V fan, thermal paste
- Sensor     : W1209 NTC probe taped to the cold plate
- Aux power  : 6-24V to 5V 3A USB Buck Converter -> green status LED only

## Important safety rules

1. The HOT side of the TEC1-4905 MUST be on a heatsink with a running fan
   BEFORE power is applied. If the hot side cannot dump heat, the Peltier
   will burn out in well under a minute.
2. Heatsink and fan sizing matters. A TEC1-4905 at 12V dumps roughly 50-60 W
   of waste heat. A tiny 40 mm fan cannot move that much air - use an 80 mm
   or 120 mm 12V fan on an extruded aluminium heatsink at least
   50 x 50 x 20 mm, with a thin layer of thermal paste between Peltier and
   heatsink. Without this, the hot side runs away even with "a fan" attached.
3. Reverse polarity on the W1209 V+ / V- terminals is DESTRUCTIVE. The
   W1209 has no reverse-polarity protection - swapping the battery leads
   can permanently damage the controller. Double-check red goes to V+
   and black goes to V- before connecting the battery.
4. The W1209 onboard relay (SRD-05VDC-SL-C, ~5A DC max) is switching the
   TEC1-4905's ~4A draw. That is inside the rating but with almost no
   headroom. Expect the relay to wear out over time and treat audible
   clicks at startup (inrush) as normal.
5. Battery choice: a 12V SLA is the beginner-safe option - chemistry is
   tolerant, no thermal runaway risk on the bench. If using a 3S LiPo,
   it MUST have a built-in BMS (battery management system) and a 5A
   inline fuse on the positive lead. Never leave a bare LiPo unattended,
   and stop using it if it puffs or smells sweet.
6. The cold side WILL sweat. Sit the build on a saucer so the puddle
   does not drown the breadboard.

## W1209 button layout

- [SET]  enters menu / confirms a value
- [+]    increases a value
- [-]    decreases a value

## One-time configuration steps

Press and hold [SET] for ~3 seconds. The display shows P0.

    P0  Setpoint                 -> set to    8 (degrees C)
    P1  Hysteresis (return diff) -> set to    2 (degrees C)
    P2  Upper-limit alarm        -> set to   50 (degrees C, safety)
    P3  Lower-limit alarm        -> set to   -5 (degrees C, safety)
    P4  Mode: C = cooling,
            H = heating          -> set to    C   <-- MUST be C
    P5  Delay before relay flips -> set to    0 (seconds)
    P6  Probe calibration offset -> set to    0 (degrees C)

Walk through the menu by tapping [SET]; change values with [+] / [-];
after the last item the board returns to the live temperature display.

## Expected behaviour (cooling mode, P4 = C)

- Display shows the cold-plate temperature in real time.
- A small dot (or LED) on the W1209 lights when the relay is closed = "cooling on".
- Cooling-mode logic with P0 = 8 and P1 = 2:
  - When temp >= 10 C (setpoint + hysteresis) -> relay CLOSES, Peltier + fan run.
  - When temp <=  8 C (setpoint)              -> relay OPENS, Peltier + fan stop.
- Cycle repeats. The 2 C gap between cut-in (10 C) and cut-out (8 C) is
  hysteresis - it stops the relay from chattering when the temp wobbles
  around the setpoint.

(If you set P4 = H by mistake the logic flips: relay would close on cold,
open on warm - exactly the wrong way around for this build.)

## Commissioning check

1. Battery DISCONNECTED. Confirm wiring against the diagram. Verify
   battery polarity at V+ / V- with a multimeter (red probe on the wire
   going to V+ should read positive when you test against V-).
2. Confirm the heatsink is mechanically clamped to the Peltier hot side
   and the 80 mm fan is wired and free to spin.
3. Connect battery. Display lights up showing ~22 C (room temp).
4. Relay clicks ON within a second (room temp is well above setpoint of 8 C
   plus hysteresis 2 C = trigger threshold 10 C).
5. Press an ice cube against the NTC probe. Watch the number fall.
6. At about 8 C the relay clicks OFF. That click is success.
7. Re-tape the probe to the cold plate. Set the can on top. Enjoy.

## Troubleshooting

- Display dark, no smoke              -> battery flat, or fuse blown. Check voltage at V+ / V-.
- Display dark, faint burning smell   -> polarity was reversed. W1209 likely damaged. Replace.
- Relay never turns off               -> probe dangling in air; tape it to the plate.
- Relay clicks when already cold      -> P4 is set to H (heating). Change to C.
- Peltier hot side untouchable in
  under 30 seconds                    -> fan not running OR fan too small OR no thermal
                                         paste OR heatsink loose. POWER OFF NOW.
- Plate barely cools                  -> battery sagging under load; charge or use a
                                         higher-capacity pack; or thicker (18 AWG) wires
                                         on the Peltier loop.

## Parts that must match the wiring diagram

    Battery 12V+ -> W1209 V+  AND  W1209 Relay COM  AND  Buck IN+
    Battery GND  -> W1209 V-  AND  TEC- (black)     AND  Fan-       AND  Buck IN-
    W1209 Relay NO -> TEC+ (red)  AND  Fan+ (12V)
    Buck 5V USB out -> 220R -> Green LED anode
    Green LED cathode -> Buck GND

projects.name: Two-Room Doorbell Pair (ESP-NOW)
projects.power_supply: Two 9V wall-warts, one per room, into MB102 power supply modules (3.3V rail for the sender ESP-01S, 5V rail for the receiver relay board)
projects.description:
**What it is**: Two little WiFi gadgets that talk straight to each other with no router in between. Press the button on one in the hallway and the other one in your bedroom blinks a red LED and clicks a buzzer. **Why it is fun**: It feels like walkie-talkies but invisible - one box ZAPS the other box across the whole house and you didn't run a single wire. You can hide the receiver under a sibling's bed and make them wonder where the buzz is coming from. ## Parts list - 1 x ESP-01S WiFi Module (the SENDER, lives at the "front door") - 1 x ESP-01S 5V Relay Module - Tasmota board (the RECEIVER, in the other room) - 1 x CP2102 USB-to-TTL adapter (only used while flashing - then you put it back in the box) - 2 x MB102 breadboard power supply modules (one for each room) - 2 x 9V wall-wart power supplies (one per MB102) - 2 x mini breadboards - 1 x push button (the doorbell) - 4 x 10K resistors (pull-ups on the sender's GPIO0, RST, CH_PD AND GPIO2 - all four pins MUST be biased HIGH at power-on or the chip refuses to boot) - 1 x 5mm red LED + 1 x 220 ohm resistor (the "ding!" light on the receiver - wired active-LOW, see below) - 1 x 5V active buzzer (wired through the Tasmota relay - low-voltage DC only) - DuPont jumper wires ## Wiring notes This project has TWO little boxes: a sender (the doorbell button) and a receiver (the buzzer + light). Each box uses one ESP-01S WiFi chip - a tiny blue board with 8 short pins on the bottom. They talk to each other directly over WiFi using a special Espressif trick called ESP-NOW (no router needed). Each box gets its own power supply. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP-01S chip:** - **VCC** - power input. The ESP-01S wants 3.3V here. Do NOT give it 5V or it will smoke. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs a GND connection. - **CH_PD** - "chip power-down". It must be held HIGH (connected to 3.3V through a resistor) for the chip to stay awake. - **RST** - reset. Held HIGH so the chip doesn't keep resetting itself. - **GPIO0** and **GPIO2** - the only two normal pins you can use on this chip. We use GPIO2 on both sides. - **rail** - the long red or blue strip running down the side of the breadboard. Red = power, blue = ground.
### Sender side (the doorbell button room) **Step 1 - Set up the sender power.** Snap one MB102 power module onto one breadboard so its pins straddle the two long red/blue rails near one end. The MB102 has two tiny black jumper caps - one for each rail. Flip BOTH caps to the **3.3V** position. The ESP-01S will be destroyed by 5V, so double-check this before plugging anything in. - MB102 +3V3 pin -> red rail of the breadboard - MB102 GND pin -> blue rail of the breadboard - 9V wall-wart -> MB102 barrel jack (do not plug it in to the wall yet)
**Step 2 - Plant the ESP-01S sender.** The ESP-01S has female header sockets, so we use male-to-male jumper wires to plug it into the breadboard. Push 6 jumper wires UP through the breadboard holes so their tops stick out, then press the ESP-01S female header DOWN onto those tops. (Or use a row of 4+4 male pin headers if you have them.) - VCC -> red rail (3.3V) - GND -> blue rail (ground)
**Step 3 - Add the four "keep-it-awake" resistors.** The ESP-01S has four pins that need to be tied to 3.3V through a 10K resistor each. Without these, the chip either won't start or will keep resetting. (We do not have a photo of the resistors on file - they are tiny brown cylinders with colored stripes: brown-black-orange-brown means 10K.) - One 10K resistor between CH_PD and the red rail - One 10K resistor between RST and the red rail - One 10K resistor between GPIO0 and the red rail - One 10K resistor between GPIO2 and the red rail **Why this matters:** Three of these pins (CH_PD, RST, GPIO0) tell the chip "you are alive, please run normally" only if they are HIGH at the moment power arrives. The fourth one (GPIO2) is the one our button will pull LOW. The 10K resistor is weak enough that the button can easily win and yank the pin down to 0V when pressed, but strong enough to hold the pin at 3.3V the rest of the time. **Step 4 - Add the doorbell button.**
tactile push-button (4 legs, no photo on file)
The tactile button is a small white-pin square switch with 4 legs. The 4 legs are paired: two are always connected to each other, and the other two are always connected to each other. When you press, the two pairs are joined. Straddle the button across the middle gap of the breadboard so its legs land on different sides. - One leg of the button -> ESP-01S GPIO2 pin - The leg on the OTHER side of the button -> blue rail (ground)
**Press the button -> GPIO2 gets shorted to ground -> chip notices and shouts "RING!" over WiFi.** That is the whole sender. **WARNING - this trips people up.** Do NOT plug in the power while you are holding the button down. GPIO2 is one of the four pins the chip checks the exact instant power arrives. If it sees ground (because you are pressing the button), the chip will refuse to boot. Plug in first, THEN press. ### Receiver side (the buzzer + light room) **Step 5 - Set up the receiver power.** Use the SECOND MB102 on the SECOND breadboard. This time flip BOTH jumper caps to **5V** (the receiver uses a relay board that needs 5V). Plug the second 9V wall-wart into its barrel jack. Do not plug into the wall yet. - MB102 +5V pin -> red rail - MB102 GND pin -> blue rail
**Step 6 - Plant the relay board.** The receiver is a special board that already has an ESP-01S socket on top AND a relay (a tiny click-switch) on the bottom. It runs on 5V (different from the sender, which is 3.3V). Push the SECOND ESP-01S chip into the socket on top of the relay board, lining up the pins. Then wire the relay board to the breadboard: - Relay board VCC pin -> red rail (5V) - Relay board GND pin -> blue rail (ground)
The relay has three screw terminals on the green block: COM (common), NO (normally open), and NC (normally closed). We only use COM and NO. When the chip fires the relay, it closes the gap between COM and NO with a quiet "click". **Step 7 - Wire the buzzer through the relay.** The buzzer is a 5V active buzzer with two wires, a + (red, longer) and a - (black, shorter). We are using the relay as a switch that completes the buzzer's ground connection. - Buzzer + (long red wire) -> red rail (5V) - Buzzer - (short black wire) -> screw into the COM terminal - A jumper wire from the NO terminal -> blue rail (ground) When the relay is OFF, COM and NO are disconnected, so the buzzer has no path to ground and stays silent. When the relay clicks ON, COM connects to NO, the buzzer gets its ground, and it beeps. **Step 8 - Add the indicator LED (this is a tricky one).**
We are wiring the LED **backwards on purpose**. Normally you would go: power -> resistor -> LED long leg -> LED short leg -> pin. Here we do the same thing, but the "pin" is GPIO2 on the receiver ESP-01S, and the chip drives that pin LOW (to 0V) only when it wants the LED to light up. The LED is the small red bulb with two legs of different lengths. The 220 ohm resistor (red-red-brown-brown stripes) limits how much current flows through the LED so it doesn't burn out. - Red rail (5V) -> one leg of the 220 ohm resistor - Other leg of the 220 ohm resistor -> LED long leg (anode) - LED short leg (cathode) -> ESP-01S GPIO2 pin on the relay board
**Why this matters:** Remember that GPIO2 has to be HIGH at boot or the chip won't start. If we did the normal LED wiring (pin -> resistor -> LED -> ground), the chip would try to source current the moment it powered on and the boot pin would be pulled low. By wiring the LED "upside-down" instead, the pin sits idle at HIGH (no current flows because both sides of the LED chain are at 5V-ish) and the LED only lights when the chip pulls the pin DOWN to 0V. The chip boots cleanly AND we still get our blinking light. **Step 9 - Flashing the chips (only the first time).** The CP2102 is a small USB stick that lets your computer talk to an ESP-01S. You only need it ONCE per chip to load the program (the "sketch"). Pop the ESP-01S out of its socket, plug it into the CP2102 with a small adapter, and hold GPIO0 to ground while you connect USB - that puts the chip into flash mode. Upload the sketch, unplug, put the chip back in its socket. Repeat for the other chip with the other sketch. After that you never need the CP2102 again (unless you change the code).
**SAFETY - very important.** The Tasmota ESP-01S relay board is for LOW-VOLTAGE DC ONLY: 5V buzzers, small LED strips, little hobby motors. It is NOT a mains-voltage relay. NEVER wire it to a wall socket, a lamp cord, or anything that plugs in to the house. The 9V wall-warts are the only things in this project that touch household power, and they handle that safely inside their own plastic cases. **What happens when the doorbell rings:** Press the button in the sender room. The sender chip wakes up, sees GPIO2 was pulled to ground, and sends a tiny WiFi message to the receiver. The receiver chip clicks its relay ON (you hear the buzzer beep) and at the same time pulses the indicator LED in a blink pattern for about 1.5 seconds. Then everything goes quiet again until the next press. ## Flash it and run it ESP-01S modules cannot be flashed by themselves - they need a USB-to-serial adapter. We use the **CP2102 USB-to-TTL UART Module** and a temporary flashing setup. **REMINDER: ESP-01S is a 3.3V part. NEVER feed it 5V on VCC even for one second, even during flashing.** Most CP2102 boards have a jumper to pick 3.3V or 5V output - double check it is on 3.3V before you plug in the ESP-01S. **Flashing rig (do this for each ESP-01S, one at a time):** 1. CP2102 3V3 out -> ESP-01S VCC AND ESP-01S CH_PD 2. CP2102 GND -> ESP-01S GND 3. CP2102 TX -> ESP-01S RX 4. CP2102 RX -> ESP-01S TX 5. ESP-01S GPIO0 -> GND (this puts it into flash mode at boot) Plug the CP2102 into the laptop USB. In the Arduino IDE: - Install the ESP8266 board package (File -> Preferences -> add `https://arduino.esp8266.com/stable/package_esp8266com_index.json` to Boards Manager URLs, then Tools -> Boards -> Boards Manager -> install "esp8266 by ESP8266 Community") - Tools -> Board -> "Generic ESP8266 Module" - Tools -> Flash Size -> "1MB (FS:64KB OTA:~470KB)" - Tools -> Port -> the COM port that appeared when you plugged the CP2102 in - Open `two_room_doorbell.ino`. For the front-door unit leave `#define ROLE_SENDER` uncommented. For the relay unit, comment out `ROLE_SENDER` and uncomment `ROLE_RECEIVER`. - Hit Upload. Once it says Done, unplug, remove the GPIO0-to-GND wire, plug back in. **MAC address pairing (REQUIRED, no shortcut this time):** flash the RECEIVER first. Open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. It prints `Receiver MAC (paste this into the sender sketch): A4:CF:12:34:56:78`. Copy those six numbers into the `RECEIVER_MAC` array near the top of the sketch, then flash the SENDER. The sender sketch refuses to send while `RECEIVER_MAC` is still all zeros - it will print a halt message in Serial. (We deliberately removed the "broadcast fallback" because on the ESP8266 the send-callback status for broadcast frames is unreliable and that masks real wiring problems.) ### Common gotchas - Forgetting **any** of GPIO0, GPIO2, RST or CH_PD pull-ups on the sender - the chip will look dead or boot into the wrong mode. All four 10K pull-ups must be in place. - Holding the button while plugging in - same effect, the chip sees GPIO2 LOW at boot and gives up. - Feeding the ESP-01S 5V instead of 3.3V - one-shot kill. - Forgetting to REMOVE the GPIO0-to-GND wire after flashing - the chip will keep booting into flash mode and the sketch won't run. - Wiring the receiver LED the "normal" way (GPIO2 -> resistor -> LED -> GND) - this ties GPIO2 to GND through the LED at the instant of power-on, pulling the boot-strap pin LOW, and the chip refuses to boot. Use the active-LOW wiring shown above. - Tasmota relay polarity backwards: if your board turns out to be active-HIGH (relay clicks at boot when sketch isn't running), flip `#define RELAY_ACTIVE_LOW 1` to `0` at the top of the sketch and re-flash. - Tiny LED flicker at every power-up: the ESP8266 ROM bootloader prints a short startup banner on GPIO2 at 74880 baud before our sketch starts. The LED may twitch for a fraction of a second. This is normal. - The Tasmota relay board ships with Tasmota firmware. We are overwriting it with our own sketch. That's fine - the relay hardware still works the same way, GPIO0 drives the coil. ## Talking points - **ESP-NOW is not WiFi-the-router-kind.** It is the two chips talking phone-to-phone directly over the same radio frequency. No internet needed. Range is about 30-50 meters indoors. - **Why a MAC address?** Every WiFi chip in the world has a unique 6-byte name burned in at the factory. The sender shouts the receiver's name on every ring so other ESP chips ignore the message. - **Why does the relay click?** A relay is a tiny electromagnet that yanks a metal switch shut. The CLICK is the metal contacts smacking together. Now you know what that sound is in your old toys. - **What is a boot-strap pin?** Some pins on a chip do double duty - the chip peeks at them at the moment of power-on to decide what mode to start in, then lets you use them as normal pins after that. GPIO0 and GPIO2 are the two famous ones on the ESP8266, and they MUST be HIGH at the instant power arrives. That is why we add the 10K pull-up resistors AND why we wire the LED upside-down. ## Things to change once it works - Replace the buzzer with a string of LED fairy lights (still low-voltage DC) for a silent visual doorbell. - Add a second button at the back door (another sender) so two doorbells trigger the same chime - check `pressCount` parity to make the LED flash a different pattern. - Put the receiver inside a 3D-printed box shaped like a bell. - Once you have learned discrete relay boards with a transistor + flyback diode, build a beefier doorbell that drives a bigger 12V DC chime - the Tasmota carrier here hides that detail so this project is about the radio, not the relay drive circuit. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project where the kid sees TWO of the same chip cooperating - same silicon inside, different jobs. It also teaches the concept of addressing (the MAC) and "fire and forget" messaging (the sender doesn't know if the receiver heard it - that's just how ESP-NOW works). Most importantly it forces a real conversation about boot-strap pins - why we add four pull-up resistors, why the LED is wired "backwards" on the receiver, and why holding the button at power-on bricks the boot. That mental model carries forward into every future ESP8266 / ESP32 build.

projects.name: Glovebox Climate Dash
projects.power_supply: 12V cigarette-lighter socket feeds the 6-24V to 5V buck converter; its USB output powers the NodeMCU V3 via the I/O Shield's micro-USB port.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A tiny dashboard that plugs into the cigarette lighter in your car and shows the cabin temperature, how humid the air is, and the air pressure right now on a little glowing screen. As you drive up a hill or down into a valley, the pressure number changes - you can actually watch the weather happen on your dashboard. **Why it is fun**: You built a real car gadget that runs off the car. Show your friends the pressure drop when you crest a mountain pass, or watch the temperature inside the car shoot up after you leave it in the sun. It's like having your own tiny weather station riding shotgun. ## Parts list - 1x **NodeMCU V3 (ESP8266, CH340G)** - the brain. The wide V3 board snaps onto the I/O Shield so we get screw terminals and a clean micro-USB power input. - 1x **NodeMCU V3 I/O Shield (pin breakout)** - the carrier that turns every pin into a screw terminal. Way nicer than poking jumper wires into the headers, especially in a bouncing car. - 1x **6-24V to 5V 3A USB Buck Converter** - the workhorse. Takes the dirty, noisy 12V from the car (which can spike up to 14.4V when the engine is running) and converts it to clean USB 5V. - 1x **DHT11 Temperature & Humidity Sensor** - reads cabin temperature in degrees C and humidity as a percentage. - 1x **GY-BMP280 Barometric Pressure Sensor** - reads air pressure in hPa (hectopascals). Sea level is about 1013 hPa; it drops as you go up. - 1x **0.96" OLED Display (I2C)** - tiny glowing screen that shows all three readings. Talks to the NodeMCU over only two wires (SDA and SCL). - 1x **Breadboard** and a handful of **jumpers** for wiring the sensors. The buck converter and NodeMCU connect via USB. - Cables you already have: a **USB-A to micro-USB cable** to go from the buck converter output into the NodeMCU (not tracked as a project allocation - grab one from the cable box). ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the NodeMCU V3 board (and its I/O Shield):** - **D1, D2, D3, ...** - the pins you can plug wires into. The number printed on the board is NOT the same as the GPIO number in the code, so always go by the printed label. - **3V3** - the 3.3V power output. The brain chip (ESP8266) only likes 3.3V, so we use this for all our sensors. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs a GND wire back to the board. - **VIN / 5V** - the 5V power output, fed by the USB cable from the buck converter. - **micro-USB port** - where the USB cable from the buck converter plugs in. - **I/O Shield** - the little board you press the NodeMCU onto. It turns every pin into a 3-pin column: the outer hole is the signal, the middle hole is +5V (we will use 3V3 instead today), and the inner hole is GND. That means you can plug a 3-wire cable straight in - no fiddling.
**Important safety note before we start.** The ESP8266 chip on the NodeMCU is a 3.3V chip. Its pins do NOT like 5V. If you wire a sensor's power to 5V, the data wire from that sensor will push 5V into a pin and slowly cook it. So every sensor in this build gets its power from the **3V3** pin, not 5V. The DHT11 is happy with 3.3V (its datasheet says 3.0V to 5.5V), so this works for all three sensors.
**Step 1 - Push the NodeMCU onto the I/O Shield.** - Line up the USB ports so they point the same way. - Press the NodeMCU straight down onto the shield's two long pin sockets. Take it slow - the pins bend easily. - Now every labeled pin (D1, D2, D3, ...) has its own little 3-hole column on the shield. This shield is the trick that makes the whole project no-soldering. Each pin is now a tiny power-plus-ground-plus-signal column.
**Step 2 - Set up the breadboard's power lanes.** We are going to use the long red strip on the side of the breadboard as our "+3.3V lane" (even though it's labeled "+", we are feeding it 3.3V, not 5V - that's fine, the strips don't care). The long blue strip is our "GND lane". - Take a red male-to-male jumper. One end into the **3V3** column on the I/O Shield. Other end into the red "+" strip on the breadboard. - Take a black male-to-male jumper. One end into the **GND** column on the I/O Shield. Other end into the blue "-" strip on the breadboard. Now any sensor that needs power can grab it from the red strip, and any sensor that needs ground can grab it from the blue strip. Super tidy.
**Step 3 - Wire up the DHT11 (temperature and humidity sensor).** Plug the DHT11 into the breadboard so its three legs land in rows A3, A5, and A7. Then run three short male-to-male jumpers: - DHT11 **VCC** (power input) in row A3 -> red "+" strip on the breadboard (that gives it 3.3V). - DHT11 **DAT** (the data leg) in row A5 -> the pin marked **D3** on the I/O Shield. In code this is GPIO0. - DHT11 **GND** (the 0V side) in row A7 -> blue "-" strip on the breadboard. Why D3 and not D4? D4 on this board is wired to the little blue light on the NodeMCU AND to a "boot helper" pin that needs to be high when the board turns on. If we used D4 for the sensor, the light would flash every reading and the board could get confused at boot. D3 is safer for our data wire.
**Step 4 - Wire up the BMP280 (air pressure sensor).** The BMP280 talks to the NodeMCU using two wires (a system called I2C - say "eye-squared-see"). Lots of sensors can share these same two wires, which is handy. Plug the BMP280 into the breadboard so its four pins land in rows A12, A14, A16, and A18. Then: - BMP280 **VCC** (power input) in row A12 -> red "+" strip. - BMP280 **GND** in row A14 -> blue "-" strip. - BMP280 **SCL** (the clock wire) in row A16 -> the pin marked **D1** on the I/O Shield. In code this is GPIO5. - BMP280 **SDA** (the data wire) in row A18 -> the pin marked **D2** on the I/O Shield. In code this is GPIO4.
**Step 5 - Wire up the OLED screen.** The OLED talks I2C too, so we are going to share the same two wires (SCL and SDA) that the BMP280 already uses. That is what makes I2C so cool - one pair of wires, many devices. Plug the OLED into the breadboard so its four pins land in rows A23, A25, A27, and A29. Then: - OLED **GND** in row A23 -> blue "-" strip. - OLED **VCC** (power input) in row A25 -> red "+" strip. - OLED **SCL** in row A27 -> jump straight across to row A16 (where the BMP280's SCL already is). Both screens now share the clock wire going to D1. - OLED **SDA** in row A29 -> jump straight across to row A18 (where the BMP280's SDA already is). Both share the data wire going to D2. Why share? Each I2C part has its own address (like its own phone number). The NodeMCU calls one at a time, and the others just stay quiet. That's how three parts can chat on two wires.
**Step 6 - Set up the buck converter.** A car's cigarette-lighter socket gives out 12V, but the NodeMCU wants 5V through its USB port. The buck converter is the little board that turns 12V into 5V. - Wire the **+** from the car cigarette-lighter plug to the **+** input screw terminal on the buck converter. - Wire the **-** (or GND) from the plug to the **-** input terminal on the buck converter. - The buck converter has a USB-A socket on its output side. Plug a USB-A to micro-USB cable in there, and plug the micro-USB end into the I/O Shield's micro-USB port. **Why this matters - do this BEFORE the NodeMCU is plugged in.** The buck converter has a tiny blue screw (a "trim pot") that sets its output voltage. If someone has turned that screw, the output could be way more than 5V - even 12V - and that would instantly kill your NodeMCU. So: 1. Plug the buck converter into the car socket WITHOUT the NodeMCU connected. 2. Touch a multimeter's red probe to the USB-A socket's center pin and the black probe to one of the side pins. 3. If it does not read 5.0V, turn the little blue screw slowly until it does. 4. ONLY THEN plug the cable into the NodeMCU. This is a tricky one to do without an adult helping. Take your time.
**Step 7 - Final check before turning it on.** - All three sensors get their red power wire from the breadboard's red "+" strip (which is fed by 3V3, not 5V). Trace it with your finger. - All three sensors have a black wire back to the blue "-" strip. - D1 goes to both SCL pins. D2 goes to both SDA pins. D3 goes to the DHT11's data leg. - The buck converter output reads 5.0V on a multimeter. If all of that is true, plug the car-socket plug in and the OLED should light up. If the OLED stays dark, unplug everything and double-check the red and black wires haven't been swapped at the shield. ## Flash it and run it 1. Install the **Arduino IDE** (or use VS Code with PlatformIO). 2. **File -> Preferences -> Additional Board Manager URLs**, add: `https://arduino.esp8266.com/stable/package_esp8266com_index.json` 3. **Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager**, search "esp8266" and install the package. 4. Plug the NodeMCU V3 into your laptop with a USB cable (not the buck converter yet - just plain laptop USB while flashing). 5. **Tools -> Board -> NodeMCU 1.0 (ESP-12E Module)**, **Tools -> Port -> COMx** (the new COM port that appeared). 6. **Sketch -> Include Library -> Manage Libraries**, install: `DHT sensor library` by Adafruit, `Adafruit BMP280 Library`, `Adafruit SSD1306`, `Adafruit GFX Library`, `Adafruit Unified Sensor`. 7. Paste the code, click **Upload**. The blue LED blinks while flashing. **Common gotchas**: - No COM port? You need the **CH340G driver** for Windows - search "CH340 driver" and install. - OLED stays blank? Some I2C OLEDs are address `0x3C`, some are `0x3D`. **The code auto-detects both - no edits needed.** If it still fails, your wiring is the suspect, not the address. - BMP280 reads nonsense? Some are `0x76`, some are `0x77`. **The code already tries both - no edits needed.** - Bench-test the WHOLE thing on your desk before taking it to the car. The car ride is not the time to debug. - Use the **buck converter** ONLY after you've confirmed it outputs 5.0V on the multimeter. The car socket is your first real-world power-supply project. ## Talking points - The buck converter is a **switching regulator** - it chops the 12V into pulses thousands of times per second and uses an inductor to smooth it back to a steady 5V. Way more efficient than the linear regulator inside the NodeMCU board would be (a linear regulator would have to burn the extra 7V as heat). - **Why I2C is amazing**: the BMP280 and the OLED both live on the same two wires. They each have a different address (like a house number on a street), so the NodeMCU just shouts "Hey 0x76, give me a reading!" and the right device answers. - Pressure in **hPa** (hectopascals) is what weather forecasts use. 1 hPa = 100 Pa = 1 mbar. Sea level standard is 1013.25 hPa. Every 8 meters you go up, pressure drops about 1 hPa. - The DHT11 is the cheap-and-cheerful sensor - it only updates once a second and is only accurate to about +/-2 degrees. Good enough for "is it hot?", not good enough for a science lab. - **3.3V vs 5V**: the ESP8266 is a 3.3V chip. Some other boards (like Arduino Uno) are 5V. Sensors that "just work" on the Uno can quietly damage the ESP8266 over weeks of use. The fix is easy: power them from 3V3 in the first place. ## Things to change once it works - Add a second OLED page that flips every few seconds to show the **trip min/max** alongside the live readings (the code already tracks tMin/tMax/pMin/pMax in memory - they just need their own screen). - Compute **altitude** from the pressure and graph it over the trip (the code already prints altitude; storing a rolling buffer and drawing a tiny line graph is the upgrade). - Add a **buzzer** that beeps if the cabin temperature goes above 30 degrees C (useful warning if you've left a window cracked and the car's been baking). - Upgrade the DHT11 to a **DHT22** or a **BME280** for better accuracy. - Use the ESP8266's WiFi to log readings to your phone when you get home over the WiFi network `GeeFam`. ## Why this is interesting This project is the first time the car becomes a power source for one of your gadgets. Up until now everything ran off a laptop's USB port - clean, friendly 5V from a known-good supply. The cigarette lighter is a totally different world: 12V nominal but actually anywhere from 11V (engine off, battery a bit tired) up to 14.4V (engine running, alternator charging) under normal conditions. Real cars also produce nasty short **transients** - load dump, cold-crank dips, inductive spikes from motors and relays - that can briefly hit 40-80V. The 6-24V buck handles the everyday range; for anything you leave installed permanently, add an **inline 1-2A fuse in the cigarette plug** (most quality plugs already have one) and a **TVS diode across the buck's input** as cheap insurance. The buck converter is the magic box that hides the everyday ugliness and gives the NodeMCU a steady 5V to live on. Once you understand this pattern - "rough power in, clean power out" - you can build gadgets that run off a 9V battery, a drone LiPo, an SLA from an old UPS, anything.

projects.name: Knock Counter Door Guard
projects.power_supply: MB102 power module on the breadboard rails (9V wall-wart into its barrel jack, switched to 5V output) feeds the Uno's 5V pin and the single big red 7-segment digit.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A vibration sensor stuck to your bedroom door counts every time someone knocks. The number of knocks shows up huge and red on a big single-digit display. Press the button to reset to zero. **Why it is fun**: You instantly know how many times your little brother tried to come in while you were away - the number is sitting there, glowing red, and he cannot delete it. It also turns one boring digit into a tiny scoreboard you can use for anything: knocks, points, lives, warnings. ## Parts list - **Arduino Uno R3** - the brain. Reads the knock sensor, drives the digit, watches the button. - **0.56" Red 7-Segment LED Display (1 digit)** - the big red number 0-9 you can see across the room. Common-cathode (the two middle pins on top and bottom share a single ground). - **SW-420 Vibration Switch Module** - our "knock" sensor. It has a little spring inside that rattles when the surface moves. (Real piezo knock sensors are not in the parts bin yet, so we use this. It works the same way for our purposes: it tells us "something just moved.") - **Tactile Push-button Switch 3x6x4.3mm (white pin)** - reset-to-zero button. - **MB102 Breadboard Power Supply Module** - sits on the rails and gives us a clean 5V from a 9V wall-wart. Way safer than running everything off the Uno's regulator with a sensor hanging off it. - **7x Resistor 220R** - one for each segment of the digit (a, b, c, d, e, f, g). LEDs always need a current-limiting resistor. - **Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points)** + **Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc** - to hold and connect everything. - **9V wall-wart with 5.5/2.1 mm barrel plug** - powers the MB102 from the wall. ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the Arduino Uno board:** - **5V** - the pin that pushes out 5 volts of power. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every circuit needs a ground. - **D2 through D13** - the pins on the top edge marked D2, D3, D4 and so on. These are the "digital" pins your code switches on and off. - **A0 through A5** - the pins on the bottom edge. We do not use any of them in this build. - **The long red and blue strips on the breadboard** - the "rails." Red carries 5V, blue carries 0V (ground). Anything you plug into a hole on the red strip gets 5V; same idea for blue and ground.
**About the digit before we start.** The big red display is one number made out of 7 little stick-shaped LEDs (plus a dot we are ignoring). Each stick is called a "segment" and has a letter name from **a** to **g**. There is a shared "short leg" hidden inside the chip that all 7 segments share - we send that to ground (0V). To light up a stick, the code sends 5V into that segment's pin (through a small resistor to protect the LED). **Step 1 - Power the breadboard with the MB102 module.** - Push the MB102 module down onto the two long rails at the top of the breadboard so its pins straddle both rails. - Set the tiny jumper on the MB102's output side to **5V** (not 3.3V). There is a label printed next to the jumper. - Plug the 9V wall-wart into the round barrel jack on the MB102. - Flip the MB102 power switch on. The little green LED on the module should light up. Now the long red strip carries 5V and the long blue strip is ground (0V). The MB102 is doing the heavy work so the Uno does not have to.
**Step 2 - Power the Uno from the same rails.** - Run a male-to-male jumper from a hole on the red strip to the Uno's **5V** pin. - Run a male-to-male jumper from a hole on the blue strip to one of the Uno's **GND** pins. Why this matters: we want the Uno and the digit to share the exact same ground. If the grounds are not connected, the Uno cannot tell what voltage the segments are actually at, and the digit will look dim or flicker. One blue rail, one shared ground - easy.
**Step 3 - Plant the 7-segment digit on the breadboard.** The digit has 10 pins, 5 on each long side. Hold it so the little decimal-point dot is in the **bottom right** corner. Now press it down across the breadboard's middle gap so its left row of pins lands in column E and its right row of pins lands in column F, with the pins covering rows 14 to 18. Pin numbers (with the dot on the bottom right): - Pin 1 = segment **e**, Pin 2 = segment **d**, Pin 3 = **COM** (shared ground), Pin 4 = segment **c**, Pin 5 = the decimal dot (we leave it alone). - Pin 6 = segment **b**, Pin 7 = segment **a**, Pin 8 = **COM** again (same shared ground), Pin 9 = segment **f**, Pin 10 = segment **g**. The two COM pins (3 and 8) are the shared "short leg" for all the segments. Both of them have to reach the blue (ground) strip. - From E16 (that is pin 3, COM), run a short black jumper to the blue strip. - From F16 (that is pin 8, COM, on the other side of the digit), run another short black jumper to the blue strip.
**Step 4 - Drop one 220 ohm resistor in front of every segment.** You need **7** of these little resistors (red-red-brown-gold bands). Resistors do not have a long leg or a short leg - either way around is fine. Plug each resistor in so it bridges from one of the digit's segment pins out to a spare row further along the board: - Segment **a** (row 17, left side): resistor from **A17 to A22**. - Segment **b** (row 18, left side): resistor from **A18 to A23**. - Segment **c** (row 17, right side): resistor from **J17 to J22**. - Segment **d** (row 15, right side): resistor from **J15 to J23**. - Segment **e** (row 14, left side): resistor from **A14 to A24**. - Segment **f** (row 18, right side): resistor from **J18 to J25**. - Segment **g** (row 14, right side): resistor from **J14 to J26**. Why this matters: LEDs are greedy. If you connect one straight to 5V, it grabs too much current and burns out in seconds. The 220 ohm resistor is a tiny speed bump that limits the current to a safe, bright level. One resistor per segment, no shortcuts - if you share a single resistor between segments, "8" looks dimmer than "1" and the lit segments look uneven.
**Step 5 - Wire each resistor's far end to the matching pin on the Uno.** Using male-to-male jumper wires, run one wire per segment from the "far" hole of the resistor back to the Uno: - A22 to Uno **D2** (this is segment **a**) - A23 to Uno **D3** (segment **b**) - J22 to Uno **D4** (segment **c**) - J23 to Uno **D5** (segment **d**) - A24 to Uno **D6** (segment **e**) - J25 to Uno **D7** (segment **f**) - J26 to Uno **D8** (segment **g**) It looks like a lot of wires, but it is the same step seven times. The code will turn each pin on and off to spell out the number on the digit. Leave pin 5 (the dot) totally unconnected - we will only show whole numbers, no decimals.
**Step 6 - Plug in the SW-420 vibration sensor.** The SW-420 is a small green board with a little metal spring on it. When the spring shakes, the module sends a quick blip to the Uno. The module has 3 pins, usually labelled **VCC**, **GND**, and **DO** (DO means "digital out" - the blip pin). Push the 3 pins of the module into rows 3, 4, 5 on column B of the breadboard: - VCC (5V in, the power input) - row B3 - GND (ground, 0V) - row B4 - DO (the signal pin) - row B5 Now jumper those rows to where they need to go: - B3 to the red 5V rail. - B4 to the blue ground rail. - B5 to the Uno's **D9** pin.
**Step 7 - Move the SW-420 to the door with female-to-male jumpers.** If you want the sensor to actually live on the door (and not on the breadboard), unplug it from rows 3-5 and use 3 female-to-male jumper wires instead. The female (cup) ends slide over the sensor's 3 pins; the male (pin) ends push into rows B3, B4, B5 just like before. Now the sensor can sit a foot away from the rest of the build. Why this matters: the SW-420 only fires when it physically shakes. If you leave it flat on the desk, banging on the door will not jiggle it. Tape it to the **inside** of the door with a strip of double-sided foam tape, near the top, where the door flexes the most. The little blue square on the module is a tuning screw. Turn it gently with a tiny screwdriver to set how big a knock has to be: turn one way and a light tap fires it, turn the other way and only a real bang counts. Plan to fiddle with this for a minute once everything is running. Aim for "real knock = counts, walking past = does not count."
**Step 8 - Add the reset button.** The small white-pin button is a 4-pin tactile switch. It has 4 legs that come out in pairs from two sides. The two legs on one side are always connected together inside the button; same for the other side. When you press the button, **all four** become connected. So the rule is simple: pick **two legs that are diagonally across from each other** (not next to each other). Wiring across the diagonal is foolproof - it will always work. - Press the button down so its legs straddle the breadboard's middle gap, with one leg in A8. - Wire from A8 to the Uno's **D10** pin (use a male-to-male jumper). - Wire from the diagonally-opposite leg of the button (the leg on the **other side** of the middle gap, one row away) to the blue ground rail. When the button is not pressed, the Uno keeps the D10 pin gently held at 5V on its own (the code turns on a little built-in helper for that called INPUT_PULLUP). When you press the button, D10 gets dragged down to ground, and the code sees that and resets the knock counter back to 0.
**Final check before plugging anything in.** - Red 5V rail goes to: MB102 5V output, Uno 5V pin, SW-420 VCC (row B3). That is it. - Blue ground rail goes to: MB102 GND output, Uno GND pin, SW-420 GND (row B4), both COM pins of the digit (E16 and F16), and one diagonal leg of the reset button. - Uno pins D2-D8 each go through their own 220 ohm resistor to one segment of the digit. - Uno pin D9 goes to the SW-420's signal pin (DO). - Uno pin D10 goes to one leg of the reset button. - The decimal-point pin (pin 5) of the digit is left empty. If a segment never lights up, the most likely fix is that its resistor is in the wrong row or its jumper went to the wrong Uno pin - trace that one wire from end to end. If the whole digit is dark, check that **both** COM pins (E16 and F16) reach the blue ground rail. ## Flash it and run it You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free download from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **One-time setup:** the Uno is supported out of the box - no extra board package needed. No extra libraries needed either; this sketch uses only built-in functions. **Every time you flash:** 1. Plug the Uno into your laptop with a **USB-A to USB-B cable** (the big square port on the Uno end). The green "ON" LED on the Uno should light up. 2. In the Arduino IDE: **Tools -> Board -> Arduino AVR Boards -> Arduino Uno**. 3. **Tools -> Port** and pick the one that just appeared (looks like `COM4` on Windows, `/dev/cu.usbmodemXXXX` on a Mac). If you only see one option, that's it. 4. No WiFi names or passwords to fill in - this sketch is offline. 5. Click **Upload** (the right-arrow icon top-left). You should see "Compiling..." then "Uploading..." then "Done uploading." The TX/RX LEDs flicker during the upload. 6. Now hook up the wall-wart so the MB102 is powering the rails. The digit lights up showing **0**. Knock on the door (or tap the SW-420 module gently). The number ticks to 1. Knock again, 2. Keep going to 9. Knock once more and it stays at 9 - that's the ceiling of one digit. Press the reset button: the digit drops back to 0. 7. Open **Tools -> Serial Monitor**, set baud to **115200**. You'll see lines like `Knock! Total = 3` every time a knock counts. **Common gotchas:** - **The digit is dim or some segments look weak.** Either you skipped a resistor, used different values for different segments, or the MB102 voltage jumpers are set to 3.3V on the wrong side. Confirm all seven segments go through a **220R** resistor and the MB102 says 5V on the rail feeding the digit. - **The number is upside-down or showing the wrong shape.** You have a couple of segment wires swapped. Look at which segment is on when you expect a different one, and re-pin the offender. The segment labels (a-g) are standard - "a" is the top bar, "g" is the middle bar, and they go round clockwise b-c-d-e-f. - **The count ticks up by itself with no one touching the door.** The SW-420 is too sensitive. Twist the blue trimpot clockwise a small amount. Conversely, if real knocks don't register, turn it counter-clockwise. - **The count jumps by 2 or 3 on a single knock.** The spring is rattling many times. The sketch already has a 250 ms "ignore further knocks" cooldown after each count, but you can bump that higher (try 400 ms) if your door rings like a bell. - **Reset button does nothing.** You probably wired two legs that are internally shorted on the same side of the switch. Tactile buttons have **two pairs** of pins - the pair across the long axis is the actual switch. Re-wire across the long axis. ## Talking points - **Why "common cathode":** all 7 of the little segment LEDs share their GND leg inside the chip and bring it out on the COM pins. That means we only need to ground COM once, and each segment becomes a single positive wire we can switch on or off independently. The other style, common anode, would have us writing LOW to turn things on - same idea, mirror image. - **Why 7 resistors and not one:** an LED draws as much current as it's offered until it dies. If we shared one resistor across all 7 segments, displaying "1" (only 2 segments on) would push each of those 2 segments at half the resistor's design current, but "8" (7 segments on) would split it 7 ways and the digit would look much dimmer. One resistor per segment means each segment gets the same brightness no matter what number we show. - **Edge detection:** we count a knock only on the *moment* the SW-420 pin drops from HIGH to LOW, not for every loop where it stays LOW. Without that, a single long rattle would rack up dozens of "knocks." Same idea as a button press: react to the change, not the held state. - **Debouncing:** after we count a knock, we ignore the sensor for 250 ms. That gives the spring time to stop rattling. If we didn't, a real fingertip rap (which makes the spring buzz for maybe 50-100 ms) would count as 3-5 knocks in a row. - **Why use the MB102 instead of just the Uno's USB:** the Uno's onboard regulator is fine for the LEDs, but as Andy adds more things (a buzzer, a relay, a bigger display) the MB102 handles it without complaint. Getting used to a power module now means later builds "just work" instead of getting brown-outs. ## Things to change once it works - Add a buzzer on D11 that does a short "beep!" on each counted knock. Instant feedback you can hear from the next room. - Switch the 0-9 ceiling to **rolling** (after 9, the next knock goes back to 0 and starts again). Useful as a "this kid has been told off N times today" counter. - Add a green LED that's only on when the count is 0 ("nobody has knocked yet") and a red LED that's only on when the count is 9 ("door has been mauled"). - Replace the SW-420 with a real piezo knock sensor (when one shows up in inventory) - that lets you read the *strength* of the knock as an analog value, so you can ignore tiny taps in software. - Wire up the decimal point (pin 5) and pulse it once per second so it works as a little "alive" heartbeat. ## Why this is interesting It's the first project that turns a sensor reading into something you can see across the room without a screen. A 7-segment digit is one of those parts that looks fancy but is just 7 LEDs wired into a single chip - once you understand that, you understand every alphanumeric display you'll meet later, all the way up to giant scoreboards. It also nails the two software ideas that come up in every event-driven build: edge detection (act on the *change*, not the held state) and debouncing (a noisy switch isn't lying, it's just bouncy - wait and re-check). Get those two right with a single sensor here, and every later button, knock, doorbell, tilt switch, or magnet sensor becomes "oh, same thing."
