projects.name: Paired Touch Lamps (Long-Distance High-Five)
projects.power_supply: One USB power bank feeds the CP2102 (set to 3.3V) which powers Lamp A's ESP-01S and LED. A second USB cable powers the MB102 Breadboard Power Supply Module on Lamp B's breadboard (set to 3.3V), which powers Lamp B's ESP-01S and LED.
projects.description:
**What it is**: Two tiny lamps that live in different rooms (or different houses on the same WiFi). When you press the button on Lamp A, Lamp B glows for five seconds. When you press the button on Lamp B, Lamp A glows. They never light themselves up - they only light the OTHER one. It is a silent way to say "I'm thinking of you" without picking up a phone. **Why it is fun**: You and a friend or sibling can have a secret signal. One press = "hi!". Two quick presses = a private joke. Because the two lamps look identical, it feels like magic that pushing this one makes that one light up across the house. Once it works on your home WiFi you can imagine using it with grandma's house too. ## Parts list - 2x ESP-01S WiFi Module (one for each lamp) - 1x CP2102 USB-to-TTL UART Module (used to flash both modules one at a time, then re-used as the 3.3V power source for Lamp A) - 1x MB102 Breadboard Power Supply Module (clean 3.3V rail for Lamp B - snaps onto the breadboard's red/blue rails) - 2x LED 5mm Red (the glow output, one per lamp - Red Vf ~2V matches the 220R on a 3.3V rail) - 2x Resistor 220R (current-limiting, one per LED) - 2x Tactile Push-button Switch 3x6x4.3mm (white pin) (the "touch" input, one per lamp) - 2x Resistor 10K (pull-up for each button - also doubles as the GPIO0 boot-strap pull-up) - 2x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) (one per lamp) - 1x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc - 1x Jumper Wire F-M, 20pc (to reach the ESP-01S female headers) ## Wiring notes You are building two identical lamps. Each lamp uses a tiny WiFi brain called an **ESP-01S**. When you tap the button on one lamp, the other lamp's red light glows. Magic? No - WiFi. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP-01S board:** - **VCC** = power input. The ESP-01S needs exactly **3.3V** here. 5V will fry it. Be careful. - **GND** = the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs a path back to GND. - **CH_PD** (sometimes labeled **EN**) = the "turn the radio on" pin. Must be connected to 3.3V or the chip just sits there doing nothing. - **GPIO 0** = a pin we use for the button. (It also picks "normal mode" vs "flash mode" at startup, which is why you only attach the button after flashing.) - **GPIO 2** = a pin we use for the LED. - **RX** and **TX** = the two pins the CP2102 uses to send code into the chip. After flashing, we leave them alone.
This guide walks through **Lamp A** step by step. Lamp B is exactly the same circuit on the second breadboard - we will note the one difference (the power supply) at the end. **Step 1 - Put the breadboard on the table.** The long red and blue strips running down the side of the breadboard are called the power strips. The red one will be **+3.3V**. The blue one will be **GND** (0V). Nothing is connected yet - we will plug things into the strips as we go.
**Step 2 - Bring power in from the CP2102.** The CP2102 is the little USB stick that you used to flash the chip. It can also power Lamp A. - First, find the tiny jumper on the CP2102 and make sure it is set to **3.3V**, not 5V. This is the most important step on this whole page. If it is on 5V, do not plug it in - move the jumper first. - Plug a USB cable from a power bank into the CP2102. - Run a wire from the CP2102's **3.3V output** to the red strip on the breadboard. - Run a wire from the CP2102's **GND** to the blue strip on the breadboard. Now the red strip carries 3.3V and the blue strip is at 0V. **Why this matters:** the ESP-01S is a 3.3V chip. Giving it 5V even for a second usually kills it. Always check the jumper before you plug in the USB.
**Step 3 - Plant the push-button on the breadboard.** The button has 4 legs but really it is just 2 switches in one. Push it down across the gap in the middle of the board so two legs land on row 8 left side and two legs land on row 8 right side. We will only use the two left-side legs.
**Step 4 - Add the 10K pull-up resistor for the button.** The 10K resistor has the color bands **brown-black-orange** (the small brown-black bands then an orange one). - One leg goes into row 5 (next to where we will land the GPIO 0 wire). - The other leg goes into the red 3.3V strip. **Why this matters:** the button by itself does not give the chip a clear "off" reading - the wire would just be floating. The 10K resistor gently pulls the wire up to 3.3V so the chip reads it as "off" when no one is pressing the button. When you push the button, it shorts the wire straight to GND, which is a stronger pull than the 10K, so the chip reads "on". One small resistor, two big jobs.
**Step 5 - Connect the button to GND and to the GPIO 0 line.** - Run a short wire from one of the button's left legs (row 8) over to row 5 (same row as the 10K resistor). This ties the button to the GPIO 0 line. - Run a wire from the other left leg of the button (across the gap, row 10 on the right side) down to the blue GND strip. Now: button not pressed = the GPIO 0 wire reads 3.3V. Button pressed = the GPIO 0 wire reads 0V.
**Step 6 - Add the 220R LED resistor.** The 220R resistor has the color bands **red-red-brown**. - One leg goes into the red 3.3V strip. - The other leg goes into row 15. **Why this matters:** LEDs are greedy. If you plug one straight into 3.3V it will gulp too much current and burn out in a second. The 220R resistor is a little speed bump that limits how much current can flow. We pick a **red** LED on purpose - a red LED lights up nicely at 3.3V, but a blue one would barely glow.
**Step 7 - Drop in the red LED.** Look at the LED carefully. One leg is **longer** than the other. The long leg is the one current goes IN to. The short leg (same side as the flat spot on the plastic dome) is the one current comes OUT of. - **Long leg** into row 15 (same row as the 220R resistor we just placed). - **Short leg** into row 17. Getting the legs the right way around matters - an LED only lights when current flows the correct direction. If your lamp does not light up at the end, this is the first thing to check.
**Step 8 - Plant the ESP-01S using F-M jumpers.**
The ESP-01S has 8 little female holes on the bottom (4 + 4). It will not plug into a breadboard directly. The fix: use the F-M (Female-to-Male) jumper wires. The female end clicks onto the ESP-01S pin, the male end pokes into the breadboard. Then we wire the male side using regular M-M (Male-to-Male) jumpers. Plug 5 F-M jumpers onto these ESP-01S pins, then push their male ends into the breadboard like this: - **VCC** (power input, must be 3.3V) -> breadboard row 20 - **CH_PD** (also marked EN) -> breadboard row 22 - **GND** -> breadboard row 24 - **GPIO 0** -> breadboard row 26 - **GPIO 2** -> breadboard row 28 (We will leave RX and TX disconnected. They were used to flash the code earlier; the lamp does not need them now.)
**Step 9 - Tie the ESP-01S into the circuit.** Now use 5 short M-M jumpers across the breadboard: - Row 20 (ESP VCC) -> red 3.3V strip. - Row 22 (ESP CH_PD) -> red 3.3V strip. The radio refuses to switch on unless this pin is held at 3.3V. - Row 24 (ESP GND) -> blue GND strip. - Row 26 (ESP GPIO 0) -> row 5 (joins the button + the 10K pull-up). Now the chip can "feel" the button. - Row 28 (ESP GPIO 2) -> row 17 (the short leg of the LED). Now the chip can drive the LED. **Why the LED is wired this way:** GPIO 2 is connected to the **short leg** side of the LED, and the **long leg** side gets 3.3V through the 220R resistor. To light the lamp, the code pulls GPIO 2 down to 0V - current then flows from 3.3V through the resistor, through the LED, into the chip. To turn the lamp off, the code lets GPIO 2 float back up to 3.3V, so there is no voltage difference across the LED and it switches off. We wire it this way (instead of the other way) because the ESP-01S has a rule: GPIO 2 must be HIGH at the moment power turns on, or the chip refuses to boot. Wiring the LED like this means GPIO 2 sits at 3.3V at startup automatically.
**Step 10 - Build Lamp B on the second breadboard.** Lamp B uses the exact same parts in the exact same places on its own breadboard - second ESP-01S, second LED, second 220R, second 10K, second button. **The only thing that changes is where the 3.3V power comes from.** Lamp B is powered by the **MB102 Breadboard Power Supply Module**: - Snap the MB102 onto the end of the second breadboard so its two metal pin rows plug straight into the red and blue power strips. - Find the tiny black jumpers on the MB102. There are usually two - one for each side of the board. Set BOTH to **3.3V**, not 5V. Same rule as before: 5V will fry the ESP-01S. - Plug a USB cable into the MB102's USB input (or a 9V wall plug into its barrel jack). - Press the little ON button on top of the MB102. The MB102 has its own power smoothing built in, which is helpful: when the ESP-01S sends WiFi, it takes a quick big gulp of current. The MB102 handles those gulps without the voltage dropping out.
**Final check before you power on:** - Both jumpers (CP2102 and MB102) set to **3.3V**. Not 5V. Look twice. - LED long leg in the row with the 220R resistor, short leg in the row that goes to GPIO 2. - CH_PD pin connected to the 3.3V strip. - Nothing touching that should not be touching. Plug in, watch for the lamps to come on dim, and tap the button. The far lamp should glow. High-five across the room - or across the world. ## Flash it and run it The ESP-01S has NO USB port. You flash it through the CP2102 USB-to-TTL UART Module. You flash both boards with the same CP2102, one at a time. 1. Wire the CP2102 to one ESP-01S: - CP2102 3.3V -> ESP-01S VCC and CH_PD - CP2102 GND -> ESP-01S GND - CP2102 TX -> ESP-01S RX - CP2102 RX -> ESP-01S TX - ESP-01S GPIO0 -> GND with a jumper (this puts it in flash mode) 2. In Arduino IDE, install the ESP8266 board package (File -> Preferences -> Boards Manager URL `http://arduino.esp8266.com/stable/package_esp8266com_index.json`, then Boards Manager -> "esp8266"). Pick board "Generic ESP8266 Module", Flash Size "1MB (FS:64KB OTA:~470KB)". 3. Open the sketch. At the top there is a constant called `MY_ROLE`. Set it to `ROLE_A` and flash Lamp 1. Then change it to `ROLE_B` and flash Lamp 2. They run the SAME sketch with one flag flipped. 4. Unplug, remove the GPIO0-to-GND flash-mode jumper (so GPIO0 reads HIGH at boot through its 10K pull-up), plug the CP2102 back in, open the Serial Monitor at 115200. You should see "Lamp A booted, IP = ..." and "mDNS started as lampa.local" within 10 seconds. 5. That is it. No second re-flash needed. Each lamp finds the other by name (`lampa.local` / `lampb.local`) using mDNS, so you never have to type an IP address. Common gotchas: - 5V on VCC will kill the ESP-01S instantly. Triple-check before plugging in. - If the Serial Monitor shows weird garbage characters, the baud rate is wrong - set it to 115200. - Flashing fails? GPIO0 was not held LOW at boot. Disconnect, move the jumper, reconnect. - Lamp boots but never lights or stays lit at boot? Double-check the LED is wired anode-to-3.3V (active-LOW). If you accidentally wire it cathode-to-GND with anode on GPIO2 you re-introduce the boot-strap problem. - WiFi never connects? The SSID and password are case-sensitive. Also the ESP-01S does NOT speak 5GHz - your router must broadcast a 2.4GHz network with the same name. - One lamp lights itself when pressed? That means it is pinging its OWN hostname. Make sure you flashed each board with the right `MY_ROLE` value. - mDNS not resolving from one lamp to the other? Some home routers block mDNS between WiFi clients. Try plugging in again, or fall back to typing the IP shown in the Serial Monitor into `peerHost()`. ## Talking points - Both lamps run the EXACT same sketch. The only difference is one constant (`MY_ROLE`). This is how real-world products often work: same firmware, different config. - The LED is wired **active-LOW** (the pin idles HIGH and pulls LOW to turn the LED on). On the ESP-01S this is not just a style choice - GPIO2 must be HIGH at boot or the chip refuses to start, so active-LOW is the safe wiring. - The 10K resistor on GPIO0 is doing two jobs at once: it pulls GPIO0 HIGH at boot (so the chip enters normal run mode, not flash mode), AND it is the pull-up for the button so the line does not "float" between HIGH and LOW. - mDNS means each lamp announces itself on the LAN as `lampa.local` / `lampb.local`. We never have to look up or hard-code an IP address - the names just work. ## Things to change once it works - Change the glow time from 5 seconds to 30 seconds in `GLOW_MS`. - Add a "double-tap" pattern: two quick presses make the OTHER lamp blink three times instead of glowing steady. - Swap one Red LED for a Yellow LED so the two ends feel like a "set" (Yellow Vf is also ~2V, so the 220R stays correct). - Add a small piezo buzzer on a second GPIO that chirps when the OTHER lamp pings YOU (so you notice even if you are not looking at the lamp). - Move from polling-each-press to a tiny pattern: hold the button for two seconds to send "long press" and make the peer fade slowly instead of snapping on. ## Why this is interesting This is your first project where two computers TALK to each other over WiFi. One pushes, the other reacts. That is the core of every chat app, every smart-home switch, every multiplayer game. We are doing it with twelve dollars of parts and a hundred lines of code, and the two lamps find each other by name with no hand-coded addresses.

projects.name: Pan-and-Tilt Joystick Cam
projects.power_supply: 12V wall-wart (or 9V battery pack) into the 6-24V-to-5V buck converter; buck USB output feeds the MB102 USB input, MB102 5V rail powers the two servos, the ESP32-CAM and the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S. All grounds tied.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little camera on a wobbly head that you aim with a joystick. Twist or push the stick and the camera turns left/right and up/down. Open a web page on a phone or laptop and you see whatever the camera is looking at, live. **Why it is fun**: It is your own spy-cam turret. Point it at the hallway and catch someone sneaking past. Aim it at the cat. Hand the joystick to your sister and let her drive it from across the room while you film yourself doing a silly dance. ## Parts list - 1x ESP32-CAM (bare module) - the camera that streams video over WiFi - 1x ESP32-CAM with MB programmer base - borrow the carrier just to flash the bare module, then move the bare module to the project - 1x ESP32 NodeMCU-32S - reads the joystick (TWO real ADC pins, no mux trickery) and drives both servos - 1x WH148 10K Stereo Potentiometer (B10K) - the joystick: one shaft, two independent wipers - 2x SG90 Servo (9g micro) - one pans (left/right), one tilts (up/down) - 1x MB102 Breadboard Power Supply Module - clean 5V rail for both servos and the camera - 1x 6-24V to 5V 3A USB Buck Converter - steps a 9-12V wall-wart down to a fat 5V, feeds the MB102 via USB-A-to-USB-A (or a USB-A to bare-wire pigtail into the MB102 USB input) - 1x Capacitor 1000uF (electrolytic, mixed voltage) - sits right on the ESP32-CAM's 5V/GND pins to soak up the brownout dips when the camera transmits - 1x Breadboard 4.5x9.5cm (~400 tie-points) - the build surface - 1x Jumper Wire M-M, 40pc - wiper-to-ESP32, signal wires, rail jumps - 1x Jumper Wire F-M, 20pc - female ends connect the servo plugs to the breadboard ## Wiring notes **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S board:** - **5V** - the pin that gives back the 5V coming in from the USB cable. We will feed 5V back IN here later. - **3V3** - a clean 3.3V power pin the ESP32 makes for itself. We use this for the joystick. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part has to share this. - **D13, D12, D34, D35** - signal pins. The numbers on the silver letters (silkscreen) match the GPIO numbers in the code. - **D34 and D35** are "read only" pins. They can listen to a voltage, but they cannot push power out. Perfect for reading a joystick.
**Step 1 - Power in: wall-wart to buck converter.** - Plug the 12V wall-wart (or a 9V battery pack) into the buck converter's input screws. **+** to **IN+**, **-** to **IN-**. - The buck converter is a tiny machine that takes any voltage from 6V up to 24V and turns it into a clean 5V on its USB-A port. - Out comes 5V on the USB-A socket on the other end. We will use that next. **Why this matters:** Servos and ESP32 chips want exactly 5V, no more. If you feed 12V straight in, you cook them. The buck converter is the bouncer at the door, only letting 5V through.
**Step 2 - Drop the breadboard and MB102 power module onto it.**
- Snap the MB102 power module down onto the breadboard so its pins line up with the long red and blue strips running down the side (those strips are called the power rails - red is 5V, blue is 0V/ground). - **Set BOTH little jumpers on the MB102 to the 5V position.** This tells the MB102 to make both rails 5V. - Take a short USB-A cable and plug one end into the buck converter's USB-A port, the other end into the MB102's USB input socket. - Flick the MB102's power switch ON. The red LED should light up. **Why this matters:** The MB102 is the "wall outlet" for your breadboard. The red rail is now 5V everywhere along the whole strip, so anything you plug into that rail gets 5V power.
**Step 3 - One ground for everybody (the most important rule).** - Use a male-to-male jumper to tie the top blue ground rail to the bottom blue ground rail. Now both blue strips are the same 0V. - Every single ground pin in this project - the ESP32 GND, the camera GND, both servo brown wires, both joystick bottom pins - will plug into one of these blue strips. **Why this matters:** If even one part has its own "different" ground, signals get confused. Servos will twitch, the camera will reboot, and you will spend an hour wondering why. One shared ground = one happy circuit.
**Step 4 - Plug in the ESP32 NodeMCU-32S.** - Press the ESP32 down across the middle gap of the breadboard so each side of pins is in its own row. - Run a jumper from the pin marked **5V** on the ESP32 to the red rail (5V). - Run a jumper from the pin marked **GND** on the ESP32 to the blue rail (ground). - For now, also plug the laptop's micro-USB cable into the ESP32's little silver USB socket. We will flash the code that way the first time. **Why this matters:** The ESP32 has TWO ways to get power - the USB cable, OR the 5V pin. Once flashed, you can unplug the laptop and the MB102's 5V rail will keep it running.
**Step 5 - Plug in the joystick (a stacked dual potentiometer).** The WH148 has 6 pins because it is really TWO knobs stacked on one shaft. Gang A is the X-axis (left/right), Gang B is the Y-axis (up/down). Each gang has 3 pins: top, middle (wiper), bottom. - Push Gang A's three pins into row 10 (positions A10, B10, C10) and Gang B's three pins into row 15 (A15, B15, C15). - **Gang A top (A10)** -> ESP32 pin marked **3V3** (3.3V power). - **Gang A wiper (C10)** -> ESP32 pin marked **D34** (this is GPIO34, an input-only pin). - **Gang A bottom (E10)** -> blue ground rail. - **Gang B top (A15)** -> ESP32 **3V3** again. - **Gang B wiper (C15)** -> ESP32 pin marked **D35** (GPIO35, also input-only). - **Gang B bottom (E15)** -> blue ground rail. **Why this matters:** Each gang is just a small adjustable voltage maker. When you tilt the joystick, the wiper slides and the voltage changes between 0V and 3.3V. The ESP32 reads that voltage and figures out which way you tilted. We feed it 3.3V (not 5V) because the ESP32's reading pins can only handle up to 3.3V safely.
**Step 6 - Plug in the Pan servo (the bottom one).** The SG90 servo has three wires: orange (signal), red (power), brown (ground). - **Orange** -> ESP32 pin marked **D13** (a fast on-off signal pin). - **Red** -> red rail (5V from MB102). - **Brown** -> blue rail (ground). This servo will spin left and right to PAN the camera (swing it side to side).
**Step 7 - Plug in the Tilt servo (riding on top of the Pan servo).** Same idea, different signal pin. - **Orange** -> ESP32 pin marked **D12**. - **Red** -> red rail (5V). - **Brown** -> blue rail (ground). This servo will TILT the camera up and down. The trick is mounting it: glue or screw it onto the horn (the little white star) of the Pan servo, so when the Pan moves, the Tilt rides along.
**Step 8 - The ESP32-CAM and its big calming capacitor.**
- Tape the ESP32-CAM module to the white horn of the Tilt servo so the lens points forward. Cellophane tape is fine. - Wire CAM pin **5V** to the red rail (5V). - Wire CAM pin **GND** to the blue rail (ground). - Now grab the big silver-can 1000uF capacitor. It has a **long leg (+)** and a **short leg (-)**. There is also a white stripe on the body next to the short leg. - Push the **long leg** into the same row as the CAM's 5V wire (A22 area). Push the **short leg** into the same row as the CAM's GND wire (A24 area). It should sit right next to the camera. **Why this matters:** When the camera's WiFi radio fires up, it suddenly grabs a huge gulp of current. Without help, the 5V rail dips, and the camera resets and the servos jerk. The 1000uF capacitor is a tiny battery that fills the dip for the half-second the WiFi needs. Plug it in BACKWARDS and it can leak or pop - so double check: long leg to +, short leg to ground.
**Step 9 - Flashing the ESP32-CAM (a two-stage trick).** The bare ESP32-CAM has no USB socket. To upload code, slide it onto the MB programmer base (the little black sled with a USB port). Plug a USB cable from the laptop into the MB programmer, hit upload, and once it says Done, **pop the camera off the MB base** and slot it back into your project breadboard wiring. You only need the programmer base for flashing. After that, the project's 5V rail powers it.
**Step 10 - Final tidy with female-to-male jumpers for the servos.** The servo wires end in little female sockets. Use female-to-male jumpers so the female end plugs onto the servo's three pins and the male end pokes into the breadboard. Three jumpers per servo, six total.
**Step 11 - Warmup and power budget check.** The MB102 can deliver about 700-800mA on the 5V rail before it sags. Two SG90 servos straining at the same time plus the CAM's WiFi kick can briefly go over that. The 1000uF capacitor smooths the spikes, but if you ever see the camera reboot: - Move the joystick more gently (the code already has a slow loop and a deadband, but you can slow it more). - Never grab both servos with your fingers and force them at the same time - that makes them pull lots of current. - If you really push the project, swap the MB102 for a stronger 5V supply.
## Flash it and run it **Two boards, two sketches** - flash them one at a time. **Sketch 1 - ESP32 NodeMCU-32S (the controller):** 1. Open Arduino IDE. File -> Preferences -> Additional Boards Manager URLs - add the Espressif ESP32 URL if not present. Boards Manager -> install **esp32** by Espressif Systems. 2. Tools -> Board -> **ESP32 Dev Module** (or "NodeMCU-32S" if listed). Port: whichever COM appears when you plug it in. Upload speed 921600 is fine. 3. Paste the controller sketch from the code section. Edit `WIFI_PASS` to your real WiFi password (SSID is already "GeeFam"). Upload. 4. Open Serial Monitor at 115200 baud. After about 5-15 seconds you should see `Controller IP: 192.168.x.x` and `mDNS: http://panctl.local/`. 5. Test: move the joystick. Both servos should respond smoothly. If one axis is reversed, swap the two outer pins on that gang of the pot (top/bottom). **Sketch 2 - ESP32-CAM (the streamer, using the stock example - much simpler than rolling your own):** 1. Push the bare ESP32-CAM module firmly into the **MB programmer base**. The base has the USB port, the auto-reset circuitry, and (on most MB boards) a built-in switch that grounds IO0 during programming. **Check your MB base**: if it has a tiny slide switch labelled "FLASH/RUN" or "PROG/COMM", set it to FLASH/PROG before upload. If it just has a button, hold the IO0 button down while you plug in the USB. Many MB carriers auto-handle it - if upload starts without you doing anything, you're done. 2. Arduino IDE -> Tools -> Board -> **AI Thinker ESP32-CAM**. Port: the MB's USB COM. 3. **File -> Examples -> ESP32 -> Camera -> CameraWebServer**. This is the official stock example - already correct, already PSRAM-aware, much shorter than a hand-rolled MJPEG handler. 4. At the top of the example, change: - `#define CAMERA_MODEL_AI_THINKER` (uncomment this line) - Comment out the other `CAMERA_MODEL_*` lines - `const char* ssid = "GeeFam";` - `const char* password = "PASSWORD_HERE";` 5. Upload. If your MB base has the slide switch, flip it back to RUN/COMM after upload completes and tap RST. 6. Open Serial Monitor at 115200. Note the **Camera IP**. Stock CameraWebServer prints something like `Camera Ready! Use 'http://192.168.x.x' to connect`. 7. Unplug, lift the bare CAM out of the MB, push it into your project breadboard wiring (5V, GND, that's it - no UART pins needed once flashed). Power on - it will rejoin WiFi and stream. **Finding both IPs the easy way:** the controller advertises itself as `http://panctl.local/` over mDNS - open that in any browser on the same WiFi and you'll see the controller status page, which also displays the **last known camera IP** if the CAM has registered itself by hitting `/register`. (The stock CameraWebServer does not register, so the first time round just grab the camera's IP from its Serial Monitor and bookmark it. After that, the controller page links to it.) **Common gotchas:** - *Servos twitching nonstop*: GNDs are not tied together. Run a jumper from MB102 GND to ESP32 GND. - *ESP32 resets when servos move*: you are powering the ESP32 from the same flimsy USB the laptop gives. Either power it from the MB102 5V rail (via the ESP32's 5V pin) or keep the laptop USB - but not run servos off the ESP32's 5V pin. - *ESP32-CAM keeps rebooting on WiFi join*: brownout. Check the 1000uF capacitor is actually wired right across the CAM's 5V/GND pins (long leg to +5V). - *Camera page is blank or 'Camera init failed'*: your specific board lacks PSRAM. In the stock example, find the `if(psramFound())` block and let it pick the smaller frame size automatically - it already handles this. If still failing, set `config.frame_size = FRAMESIZE_QQVGA;` and `config.fb_count = 1;` manually. - *MB programmer base won't enter flash mode*: hold the IO0 button while pressing RST, release RST, release IO0 - that's the universal fallback even if the auto-reset circuit is flaky. - *One axis flips backwards*: swap `top` and `bottom` on that gang of the pot, or in code change `map(raw, 0, 4095, 10, 170)` to `map(raw, 4095, 0, 10, 170)` for that axis. - *Stream stutters*: drop the frame size to QVGA (320x240) in the stock example, or move closer to the WiFi router. ## Talking points - A single shaft can carry two completely independent signals - that is what "stereo" or "dual gang" means inside the WH148. We read both at the same time because the ESP32 has more than one ADC pin. - The ESP32-CAM speaks **MJPEG**: it sends one tiny JPEG after another really fast. Your browser flips through them like a flipbook. - Servos understand a 50 Hz pulse - the ESP32Servo library hides that for us. - **Two computers, one WiFi**: the controller and the camera don't share a wire. They both join your home network and your phone is the third device watching both. - A big **decoupling capacitor** is a tiny battery sitting right next to a hungry chip. When the WiFi radio bursts, the cap delivers the spike instead of the long thin wire from the power supply sagging. ## Things to change once it works - Add a third axis (a second pot) for digital zoom-by-cropping in the browser - the stock CameraWebServer already has a resolution dropdown. - Replace the pot with the **Joystick Module (2-axis + button)** - smoother feel, and the button can be a "snap photo" trigger. - Add an LED on the camera for dark hallways (the CAM has a flash GPIO on pin 4 - the stock example already toggles it via the web UI). - Make the controller page embed the CAM stream in an `` tag so you only ever open one URL. - Auto-track motion: have the CAM detect movement in software and POST direction hints to the controller's `/nudge` endpoint. ## Why this is interesting This is two computers cooperating over WiFi - they don't share a single wire. That is the whole pattern of "edge devices": small specialised brains that talk to each other instead of one big brain doing everything. You also see how cheap a real CCTV camera actually is - the streamer is one $6 board.

projects.name: Cat-Bowl Watcher (live cam + tap-to-treat relay)
projects.power_supply: 12V wall-wart into the MB102's barrel jack feeds the breadboard rails; the 6-24V buck converter taps the 12V rail and outputs a USB-A 5V plug that powers the ESP32-CAM and the ESP-01S Relay through short USB / jumper hops.
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little camera spies on the cat's food bowl and shows the live picture on a phone web page, with a big green DISPENSE TREAT button. Tap the button and a relay across the room clicks loudly, lighting a bright red "treat fired" LED on the dispenser to tell the cat that a snack is on the way. **Why it is fun**: It is a real-deal spy-cam-plus-remote-button, just like a smart pet feeder in the shops, but you built it. You can show your friends a live picture of the cat from anywhere in the house, then make a relay CLACK across the room from your phone like a wizard. The cat learns the click means snack time and comes running before you even fill the bowl. ## Parts list - 1x ESP32-CAM with MB programmer base (the camera + the snap-on MB board used to flash it) - 1x ESP-01S 5V Relay Module (Tasmota-ready) (the WiFi relay that "fires the treat") - 1x 6-24V to 5V 3A USB Buck Converter (turns 12V into a clean 5V USB output for both boards) - 1x MB102 Breadboard Power Supply Module (snaps onto the breadboard rails, gives 5V/GND everywhere) - 1x Red 5mm LED + 1x 330R resistor (lights up bright when the relay fires - the visible "treat dispensed" indicator) - 1x Breadboard, jumper wires - A 12V wall-wart with a 5.5/2.1mm barrel plug (the regular MB102 input) - A spare USB-A to micro-USB cable (or USB-A breakout pigtail) to take 5V from the buck converter into the ESP32-CAM's 5V pin Note on the "12V vibration motor": the original sketch called for a small 12V vibration motor wedged under a treat hopper. Our inventory does not yet have one, so for the first build we wire the relay to a bright red LED that lives next to the bowl. When you do get a motor (or a tiny DC fan, or a 5V buzzer), just unplug the LED and plug the motor in its place - the rest of the project does not change. The relay is rated for low-voltage DC loads only - NEVER use it for anything plugged into the wall. ## Wiring notes This build uses two little computers that team up. The **ESP32-CAM** is the eye - it has a tiny camera and sends video to your phone or laptop. The **ESP-01S Relay** is the hand - it has a switch inside that the ESP32-CAM can tell to click ON or OFF over WiFi. When you tap a button on the web page, the switch clicks and the red LED lights up (that's the "treat" signal). **Quick glossary - words you will see on these boards:** - **5V** - the power input. Anything labelled 5V wants 5 volts coming in. - **GND** - the 0V side, called ground. Every part needs a GND wire to finish the circle. - **VIN** - "voltage in" - another name for the power input pin. - **COM / NO / NC** - the three screw terminals on the relay. COM is the common pin, NO means "Normally Open" (off until the relay clicks), NC means "Normally Closed" (on until the relay clicks). We use COM and NO. - **Rail** - the long red or blue strip running down the side of the breadboard. The red strip carries power, the blue strip carries ground.
**Step 1 - Set up the breadboard and the power module.**
- Push the **MB102 power module** down onto one end of the breadboard so its pins straddle the middle gap. - Find the two jumpers on the MB102 (little plastic caps). Set the side we are using to **5V**. The other side can be left OFF. - Plug the 12V wall-wart into the MB102's round barrel jack (do not turn it on yet). - Run a red M-M jumper wire from **row A2** (the MB102's 12V-in pin) to the **top red rail**. - Run a black M-M jumper wire from **row A4** (the MB102's GND-in pin) to the **top blue rail**. This step lights up the breadboard's top rails with 12V so the buck converter (next step) has power to munch on. Do not power up yet - finish the wiring first.
**Step 2 - Add the buck converter (the clean 5V maker).** - Place the **buck converter** further down the breadboard near row J2. - Run a red M-M jumper from **J2** (the converter's VIN+, its power input) back up to **row A2** so it grabs the 12V. - Run a black M-M jumper from **J4** (the converter's VIN-, its ground) back to **row A4**. **Why this matters:** The ESP32-CAM gets very thirsty for a split second when the WiFi turns on. If you feed it from the MB102's regular 5V, the voltage dips and the camera will reboot over and over. The buck converter is a strong, steady 5V helper that can handle those big gulps without flinching. It takes the 12V coming in and turns it into a clean 5V that comes out of its USB-A socket.
**Step 3 - Wire up the ESP32-CAM with its programmer base.** - Slot the **ESP32-CAM into its MB programmer base** (it just plugs in - line up the pins and press gently). - Place the whole MB base on the breadboard so its 5V pin lands at **J13** and its GND pin lands at **J15**. - Run a red M-M jumper from **J7** (the buck converter's USB 5V output pin) to **J13** (the ESP32-CAM 5V input). - Run a black M-M jumper from **J9** (the buck converter's USB GND) to **J15** (the ESP32-CAM GND). The MB base accepts 5V and quietly turns it into the 3.3V the camera chip actually needs inside. Always feed the 5V pin, never the 3.3V pin - the 3.3V pin would let the smoke out.
**Step 4 - Wire up the ESP-01S relay module.** - Place the **ESP-01S Relay module** further along the breadboard so its VCC pin lands at **J19**. - Run a red F-M jumper from **J7** (the same buck converter 5V output) to **J19** (the relay's VCC, its power input). - Run a black F-M jumper from **J9** (buck converter GND) to **J21** (the relay's GND). Now both little boards are sharing the buck converter's clean 5V. The relay module already has a tiny ESP-01S chip on it that is pre-flashed with Tasmota software, so it knows how to listen for click commands over WiFi.
**Step 5 - Build the "treat" indicator (LED + resistor on the relay output).**
- Find the **330 ohm resistor** (color bands: orange, orange, brown, gold). Resistors are not picky about direction. - Plug one leg of the resistor into the **bottom red rail** (the 5V side) and the other leg into **row F22**. - Take the **red LED**. The long leg is the positive side, the short leg is the negative side. - Plug the long leg into **row G22** (so it sits right next to the resistor in the same row). - Plug the short leg into **row G24**. - Run a yellow F-M jumper from **J24** (the relay's COM screw terminal) to **G24** (the LED's short leg). - Run a black F-M jumper from **J26** (the relay's NO screw terminal) to the **bottom blue rail** (GND). **Why the resistor matters:** an LED is greedy - if you connect it straight to 5V it will gulp too much electricity and pop in a flash. The 330 ohm resistor is like a narrow straw that lets only the right sip through, so the LED glows nicely instead of burning out. How the indicator works: 5V comes through the resistor, through the LED, into COM. When the relay is OFF, nothing happens - the circle is broken inside the relay. When you tap the button in the web page and Tasmota closes the relay, COM connects to NO, the circle finishes at the GND rail, and the LED snaps on. Click again and the relay opens, the LED goes dark.
**Step 6 - Final check and power-on.**
- Look over every wire one more time. Red goes to red (power). Black goes to black (ground). No red touching black anywhere except through a part. - Make sure the LED's long leg is on the resistor side (G22) and the short leg is on the GND side (G24). A backwards LED just stays dark - not dangerous, just confusing. - Plug the 12V wall-wart into the wall. You should see the MB102's little power light come on, then the buck converter's light, then in a few seconds the ESP32-CAM's red LED. **Tune note:** the ESP32-CAM is a tricky one - it sometimes takes 10 to 20 seconds to join WiFi the first time. Be patient. Once it shows up on your network, open its web page on your phone or laptop. You will see a live picture of the cat bowl and a button labelled "Treat!" - tap it and you should hear a tiny click from the relay and see the red LED flash on. That click is what would normally fire a treat dispenser. For now, the LED is your test treat. ## Flash it and run it You have to flash TWO boards: the ESP32-CAM gets your sketch (camera + web UI), and the ESP-01S Relay is already Tasmota out of the box, so it only needs WiFi setup, no Arduino IDE. You need a laptop running the **Arduino IDE 2.x** (free from [arduino.cc](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software)). **Part A - Flash the ESP32-CAM (the camera):** *One-time setup (only the first time you ever flash an ESP32):* 1. File -> Preferences -> Additional Boards Manager URLs, add: `https://espressif.github.io/arduino-esp32/package_esp32_index.json` 2. Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager, search "esp32" by Espressif, click Install. *Every time you flash:* 1. Snap the ESP32-CAM onto the MB programmer base if it is not already. 2. Plug a USB cable from your laptop into the MB base's USB port. The red power LED on the MB lights. 3. Tools -> Board -> ESP32 Arduino -> **AI Thinker ESP32-CAM**. 4. Tools -> Port -> pick the COM port that appeared when you plugged the MB in. 5. Tools -> Partition Scheme -> **Huge APP (3MB No OTA / 1MB SPIFFS)** (the default Default fails: camera library is too big). 6. Open the Cat-Bowl Watcher sketch. Edit the WiFi password to your real one. Edit `RELAY_IP` to whatever IP your relay grabs in Part B (you may need to come back here after Part B). 7. Click **Upload**. Wait for "Hard resetting via RTS pin." 8. **Important:** the MB base flashes the camera by holding the BOOT pin low automatically - if your MB does not do this, you may need to press and hold the IO0 button on the back of the MB while you click Upload, then let go after the upload starts. Most modern MBs handle this on their own. 9. Open Tools -> Serial Monitor at **115200 baud**. You should see `Camera ready` and an IP address like `http://192.168.1.123`. Type that into your phone's browser - the live camera page appears with a big DISPENSE TREAT button. **Part B - Bring the ESP-01S Relay Module online:** The ESP-01S Relay arrives pre-flashed with **Tasmota** - you do NOT need to compile or upload anything. You just connect it to WiFi. 1. Power the relay module from the buck converter's 5V/GND (DO NOT plug a separate adapter on top of this). 2. On your phone, open the WiFi list. You will see a new network called something like `tasmota-XXXX-1234`. Connect to it - no password. 3. Your phone will pop up a captive portal page. Tap **Configuration -> Configure WiFi**, type SSID `GeeFam` and your password, **Save**. 4. The relay reboots and joins your home WiFi. To find its IP: log in to your router admin page and look for `tasmota-XXXX`, OR just open the Tasmota app, OR scan your network with the "Fing" app on your phone. 5. Write that IP down. Open it in a browser - the Tasmota web UI appears. Click the big **Toggle** button. You should hear the relay click and see the LED on the breadboard turn on/off. Test passed! 6. Now go back to Part A step 6 and put that relay IP into the ESP32-CAM sketch, then re-upload. **Common gotchas:** - **CP2102 / 3.3V rule for ESP-01S modules.** The ESP-01S itself (separate from the relay board) is a 3.3V module, NOT 5V. To flash a bare ESP-01S you need a **CP2102 USB-to-TTL UART Module** set to **3.3V** logic, never 5V - 5V will kill the chip. The ESP-01S **5V Relay Module (Tasmota-ready)** in this project is different: it has its own regulator on the carrier board, so you feed the carrier 5V and it makes 3.3V for the ESP-01S internally. You only need the CP2102 if you want to RE-flash the ESP-01S yourself; out of the box it is already Tasmota and you just configure WiFi from a browser. - **ESP32-CAM keeps rebooting on every photo.** That means the 5V supply is sagging. Make sure you are using the 6-24V to 5V 3A buck converter (not the MB102 rails alone) and that your USB cable is a real data/power cable, not a charging-only one. - **`Brownout detector was triggered` in Serial Monitor.** Same root cause as above - underpowered 5V. - **The relay clicks but the LED never lights.** Swap the LED leads - the long leg (anode) must point toward the resistor / 5V side, short leg toward the COM terminal. - **Camera image is upside-down.** In the sketch, change `s->set_vflip(s, 1);` to `0` (or `1` if it was `0`). Same for `s->set_hmirror(s, 1);` if it is mirrored left/right. - **"Failed to connect" / `Camera init failed`.** Almost always wrong board picked (must be `AI Thinker ESP32-CAM`) or wrong partition scheme (must be `Huge APP`). ## Talking points - **WiFi is just a wire that goes through the air.** Your phone, the ESP32-CAM, and the relay all live on the same WiFi network. They send each other little notes ("HTTP requests") that look like `GET /dispense`. The relay reads the note and does the thing. - **One device, many faces.** The ESP32-CAM is doing FOUR things at once: capturing JPEG frames, running a tiny web server, serving an HTML page, AND firing off HTTP requests to the relay. A 5-dollar chip from 2017 multitasking like a champ. - **The relay is "dry contact" - it does not care what is on the other side.** Today it is an LED. Tomorrow it could be a 9V buzzer, a tiny DC fan, a 12V vibration motor for a real treat dispenser, an automatic cat-flap. The relay is the bridge between the digital world (`HIGH`/`LOW`) and the physical world (current flowing through stuff). - **Tasmota is firmware - software that lives on the chip and turns it into a smart-home gadget.** It comes pre-installed on this relay module so you can skip the Arduino IDE step entirely. Many smart bulbs and smart plugs from the shop run Tasmota under the hood (or can be reflashed with it). - **Camera streaming uses MJPEG**, which is a fast way to send "many JPEGs in a row" instead of a real video. That is why the picture looks a tiny bit choppy compared to YouTube - real video uses fancier compression that the little ESP32 cannot do in real-time. ## Things to change once it works - **Add a real vibration motor.** When the next parts order arrives with a 12V coin-vibration motor, unplug the LED and put the motor across COM and NO instead. The relay clicks for one second and the motor buzzes a treat down the hopper. - **Add a timer**: have the relay only stay closed for 800 ms instead of toggle-on / toggle-off. Tasmota's "PulseTime" setting does this without any code change. `http:///cm?cmnd=PulseTime%208` (= 0.8 s). - **Snap a photo when the button is pressed** instead of streaming continuously. The ESP32-CAM page can write the latest frame to SD card with a `?save=1` URL parameter, so you build a log of "every time I gave the cat a treat, here is what the bowl looked like." - **Two cats, two buttons.** Pair this with a second ESP-01S Relay and a second LED - one button per cat, treats only on their side of the kitchen. - **Motion-trigger instead of manual press.** Use the camera's built-in motion detection (or pair the PIR sensor from another project) - dispense a treat automatically when the cat sits in front of the bowl for 5 seconds. - **Phone notification when the bowl is empty.** Image-process the frame on the ESP32-CAM (compare the brightness in the bowl region) and POST to a Pushbullet / IFTTT webhook when it goes white-empty. ## Why this is interesting You have built the canonical Internet-of-Things loop: **sensor -> internet -> action**. The camera is the sensor (vision), the WiFi is the internet (transport), and the relay is the action (the world changing). Add a screen and a microphone and you have invented a Nest doorbell. Add a thermostat and a heating element and you have invented a smart kettle. The pattern - read state, expose it on a web page, accept a command, drive a relay - is exactly what every smart-home product on Earth does. Most of them just have nicer plastic. The two boards each cost less than a coffee, talk over standard HTTP (the same protocol your browser uses to read Wikipedia), and the relay does not even need code because Tasmota does it all. Once a kid sees that they can build a "spy on the cat + send a treat" gadget in an afternoon, the question stops being "could I build a smart-home thing?" and becomes "what should I build next?"

projects.name: Front-Porch Critter Cam
projects.power_supply: 12V wall-wart into the 6-24V buck converter, then a USB-A to micro-USB cable from the buck's USB-A output socket into the MB programmer base's micro-USB port
projects.description:
**What it is**: A little camera in a box near the front door. Whenever something moves past (a cat, a delivery person, your sister sneaking out for ice cream), the camera wakes up and takes a picture. Then you open a web page on your phone and see every snapshot it took. **Why it is fun**: It is your own home spy-cam. Leave it running overnight and in the morning you have a gallery of every creature that crossed the porch - foxes, raccoons, the postman at 6am - and you can show it off to your friends like a wildlife show. ## Parts list - 1x ESP32-CAM with MB programmer base (camera + the carrier that flashes it) - 1x HC-SR501 PIR Motion Sensor (the white half-dome that sees movement) - 1x 6-24V to 5V 3A USB Buck Converter (turns 12V into clean USB-5V for the camera) - 1x 12V wall-wart with barrel plug (the actual mains-side power - any 12V DC supply works) - 1x LED 5mm Red (blinks every time a photo is taken so you know it triggered) - 1x Resistor 220R (current limit for the LED) - 1x Breadboard (~400 tie-points) - Jumper wires (M-M for the breadboard rails, F-M for the PIR and ESP32-CAM headers) - 1x USB-A to micro-USB cable (connects the buck converter's USB-A output to the MB base's micro-USB port) ## Wiring notes The ESP32-CAM is a tiny camera-on-a-chip. It is hard to flash on its own, so it sits on a **MB programmer base** - a little carrier board with a micro-USB port. You plug the camera into the base, then plug a USB cable into the base. That is how we both load the code AND power the camera. No extra FTDI adapter, no soldering. **Quick glossary - words you will see on the ESP32-CAM and MB base:** - **5V** - the power input. We feed it 5 volts from the buck converter. - **GND** - the 0V side, also called ground. Every part needs a path back to GND. - **GPIO13, GPIO14, etc.** - "pins" the chip can turn on or off. The number on the silkscreen IS the pin number we use in code. - **GPIO0** - a special "boot" pin. Leave it alone with no wires on it. The MB base handles flashing for us. - **GPIO4** - drives the bright white flashlight LED that is built into the camera module.
**Step 1 - Set up power.** - Plug the 12V wall-wart into the wall. - Look at the buck converter. It has two screw terminals on one end marked **IN+** and **IN-**. Connect the wall-wart's + wire to **IN+** and the - wire to **IN-**. Polarity matters - if you swap them, nothing turns on (and you might let the smoke out). - The other end of the buck converter has a normal **USB-A socket**. It now gives clean 5V at up to 3 amps. - Take a **USB-A to micro-USB cable**. Big end goes into the buck's USB socket. Small end goes into the **micro-USB port on the MB programmer base**. The camera lights up. That is the entire power chain. The buck does the hard work of dropping 12V down to a safe 5V for the camera.
**Step 2 - Plant the breadboard rails.** The breadboard has two long red and blue strips running down each side. Those are called "rails." The red strip is for 5V (power). The blue strip is for GND (ground). Wires plugged into a rail all share the same connection. - On the MB programmer base, find the side header pins. One is marked **5V** and one is marked **GND**. - Use a **male-to-male jumper wire** (red) to connect the **5V** pin on the MB base to the top red strip (the 5V rail) on the breadboard. - Use another male-to-male jumper (black) to connect the **GND** pin on the MB base to the top blue strip (the GND rail). - Now add two more jumpers so the rails on the top of the board talk to the rails on the bottom: one red wire from the top red strip to the bottom red strip, and one black wire from the top blue strip to the bottom blue strip. Now anywhere you plug into a red strip, you get 5V. Anywhere you plug into a blue strip, you get GND. Easy.
**Step 3 - Add the motion sensor.** The PIR sensor is the white dome - it watches for warm things (like critters) moving past. It has three pins on the bottom labelled **VCC**, **OUT**, and **GND**. - Plug the PIR into the breadboard so its three pins land in holes **E5** (VCC), **E7** (OUT), and **E9** (GND). - Use a red male-to-male jumper from **E5** across to the **top red strip** (5V). That feeds the sensor. - Use a black male-to-male jumper from **E9** across to the **top blue strip** (GND). - Use a **female-to-male jumper** to connect the PIR's signal hole at **E7** to the pin marked **GPIO13** on the ESP32-CAM MB base side header. When the sensor sees motion, it lifts that wire to 3.3V and the camera notices. The PIR has two little orange screws on top. One is sensitivity, one is hold-time (how long the wire stays "on" after a trigger). Turn the hold-time screw all the way to one end. If you only get one photo per minute, turn it to the other end - different clones of this sensor turn opposite directions, so experiment.
**Step 4 - Add the status LED with its safety resistor.**
This little red light blinks every time the camera snaps a photo, so you can tell from across the room that it is working. - Take the **220 ohm resistor** (it has red-red-brown-gold stripes). Plug one leg into hole **F20** and the other leg into hole **F23**. Resistors do not care which way around they go. - Take the **red LED**. Look at its legs - one is longer than the other. The **long leg** is the + side. The **short leg** is the - side. - Plug the **long leg** of the LED into hole **J23** (which connects it to the resistor through the inside of the breadboard). - Plug the **short leg** of the LED into hole **J24**. - Use a black male-to-male jumper from **J24** down to the **bottom blue strip** (GND). - Use a female-to-male jumper from the pin marked **GPIO14** on the ESP32-CAM MB base to hole **F20**. When the code turns **GPIO14** on, current flows: GPIO14 -> resistor -> long leg -> LED lights up -> short leg -> GND. Done. **Why the 220 ohm resistor matters:** An LED is a tiny gobbler of current. If you plug it straight into a pin with nothing to slow it down, it pulls SO much current it cooks itself in a fraction of a second. The resistor is a polite traffic cop - it limits the current to a safe trickle (about 15 milliamps) so the LED glows brightly but lives a long happy life. Never wire an LED without one.
**Step 5 - The warm-up wait.** This is a tricky one. The PIR sensor needs about 30-60 seconds after power-on to calm itself down. During that warm-up time it fires its OUT wire over and over for no reason. The code already knows about this - it waits a full 60 seconds at startup before it starts believing the sensor. So when you first plug in, do not panic if the red LED blinks like crazy or no photos arrive. Walk away, count to sixty, and come back. After that, every wave of your hand should give you exactly one new picture.
**Pin notes - read these before you go hunting:** - The ESP32-CAM has a tiny red LED on its back, but it is wired to **GPIO33**, and **GPIO33 is NOT on the side header**. You cannot reach it from the breadboard. Same for **GPIO32**. That is why we add our own red LED on **GPIO14** instead. - The pins you actually have on the header are: 3V3, 5V, GND, GPIO0 (leave free - flashing pin), GPIO1, GPIO2, GPIO3, GPIO4 (already drives the bright onboard flashlight), GPIO12, GPIO13, GPIO14, GPIO15, GPIO16. - We use **GPIO13** for the PIR input and **GPIO14** for the LED output. Both are nice safe pins with no startup surprises. ## Flash it and run it 1. In the Arduino IDE, add the ESP32 board package: File -> Preferences, paste `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/espressif/arduino-esp32/gh-pages/package_esp32_index.json` into Additional Boards URLs. Then Tools -> Board -> Boards Manager, search "esp32", install it. 2. Tools -> Board -> ESP32 Arduino -> "AI Thinker ESP32-CAM". Tools -> Partition Scheme -> "Huge APP (3MB No OTA/1MB SPIFFS)". Tools -> CPU Frequency -> 240MHz. 3. Slot the ESP32-CAM module into the MB programmer base, micro-USB into the base, USB into your laptop. Pick the COM port that just appeared under Tools -> Port. 4. Open the sketch below, change `WIFI_PASS` to your real password (still set to `PASSWORD_HERE` in the code). Press Upload. 5. When upload finishes, the Serial Monitor (115200 baud) prints an IP like `192.168.1.42`. Open `http://192.168.1.42/` in your phone's browser while on the same WiFi. 6. The home page lists every photo with a timestamp. Tap one to see it. Wave your hand in front of the PIR - within a second a new entry appears. Common gotchas: - If upload fails with "Failed to connect", press the little RST button on the back of the ESP32-CAM while the IDE is in the "Connecting..." phase. Most MB bases auto-reset but a few don't. - After flashing, unplug-replug USB to actually run the sketch (some MB bases stay in download mode). - **GPIO33 / GPIO32 are not on the side header.** Don't waste 20 minutes trying to find them - they're traces buried under the module. We use GPIO14 for the external LED. - If the external LED is on solid when it should be off (or vice-versa), check polarity: long leg through 220R into GPIO14, short leg into GND. The code drives the pin HIGH for "on". - If photos look black, point the PIR away from the camera's IR LED - they can confuse each other. Or just disable the camera's onboard flash LED in code (it's already off in this sketch). - WiFi range: the ESP32-CAM antenna is tiny. Stay within sight of your router for a first test. ## Talking points - "Why does the PIR have two screws?" One sets how sensitive it is (how small a movement counts), the other sets how long it shouts after seeing something. We turned the shout-time all the way down so each new movement gets its own photo. - "Why a buck converter and not just plug USB straight in?" Because a 12V SLA brick or a car battery can run this for days, way longer than a phone charger or a power bank. The buck converter is the translator that turns big-battery 12V into the 5V the camera wants. - "Where do the pictures live?" In RAM inside the ESP32. When you reset it, they vanish. The grown-up upgrade is to save them to a microSD card or push them to a phone app. - "Why GPIO14 and not the LED already on the camera?" Because the camera's on-board red LED is wired to a pin (GPIO33) that doesn't come out on the header. We can't reach it. GPIO14 is a pin that does come out, so we hang our own LED off it. ## Things to change once it works - Add a microSD card to the ESP32-CAM's slot and write JPEGs to it - then you keep photos through reboots. - Swap the PIR for the smaller HC-SR505 if the box is too cramped. - Add a buzzer that beeps once per trigger so you can hear it through a wall. - Push photos to your phone via Telegram bot or a Pushover notification instead of a local web page. - Run it off a real 12V SLA battery in the garage - the buck converter is happy from 6V to 24V so a partly-flat SLA at 11V still works. ## Why this is interesting This is the first project where the camera is the sensor. Up to now, sensors have been little chips (temperature, light, motion) that tell you a number. A camera tells you a whole scene, and the ESP32-CAM is the cheapest WiFi-camera-on-a-chip in the world. The other big idea is power: by running off a buck converter, this project is no longer tied to a laptop or a wall socket. You can stick it in a weatherproof box on the porch with a 12V brick and forget about it for a week. That's the leap from "bench toy" to "real device".
